title: Fact Check: Does splashing water in the eyes increase eyesight?
claim_text: Filling the mouth with water, opening the eyes, and splashing clean water in the eyes after getting up in the morning can increase eyesight.
quick_take: According to a social media post, splashing water in the eyes increases eyesight. It is a suggested practice for improving eyesight. Upon conducting a fact-check, we discovered that this assertion is False.
doctor_explanation: According to the World Health Organization, there are various reasons for vision problems worldwide, including ageing, cataracts, diabetes-related eye damage, glaucoma, and needing glasses. However, it may not be possible to completely reverse certain eye conditions. But it is possible to improve and maintain good eyesight with proper eye care and certain lifestyle habits, such as maintaining a healthy and balanced diet rich in antioxidants, vitamins, and minerals, regular exercise, getting enough sleep, avoiding smoking, taking regular breaks from screens, wearing protective eyewear when necessary, and visiting an eye doctor for regular check-ups. Although there are some home remedies claimed to help improve vision impairment by consuming certain foods or performing eye exercises, scientific evidence supporting these claims is limited. There is no conclusive evidence that these remedies can improve vision or correct refractive errors. However, certain nutrients like vitamin A, lutein, omega-3 fatty acids, zinc, vitamin C, and vitamin E have been shown to maintain good eye health by reducing inflammation, protecting against oxidative damage, and supporting the function of the retina. Eye exercises may help improve eye muscle strength and coordination, but their impact on actual vision improvement is not clear. Dr Naveen Gupta, DNB (Ophthalmology) informs, 'Differentiating between the terms good for eye health and can improve vision is important as they often cause confusion. While a healthy diet and lifestyle can help maintain good eye health, they do not necessarily have the ability to improve one's vision to the extent of reducing eyeglass prescriptions. Making such claims should be avoided. Instead, it is crucial to focus on maintaining good eye health through a balanced diet and healthy lifestyle choices, which can help prevent and manage eye conditions.' Ophthalmologist Dr Aftab Alam says, 'Splashing water in eyes don't increase eyesight. Actually, this practice has its own harmful effects. It may temporarily alleviate symptoms of eye fatigue, redness, or irritation. Also splashing of water removes chemical on eye surface which is needed for tear stability.' Eyesight, or visual acuity, is determined by the clarity and sharpness of vision. It depends on the proper functioning of various structures within the eye, including the cornea, lens, and retina, as well as the neural pathways that transmit visual information to the brain. Water alone does not possess the properties or mechanisms to enhance the physiological components of vision. Splashing water in the eyes primarily helps in rinsing away debris, reducing dryness, and providing a soothing sensation, but it does not alter the underlying optical characteristics of the eye or improve visual acuity. Available scant evidence only suggests that splashing water in the eyes wont increase eyesight. Rather it can do more harm than good.

title: ABP newspaper website publishes fake news: salt water not proven COVID19 cure - THIP Media
claim_text: Researchers of The University of Edinburgh have discovered that gurgling with salt water can cure COVID-19. Salt water destroys the outer protein layer of the Novel Coronavirus.
quick_take: One of the most circulated Bengali newspaper Anandabazar Patrika published a news on its digital website anandabazar.com on 5th July claiming that researchers of The University of Edinburgh have already discovered that gurgling with salt water can cure you from COVID19. The news report further was supported by a quote from an ENT in Kolkata, Dr. Shantanu Bandopadhyay, who claimed that salt water destroys the outer protein layer of the Novel Coronavirus. We investigated and found the claims to be false.
doctor_explanation: In an article published in BBC, it is said that, 'The use of salt water in the treatment of Covid-19 is to be trialled by researchers in Edinburgh.' The report further quotes lead researcher Prof Aziz Sheikh who informed the media house that he and his associates have researched about the efficacy of salt water on normal cold and will now test the same on suspected or confirmed Covid19 patients. We reached out to Dr. Bandopadhyay asking for clarification. To our queries he sent a reply saying – 'Salt water is proved viri cidal' (virucidal = substances that can kill viruses). Dr. Bandopadhyay did not clarify further on why he thinks that salt water will act on the novel Coronavirus too OR the source of his information. We further informed him about WHO's current stand on saline water's effect on Coronavirus is negative. But he refused to comment. We have reached out to Indian Medical Association on their official stand of the issue. We will update this article once we receive a reply from them. However, we did not find any circular from any authoritative bodies in India (Ayush ministry, IMA, Health Ministry) that talks about using saline water even as a preventive against Covid19. In the meantime, below is the advisory on WHO's website about saline water (as on July 22, 2020).

title: Another fake claim about COVID-19 vaccine on Facebook - THIP Media
claim_text: Just in case you are wondering how much the media controls people, America has been vaccinating cattle for coronavirus for years, yet the news tells you it's new and gunna kill you all so go buy mask….
quick_take: A facebook post claims 'America' has coronavirus vaccine which they use for cattles. So, the current panic against the coronavirus situation is a media creation. The post also shares a photo of the claimed medicine. We investigate and find the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: First note: In the comment section of the same post the author has already mentioned that it was a meme by which he most probably intended to mean that it was posted just for fun and he was fully aware that the fact is not true. We still delve deeper to find out more. Yes. There is a medicine of that name manufactured by the company named Zoetis Inc., a company that manufactures medicines for animals. The company has listed the medicine on their official website. However, the company clearly mentions that the product is meant for veterinary use only. This corroborate the information written on the bottle (as shown on the image). The company also describes the product as – 'ScourGuard 4K is for vaccination of healthy, pregnant cows and heifers as an aid in preventing diarrhea in their calves caused by bovine rotavirus (serotypes G6 and G10), bovine coronavirus, and enterotoxigenic strains of Escherichia coli having the K99 pili adherence factor'. This is the same confusion we had seen in earlier misinformation spread about Dettol another similar vaccine confusion where users picked up the name coronavirus and equated that with the current virus pandemic across the world. So here is the explanation again. Coronavirus is a term used for a group of virus. It is not the name of a particular virus but the name of a category of virus. There are different types of coronaviruses (such as MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV). This particular virus that causes the disease Covid – 19 is a type of coronavirus named Novel Coronavirus. World Health Organization (WHO) has now officially named the virus as 'severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)'. The medicine in the picture is effective on Bovine Rotavirus (a particular coronavirus that affects animals). As on April 3, 2020, the official statement from World Health Organization (WHO) there is no vaccine invented for the 'novel' coronavirus.

title: Are birth control pills a major source of oestrogen in water supply?
claim_text: Birth control pills are a significant contributor to oestrogen levels in the water supply, causing feminisation in men and masculinisation in women.
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that birth control pills are a major source of oestrogen in the water supply. We did the fact check to term it as Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Birth control pills do release oestrogen into the water, but they are not the primary source. Natural excretions from humans and animals, along with agricultural runoff, contribute much more significantly. Modern sewage treatment effectively removes most synthetic oestrogen from contraceptives. A 2022 study shows that birth control pills account for less than 1% of the oestrogen in drinking water supplies. According to the American Chemical Society, the primary sources of oestrogen in water are natural oestrogens from humans and animals, and agricultural runoff. For instance, animal manure, which contains natural oestrogens, is a significant contributor when used untreated as fertiliser. Research suggests that animal waste alone could account for up to 90% of the oestrogen found in the environment. The synthetic oestrogen in birth control pills, 17 alpha-ethinylestradiol (EE2), is effectively removed by sewage treatment processes. According to a 2011 study, the predicted concentrations of EE2 in drinking water are significantly lower than those of natural oestrogens from other sources. All humans excrete hormones, not just women on the pill, including men, children, and pregnant women, who contribute to the overall oestrogen load in wastewater. Advanced wastewater treatment processes can remove many of these compounds, but not all. Improving these processes and reducing agricultural runoff are essential steps to addressing estrogen contamination in the water supply. In India, water pollution is a significant issue due to various contaminants, including pharmaceuticals, industrial waste, and agricultural runoff. According to the Central Pollution Control Board, the presence of endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), including oestrogens, in water supplies can pose risks to human health and the environment. The effects of chronic exposure to low levels of oestrogens in water are still being studied, but there is concern about potential impacts on fertility and reproductive health. Water treatment plants employ various methods to remove contaminants, including oestrogens, from water supplies. Techniques such as activated carbon filtration, ozonation, and advanced oxidation processes can effectively reduce the levels of endocrine disruptors in water. According to a 2014 study, advanced water treatment technologies are effective in removing a wide range of pharmaceuticals and hormones, including EE2 from oral contraceptives.

title: Fact Check: Are blood tests like HbA1c and blood pressure purely for business?
claim_text: According to a Threads post, a study by the American College of Physicians (ACP) claims that an HbA1c level of 8.4% does not indicate diabetes. The post also asserts that a Cochrane study states a blood pressure of 160/100 mmHg is not high blood pressure. Additionally, it claims that 70% of Norwegians would be considered hypertensive under Indian guidelines, yet they still live long, healthy lives, suggesting these health guidelines are flawed. The post further states that Japan is not the country with the longest lifespan. Finally, it implies that blood tests and diagnoses for diabetes and high blood pressure are merely a scheme to profit from treatments and care.
quick_take: A social media post claims that blood tests like HbA1c and blood pressure are purely for business. Our fact check shows this is false.
doctor_explanation: The claim that blood tests like HbA1c and blood pressure are purely for business is FALSE. Is there an ACP study saying HbA1c of 8.4 isn't diabetes? No, this is false. The American College of Physicians (ACP) has never published a study stating that an HbA1c of 8.4 is not considered diabetes. HbA1c measures average blood sugar over 2-3 months. Globally, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher is the standard for diagnosing diabetes, as set by the World Health Organization and the American Diabetes Association. In 2018, the ACP did release guidance suggesting that for most adults with type 2 diabetes, an HbA1c between 7% and 8% might be a reasonable treatment target—not a diagnostic threshold. This was about managing diabetes, not defining it. An HbA1c of 8.4% is well above the diagnostic cut-off and indicates diabetes. Dr Almas Fatma, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai says: "Diabetes is confirmed when HbA1c levels reach 6.5% or higher. This is recognised by global health organisations such as the American Diabetes Association and the World Health Organization. An HbA1c of 8.4% is significantly above this threshold and clearly indicates diabetes, not just an increased risk. Left unmanaged, such levels can lead to serious complications, including heart disease, nerve damage, and kidney disease." Does a Cochrane study say 160/100 mmHg isn't hypertensive? No, there is no such study. Cochrane, a respected research group, has no study claiming that 160/100 mmHg isn't hypertension. In fact, a 2012 Cochrane review examined mild hypertension (140–159/90–99 mmHg) and found that treating it didn't always reduce heart disease risk in healthy people. However, 160/100 mmHg is classified as stage 2 hypertension by almost all guidelines—such as the UK's NICE, the American Heart Association, and India's standards—where treatment is recommended due to clear risks of heart attack and stroke. There is strong evidence linking high blood pressure and diabetes, highlighting the need for proper diagnosis and management. Are 70% of Norwegians hypertensive by Indian guidelines but still healthy? No, the claim is exaggerated and unsupported. Indian guidelines define hypertension as a blood pressure consistently measuring 140/90 mmHg or higher. This matches the Norwegian guidelines. The Tromsø Study, which tracked 38,825 Norwegian adults from 1979 to 2015, shows that hypertension prevalence varies by age and time. For adults aged 30–79, it rose from 25% in younger groups to 75% in older ones by 2015. However, in a specific group aged 40–49, it dropped from 46% in 1979 to 25% in men and 14% in women by 2015. Overall, the prevalence is not 70% as the post claims. Norway's high life expectancy—around 83 years—is real, thanks to excellent healthcare, diet, and lifestyle. But there's no evidence that 70% of Norwegians exceed the 140/90 mmHg threshold yet remain healthy despite Indian standards. The guidelines are similar, and the 70% figure appears to be baseless. Is Japan not the country with the longest lifespan? No, this is wrong. Japan consistently ranks top globally for life expectancy, around 84-85 years, according to World Health Organization data. Norway's is slightly lower at 83. The claim seems to confuse or cherry-pick outdated figures. Japan's longevity is well-documented, driven by diet, healthcare, and low obesity rates. Are blood tests merely a money-making scheme? No evidence supports this. Blood tests like HbA1c and blood pressure checks are standard tools to catch diabetes and hypertension early, preventing serious issues like blindness or heart failure. Yes, healthcare involves money—pharma companies profit—but these tests are backed by science, not a conspiracy. The claim dismisses their proven role in saving lives. Dr Sanjeev Kumar, MPH, Senior Consultant (Medical), NPCCHH (MoHFW), Centre for Community Medicine, AIIMS, New Delhi says: "Blood tests are not a money-making scheme—they are essential tools for diagnosing and monitoring health conditions. Tests like HbA1c for diabetes, lipid profiles for heart disease, and kidney function tests help detect problems early, often before symptoms appear. Early diagnosis allows timely treatment, preventing serious complications. Avoiding necessary tests can put lives at risk." THIP Media Take: The claim that blood tests like HbA1c and blood pressure are purely for business is false. The Threads post twists facts and misquotes studies. No ACP study states that an HbA1c of 8.4 isn't diabetes, and no Cochrane study denies that 160/100 mmHg is hypertension. Japan's top-tier longevity is a fact, not a myth. Norway's people live long, but the Tromsø Study shows that hypertension prevalence peaks at 75% in older adults, not 70% across all age groups. Blood tests save lives, not the other way around. Trust the science—these tests are essential.

title: Are COVID-19 vaccines causing increased neurological and heart-related risks?
claim_text: COVID-19 vaccines are causing increased neurological and heart-related risks among those who have been vaccinated.
quick_take: A social media post claims that COVID-19 vaccines are causing increased neurological and heart-related risks. We fact checked this, and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Do COVID-19 vaccines cause a significant increase in neurological risks?

No, this is false. COVID-19 vaccines, including those from Pfizer, Moderna, and AstraZeneca, have been extensively studied for safety. While mild side effects like headaches are common, serious neurological issues are rare. A largestudy from 2022, which analyzed data from 8.3 million people in the UK and Spain, found no increased risk of neurological events like Bell's palsy or Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) after vaccination with Pfizer or AstraZeneca vaccines.

However, a2024 studynoted a small increased risk of GBS after the AstraZeneca vaccine—about 2.9 times higher than expected, with 190 cases observed versus 76 expected among 23 million doses. This translates to roughly 38 excess cases per 10 million doses, a very small number. In contrast, the same study found that the risk of neurological events after aCOVID-19 infection was up to 617 times higher than after vaccination. This suggests that the virus itself poses a far greater neurological risk than the vaccines.

Similarly, we've also encountered claims thatYale's study confirmed the presence of long-term symptoms and spike proteinsafter COVID-19 vaccination, which is misleading.

Are COVID-19 vaccines responsible for a rise in heart-related risks?

No,this is misleading. Concerns about heart issues, particularly myocarditis (heart muscle inflammation) and pericarditis (inflammation of the heart's outer lining), have been raised, especially in younger males after mRNA vaccines like Pfizer and Moderna. A2022 studyreported rates of myocarditis as 50–139 cases per million in males aged 12–29 after mRNA vaccines, with the highest risk after the second dose of Moderna (6.1 times higher than expected). However, these cases are rare—about 1 in 50,000 people, according to theUK's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency(MHRA) in 2023. Most cases are mild, and patients recover with rest or simpletreatment.

According to another2022 study, the risk of myocarditis after COVID-19 infection increased 11.14 times before vaccination and 5.97 times after vaccination. Additionally, a2024 studyof 45.7 million adults in England showed that the incidence of heart-related events like heart attacks was generally lower after vaccination, not higher. The data does not support a widespread increase in heart risks due to vaccines.

Similarly, another post claims thatCovishield COVID-19 vaccine is causing a new type of heart attack. However, this is misleading.

Could other factors explain neurological or heart issues in vaccinated people?

Yes.Health differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated groups often stem from factors unrelated to the vaccine. For instance, vaccinated individuals may be older or have pre-existing conditions, increasing their risk of neurological or heart problems. Lifestyle factors like stress, poor diet, or lack of exercise can also contribute. The claim specifically blames vaccines for these risks, but this isn't supported by evidence. A2024 WHO reportfound that vaccination actually lowers overall mortality and hospitalisations, demonstrating its protective benefits.

What do long-term studies say about vaccine safety?

Yes,they confirm safety. A2024 studytracked millions of vaccinated individuals over three years and found no significant rise in neurological or heart-related risks compared to unvaccinated groups. It also highlighted that vaccines lower the risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes, including heart and neurological issues caused by the virus. Ongoing monitoring by health organisations, such as the WHO, continues to reinforce the safety of these vaccines.

Despite this proven safety, misleading claims persist, suggesting thatCOVID-19 vaccines contain nanobotsorwere part of a secret military project. These assertions have no scientific basis and are simply conspiracy theories.

THIP Media Take: The claim that COVID-19 vaccines are causing increased neurological and heart-related risks isfalse. Scientific research overwhelmingly supports the safety of COVID-19 vaccines, with rare side effects far outweighed by the benefits of protection against severe COVID-19 and its complications. Promoting such unverified claims can fuel vaccine hesitancy and undermine public health efforts.

title: Are double-jointed individuals at greater risk of health problems?
claim_text: A recent Facebook post suggests that being double-jointed is linked to serious health risks, including chronic pain, gastrointestinal disorders, and other systemic issues.
quick_take: A social media post claims that double-jointed individuals are at greater risk of health problems. Our fact check shows this is half true.
doctor_explanation:
The term 'double-jointed' (medically referred to as hypermobility) is a common but inaccurate way to describe joint hypermobility, a condition where joints move beyond the normal range of motion. This happens due to the elasticity of connective tissues like ligaments and tendons. Despite the name, it doesn't mean extra joints are involved, and hypermobility is relatively common. In 2023, a study focused on General Joint Hypermobility (GJH) in young people, particularly those involved in sports like gymnastics. GJH affects 2–57% of people, with 10% experiencing symptoms such as pain or mental health issues. The study emphasized the need for further research, especially on its impact on mental health and treatment options. For most people, however, it's a harmless trait with no serious health concerns.

Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, clarifies, 'Hypermobility doesn't necessarily mean weak connective tissue. It simply means the joints can move beyond the usual range. While some people with hypermobility may have weaker connective tissues, many live without any problems. It's important to understand that hypermobility can vary from person to person, and not everyone with it will experience issues.'

Can hypermobility lead to chronic pain? Many people with hypermobility live without problems, but some may experience chronic pain or joint injuries. This is more common in individuals with hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS), as their connective tissues may not support the joints effectively. A 2023 study found that joint hypermobility affects 30% of people in the UK. While it can cause issues like pain, anxiety, and difficulty with work or school for some, not everyone with hypermobility experiences these problems.

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, says, 'Hypermobility can lead to chronic pain in some individuals, especially if the joints move too much and put strain on surrounding tissues. While not everyone with hypermobility experiences pain, it can be more common in those with additional conditions like hypermobility spectrum disorders or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. It's important to seek medical advice if pain becomes persistent.'

Are other health issues linked to hypermobility? Hypermobility is sometimes linked to systemic conditions. Studies have found connections between hypermobility syndromes and gastrointestinal issues like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Additionally, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), which affects blood circulation, can co-occur with hypermobility syndromes, particularly Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS). A 2024 study highlighted that young women with joint hypermobility, hEDS, POTS, and mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) often experience severe stomach problems, such as nausea and vomiting. However, such associations are rare and typically relate to specific conditions, not general hypermobility.

Is hypermobility a risk factor for complications from infections like COVID-19? There is no conclusive evidence that hypermobility directly increases the risk of complications from infections like COVID-19. While some conditions linked to hypermobility can affect overall health, generalized hypermobility does not weaken the immune system or make someone more prone to infections. However, a 2024 study suggests that long COVID might be linked to hypermobility. It explains that long COVID could cause inflammation and damage to connective tissues, potentially leading to hypermobility in some individuals. Similarly, a 2022 study found that fibromyalgia, a chronic pain condition, may develop in people with joint hypermobility after having COVID-19. The study highlighted that young women with joint hypermobility who experienced tendon injury during COVID-19 were particularly at risk.

THIP Media Take: While hypermobility can indicate weak connective tissues in some conditions, most hypermobile individuals have no health problems. Chronic pain and issues like gastrointestinal disorders are more common in hypermobility spectrum disorders or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. For concerns, consulting a doctor can help distinguish between benign hypermobility and more serious conditions.

title: Fact Check: Are famous people promoting a liver detox for quick weight loss?
claim_text: A Facebook post claims that famous people (Anjana Om Kashyap and Dr Deepak Chopra) are promoting a liver detox remedy that can detox the liver in 17 hours, leading to 1-2 kg weight loss daily. The post promotes the 'Guava Method' as a natural, pill-free weight loss solution for those over 35, claiming strict diets and workouts damage the pancreas, and alleges Ozempic causes 'lipase explosions' leading to metabolic breakdown and obesity.
quick_take: A social media post claims that famous people are promoting a liver detox for quick weight loss. We did the fact check and found this claim is false.
doctor_explanation: Can a liver detox concoction unblock the liver and burn fat? No, a liver detox remedy cannot unblock the liver or cause rapid fat burning. The liver does not get 'blocked.' It is a self-cleansing organ that naturally processes toxins and nutrients. Claims about 'unblocking' or 'resetting' the liver oversimplify its functions and mislead viewers about how the body works. Fat metabolism depends on multiple factors, including hormonal balance, dietary habits, and physical activity. While liver health is essential, it cannot single-handedly unlock fat-burning mechanisms or drive rapid weight loss. The idea of unblocking the liver is like saying your heart needs unblocking to beat—it's misleading and unnecessary. Is the video featuring Anjana Om Kashyap and Dr Deepak Chopra genuine? No, the video is AI-manipulated and cannot be trusted. The clip features journalist Anjana Om Kashyap and Dr Deepak Chopra, but their lip movements are not in sync with the audio, indicating digital manipulation. The pronunciations of the Hindi language are also unnatural. A review of their official social media profiles confirms they have not endorsed any liver detox or weight loss remedies. Are the weight loss claims consistent? No, the claims about weight loss timelines are inconsistent and unreliable. The caption promises weight loss within 14 days. The video, however, alternates between losing 1-2 kg daily, achieving results in 7 days, and even as quickly as 1-2 days. These conflicting statements undermine the post's credibility. From a medical perspective, healthy weight loss occurs at a steady rate of 0.5-1 kg per week. Rapid fat loss, as claimed here, is not only unrealistic but also harmful. Such weight loss often results in losing water and muscle mass, rather than fat, leading to risks like nutritional deficiencies and metabolic imbalances. Does weight gain only depend on liver function? No, weight gain involves multiple factors, including diet, calories, activity levels, and genetics. The post dismisses these key factors, oversimplifying weight gain as solely dependent on liver function. This is scientifically incorrect. Weight gain occurs when more calories are consumed than burned. Genetics, metabolism, and lifestyle choices all play significant roles in body weight. While liver health is important for nutrient metabolism, poor liver function is often a result of unhealthy habits, not the root cause of weight gain. Regular exercise, eating a balanced diet, and staying hydrated are much more effective for maintaining a healthy weight than any so-called liver detox. Can Ozempic cause 'lipase explosions' and lead to obesity? No, not true. Ozempic (semaglutide) is an FDA-approved medication for managing type 2 diabetes and aiding weight loss in certain individuals. It works by mimicking the hormone GLP-1, which regulates blood sugar levels and appetite, helping reduce weight over time. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that Ozempic causes 'lipase explosions' or leads to metabolic breakdown and obesity. Lipase is an enzyme that helps break down fats, but Ozempic does not affect its levels in this way. The most common side effects of Ozempic, which affect more than 1 in 10 people, include digestive issues like diarrhoea, nausea, and vomiting. These side effects are usually mild and short-term. In some cases, Ozempic may also lead to a serious worsening of diabetic retinopathy, which affects up to 1 in 10 individuals. Dr Almas Fatma says: 'The idea that Ozempic causes 'lipase explosions' leading to obesity is pure misinformation. Ozempic is a well-researched medication that helps control blood sugar and can aid in weight management for some individuals. It doesn't harm metabolism or trigger dramatic effects like those claimed. Such alarming statements only spread confusion. Always rely on your doctor for trustworthy advice about medications.' Dr Ashirwad Pawar says: 'Ozempic treats type 2 diabetes and supports weight loss effectively. It improves insulin sensitivity and reduces appetite, without causing harmful 'lipase explosions.' Claims that it leads to obesity or metabolic breakdown are false and misleading. Like all medications, Ozempic requires professional supervision, and its benefits far outweigh the exaggerated risks often spread in myths.'

title: Fact Check: Are famous personalities endorsing a quick weight loss remedy?
claim_text: A viral video on Facebook claims that News anchor Anjana Om Kashyap and Jagadguru Rambhadracharya are endorsing a rice water remedy for rapid weight loss. According to the video, this remedy can significantly reduce weight in just seven days and offers a permanent solution to weight problems in India.
quick_take: A social media post claims that famous personalities are endorsing a quick weight loss remedy. Our fact check termed this claim as False.
doctor_explanation:
The video features well-known personalities Anjana Om Kashyap and Jagadguru Rambhadracharya. But, there are several indications that the content is manipulated. Upon careful examination, we found that there is a noticeable lack of lip sync, with unnatural hand gestures and facial expressions. A Google Reverse Image Search revealed that the segment showing Anjana Om Kashyap was originally from a 2016 interview on The Lallantop channel, dated 16th November. Similarly, we came across another Facebook video featuring Anjana Om Kashyap promoting lemon water as a cure for eyesight problems in 7 minutes. Like this one, that video was also AI-manipulated. As for Jagadguru Rambhadracharya, identifying the original source was difficult because he often appears in the same outfit and setting across various videos. This strong online presence, combined with consistent visual elements, made it challenging to pinpoint the exact source. Moreover, it is unlikely that such respected figures would risk their reputations by endorsing quick-fix weight loss remedies. We thoroughly reviewed their social media profiles and news reports but found no evidence of them endorsing this or any other home remedy for quick weight loss. We have also reached out to them through email for confirmation but are yet to receive a response.

The video features individuals who appear to provide testimonials about the remedy. However, one woman's voice does not match her appearance; it sounds masculine, and the incorrect use of Hindi grammar suggests potential manipulation. This raises suspicion that the video might be a deepfake or AI-generated. Additionally, other individuals in the video exhibit poor lip sync, unnatural gestures, and stiff facial expressions, all pointing to signs of digital alteration.

The video's claim that the rice water remedy has been 'proven on 12,000 Indians' and boasts a '99% effectiveness rate' lacks any credible sources or scientific backing. Furthermore, it presents the remedy as a 'one and only solution for weight loss,' which is an exaggerated claim often seen in misleading advertisements.

title: Are natural ingredients as effective as lab-formulated ones?
claim_text: According to a post on Threads, your skincare routine doesn't need lab-made ingredients, but instead can rely on natural ingredients. It suggests using Greek yogurt for lactic acid, aloe vera for hyaluronic acid, bone marrow for retinol, matcha for niacinamide, lemon juice for glycolic acid, cucumber for salicylic acid, red grapes for resveratrol, rosehip oil for tretinoin, turmeric for tetrahydrocurcumin, egg yolk for tocopherol, kiwi for vitamin C, coffee for hydroquinone, raw honey for antioxidants, olive oil for amino acids, and avocado for CoQ10. The post emphasizes that nature has been providing these benefits for centuries.
quick_take: A social media post claims that natural ingredients are as effective as lab-formulated ones. Our fact check reveals this claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Natural ingredients cannot fully replicate the efficacy of lab-based actives. While some natural products may contain similar compounds, their concentration and bioavailability are not comparable to lab-formulated skincare ingredients. For instance, lactic acid in Greek yogurt exists in much lower concentrations than in skincare formulations. Lab-derived lactic acid is standardised for exfoliation and skin renewal, whereas yoghurt's concentration varies, making it less effective. Similarly, retinol, derived from vitamin A, is far more potent and stable in lab formulations than in bone marrow or natural sources. Scientific studies highlight that skincare actives have the ability to penetrate the skin at specific depths and concentrations. Natural ingredients often lack this precision, making them less effective for targeted skin concerns like acne, pigmentation, or ageing. Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, explains, 'Natural ingredients can be beneficial, but they don't work the same way as lab-based actives. For example, Greek yoghurt contains lactic acid, but the concentration is too low to give the exfoliation and skin-renewing effects you'd get from a formulated lactic acid product. Lab-based ingredients deliver specific results at the right strength and depth. Natural products can complement your routine, but they can't replace the precision and effectiveness of science-backed skincare.' Natural does not always mean safer. Many natural ingredients can cause irritation, allergic reactions, or photosensitivity (Sun sensitivity) when applied directly to the skin. For example, lemon juice, suggested as an alternative to glycolic acid, is highly acidic and can disrupt the skin's barrier, leading to irritation or burns. Lab-based glycolic acid, however, is carefully formulated to provide controlled exfoliation without damaging the skin. Similarly, turmeric, while known for its anti-inflammatory properties, can stain the skin and cause irritation when not used in refined forms. Skincare products undergo rigorous testing to ensure safety and efficacy, something raw natural ingredients lack. Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, says, 'Not everything natural is automatically safe for your skin. Many natural ingredients, like lemon juice or turmeric, can cause irritation, burns, or even allergic reactions when applied directly. Lab-based products undergo careful testing to ensure they work effectively and safely. For example, glycolic acid in skincare gently exfoliates, while lemon juice can damage your skin barrier due to its high acidity. So, while natural products might sound appealing, they're not always the better or safer choice for your skin.' Natural ingredients lack the consistency of lab-formulated products. Variations in growing conditions, processing, and storage can significantly impact the potency and composition of natural products. For instance, aloe vera gel varies in its concentration of active compounds depending on how it is harvested, the environment, and how it is stored. In contrast, lab-formulated hyaluronic acid is synthesised to deliver consistent hydration and performance. This consistency is crucial for addressing specific skin concerns effectively. While natural ingredients can complement skincare routines, they cannot replace lab-based actives for addressing specific concerns like wrinkles, hyperpigmentation, or severe acne. For example, vitamin C from kiwi or antioxidants from honey may provide mild benefits, but they are not as potent or stable as their lab-formulated counterparts. Skincare products are specially designed to deliver these actives in a form that the skin can readily absorb and utilise, something raw natural sources often fail to achieve.

title: Fact Check: Are Rajat Sharma and Dr Devi Shetty endorsing a diabetes cure?
claim_text: A Facebook video claims that Rajat Sharma endorses a baking soda remedy that has supposedly cured diabetes in over 2,17,000 Indians. doctor_explanation: The video is not authentic. There are several reasons why we say this: There is no scientific evidence to support these claims. Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) is not recognised as a treatment for diabetes. While it may temporarily neutralise stomach acid, it does not create an 'alkaline environment' throughout the body or influence insulin production. Moreover, chronic inflammation and metabolism are complex processes influenced by multiple factors, and baking soda cannot address these issues as claimed. The idea of curing diabetes within a week or a month is baseless and misleading. Similar fake videos featuring well-known personalities, including Dr Naresh Trehan promoting a diabetes cure, have circulated with false claims about quick remedies for diabetes. Another video falsely claimed that Dr Devi Shetty was endorsing a different quick diabetes remedy. Baking soda does not lower blood sugar levels. Diabetes management involves complex physiological processes that cannot rely on simple substances like baking soda. Blood sugar control depends on factors such as insulin production, cellular insulin sensitivity, diet, and medication. Baking soda has no role in regulating these processes. There is no single-step remedy for diabetes. It is a lifelong condition requiring consistent management through lifestyle changes, medication, and sometimes insulin. Medical experts advocate evidence-based approaches for diabetes management rather than quick fixes. The claim that pharmaceutical companies are hiding natural cures for diabetes is a conspiracy theory without evidence. Dr Ashirwad Pawar, Diabetologist at Sai Aashirwad Hospital in Mumbai, says, 'There is no quick remedy for diabetes. While Type 2 diabetes can sometimes be managed through lifestyle changes or medication, it cannot be cured in the traditional sense. Claims about instant cures are misleading and lack scientific backing.' The claim is a deepfake and completely false. It misleads viewers with AI-manipulated content and clickbait links.

title: Are scientists putting young girls at risk with the HPV vaccine?
claim_text: Scientists are putting young girls at risk by administering the HPV vaccine. The video implies that the vaccine is unsafe and that little girls are being used as test subjects without their knowledge.
quick_take: A video on social media claims that the HPV vaccine is putting young girls at risk. Our fact check reveals that this claim is False.
doctor_explanation: The HPV vaccine has gained attention for its vital role in preventing cervical cancer, one of the most common cancers in women. HPV, a sexually transmitted infection, can lead to cervical cancer, genital warts, and other cancers. Vaccination offers an effective way to prevent these health problems. Unfortunately, even with proven safety records, there has been a rise in misinformation related to the HPV vaccine. In countries like India, where cervical cancer rates are high, the HPV vaccine is an essential part of public health efforts to reduce the disease burden. Vaccines like Gardasil and Cervarix have been used safely for many years to protect against HPV-related diseases. Researchers have rigorously tested these vaccines, and health authorities worldwide have approved them. Scientific evidence does not support claims that these vaccines are harmful to young girls. The HPV vaccine works by stimulating the body's immune system to recognise and fight the human papillomavirus. Doctors usually give the vaccine in two or three doses over several months, depending on the person's age. It works best when given to young people before they become sexually active. This is why it is usually advisable for girls (and boys) aged 9 to 14. Dr Rakesh Kumar Sharma, a Medical Oncologist from Max Healthcare, Saket, New Delhi, explains that "Cervical cancer infections generally occur early in life. So, I recommend getting the HPV vaccine, ideally between the ages of 9 and 26, or before becoming sexually active." The HPV vaccine helps prevent infection from the most harmful strains of the virus. By doing this, it greatly lowers the chances of developing cervical cancer and other related health issues. Currently, the most widely available HPV vaccines are Gardasil, produced by Merck, and Cervarix, produced by GlaxoSmithKline. Health authorities across the globe, including the World Health Organization (WHO), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), have approved and recommended these vaccines. After years of research and clinical trials, they found vaccines like Gardasil and Cervarix to be both safe and effective. Over 100 countries recommend these vaccines as part of their national vaccination programs. Like all vaccines, the HPV vaccine can cause some side effects, but these are generally mild. For example, common side effects include pain at the injection site, headaches, fever, or mild nausea. Serious side effects are very rare. Millions of people globally have used the vaccine, and researchers have thoroughly documented its safety profile. There is no evidence that the HPV vaccine is harmful to children. Reports of serious side effects, like postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) and chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS), after the HPV vaccine are very rare. These are mostly based on common symptoms like headaches and tiredness. Large studies from Norway and the UK found no connection between the vaccine and these conditions. The European Medicines Agency also found no evidence of a link and suggested that media reports may have influenced concerns. In reality, the HPV vaccine is safe, and its benefits in preventing cervical cancer far outweigh any small risks. Dr Ayush Heda, MD, DNB (Gynaecology), MCh, European Society of Gynaecologic Oncology Fellow, Berlin, says, "HPV infection is the main cause of cervical cancer and can be prevented using vaccination and regular screening. HPV vaccine helps to develop immunity against major high risk HPV genotypes. It's safe and highly effective, especially when given at a young age, typically between 9 and 14 years. Even though there are concerns about vaccine safety, extensive studies and years of use have shown that the benefits far outweigh any minimal risks. 143 countries have already introduced it in the national immunization program and Indian Government too plans to do the same using the indigenously developed vaccine. Parents should feel confident that vaccinating their children and regular future screening will help prevent this serious health issue." No credible evidence shows that scientists are using young girls as test subjects for the HPV vaccine without their informed consent. Furthermore, the vaccine has gone through thorough clinical trials involving tens of thousands of participants of varying ages and backgrounds. These trials followed ethical guidelines and were approved by regulatory bodies.

title: Fact Check: Are vaccines more harmful than preventive?
claim_text: Dr. Suzanne Humphries objected to the role of vaccines in the prevention of infectious disease outbreaks. She even questioned the safety of vaccinations.
quick_take: A social media post questions the role of vaccines in the prevention of infectious diseases. We confirmed the assertion. Our findings indicate that the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Active immunity is the defence produced by the body's immune system. Vaccination aids in the activation of this active immunity. Vaccines reduce the risk of contracting a disease by enhancing the body's natural defences. When one receives a vaccine, the defence system responds. Vaccines are thus essential in the prevention and control of infectious disease outbreaks. They also contribute to global health security and will be crucial in combating antimicrobial resistance. It should be noted that the underprivileged in society are disproportionately troubled by infectious diseases in many countries. This is due to the combined effects of poverty, undernutrition, poor hygiene and sanitation, overpopulation, discrimination, and poor access to healthcare. Therefore, according to the World Health Organization, it is a moral imperative and a human right for every individual to have access to safe vaccines. This has led to the establishment of vaccination programs on both national and international scales. These vaccination programs ensure that mortality associated with infectious diseases is no longer a determinant of one's life. Furthermore, vaccine recipients have the potential to live longer lives. Vaccines are estimated to save six million lives each year from vaccine-preventable diseases. The most common conditions include diphtheria, poliomyelitis, pertussis, tetanus, measles, tuberculosis, and smallpox. Therefore, the most challenging scientific need of the twenty-first century is the development of safe and effective vaccines against diseases that cause significant morbidity and mortality. Regarding adverse effects: there is no such thing as a 'perfect' vaccine that not only protects but is completely safe for everyone. As a result, vaccines that induce protective immunity may cause some undesirable side effects, which are usually mild and resolve quickly. However, the vast majority of events thought to be related to vaccine administration are not due to the vaccine itself, many are simply coincidental. These events could be caused by either human or program errors. Regardless, vaccine-related adverse events can affect healthy people and should be reported as soon as possible to allow for additional research and appropriate action. WHO has established a Global Vaccine Safety Response Team to respond to vaccine safety issues in a timely, efficient, and scientifically rigorous manner. THIP MEDIA TAKE: We conclude that a vaccine program is essential for the underprivileged, particularly in developing countries. The World Health Organization's vaccination program has played a significant role in the eradication of various infectious diseases around the world. Regardless, the adverse effects following vaccination may not always be due to the vaccine itself. As a result, our analysis concludes that the assertion is mostly false.

title: Can a 5-second baking soda remedy cure vision problems?
claim_text: A viral Facebook video claims that a 5-second baking soda remedy can correct vision problems. The video features Dr Rahil Chaudhary, promising 100% results within just 24 hours, as per the voiceover. The caption, however, states that it takes 14 days.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a 5-second baking soda remedy cures vision problems. Our fact check reveals this is false.
doctor_explanation: The video is not genuine. This video is AI-manipulated, featuring an AI-generated voice that tries to mimic Dr Rahil Chaudhary's speech. However, the lip-sync is absent, which is a clear indication of manipulation. Dr Rahil Chaudhary, a renowned ophthalmologist, has not recommended any such remedy for vision correction in just 24 hours. We also searched his recent social media posts and news related to him to rule out any possibility of such promotions, and found no evidence supporting the claim. Given his strong reputation and extensive career in ophthalmology, it is highly unlikely that he would endorse such an unproven and potentially harmful remedy. Moreover, the video does not even tell the viewers what the remedy is. It doesn't give any further information to actually verify what the baking soda remedy is. This casts serious concerns over the authenticity of the video and the claims it makes. In a very similar manner, we saw another social media post, which featured Dr Rahil Chaudhary promoting lemon water for curing eyesight problems in 7 minutes. This is also an AI-generated video spreading false health advice. In a quick email interview, Dr Rahil Chaudhary refuted these claims, saying, 'We are not associated with any such video. The video must have been faked using modern AI tools.' Our findings have also been supported by the investigation of the Deepfakes Analysis Unit, which has clearly stated that this video is AI-manipulated. Baking soda cannot cure vision problems. There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that baking soda can correct vision issues. Vision problems like nearsightedness, farsightedness, or astigmatism are usually caused by the shape of the eye or the health of the retina and cannot be fixed by home remedies or external treatments like baking soda. These conditions need corrective lenses, surgery, or medical intervention, depending on the severity. There is no evidence of 100% vision correction in 24 hours. Vision correction takes time and is based on the specific condition being treated. For instance, corrective surgeries like LASIK can improve vision, but even these do not offer 100% results immediately. The claim of '100% vision correction in just 24 hours' is unrealistic and baseless as per medical research. Vision improvement is a gradual process, often taking weeks or months, depending on the treatment. You can't cure vision problems at home in just 24 hours. Issues like blurry vision or poor eyesight, especially those caused by the shape of the eye or refractive errors, need proper care from an eye specialist. There are no quick fixes or home remedies that can magically solve these problems overnight. Treatments like glasses, contact lenses, or eye surgeries take time and are based on your specific condition. Trusting viral videos or unreliable remedies can be risky and may stop you from getting the right treatment when you need it. You shouldn't trust AI-generated health content blindly. Videos with fake voices or manipulated clips can easily spread false and misleading information. In this case, using AI to twist a real doctor's video shows how technology can be misused to fool people. Diagnosis requires medical imaging techniques like angiography, Doppler ultrasound, or CT scans. title: Can a homemade drink cleanse kidneys and boost immunity?
claim_text: A viral Instagram post claims that a homemade drink made with lemon/lime, garlic, turmeric, black pepper, and honey, boiled in water and consumed every day on an empty stomach for two weeks can completely clean the kidneys, detox the liver, strengthen the immune system, get rid of digestive problems, and make kidneys 'as good as new'. The video also claims 'Mix lemon with garlic and you'll never visit a hospital again' and that just one cup can clean kidneys, boost immunity, detox liver, fix digestive issues, and reduce inflammation.
quick_take: A viral Instagram post claims that a homemade drink can cleanse kidneys and boost immunity. Our fact check found it to be false.
doctor_explanation:
## Can a homemade drink cleanse the kidneys?
No, it cannot. The kidneys naturally filter waste and extra substances from the body. This complex process is highly efficient, and there's no scientific proof that any drink can boost this function. While ingredients like lemon and garlic have some benefits, such as vitamins and antioxidants, they do not cleanse the kidneys as claimed. Drinking water and staying hydrated is essential for kidney health, but there is no shortcut for making your kidneys as good as new through a drink.

## Can this homemade drink instantly strengthen the immune system?
No, drinking this mix will not suddenly strengthen the immune system. Boosting immune health requires more than a one-time remedy; it depends on long-term habits. Ingredients like lemon and garlic do contain some immune-supporting compounds: lemon provides vitamin C, garlic has allicin with antimicrobial properties, and turmeric contains curcumin, which may help with inflammation. However, consuming these in small amounts, especially through a drink, will not cause a dramatic or immediate improvement in immunity. Furthermore, the video suggests boiling the mixture in water, which can lead to nutrient loss.

Immune health depends on various factors, including diet, exercise, sleep, and stress management. Regularly eating a balanced diet and leading a healthy lifestyle is far more effective for the immune system's health.

## Can the drink detoxify the liver and completely eliminate digestive problems?
Not really. The liver already detoxifies itself through natural processes. The body uses enzymes to break down toxins and remove waste, making external liver cleanses unnecessary. While lemon and garlic can contribute to overall health when consumed as part of a balanced diet, they do not detoxify the liver.

As for digestive issues, turmeric might have some benefits due to its anti-inflammatory properties, but the claim that this drink can eliminate all digestive problems is an exaggeration. Digestive health depends on diet, hydration, lifestyle and a well-functioning gut, not a quick-fix drink.

Dr Sharad Malhotra, Senior Consultant & HOD Gastroenterology Hepatology & Therapeutic Endoscopy, Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, says: "No single drink can cleanse the liver or fully resolve digestive problems. The liver is a highly efficient organ that naturally detoxifies the body, without needing special drinks to perform its function. While ingredients like garlic and turmeric contribute to a healthy diet, they are not miracle solutions. Addressing digestive problems often requires medical attention, a balanced diet, and lifestyle changes. True liver and digestive health comes from long-term habits, not quick fixes. Additionally, eating in moderation, staying hydrated, maintaining a healthy lifestyle, and regular exercise are far more beneficial than seeking short-term solutions for gut health."

## Does this drink reduce inflammation effectively?
Partially true, but not as the claim suggests. Turmeric's curcumin does have anti-inflammatory properties and has been studied for reducing chronic inflammation. However, small amounts of turmeric in a drink may not provide a sufficient dose for noticeable effects due to its poor bioavailability. For meaningful anti-inflammatory benefits, we would need a higher dose over time, often in supplement form.

## Does boiling ingredients reduce their nutrients?
Yes, it does. Boiling can lower the nutritional content of lime, garlic, and other ingredients. Lime contains vitamin C, which is sensitive to heat and can break down when boiled. This reduces its immune-supporting properties. Garlic's beneficial compound, allicin, is also unstable and breaks down with high heat, lowering its potential effects.

Turmeric's curcumin can lose some of its potency when exposed to high heat for too long, especially when there's no fat source to help with absorption (curcumin is fat-soluble). Although black pepper helps with curcumin absorption due to its compound piperine, boiling all these ingredients together may still reduce their overall benefits.

Soumam Dutta, PhD Scholar (Nutrition), Department of Endocrinology, ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition explains: "Boiling ingredients at high temperatures can greatly reduce their nutrient content, particularly heat-sensitive vitamins like vitamin C and some antioxidants. To retain more nutrients, it's best to cook at lower temperatures or opt for methods like steaming. This helps retain the maximum nutritional benefits, ensuring we get the most out of what we're eating."

## THIP Media Take
The claim that a homemade drink can cleanse kidneys and boost immunity is false. While these ingredients have individual health benefits, boiling them can reduce their nutrients, making the drink far less effective. title: Can a mix of spices and seeds cure diabetes completely?
claim_text: Consuming a mixture of black pepper, nigella seeds, fenugreek seeds, and jamun seed powder on an empty stomach each morning can cure any type of diabetes, regardless of severity, within 3 weeks.
quick_take: A post on Instagram says that a mix of black pepper, nigella seeds, fenugreek seeds, and jamun seed powder can cure diabetes completely within 3 weeks. We term this claim as False.
doctor_explanation: Diabetes is a chronic condition that occurs when the body cannot effectively manage blood glucose levels. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the body's immune system attacks insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, leading to an insulin deficiency. Type 2 diabetes, the more common form, is characterised by insulin resistance. Here, the body's cells do not respond properly to insulin, often combined with an eventual insulin deficiency. Both types need careful management, involving medication, lifestyle changes, and in the case of Type 1, insulin therapy. Diabetes is a long-term health issue, and diet and lifestyle changes can significantly improve management. But still, there is currently no cure for either Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes. Black pepper, nigella seeds, fenugreek seeds, and jamun seed powder have all been studied for their potential health benefits including their effects on blood sugar levels. However, this mixture cannot cure diabetes in 3 weeks. Diabetes is a complex and chronic condition that requires long-term management. The claim that this mixture can cure diabetes overlooks the need for a comprehensive approach, including medication, lifestyle changes, and regular monitoring. Currently, no cure exists for Type 1 diabetes, and while Type 2 diabetes can often be managed with lifestyle adjustments and medication, it is still not curable. Relying on such claims can be dangerous, as it might lead people to neglect proven treatments, likely worsening their condition. Dietician Kamana Chauhan says, "When it comes to diabetes, there's no magic bullet, despite what some claims might suggest. As a dietician, I've seen how easy it is to get caught up in the promise of quick fixes, but managing diabetes is a marathon, not a sprint. Ingredients like fenugreek and jamun seed powder can support blood sugar control, but they aren't a cure-all. True diabetes management requires a thoughtful balance of medical care, healthy eating, and regular exercise. Always have a discussion with your dietician or doctor before changing your routine – it's about finding what works best for you." Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, states, "Dealing with diabetes can be tough, and it's natural to look for easy solutions. But, I want to make it clear that no food or mixture can cure diabetes. Ingredients like fenugreek and jamun seed powder might help keep blood sugar in check, but they can't take the place of the treatments your doctor recommends. Managing diabetes well means sticking to your medication, eating a balanced diet, and staying active. Before trying anything new, it's always best to check in with your dietician or physician." Following unverified health advice poses several risks. Discontinuing prescribed diabetes medication or altering a treatment plan without consulting a healthcare provider can lead to uncontrolled blood sugar levels, increasing risk of serious complications such as heart disease, nerve damage, and kidney problems. While the ingredients in this mixture are generally safe in moderation, they can interact with medications or cause side effects. For instance, fenugreek can cause digestive issues, and jamun seeds might lower blood sugar levels excessively if combined with other anti-diabetic medications.

title: Fact Check: Can a person survive on water and dates?
claim_text: A person can survive solely on dates and water
quick_take: A facebook post claims that a person can live just by eating dates and water. We fact checked it and found this claim MostlyFalse.
doctor_explanation:
Fasting religiously and adhering to mono diets based on the belief that even God consumed a particular food reflect the intersection of faith and dietary choices. Across various cultures and religions, individuals embrace these practices to express their devotion and seek spiritual enlightenment. However, while such traditions hold significant spiritual meaning, science raises concerns about the potential dangers of mono diets. Mono diets involve consuming only one type of food or a limited variety, which can lead to nutrient deficiencies and health risks in long run.

What are mono diets?
Mono diets, also known as monotropic diets or single-food diets, are eating plans that involve consuming only one type of food or a limited variety of foods exclusively for a specific period. These diets often focus on a single fruit, vegetable, or food item. Proponents of mono diets claim various health benefits, such as weight loss and detoxification. However, they are highly restrictive and can lead to nutrient deficiencies if followed for an extended period. Mono diets are not considered a sustainable or healthy approach to long-term nutrition and should be approached with caution.

What are the side effects of mono diets?
Mono diets, which involve consuming only one type of food or a limited variety of foods exclusively, can have several side effects and health risks.

Can a person survive on eating water and dates?
Not really. Surviving solely on water and dates is not recommended as a sustainable long-term diet due to potential health risks and nutrient deficiencies. While dates are a good source of carbohydrates and some nutrients, they lack essential vitamins, minerals, and proteins required for overall health. Additionally, excessive consumption of dates can lead to imbalances in blood sugar levels due to their high sugar content.

Research papers suggest that a diet lacking in essential nutrients can have adverse effects on health. A study published in the International Journal of Preventive Medicine (2019) found that restricted diets, including those with limited food choices like a mono diet, can lead to nutritional deficiencies and impaired metabolic functions, affecting overall health.

In summary, while short-term consumption of water and dates may not be immediately harmful, relying solely on this limited diet for an extended period can lead to serious health issues and nutrient deficiencies. It is crucial to maintain a diverse and balanced diet to meet all nutritional requirements for sustained health and well-being.

How long can one live without food?
The human body can generally survive without food for about three to four weeks, depending on individual factors such as overall health, body composition, and environmental conditions. However, it's important to note that going without food for extended periods can lead to severe malnutrition, dehydration, and other health risks. The body requires essential nutrients found in food for proper functioning and overall well-being. It is not recommended to intentionally fast for prolonged periods without medical supervision and support. Proper nutrition is crucial for maintaining good health and sustaining life.

Sports Nutritionist Manasi Bandhu says, "To lead a long and healthy life, one needs to have a balanced diet consisting of all nutrients. Dates are rich in potassium and fibre which helps the body in retaining water. By consuming only dates and water, one can definitely survive but will have a lot of nutrient deficiencies which may lead to several diseases and loss of various body functions. Dietary supplementation may help in overcoming some of the deficiencies but it is important to have a diet consisting of all food groups for a healthy life."

According to Nutritionist Dr. Swati Dave, "A healthy individual can survive approximately 3 weeks without food, considering climatic conditions. However, extended water fasting for 4-5 days is possible for a healthy person, but temperature and humidity should be taken into account." She emphasises that a colourful diet rich in fruits and vegetables is the best way to obtain essential vitamins and minerals. When asked about a diet solely consisting of dates and water, she responded, 'That's a lot to ask for. Such a restrictive diet can lead to protein energy malnutrition and severe health consequences.'

title: Can a probiotic toothpaste make your teeth super white instantly?
claim_text: A Facebook post claims that a probiotic toothpaste (SP-4 Ultra+ Whitening Probiotic Toothpaste) can instantly make your teeth super white, with complete removal of plaque, tough stains, and significantly brighter teeth after just one brushing. The advertisement video shows very unrealistic results like complete removal of plaque, tough stains, and significantly brighter teeth.
quick_take: A Facebook post claims that a probiotic toothpaste can make your teeth super white instantly. Our fact check reveals this claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Probiotic toothpaste can offer several oral health benefits by introducing good bacteria to help keep harmful bacteria in check, reducing the risk of cavities, gum disease, and bad breath. However, there is no scientific evidence supporting the claim that it can instantly make teeth super white. Scientific analysis shows: Claim 1 (Instant teeth whitening): The product's claim that it can instantly make teeth super white is highly exaggerated. Scientifically, teeth whitening usually requires active ingredients like hydrogen peroxide, which work over time to break down stains. Probiotics and other mentioned ingredients (hydrated silicon and diamond powder) do not have the chemical properties needed for immediate whitening. Claim 2 (Removal of tough stains and plaque): The toothpaste may help in reducing surface stains and controlling plaque formation, but it is unlikely to remove tough, deeply embedded stains or hardened plaque (tartar) with just brushing. Such conditions require professional dental treatments. Claim 3 (Probiotic benefits): Probiotics' role in teeth whitening is minimal, as their main function is to balance bacteria in the mouth, not to bleach or lighten tooth enamel. Claim 4 (Plaque removal technology): There is limited evidence that any over-the-counter toothpaste can effectively remove plaque buildup like shown, in such a short span of time. Once plaque hardens into tartar, it can only be removed by a dental professional. Claim 5 (Diamond powder): Diamond powder can help in polishing teeth and removing surface stains, but excessive use can wear down enamel over time. The effectiveness of diamond powder in teeth whitening, especially in such a short timeframe, is not well-documented. Teeth whitening, especially when dealing with tough stains or yellowing, requires chemical agents like hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide that work by penetrating the tooth enamel to break down stains. The images and videos promoting such instant whitening results are likely exaggerated and misleading. Teeth whitening is a gradual process that cannot be achieved in a single brushing session, especially not with a toothpaste that primarily focuses on balancing oral bacteria rather than using strong bleaching agents. Dr Pooja Sharma states: "It's important to be cautious with products that promise instant results! Especially when it comes to teeth whitening. Professional guidance is important to ensure both the safety and effectiveness of any whitening treatment." Dr Sharma emphasises the importance of professional consultation and treatment to ensure safety and achieve desired results. Dr Snigdha says: "Probiotic toothpaste can support oral health by balancing the bacteria in your mouth, but the idea that it can instantly whiten teeth is simply not supported by scientific evidence. Teeth whitening is a process that involves more potent agents and longer time."

title: Can a teeth whitening serum effectively whiten yellow teeth?
claim_text: A teeth whitening serum can magically whiten yellow teeth without using peroxide (brand name Perfora). It claims to be safe and uses 'natural' ingredients.

doctor_explanation: Bromelain and Papain are proteolytic enzymes, meaning they have the ability to break down proteins. PAP, or Phthalimido-Peroxy Caproic Acid, is a newer compound used for teeth whitening as an alternative to Hydrogen peroxide. Acting as an alternative to hydrogen peroxide (as a whitening agent), PAP effectively targets tooth discoloration by breaking down chromogens, the molecules responsible for stains. This process lightens teeth (without the release of free radicals), which penetrate enamel and dentin to oxidise and dismantle staining molecules. Widely used in whitening gels, toothpaste, and strips, PAP offers a promising alternative to traditional hydrogen peroxide-based agents. While generally safe when used as directed, some individuals may experience temporary tooth sensitivity or gum irritation after the treatment. Yes, to some extent some of those do work. But wait, it's not that simple! The market is full of unreliable teeth whitening solutions too which can actually be harmful to the teeth enamel. One instance is the widespread use of Hydrogen peroxide in teeth whitening products. This can be harmful to the teeth if used too frequently and in high concentrations. Hydrogen peroxide causes enamel erosion (damage to the outermost layer of a tooth) and inflammation of the gums. However, the good thing about this product is that they have used PAP. This is a safer alternative when compared to Hydrogen peroxide. PAP offers reduced teeth sensitivity and there's a lesser risk of gum inflammation. Moreover, one study suggests it may still cause surface roughness (the teeth whitening serum contains Hydrated Silica, which is a mild abrasive), although results vary. Nevertheless, whitening with PAP could potentially reduce or eliminate many of the adverse side effects associated with peroxide. To add more, most PAP whitening products now include hydroxyapatite, denoted by a plus symbol as a suffix (PAP+). This addition enhances safety by not only whitening teeth but also aiding in enamel remineralization. Still, since this is a new chemical compound, there's less research about its effectiveness and potential risks. The effectiveness of PAP teeth whitening varies because some studies found it less effective than hydrogen peroxide. One study discovered that while PAP effectively removed coffee stains from teeth. But, its performance was lacking when it came to removing tea and red wine stains. Interestingly, the use of PAP actually made the appearance of teeth worse when they had tea and red wine stains. In contrast, another study determined that hydrogen peroxide produced the most significant change in tooth colour compared to PAP and bromelain. The short answer will be no. There has been a consistent concern regarding whether it is genuinely peroxide-free, despite its marketing as such. A brief investigation reveals that PubChem classifies PAP as belonging to the peroxide family. PAP is a synthetic organic peroxy acid that derives from caprolactam and phthalic anhydride. Sulfuric acid combines with hydrogen peroxide to form peroxy acid. Dr Snigdha says, 'It's important for patients to be careful when considering over-the-counter teeth whitening products. I advise consulting a dentist before starting any whitening treatment. Tooth discolouration can be due to various factors, including diet, smoking, medications, and underlying conditions. While OTC products may offer cosmetic improvements, they may not effectively address the main problem. These products can possibly harm oral tissues and worsen existing dental issues, especially with frequent and high-concentration use. Without proper diagnosis and guidance, patients may damage their gums or enamel. It's essential to recognise that natural tooth colour variations are normal. And, extra white teeth may not always be achievable or desirable.' Dr Pooja Sharma says, 'I strongly advise consulting a dentist before use. While promising quick results, their safety varies, and not all discolourations can be treated by them alone. Applying without diagnosis can worsen conditions. Teeth naturally have a shade of yellow, excessive whitening leads to unrealistic expectations. For cosmetic enhancement, options like veneers or crowns may be better under the expertise of a dentist. Overuse of such teeth whitening products can harm oral tissues, causing gum inflammation or enamel damage. Even if you are using such products, limit their use to four weeks and seek professional advice if problems continue.'
