title: Can latjeera and bamboo leaves cure all dental problems?
claim_text: A Facebook video advises that one should take 10 latjeera leaves and 10 bamboo leaves, break and dry them, then burn them. The remaining ash is to be mixed with salt and massaged on the teeth for at least five minutes daily for a week. It also suggests using a bamboo stick like a toothbrush for eight days. They claim that it can reduce swelling, clear out pus, ease tooth pain, get rid of bad breath, treat bleeding gums, and even make your teeth whiter.
quick_take: A social media post claims that latjeera and bamboo leaves can cure all dental problems. We did the fact check and termed this claim as false.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific basis to suggest that burning these leaves produces an ash capable of healing dental infections or inflammation. Modern dental science supports treatments that are evidence-based, and none of the compounds produced by burning latjeera (Achyranthes aspera) or bamboo leaves have been proven to neutralise bacteria or reduce inflammation safely in the mouth. Traditional remedies may hold cultural significance, but without rigorous testing and validation, they cannot be recommended over standard dental care. Besides, different dental issues require specific treatments rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. Dr Snigdha, BDS, MDS, from Vananchal Dental College and Hospital, Garhwa, Jharkhand says, "There is no scientific proof that latjeera and bamboo leaves ash can treat dental problems. Dental issues like cavities, gum disease, and infections need proper care, such as brushing, flossing, and professional treatment. Relying on such remedies may delay the right treatment and make the problem worse." Regarding safety: using burnt leaf ash mixed with salt on your teeth can be abrasive and potentially damaging to your enamel. Enamel is the protective outer layer of the teeth, and once it is worn away, it cannot be naturally replaced. Salt itself is a known irritant if overused, and when combined with abrasive particles, it could lead to further sensitivity, gum irritation, and even contribute to accelerated dental decay. On bamboo stems as toothbrush alternatives: some natural chewing sticks have been used as an adjunct to dental hygiene and can reduce plaque to some extent; however, they do not offer the same benefits as a regular toothbrush used with fluoride toothpaste. There is little evidence to support bamboo's efficacy compared to products that have undergone rigorous testing. Dr Sanjeev Kumar, BDS, MPH, Senior Consultant (Medical), NPCCHH (MoHFW), Centre for Community Medicine, AIIMS, New Delhi states, "No, these remedies cannot cure dental caries, gum bleeding, or bad breath. Cavities need professional treatment, bleeding gums may indicate gum disease, and bad breath often has underlying causes like poor hygiene or infections. Proper brushing, flossing, and dental check-ups are the best way to maintain oral health." There are no clinical trials or peer-reviewed studies validating the use of latjeera leaf ash, salt mixtures, or bamboo stems as a cure-all for dental problems. The absence of credible research means these practices are based solely on anecdotal or traditional knowledge, which should not override the recommendations of dental experts.

title: Can lemon ginger tea cure ovarian cysts and diabetes?
claim_text: Drinking lemon ginger tea everyday offers numerous benefits including making hair long and strong, relieving inflammation and pain, treating ovarian cysts naturally, curing diabetes, fighting indigestion, and improving skin health.
quick_take: A social media post claims that drinking lemon ginger tea can cure ovarian cysts and diabetes. Our fact check found out it’s false.
doctor_explanation:
NOT REALLY. There is no scientific evidence to suggest that lemon ginger tea can treat ovarian cysts. Ovarian cysts are sacs filled with fluid that develop either inside or on the surface of the ovaries. While most are harmless and resolve on their own, persistent or problematic cysts require medical evaluation. Ginger contains anti-inflammatory properties and may ease mild menstrual discomfort, but it does not specifically target or eliminate ovarian cysts. Similarly, lemon is rich in vitamin C and antioxidants but does not influence cyst formation or resolution. For managing ovarian cysts, consult a healthcare professional for proper guidance. Ginger may not be safe during late pregnancy, for those with past pregnancy issues, or clotting disorders.

NO, LEMON GINGER TEA CANNOT CURE DIABETES. Diabetes is a chronic condition that requires proper management through diet, exercise, and, in some cases, medication. Ginger may help in reducing blood sugar levels to a small extent by improving insulin sensitivity, as suggested by some studies. Lemon can help in hydration and provide a small dose of vitamin C, but neither ingredient can reverse or cure diabetes. Relying solely on tea for diabetes control could delay proper treatment and worsen health outcomes.

Dr P Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita School of Ayurveda, states: Ayurveda classifies diabetes into different stages based on its progression. Early-stage diabetes, known as Kapha Prameha, can often be managed and even reversed through lifestyle changes and supportive treatments. However, advanced diabetes, referred to as Pitta Prameha, is not curable but can be controlled with lifelong medication. In its most severe stage, called Vata Prameha, diabetes becomes extremely difficult to manage. Despite extensive research, no single herb or remedy has been identified as a complete cure for diabetes.

Dr V Mohan, in a previous interview with THIP Media, provided insights into diabetes cure and remission: The concepts of Diabetes Reversal or Diabetes Cure have recently gained significant attention, though they are not new ideas. The more accurate term is Diabetes Remission, as remission means the condition has temporarily subsided but can return at any time. There is no cure for diabetes yet.

NOT REALLY. Lemon ginger tea does not directly affect hair growth. Healthy hair growth relies on multiple factors, including nutrition, genetics, and scalp health. Interestingly, research shows that ginger's active compound, 6-gingerol, may actually suppress hair growth and could even act as a hair removal agent. On the contrary, another study suggests that cedrol, another compound found in ginger, may stimulate hair growth. This makes the evidence controversial at present. Lemon offers some antioxidant benefits, but drinking lemon ginger tea alone is unlikely to promote stronger or longer hair. A balanced diet rich in protein, biotin, and other essential nutrients plays a much more crucial role in supporting healthy hair.

YES, IT MAY HELP RELIEVE MILD INDIGESTION. Ginger is well-known for its ability to soothe digestive discomfort. It can ease bloating, nausea, and mild stomach upset by promoting faster gastric emptying. Lemon, with its citric acid content, may support digestion by stimulating stomach acid production. However, while lemon ginger tea can help with occasional indigestion, it is not a cure for chronic digestive issues, which require medical assessment.

TO A DEGREE, IT MAY, BUT ONLY FOR MILD INFLAMMATION AND DISCOMFORT. Ginger contains compounds like gingerol, which possess anti-inflammatory properties and may help reduce minor pain, such as muscle soreness or arthritis-related stiffness. Lemon contributes antioxidants that can combat oxidative stress. However, these benefits are modest and do not replace medical treatment for severe pain or chronic inflammatory conditions.

SOMEWHAT, BUT NOT DRAMATICALLY. The antioxidants in lemon may help protect skin cells from damage caused by free radicals, and ginger's anti-inflammatory properties may reduce redness or irritation. However, drinking lemon ginger tea is not a standalone solution for improving skin health. Hydration, a nutrient-rich diet for healthy skin, and proper skincare routines are more impactful for healthy skin.

Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, states: Lemon ginger tea is often believed to cure acne, reduce wrinkles, and brighten skin. While lemons and ginger contain antioxidants and anti-inflammatory properties, there's little scientific evidence supporting these claims. The tea may offer minor benefits like improving digestion and overall health, but it won't drastically improve skin issues. For healthy skin, focus on a proper skincare routine, sun protection, and a balanced lifestyle instead of relying on this tea as a miracle solution.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: The claim that drinking lemon ginger tea can cure ovarian cysts and diabetes is false. While the tea offers some health benefits, such as aiding mild indigestion, reducing inflammation, and providing antioxidants, it cannot treat or cure serious medical conditions. It's a healthy addition to your diet but not a replacement for evidence-based medical treatments. For chronic or serious health issues, consult a healthcare professional.

title: Can lemon grass reduce plaque and prevent heart disease?
claim_text: Lemon grass is anti-hypercholesterolemic and anti-hyperlipidemic in nature. It improves the blood flow in the vessels and reduces the risk of heart diseases by preventing the deposition of plaque in the arteries. Make a lemon grass infusion and drink one cup daily.
quick_take: A social media post claims that lemon grass reduces plaque and prevents heart disease. We did the fact check and termed it as mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
The fact check addresses three main questions. First, regarding cholesterol and lipid reduction: Studies (animal studies) suggest lemon grass may have mild effects, but evidence is limited. Lemon grass (Cymbopogon citratus) is traditionally used in herbal medicine for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits. A few animal studies showed lemon grass extracts can help lower total cholesterol and triglyceride levels. A 2011 study on rats found slight cholesterol reduction after lemon grass supplementation. However, these effects have not been conclusively proven in humans. Clinical studies on human participants (only 22 subjects) are scarce, and available evidence does not confirm that lemon grass alone can significantly lower cholesterol or lipid levels. Relying solely on it without addressing diet, exercise, or medications may not yield noticeable results.

Second, regarding plaque prevention: There is no strong scientific evidence to support this claim. Plaque formation in arteries (atherosclerosis) occurs due to build-up of cholesterol, fats, and other substances from poor diet, sedentary lifestyle, genetics, and other factors. Lemon grass contains antioxidants like flavonoids and phenolic compounds which may help reduce oxidative stress and support overall cardiovascular health. However, antioxidants alone cannot prevent or reverse plaque formation. A balanced diet, daily exercise, and proper medical treatment are far more effective.

Third, regarding daily infusion improving heart health: While lemon grass tea can be a healthy addition, it is not a magic solution. A 2011 study on rats found lemon grass helps protect the heart from damage caused by a toxic chemical - rats given lemon grass had less heart damage and more antioxidants, similar to vitamin E benefits. Lemon grass infusion is low in calories and rich in antioxidants, which can help combat inflammation and oxidative stress, indirectly supporting heart health. However, drinking lemon grass infusion alone will not address major heart disease risk factors like high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or diabetes. Managing these requires lifestyle changes, dietary improvements, and sometimes medications.

Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, states: "Lemon grass is often praised for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory benefits, but there isn't enough scientific proof to say it can stop plaque from building up in arteries. To truly protect your heart, it's important to follow a healthy lifestyle. Eating a balanced diet with lots of fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, staying active with regular exercise, and managing stress all play a key role. Avoiding smoking and limiting alcohol are also crucial for heart health. While lemon grass may offer some benefits, it's always best to talk to a doctor and rely on proven methods to keep your heart healthy."

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, advises: "To reduce the risk of heart disease, focus on healthy habits. Eating a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains helps keep your heart strong. Regular exercise, like walking or swimming, improves blood flow and keeps your heart in shape. Managing stress through relaxation techniques, avoiding smoking, and limiting alcohol can also make a big difference. Don't forget to visit your doctor for regular check-ups to stay on top of your heart health and catch any issues early."

THIP Media Take: The claim that lemon grass reduces plaque and prevents heart disease is mostly false. While lemon grass has antioxidants and mild cholesterol-lowering properties, there is no strong evidence that it prevents plaque build-up or heart disease. It can support overall health but should not replace proven medical treatments or lifestyle changes.

title: Can lemon water on an empty stomach make you lose weight?
claim_text: Lemon juice in the early morning makes you lose weight – yes, that's an accepted fact.
quick_take: A social media post claims that lemon water on an empty stomach can make you lose weight. We did a thorough fact check to term this claim as mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Can lemon juice in water help with weight loss?
No, lemon juice in water alone cannot cause significant weight loss or cure obesity. While lemon juice is low in calories and contains vitamin C, it does not possess any magic properties that target fat loss. It may, however, aid our metabolism due to its fibre content. But to get this effect you need to actually consume the pulp of lemon and not just its juice. Losing weight requires a calorie deficit, which means burning more calories than you consume. Simply drinking lemon water does not significantly impact this process.

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says: "Drinking lemon water can support hydration and digestion, but it's not a substitute for proper weight loss strategies. People often believe simple fixes will work miracles, but sustainable weight loss comes from consistent healthy eating and staying active. Lemon water is beneficial for your overall health, but on its own, it won't lead to significant weight loss." Dr Dave adds: "To get better results, have lemon water with breakfast or post-lunch. Don't add sugar or honey to it. Room temperature water is fine. Adding lemon to boiling water is a bad idea, as Vitamin C is a heat-sensitive nutrient."

Deepalakshmi Sriram, Registered Dietitian at The Cleft & Craniofacial Centre and Sree Balaji Medical College & Hospital, Chennai, shares: "Lemon water is refreshing and can be a healthy addition to your routine, but it's not a magic solution for weight loss. It can also help in hydration. The best way to manage your weight is through a balanced diet and regular exercise. While lemon juice adds flavour and vitamin C, it doesn't burn fat or boost your metabolism significantly."

Does drinking lemon juice on an empty stomach boost metabolism?
Not really. There is no solid evidence that drinking lemon juice on an empty stomach directly boosts metabolism. While lemon juice is rich in antioxidants like vitamin C, which supports overall health, it doesn't provide an instant metabolic boost. Metabolism is influenced by factors such as genetics, activity level, diet, stress, sleep, and overall health. Although stress is closely linked to weight gain, some social media posts oversimplify weight loss by claiming it's purely a mental challenge, neglecting the physical factors involved. While drinking lemon water can be refreshing, it isn't a quick fix for fat burning.

Can lemon juice replace a proper diet and exercise plan for obesity?
Absolutely not. Obesity is a multifaceted condition often caused by poor diet, lack of exercise, and other environmental or genetic factors. Relying solely on lemon water will not replace the need for a balanced diet and regular exercise. In fact, reducing calorie intake and increasing physical activity are far more effective for long-term weight management. A combination of healthy eating habits, portion control, and daily exercise is important for achieving and maintaining a healthy weight.

Is there any scientific evidence to support the claim that lemon juice can make you lose weight?
No, there is no conclusive scientific evidence that supports the claim. Numerous studies show that lemon juice, while beneficial for overall health, does not directly address the root causes of obesity. However, we found one review from 2008 that suggests lemon water can help with weight management in mice. It is true that lemons contain compounds like flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties, but these alone are not enough to cure obesity. Healthy weight loss relies on sustainable changes to one's lifestyle, such as reducing caloric intake, increasing physical activity, and improving overall nutrition.

Are there any benefits to drinking lemon water?
Yes, lemon water can be beneficial in several ways. It helps keep you hydrated, and the vitamin C in lemons supports immune function. Vitamin C intake also lowers your chances of developing heart disease. Lemon water may help with digestion and maintaining healthy skin. It can also improve your iron absorption from your diet. However, too much vitamin C can cause stomach problems for people taking iron supplements, so it's better to get iron from foods like meat, spinach, and lentils. Moreover, having lemon daily along with walking has the potential to lower blood pressure. However, these benefits are not related to weight loss or obesity treatment. They contribute to overall well-being but are not a cure for obesity.

THIP Media Take: To conclude, the claim that lemon water on an empty stomach can cure obesity is mostly false. While lemon for weight loss is very popular among people, the scientific evidence is not strong enough. Still, it can be part of a healthy lifestyle, but it will not lead to significant weight loss on its own. Sustainable weight management requires a complete approach that includes proper diet, regular physical activity, lifestyle changes, and expert consultations when necessary.

Studies suggest oxytocin can play a role in managing inflammation and promoting healing - for example, a 2021 study shows it helps regulate the immune system and reduce oxidative stress. Love can help by reducing stress and promoting healthy behaviors that support the body's natural healing processes. It's released during positive social interactions like hugging or spending time with loved ones, helping to lower blood pressure and heart rate. Oxytocin also supports childbirth by stimulating contractions and aids in breastfeeding. Its calming effects can improve emotional well-being, making it a vital hormone for both physical and mental health. Love and emotional connections can trigger the release of hormones like oxytocin, which help reduce stress, lower blood pressure, and improve overall well-being. A 2023 study did find that Mangifera indica extract (mango extract) can reduce Streptococcus mutans (a bacteria generally found in human oral cavity) when used as a rinse, which could help in preventing plaque buildup. However, this doesn't mean it can whiten your teeth. Neem is very popular for its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties, which makes it good for maintaining oral hygiene. However, it does not whiten teeth. Neem may help in preventing gum diseases or plaque build-up due to its natural antibacterial qualities, but this doesn't translate to whitening. Cinnamon doesn't whiten teeth. It is beneficial for gum health due to its antimicrobial properties, but cinnamon has no whitening capabilities. Claims that it can remove stains or make teeth brighter are misleading. On the contrary, it can actually stain your teeth, so be careful with this home remedy. Nutmeg does not whiten teeth either. Nutmeg may offer some antibacterial benefits that could contribute to oral health, but it is not a teeth-whitening agent. It does not have any properties that can change the enamel's colour or provide the brightening effects that people typically associate with teeth whitening products. It does have eugenol, which can help in tooth pain management. Home remedies like the one in the claim might help with basic oral hygiene, but they cannot replace professional whitening procedures. Ingredients like neem, cinnamon, and mango seed might contribute to better oral health, but their abrasive qualities are often overstated when it comes to whitening. In fact, excessive use of abrasive materials can damage the enamel, leading to long-term issues like tooth sensitivity. Professional teeth whitening uses bleaching agents like hydrogen peroxide, which are scientifically proven to penetrate tooth enamel and change its colour. Dr Snigdha, BDS, MDS, Vananchal Dental College and Hospital, Garhwa, Jharkhand states, 'While natural ingredients like mango seed and neem can offer some benefits for oral health, such as antibacterial properties and supporting gum health, they cannot match the effectiveness of professional whitening treatments for achieving a truly radiant smile. For those seeking significant whitening results, it's essential to consider that relying solely on natural remedies may not yield the desired brightness. Consulting with a dental professional can provide the best options for achieving and maintaining a brilliant, confident smile.' The safest and most effective way to whiten teeth is through professional treatments. Over-the-counter whitening products can help with surface stains but won't give results comparable to in-clinic procedures. title: Can massaging the lacrimal glands remove eyeglasses in a few days?
claim_text: An Instagram post suggests that massaging the lacrimal glands 30 times clockwise twice a day, alongside washing eyes 3-4 times daily and consuming a mixture of mishri (rock sugar), almonds, and fennel seeds in milk, can clear eye ducts and eliminate the need for glasses in just a few days.
quick_take: A social media post claims that massaging the lacrimal glands can remove eyeglasses in a few days. After fact checking, we found that this claim is false.
doctor_explanation:
The fact check examines three main aspects: First, regarding massaging lacrimal glands - The lacrimal glands, located above the outer corner of each eye, produce tears to keep the eyes moist and clear of debris. Massaging them may stimulate tear production or help with minor tear duct blockages, providing relief for dry eyes or irritation. A 2021 study found that short-term eye massage using Chinese eye exercises or an automated eye massager can temporarily improve blood flow and eyesight, but after 60 days of daily massage there were no lasting benefits and no direct link between increased blood flow and improved vision. There is no scientific evidence that massage can correct vision problems like nearsightedness, farsightedness, or astigmatism - these conditions result from the shape of the eyeball or cornea, which cannot be changed through massage. Vision correction requires medical interventions such as glasses, contact lenses, or surgery.

Second, regarding clearing tear ducts - Blocked tear ducts can cause watery eyes or infections, but they don't affect how light focuses on the retina, which determines visual acuity. Even if massaging helps with duct clearance, it won't reshape the eye or fix refractive errors.

Third, regarding the dietary mixture - A mixture of mishri, almonds, and saunf in milk cannot eliminate the need for glasses. While almonds provide vitamin E and fennel seeds offer antioxidants that support overall eye health and may help slow age-related conditions like macular degeneration, mishri has no proven eye benefits and if overconsumed could contribute to health issues due to its sugar content. A balanced diet rich in nutrients like vitamin A and omega-3s can support eye function but cannot correct refractive errors or replace glasses.

Dr Naveen Gupta, Ophthalmologist at Narain Eye Care, Noida, explains: "People often mistake 'good for eye health' for 'can improve vision.' Fennel contains vitamin C, which supports eye health, while almonds provide vitamin E, which may help delay conditions like age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and cataracts. However, if improving eyesight means reducing reliance on glasses, this mixture has no effect."

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, clarifies: "There is no scientific evidence to suggest that a mixture of mishri, almonds, and saunf (fennel) in milk can improve eyesight to the extent of eliminating the need for glasses. While almonds and fennel contain some nutrients beneficial for eye health, vision problems like myopia or hyperopia are primarily caused by the shape of the eye and cannot be corrected with dietary changes alone. Regular eye check-ups and proper vision correction methods, such as glasses, contact lenses, or surgery, are essential for maintaining clear vision."

Safety note: Gentle massaging around the eyes might be safe for some, but applying pressure to the lacrimal glands without proper guidance risks irritation or damage. Washing eyes 3-4 times daily is fine if using clean water, but overuse could disrupt natural tear balance. The diet mixture is generally safe in moderation, though one should avoid excessive sugar intake.

title: Can milk with jaggery improve digestion and cure anaemia?
claim_text: Drinking milk with jaggery before going to bed at night strengthens the digestive system, cures anaemia, and relieves gastric issues.
quick_take: A social media post claims that drinking milk with jaggery can improve digestion and cure anaemia. After fact checking, we found out this claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
NOT ENTIRELY. Milk and jaggery may offer some minor digestive benefits, but they are not effective digestive aids on their own. While milk with jaggery might be a comforting drink, it is unlikely to significantly improve digestion. For digestive health, a balanced diet, regular hydration, and healthy lifestyle choices are far more effective.

Regarding anaemia: No, milk with jaggery cannot cure anaemia. Although jaggery contains iron, it is insufficient for treating anaemia. Some evidence says it can help in preventing anaemia. Furthermore, certain types of anaemia like Pernicious anaemia, Aplastic anaemia, Congenital Dyserythropoietic anaemia (CDA), Fanconi anaemia, Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, and Paroxysmal Nocturnal Haemoglobinuria are incurable. Treatment for these types involves lifelong management—often including blood transfusions, iron chelation, or bone marrow transplants. Relying on milk and jaggery as a "cure" could delay necessary treatment, potentially worsening the condition.

Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai: "Milk with jaggery offers some nutritional benefits but is not a cure for anemia. Anemia often results from iron deficiency, and while jaggery contains non-heme iron, it's not easily absorbed by the body. The calcium in milk can also inhibit iron absorption, making this combination ineffective for those needing easily absorbed iron from animal sources or supplements."

Dr Fatma adds: "Jaggery can stimulate digestion, but milk may cause bloating, especially in those who are lactose intolerant, and might worsen gastric issues for some people. While they provide some nutrients, they aren't a solution for anemia. If you have anemia, consult a doctor and focus on a balanced iron-rich diet and supplements if needed."

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition: "Milk with jaggery is often seen as a comforting drink, but it's not a cure for anaemia. While jaggery does contain iron, the amount is too small to correct iron deficiency on its own. Iron from plant-based sources also doesn't absorb as well as iron from animal foods. Plus, when mixed with milk, calcium can actually compete with iron for absorption, making it even less effective. To treat or prevent anaemia, a balanced diet rich in iron, vitamin B12, and folic acid is essential. Foods like leafy greens, lentils, lean meats, and fortified cereals provide more robust support. If anaemia persists, consulting a healthcare professional is important to find the right treatment."

Soumam Dutta, PhD Scholar (Nutrition), Department of Endocrinology, ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition: "While jaggery does contain iron, we would need to consume a significant amount to meet our daily requirements. Additionally, it's generally not advisable for us to combine sources of calcium and iron in the same meal."

Regarding gastric issues: Not exactly. Traditionally, jaggery has been used for mild laxative effects, but combining it with milk may not help with gastric relief for everyone.

Regarding safety at night: Generally, yes—but it may not suit everyone. For those who tolerate it well, milk with jaggery can be a comforting evening drink. Still, if it causes digestive discomfort, it's best to avoid it at night.

Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital in Ahmedabad: "Drinking milk with jaggery at night can be a comforting and soothing habit for many. Milk, rich in tryptophan, promotes relaxation and may help in better sleep, while jaggery adds a natural sweetness. However, it's important to be mindful of your body's needs. For those with lactose intolerance or digestive sensitivities, this combination could lead to bloating or cramps." She adds: "To make the most of this drink, maintain balance and moderation. Jaggery, like sugar, contains calories and should be consumed wisely. Ensure there's a gap between dinner and milk intake, and aim to drink it about an hour before bedtime to avoid gastric discomfort or a feeling of heaviness."

THIP Media Take: The claim that drinking milk with jaggery can cure anaemia, strengthen digestion, and relieve gastric problems is mostly false. While this combination may be nutritious and comforting, it is not a substitute for medical treatment or a balanced diet.

title: Can mustard oil, cloves, and alum cure all dental problems?

doctor_explanation:
Dr Sanjeev Kumar, BDS, MPH, Senior Consultant (Medical), NPCCHH (MoHFW), Centre for Community Medicine, AIIMS, New Delhi, explains: 'Mustard oil, clove powder, and alum have been traditionally used for oral care, but they cannot treat cavities or reverse tooth decay. Clove may temporarily relieve pain, and mustard oil has some antibacterial properties, but they do not stop cavity progression. Alum, while astringent, does not repair damaged enamel. Cavities worsen over time and require professional treatment. Small cavities may be treated with fillings or fluoride applications, but for severely decayed teeth, root canals or extractions may be necessary. Ignoring proper dental care can lead to infections, pain, and tooth loss. The best way to protect teeth is by brushing with fluoride toothpaste, flossing, and getting regular dental check-ups.'

Dr Snigdha, BDS, MDS, from Vananchal Dental College and Hospital, Garhwa, Jharkhand, explains: 'Mustard oil, clove powder, and alum may offer mild antibacterial effects but do not strengthen teeth or provide deep whitening. Enamel cannot be repaired once damaged, and actually strong teeth come from a diet rich in calcium and fluoride. For whitening, surface stains may be reduced slightly, but achieving visibly whiter teeth requires professional treatments or clinically tested whitening products. Relying solely on home remedies may lead to unmet expectations and overlooked dental issues.'

Regarding cavities and tooth decay: cavities and tooth decay are caused by bacteria and cannot be reversed with home remedies. While clove powder contains eugenol, which has mild pain-relieving and antibacterial properties, it does not heal cavities. Similarly, alum has astringent effects but cannot repair decayed teeth. Some studies suggest that mustard oil may help reduce plaque and gingivitis due to its antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties, but it does not treat cavities. The only effective treatments for cavities are dental fillings, fluoride applications, and professional care. Without proper treatment, cavities can worsen, leading to infections or even tooth loss.

Regarding bad breath: Clove has antibacterial properties that may help reduce odour-causing bacteria in the mouth. Alum, with its astringent nature, can temporarily lower bacterial presence but does not provide long-term relief. Some studies suggest that mustard oil may improve gum health and help reduce bad breath by removing bacteria. While mustard oil, clove powder, and alum have some antibacterial and astringent properties, they do not rebuild enamel or provide deep whitening. Strong teeth require essential minerals like calcium and fluoride, while long-lasting whiteness comes from professional treatments or dentist-approved whitening products.

Regarding safety: These ingredients have traditional uses in oral care but lack fluoride, which is essential for preventing cavities and strengthening enamel. Overuse of alum can cause irritation and toxicity, while improper use of mustard oil may lead to gum sensitivity. High doses of eugenol, found in clove extract, can be toxic, potentially causing liver and kidney damage, coma, and low blood sugar, especially in children.

title: Can neem and guava leaves treat finger fungal infection?
claim_text: According to a Facebook video, you can treat your fungal infections between the fingers by a home remedy using ash of neem and guava leaves, alum, aloe vera gel, coconut oil and turmeric powder. The man in the video says it is a guaranteed overnight cure and will prevent any future infections of tinea pedis or tinea manuum.
quick_take: A Facebook post claims that the ash of neem and guava leaves can treat finger fungal infections at home, in just one night. We did the fact check to term this as False.
doctor_explanation: Tinea pedis, commonly known as athlete's foot, is a fungal infection that usually affects the skin between the toes, while tinea manuum affects the hands. Both infections are due to dermatophytes, a group of fungi that thrive in warm, moist environments. These infections often present as red, scaly, and itchy patches on the skin and can spread if left untreated. Fungal infections on the fingers, like tinea manuum, are often due to direct contact with contaminated surfaces, excessive sweating, or a weakened immune system. Poor hygiene, exposure to communal areas such as gyms or swimming pools, and the use of tight or non-breathable gloves can also increase the risk. Guava leaves have been traditionally used in various cultures for their antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties. The leaves are rich in bioactive compounds like quercetin, kaempferol, and myricetin, which give them strong medicinal properties. According to a 2021 review, they exhibit antioxidant, anticancer, antidiabetic, and antimicrobial effects. However, the current evidence is not yet strong enough (much of the evidence uses lab studies or animal studies) to fully confirm their effectiveness, and we need more research, especially in clinical settings. Neem leaves are very popular in traditional medicine, especially in Ayurveda, for their antifungal, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory properties. Laboratory studies show that neem extracts can inhibit the growth of certain fungi, including those responsible for skin infections. A 2016 review highlights the diverse medicinal properties of neem (Azadirachta indica), attributing its benefits to compounds like azadirachtin and nimbolide. However, it's important to note that many of these studies were conducted in laboratories (in vitro) or on animals (in vivo). Even though the findings are promising, we need more clinical trials on humans to confirm neem's efficacy and safety for medical use. When neem and guava leaves are burned to create ash, the process destroys most of the active compounds that have antifungal properties. What's left is primarily minerals and carbon residue, which do not carry the same medicinal benefits as the original plant material. The idea that mixing this ash with alum, aloe vera gel, coconut oil, and turmeric powder could cure a fungal infection overnight lacks scientific backing. And, the claim that the mixture can prevent any such infections for life is also an exaggeration. Fungal infections usually need consistent treatment with antifungal medications over several weeks. There is no evidence to support using neem or guava leaf ash as a reliable treatment for fungal infections. Dr Sachin Gupta, a Dermatologist from Amrita Hospital, Faridabad states: 'I always stress the importance of using treatments that are backed by science. Neem and guava leaves are popular for their supposed antifungal benefits, but there's not enough strong evidence to say they really work, especially the way it is being claimed or for fast results. If you're dealing with a stubborn or serious fungal infection, it's important to use proper antifungal medicines and see a doctor to make sure it's treated correctly and doesn't get worse.' Neem leaf ash does not retain the full medicinal benefits of neem leaves. The burning process destroys or significantly alters the bioactive compounds in neem leaves, such as azadirachtin, nimbin, and nimbolide, leaving behind mainly inorganic salts and minerals in the ash. For treating tinea manuum, doctors usually recommend topical antifungal creams. Most treatments take about 4 to 6 weeks, though some newer options work faster. If the infection is severe, covers multiple areas, or doesn't respond to creams, oral antifungals might be necessary. Steroids can help with severe itching or inflammation but should only be used for a short time alongside antifungal treatment.

title: Fact Check: Can Onion juice cure PCOS?
claim_text: An Instagram post claims that onion juice can cure gynaecological issues. The post recommends taking a middle-sized white onion and cutting it into four pieces. After that, put the onion in boiling water and boil it for 5 more minutes. It is suggested that drink the juice before lunch and dinner before eating anything. doctor_explanation:
Dr Shweta Mittal Gupta, Co-Director, Centre of IVF, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, New Delhi, stated: 'Since this kind of treatment does not come under allopathic medicine, I cannot give any comment. None of the treatments can be followed blindly. There needs to be some scientific reason, and not taking other treatments is not justified. So there are many naturopathic treatments. However, they cannot be validated by doctors practising allopaths. PCOS is a condition which has been present from birth. It is more associated with obesity and genetic transmission. The best way to treat PCOS or keep the symptoms under control is to lose body weight and exercise and have a proper diet which is low in carbohydrates. PCOS is also associated with a higher risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease and uterine cancer. Thus, proper follow-up with a gynaecologist lifelong is mandatory lifestyle management does help tremendously in keeping the symptoms of PCOS under control.'

Dr (Prof) Mala Srivastava, Vice-Chairperson, Gynecologic Oncology, Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, New Delhi, responded: 'Onion juice is not a scientifically proven cure for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is a complex hormonal disorder, and while some natural remedies might help alleviate symptoms for some individuals, relying solely on onion juice or any other singular remedy is not advisable. Managing PCOS typically involves a combination of lifestyle changes, medications, and sometimes medical procedures.' She outlined common PCOS management approaches: Diet and Nutrition (balanced diet high in fibre, lean proteins, healthy fats; low glycemic index foods; weight management); Exercise (regular physical activity to manage weight, improve insulin sensitivity, and reduce symptoms); Medications (hormonal birth control to regulate cycles and reduce androgen levels; Metformin to improve insulin sensitivity; anti-androgens for hirsutism and acne; fertility medications); Supplements (inositol, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin D — with healthcare provider consultation); Lifestyle Changes (stress management, mindfulness, yoga, adequate sleep); Medical Procedures (ovarian drilling in select cases).

The article further notes that while onions have nutritional benefits including quercetin (anti-inflammatory, inhibits LDL oxidation, protects vitamin E, provides cancer protection), organosulfur compounds (linked to lowering blood pressure and cholesterol), vitamin C, B6, potassium, folate, calcium, and iron, no scientific evidence supports onion juice as a cure for PCOS. A study in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Medicine (64 women with PCOS, 15 days of onion juice consumption) showed improvements in HDL, LDL, triglyceride levels and reductions in menstrual disorders, but limitations include small sample size and short duration. A study by Mehranghiz Ebrahimi-Mamaghani et al. in the Journal of Obstetrics and Gynaecology Research suggested raw red onion may lower cholesterol in women with PCOS. A Biological and Chemical Research study highlighted antioxidant properties of Allium species. However, all findings are preliminary and inconclusive. The article concludes: 'PCOS is a complex hormonal disorder that affects women of reproductive age... While onions have notable nutritional benefits, including anti-inflammatory properties and essential vitamins and minerals, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that onion juice can cure PCOS. Naturopathy may suggest onion juice for managing PCOS symptoms, but current studies have significant limitations, such as small sample sizes and short study durations; therefore, their results are not conclusive.'

title: Can onion juice with sugar dissolve gallstones naturally?

quick_take: A post on Instagram claims that onion juice with sugar can dissolve gallstones naturally. Our fact check reveals it's False.

Gallstones can be made of cholesterol, bile salts, or bilirubin, and they may cause pain, infection, or other serious health issues if they block the bile ducts. No, onion juice with sugar does not dissolve gallstones naturally. There is no scientific evidence to support this claim. Gallstones are complex formations that usually require medical intervention to treat effectively. Even though onion juice has some health benefits, its ability to dissolve gallstones has not been proven. Most medical professionals recommend treatments based on the specific type and size of the gallstones, as well as the overall health of the patient. title: Can onion, lemon, and castor oil boost beard growth in 3 days?
claim_text: According to an Instagram video, applying a blend of onion juice, lemon juice, and castor oil can significantly increase beard growth in just 3 days.
quick_take: A social media post claims that onion, lemon and castor oil can boost beard growth in 3 days. We did the fact check to term this claim as False.
doctor_explanation: The fact check examined three ingredients: onion juice, castor oil, and lemon juice. **Onion juice**: While hair care enthusiasts use onion juice for its sulphur content believed to enhance blood circulation and strengthen hair strands, scientific research on its effectiveness for beard growth is scarce. Most available studies focus on alopecia areata for scalp hair regrowth, with improvements observed over several weeks, not days. There is no conclusive evidence that onion juice can directly stimulate facial hair follicles in such a short span. Beard growth depends more on hormones like testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which cannot be altered by external applications. **Castor oil**: While castor oil is popular for its moisturising and nourishing properties, rich in ricinoleic acid that may soothe skin and reduce inflammation, there is no scientific backing for the idea that castor oil can cause new hair to grow faster or thicker. A 2015 study shows ricinoleic acid has potential for treating hair loss, but it was conducted using computer modelling in an in silico environment. Its benefits are about maintenance rather than accelerating growth. **Lemon juice**: Contains vitamin C and antioxidants that support general skin health but has no proven effects on hair growth. Its astringent properties may help cleanse skin but this does not translate into faster beard growth. Applying lemon juice directly could cause irritation, dryness, or increased photosensitivity. Dr Ekansh Shekhar states: 'Scientific evidence does not support the use of a combination of onion, lemon, and castor oil for rapid beard growth. Beard hair typically grows at a rate of 0.3-0.4 mm per day, making significant growth within 3 days unlikely. Results can vary greatly based on individual factors such as genetics, hormones, and overall health. Conditions like acne, eczema, or psoriasis may also influence how effectively these ingredients work. Furthermore, using the wrong concentration or applying them incorrectly could lead to skin irritation or allergic reactions. While these ingredients may offer some benefits, it is unrealistic to expect noticeable beard growth in just 3 days. Consistent use over 6-12 weeks might yield modest improvements, but results will still differ from person to person.' Dr Rashi Soni adds: 'Beard growth is primarily influenced by genetics, hormones, and overall health. Factors such as testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) play crucial roles in determining the thickness and speed of hair growth. Additionally, individual health, age, and even diet can impact beard growth. While some topical treatments may help with the appearance and health of existing facial hair, they cannot significantly change the natural growth rate set by these underlying factors.' Potential risks include: onion juice causing skin redness or rashes; lemon juice causing stinging, dryness, and sun sensitivity; castor oil potentially clogging pores and causing breakouts.

title: Can Oziva Hair Vitamins reduce hair fall and promote hair growth in 4 months?
claim_text: Oziva Hair Vitamins, containing biotin, iron, and a DHT blocker, claims to improve hair growth and control hair fall, with 96% of users experiencing benefits within four months.
quick_take: A social media post is promoting Oziva Hair Vitamins which claims to improve hair growth and control hair fall, with reported results showing 96% of users experiencing benefits within four months. We did the fact check to term this claim as mostly false.
doctor_explanation: The clinical trial cited by Oziva assessed the effects of SesZen-Bio™, a proprietary extract of Sesbania grandiflora (vegetable hummingbird, katurai, agati, or West Indian pea), on hair density, thickness, and ferritin levels over 56 days. Although this study showed improvements in hair metrics for the treatment group, it had several limitations. Dr Sachin Gupta, Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, says, "The paper lacks clear information about who was involved in the study, such as the type and severity of hair loss the participants had. With only 51 people studied over a short period of 56 days, it's difficult to know if these findings would hold true for more people or over a longer time. Additionally, the claim that 96% of participants saw hair growth improvement after four months isn't backed up by the study, which only lasted about two months and didn't report such high success rates." He continues, "Moreover, the critique of PRP treatment by the manufacturers of SesZen-Bio™ seems premature. PRP is a well-established treatment with proven effectiveness in various types of hair loss, including the most common type, androgenetic alopecia (AGA). This stands in contrast to the claims made for SesZen-Bio™, which are based on just this one short study." Dr Gupta adds, "While SesZen-Bio™, which mainly contains biotin and multivitamins, might help improve hair health by addressing nutritional gaps, it's not likely to work for everyone, especially not for those with AGA. AGA is caused by a mix of hormones and genetics, and simple nutritional supplements are not enough to tackle these complex causes. This means while SesZen-Bio™ could help those whose hair loss is due to missing nutrients, it's not a one-size-fits-all solution, particularly for more complex cases like AGA. Additionally, it seems likely that the authors' connections with the product's manufacturer could influence the study results. While this isn't certain, such potential conflicts of interest suggest we should approach the findings with caution." The clinical trial on Sesbania grandiflora extract (marketed as SesZen-Bio™) involved 51 participants, with only 72% of volunteers reporting an improvement in hair health after eight weeks. This percentage is significantly lower than the 96% figure advertised by Oziva. Additionally, the study's primary outcomes showed a 25% improvement in hair density and a 16.94% increase in hair thickness, rather than a near-universal benefit. Oziva likely derived the 96% success rate from internal data or marketing surveys rather than from rigorous clinical trials with independent verification. Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, says, "Hair growth and hair fall depend on a variety of factors, including genetics, hormones, overall health, and nutrition. While protein plays an important role in strengthening hair, and ingredients like biotin, iron, and DHT blockers in Oziva Hair Vitamins may help improve hair health, they may not provide the desired results for everyone. For individuals who do not have nutritional deficiencies, simply relying on Oziva Hair Vitamins might not lead to significant hair growth or reduced hair fall." Dr Shekhar adds, "Hair growth is generally slow, averaging 0.5 to 1.7 cm per month, so regrowing hair in just four months is unlikely. Oziva Hair Vitamins can help improve hair texture, reduce hair fall, and support overall hair health over time. However, this may not work for those with AGA. Also, for best results, you should use them alongside a balanced diet, regular exercise, and proper hair care. Results can vary from person to person, and it may take 3 to 6 months to see noticeable changes. It's important to consult a healthcare provider to address the root causes of hair loss before relying solely on supplements." Multivitamins can help address deficiencies that contribute to hair thinning and breakage, but they are not a cure-all. Many hair health issues are unrelated to vitamin deficiency and are instead due to genetic or hormonal factors. For individuals without nutrient deficiencies, the additional vitamins in Oziva Hair Vitamins may not produce noticeable changes. Worse still, excess vitamins and certain minerals can actually do more harm than good. For instance, taking too much of certain vitamins, like vitamin A and selenium, can make hair loss worse or affect lab test results. Also, high biotin levels can cause insomnia, increased thirst, frequent urination, and may interfere with lab tests. In addition, the biotin and DHT blocker found in Oziva Hair Vitamins are only mildly supported by research. Without a personalised diagnosis, generic hair supplements may not target the root cause of hair issues, leading to variable results among users. Oziva Hair Vitamins may benefit hair health, especially for those with nutrient deficiencies, but marketing claims likely overstate their effectiveness. The clinical trial shows some positive results, but it has limitations and conflicts of interest. Without independent verification, the 96% improvement claim is questionable, and the product should not directly compare to treatments like PRP.

title: Can paan leaf remedies cure colds, coughs, and breathlessness?
claim_text: A Facebook video suggests two remedies using paan (betel) leaves. The first involves boiling paan leaves with ajwain, ginger, cloves, and honey, claimed to treat bronchitis, colds, and blocked noses. The second remedy involves applying a paste of paan leaves soaked in mustard oil to the chest, said to instantly relieve breathing difficulties, colds, coughs, and phlegm.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a paan leaf remedy can cure colds, coughs and breathlessness. After fact checking we found that this claim ismostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Do paan or betel leaves have medicinal properties? Yes, paan leaves contain compounds with potential medicinal properties. Studies have shown that paan leaves possess antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial effects in laboratory settings. These effects are due to the presence of polyphenols, alkaloids, and other bioactive compounds. However, it's crucial to distinguish between in vitro (test tube) or animal studies and clinical trials on humans. While these initial findings are promising, we still need more research on humans to confirm their efficacy in treating specific conditions.

Can boiling paan leaves with other ingredients cure respiratory illnesses? No, boiling paan leaves with ajwain, ginger, cloves, and honey cannot cure respiratory illnesses like bronchitis or instantly clear a blocked nose. While some of these ingredients have shown potential benefits, they do not constitute a cure. For instance, ginger and honey may soothe a sore throat, and ajwain contains thymol, which has some antiseptic properties. However, these are supportive measures, not cures. Bronchitis, especially if chronic, often requires medical intervention, including antibiotics or inhalers in some cases. Relying solely on these remedies can delay appropriate treatment and potentially worsen the condition.

Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, and General Physician from Navi Mumbai, says, "While paan leaves and some of the ingredients in this remedy have mild soothing or antimicrobial properties, there is no evidence to suggest they can cure respiratory illnesses like bronchitis. These conditions often require proper medical treatment, such as antibiotics or inhalers, depending on the cause."

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, states, "Home remedies like boiling paan leaves with ginger and cloves may provide temporary relief for symptoms like a sore throat or congestion, but they are not a cure for respiratory illnesses. It's important to consult a doctor for persistent or severe symptoms."

Moreover, cloves, even in concoctions, can pose risks. They contain compounds like eugenol, which may cause skin, eye, or respiratory irritation, or allergic reactions. Cloves are also known to increase bleeding risks, particularly when taken with certain medications like warfarin. Always consult a healthcare professional before using herbal remedies to ensure they are safe for you.

Is applying paan leaf paste in mustard oil an effective treatment for breathing difficulties? No, applying a paan leaf paste soaked in mustard oil to the chest is not a proven treatment for breathing difficulties. While the warmth from the oil might provide temporary soothing relief, it does not address the underlying cause of respiratory distress. Breathing difficulties can be due to various conditions, including asthma, infections, or heart problems, each requiring specific medical management. Applying a paste to the chest is unlikely to have any significant impact on these conditions. In fact, it could potentially irritate the skin.

Similarly, people have suggested that betel leaf with mustard oil can extract worms through the navel. However, there is no scientific evidence to support this claim.

Can these remedies replace conventional medical treatment? Absolutely not. These home remedies should not replace conventional medical treatment for respiratory conditions. While they might provide some symptomatic relief for mild colds or coughs, they are not effective against more severe illnesses like bronchitis, pneumonia, or asthma exacerbations. No credible health organisation recognises these remedies as a valid treatment for such conditions, as claimed in the post. Seeking quick medical attention is essential for proper diagnosis and treatment of such conditions. Delaying or avoiding medical care in favour of unproven remedies can lead to serious health consequences.

Are there any potential risks associated with these remedies? Yes, there are potential risks. While generally considered safe in moderation, excessive consumption of paan may have adverse effects. Also, applying oil to the chest may cause skin irritation in some individuals. Furthermore, relying on these remedies instead of seeking medical advice for serious conditions can be dangerous.

THIP Media Take: The claim that a paan leaf remedy can cure colds, coughs and breathlessness is mostly false. While some ingredients in the remedy have mild symptomatic benefits, there is no scientific evidence that the described paan leaf remedies cure colds, coughs, or bronchitis. Such conditions require appropriate medical attention and cannot be effectively treated with home remedies alone.

title: Can papaya prevent baldness and keep your hair black?

quick_take: A social media post claims that papaya can prevent baldness and keep your hair black. Our fact check reveals this is false.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific evidence to suggest that papaya can prevent baldness. Baldness is often caused by genetic factors, hormonal imbalances, or health conditions. While papaya is nutritious and can contribute to overall health, there's no data supporting the claim that it specifically prevents hair loss or stops balding. Papaya does contain several vitamins and antioxidants, such as Vitamin C and Vitamin A, which support general skin and hair health. For baldness prevention, treatments like minoxidil or prescription medications are often more effective. Dr Sachin Gupta, Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad shares, 'While treatments like minoxidil and finasteride are commonly used for hair regrowth, it's important to recognise that results can vary from person to person. The effectiveness of these treatments depends on factors such as the cause of hair loss, age, and overall health. Consulting a dermatologist is essential to pinpoint the underlying cause and design a personalised treatment plan to support healthy hair growth.' Regarding hair color: While papaya is rich in antioxidants and vitamins, it doesn't directly alter hair colour or prevent greying. The natural pigmentation of your hair largely depends on genetics and the production of melanin. As you age, melanin production decreases, leading to grey or white hair. There are no studies that link papaya to stopping hair from turning grey. While papaya can help maintain overall scalp and hair health, it doesn't have the magical ability to stop the greying process. A balanced diet with adequate vitamins and minerals can slow the process, but it can't reverse or prevent it. Regarding hair roots: Papaya is a good source of nutrients like Vitamin A and C, which support the health of your hair follicles and scalp. Healthy hair roots need a good supply of nutrients, and while papaya can help in this regard, there's no strong evidence suggesting that it directly strengthens the roots or prevents hair loss. Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai explains, 'Hair growth is influenced by multiple factors, including genetics, hormonal balance, and overall health. Healthy hair doesn't occur by chance; it needs consistent care and attention to thrive.' Regarding keratin and copper: Papaya does not contain keratin, and although it contains copper, the copper content in papaya is insufficient to significantly impact hair growth. Keratin is a protein found in hair, skin, and nails, but it is not found in papaya. The claim that papaya contains keratin is misleading. Copper is essential for overall health and does play a role in melanin production, which affects hair colour. However, the amount of copper in papaya is relatively small, and consuming papaya alone is unlikely to have a significant effect on hair colour or strength. A diet rich in a variety of copper-containing foods, such as nuts, seeds, and shellfish, would be a more effective way to ensure you're getting enough of this important mineral.

title: Can Perfora teeth whitening serum effectively whiten your teeth?

doctor_explanation: Teeth whitening products are booming in the market, with numerous brands promising to deliver brighter, whiter smiles. One such product is the Perfora Teeth Whitening Serum, which claims to effectively whiten yellow teeth using innovative ingredients and theories. Let's break down the ingredients to understand better. Perfora Teeth Whitening Serum contains synthetic dyes CI 17200:1 (Red 33) and CI 42090 (Blue 1) to enhance its appearance. Both dyes are approved for use in cosmetics by regulatory bodies like the FDA and the European Commission, with concentration limits of up to 0.1% in oral care products. While generally safe, they can cause allergic reactions in some individuals. Perfora claims to utilise the colour correction theory, which involves using purple pigments to neutralise yellow tones on the teeth. According to this theory, since purple is the complementary colour to yellow on the colour wheel, applying a purple tint can temporarily mask yellow discoloration. While this can provide an immediate visual improvement, it does not remove stains or whiten teeth permanently. The effect is superficial and fades as the purple tint wears off. PAP (Phthalimidoperoxycaproic Acid) is mentioned in the brand's product page as a primary whitening agent but is not explicitly listed in the ingredients. PAP is a relatively new compound that whitens teeth by releasing oxygen radicals, similar to how hydrogen peroxide works but with a lower risk of sensitivity and enamel damage. PubChem classifies PAP as belonging to the peroxide family. PAP is a synthetic organic peroxy acid that derives from caprolactam and phthalic anhydride. Although PAP is not hydrogen peroxide, it functions similarly by releasing oxygen radicals. Claiming 100% effectiveness is unrealistic. No teeth whitening product can guarantee complete whitening for all types of teeth and stains. The effectiveness varies based on the cause of discoloration, individual dental health, and adherence to usage instructions. Here, by using colour correction theory, the product can conceal stains and neutralise yellow. It does not effectively remove stains. Moreover, concealed stains can lead to not seeking dental care even in cases where it's needed. This may give rise to delayed treatments and undesirable outcomes. The presence of hydrated silica, an abrasive, can cause surface roughness, if overused. This can possibly lead to enamel erosion over time. While nano-hydroxyapatite can help remineralize enamel, balancing the abrasive effects, careful use is essential. The Perfora Teeth Whitening Serum can provide temporary improvements in the appearance of yellow teeth due to the colour correction theory and the mild abrasive action of hydrated silica. Enzymes like papain and bromelain can help break down stains, and nano-hydroxyapatite supports enamel health. However, the absence of PAP on the ingredient list, despite its mentioned use, raises transparency concerns. Additionally, the colour correction theory conceals and neutralises yellow instead of actually removing the stains. Dr. Snigdha (BDS, MDS Oral Medicine & Diagnostic Radiology) from Vananchal Dental College and Hospital says, "It's important for patients to be careful when considering over-the-counter teeth whitening products. I advise consulting a dentist before starting any whitening treatment. Tooth discolouration can be due to various factors, including diet, smoking, medications, and underlying conditions. While OTC products may offer cosmetic improvements, they may not effectively address the main problem. These products can possibly harm oral tissues and worsen existing dental issues, especially with frequent and high-concentration use. Without proper diagnosis and guidance, patients may damage their gums or enamel. It's essential to recognise that natural tooth colour variations are normal. And, extra white teeth may not always be achievable or desirable." Dr. Pooja Sharma (BDS, MDS Orthodontics) from NIMS, Jaipur says, "I strongly advise consulting a dentist before use. While promising quick results, their safety varies, and not all discolourations can be treated by them alone. Applying without diagnosis can worsen conditions. Teeth naturally have a shade of yellow, excessive whitening leads to unrealistic expectations. For cosmetic enhancement, options like veneers or crowns may be better under the expertise of a dentist. Overuse of such teeth whitening products can harm oral tissues, causing gum inflammation or enamel damage. Even if you are using such products, limit their use to four weeks and seek professional advice if problems continue." The effectiveness of PAP teeth whitening varies because some studies found it less effective than hydrogen peroxide. One study discovered that while PAP effectively removes coffee stains from teeth, its performance was lacking when it came to removing tea and red wine stains. Interestingly, the use of PAP actually made the appearance of teeth worse when they had tea and red wine stains. In contrast, another study determined that hydrogen peroxide produced the most significant change in tooth colour compared to PAP and bromelain. Most PAP whitening products, including this one, now include hydroxyapatite, denoted by a plus symbol as a suffix (PAP+). This addition enhances safety by not only whitening teeth but also aiding in enamel remineralization. Still, since this is a new chemical compound, there's less research about its effectiveness and potential risks. To conclude, the Perfora Teeth Whitening Serum offers some potential benefits for teeth whitening, including short-term visual improvements and enamel support. However, its claims of being 100% effective and entirely natural are overstated. The product can help mask yellow tones and improve the appearance of teeth, but it is not a permanent solution. Consumers should use it with caution and seek professional dental advice for sustained whitening results.

Even traditional practices, such as those inspired by Amish or Ayurvedic approaches, require scientific evidence to confirm their effectiveness—evidence that is entirely lacking in this case. Dr Kashyap Dakshini, General Physician from Mumbai, explains, "There is no scientific evidence to support the belief that placing sliced vegetables like onions or potatoes on the body can cure respiratory conditions. While these vegetables have health benefits when consumed, there's no proof that applying them externally has any impact on illnesses like coughs or bronchitis." Dietician Voomika Mukherjee adds further clarity, "Bronchitis and persistent coughs can result from infections or environmental irritants. Onions are rich in medicinal compounds like sulfur, which have antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties. However, these benefits work when one consumes onions, as part of a balanced diet. Unverified remedies like onion application may delay appropriate care and worsen symptoms. Unlikely. title: Can pomegranate juice improve fertility and hormonal balance?
claim_text: An Instagram post suggests that drinking a glass of cold-pressed pomegranate juice every morning is essential for those trying to conceive. It states that the juice protects sperm from oxidative damage, strengthens the uterine lining, balances progesterone and oestrogen levels, and improves libido. It also highlights pomegranate as a timeless symbol of fertility.
quick_take: A social media post claims that pomegranate juice can improve fertility and hormonal balance. We did a thorough fact check and found that this is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
The fact check examined multiple claims about pomegranate juice and fertility. Regarding sperm protection: Pomegranates are rich in antioxidants like polyphenols, which may help reduce oxidative stress that can affect sperm and male fertility. However, research linking pomegranate juice directly to sperm protection in humans is limited. A 2014 study showed that pomegranate extract and galangal powder improved sperm motility in men with low semen quality, but this involved specific doses of pomegranate extract, not regular juice. Another study in 2014 showed that pomegranate juice improved sperm concentration and motility in animals, but human research is needed.

Regarding uterine lining: Pomegranate juice contains nutrients like vitamin C, folate, and potassium, which contribute to general health, but there is no strong evidence suggesting it can specifically strengthen the uterine lining. Some animal studies suggest that pomegranate seed extract (contains beta-sitosterol) may stimulate uterine activity and reduce contractions, but no clinical trials on humans have proven that pomegranate juice directly affects the uterine lining. The uterine lining's health depends on hormones, particularly oestrogen and progesterone. A 2024 study found that pomegranate juice can relax the muscles of the uterus in rats, helping to reduce contractions. This could potentially help with conditions like preterm birth and painful periods. Another study from 2022 found that pomegranate juice extract can help improve uterine damage in rats with PCOS. No clinical trials on humans have conclusively proven that pomegranate juice can have a direct impact on the uterine lining.

Regarding hormone balance: Pomegranates don't directly regulate hormones. Hormonal balance is a complex process and the endocrine system controls it. While pomegranates contain phytoestrogens—plant compounds that mimic oestrogen—their effect on human hormone levels is minimal. Consuming pomegranate juice is unlikely to significantly impact progesterone or oestrogen levels. A 2022 study did suggest that pomegranate helped improve menopausal symptoms in 78 women, but more research is needed to confirm these results. Most results are inconclusive. While pomegranates are healthy, they shouldn't replace medical treatments for hormonal imbalances.

Dr Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, explains: "Pomegranates are a great addition to your diet, packed with antioxidants and phytochemicals. While they don't directly balance hormones, their nutrient-rich profile can support overall hormonal health. By reducing inflammation and oxidative stress, pomegranates may help maintain a more balanced hormonal system over time. Enjoying this fruit regularly as part of a balanced diet can offer several health benefits."

Regarding libido: There is no conclusive evidence linking pomegranate juice to improved libido. Pomegranates have long been associated with fertility and vitality in various cultures, and some studies suggest that pomegranate juice may improve blood flow, which could support sexual health. A 2012 study found that drinking pomegranate juice for two weeks increased testosterone levels by about 24% in both males and females, along with improvements in blood pressure and mood. However, this study was small, with only 60 participants, and lasted just two weeks, so more research is needed to confirm these findings. Libido depends on many factors, and pomegranate juice alone is unlikely to have a significant impact.

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, shares: "Pomegranate juice can be a healthy addition to your diet, as it's packed with antioxidants that support overall health. There's no direct evidence linking pomegranate juice to a boost in libido. But its ability to improve blood flow and reduce oxidative stress may contribute to better overall vitality. Remember, a balanced diet, regular exercise, and managing stress are key factors for a healthy libido."

The pomegranate's association with fertility originates from ancient symbolism rather than scientific evidence. Its many seeds were seen as a representation of abundance and fertility in cultures like ancient Greece and Persia. It is a nutrient-dense fruit, but its reputation as a fertility booster is more rooted in tradition than in proven medical benefits.

title: Can potato juice and aloe vera gel reduce eye puffiness?

doctor_explanation:

Regarding potato juice: There is insufficient direct scientific evidence on the effectiveness of potato juice for reducing eye puffiness. Cold compression and cucumber slices are commonly used home remedies for reducing eye puffiness. Hypothetically, the cold application of potatoes could provide similar benefits due to their cooling and anti-inflammatory properties. However, more research is needed to substantiate its effectiveness.

Regarding aloe vera: Aloe vera is popular for its skin-healing and moisturising properties, containing vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants that benefit the skin. It is often used to soothe irritated skin, reduce inflammation, and provide hydration. While some studies suggest aloe vera may improve skin elasticity and reduce swelling, its efficacy in specifically targeting puffiness is not well-documented and mostly anecdotal. Aloe vera contains polysaccharides and glycoproteins that promote wound healing, reduce inflammation, and enhance skin permeation. A 2008 review showed its potential in reducing skin inflammation, such as significantly decreasing UV-induced erythema. However, there are no direct studies specifically addressing aloe vera gel for under-eye puffiness.

Combining potato juice and aloe vera gel: There is limited scientific evidence to support the claim that these ingredients effectively reduce puffiness around the eyes. Potatoes contain vitamin C, antioxidants, and enzymes with anti-inflammatory effects, but their efficacy for puffiness is unproven. While aloe vera is known for its skin-healing and moisturising properties, its effectiveness for puffiness is mostly anecdotal. Combining these may offer temporary soothing and hydrating effects, but these are likely short-term and not a guaranteed solution.

Dr Jyothy Kannangath, Consultant Dermatologist at Dr Thaj Laser Skin & Hair Clinic, Coimbatore, shares her expert opinion: "The internet is full of videos and blogs claiming the effectiveness of potato juice in treating puffiness, acne, pigmentation, and scars. Potatoes are often used alone or combined with ingredients like lemon juice, yoghurt, milk, or oatmeal. Although the enzyme catecholase in potatoes is believed to offer skin-healing benefits, there is no scientific evidence supporting this claim. While animal studies have shown anti-inflammatory effects of potato skin extracts, we need more research to confirm these effects in humans."

Dr Kannangath further explains: "Aloesin, a compound from aloe vera, can inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme responsible for skin pigmentation. However, there are case reports of hypersensitivity reactions and contact dermatitis from aloe vera preparations." She advises: "Before starting aloe vera-based home remedies, always conduct a skin sensitivity test."

Better treatments: For persistent puffiness, consulting a dermatologist is advisable. Medical treatments such as topical creams containing retinol, caffeine, and hyaluronic acid can be more effective. Procedures like chemical peels, laser therapy, and fillers may offer long-lasting results. Lifestyle changes including adequate sleep, hydration, balanced diet, limiting screen exposure, and wearing sunscreen can help prevent and reduce puffiness.

Safety: Generally safe with caution. Individuals with sensitive skin or allergies may experience irritation. There have been case studies of severe allergies due to potatoes or its juice. It's important to conduct a patch test before trying any new remedy. Even aloe vera gel can cause allergic reactions in some people. If irritation occurs, discontinue use immediately and consult a healthcare professional.

Conclusion: The claim that potato juice and aloe vera gel is effective for reducing dark circles and puffiness around the eyes is mostly false. These ingredients may offer temporary soothing and hydrating effects, but there is no direct scientific evidence to support their long-term efficacy for this purpose.
