quick_take: A social media post states that a person can lose belly fat and get abs without belly workouts or exercises. The narrator in the video further states that a person can get abs only with a calorie-deficit diet. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Half-true.
doctor_explanation: What are abs? 'Abs' is a term that refers to the abdominal muscles, which are located in the front of your body, between your ribs and your pelvis. These muscles are responsible for various functions, including supporting the spine and core, assisting with breathing, and aiding in the movement of the upper body. Five main muscles make up the abs, namely, Rectus abdominis, Transversus abdominis, Internal obliques, External obliques, and Pyramidalis. Rectus abdominis is the most well-known abdominal muscle and is responsible for the 'six-pack' appearance that many people strive for. Can a person get abs without exercise? Not exactly. Abs are the muscles that need to be worked and toned to be visible. A calorie-deficit diet would indeed help lose belly fat, but that can't be the sole factor in getting visible abs. A multidisciplinary approach is needed for this. Nabaruna Ganguly, Clinical dietician at D.S Research Centre for Cancer, elaborates this by stating, "Fat burning is not the matter of calories only. It depends on many other factors too. When we focus on just a calorie deficit diet, we cut down many healthy nutrients from diet to manage the calorie intake. After a certain time, a calorie deficit diet doesn't help to loose much weight as body adjusts to that system. Some hormones like insulin, thyroid etc., regulate your metabolism from inside. When metabolism lowers down then low calorie diet doesn't help much. Then you need to get the results but at this stage you lose weight by not only losing fat but muscle mass too by cannibalizing muscles by your body. So to maintain metabolism & muscle mass in a healthier level, you need to focus on exercise to work both ways, i.e., maintaining metabolism & tone your muscles which gives you the result you desire. If someone is having supplement to maintain the metabolism, proper protein (for maintaining muscle mass & strength) & maintain a proper calorie deficit diet to lower the fat percentage below normal level, with normal moderate activity, he/she can get visible abs." This fat can be subcutaneous, lying close to the skin's surface, or visceral, located deep within the abdominal cavity. The visibility of abdominal muscles decreases as the amount of fat in the body increases. Other than dietary regulations, you need to engage in regular exercise to build and tone your abdominal muscles. Incorporate strength training exercises that target your abs, such as crunches, planks, and leg raises, into your routine. Cardiovascular exercises such as running, cycling, or swimming can help burn fat and reveal your abs. Additionally, your genetics also play a major role in where you store body fat, which eventually influences the specific body fat percentage at which your abs will be visible. Nutritionist Umesh Wadhavani also clarifies this by stating, "No diet in isolation can help you reduce your belly fat in a short span that has developed because of months and months of lifestyle habits, and it can only go with the help of consistent lifestyle changes such as eating a balanced diet, proper intake of water, taking good sleep, doing regular exercise and living a stress-free life." The duration required to achieve abs is determined by factors such as an individual's body fat percentage, diet, and exercise routine.

title: Fact Check: Can a potato face pack really make you 'super white'?
claim_text: An Instagram video claims that mixing potato juice with lemon juice, curd, coffee powder, coconut oil, and besan (gram flour) makes a very powerful face pack. It says this pack can make your skin 'super white,' remove all dark spots and pigmentation from your body, work better than any cosmetic product, and be so effective that people won't need to buy skincare products anymore.
quick_take: A viral social media post suggests that a potato face pack can make you 'super white'. However, our fact check shows this claim is false.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, explains, 'Potato juice and lemon may have some mild exfoliating properties, but they won't make your skin visibly whiter. Skin tone is determined by genetics, and while certain ingredients can brighten or even out your complexion temporarily, they won't change your natural skin colour. Proper skincare, sun protection, and a healthy lifestyle are key to maintaining healthy, glowing skin.' Potato juice has antioxidant properties and can give a short-term brightening effect by hydrating and soothing the skin. Lemon juice contains vitamin C, which is known for its role in reducing oxidative stress and supporting collagen production. However, these do not have the power to drastically change your natural skin colour. Also, lemon can irritate or burn sensitive skin, especially when exposed to sunlight. Using lemon juice directly on skin without dilution or proper care may cause more harm than good.

Dr Rashi Soni, Dermatologist and Co-founder of Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, clarifies, 'While curd, coffee, coconut oil, and besan each have properties that can benefit the skin, such as moisturising, exfoliating, and improving circulation, they won't erase pigmentation. Pigmentation is often caused by deeper skin factors like sun exposure or hormonal changes, which require targeted treatments. A consistent skincare routine, along with professional advice, is the best way to address pigmentation concerns.' Curd contains lactic acid, which can gently exfoliate the skin. However, a 2015 review found limited evidence supporting its benefits and suggested more research is needed. Coffee may boost blood flow temporarily. A 2023 review found that caffeine in skincare might protect against sun damage, reduce wrinkles, improve skin tone, and reduce puffiness. Yet, most studies are small or animal-based, so more research is still needed. Besan is commonly used in home remedies to cleanse the skin, while coconut oil can help moisturise dry skin. Together, they may make your skin feel smoother or look fresher for a short while. But pigmentation, especially deeper types like melasma or sunspots, needs consistent care and sometimes medical treatment. These kitchen ingredients do not have the strength or stability to act on deep skin layers.

The face pack cannot replace clinically tested products or dermatologist-approved treatments. Cosmetic and skincare products undergo rigorous testing for safety and effectiveness. They are formulated with stabilised active ingredients in proper concentrations. The home mix mentioned in the video does not meet such standards. Even if some ingredients seem natural or beneficial, they are not suitable for all skin types. For instance, coconut oil can clog pores for those with acne-prone skin, and raw lemon juice may cause inflammation. Mixing ingredients without understanding your skin's needs can make problems worse instead of improving them.

The mention of Koreans is used to sensationalise the idea. Skincare routines in South Korea are based on years of dermatological research, and the products used are scientifically formulated. Comparing a homemade face pack to such advanced skincare, let alone claiming it is superior, is baseless. Additionally, Korean skin, climate, genetics, and diet differ significantly from those of Indians, making such comparisons irrelevant.

title: Can a powder of seeds and nuts drastically increase a child's height in 15 days?
claim_text: Take 50g of til (sesame seeds), 50g of almonds, 50g of makhana (foxnuts), and 50g of saunf. Mix all these together, roast them, and make a powder. Then, put one spoonful every day in the child's milk in the morning. In just 15 days, the height of your child will increase so much that you will have to cut their legs to make them stop growing.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a powder of seeds and nuts can drastically increase a child's height in 15 days. We fact checked it, and it turned out to be false.
doctor_explanation: Height growth in children is a complex biological process which depends on genetics, nutrition over the long term, and hormonal factors. So, adequate nutrition is crucial for healthy growth. But no single food or mixture can cause such a drastic and rapid increase in height within 15 days. The claim of needing to "cut the legs" to stop growth is an exaggeration and not based on any scientific understanding of human biology. Dr Almas Fatma, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, addresses the implausibility of such claims. She says, "It is biologically impossible for any specific food mixture, such as one made from sesame seeds, almonds, foxnuts, and fennel seeds, to cause a rapid and extreme increase in a child's height within a short period like 15 days. Human growth is a complex process governed by genetics, hormones, and consistent long-term nutrition. No single food can override these fundamental biological mechanisms to induce such a dramatic change. Claims suggesting otherwise are not based on scientific understanding." These ingredients are indeed nutritious and can contribute to a healthy diet for children. Sesame seeds offer calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, vital for bone health. Almonds provide vitamin E, magnesium, and protein, while foxnuts are a source of calcium and fibre. Makhana or foxnuts are a low glycemic index option which can be really beneficial for diabetics too. However, these seeds and nuts also contain phytates, compounds that can actually hinder the absorption of certain nutrients. Fennel seeds are popular for their digestive benefits. Although these nutrients support overall well-being and healthy development, they lack the specific compounds required to induce the rapid and extreme height increase described in the claim. Height growth in children occurs gradually, mainly during periods of growth spurts like during puberty. The bones lengthen through a process controlled by growth hormones. So, even though good nutrition can support healthy growth, there is no evidence that consuming a specific food combination can cause abnormal or accelerated growth in just two weeks. Dt. Harita Adhvaryu, Senior Clinical Dietitian at EzcureDiabetesCare in Ahmedabad, clarifies, "Height largely depends on genetics. During childhood and adolescence, our body goes through growth spurts, and proper nutrition plays a crucial role in supporting this natural process. Nutrients like calcium, vitamin D, and protein are essential for bone health and growth. However, once we reach the end of puberty, the growth plates in our bones close, which signals the end of vertical growth. After this point, no diet, supplement, or treatment can increase your height, as the bones can no longer lengthen. While some practices may improve posture or spinal alignment, they cannot add to your height once your skeleton has fully developed." Growth involves a complex interaction of genetics, physical activity, sleep, and overall nutrition. Although a balanced diet can help children grow to their maximum potential, expecting a dramatic change in height in 15 days is unrealistic. The body requires sustained nutrient intake, proper exercise, and adequate rest over a long time to grow healthily.

title: Fact Check: Can a quick home remedy restore periods?
claim_text: Drinking a combination of jaggery, ajwain, turmeric and ghee can bring back a year-old absent period/menstrual cycle within five minutes.
quick_take: An Instagram video asserts that a home remedy can restore a one-year absence of periods/menstrual cycle within five minutes. Upon fact-checking, we found this claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
The menstrual cycle is a monthly process preparing the female body for possible pregnancy, lasting 21 to 35 days. It begins with the menses phase, shedding the uterine lining if no pregnancy occurs. A typical period lasts two to seven days. The follicular phase follows, increasing oestrogen to grow the uterine lining. Ovulation then releases an egg, marking the luteal phase with elevated progesterone, preparing the uterus for pregnancy. If no fertilisation occurs, hormone levels drop, triggering the menses phase anew.

Menstrual cycles typically span four to seven days, occurring every 28 to 30 days, with variations considered normal. Factors affecting cycle length include hormonal changes, age, overall health, and medical conditions. Irregular periods involve intervals shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days, three or more consecutive missed periods, and abnormal flow. Common causes include stress, weight fluctuations, intense exercise, birth control, blood thinners, reproductive organ surgeries, and blockages. Conditions like cancer, polycystic ovarian syndrome, hormonal issues, and pelvic inflammatory disease can also contribute to irregular menstruation.

Relying solely on natural remedies carries risks. While these remedies can alleviate symptoms, they do not address the root cause. Managing menstrual irregularities and pain may involve practices like exercise, yoga, stress reduction, and dietary changes such as consuming cinnamon and ginger, while cutting back on alcohol and smoking. However, for effective relief, menstrual pain may necessitate medical pain management and adequate rest, while irregularities often require a combination of medical and surgical interventions based on the underlying cause.

This mixture may aid immunity but there is no visible evidence supporting the claim that a combination of ghee, turmeric, ajwain, and jaggery can restore a menstrual period that has been absent for a year. Turmeric is known for its anti-inflammatory properties and may have some effect on hormonal balance, but its direct impact on menstrual irregularities is not well-established. Ajwain is often used in traditional medicine for digestive issues and may have some secondary effects, but there is no scientific evidence supporting its role in regulating periods. Jaggery is a natural sweetener but has no direct connection to menstrual regularity.

If menstruation has stopped for a year, it is crucial to consult a healthcare professional promptly. This condition, known as amenorrhea, can be caused by various factors such as hormonal imbalances, stress, or underlying health issues. A thorough medical evaluation is necessary to identify the cause and determine appropriate treatment, which may involve hormonal therapy, lifestyle adjustments, or addressing any underlying medical conditions. Early intervention ensures proper management and promotes overall reproductive health.

Gynecologist Dr. Anita Gupta, Associate Director at Fortis La Femme, New Delhi, advises addressing irregular menstrual cycles by identifying and treating underlying medical or gynaecological causes. She emphasises that, in many instances, hormonal tablets prescribed by a gynecologist have proven effective in regulating menstrual cycles.

Nutritionist Anurupa Bose highlights concerns about irregular menstrual cycles, attributing them to factors like age, hormonal imbalances (such as PCOD and thyroid dysfunction), lack of exercise, irregular sleep, and high stress levels. She suggests lifestyle changes, including a balanced diet, avoidance of sugary and processed foods, and regular exercise, to manage hormonal balance, regulate menstrual cycles, and address issues like delayed menopause, ultimately impacting future fertility.

title: Can a rice-based shampoo ensure long hair in 7 days?
claim_text: चावल-शैंपू हैक: 7 दिन में बालों में आएगा असली तूफान! - A viral Instagram post claims that washing hair with a combination of rice, curry leaves, fenugreek seeds, and shampoo has the potential to accelerate hair growth in just 7 days.
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, a rice-based shampoo helps get long hair in 7 days. By fact-checking, we found that the claim is false.
doctor_explanation:
Long hair has always had significant cultural, social, and psychological implications. However, hair length alone is not an indicator of satisfactory hair health; rather, it depends on genetic factors which play a central role in determining hair growth rate, density, and maximum achievable length. In addition, nutritional deficits, hormonal disruptions, excessive heat, harsh chemicals, and mechanical damage can compromise hair integrity and lead to breakage, which eventually reduces the length that can be retained. Beyond its cosmetic significance, healthy hair growth protects the scalp from UV radiation, provides thermal insulation, and may even be an important indicator of hormonal swings and general well-being. As a result, anyone who is suffering significant hair thinning, patchy hair loss, or abrupt changes in the density and texture of their hair should get medical care right away.

Rice, curry leaves, and fenugreek seeds are being promoted because of their traditional role in hair care and scalp nourishment; nonetheless, the three nutrients' cumulative effect does not guarantee long hair. Despite the perceived benefits, the aforementioned components lack reliable clinical research establishing their ability to stimulate hair follicles or prolong the growth (anagen) phase.

Dr. Rashi Soni, Consultant Dermatologist from Rashi Hospital in Hingoli, Maharashtra, clarifies: 'Natural ingredients like fenugreek seeds, rice, and curry leaves have been used for generations to promote healthy hair, but their role in achieving significant hair growth or preventing hair loss is still uncertain.' Even though such therapies may have marginal benefits, particularly in terms of enhancing hair structure and reducing moderate hair loss, it is advised to seek professional counsel and pursue medical therapy for major concerns.

Dr. Sachin Gupta, a dermatologist from Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, adds: 'Fenugreek, rice, and curry leaves are frequently used in traditional hair care regimens; there is insufficient scientific data to support their effects on hair strength and growth.' Although they might provide the scalp and hair with some nourishment, they are unlikely to have a significant impact on their own. Dr. Gupta further emphasises that it's crucial for those who are worried about the health of their hair to consider general aspects such as nutrition, stress reduction, and using hair-type-appropriate products.

It is important to highlight that the primary determinants of hair length are heredity and variables affecting the duration of the growth phase of the hair cycle. Even though they may improve hair texture or perhaps lessen breakage, the topical administration of herbal compounds does not guarantee long hair. Reliance on such remedies overlooks the intricate elements that contribute to healthy hair development.

Regarding the 7-day claim: It is not biologically plausible to achieve long hair in just seven days. Human scalp hair grows at an average pace of 0.3–0.4 mm per day, or around 1–1.5 cm per month. The hair follicle cycle controls this growth rate and cannot be significantly accelerated in a short period of time. Therefore, no nutritional miracle, hair spray, shampoo, or topical quick fix can prolong the anagen phase or cause rapid follicular growth in a few days. Hair typically grows half an inch every month. It doesn't seem plausible that a homemade preparation could greatly expedite the process. Additionally, the available clinical evidence does not adequately support the recipe's dramatic impact. Therefore, the claim is undoubtedly exaggerated.

High-risk individuals are more likely to fall for unregulated web-based promises that ensure quick outcomes, such as those with hair loss, dietary deficiencies, hormone imbalances, and psychological distress. Hair issues should be handled by evidence-based medical advice, and such internet cures should be used cautiously because they lack sufficient scientific support.

To achieve healthy hair: Having healthy hair is preferable to having long hair since hair length does not truly reflect the condition of the hair shaft or the health of the scalp. Long-looking hair that sheds a lot, breaks easily, or is brittle is an obvious sign of an underlying issue. Hair health is determined not just by length but also by follicular integrity, proper hair cycling, and scalp physiology, necessitating an exhaustive approach. Based on the clinical assessment, doctors may suggest dietary choices that promote keratin production and help with anagen phase maintenance. Optimal scalp care is also crucial for medical management, including the management of dandruff, irritation, and infections. Pharmacological therapy can be facilitated by avoiding harsh cosmetic interventions, regulating stress, and obtaining enough sleep. Relying on viral miracle cures for hair growth may worsen pre-existing conditions and delay necessary therapy. Doctors usually recommend a personalised approach for maintaining healthy hair.

title: Can a rice remedy for high blood pressure normalise it in 24 hours?
claim_text: A Facebook video claims that a rice remedy for high blood pressure, developed by AIIMS researchers, instantly normalises blood pressure to 120/80 within 24 hours, cures related issues like cholesterol and obesity, and prevents heart attacks and strokes. It features Rajdeep Sardesai and Dr Suleman Khan, described as a famous cardiologist.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a simple rice remedy for high blood pressure, developed by AIIMS doctors, can normalise blood pressure to 120/80 within 24 hours. After fact-checking, we rated this claim as false.
doctor_explanation:
## Is Dr Suleman Khan a cardiologist?
No. Dr Suleman Khan is not a cardiologist. A reverse image search using Yandex revealed that the man shown in the video is not a cardiologist, but Hakim Suleman Khan, a practitioner of naturopathy and Unani medicine. His official website does not mention any formal medical degree in cardiology, so we could not verify any such qualification. To trace the original source of the video, we searched both Google and Yandex. While we found several YouTube videos featuring Hakim Suleman Khan in the same background and similar clothing, we could not confirm the exact origin of the footage used in the claim. Hakim Suleman Khan is a licensed herbalist and naturopath, and the founder of Atiya Herbs, a company that promotes Unani and Ayurvedic remedies. His work centres around herbal treatments, not cardiology. Promoting Dr Suleman Khan for high blood pressure and claiming he is a cardiologist is misleading. The claim misrepresents his credentials and lacks any credible medical evidence.

## Did AIIMS develop a rice remedy for high blood pressure?
No. There is no verifiable evidence from AIIMS (All India Institute of Medical Sciences) supporting a rice remedy for high blood pressure that normalises blood pressure in 24 hours. AIIMS is a reputable institution, and such a claim would require peer-reviewed studies or official statements, which are absent. The video provides no scientific backing or references to support this claim.

## Can a rice remedy work for high blood pressure in 24 hours?
No. Blood pressure management generally requires lifestyle changes, medication, or both, as advised by medical professionals. Rice, while a dietary staple, has no proven ability to instantly normalise blood pressure. Studies show that diet impacts blood pressure over time, but no single food like rice can achieve instant results. The claim of curing 377,000 people lacks credible data or documentation.

## Can a simple rice remedy prevent heart attacks and strokes?
No. Preventing heart attacks and strokes involves managing risk factors like blood pressure, cholesterol, and lifestyle through evidence-based methods. No rice remedy has been scientifically proven to clear blood vessels or prevent these conditions instantly. Such claims are misleading and lack medical evidence.

## Is the video genuine or manipulated?
Likely manipulated. The video shows signs of AI manipulation, including poor lip sync and unnatural gestures. A reverse image search suggests the footage of Hakim Suleman Khan matches other videos with different audio, indicating possible voice superimposition. The inclusion of Rajdeep Sardesai, a news anchor, in a health remedy video without any clear context further adds to the suspicion of fabrication. Additionally, the random appearance of a flashing calculator image throughout the Facebook video raises further doubts about its authenticity.

## Can rice cure cholesterol, obesity, and breathing issues?
No. Rice alone cannot cure cholesterol, obesity, or breathing difficulties. A balanced diet, exercise, and medical treatment are needed for these conditions. title: Fact Check: Can a saliva test at home detect health problems?
claim_text: A social media post claims you can detect serious health problems with a saliva test at home using a spoon. It suggests scraping morning saliva onto a spoon, sealing it in a plastic bag, and leaving it in the sun for a few hours. Different colour changes on the spoon supposedly point to specific health conditions including thyroid, kidney, blood pressure, or cholesterol issues.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a saliva test at home using a spoon can diagnose thyroid, kidney, blood pressure, or cholesterol issues. We fact checked this claim and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Saliva may dry up and leave marks or stains, but any colour change is more likely due to heat, oxidation (reaction with air), or even the material of the spoon or bag. Natural compounds in saliva can react in sunlight, but this doesn't reflect what's happening inside your body. It's similar to how tea stains or food residues change colour when exposed to sun or air, not a health test.

Thyroid and kidney problems are complex and need proper tests like blood work and hormone checks. Doctors look at things like TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), creatinine, or urea levels in the blood. Saliva alone, especially left on a spoon, cannot show these internal problems. In fact, thyroid issues do not cause any colour change in saliva. The same goes for kidney disease.

Dr Almas Fatma, General Physician, from Navi Mumbai, says, "I understand the appeal of home remedies and quick tests, but using your saliva on a spoon and checking it in the sun cannot tell you if you have thyroid or kidney problems. These are complex conditions that affect your body in ways we simply cannot see on the surface. To check your thyroid, we need to measure hormone levels through a proper blood test. For kidney function, we look at things like creatinine and urea in your blood, and sometimes test your urine too. Saliva doesn't carry the kind of information we need for these diagnoses. If you're worried about your health, it's always best to speak to a doctor and get tested properly."

High blood pressure is measured using a device called a sphygmomanometer, which checks your systolic and diastolic values. Cholesterol is checked through a blood lipid test. Neither of these conditions cause your saliva to turn purple or any other colour.

Dr Ubaid ur Rehman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, explains, "Conditions like high blood pressure and high cholesterol can be completely silent for years. You won't feel different, and there are no visible signs, certainly nothing you can see in your saliva or on a spoon. We diagnose high blood pressure using a blood pressure cuff, which gives us readings like 120 over 80. For cholesterol, we do a simple blood test that checks for different types of fats in your blood, like LDL (bad cholesterol) and HDL (good cholesterol). These are the only reliable ways to know what's really going on inside your body. Regular check-ups are key, especially if you have a family history or are over 40."

Regarding the University of Toronto claim: Claims about a saliva test at home diagnosing health conditions are among many morning saliva myths circulating online. Our thorough search of university websites and public statements found no evidence of an assistant professor or study from the University of Toronto linked to this method. Instead, an October 2023 news article from the University of Toronto's website highlights a collaboration with Alexander A. Green, a Boston University professor, who is developing a portable saliva test for health issues. This project, involving Toronto's Keith Pardee and GE HealthCare, focuses on measuring performance-related biomarkers in saliva, with results available in just 30 minutes. It's intended for potential use in homes and clinics but does not diagnose thyroid, kidney, or other conditions through color changes, debunking the saliva test myth.

Trying unverified tricks like this can give people a false sense of security, or panic. If the spoon stays white or turns orange, people may think they are healthy or sick without real reason. This can delay proper diagnosis and treatment. Many health conditions have no visible symptoms early on and need actual medical testing.

In summary, there is no scientific or medical basis for diagnosing thyroid, kidney, blood pressure, cholesterol, or infections using a saliva test at home. The colours seen on a spoon left in the sun are random and unrelated to any disease. The method is not backed by any credible institution or research.

title: Can a sea foam-based recipe effectively clear wrinkles?

Wrinkles are skin-related structural changes brought on by biological ageing, UV exposure, and collagen degradation. Our skin loses moisture, collagen, and elastin as we age, which makes it less elastic and more prone to creases, resulting in epidermal thinning, ultimately weakening the dermal support structure. Furthermore, a combination of elevated oxidative stress and reduced cellular renewal may result in the production of another cellular layer. All of this eventually causes the skin to sag, become fragile, and develop wrinkles and creases that last a lifetime. This ageing process is exacerbated by external environmental factors such as UV exposure.

Regarding the individual ingredients: Lemon juice is packed with vitamin C and polyphenols, protects skin cells from oxidative damage, and aids in collagen formation. However, these benefits depend on concentration, formulation stability, and epidermal penetration. Using concentrated lemon juice topically without a doctor's supervision is not recommended. Powdered sea foam: Processed sea foam-based skincare products may have potential to improve skin health as natural, mineral-rich detoxifiers using crystallised sea foam's high magnesium and silicon content to relax, exfoliate, and remineralise the skin. However, there isn't much scientific evidence supporting its wrinkle-reducing characteristics. Rock salt: When used as a scrub ingredient, it can be employed for mechanical exfoliation and mild skin smoothness, but there is not much evidence linking rock salt with substantial wrinkle reduction.

Even though the individual ingredients may have antioxidant properties, there is no scientific evidence that sea foam, lemon juice, and rock salt work together to minimise wrinkles. There is no online option that can make the skin absolutely wrinkle-free in a limited time frame such as one month because wrinkles are multifactorial in origin – an unavoidable outcome of ageing, hormonal changes, and inherited characteristics. It takes weeks or months for even clinically validated therapies such as topical retinoids, antioxidant-rich products, chemical peels, laser therapies, and botulinum toxin to result in noticeable and durable skin texture-related improvements.

After that, a doctor might recommend topical retinoids which encourage cell turnover and collagen synthesis. Skin-plumping moisturisers that protect the skin's barrier with ceramides or hyaluronic acid can also be used to fight off wrinkles. Individual choices are also quite significant; giving up smoking, eating nutritious foods, and getting sufficient rest can all have an important impact. In-clinic procedures like laser therapy or chemical peels may help with deeper wrinkles.

title: Can a single acupoint help recover from a cardiac arrest?
claim_text: By applying pressure to an acupoint positioned between the thumb and index finger, a person can entirely revive from cardiac arrest. (Original Hindi claim: "ये दबाने से मरते को भी जिंदा कर सकते है" - "By pressing this, you can even bring the dead back to life")
quick_take: A trending Instagram post asserts that by exerting pressure on an acupoint, an individual may fully recover from a cardiac arrest. We analysed the claim and found it to be completely false.
doctor_explanation: The fact check explains that acupoints are specific locations on the body along meridians linked to organs and physiological processes. The claim emphasizes the acupressure point in the webbing between the thumb and index finger, known as Hegu or LI4 (Large Intestine 4). LI4 is a traditional acupoint used as a neurological regulator, circulatory supporter, and pain reducer in clinical settings. It is primarily associated with reducing menstrual cramps and labour pain through local nerve stimulation that promotes microcirculation and triggers brain reactions. LI4 stimulation does not directly support medical management of heart conditions, though it may enhance cardiovascular function by promoting better blood circulation and autonomic balance. Cardiac arrest is an abrupt, unpredictable loss of heart function where the heart's electrical system malfunctions and the heart stops pumping blood efficiently. Dr. Pawan Poddar, Senior Consultant Interventional Cardiologist at Yashoda Hospitals in Hyderabad, clarifies that many confuse cardiac arrest with a heart attack, but they are not interchangeable. In contrast to a heart attack where blood supply is interrupted, cardiac arrest occurs when the heart's electrical system malfunctions. Without immediate action, death can occur within minutes. Acupressure stimulates sensory receptors in the skin and modulates autonomic nervous system activity, promoting parasympathetic tone, but no credible study suggests that Hegu or any acupressure location may restart a stopped heart or reliably influence fundamental events of cardiac arrest. This is supported by a clinical trial using LI4 with SJ6, ST25, and SP6 in patients with acute myocardial infarction, which showed it can prevent constipation without affecting heart rhythm, infarction size, or patient survival. Points like PC6 (Neiguan) have been associated with cardiovascular effects in animal studies but are not associated with resolving cardiac arrest. For cardiac arrest emergencies, evidence-based CPR and defibrillation are essential. Dr. Bushra Khan, BNYS, Naturopathy and Yoga Physician, advises that acupressure can be a useful symptom reliever but one acupoint alone is insufficient for all-encompassing treatment. It should be an adjunct to conventional allopathic medical treatment, not a substitute. Dr. Pradeep Rajanna, Head and Lead Consultant, Emergency Medicine at Vikash Hospitals, emphasizes that CPR is a simple yet powerful skill that every caregiver should learn. The article concludes that acupressure is not supported by research as a preventative strategy against acute cardiac emergencies, with no randomized controlled trials demonstrating that a single acupoint can prevent abrupt cardiac arrests or lower myocardial infarction risk.

title: Fact check: Can a single herbal powder resolve all dental concerns?
claim_text: According to an Instagram post, homemade powder is an effective remedy for over 20-30 dental concerns. doctor_explanation: Ayurveda does not offer a single, universal solution for all dental concerns. This is because oral illnesses such as caries, gingivitis, advanced gum disease, and mouth ulcers have diverse causes. These causes include bacterial biofilms, impaired immunological response, nutritional influence, and even systemic health. As a result, a single formulation may be insufficient to address all of them. While Ayurveda recommends specific herbal choices such as neem, clove, and triphala for bacterial plaque management and oral hygiene maintenance, traditional medicine tailors therapies to individual needs. Furthermore, it is critical to stress that Ayurvedic practitioners handle dental difficulties by addressing the specific condition. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, an Ayurvedic expert and MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, suggests that assumptions made in widely shared social media posts are often erroneous. Ayurveda offers significant postgraduate training in eye, ear, nose, throat, and dental procedures. These treatments, however, cannot be used in an uncertain or nonspecific fashion. Dr. Gohil maintains that "one herbal combination is insufficient to address all dental disorders, particularly severe ones such as pyorrhoea." If someone asserts that the remedy is found in Ayurvedic literature, they must offer an accurate citation. This allows skilled Ayurvedic doctors to properly examine it and guide treatment based on the particular patient's needs. While many herbal formulations may be helpful with overall oral health, they are not a cure-all. The most effective Ayurvedic therapeutic regimen involves adequate oral cleanliness, nutritious food options, healthy lifestyle choices, and professional expertise. An organic preparation composed of powders of neem, clove, turmeric, rock salt, and baking soda may carry several beneficial effects, but they are not a definitive cure for all dental conditions. Neem and clove extracts may inhibit Streptococcus mutans and Candida albicans, hence lowering plaque accumulation and fungal burden. Likewise, turmeric, which is known for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, may reduce gingival inflammation and support mild gingivitis. Finally, rock salt and baking soda may reduce microbial burden, alleviate mucosal irritation, and neutralise oral acids. However, no compelling scientific proof supports this blend as a therapeutic option for all dental concerns. It is crucial to establish the fact that dental tissues are irreparable; while herbal compositions may be used as an adjunct to the evidence-based professional intervention, preserving the viability of periodontal ligament cells or even reducing plaque and gingivitis, they cannot replace lost tooth structures. Dr. Snigdha, BDS, MDS, of Vananchal Dental College and Hospital in Jharkhand, emphasises that a homemade Ayurvedic tooth cure, such as the one suggested, won't cure serious dental issues, including cavities or gum infections. Cavities have the potential to cause permanent damage to teeth and necessitate professional treatment, such as dental fillings. Gingival pus usually indicates a serious infection, such as periodontal inflammation, which necessitates expert care. Herbal remedies may provide immediate relief but cannot address underlying issues or prevent further damage. When it comes to advanced dental caries, abscesses, extensive periodontal issues, or structural loss of the dental pulp, professional dental treatment, together with radiographic examinations and prescription medicines, is usually advised. Once lost, dental tissues are unable to repair themselves. While minor issues in their early stages can be reversed or controlled to a certain extent, moderate to severe periodontal problems or cavities cannot be addressed in 15 days without professional dental intervention. Complete management of structural damage takes much longer. While 15 days may be enough to provide evident symptomatic relief or early measurable improvements, it is rarely sufficient to completely heal or cure severe dental conditions such as caries and periodontitis. Dr. Ketan Rajput, Periodontist and Oral Implantologist, Advanced Dental Clinic and Implant Centre, Dhule, Maharashtra, suggests that minor dental issues such as mild gum inflammation, irritation, and oral malodour in otherwise healthy people can be addressed in a short period of time. However, severe dental issues, including abscesses and periodontitis, take time to heal. Dental patients should continue to brush their teeth; it is a crucial practice for preventing cavities, gum disease, and other dental illnesses. Avoiding toothbrushing permits harmful bacteria to flourish, resulting in plaque and acid that may erode tooth enamel and cause tooth decay. For optimal outcomes, dental patients should brush their teeth twice a day with toothpaste containing fluoride and a soft-bristled brush, replacing the brush every three to four months. Additionally, they should follow up with flossing and regular dental examinations. Self-medication is a prevalent practice for mild dental concerns. However, it is not recommended as an alternative to professional care. While these approaches may provide brief pain relief, they pose the risks of concealing symptoms, diagnostic delay, inappropriate medication or dosage, possible side effects and interference with current medication. Due to financial constraints or treatment-related anxiety, high-risk individuals frequently seek unsubstantiated therapies. While self-medication may provide temporary comfort, relying on it as the primary care strategy for dental issues remains risky and is not encouraged.

title: Can a single remedy effectively fix both wrinkles and age spots?
claim_text: A viral Facebook post captioned "Wrinkles & Jhayan Gone!" "Make this Magical Face Pack at home" suggests using curd and mulethi (licorice root) to effectively address age spots and wrinkles.
quick_take: A widely shared Facebook post suggests that a single at-home remedy can effectively address wrinkles and age spots. After fact-checking, we discovered that the assertion isfalse.
doctor_explanation: ## Why do age spots and wrinkles appear? Are the two conditions related? Wrinkles are folds or creases in the skin brought on by natural ageing, which results in thinning of the dermis and degradation of collagen and elastin. Likewise, age spots are aberrant pigmentation that can show up as areas of skin that are darker (hyperpigmentation) than the surrounding skin. Wrinkles and age-related hyperpigmentation are common signs of ageing skin, which originate via distinct cellular pathways. However, they share the following triggers: hereditary and metabolic processes, aggravated by external or environmental factors such as pollution, UV exposure, hormonal imbalances, and unhealthy lifestyle choices. Given that wrinkles and age spots cannot be completely prevented, they can be delayed with regular sun protection, consistent use of antioxidants, and retinoid therapy. ## Can a homemade mix of curd and mulethi help with both wrinkles and age spots? No, not really. Despite being used as skin-care remedies, the popularity of curd and mulethi is only relevant on social media. Because these ingredients are being considered for delicate issues related to ageing skin, they should be thoroughly assessed. We begin with curd. This is a traditional skin care ingredient because it contains lactic acid, a mild alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) – known to exfoliate dead skin cells. Applying it might improve hydration and collagen turnover. Regular usage of lactic acid may promote epidermal renewal by improving skin texture and minimising fine wrinkles. Next, we explore the potential of mulethi, or licorice root. This component contains a lot of glabridin, a flavonoid with known depigmenting and antioxidant qualities. Glabridin is considered to have the ability to suppress tyrosinase activity, which might reduce the synthesis of melanin in the hyperpigmented regions induced by inflammation or sun exposure. While the two ingredients have dermatologically beneficial properties, there is no scientific evidence to support their effectiveness in addressing wrinkles and age spots. Moreover, the DIY formulation lacks standardisation in terms of concentration, stability, and skin penetration. Above all, the remedy might be detrimental to those with sensitive, acne-prone skin. Dr. Gurman Singh Bhasin, Director & Chief Dermatologist, Skinclarity Clinic, Nagpur, clarifies this further by stating that while ingredients like curd and mulethi do provide some skin-soothing and moderate brightening advantages, a single home treatment cannot address ageing skin pigmentation and wrinkles simultaneously. Wrinkles involve collagen loss and deeper structural changes, whereas pigmentation requires targeted regulation of melanin production. Mulethi might help lighten slight discolouration because it has glabridin, and curd can moisturise the skin, but neither has been proven to effectively reduce signs of ageing or dark spots. For noticeable, long-term improvement, evidence-based treatments such as retinoids, peptides, sunscreen, and dermatologist-guided protocols are far more effective. ## Is it wise to depend on unverified remedies for wrinkles and age spots? No, absolutely not. As was stated previously, wrinkles and age spots are the outcome of complex biological processes. Skin ageing pigmentation is brought on by excessive or irregular melanin production, whereas wrinkles occur due to oxidative stress, UV damage, and collagen degradation. Since unverified home remedies lack standardised formulations supported by thorough clinical testing, they may not be able to deliver active ingredients in effective concentrations to the actual cause. Most significantly, frequent application of botanical or acidic extracts without pH control may damage the skin's protective layer, accelerating rather than delaying the ageing process. Dr. Sachin Gupta, a dermatologist at Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, offers his insightful perspective on the use of unsubstantiated natural wrinkle remedies. He underlines that "it is advisable to opt for treatments with proven efficacy and established clinical benefits, given the limited and inconclusive nature of studies backing such remedies." Hence, sole dependence on such untested remedies may be more harmful than beneficial. Professional assessment and evidence-based interventions remain the most reliable strategy for maintaining healthy skin. ## What is the best course of action for wrinkles and age spots? Wrinkles and age-related pigmentation both call for a personalised, evidence-based approach. Once the underlying cause has been identified, skin experts begin with sun protection, which is the cornerstone of all anti-ageing treatments. To manage wrinkles: Sun protection can be supported by topical retinoid therapy, a nutritious diet, and optimal hydration. This reduces fine wrinkles, enhances cell turnover, and encourages collagen formation. For severe cases, laser resurfacing, chemical peels, or Botox may be recommended. Dr. Rashi Soni, co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist, Aesthetician, and Hair Transplant Surgeon at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, advises that using a high-quality sunscreen every day is one of the best ways to prevent further harm. Retinoids help by encouraging collagen synthesis and cell turnover. Ceramides and hyaluronic acid-containing skin-plumping moisturisers support the preservation of the skin's protective layer. Lifestyle choices are also essential; eating a healthy diet, getting enough sleep, and quitting smoking can all make a big difference. Deeper wrinkles can be addressed with in-clinic procedures like chemical peels or laser treatments. For age spots of hyperpigmentation: Depending on the severity and kind of skin issue, dermatologists may suggest topical drugs such as hydroquinone, azelaic acid, kojic acid, or niacinamide to reduce melanin production. These therapies may be supplemented with vitamin C and vitamin E. If they are unable to resolve the problem, in-office treatments, including laser therapy, chemical peels, and microdermabrasion, may be suggested. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, explains that common reasons for persistent facial pigmentation include frequent sun exposure, hormonal changes, or skin inflammation linked to acne. When the skin is injured or irritated, it can release more melanin, which may contribute to dark spots or patches. Melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are common instances. Additionally, it's important to remember that insufficient sun protection might exacerbate pigmentation. Dr. Rashi Soni further explains: "We usually take a layered approach when it comes to stubborn pigmentation. The first and most crucial measure is to wear sunscreen every day because UV radiation aggravates pigmentation. Next, we use lotions that gradually lighten dark spots with active ingredients like vitamin C, retinoids, or niacinamide. To address deeper pigmentation, we sometimes advise laser treatments or chemical peels. With the correct strategy, we can achieve observable and long-lasting outcomes, but it's not a one-size-fits-all process, and it does require patience." Conclusion: Curd and mulethi may offer minor and supplemental benefits that may aid with dullness, texture, and uneven tone, but they cannot replace the evidence-based therapeutic intervention for wrinkles and age spots. Skin experts usually recommend a comprehensive approach to effectively and safely address signs of ageing.

title: Fact Check: Can a slimming tea help you lose weight?
claim_text: By drinking slimming tea, one can reduce 5 kg in ten days
quick_take: A video on social media claims that by drinking slimming tea, one can reduce 5 kg in ten days. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: The video promotes a slimming tea without disclosing its ingredients, despite efforts to contact the seller. It asserts that consuming the tea will result in a weight loss of 5 kilograms within 10 days. Losing 5kg (11 pounds) in just 10 days solely by adding slimming tea to your diet is highly unlikely and not recommended. While slimming teas may offer some benefits such as temporary water weight loss or appetite suppression, the amount of weight lost is typically minimal and not primarily fat loss. For significant weight loss, especially within such a short timeframe, it's essential to focus on comprehensive lifestyle changes. Relying solely on slimming tea for weight loss can be risky and may not lead to sustainable results. Additionally, drastic weight loss in a short period can have adverse effects on health, including muscle loss, nutrient deficiencies, and metabolic disturbances. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA), explains that according to Ayurveda, obesity is a challenging condition to address. Ayurvedic texts even assert that it's nearly incurable – 'na hi sthulasya bheshajam'. There are no magical solutions for obesity, and it can't be remedied by a single internal or external medicine. Instead, treatment primarily focuses on managing stress, adopting a suitable lifestyle, and following a specific diet. Medications, whether internal or external, play a supportive role. The effectiveness of the treatment is enhanced when patients adhere to a comprehensive, personalized approach to address obesity. Nutritionist Dr. Swati Dave expressed disbelief and stated that it's ridiculous that people trust such gimmicks. She emphasized that slimming tea is not a miracle weight reduction drink; it does not burn fat or promote weight loss on its own. Without knowing the ingredients, consuming ordinary spices, including green tea, daily may not be safe. Trusting such products is absurd. Dr. Dave stressed that there are no shortcuts to losing weight. Rapid weight loss leads to rapid weight regain. Misinformation from unprofessional sources can lead individuals to make unhealthy lifestyle choices, adopt unproven remedies, delay seeking proper medical advice, and contribute to anxiety, unnecessary money spending, stress, and unnecessary worry.

title: Can a smoothie help you gain 3/4 kg in 15 days?- THIP Media
claim_text: drinking a banana, jaggery, nut, and milk smoothie twice daily can lead to a weight gain of 3–4 kilos in just 15 days
quick_take: A social media post claims that consuming a smoothie made of bananas, jaggery, nuts, and milk twice a day will help you gain 3-4 kg weight. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly false.
doctor_explanation: To gain one kg of fat, you need a surplus of roughly 7,700 calories. For 3–4 kg, that's 23,100–30,800 extra calories over 15 days, or 1,540–2,053 calories daily above your maintenance needs. A smoothie with one banana (100 calories), 200ml full-fat milk (120 calories), 20g jaggery (80 calories), and 15g nuts (90 calories) totals about 390 calories per serving. Two servings provide 780 calories. For someone needing 2,000 calories daily, this creates a surplus, but not enough for the claimed gain, especially if active. Studies in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (2017) show weight gain varies widely due to metabolism and lifestyle, making precise predictions like this unreliable. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition explains: 'This smoothie can be a calorie-dense snack, but it's not a complete diet. Healthy weight gain needs variety, think whole grains, pulses, and lean meats.' She emphasises balanced diets over single foods for sustainable weight gain. Nuts and milk are nutrient-rich, but portion control is key to avoid excessive fat gain. A varied diet ensures you get fibre and vitamins missing from this smoothie alone. Jaggery's high sugar content and its overconsumption may spike blood sugar, risky for pre-diabetics. Harita Adhvaryu, Senior Clinical Dietitian at EzcureDiabetesCare, Ahmedabad explains: 'Two smoothies might help, but if you're active or have a fast metabolism, you may burn those calories.' For example, a 30-minute run burns 300–400 calories, offsetting one smoothie. Research shows consistent calorie surpluses over weeks, paired with strength training, promote muscle gain, but smoothies alone won't guarantee results. If other meals are low-calorie, the smoothie's impact diminishes. Dr Almas Fatma, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai warns: 'High-sugar ingredients like jaggery can cause insulin spikes, which isn't ideal for everyone.' Excessive milk may cause bloating in lactose-intolerant individuals, and nuts, if overeaten, add significant fat. Rapid weight gain can stress the body, raising blood sugar or cholesterol. The NHS advises gradual weight gain (0.5–1 kilo weekly) to avoid strain on organs. Over-relying on smoothies may also lead to nutrient gaps, like low fibre, increasing constipation risk. Manasi Banduni, Senior Nutritionist at Clinic Living Plus, Bangalore advises: 'Quick fixes rarely work long-term. Focus on balanced meals and exercise for healthy results.'

title: Fact Check: Can a specific food help with common health problems?
claim_text: The claimed facebook post suggests that consuming bananas, papayas, sesame seeds, yoghurt, dark chocolate, and nutmeg milk can resolve issues like low energy, eye problems, skin conditions, digestion troubles, stress, and sleep disturbances.
quick_take: A social media post claims that specific foods can directly address common health problems like low energy, poor digestion, and stress. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly True.
doctor_explanation:
## Does eating bananas instantly boost energy?
To a certain extent yes. Bananas are a good source of carbohydrates, natural sugars, and vitamin B6, which help with energy metabolism. They provide a quick burst of energy, making them a good pre-workout snack. However, their energy boost is temporary. Long-term energy levels depend on overall diet, hydration, sleep, and physical activity. Relying solely on bananas for sustained energy is misleading. A combination of protein, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fats is essential for maintaining energy throughout the day.

## Can papaya improve eye health?
Partially true, but not a magic fix. Papayas are rich in vitamin A, which is essential for maintaining eye health and preventing night blindness. They also contain antioxidants like lutein and zeaxanthin, which may help reduce the risk of age-related macular degeneration. However, consuming papaya alone will not significantly improve vision or prevent eye diseases. A diet including a variety of foods such as leafy greens, carrots, and omega-3-rich fish is more effective in supporting eye health.

## Do sesame seeds prevent skin problems?
No, but they may support skin health. Sesame seeds are packed with zinc, vitamin E, and healthy fats, which contribute to skin repair, hydration, and protection against free radical damage. However, skin problems such as acne, eczema, or dryness can stem from multiple factors, including hormonal imbalances, allergies, dehydration, and environmental stressors. While sesame seeds may offer nutritional support, they are not a cure. Proper skincare, hydration, and a nutrient-rich diet are more important for maintaining healthy skin.

## Can yoghurt fix digestion issues?
It helps, but it's not a universal solution. Yoghurt contains probiotics, which promote gut health by increasing beneficial bacteria in the digestive system. This can help ease bloating, constipation, and mild digestive discomfort. However, yoghurt is not a cure for serious digestive disorders like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), acid reflux, or Crohn's disease. Additionally, some people are lactose intolerant and may find yoghurt worsens their symptoms. A diverse diet rich in fibre, fermented foods, and adequate hydration is key for digestive health.

## Does dark chocolate reduce stress?
Somewhat, but it's not a guaranteed stress reliever. Dark chocolate contains flavonoids, which have been linked to mood improvement and reduced stress levels. It also contains magnesium, which plays a role in relaxation. Eating a small amount of dark chocolate may help boost serotonin levels, the hormone associated with happiness. However, the effects are mild, and consuming too much can lead to weight gain due to its high sugar and fat content. Managing stress effectively requires a combination of a balanced diet, regular exercise, sleep, and mindfulness techniques such as meditation or deep breathing.

## Can nutmeg milk improve sleep?
It might help, but it's not a cure for sleep problems. Nutmeg contains myristicin, a compound believed to have mild sedative effects. Warm milk, on the other hand, contains tryptophan, which can promote relaxation and potentially help sleep. Drinking nutmeg milk before bed may help some individuals feel calmer, but not everyone and it is not a guaranteed fix for insomnia or chronic sleep issues. Poor sleep is often caused by factors like stress, screen exposure before bed, irregular sleep schedules, or excessive caffeine intake. Practising good sleep hygiene, such as maintaining a consistent bedtime and reducing blue light exposure, is more effective for improving sleep quality.

## Are there better alternatives for these health concerns?
Absolutely! Instead of relying on single foods, it's better to adopt a well-rounded diet and lifestyle approach. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said, "No single food is a miracle cure, but the right nutrients can support various aspects of health. Bananas provide quick energy, but sustained vitality requires balanced meals. Papaya and sesame seeds contribute to eye and skin health, yet overall diet and lifestyle matter more. Yoghurt aids digestion, but gut health thrives on diversity. Dark chocolate may ease stress, but true well-being comes from a holistic approach. Even nutmeg milk might promote relaxation, but quality sleep depends on consistent habits. Nutrition is powerful, but it works best when combined with mindful living."

## Final Verdict
The foods mentioned in the image do offer some health benefits. But no single food can fix complex health issues on its own. A well-balanced diet, along with a healthy lifestyle, plays a far more significant role in maintaining overall well-being. Instead of focusing on 'superfoods' as miracle solutions, it's better to adopt a holistic approach to health that includes varied nutrition, exercise, proper sleep, and stress management.

title: Fact Check: Can a spoon of ghee and black pepper in water cure piles in 10 days?
claim_text: 99% of the people in the world do not know that if any of your friends is suffering from piles and it is not getting cured, mix a spoonful of ghee with black pepper, dissolve it in water, and make them drink it. This will cure piles in 10 days.
verdict_original: The claim by the user is FALSE. Hence, the user's claim is FALSE.
doctor_explanation:
The claim that ghee and black pepper in water can cure piles in 10 days is FALSE. While these ingredients may provide symptom relief, there is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that they can cure piles (hemorrhoids) in such a short time.

Dr. Vivek Kumar Singh, Consultant Gastroenterologist, Holy Family Hospital Bandra Mumbai explained, "Piles (hemorrhoids) can often be managed effectively through lifestyle changes, dietary adjustments, and medical treatments. Mild cases may resolve with increased fiber intake, hydration, and exercise. For more severe cases, treatments like medication, minimally invasive procedures, or surgery may be required. Consulting a doctor for a personalized approach is essential."

Dr. Girish SP, Surgical Gastroenterologist, Aster RV Bangalore said, "Ghee and black pepper are usual home remedies that can be used when people suffer from cold but ghee acts as a laxative. Laxative is a significant step in the treatment of piles. So, definitely, to some extent it is helpful and the black pepper usually has anti-oxidants, omega-3 fatty which may help in reducing inflammation. So, it is a general remedy, not a specific remedy for piles. So, it will also help to some extent, but in severe piles, none of them is effective."

Dr. Vivek Kumar Singh further said, "While ghee and black pepper are traditional remedies known for their digestive benefits, there is no scientific evidence to confirm they can cure piles in 10 days. They may help alleviate some symptoms, but addressing piles typically requires a comprehensive approach, including dietary changes, hydration, and medical advice."

Piles (hemorrhoids) are swollen and inflamed veins in and around the anus or lower rectum, caused by increased pressure due to straining during bowel movements, chronic constipation, or pregnancy. Complications can include blood clots in external hemorrhoids, leftover skin tags after clots dissolve, infections, strangulation of prolapsed internal hemorrhoids due to restricted blood supply, and anemia from chronic blood loss.

Hemorrhoids are classified into four grades based on severity. Grade I hemorrhoids remain inside the rectum but may protrude slightly beyond the dentate line with straining. Grade II hemorrhoids prolapse through the anus during straining but retract spontaneously. Grade III hemorrhoids protrude externally and require manual reduction. Grade IV hemorrhoids remain persistently prolapsed and cannot be pushed back. Surgical intervention is typically necessary for Grade III and IV hemorrhoids due to their severity and persistence.

Black pepper (Piper nigrum L.) offers medicinal properties including antimicrobial, antioxidant, antidiabetic, and hypolipidemic effects. Studies have shown its potential to fight infections, reduce oxidative stress, and possess anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and neuroprotective properties (PubMed: 30740986).

Ghee offers nutritional benefits as a rich source of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, supporting vision, bone health, immune function, and blood clotting. It contains phospholipids contributing to cellular health.

While studies published in the World Journal of Pharmaceutical and Medical Research and by Minhaj Ahmad et al. suggest milk and milk products like butter, buttermilk, and ghee may contribute to alleviating symptoms and supporting the management of piles, and a study in the International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition suggests black pepper may offer benefits in alleviating symptoms of piles, these findings only indicate symptom management—not a cure. Hemorrhoids are a complex condition that often requires a combination of dietary, lifestyle, and medical interventions, and ghee and black pepper lack the medicinal properties necessary to shrink or cure hemorrhoids entirely.

title: Can a strawberry a day really keep the dermatologist away?
claim_text: Eating a strawberry every day will keep one's skin so healthy that there's no need to see a dermatologist.
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that one strawberry a day keeps the dermatologist away, implying strawberries alone can prevent skin problems. We fact checked and found that the claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: The fact check examines multiple claims about strawberries and skin health. What nutrients in strawberries benefit the skin? Yes, strawberries are packed with skin-friendly nutrients. They contain lots of vitamin C and other antioxidants (like the red pigment anthocyanins). Vitamin C helps make collagen (a protein that keeps skin firm) and antioxidants help neutralise free radicals that age skin. These factors mean strawberries can support overall skin health, and even heart health. Can strawberries reduce acne or inflammation? Maybe. Strawberries have anti-inflammatory antioxidants (vitamin C, anthocyanins) that might calm skin inflammation. In theory this could ease acne, since acne flares often involve inflammation. In fact, studies note that vitamin C may help reduce some acne inflammation, and small studies with strawberry-derived vitamin C (sodium ascorbyl phosphate or SAP) showed promising results on acne. However, evidence is weak and eating strawberries isn't a cure for acne. They can complement an anti-inflammatory diet, but you should still follow your dermatologist's advice for acne treatments. Do strawberries slow skin ageing? Maybe. Vitamin C and antioxidants in strawberries help fight damage from sunlight and pollution, which can slow the signs of ageing. For example, a small study from 2019 found that a strawberry-infused vitamin C serum improved skin hydration and elasticity. But this was a special topical treatment (with microneedling), not just eating the fruit. In general, no studies show that eating strawberries alone will erase wrinkles, though a diet high in fruits can help support healthier, more youthful skin. Can eating strawberries protect the skin from sun damage? Maybe. Some laboratory tests suggest strawberry compounds can help defend skin cells against UV light. One study found that strawberry extract applied to skin cells increased their survival and reduced DNA damage from UVA rays. Scientists think anthocyanins (the berry's red pigments) may be responsible. However, this was in a lab with concentrated extracts on cell cultures. Eating strawberries isn't the same as applying them to your skin – you still need sunscreen. In short, strawberries offer some cellular protection, but they are not a substitute for sun protection measures. Dr Rashi Soni explains: 'Strawberries contain vitamin C, which supports collagen production and helps keep the skin firm and elastic. Their antioxidants may also reduce damage caused by pollution and sunlight, both of which contribute to early ageing. While strawberries can support healthier-looking skin over time, no single food can stop ageing. It's about consistent care, a balanced diet, and sun protection.' Dr Ekansh Shekhar clarifies: 'Strawberries are rich in antioxidants like vitamin C and anthocyanins, which help fight free radicals that damage skin cells. These nutrients can offer some protection at the cellular level, but eating strawberries alone won't shield your skin from the sun. Think of them as part of a skin-friendly diet, not a replacement for sunscreen or sun-safe habits.' In summary, strawberries are healthy and contain nutrients that can support skin health, but the claim that one strawberry a day alone will 'keep the dermatologist away' is misleading. There's no evidence that a single fruit can prevent acne, wrinkles or sun damage on its own. Strawberries help as part of a balanced diet, but they're not a cure-all. And, you still need proper skincare and medical advice if you have skin concerns.

title: Fact Check: Can a supplement cure all vision problems?
claim_text: Multiple Facebook posts promote herbal products claiming they can cure vision problems and eliminate the need for spectacles. The posts claim various people were cured of their vision problems after consuming the product, had clearer vision, and no longer needed to use spectacles.
quick_take: Multiple users and businesses use social media platforms to sell 'herbal' products with the claim that they can cure a patients' vision miraculously so much so that they will no longer need spectacles. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Eye specialist Dr. Pradeep Dahale, MS, DNB, explains, "Eyeglasses are given by Ophthalmologists or Optometrists to correct vision. These glasses are given to correct vision problems due to anatomical variations of eyeball dimensions. Exercises, Eye Drops or diet supplements can't alter eye dimensions like axial length, corneal curvature, etc. So it is naive to believe that you can correct your vision naturally." Dr Neha Rastogi Panda, Senior Infectious Diseases Specialist, Fortis Hospital Gurgaon, elaborates by stating, "Eye problems can be caused by various reasons, such as, allergies, dust, and unsanitary practices, such as, rubbing your eyes with unsanitised and unclean hands. Such problems require urgent treatment to prevent infections. Relying on unproven methods can be harmful. Seeking professional medical advice and evidence-based treatments are crucial for effective management and preserving eye health." Nutritionist Priyanka illustrates the importance of diet in maintaining eye health and states that diet also plays an essential role in maintaining vision or delaying age-related eye damage like macular degeneration. Many times loss of vision is a side effect of uncontrolled blood sugar or high blood pressure which can be again prevented with a healthy diet and positive lifestyle changes. But there are various eye conditions like conjunctivitis, cataracts etc. cannot be treated with diet alone. The Facebook posts also mix up "eye health" with "improving vision". While certain products can give relaxation to eyes, but there are many health conditions like Isoametropic amblyopia where spectacles become an absolute must. Dr Naveen Gupta, DNB (Ophthalmology) informs, "Differentiating between the terms 'good for eye health' and 'can improve vision' is important as they often cause confusion. While a healthy diet and lifestyle can help maintain good eye health, they do not necessarily have the ability to improve one's vision to the extent of reducing eyeglass prescriptions. Making such claims should be avoided." Ayurvedic expert, Dr. Annusuiya Gohil explains, "Triphala, Saptamrit Lauh, and Yashtimadhu are well-regarded in Ayurveda for their potential benefits in addressing eye-vision problems. They have been used in practice and have shown promising results in many cases. However, it's essential to recognize that their effectiveness in achieving a complete cure or eliminating the need for spectacles may vary depending on individual factors. Ayurveda emphasizes a holistic approach to health and well-being. It recognizes that simply relying on medicine may not be sufficient as the problem cured may re-erupt." Dr. K. Sivabalaji, Associate Professor, Dept of Shalakya Tantra, Amrita school of Ayurveda says, "It is difficult to treat a patient or give a medicine for eye disease under Ayurveda without proper diagnosis. Ayurveda eye treatment procedures remain the same for all conditions, but the choice of medicines will be different for each condition. For examples, spectacles are prescribed for multiple reasons. The treatment methodology will depend on the actual cause of the disease. So, a single medicine for all eye conditions is not feasible." Ophthalmologist Aftab Alam also states, "As an expert, it's crucial to emphasize that no product can miraculously remove the need for spectacles. While certain ingredients may support eye health, claims of spectacle elimination are false." The article notes supplements can be beneficial to eye health but cannot be guaranteed to cure all vision problems. Vision problems such as myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, and other eye conditions are complex and caused by various factors. The effectiveness of herbal supplements in treating vision problems may vary among individuals and depends on the specific underlying cause. While some herbal supplements including Triphala, Saptamrit Lauh, and Yashtimadhu are believed to have potential benefits for eye health, they have not been scientifically proven to cure all types of vision problems. Triphala has been a proven drug in maintaining health and has antioxidant properties which may aid in cataract treatment. However, all these need further verification through large-scale placebo-controlled clinical trials. Relying solely on herbal remedies can be potentially harmful due to lack of robust scientific evidence. Delaying proper diagnosis and treatment by relying on unproven remedies can lead to worsening conditions and irreversible damage. Herbal supplements may interact with prescribed medications and cause side effects.

title: Fact Check: Can a supplement enlarge penis size?
claim_text: A herbal supplement that supposedly can enlarge penis size by 2.3 inches within a few days. quick_take: A video on Instagram claims that a supplement can enlarge penis size and boost energy within days. We did the fact check to term this claim as False.
doctor_explanation: Penis size mostly depends on genetics, hormones and environment. There is no scientifically proven method to significantly increase it through supplements, exercises, or devices. Surgical options, such as penile implants or ligament release, can offer some increase in size (1-3 centimetres or 0.4-1.2 inches). However, these are invasive procedures with potential risks and complications. Non-surgical methods like vacuum pumps or stretching devices may result in minor, temporary changes, but these are not permanent or substantial. These methods do not actually increase the size, but just cause swelling. Claims of dramatic increases in penis size, especially through quick fixes like supplements, are not valid as per credible scientific evidence. Moreover, research suggests that most men have their penis size in the 'normal' range. The American Urological Association considers even penile augmentation surgeries to be unsafe and ineffective. Dr Sudeshna Mukherjee, MBBS, MD, DNB, Consultant Psychiatrist and Sexologist, says, 'Although surgical methods like tissue grafting, fat injections, and penile implants can increase penile size and are scientifically validated, they are generally not recommended for purely cosmetic purposes. These surgeries are usually performed to address anatomical defects, injuries, or in cases of micropenis (penis size less than 3 inches), where there is associated dysfunction.' Dr Mukherjee further explains, 'Individuals who are desperate for increasing their penis size may be struggling with body dysmorphic disorder. Many of them also experience depression and anxiety related to sexual performance, which can negatively impact their sexual lives. Additionally, they often suffer from low self-esteem, which affects both their personality and their relationships with others.' Dr Yogesh Tandon, an Ayurveda Sexologist, states, 'There is no pill in any branch of medicine that can definitively increase penis size. Some pills enhance blood flow to the penis, creating a temporary impression of growth, but these effects are temporary.' The website gobiotic.co raises several red flags regarding its authenticity and reliability. The claim that the product is banned in 57 countries is likely a marketing tactic. Usually, bans are due to safety concerns, but without transparency about the product, it's impossible to verify. Sexual enhancement and energy boosting products may pose several risks, as per FDA, due to the presence of dangerous ingredients. The idea that a supplement contains 393 nutrients and provides a massive energy boost within 24 hours is unrealistic and lacks scientific backing. The claim that it can eliminate all bacteria is false and dangerous, as we need good bacteria to thrive. Removing all acne within 72 hours is medically inaccurate as acne is too complex to be cured by a supplement. The notion that it can significantly boost blood flow, testosterone, and strength within a week is highly dubious. The absence of the product name or details in the video and caption is a deliberate strategy to generate curiosity and drive viewers to click the link. Deceptive marketers often use this tactic, making vague and exaggerated claims to lure consumers to a website or product page.
