doctor_explanation: Not really. Instant tan removal is largely unrealistic. While some skincare products may lighten tans temporarily, actual tanning occurs when the skin produces more melanin in response to sun exposure. This biological process cannot be reversed instantly. For effective tan removal, dermatologists often recommend gradual methods, including regular exfoliation, sun protection, and moisturisation, rather than relying on quick fixes. We reached out to Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist, Aesthetician and Hair Transplant Surgeon, Rashi Hospital, Mumbai, for her take on instant tan removal gel. She says, "No tan removal gel can instantly remove a sun tan. Tanning occurs when the skin produces melanin in response to UV exposure, and reversing that process takes time. While certain ingredients may help lighten the skin or exfoliate dead cells, immediate results are unlikely." The ingredients mentioned—walnut and turmeric—do have some skincare benefits but may not work as effectively or instantly for tan removal as claimed. While walnuts and turmeric offer some benefits for skin health and may contribute to a more even skin tone, they are not guaranteed solutions for immediate tan removal. Care should be taken with walnut shell exfoliation to avoid skin damage. No, the claims of "no side effects" should raise red flags. All skincare products can cause reactions, particularly in those with sensitive skin or allergies. Without detailed ingredient listings and customer feedback, it's challenging to determine the product's safety. It's essential to conduct a patch test before trying a new product, especially when using natural ingredients that may cause unexpected reactions. Be careful when selecting products to reduce sun tan or dark spots. Some may contain hidden harmful ingredients like steroids or mercury, even if they're not mentioned on the label. Steroids can lead to breakouts, rashes, and, with prolonged use, can thin your skin or cause lasting discolouration. We came across an interesting cream—a bee venom cream for dark spot removal. However, this product lacks safety and has a high chance of causing allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis. The absence of purchasing details, ingredient lists, and customer reviews suggests a lack of credibility. Genuine products generally provide clear information about their formulation and efficacy. In this case, the vague marketing claims coupled with negative comments under the video hint at potential issues with the product's reliability. Safer alternatives for tan removal include gentle exfoliation with natural ingredients like lactic acid or fruit enzymes, along with regular use of broad-spectrum sunscreen to prevent further tanning. Over time, products containing vitamin C or niacinamide can help brighten the skin and even out skin tone without harsh side effects.

title: Fact Check: Can a toothpowder whiten teeth in all cases? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook post with the caption 'The secret HACK to a stain-free, whiter smile' and the title 'Tired of yellow stained teeth' shares a video endorsing a product called 'MySweetSmile tooth whitening powder' showing that one can whiten their teeth after brushing with this powder.

doctor_explanation: The natural color of teeth can vary naturally. Typically, they are a light to a medium shade of yellow or grayish-yellow, influenced by genetics, age, diet, and oral hygiene. Over time, the color may darken, and stains may appear on both the surface and within the dentine. Intrinsic discoloration can result from systemic or pulpal origins, while extrinsic stains enter the dentine through defects like cracks in the tooth. Children may also exhibit intrinsic stains before tooth emergence. External staining occurs due to excessive exposure to substances that discolor tooth enamel, such as alcohol, tea, coffee, or smoking. Additionally, plaque accumulation can also cause teeth to appear yellow. Toothpowder such as MySweetSmile tooth whitening powder is designed to help remove surface stains from teeth and promote a brighter smile. However, the effectiveness of this product may vary depending on the type and severity of discoloration of your teeth. The product's effectiveness depends on the cause of the discoloration. Surface stains caused by food, drinks, and smoking can often be removed with whitening toothpowders. However, deeper or intrinsic stains caused by certain medications or trauma may not respond to toothpowders and may require professional teeth whitening treatments. Moreover, in various cases, the natural colour of the teeth is not white. However, it might be effective in a few cases due to the presence of certain ingredients, such as pentasodium triphosphate, which is a stain-dissolving agent. It can remove stains and brighten, lighten and whiten teeth. Dr. Pooja Bhardwaj comments: 'Tooth powder might contain certain abrasives like silica, Aluminium oxide, calcium pyrophosphate, charcoal, clay and herbs, which can erode the enamel. They may remove extrinsic stains from the tooth surface, thus making it look cleaner and whiter, but again it has no effect on transforming the natural colour and orientation of teeth. Herbs might promote gum health by increasing circulation. It might also lead to bleeding, gum loss and wearing of enamel. Thus it can do more harm than good.' It can damage tooth enamel if used too frequently or aggressively. It is important to follow the instructions on the packaging and consult with a dentist before using any teeth whitening product. Overall, while toothpowders may be effective for whitening teeth in some cases, they may not be suitable or effective for everyone, and it is important to discuss your options with a dental professional. Only external stains can be avoided, whereas internal stains affect the internal structure of the teeth and are challenging to prevent. Tooth discoloration can always be avoided by eating a high-fibre diet, drinking lots of water, and brushing and flossing on a regular basis. Avoiding smoking, consuming acidic juices and beverages, and limiting the consumption of foods and beverages that can stain teeth, such as cola, coffee, and red wine, are additional preventive measures.

title: Fact Check: Can a total solar eclipse make you sick?
claim_text: The solar eclipse on 8th of April has resulted in people feeling nauseated and having strange symptoms. Numerous people are reporting getting nauseated and having other strange symptoms after the eclipse today. Also, the skies everywhere were thick with MASSIVE amounts of chemtrails. More than I've ever seen. I have to think these two things are related.
quick_take: Solar eclipses, mesmerising celestial occurrences, have often been linked to conspiracy theories and superstitions. Certain cultures connect them to imminent disasters, illness, or divine anger. Scientific community has tried to refute these beliefs time and again, uncovering the eclipse as a natural event governed by astronomical principles, presenting a stunning display rather than a catastrophe. We came across a social media post that claims solar eclipse can make you sick. We did the fact check and termed it false.
doctor_explanation: A solar eclipse happens when the moon moves between the Earth and the sun, blocking out the sunlight. This occurs during the new moon phase when the three celestial bodies align in such a way that the moon casts its shadow on Earth, creating either a total or partial eclipse. 'Chemtrails' is a term used in conspiracy theories to refer to the visible trails left behind by aircraft in the sky. Some conspiracy theorists believe these trails are not just normal condensation trails (contrails) formed by aircraft exhaust but are instead chemicals deliberately sprayed into the atmosphere. There is no scientific evidence to support these claims. During the eclipse, there was a rise in air traffic expected by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) because many people wanted to view the solar eclipse from the sky. The increased flights resulted in formation of condensation trails (contrails), not chemtrails. Experts have confirmed that neither contrails nor the eclipse itself are responsible for causing illness. Eclipse sickness is not real. Despite occasional reports of people feeling unwell during solar eclipses, there is no scientific evidence to support the existence of a specific illness associated with these celestial events. Any physical discomfort or psychological effects experienced during an eclipse are more likely attributed to factors such as anxiety (Hypochondria - Illness Anxiety Disorder), dehydration, or improper viewing of the sun without adequate eye protection. There is no need to worry about a specific illness known as 'eclipse sickness'. Regarding harmful radiation: during a total solar eclipse, the only visible light we see is the corona, which is perfectly safe. The corona is the outer atmosphere of the sun, and the electromagnetic radiation it emits poses no danger to observers on Earth. Beyond visible light, there's another type of radiation produced within the sun during its nuclear fusion processes in the form of tiny particles called neutrinos. Neutrinos are extremely small, neutral particles that can pass through matter without interacting with it. During a solar eclipse, neutrinos continue their journey uninterrupted, passing through the solid body of the moon and then through the Earth. Despite the vast number of neutrinos passing through us every second (estimated to be in the trillions), they do not pose any harm to living organisms. Neutrinos are so tiny and interact so weakly with matter that they can pass through the human body and the entire Earth without any significant interactions. Occasionally, a neutrino may interact with an atom in our bodies, causing a slight change in its composition, however this process is entirely harmless and has no adverse effects on human health. Even for pregnant women, the passage of neutrinos during a solar eclipse poses no risk to the developing foetus.

title: Fact Check: Can a type of shapewear transform your body and skin?
claim_text: By wearing shapewear, one can reduce buttock acne, make the skin firm and elastic, reduce belly fat, transform their silhouette, enhance and shape their figure, look more toned, and reduce the appearance of stretch marks — all in just 3 weeks.
quick_take: A social media post claims that by wearing a type of shapewear one can reduce buttock acne, make the skin firm and elastic and reduce belly fat. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Shapewear is a type of undergarment designed to shape and contour the body, providing a smoother, more streamlined appearance. It is made from elastic materials such as nylon, spandex, or Lycra. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that wearing shapewear can reduce buttock acne, tighten the skin, or reduce fat. In fact, some experts believe that wearing shapewear can actually make these problems worse and can cause other problems such as slowing free motion of the gastrointestinal system and trapping gas inside. Regarding skin tightening: Shapewear may offer some level of compression and support, but it is unlikely to have a direct impact on reducing buttock acne or tightening the skin. Shapewear does not have the ability to tighten loose or sagging skin. Skin tightening is a complex process that involves the production of collagen and elastin. It often requires medical or cosmetic procedures, such as laser treatments, radiofrequency therapy, or surgical interventions. There is a lack of evidence proving that wearing shapewear can increase collagen or elastin production, or that it can tighten the skin in any way. In fact, some experts believe that wearing shapewear can actually hamper the skin over time. Regarding buttock acne: Buttock acne is caused by several factors, such as clogged hair follicles, excess oil production, and bacteria. Wearing shapewear or tight clothing can trap heat and moisture, which can create an environment that is ideal for acne-causing bacteria or yeast infections to thrive. Additionally, the tight fabric of shapewear can irritate the skin and make acne worse. Shapewear typically covers the buttock area, and prolonged use of tight-fitting garments may potentially increase sweating and trap moisture, which could exacerbate acne or other skin conditions. Regarding fat reduction: Reducing fat is a complex process that involves diet and exercise. There is no evidence that wearing shapewear can help to reduce fat. In fact, wearing shapewear can actually make it harder to lose weight, as it can restrict movement and make it difficult to exercise. While shapewear can provide temporary contouring and slimming effects by redistributing fat, it does not lead to permanent fat reduction. title: Can a Vaseline-based recipe remove dark circles in just 7 days?
claim_text: One teaspoon of coconut oil, one vitamin E tablet, half a teaspoon of coffee powder, and Vaseline can get rid of dark circles in just seven days.
quick_take: A well-known Facebook post claims that a Vaseline-based remedy will effectively eliminate dark circles in just seven days. We verified the notion and found it to be completely false.
doctor_explanation:
Dark circles, medically known as periorbital hyperpigmentation, may result from structural, vascular, and pigmentary changes beneath the eyes. Given that the under-eye skin is among the thinnest in the body, several contributing factors may accentuate this translucency. These alterations are both physiologically and aesthetically worrisome. Additionally, self-esteem and perceived well-being can be significantly impacted by this under-eye pigmentation. Consequently, it is essential to comprehend the fundamental mechanism that directs the targeted therapies, which would aid in the timely management of dark circles.

While the combination of Vaseline, coconut oil, vitamin E capsules, and coffee powder has been touted as an effective remedy for dark circles on social media, its relevance is confined to social media platforms. As previously stated, the under-eye skin is the thinnest; hence, all four ingredients should be comprehensively evaluated.

We begin with Vaseline. The petroleum jelly-based product is considered for its occlusive properties, which may reduce transdermal water loss and momentarily smooth the skin beneath the eyes.

Coconut oil comes next. The skin barrier may be supported by this ingredient's mild, emollient, and anti-inflammatory effects.

This is followed by the most popular skincare ingredient, vitamin E capsules. It is widely recommended for its antioxidant potential – it helps reduce oxidative stress and supports skin repair.

And finally, we explore the potential of coffee powder. Because the ingredient is packed with caffeine and polyphenols, it may temporarily reduce puffiness and enhance the appearance of vascular under-eye darkness.

Despite these benefits, the scientific evidence supporting the effectiveness of the aforementioned components for dark circles remains inconclusive. Moreover, periorbital hyperpigmentation is multifactorial in origin; a single home remedy is unlikely to address the entire spectrum of underlying mechanisms. While the at-home formulation may offer mild short-term cosmetic benefits, it should not be considered as a primary therapeutic intervention for dark circles.

No therapeutic approach can remove dark circles in 7 days. This is because dark circles could stem from several causes, necessitating targeted, regular supervision. Considering any therapeutic intervention would work by enhancing collagen, decreasing melanin, or correcting volume loss over time, no therapy can yield results in just seven days. As a result, any medically approved procedure—such as topical prescription medications, chemical peels, under-eye fillers, or laser therapy—usually takes several weeks of regular application to demonstrate outcomes. Always consult a well-qualified dermatologist for the right guidance.

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetician, Trichologist, and Consultant for Aesthetic Medicine in Lucknow, clarifies that not all botanical remedies are beneficial for the skin. When applied topically, several organic substances, such as turmeric or lemon juice, might result in allergic responses, burns, or irritation. Lab-based products are put through a rigorous testing process to guarantee their safe and efficient performance. For instance, the strong acidity of lemon juice may damage the skin's barrier, yet glycolic acid in skincare products softly exfoliates skin. Therefore, even if they might seem enticing, homemade skincare products aren't always the best or safest option for your skin.

Dr. Iftekhar Khan, MD (Dermatology), Assistant Professor at SMS Medical College in Jaipur, provides support by stating that, contrary to popular belief, home remedies are not a suitable approach for addressing under-eye discolouration. Because the skin beneath the eyes is much thinner and more delicate, using unsupervised therapies could worsen the condition. Effective under-eye therapy requires a comprehensive evaluation of the issue along with persistent effort.

Dermatologists use an evidence-based personalised therapeutic approach to manage dark circles. The root cause determines the approach to management. For pigmentary dark circles: Prescription hydroquinone, azelaic acid, vitamin C, or retinoids are typically recommended. Vascular under-eye pigmentation: laser therapies and caffeine-based formulations may help enhance the condition. Structural Deficits: Techniques including hyaluronic acid fillers, chemical peels, microneedling, and platelet-rich plasma can help restore the volume and texture of the skin. Dermatologists can additionally manage related causes, such as atopy, UV exposure, or nutritional deficiencies, which may aid in preventing recurrence. While certain home-based solutions may provide short-term benefits, they can neither correct melanin overproduction nor thicken structurally thin skin. Therefore, a comprehensive, scientifically supported strategy ensures safer and effective outcomes.

title: Can a vinegar-based recipe whiten teeth in just 3-4 days?
claim_text: An Instagram post promoting a formulation composed of vinegar, regular toothpaste and black or pink salt as a definitive home remedy for teeth whitening that can whiten teeth in just three to four days.
quick_take: According to a well-known Instagram post, teeth can be efficiently whitened in just three to four days using a vinegar-based recipe. We fact-checked and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation: Teeth whitening is the intentional lightening of a tooth's natural shade. The process involves chemical oxidisers, which may help alter intrinsic chromophores and minimise extrinsic surface stains. Even though teeth whitening is not a therapeutic intervention, people want it for aesthetic reasons. There is no scientific evidence to support the claims that pink salt, white vinegar, and regular or any toothpaste are effective natural teeth whiteners. Regarding white vinegar: even though the component contains acidic properties that may temporarily remove some surface stains, its concentrated form can erode tooth enamel, causing irreparable damage, increased sensitivity, and surface roughness, making the teeth more susceptible to subsequent staining. Regarding regular toothpaste: this primarily works via mild abrasives that may help remove surface stains, but it may not have an effect against intrinsic discolouration brought on by age, trauma, or certain medications. Regarding pink or black salt (Kala Namak): although this ingredient's high trace mineral content may help remove surface stains, regular usage or application may raise the risk of enamel erosion. Dr. Ketan Rajput, Periodontist and Oral Implantologist at Dr. Rajput's Advanced Dental Care and Implant Centre in Dhule, Maharashtra, underlines that no natural remedies can effectively whiten teeth. Certain do-it-yourself measures can be used to remove surface stains, but their efficacy demands careful consideration. Furthermore, they are not meant to replace professional dental procedures. Always seek professional advice to ensure the greatest results from the procedure. Dr. Gagandeep Singh Sodhi, a dental expert in Delhi, concurs, saying that adopting unreliable teeth-whitening techniques at home before seeing a dentist could delay critical care and result in unanticipated health issues. While some of these natural remedies might complement professional teeth-whitening techniques, they cannot replace them. Web-based claims that some quick solutions or home remedies can whiten teeth in as little as three to four days are scientifically unrealistic. The whitening procedure relies on the controlled chemical oxidation of stains in dentin and enamel, which calls for sufficient exposure time and expert supervision. Online unregulated at-home remedies like charcoal, baking soda, and apple cider vinegar might just provide surface cleaning, but if applied improperly, they could damage enamel or result in uneven discolouration. Furthermore, an online topical treatment cannot erase intrinsic discolouration brought on by ageing, medications, or tobacco use in a matter of days. Most importantly, teeth cannot be properly whitened in three to four days using even the scientifically proven method without risking the danger of structural or cosmetic damage. Therefore, effective whitening must be gradual, professionally supervised and customised to individual requirements. Professional teeth whitening involves in-office procedures using higher concentrations of peroxide gels activated by light or laser or LED, with results visible in about 30 to 90 minutes, or at-home whitening kits involving the use of custom-fitted trays with lower peroxide concentrations. Professional tooth whitening is a safe process, but too much of it can cause biological problems due to peroxide diffusion which can momentarily increase dentin permeability, resulting in tooth sensitivity and pulpal discomfort.

title: Fact Check: Can abortion be done at home safely and naturally? - THIP Media

quick_take: A social media post is claiming that abortion can be done at home safely and naturally. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Manzer Altamash Shaikh, Consultant Obstetrician, Gynaecologist, and Fertility Specialist, Masina Hospital, Mumbai, explains, "Self-induced abortion is an abortion performed by the pregnant woman herself or with the help of untrained non-medical personnel either by over-the-counter medications or through a quack. It is associated with many complications, some being life-threatening. These methods are often tried during first two months of pregnancy." Dr Shaikh further narrates, "Some of the side effects of self-abortion are incomplete abortion leading to continuous vaginal bleeding, anemia, infection of the womb, or sepsis spreading in the whole body. If done through quacks can cause perforation of the uterus and may be potentially lethal to the life of the pregnant woman causing death." According to the World Health Organization, an estimated 22 million abortions continue to be performed unsafely each year, resulting in the death of an estimated 47,000 women and disabilities for an additional 5 million women. Plus, about 1 in 4 women who have an unsafe abortion are left with serious health issues that require ongoing medical care. Almost every one of these deaths and disabilities could have been prevented through proper sex education, family planning, and the provision of safe & legal abortion and care for complications of abortion. The results of a study on rats indicate that unripe fruits of papaya interrupt the estrous cycle and induce abortions. The abortifacient property seems to decrease as the fruit becomes stale or ripe. Exogenous progesterone (a hormone) counteracts partially the adverse effects on pregnancy and the surviving fetuses are without any distinct malformations. Another study suggests that normal consumption of ripe papaya during pregnancy may not pose any significant danger. However, the unripe or semi-ripe papaya (which contains a high concentration of latex that produces marked uterine contractions) could be unsafe in pregnancy. Though it doesn't necessarily lead to miscarriage, it may lead to certain complications, therefore should be avoided. There is no credible scientific information suggesting that vitamin C has any effect on pregnancy, implantation, or menstruation. A 2016 review of existing studies found that taking vitamin C had no effect on someone's risk of having a spontaneous miscarriage. According to Dr Shaikh, "Traditionally and culturally, many food taboos have been associated with pregnancy and are linked to abortion. And these are used for self-abortion. Two of the commonly used foods for self-abortion are papaya and pineapple. However, consumption of any fruit or food item can't cause abortion." Another social media post suggests that chemical abortion pills are not safe. They carry the risk of infection, surgery, infertility, depression, horrifying pain, & death. Another social media post suggests that consuming Vitamin C after unprotected sex can prevent pregnancy. Papaya or raw papaya (Carica papaya linn) interrupts certain pregnancy hormones and may induce some uterine contractions however it's insufficient to cause an abortion. Likewise, pineapple (Ananas comosus) has been traditionally linked to abortion which is untrue. Therefore, the myths that diet can induce self-abortion needs to be strongly busted, and patients should be encouraged to seek medical help. Medical or surgical abortion is recommended as trying abortion on your own is absolutely not safe and pregnant women are requested to abstain from trying such procedures as it may lead to many complications or may even be fatal.

title: Fact Check: Can activated charcoal whiten teeth effectively?
claim_text: A YouTube video "Activated Charcoal: Weird Way to Get White Teeth" recommends using activated charcoal with a toothbrush up to five times per week.
quick_take: According to a well-liked YouTube video, activated charcoal can be effective as a tooth whitener. We verified the assertion. As per our research, the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Stains and tooth discoloration are frequent dental concerns that can happen for a variety of reasons. There are three main categories of tooth stains. They are internal, external, and even age-related tooth stains. External tooth staining, which can happen for a variety of reasons, can happen to anyone. Frequently, the cause is the consumption of foods, beverages, and tobacco products with colour, such as cigarettes, cigars, or chewable tobacco. It is possible for internal tooth staining to be brought on by tooth decay, injury, and even some medications. These tooth stains could be yellow, brown, grey, or even black in colour. Yes, the colour of the teeth can also be influenced by genes. The enamel's thickness can be inherited, so depending on what runs in one's family, it may be thicker or more transparent. When the enamel is thin, the yellow-brown layer (dentin) underneath is more visible, giving the appearance of a darker or more yellow smile. Regrettably, whitening products and toothpaste might not be able to brighten the teeth of people who were born with naturally yellow teeth. It should be noted that genes may have an effect on both baby and permanent teeth. No, not right away. Activated charcoal is a common component of teeth-whitening toothpastes, but there isn't any substantial proof that it works to whiten teeth. It is important to note that activated charcoal is essentially a fine-grained powder made from wood, coconut shells, and other natural materials that have been oxidized at high temperatures and might serve as an occasional surface cleaner and help with bad breath. However, daily use of activated charcoal could harm enamel because of its abrasive nature. Furthermore, it has no effect on stains that seep beneath the enamel surface. Aside from these detrimental effects, activated charcoal can also result in tooth sensitivity, tooth staining, and cavity fillings. Concerns have also been raised regarding its safety and long-term effectiveness for teeth whitening. Dr. Pratyasa Bagchi, our dental expert, stated: "there was no proof that activated charcoal whitened teeth. The fact that activated charcoal acts as an abrasive cannot be ignored, despite the fact that it has been widely used in toothpastes for teeth whitening. However, while it undoubtedly gets rid of some surface stains, it cannot stop severe stains like yellowing or plaque development. Thus, it should only be used in moderation under the guidance of your dentist." Maintaining good oral hygiene requires the development of healthy habits. With a few clear and simple lifestyle changes, one might be able to prevent tooth discoloration. If one consumes a lot of coffee, one might want to cut back or switch to a suitable alternative. Additionally, a smoker should seek assistance to quit because smoking harms a lot more than just your oral health. Through daily tooth brushing, daily flossing, and biannual dental cleanings, one could improve their oral hygiene.

title: Fact Check: Can acupressure cure common cold? - THIP Media
claim_text: Acupressure can cure common cold

doctor_explanation: Common cold is caused by many types of viruses; rhinoviruses are the most common cause. The virus enters the human body through one's mouth, eyes or nose. The virus then spreads through droplets in the air when someone who is sick coughs, sneezes or talks. Acupressure is a type of complementary treatment procedure used to remove immune ailments to emotional disorders. This treatment relieves diverse pains and manages multiple symptoms among different people. This may help people feel better when suffering from cold. Not exactly. No evidence shows how acupressure procedures fight the viruses that cause common cold. A review published in 2010 informs that the effectiveness of acupressure against common cold is currently not well documented. This conclusion is in sharp contrast to claim made in the YouTube video. However, in case of allergic rhinitis, a condition that also make people sneeze, acupressure exercise on the face can help. A research paper published in 2010 shows that common cold is a viral infection. But allergic rhinitis is a reaction by immune system to an allergic trigger. The symptoms of allergic rhinitis begins immediately upon exposure to a trigger. But common cold symptoms often starts after 2-3 days of viral exposure. A few research papers have shown that acupressure can relieve irritated sinus gland on the face to relieve allergic rhinitis. In most of these patients, the immune system is compromised and we need to buildup the immunity of the patient. There are specific acupuncture points on which needling is done to improve the immunity. Some local points are also used along the nose for giving symptomatic improvement.' However, no evidence proves acupressure cures common cold. In another fact-check 'common cold is a cure but not an illness' we have shown that there exist no cure for common cold. The condition is caused by different viruses, so it is difficult to develop a single drug to fight all these viruses. Several posts on social media claim that heating the orange and consuming it will cure cold or a single acupressure point can cure all diseases. These claims remain false due to the lack of scientific evidence.

title: Can ACV and spices reduce insulin resistance and sugar spikes?
claim_text: Drinking a mix of apple cider vinegar, lemon, soaked fenugreek seeds, turmeric and black pepper daily can help you "say goodbye" to insulin resistance and permanently stop sugar spikes.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that consuming apple cider vinegar along with various spices can help "say goodbye" to insulin resistance and permanently stop sugar spikes. We fact checked and found the claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Insulin resistance doesn't happen because your diet is missing vinegar, spices or herbs. It develops gradually, when the body's cells, mainly in the muscles, liver and fat tissue, stop responding properly to insulin. This usually builds up over years, shaped by factors like excess body fat (especially around the waist), low physical activity, ongoing inflammation, genetic susceptibility, poor sleep and repeated exposure to high blood sugar levels. Because the problem is long-term and multi-layered, the solution has to be the same. Scientific research consistently shows that insulin resistance improves with sustained changes, not quick remedies. Weight loss where needed, regular physical activity (particularly strength training), balanced carbohydrate intake and, for some people, medication are what actually improve insulin sensitivity at a cellular level. To date, no clinical trials have shown that any home drink or ingredient combination can simply "switch off" insulin resistance. Some components of this mix have been studied individually, and a few show modest benefits. But those effects are supportive, not curative. Framing this drink as a cure oversimplifies a complex condition, and risks people delaying the kind of care that genuinely helps.

Apple cider vinegar has been researched for its effect on post-meal blood sugar levels. The acetic acid in vinegar can slow the rate at which food leaves the stomach, meaning glucose enters the bloodstream more gradually. Some studies also suggest a small improvement in insulin sensitivity when vinegar is consumed before meals. That said, the impact is modest. Vinegar does not neutralise the effects of large portions of refined carbohydrates, sugary foods or frequent snacking. In real-world settings, the reductions seen are usually small and short-lived, nowhere near enough to normalise blood sugar levels in people with insulin resistance or diabetes. Most importantly, vinegar does nothing to address the underlying drivers of sugar spikes, such as low muscle mass, excess visceral fat or a consistently high carbohydrate load. It may help at the margins, but it is not a protective shield. Voomika Mukherjee, a certified dietitian and health coach, cautioned that ACV cannot replace prescribed diabetes medications. She noted that including it as part of a balanced diet may help support symptom management, but they should be used alongside, not in place of, standard treatment.

Fenugreek seeds are rich in soluble fibre and contain compounds that can slow carbohydrate digestion and reduce glucose absorption in the gut. Some clinical studies show improvements in fasting blood glucose and insulin response when fenugreek is taken regularly, particularly in people with impaired glucose tolerance. However, these benefits are gradual rather than dramatic. Fenugreek works best as part of a fibre-rich, balanced diet, not as a standalone fix. Soaking the seeds may make them easier to digest, but it does not turn them into a metabolic game-changer. Fenugreek cannot override poor dietary patterns, physical inactivity or hormonal contributors to insulin resistance. Its role is supportive at best, not transformative. Dr Ganesh Srinivasa Prasad P, MBBS, Consultant Nephrologist and Transplant Physician at Narayana Health City, Bengaluru, explained that fenugreek seeds have traditionally been considered beneficial for health, particularly in diabetes, but scientific evidence remains limited and inconsistent. Diabetes affects individuals differently - type 1 diabetes requires insulin, while type 2 diabetes is influenced by multiple factors so a single remedy does not work for everyone. Fenugreek may not provide benefit in all cases, which is why medical guidance is important. Managing diabetes early and appropriately helps reduce the risk of complications such as kidney disease, heart disease and kidney stones.

Turmeric's active compound, curcumin, is well known for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Since chronic, low-grade inflammation plays a role in insulin resistance, curcumin has been studied for potential metabolic benefits. Some research suggests that curcumin supplementation may slightly improve markers of insulin sensitivity. However, these effects are usually seen with concentrated extracts taken consistently and in therapeutic doses, not with small culinary amounts stirred into a drink. Black pepper does enhance curcumin absorption, but it does not elevate turmeric to a treatment-level intervention. Turmeric may support overall metabolic health, but it does not reverse insulin resistance or replace proven lifestyle and medical strategies. Dr Ritesh Bansal, Founder and Senior Consultant Diabetologist at Saroj Diabetes & Research Centre in Delhi, notes that dietary modifications can support diabetes management but should not be treated as a replacement for prescribed medications. He adds that healthy food choices may help reduce the intensity or amount of medication required in some cases. Dr Bansal also emphasises the importance of seeking professional guidance before making any dietary changes as part of a diabetes treatment plan.

There is no scientific evidence showing that combining apple cider vinegar, lemon, fenugreek, turmeric and black pepper creates a powerful synergy capable of fixing insulin resistance or preventing sugar spikes. Stacking several mildly helpful ingredients does not multiply their effects in a clinically meaningful way. This idea often comes from wellness culture, where mixing "natural" ingredients creates a sense of control and hope. In reality, metabolic health improves through consistency, not concoctions. This drink is unlikely to be harmful for most people, but it is not a cure. At best, it may offer small, short-term support when paired with balanced meals. Real improvements in insulin resistance come from long-term habits: adequate protein and fibre, regular movement, strength training, good sleep, stress management and, when needed, medical care. No drink, no matter how natural, can replace that foundation.

title: Fact Check: Can adding a disclaimer enable misinformation sharing?
claim_text: Several facebook post are making inconsistent health claims mere putting a disclaimer give you a free hand in spreading misinformation. The disclaimer reads, 'Note: These tips are general in nature; and it's always a good idea to consult a healthcare professional or expert for personalized advice'.
quick_take: Several social media post are spreading health misinformation online putting a disclaimer that the tips are general and recommends to consult a doctor before taking a decision. We factchecked the claims and put them under mostly false category. Even though the claims made are correct to a certain extent, mere putting a disclaimer does not give you a free hand in spreading misinformation.
doctor_explanation: Not always. Social media is easy to use, but it doesn't always give us the right information. Even in the claimed videos, the information is not entirely accurate. In one video, there are claims that suggest that thin individuals can gain weight by consuming a combination of chickpeas and dates. Conversely, another video asserts that drinking fennel water on an empty stomach can lead to weight loss in just 10 days, while applying ghee to chapati can promote weight gain. Additionally, it is suggested that consuming jaggery with onion juice can increase height. We have previously conducted comprehensive research that shows fennel alone cannot induce weight loss, and the combination of ghee and roti cannot lead to weight gain, strengthen bones, or prevent hair loss. These conditions can occur due to various factors, including nutritional deficiencies, certain diseases, or other underlying causes that cannot be solved by ghee or roti alone. Similarly, it would be an exaggeration to claim that dates or chickpeas, jaggery with onion juice alone, can produce miraculous results on their own. In a different social media video, it proclaims that moringa is more nutritious than oranges, bananas, milk, and meat. It suggests that consuming moringa can prevent low immunity, hair fall, asthma, diabetes, and obesity. However, even though moringa has health benefits, it is still better to consult a doctor before eating it. Each of these conditions has specific treatments that individuals should seek out, rather than relying solely on these quick remedies. The nuances of misinformation are further complicated when considering the role of social media in disseminating health information. This concern is particularly relevant when evaluating the trustworthiness of online sources for topics like treating parasitic wounds. Yet another social media video claims that applying potato to the skin can remove pigmentation. However, it may only reduce the appearance of pigmentation and may not target the root cause in every individual. For a comprehensive approach, a doctor can prescribe lightening creams, retinoids, chemical peels, laser therapy, and microdermabrasion to address the root cause of pigmentation. Similarly, relying solely on cashews to improve the quality and appearance of skin and hair, or drinking hot water with black pepper to boost stamina, is not recommended. These measures can complement proper treatment taken to address specific health issues. Disclaimers do convey the message that the information presented in the content should not be taken seriously. However it is important to emphasize that adding a disclaimer to misinformation does not give you a free hand in spreading it. A disclaimer is simply a statement that warns the reader or viewer that the information may not be accurate or reliable. It does not minimise your responsibility of ensuring that the information you are sharing is true and accurate. In fact, putting a disclaimer on misinformation can be seen as a way to try to avoid responsibility for the consequences of spreading it. It is a way of saying, 'I know this information may not be true, but I am sharing it anyway, and it is your fault if you believe it.' In addition to this, we have observed that these social media videos are generated using AI tools, which makes it challenging to engage with their creators. For instance, the claimant of the social media video mentioned in this story is a prime example of this challenge. Furthermore, we have identified the creator of these social media videos as a page named 'doctorji_ai_sb.' This page has published numerous similar videos, and it is difficult to establish communication with the individual behind these posts. Moreover, these videos often include hashtags that are unrelated to the claims made in the video. This practice is commonly employed by social media users seeking to promote their content through the use of popular or viral hashtags. In conclusion, it is important to remember that misinformation can have serious consequences. It can lead people to make wrong decisions that can negatively affect their lives.

title: Fact Check: Can adding vodka to shampoo strengthen hair?
claim_text: Adding vodka to your shampoo can strengthen your hair, prevent dry scalp, and stop dandruff.
quick_take: A social media post claims that adding vodka to shampoo can strengthen hair. We did the fact check to term this claim asfalse.
doctor_explanation: Vodka does not strengthen hair. Hair is made of keratin, a protein that cannot be 'strengthened' externally by alcohol. While some believe vodka's acidic nature can help 'close' the hair cuticle, there's no scientific evidence to support this claim. In fact, alcohol can strip natural oils from hair, making it brittle and prone to breakage over time. Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, clarifies: 'While vodka may have some antibacterial properties, it's unlikely to significantly strengthen your hair. The alcohol in vodka can strip the scalp of its natural oils, leading to dryness and irritation. In fact, over time, this can weaken your hair, making it more prone to breakage. For healthier hair, it's better to focus on nourishing ingredients that support hydration and strengthen hair from the inside out.' Regarding dry scalp: vodka may actually worsen a dry scalp. Alcohol is a drying agent. Applying vodka to your scalp can strip away natural moisture, leaving your scalp drier than before. This is especially harmful for individuals already dealing with dryness or sensitive skin. Regarding dandruff: vodka is not a proven remedy for dandruff. Dandruff can arise due to factors like an overgrowth of a yeast-like fungus called Malassezia, excessive oil production, or skin conditions like seborrheic dermatitis. Vodka, with its high alcohol content, does not address these underlying causes. In fact, the drying effect of alcohol could irritate your scalp further, potentially exacerbating dandruff. Regarding alcohol in hair care: While some hair care products contain specific alcohols (like cetyl or stearyl alcohol) to help with texture and hydration, these are fatty alcohols, not the type found in vodka. Ethanol-based alcohols, like those in vodka, are generally not recommended for regular hair application because they are highly drying. Vodka's alcohol content is around 40%, while disinfectants typically require at least 60-90% alcohol to be truly effective. Even though it may have some antibacterial effects, this potential benefit is overshadowed by vodka's tendency to dry out the scalp and cause irritation. title: Fact Check: Can ADHD Be Treated Through Diet?
claim_text: In India, 58% of people are suffering from mental and emotional problems like ADHD, GAD, stress, depression, etc., and these can be cured only and only through lifestyle changes and diet.
verdict_original: The claim by the user is FALSE.
quick_take: Dietary changes alone are not a proven treatment for ADHD. While certain nutrients and dietary adjustments may help manage some symptoms, there is no strong scientific evidence that diet by itself can treat or cure ADHD. Effective ADHD management typically requires a combination of behavioral therapies, medications, and supportive strategies.
doctor_explanation:
The claim that ADHD can be treated through diet is False. ADHD is primarily neurobiological and genetic in origin. Diet may influence general health and help in management, but it alone cannot treat ADHD.

National Institute of Mental Health defines ADHD as a disorder characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that disrupts functioning or development. Individuals with ADHD may struggle to stay focused, organized, and on task, not due to defiance or misunderstanding but because of these core symptoms.

Dr Rahul Chawla, Associate Consultant, Department of Neurology, PSRI Hospitals, New Delhi, explained: 'Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, which significantly impair daily functioning. Diagnosed primarily in childhood but often persisting into adulthood, ADHD affects around 5-7% of children globally. Symptoms include difficulty focusing, excessive fidgeting or talking, and impulsive actions. Diagnosis is based on criteria from the DSM-5, typically involving professional assessments. Treatment usually involves a combination of behavioral therapies and medications, particularly stimulants, which help manage symptoms. Without treatment, ADHD can lead to academic, social, and occupational challenges, along with an increased risk of co-occurring mental health issues.'

Researchers have been investigating the impact of nutritional supplements on managing symptoms of ADHD. A recent study published in the Current Nutrition Reports explored the role of micronutrient supplementation in managing ADHD symptoms. The study found that supplementing the diet with zinc and iron was associated with a reduction in the severity of ADHD symptoms. Studies have also examined how dietary patterns may influence the severity of ADHD symptoms. A study led by Olweya Mohammed Abd El Baaki et al. reported that reduced intake of carbohydrates and proteins was linked to improvements in ADHD symptoms.

Dr Rahul Chawla responding to the claim: 'The claim that ADHD can be treated solely through diet is false. While certain dietary modifications, like reducing processed foods, artificial additives, and ensuring balanced nutrition, may support overall brain health and behavior, they do not cure or treat ADHD. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with complex genetic and neurological factors. Evidence-based treatment primarily includes behavioral therapy and medications such as stimulants. Dietary interventions can complement, but not replace, medical management. Always consult a neurologist or psychiatrist for accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment options.'

Dr Divya Tripathi also explained: 'While maintaining a balanced diet rich in essential nutrients like omega-3 fatty acids, iron, zinc, and vitamins supports overall brain function, there is no strong scientific evidence that diet alone can treat ADHD. Eliminating processed foods, sugar, or artificial additives may help reduce some behavioral symptoms in certain children but cannot replace medical therapies. Hence, the claim that ADHD can be treated solely through diet is false. ADHD requires a multidisciplinary approach, including medication and behavioral therapy, not just dietary changes.'

Dietary strategies may complement other treatments and promote overall health, but they are not effective as a standalone therapy for ADHD. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to back the claim that ADHD can be cured solely through diet.

title: Fact Check: Can AirPods cause brain cancer?

doctor_explanation: Electromagnetic fields (EMF) are areas of energy that surround electronic devices. Non-ionizing radiation, which includes the EMF from wireless devices like AirPods, is generally not harmful because the energy levels are too low to cause the ionisation of atoms and damage DNA. Regulatory bodies such as the FCC and WHO have set safety limits for EMF exposure from consumer electronics that are well below harmful levels. The Specific Absorption Rate (SAR) for AirPods is well within safety limits. The claim that AirPods are miniature microwave ovens is an exaggeration - microwaves operate at much higher power levels and frequencies designed to heat food, while AirPods operate at frequencies designed for wireless communication with power output in the milliwatt range, compared to hundreds of watts for microwave ovens. Think of it as a helpful spice, not a cure-all. A balanced diet, regular meals, and staying hydrated are still the most effective ways to keep your gut healthy.' Digestive issues have many causes, such as diet, gut health, and underlying medical conditions. Not all digestive problems can be fully managed by a single spice. (2) Can black salt help with digestion? Black salt (kala namak) contains small amounts of sulphur compounds, which give it a pungent smell and are believed to aid digestion. title: Fact Check: Can alkaline water prevent cancer?
claim_text: Drinking alkaline water can prevent or save you from cancer. quick_take: An Instagram post claims that drinking alkaline water can prevent cancer. We did the fact check to term this claim as False.
doctor_explanation: Alkaline water refers to water that has a higher pH level than regular drinking water, usually around 8 or 9 on the pH scale. It is still not conclusive that alkaline water is better than regular safe drinking water. Supporters of alkaline water claim that it can neutralise the acid in the body, leading to various health benefits, including cancer prevention. Our bodies are incredibly good at keeping pH levels stable, especially in the blood. This balance is tightly controlled by systems like our kidneys and lungs, ensuring the blood's pH stays within a narrow range of 7.35 to 7.45, no matter what we eat or drink. Drinking alkaline water might briefly change the pH of your saliva or urine. But, it doesn't impact the blood's pH or the overall body's pH. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that drinking alkaline water can prevent or cure cancer. Cancer is a complex group of diseases with various causes, including genetic factors, lifestyle choices, and environmental exposures. The idea that altering the body's pH through drinking alkaline water can affect cancer cells is not supported by credible scientific research. Cancer cells thrive in both acidic and alkaline environments. The kidneys, lungs, and buffer systems regulate the body's pH. This makes it nearly impossible to change blood pH significantly through diet or water consumption. Dr Pooja Khullar, Radiation Oncologist from Dharamshila Narayana Superspeciality Hospital, New Delhi says: "The concept of alkaline water preventing cancer might sound promising, but there's no solid science to back it up. Cancer is a complicated disease, and drinking water with a different pH level won't stop it from developing. Alkaline water is just like bottled water with different mineral content. Alkaline water also can't change the pH of your blood." Dr Khullar further explains: "Some studies have shown that acidic environments help cancer cells grow. So the idea is that a diet high in alkaline foods (high pH) and low in acidic foods will raise the body's pH levels (make the body more alkaline) and prevent or even cure cancer. It should be noted that these are studies of cancer cells in a dish and do not represent the complex nature of how tumours behave in the human body. And food cannot change the pH of your blood. Research shows that there's no one diet or food that can cure and prevent cancer. The best way to reduce your risk of cancer is to focus on a healthy lifestyle—eating a balanced diet, staying active, and avoiding things like smoking and too much sun. It's important to stick to proven methods rather than getting sidetracked by unproven claims." Copper and silver have antimicrobial properties, and storing water in copper or silver vessels can reduce bacterial contamination. However, these metals do not make water alkaline or have any effect on cancer prevention. Similarly, storing water in earthen pots may help keep it cool and slightly enrich it with minerals, but it does not provide any cancer-fighting properties. Adding vegetables like cucumber, ginger, lemon, and carrot to water can add some flavour and provide minimal nutrients. However, it does not significantly alter the pH of the water, nor does it imbue the water with any cancer-preventing qualities. Excessive copper intake can lead to copper toxicity, which may cause symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and headaches. In severe cases, it can result in liver and kidney damage, neurological problems, and even death. Long-term exposure to high levels of copper can also increase the risk of liver disease and anaemia. Health claims like the one in this video are misleading because they provide false hope. These health claims further divert attention from scientifically proven methods of cancer prevention and treatment. Relying on unproven remedies like alkaline water can delay seeking appropriate medical care which can lead to worse outcomes.

title: Fact Check: Can almonds and butter cure stammering in kids?
claim_text: According to an Instagram post, you can cure stammering in kids by using almonds and butter.
quick_take: A social media post claims that almonds and butter can cure stammering in kids. We did the fact check to term this as False.
doctor_explanation:
No, food cannot cure stammering. Stammering, also known as stuttering, is a speech disorder that can involve repeating sounds, syllables, or words. It can be influenced by a combination of genetic, neurological, developmental, and environmental factors. There is no scientific basis to suggest that consuming specific foods, such as almonds and butter, can cure stammering. In fact, there is no cure for stammering as of now. Stammering often requires speech therapy, cognitive behavioural strategies, and, in some cases, medical interventions. While a balanced diet, including almonds and butter, is important for overall health, it does not target speech-related disorders.

We reached out to Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, for her expert insights. She says, "No, food alone cannot cure stammering. While maintaining a healthy diet is important for overall brain development and cognitive function, speech disorders like stammering require targeted speech therapy for proper management. There's no evidence that specific foods can directly improve or cure stammering."

Almonds and butter do not have a direct impact on speech development. Almonds are a great source of nutrients like vitamin E, magnesium, and healthy fats. On the other hand, butter contains fats and vitamins such as A and D. These foods can contribute to a child's overall nutritional needs, but they have no proven link to improving speech disorders like stammering. Speech and language development in children is a complex process that involves various factors, including brain development and motor skills. No studies show that specific foods can address these complexities in a way that cures stammering.

Speech therapy is the most recognised and effective treatment for stammering. Evidence-based treatments for stammering include speech therapy, cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), and sometimes the use of electronic devices to assist with fluency. Speech therapists work with children to develop communication techniques that help manage stammering, such as breathing exercises, slow speech practices, and learning to cope with anxiety that may worsen the condition.

Not exactly, but it's not that simple. While stammering cannot currently be cured, it can be effectively managed, especially in cases of developmental stuttering in kids. Since the causes of stammering vary between individuals, the management approach may also differ. Developmental stammering, which often begins in childhood, can improve with speech therapy and other interventions, but it doesn't have a definitive cure. On the other hand, stammering that develops in adulthood due to brain injury, stroke, or neurological conditions is usually much harder to treat and may not fully go away. These types of stammering are often referred to as acquired or neurogenic stuttering.

Researchers are investigating the early identification and treatment of stuttering, including studying genetic causes linked to stuttering in families. They have identified gene variants related to cell trafficking that may affect speech fluency. Brain imaging tools like MRI and PET scans are being used to study brain activity and structure in people who stutter, with the goal of improving treatment. Scientists are also working to help speech-language pathologists predict which children will outgrow stuttering and which are at risk of continuing into adulthood.

Misinformation about stammering can delay effective treatment and create false hope. Believing in unproven remedies, such as certain foods curing stammering, can prevent parents and individuals from seeking professional help, like speech therapy. Early intervention is important, particularly in children. Because, it can significantly improve long-term outcomes.

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, "There isn't a specific food that can directly cure or improve speech disorders like stammering. These conditions are usually treated with specialised therapies, such as speech and language therapy. That said, good nutrition—especially omega-3s, vitamins B12 and D, and antioxidants—supports brain health and development, which can indirectly help with speech. However, a balanced diet can't replace the need for professional therapy to manage speech disorders."

title: Fact Check: Can almonds, saunf, black pepper and mishri powder with milk increase eyesight and get rid of reading glasses?
claim_text: Combining almonds, saunf (fennel seeds), black pepper, and mishri powder mixed with milk can enhance eyesight and eliminate the need for reading glasses. verdict_original: This claim made by Instagram User is False. Eye glasses cannot be removed without surgical interventions.
quick_take: While almonds, saunf, black pepper, and milk are nutritious and beneficial for overall health, there is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that a mixture of these ingredients can improve eyesight or eliminate the need for reading glasses. doctor_explanation:
Dr. Rita Dash, Senior Consultant Ophthalmology at Manipal Hospital, Bhubaneshwar, explained: 'Your eyes are essential sensory organs, allowing you to perceive the world by capturing light and turning it into signals that your brain uses to create vision. Understandably, many of us are concerned about maintaining good eyesight, which leads people to seek remedies and follow social media advice, hoping to eliminate the need for glasses. One such idea is the consumption of almonds, saunf (fennel seeds), mishri (rock sugar), and black pepper with milk for improving vision. While these ingredients are undoubtedly nutritious and beneficial for overall health, they cannot eliminate the need for glasses or correct genetic factors that affect vision. Here's why: 1. Genetic Factors: The size and shape of your eyes are genetically determined. People with elongated eyeballs need minus-power (-) lenses to correct their vision, while those with shorter eyeballs need plus-power (+) lenses. These structural issues cannot be corrected with food. 2. Age-Related Vision Changes: As people age, particularly after 40, they often require reading glasses due to a condition called presbyopia. This occurs naturally as the lens of the eye becomes less flexible, making it harder to focus on close objects. No food or supplement can prevent or reverse this condition. 3. Cylindrical Lens Needs: People with astigmatism, where the shape of the cornea is irregular, require cylindrical lenses for correction. Nutritional supplements cannot change the shape of the cornea or cure astigmatism. 4. Benefits for Vitamin Deficiency: While the mentioned foods are rich in nutrients, they primarily benefit individuals with specific deficiencies. For example, children with dry eyes due to vitamin A deficiency may see improvements with proper nutrition, including foods like almonds and milk, which are rich in vitamins and healthy fats. However, this is different from correcting refractive errors like myopia (nearsightedness) or hyperopia (farsightedness).'

Dr. Sukanya Meikandasivam, Consultant - Ophthalmology at Gleneagles BGS Hospital, Kengeri, Bengaluru, explained further: 'The combination of saunf, mishri, black pepper with milk has nutritive value to ensure healthy eyes. Almonds are rich in vitamin E and omega fatty acids. Mishri, black pepper also have antioxidants to help in good eye health. The combined effect helps in cell regeneration, and reduce brain fog. Drinking it at bedtime can help in inducing sleep due to presence of tryptophan, that relaxes the nerves. However, as refractive error is due to axial length and growth related measurements, one cannot totally avoid glasses.'

Scientific evidence cited in the article:
- Fazira Latib Ratib et al.'s article reports that Tocopherol and Tocotrienol, two forms of vitamin E, exhibit antioxidant and neuroprotective effects, which may help lower intraocular pressure and safeguard optic nerve cells.
- An article published in Ophthalmology Research: An International Journal highlights conflicting evidence concerning the role of vitamins A and E in preventing eye diseases. Several epidemiological studies associate low vitamin E levels with a higher risk of nuclear or cortical cataracts. Furthermore, some research indicates that nutrition, especially oxidative stress, may impact intraocular pressure and the risk of developing glaucoma.

The article states there is no scientific evidence indicating that black pepper, mishri, or milk contribute to eye health once you need glasses. No evidence or medical consensus supports the claim that a mixture of almonds, fennel seeds (saunf), black pepper, and mishri with milk can improve eyesight or eliminate the need for reading glasses. Glasses can only be removed through LASIK, a type of refractive surgery.

A 2009 study in the Annals of Dermatology found that women over 45 who consumed 1,200 mg of aloe vera gel daily showed improvements in facial wrinkles and increased skin elasticity over 90 days. The researchers suggested that aloe's compounds helped stimulate collagen production and improve skin hydration. However, the effect is gradual and mild. It does not yield the quick, dramatic results that Botox offers. Aloe vera may reduce the appearance of fine lines, but calling it a replacement for Botox overstates its abilities. There is no actual collagen in aloe vera. However, aloe contains compounds such as glucomannan, vitamins C and E, and amino acids, which may help stimulate the skin's natural collagen production. By reducing oxidative stress and inflammation, aloe vera can create a favourable environment for collagen synthesis. But again, this is a long-term benefit, not a quick fix. Claims that aloe vera can do what serums and Botox can't are misleading. Serums are formulated with potent ingredients like hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and retinol, which penetrate the skin barrier and target specific issues like pigmentation or ageing. Botox works at the muscular level. Aloe vera is beneficial in its own right, it hydrates, soothes, and helps maintain a healthy skin barrier. It's a useful addition to a skincare routine, but not a replacement for scientifically designed products or procedures. Marketing aloe vera as superior to both injectables and topical serums distorts the science and can lead to false hope. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist & Aesthetic Medicine Consultant from Lucknow said, "Consuming aloe vera may help reduce the appearance of wrinkles, though its role as a natural Botox substitute is still under study. Its skin benefits come from its soothing properties, promoting hydration and regeneration, and a rich nutritional profile full of skin-supporting vitamins and minerals. Some studies suggest aloe vera supplements may improve skin elasticity, not by freezing muscles like Botox, but by locking in moisture and encouraging new cell growth. To harness aloe vera's full skin benefits, apply it topically as a gel or cream, or consume it as a supplement after medical consultation. For best results, combine it with a nutrient-rich diet and proper hydration. Individual results may vary, but consistency is key." While aloe vera is generally safe when applied to the skin, consuming it especially in large amounts or over long periods can lead to side effects.

title: Fact Check: Can aloo bukhara and imli cure fatty liver in 2 months?

Fatty liver is a multifactorial metabolic condition influenced by obesity, insulin resistance, diet, physical activity, and genetics. While dietary fiber in general plays a beneficial role in managing cholesterol levels by reducing its reabsorption in the intestines — which can indirectly support liver health as elevated cholesterol is a contributing factor in NAFLD — fiber-rich foods like aloo bukhara and tamarind cannot be considered a standalone cure.

Dr. Lohit Shetty Raju, Consultant - HPB and Liver Transplantation Surgery, Manipal Hospital Old Airport Road Bengaluru, stated: 'Fatty liver is typically a generalized condition, much like how fat accumulates throughout the body due to a sluggish metabolism or sedentary lifestyle, often linked to obesity from various causes. In such scenarios, fat also begins to deposit in the liver—this marks the earliest stage, transitioning a healthy liver into what is termed "fatty liver." While dry plums (aloo bukhara) and tamarind (imli) are both rich in fiber and antioxidants, there is currently no scientific evidence or peer-reviewed research that supports their direct role in curing fatty liver disease. However, fatty liver is a multifactorial metabolic condition influenced by obesity, insulin resistance, diet, physical activity, and genetics. Therefore, while fiber-rich foods like aloo bukhara and tamarind may assist in broader dietary strategies to manage fatty liver, they cannot be considered a standalone cure.'

Dr Piyush Ranjan, Vice-Chairperson, Institute Of Liver Gastroenterology & Pancreatico Biliary Sciences, Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, further stated: 'Diet is an important part of fatty liver management and it involves calorie reduction and fat control avoiding sugar. Things like taking Alu Bukhara and Imli are just fads.'

A study featured in Advances in Nutrition highlights five key dietary strategies for preventing and managing fatty liver disease: following traditional eating patterns such as the Mediterranean diet; cutting down on fructose intake by avoiding processed foods and sugary drinks; substituting saturated fats with healthier fats like polyunsaturated fats (PUFAs) — particularly long-chain omega-3s — and monounsaturated fats (MUFAs); replacing fast food, baked goods, and sweets with fiber-rich, whole foods such as whole grains, vegetables, fruits, legumes, nuts, and seeds; and minimizing alcohol consumption. Tiziana Fernández et al. found that lifestyle changes are effective in managing NAFLD, with a combination of dietary improvements and physical activity offering greater benefits than either approach alone. This combined strategy led to more significant improvements in liver enzyme levels and HOMA-IR, an indicator of insulin resistance.

The article concludes: 'A healthy diet significantly contributes to the prevention and control of fatty liver disease but it cannot cure fatty liver.'

title: Can alum and vitamin E permanently remove wrinkles?
claim_text: An Instagram post promotes a DIY serum consisting of alum and vitamin E capsules with the caption '100 साल तक झुर्रियाँ नहीं – फिटकरी और विटामिन E का गुप्त नुस्खा' (No wrinkles for 100 years – the secret recipe of alum and vitamin E), claiming the combination is particularly helpful for skin texture, spots and even wrinkles, and that it is a permanent solution to wrinkles.
quick_take: According to a widely shared Instagram post, wrinkles can be permanently removed by using a combination of alum with vitamin E. We analysed the claim and determined that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Wrinkles are folds, creases, or lines that appear on the skin's surface, occurring when skin loses structural integrity and resilience over time. They are caused by two major contributors: Intrinsic ageing (natural, time-dependent, genetic phenomenon where skin loses collagen, elastin, and hydration, leaving it less elastic) and Extrinsic ageing (caused by external variables like UV radiation, smoking, pollution, sedentary lifestyle, repetitive facial expressions). Alum and vitamin E have been suggested as a DIY skincare solution for wrinkles because they are thought to be safe and natural. While they might not have severe detrimental impacts, their all-encompassing impact could not be beneficial for wrinkled skin. Vitamin E is a thoroughly studied dermatological component - a fat-soluble antioxidant that can help neutralize reactive oxygen species. This may help stop collagen deterioration, inflammation, and photodamage. Furthermore, limited preliminary evidence suggests that it may help prevent or delay certain symptoms of ageing, particularly when coupled with other vitamin C-rich therapeutics. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetician, Trichologist, and Consultant in Aesthetic Medicine in Lucknow, elaborates that vitamin E may offer some protection against dryness and early signs of ageing and may additionally keep the skin moisturised. Given that wrinkles develop by deeper structural changes in the skin over time, they are frequently addressed with more specialised skincare products that include tried-and-true components such as retinoids, peptides, and sunscreen. Vitamin E can be incorporated into a moisturising regimen, but it shouldn't replace dermatologist-recommended therapies or the appropriate sunscreen. Alum (phitkari) has anti-inflammatory, tissue-constricting, and soothing effects and can be used in various medicinal or cosmetic preparations. Nevertheless, there is a dearth of reliable evidence supporting the use of alum to restore collagen or elastin in order to reverse wrinkles. While vitamin E may help delay the development of wrinkles and enhance the appearance of those that are already there, there are no compelling scientific trials to support the combination as a permanent miraculous remedy for wrinkle removal. Dr. Sachin Gupta, Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, emphasises that 'considering the limited and inconclusive nature of studies backing such remedies, it is advisable to opt for treatments with proven efficacy and established clinical benefits.' Wrinkles are primarily caused by enhanced oxidative stress and collagen breakdown, which cannot be addressed with unregulated local herbs. These can moisturise the skin temporarily, but they can't restore the structure of the skin. Moreover, improper or excessive use of some of these DIY therapies may cause skin irritation, allergic responses, or even accelerate skin deterioration. Dermatologists approach wrinkles with a well-crafted, evidence-based therapeutic regimen encompassing both treatment and prevention: Photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreens to address ultraviolet radiation), Topical applicants (retinoids for collagen synthesis and cell turnover, Vitamins E and C for antioxidants), and In-office interventions (laser resurfacing, dermal fillers, chemical peels, microdermabrasion, botulinum toxin injections). Dr. Rashi Soni, co-founder and consulting dermatologist, aesthetician, and hair transplant surgeon at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, explains that one of the most effective strategies for preventing more harm is to apply a high-quality sunscreen on a daily basis. Retinoids aid by promoting cell turnover and collagen production. Skin-plumping moisturisers that contain ceramides or hyaluronic acid help maintain the skin's protective layer. Lifestyle decisions are also critical - nutritious food, adequate sleep, and giving up nicotine can all have a noticeable impact.
