title: Can alum, coconut oil, or vitamin E remove wrinkles in a week?
claim_text: The combination of alum, coconut oil, or vitamin E can remove wrinkles in just a week.
quick_take: A well-shared Instagram post suggests that the combination of alum, coconut oil, or vitamin E can remove wrinkles in just a week. We fact-checked and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Wrinkles are fully developed, mature fine lines that originate from a confluence of environmental and chronological variables. Ageing is the primary contributor that results in deep lines and wrinkles. As fibroblast activity decreases over time, two vital structural proteins—collagen and elastin—are reduced, causing the skin to become thinner and less flexible. Excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation may accelerate ageing by generating reactive oxygen species, which induce matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) responsible for collagen and elastin degradation. While facial lines and wrinkles are a natural phenomenon, they raise concern when they reflect underlying skin damage, such as deep, coarse lines in sun-exposed areas, rapid onset, or accompanied by changes in skin texture, pigmentation, or loss of elasticity.

Do alum, coconut oil, and vitamin E really work well for wrinkles? No, not really. While anecdotal reports support their role, the combination lacks scientific validation, especially for deep, structural wrinkles.

Alum (fitkari): Alum is a common home product that can momentarily lessen the appearance of facial wrinkles due to its skin-tightening, astringent, and antioxidant qualities that combat free radicals. Nevertheless, no clinical studies have shown that alum can restore elastin or collagen to repair wrinkles. Furthermore, applying it on the face daily may cause dryness, irritation, or allergic reactions in those with sensitive skin.

Coconut oil: It is a well-recognised moisturiser that can effectively promote skin hydration, and along with stem cell extract, it may help reduce fine wrinkles and may increase collagen density. These results, however, are limited to preliminary studies. Furthermore, there is insufficient scientific evidence to support its effectiveness in minimising or smoothing deep or age-related wrinkles.

Vitamin E capsules: It is a lipophilic antioxidant that exhibits anti-inflammatory, barrier-stabilising, and photoprotective characteristics. While the constituent may improve skin texture, there is a dearth of scientific evidence supporting vitamin E's anti-wrinkle effect.

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetician, Trichologist, and Consultant in Aesthetic Medicine in Lucknow, explains that vitamin E may provide some protection against dryness and early signs of ageing and additionally keep the skin moisturised. However, wrinkles frequently respond to more specialised skincare products which incorporate tried-and-true ingredients such as retinoids, peptides, and sunscreen, as they originate from deeper structural changes in the skin over time. While vitamin E can be added to a moisturising routine, it shouldn't replace dermatologist-recommended therapies or a suitable sunscreen. Even while these ingredients have been labelled as safe, natural and even chemical-free, they are unlikely to reverse deep wrinkles. Established anti-ageing interventions remain the most dependable option for wrinkles.

Can any remedy or treatment visibly remove wrinkles in just one week? No, not exactly. This is due to the fact that wrinkle therapies usually take weeks to months to fully stimulate collagen or restructure the dermis. Prescription retinoids, such as retinol or tretinoin, can only significantly reduce wrinkles after a few weeks to months of application. Moreover, even while growth factors, peptides, and a specific topical anti-ageing product may show surface hydration and smoothing, meaningful wrinkle reduction may take weeks to manifest.

Dr. Sachin Gupta, Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, points out that "because of the limited and inconclusive nature of studies backing such remedies, it is advisable to opt for remedies with validated effectiveness and established clinical benefits." Claims that overpromise and use surface-level effects in a single week should be approached with caution. Real, long-lasting progress requires evidence-based, long-term therapy rather than quick fixes.

How are wrinkles addressed by dermatologists? Skin specialists take a personalised, multifaceted approach to facial wrinkles. The therapeutic intervention is usually based on whether the lines are deep, static, or superficial. Topical retinoids may be advised for long-term remodelling, helping in the production of collagen and improving the skin's texture by enhancing dermal collagen and anchoring fibrils. Dynamic wrinkles brought on by facial muscle activity may be addressed with botulinum toxin A injections, which may relax the muscles, smoothen expressive lines and may even induce some collagen formation over time. Skin care practitioners may also employ hyaluronic acid fillers to restore volume and fill deeper creases. In-office procedures like chemical peels or laser resurfacing may be beneficial for aggressive resurfacing, facilitating the removal of damaged upper skin layers and encouraging dermal repair. The dermatological anti-wrinkle regimen can be supported by antioxidants, UV protection, and lifestyle modifications.

Dr. Rashi Soni, co-founder and consulting dermatologist, aesthetician, and hair transplant surgeon at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, explains that when it comes to wrinkle reduction, doctors usually use methods with robust scientific support. Usually, the first step in the management procedure is to use a premium sunscreen that prevents further skin damage. After that, a doctor might give topical retinoids that encourage cell turnover and collagen synthesis. Wrinkles may also be dealt with using skin-plumping moisturisers that contain ceramides or hyaluronic acid to protect the skin's barrier. Individual decisions are also quite important; quitting smoking, maintaining a good diet, and getting adequate sleep can all have a big impact. Deeper wrinkles may benefit from in-clinic treatments like chemical peels or laser therapy.

title: Fact Check: Can alum tighten the vagina?
claim_text: An Instagram video claims that applying alum as a wash, douche, or paste to the vagina can tighten the muscles, enhance sexual pleasure, and even 'restore virginity.' It promotes alum as a quick and natural solution for vaginal tightening.
quick_take: A viral claim on social media suggests that alum can tighten the vagina. After investigating, we found this claim to be entirely false and potentially harmful.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Almas Fatma, General Physician from Navi Mumbai with a Diploma in Family Medicine and a PG in Digital Health, explains, 'Alum's astringent effect may cause a temporary tissue contraction, but this is only superficial. It does not strengthen the pelvic floor muscles, which actually determine vaginal tone. It's biologically incorrect to say the vagina becomes loose after childbirth or regular intercourse—the vagina is a highly elastic organ that naturally returns to its original shape over time. No products like alum should be applied to such a sensitive area, as they can cause rashes, irritation, or even infections.'

Dr Ayush Heda, MD, DNB (Gynaecology), MCh, Fellow of the European Society of Gynaecologic Oncology, Berlin, warns, 'Using alum vaginally is like applying a harsh chemical to sensitive skin; it can cause immediate irritation and long-term damage, including vaginal scarring. In some cases, such irritation can increase the risk of infections, which, if left untreated, could spread to the uterus or fallopian tubes, leading to more serious health issues, including infertility. Repeated use of alum may also contribute to chronic inflammation, potentially affecting the vagina's natural elasticity. This can lead to discomfort during sexual activity or daily life.'

Physiotherapist Prachi Bharwani explains, 'Kegel exercises are a game-changer for many of my patients. They're simple, free, and empower women to improve vaginal tone naturally. In addition to Kegels, certain yoga poses, such as Bridge, Child's Pose, or Goddess Pose, can engage the pelvic floor muscles and offer a holistic approach. For those needing additional support, pelvic floor physiotherapy can provide personalised exercises.'

The article further explains that alum does not tighten the vagina in any meaningful way. After childbirth, the vagina typically returns to its original elasticity over time. Scientifically, there is no such thing as a 'loose' vagina. Alum, being an astringent, causes a temporary shrinkage of tissues, creating a fleeting sensation of tightness. It does not strengthen the muscles responsible for vaginal tone. Applying alum to the vagina is unsafe and can lead to significant harm. The vaginal lining is delicate, and alum's corrosive properties can cause irritation or even burns. This not only disrupts the natural pH balance but also harms the healthy bacterial ecosystem of the vagina, increasing the risk of infections like bacterial vaginosis and yeast infections. A 2010 study highlighted that some Latina women use alum for vaginal tightening due to cultural beliefs, but there is no scientific evidence supporting its effectiveness or safety for this purpose. The study also emphasized the risks associated with vaginal douching, including alum use, which can lead to pelvic infections, reduced fertility, and other gynecological issues.

title: Can alum work as a spot and acne treatment for skin? - THIP Media

doctor_explanation:
Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow said, "Alum's effectiveness against acne-causing bacteria is debated. It has antibacterial properties, disrupting bacterial cell membranes and reducing pH levels. However, there's limited scientific evidence to confirm it kills bacteria like P. acnes. Alum may help reduce inflammation and dry out pimples, but it's not a proven bacteria-killer." 

Alum does have mild antibacterial properties, but that doesn't mean it can kill the bacteria responsible for acne, mainly Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes). In laboratory settings, alum (potassium aluminium sulphate) shows limited antibacterial effects against common pathogens. However, these studies are not specific to acne bacteria on human skin. The concentrations used in labs are much higher than what people typically apply topically. There are no clinical studies proving that alum can reduce acne or inflammation when used directly on the face. At best, alum can temporarily shrink the appearance of pores or dry out surface oil because it's an astringent, meaning it tightens tissues and reduces moisture. But this effect is cosmetic and short-lived. It does not target the deeper infection or inflammation that causes pimples. In fact, dermatologists warn that excessively drying the skin can worsen acne by triggering the sebaceous glands to produce more oil, creating a rebound effect.

Regarding fading dark marks or scars: The claimant in the video is claiming that alum can "lighten" dark spots due to its exfoliating and brightening properties, but there's no solid evidence to support this. Scientific research on alum's skin-lightening potential is extremely limited. A few studies have explored its use in reducing melanin production in lab conditions, but these findings don't translate into safe or effective results for humans. Moreover, alum's drying and irritating nature can cause post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, the very problem people often try to treat. Over time, continuous use of alum may damage the skin barrier, making it more prone to uneven tone, redness, or even tiny chemical burns.

Regarding safety: Alum is a natural salt compound that can irritate delicate facial skin. It's sometimes used after shaving because of its antiseptic and tightening effects, but even then, it's applied briefly and only on small areas of tougher skin. Repeatedly applying alum on the face, especially near sensitive areas like the eyes, mouth, or nose, can lead to skin damage. A report published in the Journal of Dermatological Treatment notes that natural mineral salts like alum can disturb the skin's acid mantle, the thin protective layer that keeps bacteria out and moisture in. Once that barrier is compromised, the skin becomes more vulnerable to inflammation and infections. If you have acne-prone or sensitive skin, using harsh astringents like alum can worsen your condition instead of improving it.

Safe, evidence-based options for fading acne marks include ingredients like niacinamide, azelaic acid, and topical retinoids, all backed by dermatological research.

title: Fact Check: Can aluminium foil relieve pain?

doctor_explanation:

Chronic pain, on the other hand, lasts much longer and can be due to conditions like arthritis, nerve damage, or ongoing inflammation. This long-lasting pain can significantly affect a person's daily life and often requires specialised treatment. Pain is also influenced by our emotions and mental state. Stress, anxiety, and depression can make pain feel worse. How we think about pain can also affect its intensity; focusing on pain or worrying about it can amplify the sensation. Effective pain management involves treating both the physical and emotional aspects of pain. This can include using medications, physical therapy, lifestyle changes, and alternative treatments like acupuncture or massage to help alleviate symptoms and improve quality of life.

No, not really. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that aluminium foil can relieve pain. Pain relief methods need to undergo rigorous testing and validation through clinical trials. Aluminium foil has not been shown to have any therapeutic benefits in pain management. While some alternative medicine practices might suggest unusual remedies, it's important to rely on treatments that have been proven effective through scientific research.

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi says: "I want to clear up some confusion about a recent claim that wrapping aluminium foil around body parts can relieve pain. To conclude, the claim that aluminium foil can relieve pain is false. There is no scientific evidence to support this notion, and it is always best to use proven methods for pain relief. quick_take: A social media post claims that mixing 4–5 cashews, one spoon of black chickpeas, half a spoon of white sesame seeds, jaggery, and honey, grinding them together and drinking it with a glass of milk can increase your 'bed timing' or sexual stamina. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Dr Yogesh Tandon, a Delhi-based sexologist, states that it cannot be confidently said that consuming this mixture will cure premature ejaculation or improve sexual timing. While this combination may significantly help in boosting overall strength and vitality, claiming that it can increase timing or prevent premature ejaculation is an exaggeration. Dr Mohit Sandhu, an Ayurveda Consultant and Kshar Sutra expert from Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh, shared that such videos are created purely for viewership. He pointed out that using appealing words attracts people, especially as social media and digital platforms have heavily influenced perceptions about sexual performance and timing. As a result, many try to copy these remedies and fall for these DIY suggestions. He clearly stated that the claim that this mixture can help with premature ejaculation or increase sexual timing is completely false, not mentioned in any Ayurvedic texts, and has no scientific evidence to support it. The article further explains that sexual stamina depends on a variety of factors: physical fitness, circulation, hormone levels, mental health, and energy levels. Good food supports these areas, but food alone won't solve stamina issues. If you're stressed, anxious, or physically unfit, no amount of nuts and seeds can magically extend your performance. While cashews contain zinc which supports testosterone production if someone is deficient, black chickpeas and sesame seeds contain nutrients generally good for hormone health, these benefits come from regular, balanced consumption over time, not from grinding everything into a paste and taking it with milk. There is no scientific proof that this combination can prevent premature ejaculation or directly increase bed timing.

title: Fact Check: Can an air fryer cause high antimony levels in a child?
claim_text: A mother's daily use of an air fryer resulted in astronomically high levels of antimony in her child's bloodwork. The antimony, a toxic metal, came from the air-fryer cord and contributed to her child's health issues, including autism.
quick_take: A social media video claims that an air fryer caused high antimony levels in a child's blood. We did a fact check and termed it as False.
doctor_explanation:
What is antimony? Antimony is a metallic element with the chemical symbol Sb and atomic number 51. It is abundant in nature primarily as the sulphide mineral stibnite (Sb2S3). Antimony has a variety uses in industrial applications including flame-retardant materials, lead-acid batteries, and microelectronics. It also has uses in some medical treatments for parasitic infections such as leishmaniasis. Although antimony compounds can be toxic, typical exposure levels for the general population are very low. It is generally less than 1 part per billion (ppb) in food and regulated to be below 6 ppb in drinking water.

Did the use of an air fryer lead to high antimony levels in the child? No, the use of an air fryer did not lead to high antimony levels in the child's blood. There is no scientific evidence or documented cases supporting the claim that air fryers can cause high levels of antimony in food or the human body. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) has issued recalls for various air fryers, but these were due to fire, burn, and laceration hazards, not because of antimony contamination. The woman in the Facebook video did not provide any proof or scientific data showing that her air fryer emitted antimony. Also, anything that's present in the cord of an air fryer cannot possibly contaminate the food.

Is there evidence that an air-fryer cord can release antimony into the food? No, not really. The claim lacks credible evidence. Plus, even if antimony were present in the jacketing of the cord, there would be no possibility for it to contaminate food cooked in the fryer. Electrical cords are usually insulated and separated from the cooking chamber, making it highly unlikely for any substance from the cord to leach into the food. The video mentioned provides no testing results or scientific validation of the cord containing or releasing antimony.

Do air fryers release toxic metals into food? No, they are not known to release toxic metals. Air fryers, like all kitchen appliances, must meet safety standards and regulations that prevent the release of harmful substances. Materials used in these appliances are evaluated for safety and compliance with health standards. The CPSC has not issued any recalls related to the release of toxic metals, including antimony, from air fryers. The main concerns addressed by the CPSC have been related to mechanical and electrical safety, not chemical contamination.

What levels of antimony exposure are considered normal? Low levels, usually measured in parts per billion (ppb). According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the general population can be exposed to low levels of antimony from food, drinking water, and dust. Typical antimony levels in food are less than 1 ppb. And, in drinking water, they should be below 6 ppb by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). These levels are safe for human health and do not pose significant risks. In contrast, the claim suggests astronomically high levels of exposure without providing specific measurements or context.

Could antimony exposure from air fryers cause autism? No, there is no evidence to support this. Autism is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder due to genetic and/or environmental factors. There is no credible scientific research linking antimony exposure from air fryers to autism. The video's suggestion that high antimony levels could be the cause of autism is speculative and not supported by existing scientific literature. Experts emphasise that environmental factors can contribute to autism. But, no single toxin has been definitively linked to its development.

How should consumers use air fryers safely? Air fryers are generally safe when used according to the manufacturer's instructions. It is important to follow safety guidelines to avoid mechanical hazards. Consumers should regularly inspect their appliances for any signs of damage, such as frayed cords or malfunctioning parts, and adhere to the recommended usage and maintenance procedures. Proper use and care of air fryers minimise risks and ensure safe cooking practices.

What is the regulatory context in India? India has strict safety standards for kitchen appliances. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) oversees the regulation of consumer products, including kitchen appliances like air fryers. Appliances must conform to the standards set by the BIS, which include specifications for electrical safety, materials used, and overall product safety. The BIS certification ensures that products meet rigorous safety and quality standards before they reach consumers. In addition, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) regulates food contact materials to ensure they do not release harmful substances into food. This regulatory framework ensures that products like air fryers are safe for use and do not pose health risks due to chemical contamination.

What are the health hazards of antimony exposure? Exposure to antimony, a metallic element, poses several health risks depending on the duration and level of exposure. According to the EPA, health hazards of antimony exposure can be: Acute effects: Acute exposure primarily affects the skin and eyes. Inhalation can cause skin rashes known as antimony spots and eye irritation like conjunctivitis. Oral exposure can lead to gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea. Animal studies have shown effects on the lungs, cardiovascular system, and liver from high-level inhalation. Chronic effects (Non-cancer): Chronic inhalation exposure can result in respiratory issues such as pneumoconiosis (lung inflammation), chronic bronchitis, and emphysema. Other effects include cardiovascular problems like increased blood pressure and altered EKG readings, as well as gastrointestinal disorders. Reproductive/Developmental effects: Reproductive issues reported include increased spontaneous abortions and menstrual disturbances in women exposed to antimony, though these studies are not definitive. Animal studies have also noted decreased offspring and reproductive process disturbances. Cancer risk: Human studies are inconclusive. But, animal studies have shown lung tumours in rats exposed to antimony trioxide. The EPA has not classified antimony for carcinogenicity due to insufficient evidence.

In conclusion, there is no scientific basis for the claim that air fryer cords can contaminate food with antimony. The materials and design of air fryers are intended to prevent such contamination. Every new invention like the refrigerator or the microwave has met with criticism and been a subject of several conspiracy theories. For instance, there's an ongoing claim that microwave ovens can cause cancer. Similarly, there's also a viral claim saying that wireless personal audio devices like AirPods can cause brain cancer. All these remain unproven and hence false. You should always rely on credible health organisations for correct healthcare information.

title: Can an almond-based recipe remove dark circles naturally?
claim_text: According to a trending Instagram post with the caption "डार्क सर्कल्स का खात्मा – 100% देसी इलाज", a combination of crushed almonds, honey and milk can efficiently remove dark circles.
quick_take: An Instagram reel is promoting an almond-based recipe for removing dark circles. Our fact-checking suggests that the claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Periorbital discolouration, also referred to as dark circles, is a frequent aesthetic challenge that gives the appearance of premature ageing or excessive exhaustion. This under-eye hyperpigmentation is usually triggered by interrelated contributing factors including sleep deprivation, excessive screen time, prolonged exposure to sunlight, frequent eye washing, allergies, and atopic issues. Since dark circles are an outcome of both internal and environmental variables, medical intervention is required for under-eye pigmentation. Analysis of each ingredient: ALMONDS: Due to their high vitamin E and antioxidant content, almonds and almond-based products are frequently used in topical skin care products. Although eating dietary almonds as part of a balanced diet has been demonstrated to enhance skin texture and reduce the intensity of face pigmentation, there is no clinical evidence to support their ability to eliminate dark circles under the eyes. MILK: Contains lactic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid that is mostly utilised as a skin brightener and moderate exfoliator. Even though using a milk mask or plain milk may enhance the appearance of the skin, there is no solid evidence that it may eliminate dark circles. HONEY: Has a high bioactive profile and antibacterial and anti-inflammatory qualities, has been demonstrated to be helpful in wound healing and may help with skin restoration, despite conflicting clinical evidence about its efficacy in treating under-eye hyperpigmentation. Dr. Rashi Soni, a Consultant Dermatologist at Mumbai's Rashi Hospital, states that while the aforementioned ingredients may appear to be natural substitutes, they are ineffective at reducing dark circles. Home therapies are insufficient to address under-eye pigmentation, which can be caused by a number of factors, including thin skin, ageing, lack of sleep, and genetics. Certain medications may offer slight cosmetic benefits, but they don't address the primary issue. Successful outcomes frequently call for persistence, perseverance, and a personalised skincare regimen supervised by a specialist. While milk, honey, and crushed almonds may exhibit modest exfoliating, moisturising, and antioxidant properties, they cannot replace evidence-based treatments designed to address the root causes of infraorbital dark circles. Dr. Iftekhar Khan, MD (Dermatology), Assistant Professor at SMS Medical College in Jaipur, reinforces that contrary to general consensus, home remedies are not the best approach to address under-eye discolouration. Due to the thinner and more sensitive skin behind the eyes, there could be negative consequences, and the problem could get worse. A thorough evaluation of the problem and persistent perseverance are necessary for under-eye therapy to be successful. Dark circles constitute a challenging cosmetic concern that is brought on by several factors, including genetics, vascular congestion, pigmentary alterations, skin thinning, and structural shadowing. Due to its intricacy, no single untested online recipe can ensure that dark circles are completely eliminated. Such trending assertions may not only oversimplify a specific multifactorial condition with multiple origins but may also ignore the significance of the critical dermatological assessment. Additionally, most of these inaccurate online hacks lack standardisation in terms of safety testing and clinical approval. Although such online remedies may be viewed as supportive measures, these require rigorous large-scale clinical trials to be established as a primary therapeutic intervention for dark circles.

title: Can an at-home formulation whiten skin in just 15 days?
claim_text: Applying alum, coconut oil, aloe vera gel, rose water, and a vitamin E capsule together can whiten skin in just 15 days.
quick_take: An Instagram reel is promoting an organic skin-whitening preparation that promises results in just 15 days. After fact-checking, we discovered that the claim is completely false.
doctor_explanation:
Skin colour is the visible hue of the skin that depends on the amount and type of melanin production. Skin pigmentation varies considerably from individual to individual and is generally determined by the presence of melanocytes, carotene, oxygenated haemoglobin, and regional blood circulation. Genetics are the primary determinant of an individual's baseline or constitutive skin colour; over 150 genes have been identified that influence skin pigmentation. Environmental factors also significantly affect skin appearance by changing the amount of melanin synthesised, with UV radiation from sunlight playing a significant role. Endocrine variables may also impact skin pigmentation; hormonal swings during pregnancy or as people age can significantly impact melanin synthesis, resulting in age spots or melasma. Additionally, certain medications and compounds may result in pigmentation by suppressing melanocyte activity.

The combination of alum, coconut oil, aloe vera gel, rose water, and vitamin E is often touted in home remedies for whitening skin, but scientific evidence for its effectiveness in modifying skin pigmentation is limited. Dr. Sachin Gupta from Amrita Hospital (MBBS, MD Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi) warns: 'In the field of dermatology, natural ingredients are not always synonymous with safety or efficacy, and what might seem harmless can actually be risky.' Dermatologists offer customized treatment based on scientific research, clinical expertise, and understanding of each patient's skin physiology.

Regarding the 15-day claim: no known measure can yield such significant outcomes in such a short period of time because random inheritance plays a major role in skin pigmentation. While regular application of certain local or botanical extracts might exhibit a moderate effect, such dramatic results in just two weeks are impossible.

Regarding unverified home remedies: relying on random online home remedies could lead to safety concerns as they lack strong scientific backing. Many DIY remedies are sold under the guise of Ayurveda, but the term is frequently used incorrectly to advertise skin-lightening modalities that frequently lack scientific backing. Long-term use of these formulations can cause neurological, renal, and cutaneous reactions.

Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, states that skin fairness primarily depends on genetics, followed by environmental triggers. While there are several approaches to make the skin more radiant, skin pigmentation itself can only be enhanced; it cannot be changed. It is possible to restore the natural skin colour that may have been diminished over time due to ageing, exposure to harsh environments, and other factors including diet and medication, but skin colour cannot be altered by topical remedies.

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, dermatologist, cosmetician, trichologist, and consultant for aesthetic medicine in Lucknow, further states that a cure is not necessarily appropriate for your skin simply because it includes ingredients from the kitchen. Using unrefined or untested blends could irritate your face's sensitive skin, cause an allergic reaction, or even make pre-existing conditions worse. In skincare, 'natural' does not necessarily mean 'harmless'. The promotion of natural skin-whitening remedies frequently reinforces negative beauty standards, causing psychological discomfort for those who feel compelled to conform to these ideals.

Maintenance of healthy skin necessitates a comprehensive approach. Environmental variables and genetics play a major role in controlling skin pigmentation. While an unproven topical herbal composition might hydrate and moisturise the skin, it might not have any effect on skin whitening. Therefore, one should consult a dermatologist for an individualised skincare regimen.

title: Fact Check: Can an at-home routine clear dark spots in 7 days?
claim_text: A popular Facebook post with the caption "कितनी भी पुरानी झाइयों को 7 दिन में ठीक करें" claims that dark spots can be successfully removed by applying a shredded potato scrub with milk, followed by a blend of egg whites and potato juice – with starch – along with corn flour.
quick_take: According to a trending Facebook post, an at-home routine can effectively clear dark spots in 7 days. We verified the claim and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Dark spots, or hyperpigmentation in clinical terms, are patches of skin that seem darker than the surrounding tissues. They usually develop when melanocytes are overstimulated by external or internal stimuli. Melasma is an established form of hyperpigmentation that is prevalent in women due to its significant correlation with sun exposure, oral contraceptives, and pregnancy. It is not, however, the only type. Additional common types include those linked to excessive melanin production or deposition. Although most age spots are harmless, if they develop changes in size or colour, are irregular, bleed, or persist, a dermatologist should be consulted immediately to rule out any underlying pathology.

Can a potato-milk scrub effectively address hyperpigmented skin? No, not exactly. While the scrub of shredded potato and milk is a popular home remedy for hyperpigmentation, the recipe lacks substantial scientific evidence. Potatoes are a popular ingredient utilised for skin care because they contain catecholase and small amounts of vitamin C, which may exert modest antioxidant effects. Milk is under consideration, as it contains lactic acid, an alpha-hydroxy acid known to promote gentle exfoliation and improve skin texture. Despite these advantages, it is important to recognise that the concentration of the active ingredients in milk and potatoes is neither scientifically proven nor standardised to correct pigmentation. Furthermore, frequent physical scrubbing, particularly on sensitive or acne-prone skin, can damage the skin barrier and aggravate post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Should one rely on egg white, potato juice with its starch, and corn flour for dark spots? No, not really. There is no clinical evidence that egg white, potato starch or corn flour may manage established hyperpigmentation or melasma. Contrarily, the excessive use of such unregulated topical preparations can be more detrimental than beneficial. Importantly, hyperpigmentation, especially melasma, is a complex pigmentary condition driven by UV exposure, hormones, vascular factors, and melanocyte hyperactivity – mechanisms that cannot be addressed by such home preparations.

Why are alternative therapies becoming popular for dark spots? Do they work in 7 days? Unregulated web-based remedies often are promoted as safer, gentler, and more culturally acceptable than potent prescription medications. Certain plant elements may have mild antioxidant or melanin-inhibiting effects, but they do not undergo the identical rigorous scientific testing as pharmaceutical products. It is also crucial to distinguish between brightness brought on by better skin health and reduced pigmentation. Although these therapies may enhance skin quality, there is no medical evidence that they can safely or substantially lighten skin. Another crucial consideration is that the claim that dark spots can be removed in just 7 days is unrealistic and unscientific. This is because the skin's normal regeneration cycle takes much longer and the melanin that forms the spot is deeply embedded in the skin's layers. Most treatments show results in two to three weeks, but major fading often takes several months.

Dr. Sachin Gupta (MBBS, MD Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi) of Amrita Hospital explains: "Organic ingredients are not always synonymous with safety or efficacy, and what could seem harmless can actually be harmful."

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Lucknow-based Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic medicine consultant adds: "A natural cure isn't always beneficial for your skin simply because it uses everyday products. Using unproven or experimental mixes may cause allergic responses, irritate the delicate skin on your face, or even exacerbate pre-existing conditions. Certain compounds, for instance, may be very abrasive, clog your pores, or alter the natural balance of your skin. Always begin with patch testing, and if you're not sure, consult a dermatologist. When it comes to skincare in particular, natural does not always equate to safe."

Dermatologists manage hyperpigmentation using a standardised, clinically established methodology that prioritises melanin production and skin turnover in addition to addressing the root causes. Regular ultraviolet protection is the first step in controlling hyperpigmentation. Frequent application of a suggested broad-spectrum sunscreen may help prevent UV-induced melanocyte activation and reduce pigmentation deterioration. Dr. Swati Watwani, Medical Director, Co-Founder, and Chief Consultant of Persianlay – Skin/Hair/Aesthetics/Ayurveda Clinic states: "Topical creams like hydroquinone, tretinoin, topical steroids, alpha hydroxy acid creams, azelaic acid, arbutin, liquorice, and kojic acid can reduce melasma, photomelanosis, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation." Other therapies could be employed if these medications fail to resolve the issue. Supportive practices, including following a sun protection schedule, avoiding unsupervised harsh products, and exfoliating excessively, can help contribute to the recommended therapy.

Conclusion: Certain at-home remedies may be beneficial for mild or early pigmentation, but they shouldn't be the primary therapy for multifaceted conditions such as pigmented patches. Evidence-based therapies are still more effective.

title: Fact Check: Can an Ayurvedic juice cure lumps naturally?
claim_text: A trending Facebook post promotes an Ayurvedic juice made from 2 leaves each of banyan, peepal, and guava; 4-5 paan leaves; 15-20 leaves of curry, mint and coriander; some kadi patta; 50-70 grams of methi, spinach, nearly a whole turmeric root, ginger, amla, and beetroot. The post claims that drinking this preparation daily can help eliminate lumps like cancerous cysts and tumours.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that drinking an ayurvedic juice may completely eradicate lumps such as malignant cysts and tumours. After verifying the claim, we determined that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: According to the American Society of Cancer, tumours and cysts are regarded as abnormal bodily growths. However, their components, structure, and clinical implications are entirely distinct. A tumour is a dense, aberrant mass of tissue that usually develops when cells proliferate uncontrollably due to genetic mutations that interfere with cellular division and apoptosis pathways. A tumour's cellular behaviour determines whether it is benign, premalignant, or malignant. A cyst is a sealed sac or lump of tissue that contains fluid, semi-solid, or gaseous content, often benign or non-cancerous in origin, arising from infections, chronic inflammation, or duct obstructions. Cystic lesions are usually benign, but the rare potential for transformation into cancer depends on cyst type, location, age, and medical history. Malignant transformation may be visible in kidneys, ovaries, and pancreas. Complex ovarian cysts in postmenopausal women may be a sign of early-stage ovarian cancer. Determining if a cyst is malignant requires thorough clinical assessment with CT, MRI, and biopsy. Elevated tumour markers like CA-125 in ovarian cysts help in diagnosis. In Ayurvedic scriptures, a lump or cystic lesion is referred to as Granthi, developing from dosha imbalances with reduced metabolism. While Ayurveda recommends herbal juices and decoctions to balance doshas and detoxify, scientific validity for managing lumps like tumours or cysts is lacking. Guava leaves (Psidium guajava) possess potent antibacterial and anti-inflammatory characteristics and may influence inflammatory enzymes and tissue healing. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) and turmeric (Curcuma longa) have anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-proliferative qualities linked to cancer prevention. Methi or fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is high in phytoestrogens and saponins with lipid-lowering and hormonal balancing properties beneficial for PCOS-related cystic lesions. Antioxidant profiles in amla (Emblica officinalis), beetroot, mint, and coriander support liver function and detoxification. Peepal (Ficus religiosa) and banyan (Ficus benghalensis) leaves have Rasayana or rejuvenative properties with limited evidence for antibacterial and wound-healing benefits. However, paan or betel leaves should be used with caution as excessive or long-term consumption has been linked to mucosal alterations and carcinogenic outcomes. According to Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita School of Ayurveda, lumps, fibroids, and tumours can have a wide range of causes and forms; hence, there is no specific treatment for them. Every disease needs a precise diagnosis and treatment plan. Furthermore, he stated that while some herbs may show promise in lab studies, there is insufficient clinical evidence to support their application as proven human treatments. Using these treatments without a doctor's advice can cause delays in receiving the care you need. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, backs this up by stating that Ayurveda is a comprehensive medical system that goes beyond simple herbal beverages and home cures. It entails a thorough diagnosis and course of therapy based on the individual's body type and the nature of a medical condition. Therapies such as Panchakarma, food, lifestyle modifications, and botanicals can all be used as treatments. Ayurvedic medicine is not restricted to consuming herbs or liquids without proper advice. Dr. Gohil also cautions that endorsing unverified cancer therapies is not only reckless but also inappropriate from a scientific standpoint. Hence, anyone with lumps or even cancer must consult an experienced doctor, whether they practise Ayurveda, modern medicine, or both. Ayurvedic practitioners may help alongside modern allopathic treatments with supportive therapies. Even though many ingredients in this juice recipe may offer potential benefits, there is a lack of credible scientific clinical evidence to support its effectiveness in curing or reversing cystic or cancerous growths. Since these outgrowths can be complex, relying solely on such preparations can delay critical medical care. Such remedies should only be used as adjunct therapy and always under the guidance of a multidisciplinary team of medical experts. For malignant cystic lumps, treatment includes surgical excision as the mainstay, often combined with radiation therapy or chemotherapy. Immunotherapy or targeted medications may help in inoperable cases with modifiable molecular changes. Hormonal therapy may be used when hormone receptors play a part. Tumour markers and follow-up imaging are crucial for post-treatment surveillance.

title: Can an eye exercise permanently improve vision without surgery or glasses?
claim_text: A simple eye exercise, performed for one minute a day, can permanently improve vision. The post also claims it can cure eye strain, blurry vision, and dry eyes, and eliminate the need for glasses, surgery, or drops.
quick_take: A social media post claims that an eye exercise can permanently improve vision without surgery or glasses. We fact checked this claim and found that this is false.
doctor_explanation: Eye exercises cannot simply improve vision. While these exercises can help with certain aspects of eye health, they cannot permanently improve refractive errors like myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), or astigmatism. These conditions are usually caused by the shape of the eye, which eye exercises cannot alter. Vision correction often requires corrective lenses or surgery, which address the structural issues. Similarly, there are claims that Mudras or hand exercises can improve vision. However, this is entirely false. The claim that eye exercises can replace glasses or surgery is not supported by scientific evidence. Glasses correct vision by refracting light to focus it properly on the retina, while surgeries like LASIK reshape the cornea to correct refractive errors. Unlike these methods, eye exercises do not alter the physical structure of the eye. Dr Aftab Alam, Consultant Ophthalmologist and Eye Surgeon at Dr Aftab Eye Care, Bareilly, explains that regular eye exercises can support overall eye health and ease discomfort caused by prolonged screen time. While these exercises may help reduce strain and irritation, they do not eliminate the need for glasses or cure eye conditions. If discomfort persists, consulting a medical professional is essential. Maintaining good eye care habits is crucial for long-term vision health. Dr Pradeep Dahale, Consultant Ophthalmologist at Manipal Hospital Baner, Pune, states that while eye exercises can improve comfort and reduce strain, they cannot correct refractive errors or enhance vision. He emphasises that these exercises, though beneficial for eye health, cannot replace glasses, contact lenses, or medical treatments needed for vision correction. Some eye exercises can help ease eye strain and dry eyes by promoting relaxation and increasing blood flow. For instance, the 20-20-20 rule (looking at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes) can reduce eye strain. Blinking exercises can help with dry eyes by stimulating tear production. However, these exercises do not cure the underlying causes of these conditions; they only provide temporary relief. Blurry vision can result from various factors, including refractive errors, dry eyes, or more serious medical conditions, and exercises alone cannot address all of these. While they may help delay or prevent refractive errors to some extent, they are not a substitute for proper eye care. Certain eye exercises can improve blood circulation to the eyes. For instance, moving the eyes in different directions can stimulate blood flow. This improved circulation can potentially nourish eye tissues to some extent. However, the claim that this alone will lead to significant or permanent vision improvement lacks strong scientific evidence. Ophthalmologists are aware of eye exercises. They often recommend them for managing eye strain and dry eyes. However, they do not promote them as a cure for refractive errors or as a replacement for glasses or surgery because there is no scientific evidence to support such claims. The assertion that "90% of ophthalmologists never mention this" is likely a sensationalised statement meant to mislead viewers.

title: Fact Check: Can an intimate whitening cream work instantly? - THIP Media
claim_text: 10 Seconds Instant Whitening Cream - Whiten all skin areas: underarms, necklines, private areas, shoulder straps, cuffs and bikini prints, and for elbows and toes… Only PHP 1/day, instantly smooth pink and white skin Confident in bikini showing off hot body. We use an innovative and advanced formula for this dark spot cream to evenly and gently improve uneven skin tone, and insist on using it to significantly improve dull skin.
quick_take: A social media post claims that one can instantly whiten their skin, especially their private parts, armpits, knees and elbows by applying a cream. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
Human skin is available in a variety of tones and colours. Several factors influence skin colour, but genetics determines constitutive skin colour. The enzyme tyrosinase is primarily responsible for the genetic mechanism that controls human skin colour. Melanin, the primary determinant of human skin colour, is produced in the skin by melanocytes. Thus, it should be noted that the genes that determine skin colour are controlled by melanin quantity and quality. Also, genetic factors influence skin color, but this can be further affected by exposure to sunlight, which can trigger the production of melanin and tanning reactions. Vitamin D, like melanin, has been shown to regulate cellular proliferation and differentiation in various tissues, including the skin, which may influence skin colour.

Not exactly. There is no scientific evidence to support that an intimate whitening cream can whiten skin in 10 seconds. In fact, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved any over-the-counter skin whitening creams that can whiten skin instantly. Some skin whitening creams contain ingredients that can lighten the skin over time, but these ingredients do not work instantaneously. Skin-lightening products usually work by reducing the production of melanin, a pigment that gives color to the skin. These ingredients include hydroquinone, kojic acid, and azelaic acid. These products usually require regular and consistent use over a period of time to see any noticeable results, and individual results can vary. However, these ingredients can also irritate the skin, and they should only be used under the supervision of a doctor. Apart from the potential risks, the effects will quickly dissipate.

On redirecting to the mentioned link on the claim, we found the product named, "Body Whitening Cream Intimate Area Pink Essence" which claims to lighten various skin areas. However, throughout the description of the products, no list of ingredients could be found which can either confirm that its ingredients might be helpful in changing the skin color. The purported use of this product doesn't have any scientific evidence as no record could be found for its clinical testing. Skin whitening products, including creams and lotions, often claim to lighten or brighten the skin tone. However, it is important to approach such claims with caution. Instant skin whitening is not possible with any cream or product.

Dr. Jyoti Agarkar, MD (Dermatology) sums it up by stating, "God has given us a very beautiful body and skin. We should cherish it instead of trying to change its colour. I always prescribe my patients a healthy diet, regular exercise, enough sleep, and good water consumption. This helps in bringing out a natural glow that cannot be matched by any artificially induced whitening products. Also, when choosing skincare products, choose according to your skin type."

doctor_specialization: MD (Dermatology)

title: Can an IV drip really transform your skin and mood fast?
claim_text: An Instagram post suggests that IV drip can manage internal stress caused by lifestyle, fatigue, and pollution. The woman in the video claims that it can offer glowing skin, better hydration, high energy, and a fresher mood, all from the inside, in just half an hour. She also claims it works by providing vitamin C, B complex, hydration, and glutathione directly into the bloodstream, meeting all nutritional needs of the skin.
quick_take: A social media post claims that an IV drip can transform your skin and mood quickly, in just 30 minutes. However, our fact check finds this claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist, Aesthetician, and Hair Transplant Surgeon at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, explains, "An IV drip may help with quick hydration and deliver some vitamins directly into the bloodstream, which can make you feel refreshed for a short while. But it can't fully recharge the body from late nights, stress, or traffic-related exhaustion. These issues build up over time and need a complete approach, like proper sleep, good nutrition, sun protection, skincare, and stress management. An IV drip can support your routine, but it isn't a shortcut to glowing skin or lasting energy." Dr Sachin Gupta, Senior Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, says, "IV drips can deliver certain vitamins like C and B complex, and antioxidants like glutathione, which may support skin health to some extent. But no single drip can meet all the skin's nutritional needs. Healthy, glowing skin comes from a mix of things—balanced diet, hydration, sun protection, sleep, and skincare. An IV drip might give a mild boost, but it's not a magic solution. Real skin health builds from the inside and the outside, over time." The article explains that IV drips can provide immediate hydration and may offer a short-lived energy boost by delivering fluids, electrolytes, and certain vitamins directly into the bloodstream. However, they cannot "fully recharge" the body in a complete or lasting way. A 2024 study shows that IV drips may offer some short-term skin benefits, like improved hydration and a mild glow, but the effects are neither instant nor dramatic, and results vary widely between individuals. Multiple sessions are often required, and it's far from the quick fix portrayed in the Instagram post. While IV drips can deliver vitamins and antioxidants like Vitamin C, B complex, and glutathione directly into the bloodstream, bypassing the digestive system which theoretically allows for higher absorption, the claim that it provides "all" nutritional needs for the skin is an overstatement. Skin health is complex and influenced by a multitude of factors, including a balanced diet, proper skincare, sun protection, genetics, and overall health. The idea of an "inside out glow" through an IV drip is more of a marketing concept than a scientifically proven, comprehensive dermatological solution. Achieving "soft skin, high energy, and a fresh mood" as a complete and lasting transformation in just 30 minutes is an exaggeration. The immediate effects are primarily due to rehydration. For long-term changes in skin texture, sustained high energy levels, or improved mood, addressing lifestyle factors, dietary habits, and underlying health conditions is far more critical and effective than a single 30-minute IV infusion.

title: Fact Check: Can an oil-based navel therapy help with digestion?
claim_text: Applying an Ayurvedic oil to the navel enhances digestion, detoxification, and helps in the production of serotonin (the happy hormone) which is primarily synthesised in the gut rather than the brain.
quick_take: According to a social media post, applying an Ayurvedic oil to the navel enhances digestion and detoxification. We verified the assertion and found that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Nabhi Chikitsa, or Navel therapy, is the term used in Ayurveda to describe the application of oil to the navel. The most commonly utilised oils are coconut, neem, and mustard. The therapy is gaining popularity because the navel, where the umbilical cord attaches during foetal life, is a focal point of energy linked to digestion, emotional balance, and even skin health. As a result, it is believed to enhance facial brightness and aid with musculoskeletal, digestive, immunological, and fertility issues. Despite the practice's supposed subjective benefits, its application should be viewed as complementary rather than therapeutic. As per certain traditional practices, it is believed that the oil can be absorbed into the body through the navel. This could be attributed to the absorption of certain medications and oil-based compounds through the transdermal route, which may include the peri-umbilical region. Transdermal delivery systems (TDDS) are known for their ability to deliver substances by bypassing hepatic metabolism, potentially enabling both localised and systemic absorption based on the biochemical properties of the molecules involved. However, scientific evidence backing the absorptive capabilities of the skin surrounding the navel remains insufficient. Additionally, the idea that the Pechoti gland, which is supposedly located behind the navel, serves as the conduit for oil absorption has not much anatomic and histologic scientific basis. Hence, it is critical to clarify that applying oil to the navel skin may be calming and hydrating, but it may not offer any therapeutic benefits. This is further confirmed by Dr P. Rammanohar, Research Director at Amrita School of Ayurveda, who clarifies that 'applying oils on the navel for curing diseases is not supported by traditional Ayurvedic texts and has no scientific validity.' He further points out that although Ayurveda utilises oils in massage and therapies, true Ayurvedic practice does not include the idea that the navel is a healing centre for all health issues. Additionally, Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, supports this by explaining that menstruation and digestive problems frequently result from underlying imbalances in the body, such as weak digestive fire (agni) or disruptions in the doshas. Managing these illnesses in Ayurveda entails dietary adjustments, lifestyle changes, internal herbal remedies, and a thorough grasp of the patient's constitution. Hence, as per the traditional Ayurvedic therapy, merely applying oil on the navel won't resolve digestive issues. Although safe for otherwise healthy people, applying oil to the navel cannot be a conclusive medical procedure. The benefits of essential oil application primarily include: Massage therapy - applying extra virgin olive oil to the area of the abdomen surrounding the navel (rather than the navel itself) may help relieve constipation; Chinese medicine belly button application - putting certain herbal remedies in the navel may help in paediatric diarrhoea via localised transdermal and thermoregulation effects. There is no reliable scientific evidence to support the practice of putting oil in the navel, and such assertions should always be viewed with caution. As per the post, the Ayurvedic preparation consists of coconut oil, sesame oil, castor oil, and powdered herbs, including asafoetida, fennel, ginger, triphala, and carom seeds. It should be clarified that most of these ingredients exhibit respective digestive benefits, provided they are administered through established routes. The aforementioned ingredients may be beneficial, they cannot cure digestive issues brought on by underlying medical illnesses. While oil-based navel therapy might provide short-term relief, hydration, or relaxation, it is not a reliable treatment for any long-term or severe digestion-related health issues. To substantiate the notion that oil-based navel therapy improves digestion, large-scale, randomised, placebo-controlled investigations are required.

doctor_specialization: Research Director, Amrita School of Ayurveda; MD Scholar, All India Institute of Ayurveda

label: Mostly False

title: Fact Check: Can an oil massage cure paralysis in just 2 minutes?
claim_text: A viral Facebook video claims that an unnamed 'chamatkari' (magical) Ayurvedic oil made from rare herbs can completely cure paralysis from the roots in just 2 minutes through massage. The speaker in the video also claims he can treat any illness with this oil.
quick_take: A social media post claims that an oil massage can cure paralysis in just 2 minutes. After fact checking, we found it to be false.
doctor_explanation: Paralysis cannot be cured in 2 minutes by any oil or massage—Ayurvedic or otherwise. It occurs due to nerve damage or brain injury, such as from stroke, spinal cord injury, or neurological conditions. Recovery, if it happens at all, takes time, therapy, and proper medical care. No scientific or medical evidence supports instant or very quick recovery from paralysis through topical oils or massage. Even in Ayurveda, treatment of paralysis (Pakshaghat) involves a long-term approach using therapies, herbs, diet, and Panchakarma. It does not offer instant cures. Dr Mohit Sandhu, Consultant Ayurvedic Practitioner at AgniShalya Ayurvedic Hospital and Research Centre, Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh, explains: 'No, not even according to Ayurveda can paralysis be fully cured in just 2 minutes by any oil massage. However, applying specific medicated oils like Mahanarayan tail, Ksheerabala tail, or Dhanwantaram tail, along with vigorous massage (Abhyanga) and heat therapy (Swedana), may help stimulate the nerves, improve blood circulation, and bring some temporary movement or sensation. In very rare and early-stage cases, especially when the paralysis is functional, such as in hysterical paralysis or mild Bell's palsy, some minor movements might return quickly. But this is not a cure; it is only short-term relief of symptoms.' He continues: 'The Ayurvedic approach to paralysis includes a combination of therapies. These may involve Snehana (internal and external use of medicated oils), Swedana (fomentation to ease stiffness and pain), and Basti (medicated enema), which is considered especially effective for Vata-related conditions. Treatments like Nasya (for head and neck issues), Shirodhara or Shirobasti (to calm the nervous system), and Rasayana therapy (to help with nerve regeneration and vitality) are also used. In some cases, practitioners may also use Marma Chikitsa or Agnikarma to stimulate neuromuscular points.' Dr Sandhu concludes: 'Ayurveda offers a holistic and step-by-step approach to managing paralysis. It does not support instant cures. Claims of a '2-minute cure' are misleading and classical Ayurvedic texts or real clinical experience do not back this.' Dr Muskan Thakur, BAMS, an Ayurveda Consultant from Indore, says: 'Classical Ayurvedic texts or scientific evidence do not support this claim. In Ayurveda, paralysis (Pakshaghat) is a serious condition which happens due to an aggravated Vata dosha, affecting the nervous system. Treatments involve a holistic and gradual approach, including medicated oil massages (Abhyanga), Panchakarma therapies (such as Pizhichil and Basti), internal herbal medications, and lifestyle modifications. While oils like Mahanarayana Taila or Dhanwantaram Tailah help nourish the nerves and improve function over time, no Ayurvedic oil can cure paralysis instantly.' She adds: 'Also, the claim that a single oil can treat all illnesses contradicts Ayurveda's principle of individualised treatment based on dosha, dhatu, and roga. Hence, such statements are misleading and people should be careful before believing such claims.' Without knowing what the oil contains, it is impossible to assess its safety or effectiveness. The video does not mention any herbs, manufacturing details, or official approvals. It also fails to provide proper product information or verified credentials of the so-called 'Vaidya,' the Ayurvedic doctor featured in the video. It provides only a phone number for placing orders. Ayurveda does use certain herbs to support nerve and muscle health, but these remedies do not work instantly. It is also important to use any medication only under proper medical guidance. Without clear information about the ingredients, users risk skin reactions, allergies, or even falling victim to financial scams. In India, a qualified Ayurvedic doctor must have a BAMS (Bachelor of Ayurvedic Medicine and Surgery) degree and be registered with a recognised medical board. The person in the video makes big claims but does not provide any name, registration, or proof of qualifications. Falsely presenting oneself as a doctor is a punishable offence under Indian law. According to the Indian Penal Code Section 419, cheating by impersonation—including pretending to be a doctor—can lead to up to three years in prison, a fine, or both. Trusting such unverified sources can delay proper treatment and cause harm. Treatment for paralysis focuses on helping the person move better, manage everyday tasks, and live more independently. A team of experts, including physiotherapists and occupational therapists, work with the patient to build strength and improve movement. Speech therapists may also help if the person has trouble speaking or swallowing. Depending on the cause, doctors may give medicines like blood thinners after a stroke or recommend surgery if nerves are under pressure. People often use support tools such as wheelchairs, braces, or walking aids. Recovery usually takes time. In many cases, full recovery may not be possible, so the aim is to make the best use of the abilities that remain.

title: Fact Check: Can an orange-mint drink burn fat in 4 days?
claim_text: A drink made from 2 oranges, 3 limes, 4 mint leaves, 1 cup of ice, and orange juice will "burn fat" and give visible results in 4 days.
quick_take: A social media post claims that an orange-mint drink can burn fat in 4 days. After fact checking, we found that this claim is false.
doctor_explanation: The concept of a specific food or drink actively "burning" fat in the body is a common misconception. Fat loss, scientifically known as reducing adipose tissue, primarily occurs when you are in a calorie deficit. This means you consistently consume fewer calories than your body uses over time. Your body then taps into stored fat for energy. Ingredients like citrus fruits offer vitamins and hydration, but they do not contain compounds that directly trigger fat burning or significantly boost metabolism to achieve this effect on their own. The calories consumed from the orange juice in the recipe would also contribute to your overall daily intake, potentially counteracting any minor metabolic effect. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, "No drink, whether it includes oranges, limes, mint or juice, can directly burn fat. These ingredients are refreshing and full of nutrients, but they don't trigger fat loss on their own. Sustainable fat loss comes from creating a calorie deficit through healthy eating and regular physical activity; it doesn't happen overnight." Achieving visible results in terms of fat loss in only four days is highly unrealistic for the vast majority of people through dietary changes alone, let alone by simply adding a single drink to their routine. Significant and visible fat loss requires a sustained calorie deficit over a longer period, typically weeks or months, combined with regular physical activity. Your body weight might fluctuate slightly day-to-day due to water retention or other factors, but these changes are not visible fat loss. A healthy rate of fat loss is generally considered to be around 0.5-1 kg per week, which would take much longer than four days to show a noticeable difference in appearance. Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, says, "It's very unlikely that any drink can give visible fat loss results in just four days. Our bodies need time to respond to changes in diet and lifestyle. Real fat loss happens gradually, through a combination of eating fewer calories, staying active, and being consistent. Drinks like these may help you feel fresh or reduce bloating for a short while, but they won't melt fat or change your body shape overnight." Dr P Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA), explains from an Ayurvedic perspective: "Ayurveda considers obesity a complex condition that needs a long-term, personalised approach. The classical texts describe it as 'na hi sthulasya bheshajam', meaning there is no single medicine that can cure it. No drink or herbal remedy alone can lead to fat loss or visible results in just a few days. Ayurveda focuses on bringing balance to the body through lifestyle changes, stress management, and tailored diets. Medicines or herbal preparations may support the process, but lasting results come from consistent and holistic care." Regarding citrus fruits and mint: Oranges and limes are low in calories and provide valuable vitamins (especially Vitamin C) and fibre (if the whole fruit is used, though juicing reduces fibre content). Fibre can help you feel fuller for longer, which can indirectly support weight management by helping to control appetite and overall calorie intake. Mint is also very low in calories and can add flavour without sugar. Staying hydrated by drinking fluids, including water or low-calorie infused water like this (minus the added orange juice, which adds calories), is important for overall health and can play a minor role in metabolism. However, these benefits are part of a balanced diet and healthy lifestyle and do not equate to a magic "fat burning" effect or guarantee rapid results, particularly from just one drink. The added orange juice in the recipe also contains natural sugars and calories, which need to be accounted for in total daily intake.
doctor_name: Dr Swati Dave; Shruti K Bhardwaj; Dr P Rammanohar
doctor_specialization: PhD in Food and Nutrition; Chief Clinical Nutritionist @ Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad; Research Director at Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda
key_medical_terms: calorie deficit|adipose tissue|fat loss|metabolism|Vitamin C|fiber|obesity|Ayurveda|hydration
label: False

title: Fact Check: Can animal milk weaken bones?
claim_text: An Instagram reel suggests that animal milk weakens bones and is responsible for conditions like diabetes, obesity, allergies, migraines, sinusitis, acidity, and fungal infections. The video suggests eliminating milk for three months to see improvements.
quick_take: A social media post claims that animal milk can weaken bones. We did the fact check to term this claim as mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
## Does animal milk weaken bones?
No, there is no strong evidence that milk weakens bones. In fact, milk is a well-known source of calcium, which helps maintain bone density and strength. Studies have shown that adequate calcium intake from dairy products can reduce the risk of osteoporosis and fractures. While some older studies suggested a link between high milk consumption and increased fracture risk, these findings are inconsistent and do not establish a cause-and-effect relationship. More recent research provides clearer insights. For example, a 2022 study of 14,711 Chinese adults found that consuming 0.1–100 g of dairy per day was associated with a lower risk of fractures, while higher intake showed no effect. This reduced risk was mainly due to the nutrients in dairy, with minimal influence from factors like height or BMI. Similarly, a 2019 study of 2,466 children in Toronto found no link between the amount or fat content of cow's milk consumed at ages 1–3 and the risk of fractures between ages 3–10. This suggests that while cow's milk may not offer extra protection against fractures in later childhood, it does not increase fracture risk either.

Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, says: "There's a common myth that drinking animal milk can weaken your bones, but that's simply not true. In fact, milk is rich in calcium and vitamin D, both of which are essential for strong, healthy bones. These nutrients help maintain bone density and reduce the risk of fractures. Unless someone has a specific condition like lactose intolerance or a dairy allergy, milk can actually support bone health, not harm it."

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, explains: "Animal milk doesn't weaken bones—in fact, it does the opposite. It's a great source of calcium, vitamin D, and protein, all of which are vital for maintaining bone strength. These nutrients work together to support bone density and overall health. Of course, if someone doesn't consume milk, there are other ways to get these nutrients, but for many people, milk is an easy and effective option."

If you're curious about the benefits of donkey milk, it's important to remember that consuming raw milk—whether from cows or any other animal—can pose health risks. Always ensure it's properly pasteurised before consumption.

## Can milk contribute to osteoporosis?
No, milk does not cause osteoporosis. Osteoporosis is a condition where bones become weak and brittle, often due to low calcium, vitamin D deficiency, and hormonal changes. Dairy products are among the best sources of calcium, and consuming them in moderation supports bone health. While excessive milk intake may not provide extra benefits, moderate consumption is generally safe. Similarly, some claims suggest that milk, ghee, and mishri can cure all physical, mental, and brain-related weaknesses. This, however, is misleading.

## Does eliminating milk cure diabetes, obesity, allergies, or other conditions?
No, eliminating milk does not cure diabetes, obesity, allergies, or other conditions. There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that avoiding dairy can reverse diabetes, obesity, allergies, migraines, or fungal infections. In fact, research suggests the opposite in many cases. For example, a 2019 study found an inverse link between dairy consumption and the risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Another study from the same year highlighted that increased dairy intake, especially milk proteins, may help lower this risk. Milk proteins can improve insulin response and reduce blood sugar levels after meals, though the exact mechanisms remain unclear. When it comes to obesity, a 2022 study showed that children who drank white milk were 33% less likely to be overweight or obese compared to those who didn't drink milk. Additionally, a 2016 review found that dairy intake may help reduce the risk of childhood obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, particularly stroke. It also showed benefits for bone health and a lower risk of certain cancers, such as colorectal and breast cancer. Importantly, dairy consumption was not linked to all-cause mortality or major adverse effects. Regarding migraines, the evidence is mixed. A 2022 study found that higher low-fat dairy intake may reduce the risk of migraines in children aged 7–14, with up to 53% lower odds of experiencing migraines. This effect could be due to the micronutrients and bioactive compounds in dairy. However, a 2024 review highlighted a complex relationship between dairy intake and headaches, with some studies showing a positive association, others no effect, and some suggesting benefits from dairy restriction. Factors such as individual health conditions and headache types may influence these outcomes. That said, people with lactose intolerance or dairy allergies may feel better when they avoid milk. However, this does not mean dairy is harmful to everyone. For most people, dairy can be part of a healthy, balanced diet.

## What about acidity and sinusitis?
There is no conclusive evidence that milk causes acidity or sinusitis. Some people report increased mucus production after consuming dairy, but studies suggest this is more of a perceived effect rather than an actual increase in mucus. As for acidity, milk can temporarily soothe acid reflux, but excessive consumption—especially of full-fat dairy—may contribute to digestive discomfort in some individuals.

## THIP Media Take
The claim that animal milk can weaken bones is mostly false. Milk is a good source of calcium and other nutrients essential for bone health. While some people may have sensitivities to dairy, there is no scientific basis to say milk is harmful to bones or causes multiple health conditions. Eliminating milk is not a universal solution, and claims suggesting otherwise are misleading.

doctor_specialization: General Physician; PhD in Food and Nutrition
