title: Fact Check: Can animal milk weaken your bones?
claim_text: The reason why your bones are weak and brittle is because of animal milk. Animal milk which we consume as a blessing and we think it's good for our bones is what is harming us. If you are suffering from diabetes, obesity, allergies, migraine, sinusitis, acidity or fungal infections leave milk for 3 months and resume after 3 months.
quick_take: An Instagram post claiming that animal milk can weaken your bones is FALSE. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to support this claim. While it is important to acknowledge that excessive milk consumption may affect bone health, studies show that animal milk contains essential minerals like calcium and phosphorus, which contribute to bone strengthening.
doctor_explanation:
Dr. Kumardev Arvind Rajamanya, Head of Department (HOD) & Lead Consultant - Orthopaedics, Aster Whitefield Hospital, Bengaluru, explained: 'Many causes can lead to bone damage, such as trauma which can cause fractures or breaks. Some medical conditions, like osteoporosis, weaken bones and make them more susceptible to damage. Chronic diseases such as arthritis and certain cancers can also cause bone tissue to gradually deteriorate over time. Infections, such as osteomyelitis and nutritional deficiencies, especially in calcium and vitamin D, contribute to bone degeneration. In addition to these, excessive use, repeated stress or genetic diseases such as osteogenesis imperfecta make bones fragile and prone to breaking as well.'

Scientific evidence consistently refutes the claim. Animal milk is a nutrient-dense food, supplying energy and high-quality protein with essential micronutrients like calcium, magnesium, potassium, zinc, and phosphorus in an easily absorbed form. Milk minerals are crucial for human health and development throughout life. Milk is rich in nutrients essential for good bone health, including calcium, protein, potassium, and phosphorus (source: PMC6723869).

The National Institutes of Health emphasizes that dairy products such as milk, cheese and yogurt are excellent sources of calcium, an essential mineral vital for building and maintaining the structure of bones and teeth. A study by Alicja Ewa Ratajczak et al. highlights that milk is amongst the most important sources of calcium and phosphorus which are essential for bone health. Milk consumption throughout life is crucial to prevent bone mass loss (source: PMC8072827).

An article published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found that adequate dietary calcium and protein intakes found in milk are essential and may help to achieve optimal peak bone mass during skeletal growth and to prevent bone loss in the elderly.

Dr Ankur Bambhania, Consultant Critical Care, HCG Hospitals, Bhavnagar, told the Medical Dialogues Fact Check Team: 'While animal milk is often celebrated as a source of calcium for strong bones, excessive consumption may have the opposite effect. The acidic nature of animal protein can lead to calcium loss as the body works to neutralize the acid. Over time, this could weaken bone health instead of strengthening it. However, this doesn't mean milk is harmful in moderation. A balanced diet, including plant-based calcium sources such as leafy greens, almonds, and fortified alternatives, alongside regular exercise, is essential for maintaining optimal bone health. Understanding the impact of dietary choices can help foster healthier habits for stronger bones.'

Dr. Kumardev Arvind Rajamanya further said: 'Consumption of animal milk has a complex relation with bone health. Milk has traditionally been considered one of the best foods for maintaining a healthy skeletal system. Research findings suggest that consuming milk is important due to its nutrients that support bone density. Adulterated milk may have certain ill effects, but no such negative effects have ever been noticed by consuming normal animal milk. However, moderation and a balanced diet are very important in optimizing the health of the bones.'

The article does note one nuance: A study by Karl Michaëlsson et al. found that high milk consumption has been linked to higher mortality rates and an increased risk of fractures in women (source: PMC4212225). However, this pertains to excessive consumption, not milk consumption in general, and does not support the blanket claim that animal milk weakens bones.

Conclusion: Milk is a valuable source of proteins and essential minerals such as calcium and phosphorus, contributing to bone health. The user's claim that animal milk weakens bones is false. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to support the claim that milk weakens bones. Moderation and a balanced diet are essential for optimizing bone health.

title: Fact Check: Can animals also suffer from Down Syndrome? - THIP Media
claim_text: A video on Instagram with the title 'Animals With Down Syndrome' slideshow images of what was said to be a tiger and an owl with Down syndrome.
quick_take: A social media post claims that various animals, such as tigers, owls, etc., can also suffer from Down syndrome. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Down syndrome occurs when an abnormal cell division involving chromosome 21 leads to an extra partial or full chromosome 21. It cannot be prevented. This extra genetic material is responsible for Down syndrome's characteristic features and developmental problems. According to the National Down Syndrome Society, maternal age is the only factor that has been linked to an increased chance of having a baby with down syndrome. There are three types of Down syndrome, each caused by a different mechanism. It is important to note that Down syndrome is not caused by anything the parents did or did not do, and it is not inherited in a predictable pattern. Rather, it is caused by a random event that occurs during the formation of the egg and sperm or at conception. Down syndrome is a genetic condition that affects humans and is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21. The condition is not seen in animals in the same way that it is seen in humans. But, animals can have genetic abnormalities of their own. However, there are some animal species in which similar genetic changes have been observed, leading to physical and behavioural abnormalities. Since animals, such as apes, chimpanzees, etc., possess a DNA similar to that of humans, there can be similarities in the genetic abnormalities, such as Great apes (Pongidae) possess a chromosome similar to human chromosome 21 (HSA21), whose trisomy was described in both chimpanzee and orangutan. Additionally, a trisomy of chromosome 16 has been found in laboratory mice, but it is not as similar to that of Down syndrome. Long ago, in 1999, researchers also described in the journal Acta Veterinaria Scandinavica a case report of a Hereford calf born with a case of trisomy 22. Similarly, research on cats found a rare chromosomal abnormality in male cats for an extra chromosome that results in a condition similar to Klinefelter syndrome in humans or when a boy is born with an extra copy of the X chromosome. Our veterinary expert, Dr. Vivek Arora, B.V.Sc. & AH, MIVIS, explains, 'Animals, such as dogs don't suffer from Down's syndrome. However, there are certain chromosomal defects that can be present in animals, which are different from Down syndrome.' It is also worth noting that animals can suffer from other genetic conditions and health problems that can cause similar symptoms to those seen in people with Down syndrome. However, these conditions are not the same as Down syndrome and are not caused by the same genetic mechanisms.

title: Can anti-dandruff shampoos combat comedonal acne?
claim_text: Your anti-dandruff shampoo has a secret superpower! Using an anti-dandruff shampoo helps get rid of comedonal acne. The key antifungal and antibacterial ingredient in anti-dandruff shampoos such as Head & Shoulders, zinc pyrithione (ZPT), facilitates the fight against Malassezia, responsible for fungal acne.
quick_take: A social media post claims that using an anti-dandruff shampoo helps get rid of comedonal acne. We analysed the assertion and determined it isfalse.
doctor_explanation: Comedonal acne, which usually manifests as whiteheads or blackheads, gets its name from the word 'comedo,' which means 'plug of keratin.' Classically, comedones have been linked to acne and acne-related issues. Nonetheless, they may co-exist with dermatological illnesses other than acne. The non-inflammatory form of acne develops when hair follicles get clogged with excess sebum, dead skin cells, or external environmental contaminants. The comedonal bumps usually appear on the forehead, chin, nose, chest area, and upper back. Compared to pustular or cystic acne, comedonal acne usually involves less redness and irritation. The condition is primarily triggered by hormonal abnormalities, particularly those brought on by androgens, as well as the use of certain cosmetic skin care products, genetic predispositions, stress, humidity, pollutants, and unhealthy eating patterns. Adolescents are particularly at a higher risk, along with adults who have oily skin or a family history of acne. While both can manifest as little bumps on the skin, it is critical to acknowledge that comedonal acne and fungal acne are distinct forms. Dr. Gurman Singh Bhasin, Director & Chief Dermatologist, Skinclarity Clinic, Nagpur, explained that comedonal acne is caused by clogged pores, either open or closed comedones, caused by excess sebum, dead skin, and keratin—not fungus. In contrast, fungal acne (Malassezia folliculitis) is actually a yeast infection of hair follicles and presents as itchy, monomorphic papules or pustules rather than comedones. Anti-dandruff shampoos contain active ingredients like zinc pyrithione (ZPT), ketoconazole, salicylic acid, and selenium sulphide, which are designed to address dandruff by reducing fungal overgrowth and scalp inflammation. ZPT primarily regulates keratinisation and helps heal the scalp by restoring normal sebum production, epithelium keratinisation, or both. While ZPT has shown promise in addressing Malassezia-related disorders such as dandruff and seborrheic dermatitis, its effectiveness in managing nonfungal comedonal acne is yet unclear. This is because comedonal and fungal acne have distinct pathophysiologies, making antifungal agents less relevant in such cases. Dr. Gurman Singh Bhasin also supports this by stating that anti-dandruff shampoos may help reduce spillover and prevent worsening of acne around the forehead and temples. However, comedonal acne is better managed with keratolytics like salicylic acid or retinoids like adapalene and not antifungals. Dr. K Kranthi Varma, Consultant Dermatologist at Renova Hospitals in Sanath Nagar, Hyderabad, explains that the management of comedonal acne is usually a combination of personal hygiene and prescribed medications. After medically supervised gentle scrubbing, doctors usually prescribe topical retinoids. These are vitamin A derivatives that unclog pores and prevent the formation of new comedones. In case they are ineffective, salicylic acid, benzoyl peroxide, glycollic acid, or other AHAs may be prescribed. Oral medications such as low-dose isotretinoin may be prescribed in cases that are resistant or chronic. The three primary in-office procedures—chemical peels, comedone extraction, and microdermabrasion—are usually employed for resistant cases. ZPT antidandruff shampoos may have nonspecific benefits, but they cannot substitute for the evidence-based treatments for acne. Reliance on such uncertain remedies may do more damage than good by delaying the essential therapy.

title: Fact Check: Can Anulom Vilom Cure Migraine in 3 Minutes and High BP in 5 minutes?
claim_text: Anulom Vilom (alternate nostril breathing) can cure migraine in 3 minutes and bring high blood pressure under control in 5 minutes. The claim is based on the idea that the right nostril is associated with the Surya Nadi (sun channel) which generates heat, while the left nostril activates the Chandra Nadi (moon channel) which brings coolness and calmness — so breathing only through the left nostril can stimulate cooling energy, relieve headache, ease migraine, and normalize high BP.
quick_take: Anulom Vilom may offer long-term health benefits, but there is no scientific evidence that it can cure migraines in 3 minutes or normalize blood pressure in 5 minutes. Both conditions are chronic and require comprehensive medical treatment.
doctor_explanation:
Both consulted doctors categorically rejected the claim that Anulom Vilom can cure migraine in 3 minutes or normalize high blood pressure in 5 minutes.

Dr. Avinash Kulkarni, Consultant Neurologist at Gleneagles BGS Hospital, stated: 'The short answer is no, because both blood pressure and migraine are chronic conditions — there is no concept of a complete cure. Now, is the claim entirely false? Not really. It is partially true. Breathing patterns play an important role. The way we breathe influences changes in the brain. They are interconnected. In patients with migraine, certain breathing patterns — especially the Indian practice of anulom-vilom or pranayama — have been shown to alter brain chemistry in a way that reduces headache episodes. This can decrease the overall frequency of attacks. However, it does not cure migraine. The same applies to blood pressure. Research has shown that deeper, slower breathing lowers blood pressure. During anulom-vilom, one breathes deeply and the number of breaths per minute comes down. This calm breathing pattern leads to a reduction in blood pressure to near-normal levels. But this effect is transient. It does not mean blood pressure is cured. Patients should therefore not believe claims that migraine or hypertension can be cured, nor should they stop their prescribed medicines in favor of breathing exercises alone. Doing so can result in serious complications such as stroke or heart attack. Breathing exercises like anulom-vilom should be considered only as a supportive measure, to be practiced alongside proper medical management under the guidance of a neurologist or cardiologist.'

Dr. Umesh Tukaram, MBBS, MD (General Medicine), DM (Neurology), Clinical Director & Senior Consultant Neurology at CARE Hospitals, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, added: 'Anulom Vilom, also known as alternate nostril breathing, is a yoga technique that is believed to calm the nervous system, reduce stress, and improve overall well-being. Regular practice is often said to help in controlling blood pressure and reducing the frequency and intensity of migraine attacks. However, it is very important to clarify that no breathing exercise, including Anulom Vilom, can cure migraine within three minutes or normalize high blood pressure in five minutes. Migraine and hypertension are medical conditions influenced by multiple factors such as genetics, lifestyle, diet, and stress. While yoga and breathing exercises can be excellent complementary therapies, they should never replace medical treatment. If someone is experiencing frequent migraines or high blood pressure, I strongly recommend consulting a qualified medical professional for proper diagnosis and treatment.'

The article cites WHO's definition of hypertension as blood pressure consistently at or above 140/90 mmHg, noting that untreated hypertension can lead to serious health problems and does not have a permanent cure — it can only be managed with lifestyle changes and prescribed medications. Migraine is described as a neurological condition with a genetic basis, marked by repeated episodes of moderate to severe headache, usually one-sided, accompanied by nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia; attacks may last hours to days and are a major contributor to disability.

Scientific evidence cited in the article includes: a study in Acta Scientific Medical Sciences showing Anulom Vilom boosts lung function, increases vital capacity and breath-holding time, and strengthens respiratory muscles, supporting better cardio-respiratory performance and higher energy levels; a study in the International Journal of Science and Healthcare Research finding that four weeks of regular practice reduced certain cardiovascular parameters in hypertensive patients (but with no evidence of effect within 5 minutes); and a study by Anjana Kaushal et al. (PMC10666878) reporting that pranayama may complement migraine treatment by reducing headache severity and frequency and shortening episode duration — but with no evidence supporting a 3-minute cure.

The article explicitly states that while Anulom Vilom may support respiratory health, aid in hypertension management over time, and yoga can complement migraine treatment, there is no scientific evidence that it can cure migraines in 3 minutes or lower high blood pressure in 5 minutes.

title: Can any herbal eye drops help to get rid of eye glasses?
claim_text: One can get rid of spectacles within 60 days with herbal eye drops.
quick_take: A Facebook reel has shared home remedies to remove spectacles. The post claims to remove glasses at home with the use of herbal eye drops. We did the fact check and termed it as false.
doctor_explanation: We need glasses mainly because of refractive errors in our eyes, which can cause blurry vision. These errors include myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia or hypermetropia (farsightedness), astigmatism, and presbyopia (poor vision due to advancing age). Glasses correct these refractive errors by adjusting the way light enters our eyes, allowing for clearer vision. They bend light rays such that it compensates for the imperfections in our eye's shape or the focusing mechanism. Hence, glasses act as optical aids, providing a clearer and sharper vision for those with visual impairments. The claim suggesting herbal eye drops as a universal remedy to eliminate the need for eye glasses within a fixed timeframe, such as 60 days, is deceptive. This claim does not acknowledge the diverse nature of vision-related issues and overlooks key factors that influence eye health. Firstly, the idea of relying solely on herbal eye drops as a home remedy to remove spectacles oversimplifies the complexities of vision correction. Vision problems, ranging from myopia to presbyopia, stem from various underlying factors. These include genetics, lifestyle, and age-related changes. A one-size-fits-all approach, such as herbal eye drops, cannot properly address the needs and complexities of different people's eyesight. Secondly, the claim's promise of quick and permanent vision improvement within a rigid timeframe completely disregards established medical science. Vision correction requires thorough evaluations by qualified eye care professionals. It is then followed by personalised solutions like eyeglasses, contact lenses, or surgical interventions. These approaches are customised to each individual's unique needs and may involve ongoing management and adjustments over time. Furthermore, certain home remedies may offer general health benefits, but their efficacy in addressing specific eyesight problems like refractive errors remains unproven. Vision care requires evidence-based approaches supported by clinical trials and professional expertise, instead of unsubstantiated claims promoting quick-fix solutions. Therefore, the notion of using herbal eye drops as a blanket solution to eliminate the need for eye glasses is misguided. Not only that, it can be potentially harmful too. Dr Sahebaan Sabharwal Sethi, Ophthalmologist, Arunodaya Deseret Eye Hospital, Gurugram, regarding the widespread use of home remedies to remove spectacles, says, "Herbal eye drops cannot help you get rid of spectacles. Eye glass number comes as a result of the size of the eyeball and the shape of the cornea which cannot be altered by any eye drop. On the other hand, acidic or extremely alkaline ingredients in herbal remedies can alter the normal pH of the eye and cause serious injuries or dryness." Ophthalmologist Dr Isha Agarwalla for her opinion on 'natural remedies for eye problems' says, "Herbal remedies claiming to cure cataracts and other eye ailments are proliferating, but beware: they're often completely false. While some herbs may have minor benefits for eye health, they're no match for proven medical treatments. Trusting in these unverified remedies could delay proper care and exacerbate conditions. Always consult with qualified medical professionals for accurate diagnosis and treatment options." Unfortunately, no medicine can remove spectacles. Because eye health is pretty complicated, home remedies to remove spectacles usually don't help. That's why many people with eyesight issues go for contact lenses or glasses. If you want to get rid of your eye glasses, laser eye surgery is the main and only option available. It is important to understand that we cannot correct our eyesight without any professional help. Eye exercises and home remedies to remove spectacles, unfortunately, do not work and won't help you get rid of your eye glasses. You should not rely upon such claims.

title: Fact Check: Can eating any kind of rusk lead to celiac disease?
claim_text: According to a social media post with the title "Rusk Side Effects: 6 Reasons Why You Must Not Eat Too Many Toasts," any type of rusk, which is a popular breakfast food, may cause a number of health issues, with celiac disease being the main concern.
quick_take: It has been suggested on social media that eating rusks can cause celiac disease. We verified the assertion. We discovered that the claim is onlyHalf True.
doctor_explanation:
Celiac disease is a condition brought on by eating gluten and results in an immune reaction in the small intestine. Over time, this reaction thins out the lining of your small intestine and impairs the absorption of some nutrients. The precise cause of celiac disease is unknown, but it may be influenced by your genes, consuming gluten-containing foods, and other factors. Additionally, infant feeding practices, gastrointestinal infections, and gut bacteria may be involved. Intestinal damage frequently results in diarrhoea, exhaustion, weight loss, bloating, and anaemia and can have serious consequences. The small, hair-like projections that line the small intestine are harmed when the body's immune system overreacts to gluten in food.

Regarding rusk varieties: Whole-wheat rusk is made from wheat flour and contains gluten. However, other varieties of rusks primarily consist of semolina, gluten-free rusks, and those supplemented with flax seeds, chia seeds, and millets. These modifications have greatly decreased their gluten content while also improving their nutritional value. Only wheat rusks were found to contain gluten in the study; other rusk varieties were found to be gluten-free.

Tea contains tannins, a subclass of compounds known as polyphenols. These tannins may be hydrolysable and condensed. Various edible and inedible plants, such as tree bark, leaves, spices, nuts, seeds, fruits, and legumes, naturally contain these compounds. They are typically produced by plants as a natural defense against pests, and they also give plant foods their colour and flavour. Tea, coffee, wine, and chocolate are some of the richest and most popular dietary sources of condensed tannins. Additional findings from the research showed that wheat gluten and condensed gluten can crosslink. However, it is unclear what processes lead to these interactions.

Despite this, the research found no convincing evidence to suggest that eating gluten-containing foods, such as wheat rusks, significantly increases the risk of developing celiac disease. This is a result of the debate over wheat's role and other possible causes of the rising incidence of celiac disease. According to some theories, factors that contribute to the toxicity of wheat in genetically vulnerable people include daily gluten consumption, variation in the types of wheat gluten consumed, and agricultural practices that affect wheat protein content.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: Even though gluten is a very important celiac disease trigger, it is not present in all of the rusk varieties. Additionally, there is no strong evidence to support the claim that eating any kind of rusk increases your risk of developing celiac disease. However, caution is required due to the excessive consumption of wheat rusks, especially with tea. Therefore, the claim is only half true.

title: Can Apamarg root water break kidney stones up to 25mm? - THIP
claim_text: Apamarg roots can dissolve kidney stone as big as 25 mm in just 15 days
quick_take: A social media post suggests that drinking water boiled with Apamarg root can break down kidney stones up to 25mm in size. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: The Fact Check section covers four main areas: 1) Is Apamarg scientifically proven to treat kidney stones? Apamarg has been around for centuries in traditional Indian medicine, praised for its diuretic qualities (helps you urinate more, which might flush out small debris). Studies, mostly on animals or in labs, show mixed results. One experiment on rats found that extracts from Achyranthes aspera could prevent calcium oxalate stones from forming or reduce their size slightly. Another lab test suggested a saponin-rich part of the plant might dissolve tiny calcium crystals in test tubes. There's even a small human study on an herbal mix including Apamarg that helped expel small stones and cut pain, but it wasn't just Apamarg alone, and the group was tiny. Most research is preliminary, like petri dish stuff or rat models, not real-life humans with stubborn stones. 2) Can drinking Apamarg root water handle stones as big as 25mm? Definitely not. A 25mm stone is about the size of a cherry pit, lodged in your kidney. Small stones, under 5mm, often sneak out with water and time. But giants like 25mm block things up, causing sharp pain, infections, or worse. Apamarg's compounds, like triterpenoid saponins, show some stone-dissolving potential in labs for wee crystals. One study on ethylene glycol-induced stones in rats hinted at reduced growth, but again, rats aren't people, and the stones weren't 25mm. In humans, there is no research that proves it works on large ones. While Apamarg might tweak urine pH or boost flow mildly, it's no match for big blockers. Experts agree: for anything over 10mm, natural remedies fall short. 3) What risks come with trying herbal fixes like Apamarg for stones? Apamarg can cause tummy upsets, allergies, or skin rashes in some. More worryingly, if it's not pure, say, contaminated with heavy metals or pesticides, it might harm your kidneys further. Studies link herbal remedies to kidney damage, like acute injury from toxins or interactions. One review highlighted how traditional brews led to electrolyte imbalances or tubular defects in kidneys. If you have existing kidney issues, it's dicey; herbs can worsen chronic disease or clash with blood thinners. And for stones? Delaying proper care risks infections spreading or stones growing, potentially leading to surgery you could've avoided. Cases show people with herbal-induced toxicity ending up on dialysis. 4) How do doctors actually deal with kidney stones this size? Doctors use proven methods. A 25mm stone is too big to pass naturally and can be very painful. First, a CT scan checks the stone's size and location. Then, doctors decide the best approach. One method, called shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), uses sound waves to break the stone into tiny pieces you can pass more easily. It's usually done without an overnight stay. For tougher stones, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) removes pieces through a small cut in your back, requiring a short hospital stay. Another option, ureteroscopy, uses a tiny camera and laser to zap the stone. Medicines like alpha-blockers help relax your urinary tubes, and painkillers ease discomfort. ESWL clears 70-90% of stones, PCNL even more for big ones. Dr. Archana Daftardar, a kidney specialist and transplant doctor at Renova Hospitals in Kompally, Hyderabad, warns that many myths surround kidney stone prevention and treatment. Relying on untested natural remedies can worsen the problem instead of helping. For the best results, consult a qualified Ayurvedic or allopathic doctor. Dr. Bhanu Mishra, a kidney specialist at BLK Max Hospital in Delhi, clarifies that the mentioned herbal preparation doesn't dissolve kidney stones. The idea that a drink can completely break down and flush out stones is not trustworthy, though staying hydrated and getting enough calcium can help prevent stones from forming. While certain juices or homemade brews might support kidney health, there's no solid evidence showing that combining them with rock salt effectively eliminates kidney stones.

title: Can Apamarga root extract effectively dissolve kidney stones?
claim_text: Consuming Apamarga root extract on an empty stomach may dissolve kidney stones of any size
quick_take: An Instagram reel is promoting Apamargaroot extract for the management of kidney stones. After fact-checking, we discovered that the claim ismostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Kidney stones are mineral precipitates in the renal calyces and pelvis that are either free or attached to the renal papillae. They originate when urine becomes supersaturated with both organic and crystalline components, such as calcium, oxalate, or uric acid. Most stones are usually composed of calcium oxalate. These are usually caused by the following conditions. Even though smaller kidney calculi are typically painless (asymptomatic), larger ones can impede urinary flow, causing severe discomfort (renal colic), nausea, vomiting, and even blood in the urine. Pain from a kidney stone typically starts in the side or lower back and might spread to the groin as the stone passes through the urinary system. If the issue is not addressed appropriately, it may result in serious complications; therefore, if there is any discomfort, one should consult a doctor right away.

Apamarga, also known as the prickly chaff-flower, is a widely used Ayurvedic herb. The traditional medicine utilises the plant's root and ash (kshara) for its diuretic, anti-inflammatory, and alkaline characteristics. Its high bioactive profile (flavanoids and saponins) may also have a major impact on the urinary biochemistry. Although the saponin-rich fraction of Apamarga may facilitate and encourage the breakdown of CaOx crystals, these results are limited to preliminary experimental investigations. Furthermore, because there is a dearth of high-quality clinical studies, the formulation should not be used in clinical practice for all stone types or sizes. Most significantly, Apamarga's root extract may not work for larger aggregates, staghorn calculi, cystine stones, or radiopaque infection stones; instead, urological intervention or other medical dissolving techniques may be essential.

While home remedies could be beneficial for digestive or urinary health, Dr. Sharad Malhotra, HOD Gastroenterology, Hepatology & Therapeutic Endoscopy, Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, advises against utilising them as a long-term kidney stone treatment. Additionally, Dr. Malhotra states that these unregulated remedies shouldn't be considered a substitute for conventional medical therapies for renal calculi because they lack strong scientific support. Apamarga root extract may therefore be used extensively due to its possible anti-nephrolithiasis (stone-dissolving) and diuretic qualities. However, until thorough clinical trials determine its safety, dosage, and efficacy, it should only be used as an adjuvant or complement to evidence-based medical therapy for renal calculi.

Claims that kidney stones resolve on their own in a few days are unsupported by scientific data. For asymptomatic calculi less than 5 mm, it usually takes weeks instead of days. Additionally, the symptomatic stones, which range in size from 5 to 10 mm, require cautious treatment for a few weeks to a month.

Dr. Archana Daftardar, a Consultant Nephrologist, Hypertension Specialist, and Transplant Physician at Renova Hospitals in Kompally, Hyderabad, further supports this by pointing out that there are many misconceptions about kidney stone prevention and treatment. Unsubstantiated alternative therapies might actually make the illness worse rather than better. It is advised to seek advice from licensed Ayurvedic or allopathic specialists.

The management of kidney stones depends on stone size, location, and composition. For small verified cases, specialists may recommend dietary modifications, analgesics, and hydration therapy. Larger and obstructive calculi may require medical or surgical interventions. Medical expulsive therapy with alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin has been beneficial in stone transit. When conservative strategies fail, nephrologists may recommend minimally invasive treatments like ureteroscopy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), and extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL). Targeted therapy may also be suggested once underlying causes such as hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, or uric acid imbalance have been identified.

Given that kidney stones vary widely in terms of dimensions and composition, a medical assessment supported by laboratory and diagnostic imaging procedures is the cornerstone for kidney stone care. Therefore, relying on unsupported alternative therapies like Apamarga root extract may not only delay the necessary intervention but may also increase the risk of complications, including infection, blockage, or renal impairment.

title: Fact Check: Can apple cider vinegar cure fatty liver?
claim_text: Replacing morning tea with apple cider vinegar (ACV) diluted in water can "cure fatty liver from the roots" and is a "100% guaranteed remedy" for fatty liver.
quick_take: A social media post claims that apple cider vinegar can cure fatty liver from the roots. After fact-checking, we found that the claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: No, it cannot cure fatty liver. There is no scientific proof that apple cider vinegar alone can cure fatty liver, whether alcoholic or non-alcoholic. Fatty liver disease is a complex condition that needs a combination of medical care, diet changes, physical activity, and sometimes medication. A drink like ACV cannot address the root causes or repair liver cells on its own. Not directly. Some small studies suggest mild benefits of apple cider vinegar (ACV), but not a cure for fatty liver. Animal studies and limited human trials hint that its acetic acid content may help reduce fat buildup in the liver. For instance, a 2024 animal study found that adding a small amount of ACV to fish feed slightly reduced fat in liver cells of sick trout, though it didn't lead to major changes in weight or key liver enzymes. A 2021 review of human trials showed that ACV helped lower blood sugar and cholesterol slightly, especially in people with type 2 diabetes, but had no effect on other important health markers. These effects were modest and not specific to curing fatty liver disease. No study so far has proven that ACV can treat or cure fatty liver in humans. At best, it may support liver health indirectly by helping reduce blood sugar and cholesterol—when combined with other lifestyle changes like balanced nutritious diet and regular exercise. Yes, it can cause side effects. Drinking undiluted or even diluted apple cider vinegar daily, especially on an empty stomach, can irritate the stomach lining, induce nausea, reduce appetite, damage tooth enamel, throat burns, and lower potassium levels over time. It may also interact with medicines for diabetes, diuretics and heart conditions. People with acid reflux or ulcers might experience worse symptoms. No, it's not a recommended treatment. Doctors and dietitians do not list apple cider vinegar as a treatment for fatty liver in any major guideline. The best way to manage fatty liver is through a balanced diet (like the Mediterranean diet), regular exercise, weight loss (if overweight), and avoiding alcohol. In some cases, medication might be needed. Dr Sharad Malhotra said: "Fatty liver usually develops silently and doesn't show symptoms early. There's no quick fix—definitely not something that can cure it in just 14 days. The best way to manage it is through long-term changes like eating healthy, cutting down on sugar and alcohol, staying active, and gradually losing weight. Even a 5–10% weight loss can improve liver health." Dr Malhotra added: "It's important to get a yearly abdominal ultrasound and liver function tests to catch fatty liver early. In some cases, tests like Fibroscan or even a liver biopsy might be needed. Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and avoiding unproven herbal remedies or unnecessary medicines also plays a big role. A healthy liver takes time and consistent effort—not shortcuts." Chhavi Kohli explained: "Reversing fatty liver isn't that quick—it needs steady lifestyle changes over months. One important factor is the gut-liver connection. Eating poorly and not moving enough can disturb gut bacteria, which lets harmful substances reach the liver and increase inflammation." title: Can applying clay pack flatten your tummy within 2 days?
claim_text: Spreading a clay pack (mitti patti) around the stomach can completely flatten a bulging belly within just two days.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that applying clay pack on the stomach will flatten the stomach in two days. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: No. There is no physiological mechanism by which a topical clay or mud pack (mitti patti) can remove or "melt" subcutaneous fat in 48 hours. Body fat sits beneath the skin in adipose tissue; to reduce it the body must metabolise stored triglycerides through biochemical pathways (lipolysis) that are driven by overall energy balance (calorie deficit), hormones and sustained metabolic demand. The skin itself, especially the outermost layer, the stratum corneum, acts as a barrier. Most topical substances do not penetrate deeply enough to reach fat cells, and even those that penetrate act on skin or superficial tissues, not on adipocyte metabolism. What people notice after a clay pack is usually temporary: the mask can dry and tighten the top layers of skin, and you may lose water through mild sweating; both make the abdomen appear a little firmer for a few hours. That visual change is cosmetic and reversible once you rehydrate or wash the skin. Short-term centimetre reductions after a mud pack are almost always explained by measurement variability, temporary loss of surface water, or posture changes, not by removal of adipose tissue. Scientific studies that look at "spot reduction" consistently show that neither local creams nor exercises target fat loss from a single area; fat is mobilised systemically. Sustained, measurable waist reduction requires a negative energy balance over time so the body oxidises stored fat. Clinically proven targeted methods exist (for example, liposuction physically removes fat; cryolipolysis cools fat cells leading to gradual loss), but these are medical procedures with defined time courses and risks, and they are not comparable to applying clay at home. A search of reputable medical literature shows no credible peer-reviewed evidence that topical clay, mud, or similar household masks penetrate to adipose tissue and trigger fat loss. Research into non-surgical fat reduction focuses on systemic interventions (diet, exercise, drugs that alter metabolism) or device-based approaches that deliver energy (cold, heat, ultrasound) to deeper tissues under controlled conditions. The idea that a home topical pack can alter adipocyte biology contradicts what we know about skin permeability and fat metabolism. Beyond the lack of benefit, there are small but real risks: contaminated mud can cause skin infections; fragrances or additives can provoke allergic contact dermatitis; vigorous rubbing or occlusion can irritate sensitive skin. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said: "Clay packs offer a temporary tight-skin feeling by absorbing moisture and constricting the surface, but it's superficial, no fat loss, just effects that fade in hours as skin rehydrates. For real fat reduction, focus on science: a nutrient-rich diet with a mild calorie deficit, plus 150 minutes of weekly moderate exercise like walking or strength training. Prioritize lean proteins, veggies, and healthy fats to curb hunger and sustain habits. Clay packs can be fun self-care, but let's prioritize lasting changes." Hakim Bharmal, Master Trainer and Contest Prep Coach said: "Safe, lasting reductions in abdominal fat come from sustained, evidence-based habits: modest calorie reduction (not extreme dieting), a mix of cardiovascular activity and resistance training, adequate protein and fibre to support satiety, and better sleep and stress management because hormones (cortisol, insulin) influence fat storage. Core exercises improve muscle tone and posture so your midsection looks firmer, but they don't selectively burn belly fat. Keep expectations realistic: health and body shape change slowly. Small, consistent improvements are the safest and most reliable route."

title: Fact Check: Can applying cloves, bay leaves and coffee reverse gray hair in just 4 minutes?
claim_text: Gray hair will disappear forever in just 4 minutes with this natural remedy. First, you will need a spoonful of cloves. quick_take: The claim that applying a mixture of cloves, bay leaves, and coffee can reverse gray hair in 4 minutes is false and scientifically unsupported. While these ingredients might offer certain health benefits, and coffee might provide minor or temporary staining effects, they do not affect melanin production or reverse graying.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Priyanka Kuri, Consultant - Dermatology, Aster Whitefield Hospital, Bengaluru, stated: 'Several newer molecules and supplements—such as dark nail extract, melatonin, caravis, biotin, and calcium pantothenate—have been studied for their potential to stimulate alpha-melanocyte–stimulating hormone, which may promote melanin production. While these may help, results for grey hair reversal are slow and limited. Simple home remedies like clove, bay leaves, or coffee cannot reverse grey hair in minutes. They are rich in antioxidants and can support overall hair health, but reversal of greying is extremely difficult. Most treatments aim to delay or prevent new greying rather than reverse existing grey hair. Greying is often genetic, but other factors—vitamin deficiencies (especially B12), lack of antioxidants, stress, and pollution—also play a role. Damage to melanocytes (pigment cells) reduces melanin in hair follicles, and current medicine has limited ability to restore them. For supportive care, experts recommend: Maintaining an antioxidant-rich diet; Protecting hair from excessive pollution and UV radiation (e.g., using an umbrella when outdoors); Correcting vitamin deficiencies and following a healthy lifestyle. In short, lifestyle modification, nutrition, and protection may help slow greying, but complete reversal remains very challenging with current treatments.' Dr. Divya Siddavaram, Senior Dermatologist, CARE HOSPITALS, Hyderabad, further stated: 'No, this is not possible. Hair turns gray when pigment cells stop working, and once that happens, the natural color cannot return. Cloves, bay leaves, and coffee may improve scalp health, add shine, or give a temporary dark tint, but they cannot reverse graying. Claims of "permanent hair removal in 4 minutes" are also myths—only medical treatments like laser or electrolysis can do that. Oils like "Spoil Betona" may nourish the scalp and reduce dryness, but there is no scientific evidence that they restore lost pigment. Such remedies should be seen as supportive, not curative.' Scientific background: Hair naturally turns gray or white with age due to a reduction in melanin, the pigment that gives hair its color. Melanin is produced by melanocytes, which are replenished by melanocyte stem cells (McSCs) during each hair growth cycle. Over time, these stem cells can become displaced within the follicle, losing their ability to produce new melanocytes. Since hair gains its color only during the anagen (growth) phase, the absence or malfunction of pigment-producing cells results in gray or white hair. Once melanin production stops entirely, the hair loses its color permanently. Once hair turns white, the change is permanent—it may shed and regrow, but the original color will not return. While clove oil has documented antifungal, antibacterial, and hair growth-stimulating properties (International Journal of Creative Research Thoughts), there is no scientific evidence that clove oil can reverse gray hair. Bay leaf has documented wound healing, antioxidant, antibacterial, antiviral, immunostimulant, anticholinergic, antifungal, insect repellent, anticonvulsant, antimutagenic, and anti-inflammatory properties (Saima Batool et al., PMC7152419), but no evidence for reversing gray hair. Coffee may act as a natural dyeing agent imparting subtle, earthy brown tones (World Journal of Pharmaceutical and Life Sciences), but this is a cosmetic staining effect, not melanin restoration.

title: Fact Check: Can applying egg white, milk, and apple eliminate wrinkles and age lines?
claim_text: You can get rid of wrinkles and age lines by applying a mixture of egg white, milk, and grated apple.
quick_take: A social media post claims that you can get rid of wrinkles and age lines by applying a mixture of egg white, milk, and grated apple. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False. Even though these ingredients separately might have some anti-aging effects, there is no scientific evidence that this mixture can eliminate wrinkles and age lines as aging is a natural process.
doctor_explanation: Wrinkles are creases, folds, or ridges in the skin which appear naturally as people get older. As a person ages, the skin becomes thinner and less elastic over time. However, certain other factors such as sun exposure, smoking, dehydration, some medications and environmental and genetic factors also play a vital role. Blemishes and wrinkles are signs of skin ageing. Both signs occur due to irreversible structural and biological changes in the layers of the skin. However medical treatments under the guidance of experienced doctors can reduce the appearance of blemishes, wrinkles and other visible signs of ageing. Our Dermatology expert, Dr. Jyothy Kannangath, describes the etiology behind wrinkles by stating, "Wrinkles occur as people age or due to repeated muscle contractions. As we age, the skin cells divide more slowly, and the middle layer of your skin, the dermis, begins to thin. The dermis has a network of elastin and collagen fibres, which offer support and elasticity. As this network loosens and becomes weak, depressions form on your skin's surface. Aging skin is also less able to retain moisture, less efficient in secreting oil and slower to heal. All of these factors contribute to the development of wrinkles." Many factors affect the elasticity of the skin, such as sun exposure and diet. Getting wrinkles and age lines is a natural process and reversing it or eliminating it through an external application is not possible. Moreover, on researching, we could not find any credible scientific evidence that proves that a mixture of egg white, milk and apple helps eliminate wrinkles and age lines. However, some studies on individual ingredients of this mixture that indicate anti-aging properties. However, one needs further research to prove this. Eggs contain vitamin A, and applying vitamin A to the skin may promote wound healing and reduce wrinkles. A study that evaluated the effects of water-soluble egg membranes (WSEM) on wrinkle reduction concluded that applying WSEM can significantly reduce wrinkle depth by protection from free radical damage at the cellular level and induction of several antioxidant response elements. However, there can be certain disadvantages of using eggs on the face for a few people. It can lead to skin irritation. Some people might have an allergic reaction and can experience specific symptoms such as severe itchiness, rash, hives, and breathing difficulties from using egg whites on their face depending on the severity of the disease. Similarly, if you have any recent cuts, scrapes, or wounds, the use of raw egg whites could potentially cause a secondary infection. Similarly, apple is speculated to have anti-aging properties due to the presence of essential fatty acids that keeps the skin moist and plump. It is considered to minimize fine lines and wrinkles due to vitamins E and C. Research on anti-aging facial serum containing apple stem cell extract showed significant improvement in aging skin signs. Similarly, milk is also considered to have anti-aging properties. Milk is considered to improve the skin's condition through various means, including antiaging effects. Furthermore, the amino acids also have positive effects on the skin, such as proline has antiaging properties, which reduce wrinkles and sagging. However, further studies are needed to prove the efficiency of the application of these agents on the skin concerning the reduction or elimination of wrinkles and age lines. Dr. Kannangath further clarifies this by stating, "Egg white, apple and milk are used as face masks which claim to tighten the skin. However, there is no scientific evidence to prove that this mask can reduce wrinkle formation, as skin ageing is an internal process. Also, before applying egg whites to your face, do a patch test as it can cause an allergic reaction. This test involves applying a small amount of egg white to the back of the hand, under the chin, or behind the ear to see if it causes any allergic reaction."

title: Can applying ghee and coconut oil to the navel enhance eyesight?
claim_text: Applying desi ghee and coconut oil to the navel can enhance eyesight in both adults and children. The trending reel emphasises that applying the combination to the navel is beneficial as it stimulates the medulla oblongata of the brain when massaged under the armpit.
quick_take: A popular Instagram post claims that putting ghee and coconut oil on the navel can enhance eyesight. After fact-checking, we found that it is completely false.
doctor_explanation: While navel therapy, often referred to as 'nabhi chikitsa', is widely considered to originate from Ayurvedic principles, credible scientific evidence supporting its therapeutic efficiency is limited. The navel, or nabhi, is regarded in ancient Ayurvedic medicine as a crucial energy centre that links several physiological systems via channels referred to as strotas. Navel oiling, believed to help with tridosha balance, influencing overall health, is primarily backed by anecdotal reports, and there is no concrete scientific evidence supporting its role in treating any health condition, but not improving eyesight. Applying oils to the navel for curing diseases is not supported by traditional Ayurvedic texts and has no scientific validity, confirms Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at Amrita School of Ayurveda. He underlines that while oils are used in massage and certain Ayurvedic therapies, the notion that the navel is a healing locus for all medical conditions is at odds with authentic Ayurvedic practice. Ayurveda takes a comprehensive approach to eye health, including dietary control, lifestyle modifications, triphala usage, and netra tarpana (lubricating therapy). While ghee and coconut oil have been touted for their nourishing, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and eye-supporting benefits, there is no conclusive scientific evidence that applying them to the navel can enhance vision. Furthermore, ghee and coconut oil are natural fats that contain vital fatty acids and vitamins, especially vitamin E, which may help preserve cellular integrity and reduce oxidative stress associated with eye ageing and dryness. Despite the fact that it is believed to enhance circulation and balance the three doshas, there is no conclusive scientific evidence that navel therapy affects or enhances vision. Scientific literature acknowledges the benefits of ghee and coconut oil through dietary or topical ocular pathways instead of systemic absorption via one's navel. Most significantly, social media endorsement for navel oiling's ability to improve vision fails to demonstrate that it is the best approach or substitute for medically validated vision correction therapies. This is further supported by Dr. Satyanarayana Kada, MS (AIIMS), FVRS (Aravind Eye Institute, Madurai), Senior Consultant Ophthalmologist & Retina Specialist, Renova Century Hospitals, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, who emphasises that there is no scientific or anatomical basis to support the belief that applying ghee, coconut oil, or any other oil to the navel can improve eyesight in any age group. Given that there is no physiological link between the navel and eyes that could offer such benefits, this practice stems from age-old beliefs rather than scientific evidence. The medulla oblongata, situated near the base of the brainstem, regulates essential autonomic processes but oil absorption from the navel and underarms cannot affect medullary activity since these skin locations do not directly share neuronal or circulatory routes with the brainstem. Furthermore, visual processing mostly takes place in the occipital lobe, which includes the optic nerves, retina, and visual cortex; the medulla oblongata is not related to vision or eyesight. Therefore, there is no physiological or neuroanatomical link between these practices and visual function or the medulla oblongata. For adults: regular eye examinations are crucial for early detection of conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. For children: Dr. Bhanu Prakash M recommends using prescription Myatro 0.01% eye drops to address myopia, along with ZEISS Myopia Management glasses, and limiting screen time.

title: Fact Check: Can applying ginger and garlic to the navel help with indigestion?
claim_text: putting ginger powder and garlic in navel helps with indigestion
quick_take: According to a social media post, applying ginger and garlic to the navel is said to help with indigestion. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: The belly button is simply a scar left behind after the umbilical cord is cut at birth. Once we are born, that cord no longer exists, and there is no open channel linking the navel directly to the stomach or intestines. Many online explanations describe the navel as a "centre" that connects to internal organs. This idea may sound appealing, but anatomically, it is incorrect. Under the belly button are layers of skin, fat, muscle, and connective tissue, no hidden passage to the gut. Sensations felt in this area are related to skin nerves, not digestive activity. Human skin acts as a strong protective barrier. Its main role is to prevent substances, from bacteria to chemicals, from entering the body. Only specially designed medicines, delivered through medical skin patches, can reliably pass through the skin in meaningful amounts. A homemade ginger and garlic paste is not designed for this purpose. Even if tiny traces of compounds were absorbed, they would be far too small to influence digestion in any significant way. There is no evidence that these ingredients, when applied to the navel, can reach the digestive system or change how it works. Dr P. Ram Manohar, Research Director at the Amrita School of Ayurveda, states that there is no scientific evidence backing this practice. He adds that it is not a recognised part of Ayurveda and is not mentioned in classical Ayurvedic texts. Dr Annusuiya Gohil, an MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, explains that digestive problems usually arise from deeper imbalances in the body, such as disturbed doshas or impaired digestive fire (agni). She notes that Ayurvedic management focuses on understanding an individual's constitution, along with internal herbal medicines, dietary changes, and lifestyle modifications. According to classical Ayurvedic principles, applying ginger and garlic to the navel does not treat digestive disorders. Feeling better does not always mean digestion has improved. Several factors can explain this experience. Applying something warm or aromatic to the abdomen can be soothing and relaxing. Lying down, breathing slowly, or gently massaging the belly can also ease tension. Since stress and anxiety often worsen bloating and discomfort, relaxation alone can make symptoms feel milder. Expectation also plays a role. When someone strongly believes a remedy will help, the brain may dampen discomfort signals. This does not mean the relief is fake, it simply means the effect comes from perception and relaxation, not from the paste altering digestion. Garlic, in particular, can be harsh on the skin. It contains natural chemicals that can irritate tissue, especially when crushed and left in contact with the skin for long periods. There are well-documented cases of redness, blistering, and burn-like injuries from applying garlic directly to the skin. The belly button is a small, folded area where moisture can get trapped. This increases the risk of irritation, especially if the paste is covered with a bandage or left overnight. Ginger can also irritate sensitive skin, though garlic is more commonly associated with severe reactions. Simple habits work better. Eating slowly, avoiding very large meals, staying hydrated, and identifying foods that trigger bloating are far more effective than navel therapy. If ginger suits you, using it in cooking or tea is a safer, evidence-aligned option. Persistent digestive discomfort should not be ignored. Ongoing bloating, pain, or unexplained changes in digestion deserve medical attention rather than home remedies that may cause harm.

title: Can applying neem oil to the anus help get rid of piles? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook post claims that applying neem oil around the anal area can help cure piles.
quick_take: A social media post claims that applying neem oil to the anal area can help prevent piles. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
There’s a big difference between “this plant has interesting properties in a lab” and “this reliably treats haemorrhoids in real people.” At the moment, piles guidance and medical reviews focus on things like fibre, fluids, avoiding straining, warm sitz baths, and (when appropriate) short-term topical treatments, because those have clearer evidence for symptom relief and prevention. Neem (Azadirachta indica) does show anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial activity in some contexts, and it’s used in traditional medicine. But that does not automatically translate into “it shrinks haemorrhoids.” Piles are essentially swollen blood vessels and tissue in/around the anal canal. To “get rid” of them, you’d need either: [procedures that remove or shrink the tissue]. Neem oil hasn’t been shown to do either of those jobs in robust clinical trials for haemorrhoids. So if someone says, “It cured my piles,” it may be coincidence, the piles may have improved naturally, or the person may not have had piles in the first place.

Is neem oil safe to apply on anal skin?
No, it can be unsafe for some people, especially in such a sensitive area. The skin around the anus is thin, easily irritated, and often already inflamed when piles are present. Neem oil can cause allergic contact dermatitis, meaning the immune system reacts to it and you can develop redness, burning, swelling, itching, or an oozing rash. This isn’t a rare “internet myth”, there are published case reports and reviews documenting allergic reactions to neem oil (PubMed link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29059091/). Piles symptoms (itching, soreness, irritation) can look very similar to an allergic rash. So someone might apply neem oil, feel a brief “oily soothing” effect, and then later experience worse burning and itching, and assume their piles are “getting worse,” when actually the skin is reacting to the oil. The more you scratch or rub (which is very tempting), the more the skin barrier breaks down, and the cycle continues. Also, many home remedies involve undiluted neem oil or mixed “cocktails” (neem + camphor + other oils). That increases the chance of irritation.

Could neem oil still reduce itching or swelling even if it doesn’t cure piles?
No, not reliably, and the risk often outweighs the benefit. Some people report short-term relief with oily products because they reduce friction (like a temporary barrier). But that’s not a targeted haemorrhoid treatment. And because neem oil can irritate or trigger allergy, it’s a gamble, especially on anal skin. If itching is the main symptom, it can also be caused by things that aren’t piles at all: skin irritation from harsh wiping, scented products, leakage after bowel movements, fungal irritation, or tiny tears. Adding neem oil can mask the real cause, delay proper treatment, and make the skin angrier.

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic in New Delhi, explains that while home remedies can sometimes offer temporary comfort, they should not be considered a substitute for proper medical care. In cases of piles particularly when there is bleeding, significant pain, or repeated flare-ups a thorough medical evaluation is important. He cautions that depending solely on herbal drinks or household spices may delay appropriate treatment and potentially worsen the condition. According to him, doctors strongly support healthy lifestyle practices, but it is equally important for individuals to recognise when symptoms require professional medical attention rather than self-treatment.

Dietician Kamna Chauhan clarifies that piles are not something that can be eliminated with a quick home fix. Proper management depends on steady lifestyle changes — especially a well-balanced diet, adequate fluid intake, and healthy daily habits. She explains that including fibre-rich foods in the diet and drinking sufficient water helps keep stools soft. Softer stools pass more easily, which reduces straining, discomfort, and irritation around the anal area. According to her, consistency is key.

Dr Mohit Sandhu, an Ayurveda consultant and Kshar Sutra specialist based in Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh, explains that from an Ayurvedic perspective, taking a warm salt sitz bath may offer short-term relief in cases of haemorrhoids. He notes that the warmth and salt can sometimes help soothe the area and may slightly reduce swelling, which can ease pain and discomfort. However, he emphasises that this is not a rapid or permanent solution.

Dr Almas Fatma, a General Physician based in Navi Mumbai, explains that surgery is usually not the first line of treatment for piles. Most cases are initially managed with lifestyle changes and medication. However, she points out that in certain situations such as when piles are large, repeatedly bleed, cause significant pain, or fail to improve with conservative treatment surgery may become the most effective option. She adds that many modern surgical techniques are minimally invasive, relatively quick, and often do not require a prolonged hospital stay.

title: Fact Check: Can applying Nutmeg (Jaiphal) on forehead relieve migraine headaches?

It is valued for its aroma and flavour in cooking, and in some traditional systems, it is thought to have calming effects. However, scientific research into nutmeg and its medicinal properties is very limited. A migraine is not just a simple headache, it is a neurological condition involving abnormal brain activity, changes in blood flow, and activation of pain pathways. To date, there is no medical evidence that nutmeg, when applied to the skin, can influence these complex mechanisms. At best, the cool sensation of applying a paste to the forehead may provide a temporary distraction from pain, but this is not the same as genuine migraine relief. Dr. Utkarsh Bhagat, Neurosurgeon at Narayana Hospital, Gurugram, explained that migraines are far more than just intense headaches. They are a complex neurological disorder that can cause pulsating pain, nausea, and heightened sensitivity to light and sound. Triggers often include stress, hormonal changes, specific foods, and environmental influences. To manage this debilitating condition effectively, preventive measures and medications can help lessen the frequency and severity of attacks, while alternative therapies may provide relief from its symptoms. People believe nutmeg helps because of cultural traditions and its mild calming reputation, but this is not backed by clinical research. In Ayurveda and Unani medicine, nutmeg has been described as having sedative and warming properties. This may have led to its use in managing pain, stress, or sleep issues. Over time, such uses have been passed down as home remedies for headaches. The act of applying a paste to the forehead can feel soothing. Many traditional practices use this approach with sandalwood, camphor, or herbal balms. The relief people experience may come from the cooling effect, the pleasant smell, or simply the belief that the remedy will work, what scientists call the placebo effect. But importantly, placebo relief is not the same as treating the root cause of migraine. Belief can sometimes ease perception of pain, but it cannot replace proper care. Dr. Varun Kodam, Consultant Neurologist at TX Hospitals, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, explains that migraine is a common headache disorder with several known triggers. He clarifies that no specific food can cure migraines, despite popular claims on social media. The most effective strategy is to identify and avoid foods that may trigger attacks—such as alcohol, monosodium glutamate (MSG), and caffeine—which can help reduce how often migraines occur. Dr. Zahoor Ahmad Parry, Specialist Neurologist at NMC Healthcare, UAE, states that modern medicine is guided by strong scientific evidence, and there is no proof that applying nutmeg paste can treat or prevent migraines. He emphasises that treatments are based on well-established research, and currently, no studies support this combination as an effective remedy for migraine relief. Nutmeg on the skin can sometimes cause harm, especially if overused or if someone is sensitive to it. Nutmeg contains compounds like myristicin and safrole. In high amounts, these can be toxic when ingested, causing nausea, dizziness, or even hallucinations. While applying nutmeg on the forehead is less likely to reach dangerous levels, skin irritation and allergic reactions are possible. Some people may develop redness, itching, or rashes after applying spice pastes. Since nutmeg is not designed or tested for topical medicinal use, there is no safety guarantee. Using it repeatedly on delicate skin like the forehead could do more harm than good. Not only is nutmeg ineffective for migraines, but it may also pose risks if used carelessly. Migraines require evidence-based management, not untested home pastes. Research suggests nutmeg may have mild antioxidant and antimicrobial properties. Some studies also mention sedative effects, which is why it has been used in traditional remedies for sleep. However, these effects are mostly noted in laboratory studies or animal research, not in well-designed human clinical trials. Even if nutmeg does help promote relaxation when consumed in very small amounts, applying it on the skin does not translate to any neurological benefit. A spice that flavours curries and sweets cannot tackle a condition as complex as migraine.

The claim that applying oils or liquids to the navel can cure all health problems is false. There is no medical or scientific basis for this practice. While oil massages may help with relaxation or dry skin, they cannot cure diseases like diabetes, heart problems, or depression.

That said, there is very little scientific evidence to show that the skin around the navel can absorb oils in a way that leads to real health benefits. The popular idea of a Pechoti gland located behind the navel, which supposedly helps draw oils into the body, does not have solid anatomical or histological support in modern medicine. In reality, applying oil to the navel may feel comforting and help keep the skin soft and hydrated. However, it is unlikely to deliver any meaningful therapeutic effect beyond local skin care or relaxation. Dr P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita School of Ayurveda, explains that applying oil to the navel as a treatment for indigestion is neither mentioned in classical Ayurvedic texts nor supported by scientific evidence. He adds that while Ayurveda does make extensive use of oils in massages and therapeutic procedures, it does not recognise the navel as a universal healing centre for all health problems. Supporting this perspective, Dr Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, notes that digestive and menstrual concerns in Ayurveda are usually linked to deeper imbalances in the body, such as a weakened digestive fire (agni) or disturbances in the doshas. Addressing these issues typically involves personalised dietary changes, lifestyle modifications, internal herbal treatments, and an understanding of an individual's body constitution. From this traditional Ayurvedic standpoint, simply applying oil to the navel is unlikely to correct digestive problems. Additionally, applying turmeric and mustard oil to the navel is unlikely to genuinely improve gut health, gastritis or digestion. While both ingredients are often praised for their health-supporting properties, there's no solid scientific evidence to show that rubbing them on the navel helps the digestive system work better. The skin in this area acts as a protective barrier, and oils applied externally don't travel inward to the gut in any meaningful way. The idea that the navel serves as a direct pathway to the digestive organs isn't supported by anatomy or medical science. Even within traditional practices like Ayurveda, digestion is improved by what you eat, how you live, and how well your digestive fire (agni) functions not by topical applications alone. At best, oiling the navel may feel calming or help keep the skin soft, but it shouldn't be seen as a reliable solution for digestive or gut-related concerns. Indigestion is best managed by addressing what's happening inside the digestive system, rather than relying on external remedies like navel oiling. Evidence-based approaches focus on calming irritation in the stomach, improving digestion, and preventing triggers that worsen symptoms. This usually starts with simple dietary changes, eating smaller, regular meals, avoiding very oily, spicy, or late-night foods, and limiting caffeine and alcohol. Chewing food slowly and managing stress also play an important role, as digestion is closely linked to the nervous system. For some people, antacids or acid-reducing medicines may be helpful, especially when indigestion is linked to excess stomach acid or reflux. In other cases, probiotics, fibre-rich foods, and adequate hydration can support a healthier gut environment. These methods are backed by research and work from within the body, helping the stomach lining heal and digestion function more smoothly. Unlike navel therapy, they target the root cause rather than offering surface-level comfort.

title: Fact Check: Can applying turmeric paste disappear pimples? THIP Media
claim_text: A YouTube video claims that turmeric has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties that help in fading the spot scars and making our skin glow.
quick_take: A social media video claims that applying turmeric paste disappears pimples. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Half True.
doctor_explanation: To a certain extent. It is often claimed that home remedies can cure skin problems. However, it is not always the case. Applying turmeric paste may disappear or fade away pimples in some cases. But the effectiveness of turmeric paste in treating pimples can vary from person to person. Turmeric has been touted for its antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-tumor effects. Even research published in 2016 indicates that a chemical named curcumin in turmeric may provide therapeutic benefits for skin health. Another article published in 2013 informs that curcumin has an antibacterial effect against the bacteria named Propionibacterium acnes which mostly causes pimples on the skin. These properties may help reduce redness, swelling, and bacterial growth associated with pimples. So, some individuals may experience improvements in their pimples by applying a turmeric paste directly to the affected areas. However, turmeric paste is not a miracle cure for everyone. Pimples can have various causes, such as hormonal imbalances, bacteria, clogged pores, or underlying skin conditions that turmeric paste cannot cure completely. While turmeric's anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties may provide some relief to the symptoms associated with pimples, it might not address the root causes of acne. So, it is essential to maintain realistic expectations and consider a comprehensive approach to skincare, including proper cleansing, a balanced diet, and, if necessary, consultation with a dermatologist for more effective and personalized treatment options. This isn't the first time we have found inconsistent claims that suggest home remedies can disappear pimples completely. We have previously debunked ice therapy cures pimples and toothpaste dries out pimples. What are the causes of pimples? Pimples result from a combination of factors including excess skin oil (sebum), clogged hair follicles, bacterial growth, hormonal changes (especially during puberty), genetics, diet, stress, and environmental factors. Medications and friction can also play a role. What is the difference between pimples and acne? Acne and pimples are often used interchangeably, yet there is a subtle distinction between them. A pimple is a small, raised bump resulting from blocked pores and may include redness, inflammation, and pus. Acne, on the other hand, encompasses a chronic skin condition involving pimples, blackheads, whiteheads, and more. It stems from factors like hormones, excess oil, and bacteria, leading to various blemishes such as papules, pustules, nodules, and cysts. While a pimple is a singular bump, acne comprises a range of lesions requiring comprehensive treatment. What can be the side effects of relying solely on home remedies and not seeking proper medical treatment? Relying solely on home remedies and not seeking proper medical treatment can worsen the condition. Research shows that turmeric can cause allergies in some people. Evidence shows that some people are allergic to curcumin. Research published in 2015 shows that people allergic to curcumin can suffer from rashes due to contact dermatitis. Another research published in 2018 shows that turmeric can stain the skin yellow.
