title: Fact Check: Can clove detox a smoker's lungs? - THIP Media
claim_text: Drinking clove water can cleanse a smoker's lungs and also kill stomach parasites
quick_take: A social media post suggests that drinking clove water can cleanse smoker lungs. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: The lungs don't 'detox' the way the liver or kidneys do. Once cigarette smoke is inhaled, thousands of chemicals, tar, carbon monoxide, and other irritants settle deep into the airways and lung tissue. This damage builds up slowly over time, and it cannot be undone by chewing a spice or drinking an herbal mix. Cloves do contain eugenol, a compound known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in laboratory studies. But antioxidant activity is not the same as detoxification. There is no clinical evidence showing that clove or eugenol can remove smoke residues, dissolve tar, or reverse smoking-related lung damage in humans. Tar is a thick, sticky residue that accumulates in the airways with repeated smoking. It isn't water-soluble, and it can't be flushed out by food, herbs, or drinks, no matter how natural they sound. The lungs clean themselves using a built-in system called mucociliary clearance. Tiny hair-like structures, known as cilia, constantly move mucus upward so trapped particles can be coughed out or swallowed. Smoking damages these cilia, slowing this process or stopping it altogether. What actually restarts lung cleaning is quitting smoking, not adding clove to the diet. Once smoking stops, cilia gradually recover, mucus starts moving again, and the lungs begin clearing debris on their own. This recovery takes weeks to months, and sometimes longer. Clove does not repair cilia or speed up this process in any proven way. According to Dr Rohan Bartake, the idea of 'detoxifying' the lungs is often misunderstood. He explains that once lung damage occurs such as tar accumulation or destruction of the alveoli it cannot be reversed by any food, drink, or herbal remedy. While a nutritious diet and healthier lifestyle can support overall body function, improve breathing efficiency, and help prevent further harm, they do not cleanse the lungs directly. Measures like quitting smoking, reducing exposure to pollutants, and staying well hydrated allow the lungs to use their own repair mechanisms, but herbal teas or specific foods do not have the ability to physically clean or detox the lungs. Clove has been studied for general antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effects, mostly in lab and animal research. While these findings are scientifically interesting, they cannot be directly applied to a smoker's lungs. There are no human studies showing that clove improves lung function, reverses smoke damage, or lowers long-term respiratory risks in smokers. At best, clove is a flavourful spice with some biological activity. That does not make it a lung detoxifier. According to Dr Muskan Thakur, an Ayurveda consultant based in Indore, cloves are valued in Ayurvedic practice for their warming nature and antimicrobial properties, which may help soothe throat irritation and support overall respiratory comfort. However, she cautions that cloves on their own are not a treatment for bronchitis or other respiratory infections. Ayurveda follows an individualised, holistic approach that combines dietary guidance, herbal support, and lifestyle adjustments. For symptoms that are persistent or severe, Dr Thakur advises seeking care from a qualified medical professional to ensure proper evaluation and treatment. The only approach consistently proven to allow the lungs to heal is stopping smoking. After quitting, supportive habits, staying hydrated, gentle physical activity, vaccinations, and timely medical check-ups can support lung health. But none of these truly 'detox' the lungs on their own.

title: Fact Check: Can clove water effectively manage acne?
claim_text: A Facebook post titled '8 Surprising Benefits of Drinking Clove Water – A Natural Health Booster' implies that clove water is a potent therapeutic option for acne because of its antibacterial and antifungal qualities.
quick_take: According to a Facebook reel, clove water can effectively manage acne. We fact-checked the notion and found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Acne (acne vulgaris) is a prevalent, persistent inflammatory dermatological condition caused by clogged hair follicles underneath the skin's surface. It manifests as whiteheads, blackheads, pimples, and sometimes deeper cysts when dead skin cells and sebum clog the pores. Its multifaceted pathogenesis includes follicular blockage, excess sebum, bacterial contamination, and immunological responses. Adolescents, those with a family history, those experiencing hormonal swings, and those eating foods with a high glycaemic load are particularly at risk. There is no substantial scientific evidence to suggest the application or consumption of clove water, a moderate aqueous homemade infusion, as a reliable cure for acne. Due to the presence of eugenol, clove (Syzygium aromaticum) has long been evaluated for its antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant effects. Clove oil and its extracts may suppress Cutibacterium acnes (previously Propionibacterium acnes) along with other skin bacteria associated with acne by rupturing bacterial membranes and reducing inflammatory mediators. Furthermore, topical formulations that combine clove oil with other therapeutic agents, such as curcumin, may help reduce lesion counts. However, these beneficial findings are confined to preliminary in-vitro research. Therefore, extensive clinical human trials are needed to prove that clove-based compositions are effective therapies for acne. The potency and concentration of active ingredients in clove water are significantly lower than those of regulated extracts used in controlled trials. Natural concoctions are unregulated and vary significantly in terms of safety, purity, and dosage. Due to its lack of standardisation, the at-home formulation cannot replace clinically validated acne therapies. Moreover, overuse of concentrated clove oil may irritate the skin and result in allergies and dermatitis. While some plant extracts such as rosemary and tea tree may have modest antibacterial or anti-inflammatory effect, their formulations are not standardised or regulated, their trials are inconsistent, and they lack high-quality evidence. Unregulated natural remedies could help with acne's surface symptoms but not its underlying cause. Additionally, applying them excessively or incorrectly might irritate or damage the skin's barrier, exacerbating breakouts or causing redness. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar clarifies: 'A balanced diet, appropriate hydration, and using mild skincare products are all important components of healthy, radiant skin.' Even though home remedies can help hydrate the body and provide vital nutrients, they cannot prevent acne on their own. Maintaining a regular skincare routine, regulating stress, and getting adequate sleep are all equally crucial for clear skin because hormones, stress, and clogged pores all contribute to acne. Dr. Sachin Gupta emphasises that 'acne is a medical concern that calls for targeted care based on the individual's skin type and severity of the condition.' For more persistent cases, using evidence-based treatments such as topical retinoids or benzoyl peroxide or speaking with a dermatologist are crucial. Opting for unregulated at-home options for skin issues such as acne may worsen the condition by delaying required intervention.

title: Can clove water spray help in skin whitening?
claim_text: An Instagram post suggests that clove water, if used topically, can lighten your skin color.
quick_take: A social media post suggest that spraying clove water on the skin can lead to skin whitening. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Skin colour is determined mainly by melanin, a pigment produced by specialised skin cells. To truly "whiten" or lighten skin, something would need to safely reduce melanin production or distribution in human skin and clove water has not been proven to do this. There are no well-designed human clinical studies showing that clove water spray can lighten skin tone. Most claims online are based on personal anecdotes or misunderstandings of laboratory research, not real-world evidence. Dr Sachin Gupta, MBBS, MD (Dermatology and Venereology, AIIMS Delhi), Amrita Hospital, cautions: "In dermatology, 'natural' does not automatically mean safe or effective. Substances that appear gentle or harmless can still pose risks to the skin." For any persistent or concerning skin issue, consulting a qualified dermatologist remains the safest option. Dermatologists design treatment plans based on scientific evidence, clinical experience, and a clear understanding of individual skin physiology. This personalised, evidence-based approach helps ensure that skin treatments are both effective and appropriate for a person's specific needs. Some laboratory (test-tube) studies have explored clove extracts and compounds like eugenol for their effect on melanin-producing cells. In very controlled lab conditions, certain extracts showed an ability to influence melanin pathways. However, lab studies are not the same as skincare evidence. These experiments use isolated cells, precise concentrations, and purified compounds. Human skin is far more complex, it has protective barriers, blood flow, immune responses, and constant exposure to sunlight and pollution. What works in a petri dish does not automatically work on a face. Even more importantly, not all research points in the same direction. Some experimental studies suggest that eugenol can stimulate melanocyte activity under certain conditions, which could theoretically increase pigmentation rather than reduce it. This inconsistency alone makes clove a poor candidate for "whitening." Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, an MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, also explains that skin pigmentation is largely influenced by genetic makeup and environmental exposure. Although various measures can help improve overall skin brightness and appearance, a person's natural skin pigmentation cannot be changed, only enhanced or managed to some extent. Clove contains eugenol, a biologically active compound that can irritate the skin. When applied repeatedly especially in homemade, unmeasured concentrations it may cause skin irritation. When skin becomes inflamed, the body responds by increasing melanin production during healing. This process, called post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, is a common cause of stubborn dark patches particularly in medium to deeper skin tones. Ironically, a remedy used for "whitening" can leave skin looking darker and patchier over time. While clove oil is more concentrated and clearly risky, clove water is still unpredictable. There is no standard recipe. One person may soak two cloves, another may boil ten. Spray frequency, skin sensitivity, sun exposure, and existing acne or damage all change how skin reacts. "Natural" does not mean gentle. Many plant compounds are potent precisely because they are biologically active. Without proper formulation and testing, even diluted preparations can cause harm. Some people notice a brief tightening or refreshing sensation after using clove water. This is not whitening. It is usually due to mild astringent or irritant effects that temporarily reduce oil or tighten pores. Once washed off or once irritation sets in the effect disappears. Temporary brightness is often mistaken for long-term skin improvement, which fuels misleading claims online. Evidence-based skincare works better and is safer. If the goal is an even, healthy-looking complexion (not changing natural skin colour), professional guidance and evidence-based skincare products are far more effective than DIY remedies.

title: Can Cloves Really Grow Your Eyelashes in Just Three Days? - THIP
claim_text: A Facebook post claims that a paste prepared from roasted cloves, aloe vera, vitamin E capsules and castor oil can make eyelashes grow within just three days.
verdict_original: found the claim to be false
quick_take: A social media post suggests that cloves paste with castor oil make your eyelashes grow in three days. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Eyelashes simply cannot grow to a noticeable length within three days because of the way the hair growth cycle works. Every eyelash grows from a hair follicle embedded in the eyelid. These follicles follow a structured biological cycle made up of three stages: the growth phase (anagen), the transition phase (catagen) and the resting phase (telogen). For eyelashes, the active growth phase is relatively short, around 4 to 6 weeks, and growth happens gradually. On average, lashes grow about 0.1 to 0.2 millimetres per day. That means in three days, the total growth would be less than one millimetre. Less than one millimetre is barely noticeable to the naked eye. It certainly does not translate into visibly longer, fuller lashes in a dramatic way. For any ingredient to produce such rapid change, it would need to dramatically accelerate cell division inside the follicle, something no cosmetic oil or home mixture has been shown to do.

There is no scientific evidence showing that cloves can stimulate eyelash follicles to grow faster. Cloves contain eugenol, a naturally occurring compound known for its antioxidant and mild anti-inflammatory properties. In laboratory research, certain plant compounds have been studied for their potential effects on scalp circulation. However, this is very different from proving that a ground clove paste applied to eyelashes causes hair growth in humans. There are no clinical trials examining clove application on eyelashes. There is no dermatological evidence showing that eugenol can extend the anagen phase or activate dormant follicles in the eyelid area. In fact, cloves are considered quite potent and can be irritating. Clove oil is commonly diluted before being used even on thicker skin areas like the scalp. The eyelid, by contrast, has some of the thinnest and most sensitive skin on the body. Applying a concentrated spice preparation near the eyes is more likely to cause burning or redness than follicle stimulation.

These ingredients may condition lashes, but they do not create rapid biological growth. Castor oil is thick and coats the hair shaft. When applied to lashes, it can make them appear darker, shinier and slightly thicker because the oil adds weight and sheen. This cosmetic effect can create the illusion of fuller lashes. However, coating the hair shaft does not change what is happening inside the follicle beneath the skin. Vitamin E is an antioxidant that supports skin health and protects cells from oxidative stress. While it plays a role in general skin integrity, there is no solid scientific evidence showing that topical vitamin E accelerates eyelash growth. Aloe vera is soothing and hydrating. It can calm irritated skin and improve moisture levels. But again, hydration does not equal accelerated hair production. None of these ingredients alter the internal growth cycle of the lash follicle in a matter of days.

Dermatologist Dr Sachin Gupta of Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, explains that there is no quick fix for faster hair growth. He notes that unregulated products rarely work because hair growth depends on hormones, nutrition, genetics and overall health. A balanced diet, proper hair care and medical advice for underlying issues are far more effective.

Dr Sandeep Arora, consultant Dermatologist at Mehektagul Dermaclinic, Delhi, explains that there is no instant solution for making eyebrows or eyelashes thicker. Even medically prescribed treatments require time to show visible results. He also warns that using home remedies in unregulated or unknown concentrations can trigger serious allergic reactions and should therefore be avoided.

Applying roasted clove powder near the eyes carries real risk. The eyelids are extremely delicate. They contain thin skin, minimal fat and a high density of nerve endings. Clove compounds such as eugenol can cause irritation, stinging or allergic contact dermatitis. If even a small amount enters the eye, it may cause watering, burning, swelling or blurred vision. Grinding roasted cloves into powder also introduces the risk of tiny abrasive particles. These particles can scratch the surface of the eye (the cornea) if they migrate during blinking. Eye irritation is not only uncomfortable, it can lead to infection if the protective barrier is disrupted. The spoolie brush itself can introduce bacteria if not properly cleaned.

If someone genuinely struggles with thinning lashes, there are medically approved options. Certain prescription treatments containing prostaglandin analogues have been clinically tested and shown to prolong the growth phase of eyelashes. These are regulated, studied for safety and prescribed under medical supervision. They work by extending the anagen phase, something cosmetic oils do not do. Beyond medication, maintaining good overall health matters. Adequate protein intake, sufficient iron levels, thyroid balance and avoiding excessive mascara or harsh lash extensions all support natural lash health. But even with proper support, lash growth is gradual. Visible change takes weeks, not days.

title: Fact Check: Can Coconut and clove Oil Pulling with Herbal Rinses Reverse Tooth Decay?
claim_text: Oil pulling with coconut oil and clove oil, along with rinsing with saltwater and using black cumin seed oil, can reverse tooth decay.
doctor_explanation:
Tooth decay, also known as tooth cavity or dental caries, is defined by Shafers in 1993 as an irreversible microbial disease of the calcified tissues of the teeth, characterized by demineralization of the inorganic portion and destruction of the organic substance of the tooth, which often leads to cavitation. This widespread chronic condition is primarily caused by cariogenic bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans, which attach to the teeth. These bacteria break down sugars into acid, causing the gradual erosion and weakening of the tooth structure. The formation of dental caries depends on four key factors: bacterial biofilm (plaque), fermentable carbohydrates, dental hard tissues, and sufficient time. Tooth decay cannot be cured or reversed once it has formed.

Dr. Bhumika Gupta Dani, Dental Surgeon, Dani Dental Clinic, Kawardha, Chhattisgarh, told Medical Dialogues: 'Oil pulling with coconut oil or clove oil can be a helpful addition to your oral hygiene routine for reducing bacteria or improving gum health, but it cannot reverse tooth decay. Once decay sets in, the damage to the tooth structure is permanent and needs professional treatment. While oil pulling has its benefits, it's important to focus on prevention through proper brushing, flossing, and regular dental checkups to keep your teeth healthy.'

A systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of the International Oral Health emphasized coconut oil's antimicrobial properties in reducing bacterial colonization and improving oral hygiene through oil pulling. However, it does not support the claim that coconut oil pulling can reverse tooth decay. There are no scientific studies on the effectiveness of clove oil pulling in reversing tooth decay. One study in the International Journal of Dentistry found that clove-oil-treated teeth showed reduced decalcification, but the study does not mention clove oil pulling or its role in reversing tooth decay.

Regarding Pink Himalayan salt water: There are no studies that discuss the role of rinsing with Pink Himalayan Salt water in reversing tooth decay. One study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health mentions that using a sea salt-based mouthwash as part of daily oral hygiene can reduce the bacterial levels of S. mutans, but this study does not mention that sea salt can reverse tooth decay once it has occurred.

Regarding Black Cumin Seed Oil (Nigella sativa L.): A study on the effects of black seed on teeth, published in the Indian Journal of Public Health Research & Development, found that water extract of black seed (Nigella sativa) can reduce the loss of potassium and zinc ions from teeth, which may strengthen teeth and improve resistance to acid attacks. However, this study does not highlight the role of black cumin seed oil in the reversal of tooth decay.

Dr. Deepika Jain, Orthodontist, Samda Superspeciality Hospital, Rajnandgaon, C.G., told Medical Dialogues: 'Using remedies like rinsing with Pink Himalayan salt water or applying Black Cumin Seed Oil may have some general oral health benefits, but they cannot reverse tooth decay once it has occurred. Tooth decay causes permanent damage to the tooth structure, and no home remedy can undo that. The best approach is to focus on prevention through good oral hygiene, a healthy diet, and regular dental checkups to address any issues early.'

Medical Dialogues Final Take: While oil pulling with coconut oil or clove oil, rinsing with Pink Himalayan salt water, or using Black Cumin Seed Oil may support oral health and reduce bacteria, they cannot reverse tooth decay once it has occurred. Tooth decay is a permanent process that damages the tooth structure and requires professional dental treatment to prevent further progression and restore the affected areas.

title: Can coconut oil, cloves, and salt mixture cure all dental issues?
claim_text: Oil pulling with a mixture of coconut oil, cloves, and salt, stored in a glass jar, can cure bleeding gums, cavities, and yellow teeth. It promises guaranteed results for all dental problems and eliminates the need for visiting the dentist.
quick_take: A social media post claims that coconut oil, cloves and salt mixture can cure all dental issues. Our fact check shows that this claim is false.
doctor_explanation:
Oil pulling is an ancient practice of swishing oil in the mouth. This practice may help reduce bacteria that contribute to gum inflammation, a common cause of bleeding gums. Coconut oil has antibacterial properties due to its lauric acid content, and cloves contain eugenol, known for its anti-inflammatory effects. Moreover, a 2016 study suggests that oil pulling with coconut oil might offer slight improvements in gum health. However, it's important to note that bleeding gums can also signal more serious issues, including conditions such as gingivitis or periodontitis, which require professional dental care. This mixture isn't a guaranteed cure-all, and its benefits are limited.

Cavities are holes in tooth enamel caused by bacterial acid eroding the surface, and once formed, they cannot be reversed by oil pulling or any home remedy. Since enamel doesn't regenerate naturally, repairing damaged teeth requires professional care. While coconut oil may reduce some oral bacteria, it doesn't have the ability to heal cavities. Similarly, cloves and salt offer no proven cavity-curing benefits. Cloves may provide temporary relief from toothaches, but they cannot treat or cure tooth decay. Only a dentist can properly treat cavities with fillings or other interventions.

Coconut oil pulling cannot whiten teeth. There's no solid evidence that oil pulling with coconut oil—let alone with added cloves and salt—significantly whitens teeth. A 2015 study showed that coconut oil pulling reduces plaque and gingivitis over 30 days, but it didn't assess tooth colour or whitening. Plaque reduction might slightly lessen surface stains over time by clearing debris that traps discolouration, but this is unproven and far from significant. Cloves and salt don't have bleaching properties, and no research supports this mixture as a whitening agent. For noticeable whitening, professional treatments with bleaching agents like hydrogen peroxide are proven to work far better.

Dental problems range from plaque buildup to tooth decay, gum disease, and even oral cancer. This mixture might slightly reduce bacteria or inflammation, but it's not a universal fix. The claim of 100% guaranteed results lacks evidence—science doesn't support such absolute promises. A 2017 review found oil pulling has mild benefits for oral hygiene, but it's no substitute for brushing, flossing, or dental care. The idea that it replaces dentists is baseless. Dentists diagnose and treat issues this mixture can't touch—like hidden decay or gum disease progression. Ignoring professional care risks worsening problems. The American Dental Association stresses regular check-ups for prevention and early treatment. Relying solely on this remedy could cost more in the long run—both in money and health.

title: Fact Check: Can Coconut Oil Pulling Heal Gingivitis or Gum Inflammation?
claim_text: Oil pulling can help to heal the gums. One lady told me that she had infected gums called gingivitis. The dentist advised her to take antibiotics. And she asked for my advice. I said to her I wouldn't take the antibiotics. I would oil pull three times a day. And she oil pulled three times a day. She emailed me a week later and said her gums were totally healed. And oil pulling is putting a spoonful of coconut oil in your mouth and then swishing it around. You might swish for 10 seconds, rest for 10 seconds, swish for 10 seconds, rest for 10 seconds, and do it like this for 10 minutes. Now, the reason why it's called oil pulling is it pulls waste out of your tongue. It pulls waste out of the glands and the blood vessels under your tongue. It also seems to pull from the sinuses, and when you've pulled that waste into the oil after 10 minutes, then you release it out.
quick_take: Coconut oil pulling is known to provide oral health benefits, such as reducing inflammation, bleeding gums, dry mouth, and bad breath. However, there is no scientific evidence or dental consensus supporting the claim that it can heal gingivitis or gum inflammation on its own. Gingivitis has multiple causes, and proper dental care, professional treatment, and good oral hygiene are essential for managing the condition. Relying solely on oil pulling without consulting a dentist may lead to untreated gum disease and further complications.
doctor_explanation:
Gingivitis is a condition where the gums become inflamed, usually due to a bacterial infection. It causes redness, swelling, and irritation in the gum tissue but does not lead to loss of attachment between the gums and teeth. If left untreated, it can worsen and lead to more serious gum diseases. Poor oral hygiene causes bacterial plaque buildup, which can trigger gum inflammation (gingivitis) in less than a week. In the early stage, the gums produce more fluid and immune cells to fight the bacteria, leading to swelling and irritation. As gingivitis progresses, the immune response weakens gum fibres and creates pockets between the gums and teeth. If left untreated, this can damage the bone and ligaments supporting the teeth, potentially leading to tooth loss. There are various causes or types of gingivitis, including bacterial plaque, necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG), medication-influenced gingivitis, infection-related gingivitis, allergic gingivitis, and systemic disease-associated gingivitis.

Coconut oil is rich in medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs), unlike most other dietary oils which contain long-chain fatty acids. About 50% of these MCFAs are lauric acid, which has antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties and is effective against harmful bacteria like Streptococcus mutans and Candida albicans. Coconut oil pulling is a traditional Ayurvedic practice from ancient India for maintaining oral hygiene involving swishing coconut oil in the mouth to help reduce inflammation, bleeding gums, dry mouth, and bad breath.

Coconut oil pulling offers various health benefits helping reduce inflammation, bleeding gums, dry mouth, and bad breath, and improving overall oral health. Although there are studies that have demonstrated that coconut oil pulling helps reduce plaque-induced gingivitis, there is no consensus or scientific evidence that supports the claim that coconut oil pulling heals gingivitis or gum inflammation on its own.

A study published in The Nigerian Medical Journal concluded that oil pulling with coconut oil may serve as a beneficial supplementary practice in reducing plaque buildup and managing plaque-induced gingivitis, but did not highlight the standalone role of coconut oil pulling in curing gingivitis, nor did it address all types and causes of the condition.

Another study published in the European Journal of Dentistry demonstrated significant and promising improvements in reducing plaque buildup and gingivitis, but does not claim that coconut oil pulling alone can heal gingivitis.

Yet one more study published in the Journal of the Indian Association of Public Health Dentistry found that coconut oil pulling when used as a supplementary oral hygiene practice is effective in reducing plaque buildup and plaque-induced gingivitis. This study does not state that coconut oil pulling alone can heal gingivitis.

Dr Prithvi Dani, BDS, Dental Surgeon, Dani Dental Care, Kawardha, C.G. told Medical Dialogues: 'Coconut oil pulling is a great addition to an oral care routine and may help with issues like bad breath, dry mouth, and mild gum inflammation. However, it should not replace proper dental care. Gingivitis has multiple causes, and the best way to treat it is through good oral hygiene, regular dental checkups, and professional treatment when needed.'

Dr Ritu Thawait, Dental Surgeon, Medical Officer, CHC, Risali, Durg, C.G. added: 'Many people try coconut oil pulling for better oral health, and while it can be a useful practice, it's not a cure-all. Gingivitis needs proper care, including brushing, flossing, and professional cleanings. If your gums are swollen, bleeding, or painful, don't rely on home remedies alone—visit a dentist to get the right treatment before it worsens.'

title: Can Coconut Water and Olive Oil Dissolve Kidney Stones? - THIP
claim_text: Drinking coconut water mixed with olive oil can dissolve kidney stones naturally and flush them out of the body without medical treatment.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that coconut water and olive oil can dissolve kidney stones of any size. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Coconut water cannot dissolve kidney stones that have already formed. Kidney stones are not soft deposits that can be 'washed away.' They are hard, solid crystals made when minerals in urine, such as calcium, oxalate, or uric acid, bind together over time. Once a stone forms, it behaves much more like a tiny rock than something that can melt or break apart with fluids. Coconut water is often promoted because it feels natural, gentle, and hydrating. Hydration is important for kidney health, but hydration alone does not dissolve stones. Drinking coconut water may help dilute urine and reduce the chance of new crystals forming, but it cannot reverse a stone that is already there. There's also a practical concern: people trying this remedy often drink large quantities daily. Coconut water is naturally high in potassium, which can be risky for people with kidney disease or reduced kidney function, especially when stones are already stressing the kidneys. Olive oil does not break down kidney stones or help push them out of the kidneys. This idea comes from detox and 'cleanse' myths that blur the line between digestion and urinary function. Olive oil is digested in the gut. Kidney stones form in the kidneys and urinary tract. These systems do not connect in a way that allows oil to reach or act on stones. Some people report passing 'stones' after drinking olive oil mixtures. However, medical analysis has shown that what is passed in these cases is often soft, waxy material formed from oil and digestive secretions, not actual kidney stones. Real kidney stones are dense, mineral-based, and typically very painful to pass. Olive oil is a healthy fat when used in normal cooking, but it does not dissolve stones or flush them out. There is no credible scientific evidence to support this claim. Kidney stone treatment depends on the stone's composition. The most common type, calcium oxalate stones, cannot be dissolved by foods or drinks. Some uric acid stones may be dissolved, but only with prescription alkalising therapy under medical supervision. If coconut water or olive oil truly dissolved kidney stones, they would be part of standard medical treatment but they are not. Dr. Archana Daftardar, Consultant Nephrologist, Hypertension and Transplant Physician at Renova Hospitals, Kompally, Hyderabad, notes that citrus fruits such as lemons can increase urinary citrate levels, which may help lower the risk of calcium stone formation. She also mentions that coconut water may encourage better overall fluid intake. However, she points out that there is limited evidence to support any added benefit of combining coconut water with olive oil and lemon juice. Dr. Ganesh Srinivasa Prasad P, Consultant Nephrologist and Transplant Physician at Narayana Health City, Bengaluru explains that 'Once kidney stones have formed, they usually require medical treatment for removal. However, certain lifestyle and dietary measures can help reduce the risk of new stones developing. Management depends on the type of stone, and there is no scientific evidence to show that coconut water or lemon juice can prevent kidney stones. Instead, he highlighted the importance of adequate hydration, limiting salt intake, consuming enough calcium from food, avoiding foods high in oxalates, and maintaining a healthy body weight. For individuals prone to uric acid stones, he added that reducing meat, sugar, and refined carbohydrates, along with avoiding alcohol and smoking, may help lower the risk.'

title: Fact Check: Can coffee cause cancer? - THIP Media
claim_text: Coffee is proven to cause certain types of cancer

title: Fact Check: Can coffee, cinnamon and onion grow hair faster?
claim_text: According to a Facebook video, you can make your hair grow faster by using a blend of onion, coffee and cinnamon.
quick_take: A Facebook video claims that a blend of coffee, cinnamon and onion can make the hair grow faster. We did the fact check to term it as Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
Hair grows from follicles located in the skin, and each follicle goes through a growth cycle comprising three phases: anagen (growth phase), catagen (transitional phase), and telogen (resting phase). During the anagen phase, hair grows approximately half an inch per month. Factors influencing hair growth include genetics, hormones, diet, and overall health. Some topical treatments can support scalp health. But, they cannot dramatically speed up the inherent growth rate determined by these factors.

Can a blend of onion, coffee and cinnamon make the hair grow faster?
No, not really. These ingredients may offer some benefits for scalp health, there's no scientific evidence to support the claim that they can significantly accelerate hair growth. Onions contain sulphur, which can improve blood circulation and deliver essential nutrients to hair follicles. However, the evidence supporting onion juice as a hair growth treatment is mostly anecdotal. Similarly, coffee contains caffeine, which may stimulate blood circulation and improve follicle health, but its impact on actual hair growth remains minimal. Cinnamon, known for its antimicrobial properties, might improve scalp health, yet it does not enhance the speed of hair growth significantly.

There is a widespread practice of using home remedies for hair growth like neem oil, fenugreek seeds, coconut oil concoction, eating fennel seeds, etc. But, just like onion, coffee and cinnamon mixture, even these lack the clinical evidence. We need more research to substantiate these home remedies for hair growth.

Dr Sachin Gupta, Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, offers a professional perspective: "There is little to no scientific backing for the claim that onion, coffee, and cinnamon can speed up hair growth. These ingredients may improve scalp health for some people. But they should not be relied upon as a primary method for hair growth. It is essential to focus on overall health, proper nutrition, and proven treatments."

Is onion good for hair?
Onion juice has gained popularity as a home remedy for hair loss. It contains sulphur, which can improve blood circulation, providing follicles with nourishment and promoting hair health. Some small studies and informal evidence suggest that applying onion juice might help with hair loss and improve hair strength. However, these findings are not conclusive, and we need more research to validate onion juice as an effective hair growth treatment.

Science shows that onion juice can help with hair loss due to its high sulphur content. Sulphur is essential for protein formation, including keratin, which is crucial for strong hair. Applying onion juice to the scalp provides extra sulphur, promoting strong and thick hair, and may also enhance collagen production, supporting healthy skin and hair growth. Additionally, onions may boost circulation, improving blood supply to hair follicles. A 2002 study found that participants who used onion juice experienced more hair growth than those who used tap water. However, the study is old and incomplete, necessitating further research. Onion juice can stimulate and protect existing hair growth but is not a cure for hair loss conditions like alopecia or pattern baldness.

Is coffee and cinnamon good for your hair?
Coffee, with its high caffeine content, is sometimes used in hair treatments. Caffeine can stimulate blood circulation to the scalp, potentially promoting a healthier environment for hair growth. Coffee also contains antioxidants, which can help combat free radicals and maintain scalp health. However, these benefits are mild and do not translate into significantly faster hair growth. Also, there isn't much research available on the efficacy of caffeine for hair growth. We found one lab study which looks at the positive effect of caffeine on hair growth. Once again, we need more research on animals and then humans to come to a conclusion.

Cinnamon's antimicrobial properties help keep the scalp healthy by preventing infections and creating a clean environment for hair to grow. A 2019 review looked at procyanidin, a compound in cinnamon, and found older studies linking it to hair growth, although these studies used procyanidin from apple juice. A 2018 animal study showed that cinnamon oil could improve hair length in male rats as effectively as 2% minoxidil (Rogaine). Researchers believe this effect is due to cinnamaldehyde, which increases circulation and blood flow to hair follicles. However, we need more research on procyanidin from cinnamon and further human studies.

What are the disadvantages of coffee in hair?
Coffee may have some benefits, but using it on your hair can lead to potential downsides. Applying coffee to your hair can result in dryness and brittleness, especially if you don't rinse it out thoroughly. The caffeine in coffee might also cause irritation or allergic reactions in some individuals. Overusing coffee in hair treatments can strip moisture from the hair, making it more prone to breakage. It's important to use coffee treatments in moderation and follow up with a conditioner to maintain moisture balance.

What are the side effects of using onion and cinnamon for hair?
Onions and cinnamon can cause allergic reactions in some individuals. Onions can sometimes irritate the skin, causing redness and itching. Mixing onion juice with soothing substances like aloe vera or coconut oil can help reduce these effects. But remember, onion juice won't cure conditions like alopecia. For people with alopecia, hair transplants may be the only solution. Also, certain medications, like aspirin, can make your skin more sensitive to onion juice, so it's wise to do a skin test or ask your doctor before using it. Similarly, cinnamon oil and ground cinnamon may irritate the skin too, causing redness or a burning feeling. To lower the risk, dilute cinnamon oil (or the powder) and test it on a small area of skin first. Even though cinnamon is safe to eat, be careful with the oil—it can cause skin reactions in some people.

How to grow hair faster?
Expecting significant hair growth in just one week is unrealistic. But you can take steps to optimise hair health and create the best conditions for growth. You should keep in mind that these methods can only support overall hair health. But they will not lead to dramatic results in just one week. Consistency and a holistic approach to health and hair care are key to achieving and maintaining healthy hair growth over time.

In conclusion, the claim that a blend of onion, coffee, and cinnamon can accelerate hair growth is mostly false. These ingredients may offer some benefits for scalp health, but they do not make the hair grow faster. Focusing on a balanced diet, proper scalp care, and proven hair treatments is a more reliable approach to achieving healthy hair.

title: Fact Check: Can coffee enema detoxify our bodies safely? - THIP Media
claim_text: Yes, pouring a quart of coffee up your butt sounds weird, but it's one of the fastest and most effective ways to get rid of a whole lot of toxins all at once, and it's really not that big of a deal.

doctor_explanation: An enema is a medical procedure that involves introducing liquid into the rectum and colon through the anus. It must be noted that colon cleansing is not considered necessary as our digestive system and bowel already eliminate waste material and bacteria from our bodies. The fundamental causes of dark circles include ageing, hereditary predisposition, thinning of the periorbital skin, hyperpigmentation, impaired blood circulation, and unhealthy lifestyle choices. Extended periods of screen time, the tendency to touch one's eyes, and specific allergies can all be significant influences. While the combination of coffee, turmeric, and aloe vera gel is gaining popularity as a natural alternative for under-eye dark circles, its relevance is limited to social media and lifestyle blogs. Additionally, caffeine has demonstrated quantifiable effects in reducing pigmentation and puffiness when utilised in formulated products. Turmeric (Curcumin): Because the golden spice contains curcumin, which has been demonstrated to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant qualities, it may be beneficial for skin health. Aloe vera gel (Aloesin): In addition to its recognised hydrating and moisturising attributes, aloesin may help prevent melanin production, ultimately enhancing skin quality. Although the aforementioned components may have a slight melanin-reducing effect, preclinical studies are the only ones that have demonstrated these benefits. To confirm the efficacy of the homemade formula for eliminating dark circles, more thorough, extensive clinical trials are required. Dr. Rashi Soni, a Consultant Dermatologist at Mumbai's Rashi Hospital, concurs, maintaining that while the aforementioned ingredients may appear to be natural substitutes, they are ineffective for getting rid of dark circles. Several variables, such as thin skin, ageing, lack of sleep, and inheritance, may contribute to under-eye pigmentation, and home remedies are inadequate to remove the condition. While certain components could be aesthetically pleasing, they fail to resolve the core issue. Perseverance, patience, and a personalised skincare routine closely supervised by a dermatologist are frequently necessary for attaining results. While the blend of coffee, aloe vera gel, and turmeric may be a safe substitute for clinically established therapies, it cannot serve as their replacement. It is impractical and unscientific to claim that dark circles may be removed in a week, especially with an unapproved home cure. This may be explained by the fact that under-eye pigmentation is a multifaceted concern—usually a combination of genetics, pigmentation, thin skin, blood vessel visibility, and structural shadows from tear troughs or volume loss—that cannot be completely resolved with quick fixes. An obvious decline in pigmentation usually calls for weeks to months of consistent application of prescribed skincare formulations. Dr. Iftekhar Khan, MD (Dermatology), Assistant Professor at SMS Medical College in Jaipur, maintains that home remedies are not the most efficient means for addressing under-eye discolouration. title: Fact Check: Can cold cough home remedies cure symptoms in one use?

doctor_explanation: Can cold cough home remedies cure symptoms quickly? No. Natural ingredients like onion, garlic, lemon, cinnamon, and honey have health benefits, but they cannot cure a cold, cough, or fever in one use. Colds are caused by viruses, and the body typically needs 7-10 days to recover, even with treatment. These ingredients may help ease symptoms, but scientific evidence does not support a one-use cure. For example, honey can soothe a sore throat, and garlic has antibacterial properties, but they do not eliminate viruses instantly. Do onion garlic for cough fight viruses effectively? Maybe. Onions and garlic contain compounds like allicin, which have some antiviral and antibacterial properties. Small studies suggest garlic might reduce the severity of cold symptoms if taken regularly. However, there is no evidence that boiling onion garlic for cough and drinking them once will cure a cold or fever. The body's immune system primarily fights the virus, and these foods may only offer mild support. Can lemon and cinnamon boost recovery speed? No. Lemons are rich in vitamin C, which helps support the immune system. But studies show that vitamin C doesn't prevent colds for most people. Taking it every day might help you recover about a day faster, but it won't stop the symptoms or make them milder. Starting vitamin C after catching a cold doesn't help either. Most people get enough from food, and the extra is flushed out in urine. Only people who do heavy physical activity in cold weather, like athletes or soldiers, may see some benefit. Moreover, cinnamon has anti-inflammatory properties, but there is no research proving it can cure cold cough home remedies in one dose. These ingredients may make you feel better temporarily, but they do not address the virus directly. Is honey effective for cough and fever relief? Yes, but not for a complete cure in one use. Honey is proven to help reduce cough severity, especially in children, as shown in a 2018 study. It can coat the throat, easing irritation. However, honey does not cure the underlying viral infection or reduce fever significantly. Its effect is limited to symptom relief, not a one-time cure. Dr Muskan Thakur, Ayurvedic Consultant, from Indore, explains, "In Ayurveda, honey (Madhu) is described as having the gunas of Ruksha (dry), Laghu (light), and Ushna Virya (hot potency), with Madhura (sweet) and Kashaya (astringent) rasa. Its Ushna nature makes it effective in reducing aggravated Kapha dosha, which is commonly associated with cough, congestion, and throat irritation. The dry and light qualities help break down mucus, while its astringent action tones the mucous membranes. Though honey does not act as a direct antipyretic, it supports strength (Balya) and quick recovery during fever by providing nourishment and aiding digestion (Deepana)." Are there risks in relying on a home remedy alone? Yes. Relying solely on cold cough home remedies could delay proper treatment. Fevers, especially if high or persistent, may signal a more serious condition requiring medical attention. While these ingredients are generally safe, they are not a substitute for rest, hydration, or, in some cases, medical care like antipyretics for fever. Always consult a doctor if symptoms worsen or last longer than expected. Dr Ubaid ur Rehman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, says, "Relying only on home remedies like lemon or vitamin C for colds can be risky. While these remedies may offer some comfort or mild benefit, they can't replace proper medical advice, especially if symptoms get worse or last too long. It's also important to remember that taking too much vitamin C doesn't boost your immunity further, your body just flushes out the extra. The best way to support your immune system is by eating a balanced diet, getting enough sleep, staying active, and keeping up with regular health checks. If you're unsure, always speak to your doctor rather than self-diagnosing or overloading on supplements." Similarly, there are claims that ginger and turmeric can instantly cure a cough and cold. However, this is also misleading. In summary, the claim is false. While onion, garlic, lemon, cinnamon, and honey have health benefits and may ease some symptoms of a cold or cough, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that cold cough home remedies can cure cold, cough, and fever in just one use.

Migraine is a genetically influenced neurological disorder characterized by recurrent moderate-to-severe headaches, often one-sided, accompanied by nausea, light sensitivity, and sound sensitivity. Migraine triggers are diverse and include stress, hormonal fluctuations, certain foods, and environmental factors.

Dr Rahul Chawla (MBBS, MD General Medicine, DM Neurology), Consultant Neurologist at IBS Hospital, New Delhi, stated: "Early signs of a migraine can include mood changes, fatigue, food cravings, and neck stiffness. Some people experience an aura, with visual changes. As the headache sets in, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound are common. If these symptoms recur, consult a doctor for proper diagnosis."

Studies on cloves for headaches: A mini-review in Applied Food Research noted that sniffing the strong aroma of clove buds may reduce headache, irritability, and drowsiness, but does not recommend clove specifically for migraines. A review by Mayank Agrawal et al. noted clove oil has analgesic properties offering temporary pain relief for headaches, but no direct evidence supports cloves as a complete cure for migraines.

Dr Rahul Chawla further stated: "Although apples and cloves have some nutritional benefits, there's no scientific evidence to support that they can cure them. While they may provide minor relief due to their nutritional properties, they're not a proven solution. For effective management of migraines, it's essential to consult a healthcare professional and consider evidence-based treatments tailored to your condition."

**On Acidity:**
Acidity (heartburn) is a burning sensation in the chest or throat caused by stomach acid entering the oesophagus, resulting from acid reflux or GERD. Frequent heartburn linked to GERD can lead to serious oesophageal issues.

Dr Prakhar Gupta (M.S General Surgery, FNB Minimal Access Surgery, FMBS), Gastrointestinal, Bariatric and Advanced Laparoscopic Surgeon, explained: "Acid reflux is commonly triggered by factors like overeating, spicy or fatty foods, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, and lying down soon after meals. Stress, obesity, and certain medications can also contribute. To minimize it, try eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoid known trigger foods, and maintain a healthy weight."

Research on apples and acidity: A study in Nutrients journal mentioned various natural active ingredients including apples that may help reduce stomach acid secretions. Research on cloves and acidity: A review in Biomolecules noted clove possesses gastroprotective efficacy, but no study exists on clove in reducing stomach acidity or relieving heartburn.

Dr Prakhar Gupta concluded: "Apples and cloves do have some beneficial properties, but they aren't a cure for acid reflux or chronic acidity. While apples may provide temporary relief and cloves can offer mild soothing effects, they're not effective treatments. For lasting relief and proper care, it's best to consult a healthcare professional."

The method described — leaving cloves inside an apple for 12 hours — has no basis in medical literature or naturopathic principles for treating migraines or acidity.

title: Fact Check: Can community swimming pools cause HIV infection?
claim_text: A Facebook post claims: "No pools for me this summer!!" The post claims that community swimming pools can cause HIV infection. The post further goes on to say that, "4th person tested positive this week. Make sure everyone that visited this pool gets checked. The pool wasn't cared for and chemicals were not used."
quick_take: A post on Facebook claims that community swimming pools can cause HIV infection. We fact checked and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation: The claim that four individuals contracted HIV from a swimming pool lacks evidence. There have been no documented cases of HIV transmission in such a setting. HIV primarily spreads through unprotected sexual intercourse, needle sharing, or from mother to child during childbirth, breastfeeding, or pregnancy. Additionally, important details such as the location of the contaminated pool in the claim are not available. It is important to clarify that HIV cannot survive in swimming pools or hot tubs. The virus is highly delicate and cannot survive for long outside the human body. Therefore, the notion that HIV can transmit through swimming in the same pool as an HIV+ individual is baseless. Also, it cannot spread through sweat, urine or saliva. Dr Amit Harshana (MBBS, MD Community Health & Preventive Medicine, HIV Specialist) provides expert advice: "I want to reassure everyone that HIV does not transmit through casual contact, including swimming in community pools. The virus is fragile and cannot survive outside the body for long periods. However, it's important to understand that HIV can spread through specific bodily fluids, such as blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk, during activities like unprotected sex, sharing needles, or from mother to child during childbirth. To protect yourself and others, practice safe sex and avoid sharing needles or syringes." Dr Harshana further continues, "Getting regular tests for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections is necessary, as early detection can lead to better treatment outcomes. One important thing to note is that after accidental exposure, you must consult with an expert for post-exposure prophylaxis and follow the advice religiously. Initial tests after the exposure can remain negative for some time as the person might be in the window period and that's why it is important to follow the advice of follow up tests till you get final confirmation. It's essential to approach people living with HIV with empathy and understanding. People living with HIV face stigma and discrimination, which can affect their mental and physical well-being." HIV spreads through certain bodily fluids including blood, semen, vaginal fluids, and breast milk. The most common way HIV spreads is through unprotected sex with someone who has HIV. Sharing needles or syringes with someone who has HIV also puts you at risk. HIV can pass from a mother to her baby during childbirth, breastfeeding, or pregnancy. In rare cases, HIV transmission can occur through blood transfusions or organ transplants from infected donors. HIV cannot spread through casual contact like hugging, kissing, or sharing food or drinks. Currently, there is no cure for HIV. While there's significant progress in managing the virus through antiretroviral therapy (ART), which helps control HIV replication and slows down disease progression, it does not eliminate the virus from the body. HIV remains in the body for life, even when viral load becomes undetectable with treatment.

title: Fact Check: Can consuming alkaline foods cure cancer?
claim_text: A Facebook post by Shuddhi promotes an alkaline (ayurvedic) juice for cancer prepared from turmeric root, radish, banyan, betel, curry, spinach, methi, and guava leaves. The post claims these natural remedies support the body's cleansing mechanism and enhance holistic healing, with the underlying message that making the body alkaline can prevent cancer cells from thriving in an acidic environment and potentially restore normal function.
quick_take: A social media post claims that consumption of alkaline foods can manage and even reverse cancer, a potentially fatal illness. After verifying the assertion, we found that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
## Can a diet make the body more alkaline?
No, not exactly. Alkaline diets have gained a lot of popularity, particularly in wellness circles, due to their alleged potential to reduce inflammation, prevent certain medical conditions, and even combat cancer. They might not, however, be able to influence the body's pH.
It is thought that by including certain food types—known as alkaline-forming foods—and consuming less meat, dairy, and processed food, the body's internal environment may be altered to become less acidic, potentially lowering the likelihood of disease. While such plant-based diets have definite health benefits, it is crucial to note that there is no scientific evidence to support the primary assertion that alkaline foods may change the body's pH.
Another significant factor to consider is that the body regulates the blood pH within 7.35 to 7.45, and any deviation from this range is rectified by the lungs, kidneys, and buffering systems. Furthermore, food may influence the urine's pH. Therefore, the benefits of alkaline diets lie in their food density rather than modifications to the body's pH.

## Can cancer be cured through an alkaline diet?
No, not exactly. This is because alkaline foods may assist cancer patients in maintaining a balanced lifestyle and enhance general health, but there is no solid scientific evidence to support the claim that they may reverse or cure cancer.
In an Interview with THIP Media, Dr Manish Singhal, Oncologist, Apollo Hospital, Delhi, advises that while cancer cells may create an acidic tumour microenvironment around themselves, potentially supporting their growth and spread. While nutrition may have an effect on general health, it has no effect on the body's alkalinity or the acidity of the tumour microenvironment. However, these results are limited to controlled conditions and may not accurately mirror the complexities of the actual human body. Also, excessive alkaline circumstances negatively impact the body's natural functioning, potentially requiring hospitalisation.
Dr. Pooja Khullar, radiation oncologist at Dharamshila Narayana Superspeciality Hospital in New Delhi, supports this further by stating that some research has indicated that acidic surroundings promote the growth of cancer cells. Therefore, the theory goes that a diet low in acidic foods and high in alkaline foods (high pH) will increase the body's alkalinity and prevent or even cure cancer. However, Dr. Khuller mentions that these studies focus on cancer cells in a dish and do not capture the complexity of tumour behaviour in the human body.
Therefore, no specific food item or diet can both prevent and cure cancer. The best way to reduce your risk of cancer is to focus on adopting a healthy lifestyle, which includes eating a balanced diet, exercising, and avoiding unhealthy habits like smoking and too much sun exposure. It's crucial to stick to proven methods rather than getting sidetracked by unsubstantiated claims.

## Is the recommended juice recipe a proven cancer medication?
The post recommends the consumption of an alkaline preparation composed of turmeric root, radish leaves, banyan leaves, betel leaves, curry leaves, spinach, methi (fenugreek) leaves, and guava leaves.
It is important to emphasise that each of these components exhibits specific health benefits. Nonetheless, their efficacy in cancer prevention and treatment requires careful consideration.
We begin with radish leaves, which possess antibacterial, antioxidant, antimutagenic, and anticarcinogenic characteristics – likely due to the presence of certain phytoconstituents. While they may be beneficial to human health in terms of nutrition and therapy, additional research is required to establish their role as a reliable cancer remedy.
Next are the Banyan leaves, which are utilised in a variety of traditional therapies and contain a range of bioactive chemical substances involved in several biological processes. While the medicinal herb is widely used in the Ayurvedic medical system, there is not much data to support its role in cancer therapy.
After that is turmeric, whose active ingredient, curcumin, has been the subject of extensive research. According to preliminary clinical trials and laboratory studies, it exhibits anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-cancer properties. However, there are still issues with its bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy in large-scale trials.
Curry leaves contain alkaloids called carbazole, which in animal models exhibit chemopreventive properties. Rich in lutein and folate, spinach has antioxidant properties, yet there is disparate evidence regarding its direct ability to prevent cancer. Guava leaves have also demonstrated their anticancer potential, whereas fenugreek leaves may have hypoglycaemic and anti-cancer properties.
Among all, betel leaves should always be consumed with caution; while they are used in traditional medicine for digestion and antimicrobial activity, they exhibit carcinogenic impact, especially when chewed with tobacco or lime.
The moderate and preventive healthy benefits of such preparations cannot be denied. However, Ayurvedic care employs a personalised approach; hence, as per any medicine system, including the traditional Ayurvedic practice, cancer treatment cannot depend on unsupervised, generic preparations; rather, it depends on the condition's location, severity, and overall wellness of the patient.
Consequently, the suggested alkaline preparation can be considered as a preventive or supporting intervention rather than a miracle cure for a possibly fatal illness.

## What are the risks of stopping conventional cancer treatment?
Conventional allopathic cancer treatment options, primarily including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, and surgery, are backed by decades of thorough clinical research. These therapies consider the following factors: Type of tumour, Stage of the condition, Genetic alterations, Patient-specific characteristics. While these maximise the survival rates and enhance quality of life, they are constantly being refined via extensive clinical trials.
Complementary therapies such as Ayurveda, acupuncture, yoga, and dietary modifications may be beneficial in symptom relief, psychological support, and even enhancing tolerance to side effects. However, these are not a reliable option for the management of grave illnesses like cancer.
Furthermore, several studies have shown that delaying or discontinuing evidence-based treatments might accelerate the progression of the medical condition, reduce survival rates, and raise the likelihood of recurrence. This might be particularly concerning in cases of aggressive or advanced cancers, where timely and consistent therapy is crucial.
Please be advised that while adjunct therapies may be helpful, they are not a substitute for conventional evidence-based cancer treatment. Therefore, decisions for managing conditions such as cancer should only be made after consulting with certified oncologists rather than depending only on unsubstantiated online assertions.

title: Can consuming dry almonds be fatal to health? - THIP Media
claim_text: Eating dry almonds without soaking them can be fatal to your health
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that eating dry almonds without soaking them could be harmful to your health. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Almonds are widely regarded as a healthy snack, packed with vitamins, minerals, and beneficial fats. However, misinformation surrounding their safety has led some to question whether eating dry almonds could be harmful, or even fatal. The claim that dry almonds can be deadly is far from accurate, but there are some nuances that should be clarified. While it is crucial to understand the risks involved, it's important to approach almonds not with fear, but with knowledge and awareness. Dry almonds are not toxic to health when consumed in moderation. One of the most common misconceptions about almonds stems from the presence of a compound called amygdalin. Amygdalin is found in bitter almonds and can release cyanide when metabolised. Cyanide is a toxic substance that can be harmful in large amounts. However, the almonds typically sold in grocery stores are sweet almonds, which contain very low levels of amygdalin. Sweet almonds are entirely safe for consumption and are not toxic. In fact, bitter almonds (which are used primarily for almond oil and flavouring) are not sold as food for the general public due to their higher amygdalin content. Even if someone were to consume a large number of bitter almonds, it would still require a substantial amount (hundreds of almonds) to cause poisoning. For this reason, sweet almonds are completely safe and not a cause for concern when eaten in normal, reasonable quantities. There is a difference between eating dry almonds and soaked almonds, but the differences are not vast. Soaked almonds are often preferred because soaking helps to remove tannins and phytic acid from the almond's skin, which can inhibit nutrient absorption not because it becomes less fatal than dry almonds. This makes soaked almonds easier to digest and may enhance nutrient availability. Raw almonds, on the other hand, are consumed with their skins intact and retain their natural crunch, but some people may find them harder to digest. Nutritionally, both are rich in vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats, but the soaking process can slightly improve their bioavailability. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, stated: 'No, dry almonds are safe to eat, and they provide a wide range of health benefits. While consuming large amounts of almonds may cause digestive discomfort or contribute to weight gain, the risks are relatively low when eaten as part of a balanced diet. The claim that dry almonds can be fatal to health is unsubstantiated. In fact, almonds offer heart-healthy fats, antioxidants, and essential vitamins, making them a valuable part of a healthy lifestyle. As with any food, moderation is key. Be mindful of portion sizes, chew thoroughly, and avoid consuming them in excessive quantities. For those with nut allergies or swallowing difficulties, alternative options like almond butter or chopped almonds may be safer choices.' Dietitian Harita Adhvaryu, a senior dietician and diabetes educator from Ahmedabad, clarified that almonds are safe to eat whether dry or soaked. She explained that dry almonds are more convenient, while soaked ones require extra effort. She also debunked the myth that almonds must be peeled before eating, emphasising that the sweet almonds we commonly consume are safe, unlike bitter almonds, which can be toxic.

title: Fact Check: Can consuming hot sauce eliminate back pain? - THIP Media
claim_text: Why is hot sauce one the best things for Back Pain? #BackPain#SpineHealth#HealthTips
quick_take: A social media post claims that consuming hot sauce can eliminate back pain. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that consuming hot sauce can eliminate back pain. While some people may experience temporary relief from back pain after eating spicy foods, this is likely due to the distraction caused by the heat rather than any direct effect on the pain itself. Hot sauce contains a compound called capsaicin, which is what gives chili peppers their heat. When capsaicin comes into contact with the body's tissues, it triggers a pain response along with a burning and irritant effect. However, this pain response is caused by the release of endorphins and dopamine, which are hormones that have pain-relieving effects. The release of such hormones can provide temporary relief from pain, but it does not address the underlying cause of the pain. Back pain can result from various factors such as muscle strain, injury, or underlying medical conditions, such as arthritis, or a herniated disc. Managing back pain typically involves a comprehensive approach, including proper rest, exercise, physical therapy, and, if necessary, medical interventions prescribed by healthcare professionals. Hot sauce will not help to treat any of these conditions. In addition, eating too much hot sauce can actually worsen back pain. Spicy foods can irritate the digestive system, leading to symptoms such as heartburn, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps. These symptoms can be uncomfortable and can make it difficult to focus on anything else, which can make back pain seem worse. Dr Rachit Gulati, orthopaedician and Medical Director at SAAOL Ortho Care states, "Hot sauce contains capsaicin, which has anti inflammatory and anti oxidant properties. These properties can help in keeping our body healthy and reduce inflammation. However, it cannot cure your back pain. Diet can have an adjuvant effect on back pain treatment. That means, good diet can improve treatment outcomes and bad diet can downgrade it. But the mainstay of back pain treatment includes medications, minimally invasive interventions, physiotherapy, posture correction, weight loss and lifestyle changes." Consuming hot sauce is unlikely to have a significant impact on the physiological factors contributing to back pain. If you are experiencing persistent or severe back pain, it is important to consult with a healthcare professional for a proper diagnosis and appropriate treatment plan. Relying on unproven remedies like practicing chiropractic treatment or consuming hot sauce may not address the root cause of the pain and could potentially lead to delayed or inadequate treatment.

title: Fact Check: Can Consuming kulthi dal water continuously for 15 days help in removing gall stones?
claim_text: Consuming kulthi dal (horse gram dal) water continuously for 15 days helps in removing gall stones
quick_take: Gallstones generally cannot be dissolved through diet or non-surgical methods. Surgical removal, such as cholecystectomy, remains the treatment for gallstones. There is no medical consensus or scientific evidence that consuming kulthi dal water continuously for 15 days helps in removing gall stones.
doctor_explanation: Dr Sachin Choudhary, MBBS, MS (General Surgery), FMAS,FIGS, Assistant Professor (General Surgery), Army College of Medical Sciences said: 'Kulthi dal is beneficial for digestive health due to its high fiber content and diuretic properties, it cannot dissolve or remove gallstones from the body. Gallstones are solid deposits that form in the gallbladder and typically require medical intervention, such as medication or surgery, for removal. Kulthi dal water may support digestion, but it cannot address the underlying issue of gallstones. Gallstones cannot be removed without surgery. If you experience symptoms like pain, nausea, or jaundice, it's crucial to seek doctors' advice rather than relying on home remedies alone. Maintaining a healthy diet is important for health, but when dealing with gallstones, traditional remedies should not replace proper medical treatment.' Dr. Uddhavesh Paithankar, Consultant Gastroenterology, Manipal Hospital, Gurugram added: 'This is completely false as there are no medical trials to prove that consuming water from this dal would remove gall stones or any other stones from the body. If it were true wouldn't the pharma companies be manufacturing this compound in bulk and selling it like hotcakes? Spreading such false news not only creates doubt regarding the medical community in mind of patients but can also be detrimental due to the volume of fluid consumed per say would be too much for the body to handle.' The article explains that gallstones (Cholelithiasis) are hardened deposits of digestive fluid forming in the gallbladder. Three main pathways lead to their formation: (1) Cholesterol supersaturation — when the liver produces more cholesterol than bile can dissolve, leading to crystal precipitation; (2) Excess bilirubin from red blood cell breakdown contributing to stone formation; (3) Gallbladder hypomotility — impaired contractility causing bile concentration. Gallstones are removed through surgery (cholecystectomy) because they are located in the gallbladder where there is no duct for them to pass through naturally. While Kulthi Dal (Macrotyloma uniflorum) is recognized in traditional medicine for bioactive properties such as anti-diabetic, anti-obesity, and antioxidant effects, and may support gut health, there is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that kulthi dal water consumption helps in removing gallstones. The article cites the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases for prevention guidance (high-fiber foods, reducing refined carbs, healthy fats), but notes these are preventive measures, not treatments for existing gallstones.

title: Fact Check: Can consuming makhana, khas khas and desi ghee powder with milk increase height of kids?
claim_text: For all the kids who want to increase their height and want to build strength in their body, you have to take 100 grams of makhana and 50 grams of khas khas — khas khas are small seeds. Now, what you have to do is roast them lightly in desi ghee. After that, you have to grind them into a powder and keep it. Take one spoon either in the morning and evening, or once a day with a glass of milk. This is for those whose height is not increasing and those who want to gain weight. It is comfortable for everyone.
verdict_original: The claim by the user is FALSE. Hence, the user's claim is FALSE.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Pallavi Gupta, Senior Resident, Department of Pediatrics, ESIC Hospital, stated: Height growth is a common concern, especially among adolescents and young adults. Recently, claims have been circulating that consuming a mixture of makhana (fox nuts), khas khas (poppy seeds), and desi ghee powder with milk can significantly increase height. However, this claim is false and lacks scientific backing. Height is primarily determined by genetics. Studies estimate that about 60-80% of a person's final height is influenced by genetic factors, specifically parental height and genetic coding. The remaining percentage may be influenced by external factors such as nutrition, hormonal balance, physical activity, and general health during the growing years, particularly before the closure of growth plates (epiphyseal plates) around the age of 18-21. While makhana, khas khas, and desi ghee are nutritious—offering healthy fats, calcium, and proteins—they cannot override genetic predisposition or reopen growth plates once they are fused. There is no clinical evidence suggesting that consuming these ingredients together with milk can stimulate growth hormones or elongate bones in adults or adolescents beyond their natural potential. For optimal growth during childhood and adolescence, a balanced diet rich in proteins, calcium, vitamins D and C, regular physical activity, and adequate sleep are important. Once puberty ends and growth plates close, height increase through diet or supplements becomes biologically impossible. Also, it is important to note that short height can be physiological and pathological where physiological can be due to familial short stature or due to delayed puberty whereas pathological causes are multiple and not only diet-related.

Dr Sabina Vij, Pediatrician, Vij Clinic, Greater Kailash, stated: If height and weight could increase with makhana and khus khus and milk powder, we all would be tall. No one would remain short. Height of a child depends on his/her genetic makeup and epigenetics, protein and diet intake and the level of physical activity throughout childhood. So think about it before falling prey to the food fads. Visit your pediatrician regularly for weight and height monitoring and for guidance.

Supporting scientific context from the article: Height is influenced by multiple factors including genetics, exercise, sleep, diet, and hormonal regulation. Exercise promotes height by stimulating growth hormone (GH) secretion. Adequate sleep boosts GH release. GH and IGF-1 critically regulate height, with IGF-1 levels peaking during puberty (Tanner stages III-IV) and declining thereafter. Height increase ceases permanently after puberty when bone growth plates fuse. The article cites studies: Rahul Vishnu Rathod et al. on makhana's nutritional and therapeutic value; Sk. Md. Kaleem Basha et al. on poppy seeds supporting bone health due to calcium content and dietary fiber for digestion; Anil Kumar et al. on ghee's short-chain fatty acids, anti-cancer benefits, and fat-soluble vitamin delivery; Hanna Górska-Warsewicz et al. on milk as a source of energy, high-quality protein, calcium, magnesium, potassium, zinc, and phosphorus in bioavailable form for bone health. The article also notes that childhood obesity is associated with disrupted growth and earlier puberty.
