title: Fact Check: Can drinking milk with jaggery before bed cure anemia?
claim_text: Milk and jaggery before bed is an Ayurvedic combo which is a natural powerhouse for digestive health. Drinking this delicious nightcap cures anemia and relieve gastric problems.
doctor_explanation:
Anemia is a condition in which the number of red blood cells or the hemoglobin concentration within them is lower than normal (per WHO). It may be caused by nutrient deficiencies, infections (malaria, parasitic infections, tuberculosis, HIV), inflammation, chronic diseases, gynecological and obstetric conditions, and inherited red blood cell disorders. The most common nutritional cause is iron deficiency, though deficiencies in folate, vitamins B12 and A are also important causes. Common types of anemia include Iron deficiency anemia, Vitamin B12–deficiency anemia (cobalamin deficiency), and Hemolytic anemia. Uncommon types include Aplastic anemia, Sickle cell anemia, and anemia caused by other diseases. Milk is nutrient-dense, supplying energy and high-quality protein with calcium, magnesium, potassium, zinc, and phosphorus, and is beneficial for bone health. However, milk is not a significant source of iron. Jaggery is a natural sweetener from sugarcane or palm sap, rich in iron, magnesium, potassium, and phosphorus. While jaggery can help increase iron levels in the body due to its iron content, aiding in the management of anemia, there is no evidence that milk cures anemia or significantly boosts iron levels. No scientific evidence was found to support the claim that drinking milk with jaggery before bed cures anemia. Additionally, some forms of anemia — particularly those with a genetic basis such as Fanconi anemia, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, and Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria — are currently considered incurable and require lifelong management including blood transfusions, iron chelation therapy, or bone marrow transplantation.

Dr Pallavi Gupta, Senior Resident, Department of Pediatrics, ESIC Hospital: 'Milk and jaggery can be part of a healthy diet, as milk provides calcium and other nutrients, while jaggery is a good source of iron. However, anemia is a complex condition that typically requires more than dietary changes. While incorporating iron-rich foods like jaggery into your diet can help, it is unlikely to be sufficient on its own. Treatment for anemia often involves taking iron supplements and sometimes medications, depending on the underlying cause. Individuals with anemia must consult a healthcare provider to get a proper diagnosis and tailored treatment plan. Furthermore, it is important to note that jaggery is a form of sugar, which can pose risks for individuals with diabetes. Consuming jaggery can lead to spikes in blood sugar levels, which can be harmful for diabetic patients. In conclusion, while milk with jaggery might be a healthy addition to some diets, it should not be relied upon as a cure for anemia. Additionally, those with diabetes should be cautious with jaggery consumption. Proper medical treatment and guidance from a healthcare professional are essential for effectively managing and curing anemia.'

Dr. Divya Tripathi, Assistant Professor, Department of Nutrition and Dietetics, Manav Rachna International Institute Of Research and Studies: 'Anemia is typically treated with iron supplements and dietary changes under medical supervision. Jaggery, a traditional form of unrefined sugar, is packed with several nutrients, including small amounts of iron, which can help prevent iron deficiency anemia when included in a balanced diet. It also aids digestion, detoxifies the liver, boosts immunity, and provides a steady source of energy due to its complex carbohydrate content. However, it's important to note that jaggery is still a form of sugar, and excessive consumption can lead to harmful effects such as weight gain, increased blood sugar levels, and dental problems. For those with anemia, it's crucial to incorporate a variety of iron-rich foods such as leafy greens, beans, lentils, and fortified cereals, alongside medical treatment. While adding jaggery to your diet can be beneficial, it should not replace other essential treatments and dietary sources of iron. Effective anemia management requires a comprehensive diet and medical care under doctors and experts guidance.'

title: Can Drinking Milk with Lemon Cure Piles in Just Three Days?- THIP
claim_text: Drinking cold milk followed by lemon can cure piles in just three days.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that drinking cold milk with lemon cure piles in just 3 days. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Piles, medically known as haemorrhoids, are enlarged and inflamed veins in the lower rectum or around the anus. They develop because of increased pressure in that region. The most common triggers include chronic constipation, repeated straining, prolonged sitting on the toilet, pregnancy, obesity, and low fibre intake. Once veins become swollen, they behave like varicose veins in the legs. They do not 'disappear' overnight. Mild cases may settle within days if bowel habits improve, but that improvement comes from reducing pressure and irritation, not from a specific drink. There is no clinical trial, no gastroenterology guideline, and no peer-reviewed study that recognises milk with lemon as a treatment for haemorrhoids. The idea of a strict three-day cure oversimplifies a condition that often develops over months or years. Dr Sharad Malhotra, Sr. Consultant & HOD – Gastroenterology, Akash Hospital, clarified that while diet does not cure haemorrhoids, it plays a significant role in improving symptoms. According to him, meals should focus on whole grains, legumes, fruits eaten with their peel, and adequate fibre in any form to prevent constipation. He also advised limiting foods high in processed fats and refined carbohydrates, as these can slow bowel movement and worsen constipation. Dr Malhotra further explained that treatment for piles typically involves adopting a fibre-rich diet, using laxatives or stool softeners when necessary, avoiding medicines or foods that trigger constipation, and prescribing medications that help reduce pressure in the anal veins. In certain cases, minimally invasive procedures such as endoscopy-guided injection therapy or banding may be required, and surgery may be considered to remove severely affected veins. Regarding biological mechanisms: Lemon contains vitamin C and citric acid. Milk contains protein, fat, calcium, and lactose. None of these ingredients directly shrink swollen veins in the rectum. Some people assume lemon 'cleanses toxins' or that milk 'coats and soothes the gut.' However, piles are not caused by toxins. They are mechanical and vascular in nature. The problem is pressure on veins, not acidity, infection, or internal impurities. When lemon is added to milk, it curdles. This happens because the acid in lemon causes milk proteins (casein) to coagulate. While this reaction is harmless for most people, there is no evidence that consuming this mixture has any targeted effect on haemorrhoidal tissue. The digestive system will break down the drink like any other food. It does not travel specifically to the anal veins to 'heal' them. Regarding potential harm: Many adults have some degree of lactose intolerance. Drinking milk may cause bloating, abdominal discomfort, gas, or even constipation in sensitive individuals. Constipation is one of the strongest risk factors for piles because it leads to hard stools and straining. Straining increases pressure in the rectal veins, which can worsen swelling, pain, and bleeding. In some individuals, dairy may cause loose stools. Frequent diarrhoea can irritate the anal region and aggravate existing haemorrhoids. Lemon's acidity may also trigger gastric discomfort or reflux in susceptible people. While this does not directly cause piles, digestive discomfort can disrupt regular bowel movements. So, instead of curing the problem, this combination might delay proper management. Dietitian Shikha Sharma, MSc in Foods and Nutrition, Noida, says, 'This is one of the most bizarre claims I have come across in my professional practice. There is absolutely no scientific or medical basis to suggest that drinking cold milk followed by lemon can cure piles. Haemorrhoids require appropriate dietary management, lifestyle modification, and in some cases medical treatment not unproven home remedies.' What actually improves piles symptoms based on medical evidence: Lifestyle and bowel management are the cornerstone of treatment. The primary aim in managing haemorrhoids is to reduce straining and allow the swollen veins to settle. Increasing dietary fibre is one of the most strongly supported interventions. Fibre softens stools and increases bulk, making bowel movements easier to pass. Vegetables, fruits, whole grains, seeds, and pulses are excellent sources. When diet alone is insufficient, fibre supplements such as psyllium may be recommended. Adequate hydration is equally important. Fibre works effectively only when paired with sufficient water intake. Toilet habits matter significantly. People should avoid sitting on the toilet for prolonged periods, especially while using phones. Responding promptly to the urge to pass stool reduces unnecessary pressure. Warm sitz baths can provide symptom relief by improving local blood flow and relaxing the muscles around the anus. Short-term topical treatments prescribed by a pharmacist or doctor may help reduce itching and inflammation. These measures do not sound dramatic, but they directly address the root cause, pressure and irritation. When should medical advice be sought: Professional evaluation is necessary if symptoms do not improve. If there is persistent bleeding, severe pain, a painful lump that does not settle, or no improvement after a week of home measures, medical review is essential. Not all rectal bleeding is caused by piles. Conditions such as fissures, inflammatory bowel disease, or other gastrointestinal disorders need to be ruled out. Early assessment prevents complications and provides reassurance. So milk with lemon is not a scientifically proven cure for piles. There is no evidence that it can reverse swollen rectal veins in three days, or at all. At best, it is an unproven home remedy. At worst, it may worsen digestive symptoms in some individuals. When it comes to haemorrhoids, consistency and evidence-based care will always be more reliable than viral quick fixes.

Diabetes is a chronic condition that requires long-term management. A healthy diet is a vital aspect of managing diabetes and controlling blood sugar levels. title: Fact Check: Can Drinking Raisin Water Purify Blood in 30-45 Days?
claim_text: Drinking raisin water daily with empty stomach for 30–45 days. It helps to remove acne/pimples providing glowing skin. It works as a blood purifier.
quick_take: There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to support the claim that drinking raisin water can purify blood in 30-45 days. While raisins have nutritional benefits, the kidneys and liver naturally purify blood — no single food or drink can change how blood works.
doctor_explanation: The kidneys are essential for blood purification, filtering about half a cup of blood every minute to remove waste and excess water, which are excreted as urine. When kidney function fails, blood purification is carried out through specialized therapies outside the body — including dialysis, filtration, or adsorption. These methods act rapidly and are used in emergency situations (e.g., plasmapheresis to remove toxins), life-sustaining treatments (e.g., hemodialysis for kidney failure), and managing immune or metabolic conditions (e.g., immunoadsorption for autoimmune disorders). Dr Poojitha Byreddy, Senior Haematologist, CARE Hospitals, Hi-tech City, Hyderabad, said: 'Some people believe that drinking raisin water can clean or purify the blood in 30 to 45 days, but there is no medical proof for this. Our body already has a natural way of removing waste and toxins through the liver and kidneys. While raisins do have healthy nutrients like iron and antioxidants, raisin water alone cannot clean your blood. It is important to remember that no single food or drink can change how your blood works. Eating a balanced diet and staying healthy is more effective. Always talk to a doctor if you have any concerns about your blood.' Dr Imran Khan, Senior Consultant – Internal Medicine, CARE Hospitals, Musheerabad, Hyderabad, said: 'Raisin water might help with digestion and give your body some energy, but it will not purify your blood. The idea that a drink can clean your blood is a common myth and not backed by science. Your liver and kidneys already do that job naturally every day. Good health does not come from just one drink. It comes from eating a variety of healthy foods, drinking enough water, and staying active. If you are worried about your health or have specific problems, it is best to speak with a doctor rather than relying on home remedies.' A review published in the Journal of Nutrition and Health reported that consuming raisins, when compared to other carbohydrate-rich snacks with equal caloric value, can lead to reductions in LDL (bad) cholesterol and blood pressure, and is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease. A study by Margaret J. Schuster et al. found that consuming raisins offers several health benefits, contributing to overall wellness and helping prevent various chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, gastrointestinal disorders, and dental caries. While raisins have some health benefits, no scientific evidence or medical consensus supports the claim that raisin water can purify, detoxify, or cleanse the blood in 30-45 days.

## Can drinking water actually be dangerous?
No. But excessive water intake can be harmful and, in extreme cases, even fatal.
Drinking too much water in a short period can overwhelm the kidneys, which are responsible for filtering excess fluids. This can lead to a condition called hyponatraemia, or water intoxication, where sodium levels in the blood drop dangerously low.
Sodium is an essential electrolyte that helps regulate fluid balance, nerve signals, and muscle contractions. When the body is flooded with too much water, sodium levels become diluted, leading to swelling in cells. This can affect various organs, including the brain, causing headaches, nausea, confusion, and, in severe cases, seizures, coma, or even death.
Several cases of fatal water intoxication have been reported. For example, in 2007, a woman in the United States died after participating in a water-drinking contest. She consumed several litres in a short period without allowing her body to process it, leading to fatal hyponatraemia.

## How much water is considered 'too much'?
There is no universal answer, but drinking beyond your body's ability to excrete water is risky. The kidneys can process about 0.8 to 1 litre of water per hour, but this can vary based on individual factors such as kidney function, activity level, and overall health. Consuming significantly more than this—especially in a short period—can put you at risk of water intoxication.
Hydration needs vary widely. Someone sweating heavily due to exercise or heat may need more water than someone with a sedentary lifestyle. However, forcing yourself to drink excessive amounts beyond thirst, especially over a short duration, can be dangerous.
The general recommendation for water intake is 2-3 litres per day, but this should be adjusted based on thirst, diet, climate, and activity level rather than an arbitrary target.

## Does drinking more water always mean better hydration?
No, more water does not necessarily mean better hydration.
Hydration is not just about water intake but also about maintaining a balance of essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium. Drinking too much water can flush out these electrolytes, leading to an imbalance that affects muscle function, nerve signalling, and heart health.
Signs of overhydration include headaches, dizziness, swelling in the hands or feet, nausea, and confusion. If hydration were simply about drinking more water, we wouldn't need electrolytes in our diet. Instead, hydration should be approached holistically—by consuming water in balance with food and essential minerals.
Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, stated, "As doctors, there are certain things we can't dictate because your body knows best how much water it needs based on your thirst levels. However, if someone has a kidney condition, we can assess their reports and provide specific guidance on water intake accordingly."

## Can excessive water intake affect brain function?
Dr Almas Fatma, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai said, Yes, too much water can cause brain swelling, leading to serious neurological effects.
Hyponatraemia causes excess water to enter brain cells, leading to swelling. Since the skull cannot expand, this puts pressure on the brain, potentially causing symptoms like confusion, drowsiness, blurred vision, and, in severe cases, seizures or coma.
In extreme cases, this swelling can be life-threatening. Military training programs, marathon runners, and people engaging in endurance sports without replenishing electrolytes have been known to suffer from water intoxication.

## Should you force yourself to drink water even when not thirsty?
No, drinking water when you're not thirsty can be unnecessary and potentially harmful.
The body has a natural thirst mechanism that signals when hydration is needed. While mild dehydration can sometimes go unnoticed, forcing excessive water intake when you're not thirsty can lead to overhydration.
Some health trends encourage drinking large amounts of water regardless of thirst, claiming it helps digestion, detoxification, or skin health. However, the kidneys are highly efficient at filtering waste, and excessive water does not necessarily enhance this process—it may even burden the kidneys unnecessarily.
Instead of blindly following hydration myths, listen to your body. Drink when thirsty, and adjust your intake based on activity levels, climate, and diet.

## Is it possible to die from drinking too much water?
Yes, in extreme cases, water intoxication can be fatal.
Although rare, excessive water consumption in a short period can cause fatal complications. Several documented cases have shown that drinking excessive water too quickly can result in life-threatening hyponatraemia.
One of the most well-known cases involved a 40-year-old woman from Hyderabad who experienced seizures and lost consciousness after consuming an excessive amount of water in the morning.
Similarly, some marathon runners and military personnel have suffered fatal consequences due to excessive water intake without sufficient electrolyte replacement.

## Final Verdict
While hydration is crucial for good health, drinking excessive amounts of water can have dangerous consequences. Overhydration can lead to water intoxication, electrolyte imbalances, and in extreme cases, death. The key to safe hydration is balance. Instead of following hydration myths, rely on your body's natural signals and adjust water intake based on your needs, physical activity, and environment. Drinking water is essential, but too much of a good thing can be harmful.

It's a condition influenced by a mix of factors, often including genetics (family tendency), how the body responds to insulin (the hormone that manages blood sugar), long-term weight changes, sleep patterns, stress, and sometimes other hormone-related conditions. Think of it like a setup that builds over time, not something that flips on or off based on one drink. Prevention claims need strong proof: studies would have to follow people without PCOD and show that those drinking turmeric-ghee water develop PCOD less often than those who don't. We don't have that kind of evidence. What we do have are smaller studies looking at curcumin supplements in women who already have PCOS, checking whether markers like fasting insulin, blood sugar, or inflammation move in a better direction. That's not the same as preventing the condition. Turmeric is not a hormone-balancing treatment in the way people mean it online. PCOD/PCOS hormone changes can include higher androgens (male-type hormones), irregular ovulation, and disrupted signalling between the brain, ovaries, and insulin pathways. Fixing that usually needs sustained lifestyle steps, and sometimes medicines, because the hormone shifts are not superficial. Curcumin has been researched because it can reduce inflammation and oxidative stress in the body, and it may slightly improve insulin resistance in some cases. Insulin resistance matters because higher insulin levels can push the ovaries to produce more androgens in some women. So the logic is: if insulin improves, some hormone effects might improve too. But in real-world outcomes, the changes seen in studies are often modest and not consistent enough to claim turmeric balances hormones reliably. Another practical issue: the dose. If someone is already struggling with weight gain, belly fat, high triglycerides, fatty liver, or high LDL cholesterol, adding daily ghee water may quietly increase daily calorie intake without adding much satiety (that full feeling). She adds that effective PCOD management relies on maintaining a nutritious diet, regular physical activity, and, in some cases, appropriate medical treatment. The liver processes toxins, the kidneys filter waste from the blood into urine, and the skin eliminates some waste through sweat. The term 'toxin' is often used vaguely in health claims, but in medical terms, it refers to specific harmful substances like waste products or environmental pollutants. The body or liver detox are mostly misleading marketing strategies. The body's detoxification systems work continuously, not just when you drink water or have a special detoxification diet. Drinking water supports the body's natural detoxification processes. Water helps the kidneys filter waste products, such as blood urea nitrogen, from the blood, which are then excreted in urine. It also helps in digestion by helping move waste through the intestines, preventing constipation. Scientifically, adequate hydration ensures urine flows freely, helping the kidneys remove waste efficiently. However, this benefit applies to water at any temperature, not just warm water. There is no scientific evidence that warm water is more effective at removing toxins than room-temperature or cold water. Some animal studies suggest warm water may help in digestion by helping the stomach break down food or by promoting bowel movements. A 2016 study showed warm water helped intestinal movements after surgery, but this is not specific to toxin removal or empty stomach conditions. The temperature of water may affect comfort or digestion for some people, but it does not uniquely enhance detoxification. Similarly, some claim that drinking warm water can boost immunity. However, this too lacks scientific evidence. There is no evidence that drinking water on an empty stomach is more effective for toxin removal than drinking water at other times. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, notes that while drinking water in the morning can help rehydrate the body after sleep, there's no specific benefit to doing so on an empty stomach. The body's detoxification processes, like kidney filtration and liver metabolism, occur continuously and are not significantly influenced by the timing of water intake. Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi says: 'Drinking enough water every day is essential for good health. It helps with digestion, keeps the kidneys functioning well, and supports many other body processes. According to Ayurveda, sipping warm water regularly can be a gentle way to support health. While staying hydrated is crucial for supporting the body's natural detoxification processes, there is no scientific evidence that warm water or drinking it on an empty stomach offers unique benefits in this regard. Drinking water, regardless of temperature or timing, helps maintain overall health.

verdict_original: This claim made by the user is FALSE. Drinking water while standing does not cause joint damage.
quick_take: There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to support the claim that drinking water while standing can directly lead to joint damage. This claim is largely a myth with no backing from medical research. Joint damage typically results from causes like osteoarthritis, injuries, autoimmune diseases (like rheumatoid arthritis), or wear and tear due to repetitive movements or excess body weight. On the other hand, research indicates that drinking water regardless of position, and maintaining good levels of hydration positively affect bone health.

Without this cushion, the bones can grind against each other, leading to pain, swelling, and stiffness. If the damage is severe, the joint might become deformed, making it hard to move without discomfort. There are other causes of joint damage too. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition where the body's immune system attacks the joint lining. Injuries like fractures or torn ligaments can also damage joints, especially if they aren't treated properly. Everyday wear and tear, carrying extra weight, or even conditions like gout can worsen joint health over time.' He further added: 'Drinking water while standing does not lead to joint damage, contrary to popular myths. This misconception likely arises from traditional beliefs rather than medical facts. The health of your joints is influenced by several key factors, including maintaining an active lifestyle, a balanced diet, and staying at a healthy weight. Water plays an essential role in joint health, as it helps maintain the lubrication and cushioning of joints by supporting the production of synovial fluid, which reduces friction and helps prevent joint wear. However, how you drink water—whether standing or sitting—does not change how your body absorbs and utilizes it for joint health. Instead, focusing on staying adequately hydrated throughout the day is more important. To prevent joint issues such as osteoarthritis, it's recommended to engage in regular exercise, maintain appropriate body weight, and ensure that your diet includes essential nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D.'

Dr. Anup Khatri, Senior Consultant-Orthopedics at Gleneagles Hospital, Parel, Mumbai, reacted to the claim: 'Many people are in a hurry and end up drinking water while standing. Moreover, it is a common practice, and many believe that it can contribute to various health concerns, including joint damage. However, one has to be cautious when it comes to believing in such claims and consult an expert without any delay. There are no studies or evidence available that prove the connection between drinking water while standing causing joint damage. The body's posture during hydration could affect digestion and nutrient absorption, increasing the stress on the joints and one can experience discomfort. The common causes of joint damage are injuries such as falling, twisting of an ankle, ligament strain, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and psoriatic arthritis, gout, wearing the wrong shoes, smoking and stress. It will be better to sit and drink the water instead of standing which can also facilitate improper swallowing or rapid gulping actions. The symptoms can be pain, stiffness in the joints, fatigue, limited range of motion, swelling, redness and tenderness. So, it will not be correct to associate joint damage with drinking water while standing or create any misconceptions among people. A study by Joseph P. Crolla et al. found that dehydration may lead to an increase in cartilage stiffness, which may contribute to increased joint stiffness and pain, highlighting the importance of proper hydration in maintaining joint health. The myth that drinking water while standing causes joint damage originates from traditional or cultural practices that promote proper posture and digestion. As per traditional beliefs, sitting while drinking is thought to be healthier and believed to aid digestion and overall health. However, joint damage typically results from factors like injury, aging, osteoarthritis, or overuse, and there is no scientific evidence to support the idea that drinking water while standing leads to joint damage.

title: Can drinking your own urine really speed up bone healing?
claim_text: Drinking your own urine every morning for 15 days after a knee injury can speed up bone healing and surprise doctors with the results.
quick_take: In a viral YouTube video, Paresh Rawal claims that drinking your own urine can speed up bone healing. However, our fact check found this claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: The fact check addresses several aspects of this claim: 1) Does urine contain anything that helps bones heal faster? No, there is no scientific proof that drinking urine can heal bones. Urine is made up mostly of water, along with salts, urea, and other waste products that the body needs to eliminate. None of these components are known to support bone growth or repair. While an older study from 1999 suggests that urine may have uses in treating bacterial and viral infections, it makes no mention of any benefits for bone healing. Doctors treat bone injuries using rest, immobilisation, physiotherapy, and sometimes surgery or medication. Proper nutrition, especially calcium, vitamin D, and protein, plays a key role in the healing process. But urine does not contribute to any of these nutrients. 2) Do athletes or fighters use urine therapy to heal bone injuries? No, urine therapy is not used in professional sports or medicine. Some alternative health groups advocate for urine therapy as a treatment for various conditions, but mainstream medicine does not support this. There are no guidelines or expert recommendations that suggest drinking urine can help athletes recover from injuries. Senior Physiotherapist Upma Lal says, "Throughout my career, I have worked with numerous athletes recovering from injuries. I have never encountered any reputable treatment protocol that includes urine therapy. The healing process for injuries is complex and requires appropriate rehabilitation techniques, such as targeted exercises, physical therapy, and medical interventions when necessary. Urine therapy lacks scientific evidence and could present health risks by introducing waste products back into the body. Athletes should rely on proven, safe methods to ensure a full recovery." Physiotherapist Prachi Bharwani clarifies, "Urine therapy is not a scientifically validated treatment for sports injuries or bone healing. As a sports physiotherapist, I focus on evidence-based practices such as physiotherapy, stretching, strengthening exercises, and proper nutritional support, including calcium, vitamin D, and protein. These methods are backed by years of clinical research and are proven to aid in recovery. Drinking urine, on the other hand, offers no therapeutic benefit and could potentially interfere with a more effective recovery process." 3) Can belief in a remedy affect how fast someone recovers? To some extent, yes, but not for physical healing like bone repair. This is called the placebo effect, when someone feels better after a treatment simply because they believe it will work. It can reduce stress or pain, and boost mood. But it cannot speed up how quickly a bone repairs itself. In Rawal's case, rest, nutrition, and medical care were likely the main reasons for his recovery. Urine-drinking might have felt meaningful to him, but it wouldn't have changed his body's healing timeline. 4) Can any home remedy affect what shows up in an X-ray? No, X-ray images reflect real healing, not miracle remedies. Bone healing shows up as new white areas on an X-ray. These changes come from natural biological processes. How quickly they appear can vary from person to person depending on age, health, and the type of injury. There's no evidence that drinking urine, or any other unproven remedy, can speed up the appearance of bone healing in X-rays. 5) Is it safe to drink your own urine? Not really. Drinking urine can be harmful. A small sip once may not cause serious harm, but urine is a waste product. It contains salts, toxins, and bacteria, even in healthy people. Studies have shown that urine is not sterile as once believed. Drinking it often can stress your kidneys and increase the risk of infections. Contrary to popular belief, drinking urine will not hydrate you in an emergency. In fact, it can dehydrate you. There is no proven health benefit, and since your body is trying to remove these substances, putting them back in can be unsafe. Drinking it goes against how our system works. Some people believe urine has healing powers, but there's no science behind that. In fact, drinking it can upset your body's balance and may do more harm than good. Clean water and good hygiene are always the best choices for health." The article also references previous fact checks on cow urine being good for human health and human urine improving eyesight, both of which were debunked as having no scientific evidence and being potentially harmful.

title: Fact Check: Can dusted eggshell powder & baking soda restore teeth enamel?
claim_text: A website post titled '8 Home Remedies to Naturally Get Rid of Tooth Cavity' is currently circulating widely. The post suggests using a mixture of powdered or dusted eggshells and baking soda to restore enamel.
quick_take: A post claiming that dusted eggshell powder, when combined with baking soda, can help restore enamel has been widely circulated. However, after conducting a thorough fact-check, we have determined that this claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
Enamel, the outer layer of teeth that protects them, is the strongest substance in the body, even stronger than bones. However, factors like dental plaque, acidic foods, and oral bacteria can cause enamel to deteriorate over time. To maintain dental health, it is important to promote enamel remineralisation, a natural process that reintroduces lost minerals, particularly calcium and phosphate, into the enamel structure. Fluoride has been implicated as an effective way to enhance enamel remineralization, making it more resistant to acid attacks and decay. Saliva also plays a critical role by providing necessary minerals and creating an ideal pH environment for remineralization.

Eggshell powder has been gaining attention in natural health and alternative medicine circles as a potential remedy for restoring tooth enamel. It is claimed that the calcium and minerals found in finely crushed (dusted) eggshells can promote enamel remineralization and strengthen teeth. Eggshell powder is rich in calcium phosphate, organic matter, and magnesium carbonate, with minimal levels of strontium, fluoride, manganese, zinc, and copper ions. It plays a significant role in bone and dental metabolism and can contribute to the formation of high-quality hydroxyapatite. However, the scientific evidence supporting the use of eggshell powder for enamel remineralization is currently limited, despite its calcium content and recognized role in dental health.

The effectiveness of using a mixture of baking soda and eggshell powder for enamel remineralization may not be substantial, as the primary factor influencing this natural process is the presence of minerals in saliva. Nevertheless, baking soda can be beneficial in neutralising acids in dental biofilm, which can help prevent gum diseases. However, it is important to note that there is currently insufficient evidence to support the idea that baking soda plays a role in restoring or maintaining healthy enamel. Enamel health and remineralization are influenced by various factors, including oral hygiene, dietary habits, the presence of harmful oral bacteria, and overall individual health.

title: Fact Check: Can ear candling technique safely remove ear wax?
claim_text: The Facebook reel titled 'Benefits of Ear Candling' suggests that the technique can soften ear wax. Further it can relieve sinus pressure and headaches, improve lymphatic flow, and enhance the sense of smell. Additionally, it can be used for itchy, plugged, and swimmer's ears.
quick_take: A Facebook post claimed that the ear candling technique is highly beneficial for removing ear wax by softening it. However, after fact-checking, the claim was found to be false.
doctor_explanation: Earwax, also known as cerumen, is a natural waxy substance present in the ceruminous glands of the ear canal. Its primary function is to maintain ear health by trapping dust and debris. This prevents the entry of foreign particles into the delicate structures of the ear. Composed of dead skin cells, hair, and gland secretions, earwax forms a protective barrier. Its lubricating and antimicrobial properties help prevent dryness, irritation, and infection in the ear canal. Additionally, earwax acts as a self-cleaning mechanism. It gradually moves from the ear canal to the ear opening, where it dries up and eventually falls out. According to Dr. Priyajeet Panigrahi, ENT specialist (MBBS, DNB, MNAMS), the bulk of earwax is made up of dead epithelial cells, keratin, and fatty acids. A higher concentration of keratin and dead cells is often associated with dirt, causing the wax to turn black, as typically observed in older people. Conversely, a higher percentage of fatty acids will make the wax look yellowish, more prevalent in children and older individuals. While earwax is generally beneficial, excessive earwax buildup can happen due to overproduction or improper migration towards the ear opening, leading to symptoms such as hearing loss, earache, tinnitus, or dizziness. Impacted earwax, caused by pushing it deeper into the ear during cleaning attempts or by using earplugs, hearing aids, or earphones, may require intervention. The Ear Candling Technique is a controversial alternative therapy that involves placing a hollow, cone-shaped candle into the ear canal and lighting the opposite end. Also known as ear coning, this practice is purportedly designed to remove earwax, debris, and impurities from the ear canal. Proponents claim that as the candle burns, a suction force is created, drawing out earwax and other toxic substances. Evidence-based scientific research widely discredits the effectiveness of ear candling. Studies consistently show that any apparent removal of debris during ear candling is more likely due to residue from the candle itself than actual earwax. The claimed benefits of ear candling, such as improved hearing and relief from ear infections, lack evidence to support them. According to the FDA, there are significant risks associated with ear candling, including burns or injuries to the face, hair, ear canal, or perforation of the eardrum, as well as the potential for damage to the ear and an increased risk of candle wax or ash entering the ear. Dr. Panigrahi explains that modern medical science is evidence-based. As an ENT specialist, he has never performed or recommended the unsafe practice of wax removal. However, there are many safe and painless techniques available, such as using wax solvents and suction cleaning. People should consider safer and evidence-based methods, such as ear drops and irrigation, as advised by doctors, for addressing earwax concerns. Dr. Panigrahi advises against using chemicals and natural substances including almond oil, olive oil, hydrogen peroxide, sodium bicarbonate, paradichlorobenzene, chlorobutolol, turpentine oil, and benzocaine to soften ear wax. Complete softening of the wax usually takes around 5-7 days, and no agent can provide immediate results. ENT specialists may use specialised medical devices to physically remove impacted earwax under direct visualisation using an otoscope to ensure precision and avoid injury to the delicate structures of the ear.

title: Fact Check: Can Eating 1 grapefruit a day for 9 months clear plaque in Arteries?
claim_text: Eating 1 grapefruit a day for 9 months can clear plaque in Arteries.
verdict_original: The claim made by the Pinterest user is Misleading.
quick_take: While Grapefruits has some evidence in case of helping to reduce atherosclerosis (buildup of plaque on arteries) and support cardiovascular health, eating 1 grapefruit for 9 months cannot completely clear plaque in arteries. The claim exaggerates the role of grapefruit in heart health by suggesting that it can directly clear plaques, which is not supported by evidence. However, grapefruit can have some positive cardiovascular effects, like improving cholesterol or reducing inflammation, which might reduce plaque risk over time.
doctor_explanation: Dr Prem Aggarwal, MD (Medicine), DNB, Cardiology, Director, Sanjeevan Hospital, Daryaganj, Delhi explained: "While grapefruit is a nutritious fruit that can support heart health in terms of improving cholesterol levels, it cannot clear plaque from the arteries. Plaque build-up is a complex process involving cholesterol, inflammation, and calcification, often requiring a combination of medications, dietary changes, and lifestyle interventions for management. Eating grapefruit may contribute to overall heart wellness as part of a balanced diet, but expecting it to completely clear arterial plaque is highly unrealistic. Always consult a doctor for proper treatment and management of plaque buildup in arteries." Dr Manav Aggarwal, MBBS, DM, Interventional Cardiologist, Sanjeevan Hospital, New Delhi further said: "Grapefruit has its perks—it’s rich in vitamin C, fiber, and antioxidants, which can contribute to heart health in general. But let’s be clear: it won’t scrub your arteries clean. Plaque reduction and reversal are complicated processes that involve more than just dietary tweaks; they often require medications, exercise, and a comprehensive diet plan to truly make a difference. While adding grapefruit to your meals is a good move for overall wellness, it’s not a miracle fix for artery plaque. It is important to seek doctors' advice to prevent potential complications arising from plaque build-up in the arteries." The article also cites scientific evidence: A study by J.J. Cerda et al. discovered that grapefruit pectin reduced the severity of atherosclerosis in both the aorta and coronary arteries through a mechanism not related to cholesterol levels. A study published in Frontiers in Nutrition indicates that regular intake of flavanones found in grapefruit juice may influence gene expression, potentially aiding in the prevention of vascular dysfunction and reducing cardiovascular disease risk. Peter M.O. Owira et al. found that flavonoids in grapefruit such as naringin and hesperidin may help in the prevention of diabetes and heart disease. A study in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry found that fresh red grapefruit has high bioactive compounds and higher antioxidant potential, positively impacts serum lipid levels particularly triglycerides, and increases serum antioxidant activity. While grapefruit has shown to help improve cardiovascular health by enhancing serum lipid levels, boosting antioxidant activity, and potentially reducing the severity of atherosclerosis, there is no scientific evidence supporting that eating 1 grapefruit a day for 9 months can clear plaque in arteries. As per NIH: "Atherosclerosis develops slowly as cholesterol, fat, blood cells and other substances in your blood form plaque. When the plaque builds up, it causes your arteries to narrow. This reduces the supply of oxygen-rich blood to tissues of vital organs in the body." Plaque gradually builds up inside the arterial walls, leading to atherosclerosis, which can impact most arteries including those in the heart, brain, arms, legs, pelvis, and kidneys. Reduced blood flow can cause symptoms like angina, while plaque rupture may result in clots that block arteries, leading to heart attacks, strokes, vascular dementia, and even death.

title: Can eating 15 almonds provide the same benefits as aspirin? - THIP
claim_text: some studies show eating 15 almonds is equivalent to 1 aspirin for headaches
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that eating 15 almonds can alleviate headaches similarly to a standard aspirin. We couldn't find any study about 15 almonds. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Saurabh Gaba, Associate Consultant in Internal Medicine at Paras Hospitals, Panchkula, states, "The idea that 15 almonds can substitute aspirin for treating certain health conditions is a misconception. While almonds are healthy, there is no scientific evidence to support their effectiveness in relieving headaches or specifically migraines." Dr Sudhir Kumar, Prof & HOD, Neurology Dept, Apollo Hospitals, Hyderabad, says, "Aspirin is one of the various options for treating headaches. It is quite effective too. Other commonly used analgesics such as paracetamol and naproxen are also effective in providing quick pain relief in people suffering from headaches. It is important to note that pain-relief medications are recommended for those who suffer from infrequent headaches (lesser than three times in a month). Those who suffer from frequent headaches should be started on prophylactic medications to reduce the frequency, severity and duration of headache episodes." The article explains that aspirin is a medically validated pain reliever that contains acetylsalicylic acid. This compound specifically targets pain, inflammation, and fever by inhibiting enzymes involved in the production of prostaglandins—substances that promote pain and inflammation in the body. A typical dose of aspirin is designed to provide effective pain relief for a variety of conditions, including headaches, joint pain, and muscle aches. Aspirin works quickly and reliably due to its active ingredients, making it a well-established treatment for pain. Almonds, on the other hand, contain only trace amounts of salicin, a compound that can be converted into salicylic acid in the body. However, the amount of salicin in almonds is so small that it has no meaningful effect on pain relief. Even if you consumed large quantities of almonds, it would not provide the therapeutic dose needed to alleviate pain in the way that aspirin does. While almonds have been touted for their heart-protective properties and are considered a "superfood" rich in healthy fats, vitamin E, magnesium, fibre, and protein, these nutrients offer general health benefits but not pain relief. Interestingly, magnesium, which is present in almonds, has been linked to a reduction in migraine frequency for some people who suffer from chronic migraines. However, this effect is gradual and does not provide immediate relief like aspirin. Magnesium's benefits are associated more with prevention than with curing a headache once it begins. A 2015 study has mentioned that eating almonds can help people with headaches but there was no proof in the paper about its mechanism. So, while a diet including almonds may offer long-term health benefits, eating them during a headache won't provide the immediate pain relief one might need.

Dr Chirag Bhandari, MBBS, MS(Andrology), FECSM (Fellow of The European Committee of Sexual Medicine), told Medical Dialogues: "The claim that eating two cardamoms at night can cure impotence in men lacks scientific backing. Lifestyle choices such as smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, obesity, high cholesterol levels, and lack of physical activity are major contributors to ED. Consulting a healthcare professional is essential for accurate diagnosis and effective management."

The article further explains: While some studies have highlighted cardamom's aphrodisiac properties that may help treat impotence, there is no scientific evidence and medical consensus that support the claim that eating 2 cardamoms regularly at night eliminate impotence in men. A research article published in the International Journal of Environment and Health Sciences mentioned that cardamom has aphrodisiac properties, meaning it can enhance sexual desire, performance, and pleasure — however, the article does not state that cardamom alone can eliminate impotence. A narrative review published in Nutrition Today notes that cardamom is used in cases such as impotence, but does not specifically mention its ability to eliminate impotence on its own. Another review article published in the Research Journal of Pharmacy and Technology mentioned that cardamom oil has an arousing effect that may help treat sexual weakness, erectile dysfunction, and impotence — however, this article also does not attribute the ability to eliminate impotence in men to cardamom alone. These studies have emphasized the potential of cardamom in aiding the treatment of impotence, but they do not attribute a standalone ability to cardamom for eliminating impotency in men, and there is no medical consensus supporting the claim that consuming two cardamoms daily can eradicate impotence in men.

Impotence (now called erectile dysfunction or ED) refers to the inability to get or keep a firm enough erection for satisfying sexual activity. It is a common issue in men over 40, and its likelihood increases with age and other health problems. ED can be a sign of various underlying health issues including heart problems, diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and mental health conditions like depression and performance anxiety. Any condition that affects the blood vessels, nerves, hormones, smooth muscle, or tissues in the penis can lead to ED.

title: Fact Check: Can eating a raw garlic clove at night purify blood and strengthen the heart?
claim_text: Swallowing one raw garlic clove with water before going to bed at night. It cleans the blood so thoroughly that the heart's arteries open up and the heart becomes as strong as iron.

doctor_explanation: Dr Almas Fatma, a diabetologist in Mumbai, clarifies that no herb or natural remedy can truly "purify" the blood in the way dialysis does for patients with kidney failure. Dialysis is a specialised medical treatment that removes waste, excess fluids, and toxins when the kidneys are unable to do so. Although certain herbs may be thought to aid liver or kidney health, they cannot take over the organs' function or carry out the complex process of filtering the blood. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, explains that turmeric does not "purify" the blood as suggested in some traditional practices. The idea of "blood purification" itself is vague and does not have a clear or scientifically recognised medical meaning. Garlic contains sulphur compounds like allicin, which have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, but these do not scrub the blood clean like a detergent. Some studies show garlic can modestly lower cholesterol and blood pressure when consumed regularly. However, this is not the same as purifying blood in a single night. The idea of instant blood cleansing from a single clove of garlic is an exaggeration with no scientific proof. Regarding heart arteries: Heart blockages are caused by plaque build-up, made of fat, cholesterol, and calcium, over many years. Once these deposits harden and narrow the arteries, only medical treatment, such as stents, surgery, or prescribed medication, can manage them. Garlic cannot dissolve or wash away these blockages. Research does suggest that garlic may slow down plaque progression when consumed over time. A study published in The Journal of Nutrition (2016) found that aged garlic extract reduced the build-up of soft plaque in arteries among people with metabolic syndrome. But this effect was mild and gradual, not a magical unclogging. Regarding "heart stronger like iron": The heart's strength depends on overall health, including regular exercise, balanced nutrition, not smoking, and managing conditions like diabetes and hypertension. Garlic can help reduce some risk factors for heart disease, such as high blood pressure and high cholesterol, but it does not transform the physical strength of the heart muscle. This expression is a metaphor often used in traditional beliefs. Swallowing a raw garlic clove at night may offer small benefits like supporting general wellness, but these are gradual effects, not overnight miracles. Also, eating raw garlic can sometimes irritate the stomach, cause bad breath, or trigger acidity, especially if eaten on an empty stomach.

Dr. Sreenivas Meenakshisundaram, Consultant Neurologist at MGM Healthcare, Chennai explained that there's no scientific link between consuming apples and any real reduction in headache. Apple skin contains polyphenols, which are antioxidants with anti-inflammatory properties, but the amount of these compounds in apple skin is minimal compared to other anti-inflammatory foods like turmeric or fatty fish. Not all headaches are caused by inflammation - tension headaches are often triggered by stress, tight muscles, or environmental factors. Apple skin is an excellent source of fibre, which is great for digestion and maintaining overall health, but its effect on actual headache relief is negligible. Headaches that arise from constipation or dehydration might improve with better hydration or fibre intake, but eating an apple skin alone won't solve the problem. Apples, skin included, contain a good amount of water - about 85% of the fruit is made up of water. Staying hydrated is essential for preventing dehydration headaches, but the effect on headaches is more about overall hydration rather than any magical quality of the apple skin itself. While apples are a healthy choice and contribute to overall well-being, the idea that their skin has special powers to cure or alleviate headaches is a myth.

title: Can apples and bananas with cloves prevent thyroid and acidity?
claim_text: Consuming apples and bananas with cloves inserted into them during winter months offers a permanent cure or protection against thyroid disorders, acidity, and migraines
quick_take: An social media post suggests that eating apples and bananas with cloves poked into them during winter can guarantee lifelong protection from thyroid issues, acidity, and even migraines. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific evidence that supports the idea that eating fruits with cloves poked into them can prevent, or permanently 'cure', thyroid disorders. This claim is not only unproven but medically misleading. Thyroid conditions like hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism are complex hormonal imbalances often triggered by autoimmune factors, iodine deficiencies, or genetics. They require medical evaluation and in many cases lifelong treatment and monitoring. The idea that poking cloves into these fruits somehow makes them powerful enough to ward off thyroid disorders is absurd. There's no known reaction or enhancement that occurs when cloves are stuck into fruit that would offer any therapeutic benefit, let alone cure a hormonal disorder. For acidity: It doesn't cure or prevent acidity. Acidity or acid reflux is a digestive issue caused by excess stomach acid or weakened muscles in the food pipe. Managing it usually involves dietary changes, stress management, and sometimes medication. Poking cloves into fruit does nothing to enhance their anti-acidity properties. And storing such combinations improperly can lead to bacterial growth, which may worsen digestive symptoms. Sports nutritionist Manasi Bandhuni says 'While foods like bananas and apples can offer temporary relief from acid reflux symptoms due to their natural antacid-like properties, they are not cures. True management comes from a balanced, low-acid diet, portion control, and lifestyle tweaks consulting a professional for personalized advice is key to avoiding flare-ups.' For migraines: Adding to the list of claims is the idea that this fruit-and-clove combo can also cure migraines. This is completely unfounded. Migraines are a neurological condition, often linked to hormonal changes, stress, diet, sleep, and environmental triggers. They are not caused, or cured, by anything that can be addressed through poked fruits. There is zero scientific logic to the belief that inserting cloves into apples or bananas could have any effect on migraine pain or frequency. It's a leap from food-based wellness to pure pseudoscience. Dr Vivek Barun, Senior Consultant Neurologist and Epileptologist at Artemis Hospitals, Gurugram explained, 'Migraine is a complex condition that needs proper treatment. Managing it usually involves two types of approaches, one to relieve the pain during an attack, and another to help prevent future attacks. While apples do have some minerals like magnesium, which might slightly help reduce how often or how severe migraines get, they definitely can't cure it.' Dr Sreenivas Meenakshisundaram, Consultant Neurologist at MGM Healthcare, Chennai said, 'There's no link between cloves or apples/bananas and migraine relief. The only nutrients that have shown some benefit in reducing migraine attacks are magnesium and vitamin B2 (also called riboflavin). While apples do contain small amounts of these, it's not nearly enough to actually prevent migraines.' Regarding cloves specifically: While cloves do have some antimicrobial and antioxidant properties, inserting them into fruit does not improve their health effects. In fact, cloves lose potency when exposed to air and moisture over time. So, sticking them into fruit and leaving them for hours or days might reduce their already minimal benefit. This practice seems rooted in folk traditions rather than any nutritional or medicinal science. It may appear ritualistic, but it holds no clinical value. Fruits and spices are important parts of a healthy diet, but they should never be viewed as a replacement for medical care. Especially for conditions like thyroid disorders and chronic migraines, delaying treatment in favour of unverified 'natural cures' can lead to serious complications. Migraines may require lifestyle adjustments, medications, or neurological assessments. Thyroid issues need hormone tests and possibly long-term therapy. Acidity may be managed with diet, but not with unverified clove poking claims.

title: Fact Check: Can eating apples relieve migraine pain? - THIP Media
claim_text: eating an apple on an empty stomach relieves migraine pain
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating apples relieve migraine pain. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation:
Migraine is a type of headache that typically affects one side of the head and causes intense throbbing pain or a pulsing sensation. Along with the pain, individuals often experience sensitivity to light and sound, nausea, and vomiting. Migraine attacks can last anywhere from a few hours to several days and can significantly interfere with daily activities. Fortunately, there are medications available that can help prevent some migraines and lessen their severity. Combining medication with self-help remedies and lifestyle adjustments may also be beneficial in managing the condition.

Can eating apples relieve migraine pain? Not exactly. There is no concrete scientific evidence to suggest that apples can alleviate migraine pain. But research published in 2020 indicates that diet plays a significant role in triggering or relieving migraine symptoms. As such, dietary changes are an essential risk factor to consider in managing migraine pain. Further research is needed to fully understand how diet impacts migraine. The research also informs that there is a risk of nutritional imbalances that could lead to adverse effects if not carefully monitored by a qualified healthcare provider. Therefore, paying attention to lifestyle and behavioral changes that may help prevent or delay migraine attacks, such as maintaining proper nutrition and hydration, practicing good sleep hygiene, relaxation techniques, and social activities is crucial. By taking a holistic approach, individuals with migraines can improve their quality of life and manage their symptoms more effectively.

Dr Abhishek Juneja, Neurologist explains 'Consuming a healthy diet that includes fresh fruits and leafy greens, which are rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, can be beneficial for mental health. However, while apples are a nutritious fruit, there is no evidence to suggest that they are specifically effective in relieving migraines'.

What can be the dangers of trying to cure migraine at home by eating apples and not seeking medical advice? While apples are generally a healthy food choice, relying solely on them to cure migraines without seeking medical advice can be risky. Migraines can have multiple triggers and not all migraines are caused by dietary factors. It's possible to mistake migraines for other types of headaches or misdiagnose the cause of migraines by assuming they are caused by diet. This can lead to delayed or inappropriate treatment and potentially worsen the condition.

Nutritionist Priyanka informs 'Migraine attacks triggered by certain foods are common, and identifying and avoiding these food triggers can help alleviate symptoms. However, since migraines are a complex condition requiring a multifaceted approach, simply eating an apple on an empty stomach cannot reliably relieve migraine pain'. Also, eating only apples or relying on a limited diet to manage migraines can lead to nutritional deficiencies and imbalances. This can negatively impact overall health and well-being and exacerbate migraine symptoms. Moreover, eating too many apples or making significant changes to your diet without medical supervision can cause adverse effects, such as gastrointestinal discomfort, allergic reactions.

Besides this, if migraines have occurred because of an underlying medical condition, such as a hormonal imbalance or neurological disorder, relying solely on apples to treat the symptoms may delay proper medical treatment. This can lead to the progression of the underlying condition and further complications. Previously, The Healthy Indian Project (THIP Media) has cautioned that apple seeds can be poisonous enough to kill people. They can be harmful if crushed or chewed. Additionally, a Harvard School of Public Health article suggests that pesticides can remain on apple skin and seep into the fruit. Therefore, washing and peeling apples can help to prevent the ingestion of these pesticides.

title: Can eating banana and flaxseed together help control hair fall?
claim_text: Consuming banana and flaxseed together can reduce hair shedding, promote hair growth, and help manage excessive hair fall.
verdict_original: found the claim to be false
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating banana and flaxseed will help control excess hair fall. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Hair shedding is usually driven by what's happening inside the hair cycle, not by one food pairing. A very common pattern is telogen effluvium, a temporary surge in shedding that often shows up 2–3 months after a trigger such as fever/viral illness, major stress, surgery, childbirth, rapid weight loss, or a new medication. In this situation, many hairs shift into the 'resting and shedding' phase together, so you see more strands on the pillow, in the shower, and on the comb. That's scary, but it's not something banana + flaxseed can switch off overnight. Medical references describe telogen effluvium as diffuse shedding after a stressor or body change, and the best management is usually identifying and addressing the trigger while giving the cycle time to settle. Dr Gurman Singh Bhasin, Director & Chief Dermatologist, Skinclarity Clinic, Nagpur, states: "In conditions like telogen effluvium, hair shedding occurs because a large number of hair follicles prematurely enter the resting phase following a physical or emotional stressor. This process is internally regulated and cannot be reversed by eating a particular food or food combination. Once triggered, the shedding runs its course over several months, and recovery depends on removal of the underlying cause rather than dietary 'quick fixes'. Banana/flaxseed are healthy as part of an overall balanced diet (protein/iron/Vit D/B12/omega-3), but they don't 'stop' hair fall by themselves – especially in telogen effluvium." Banana offers carbohydrate energy and small amounts of vitamins and minerals; flaxseed adds fibre and healthy fats. That can support overall diet quality, especially if meals are irregular or low in plant foods. But when hair fall is linked to nutrition, the usual culprits are bigger-picture issues: not eating enough overall, too little protein, or specific deficiencies (often iron-related in some people, though the science on iron and hair loss is mixed and not as simple as 'low ferritin = hair fall'). One review notes there isn't clear-cut evidence proving iron deficiency directly causes all non-scarring hair loss types, which is why blanket self-treatment is risky. Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital, Mumbai, explains that hair fall cannot be managed through diet alone and needs a well-rounded approach. She notes that eating a balanced diet with enough protein, vitamins, and key minerals helps support normal hair follicle function and improves hair strength from within. Alongside nutrition, good scalp care plays an important role, including avoiding frequent chemical treatments and excessive heat styling, which can weaken hair and worsen breakage. She adds that when hair loss is connected to hormonal changes or genetic factors, medically proven options such as minoxidil or doctor-prescribed treatments may be necessary. According to her, seeing a dermatologist is essential to correctly identify the cause of hair loss and to design a treatment plan tailored to the individual, rather than relying on one-size-fits-all remedies. Regarding flaxseed omega-3: Flaxseed contains ALA, a plant omega-3, but the body converts ALA into the longer-chain omega-3s (EPA/DHA) only in small amounts, and conversion to DHA can be very low. Also, the more convincing hair-related studies don't test 'flaxseed with banana.' One well-known trial looked at a multi-ingredient nutritional supplement (omega-3 & omega-6 plus antioxidants) and found improvements in some hair measures over months, but that result cannot be pinned on flaxseed alone. The claim also leans on the biotin myth - 'more biotin = less hair fall' - but biotin helps when someone is deficient, and marketing for routine use in healthy people is not well supported by evidence.

title: Fact Check: Can eating bananas help quit smoking?
claim_text: Eating two bananas daily can help quit smoking.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Meenakshi Jain, Assistant Professor of Psychiatry at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, stated: 'More than 267 million adults in India are tobacco users. They face multiple physical and mental health issues like COPD, heart attacks, lung cancer, oral cancer, depression, anxiety, etc. Beyond morbidity, tobacco use can also result in death. According to the WHO regional office for South East Asia WHO Face Sheet 2018, more than 1 million adults die each year in India due to tobacco use.' She explained that more than half of smokers wish to stop smoking at least once in their lifetime, but due to lack of knowledge, withdrawal symptoms, or lack of support, quitting is difficult. The most common method involves NRT (Nicotine Replacement Therapy). Those who do not wish to take NRT can utilize multiple techniques and nonpharmacological methods: (1) Find a personalized reason/motivation to quit smoking — listing advantages such as improved physical health, reduced risk of illness, improved mental health, financial gain, improved cognition; (2) Understand why it is difficult to quit — physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms like mood swings, irritability, sleep disturbances, depressive symptoms, constipation, anxiety), psychological dependence (using tobacco to handle stress), and conditioning (smoking associated with environmental/social cues); (3) Set a quit date — within two weeks, using either nicotine fading technique (progressively lowering cigarettes per day) or cold turkey method; (4) Throw away all nicotine/tobacco products on the night before the quit date and ensure total abstinence; (5) Overcome psychological dependence/conditioning — identify triggers, practice coping skills, meditation, deep breathing, distraction techniques; (6) Anticipate triggers and challenges — practice coping responses; (7) Avoid alcohol as it is the most common cause of relapse; (8) Find support from family, friends, support groups, online cessation groups, counselling; (9) Visit a mental health professional for withdrawal symptoms; (9) Follow the Five Ds for handling urges: Delay, Distract, Drink water, Deep breath, Discuss; (10) Counselling and therapy — behaviour therapy and motivation enhancement therapy play significant roles; (11) Manage failure — learn from failed attempts and try again.

Dr Neatu Narang, Professor and Senior Consultant at Amrita Hospital Faridabad, added: 'While bananas themselves may not directly help in quitting smoking, incorporating healthy habits like eating fruits such as bananas can be part of a holistic approach.' She outlined potential supportive roles: (A) Control of Craving — Bananas can be a good snack option to curb cravings and provide essential nutrients; (B) Stress relief — Bananas contain magnesium and vitamin B6 that can help relax muscles and calm the mind, potentially reducing stress; (C) Increased energy — Bananas are a source of natural sugars and carbohydrates that can provide a quick energy boost during the quitting process. She concluded: 'Adding bananas to your diet as a healthy snack option can be a small but helpful part of a comprehensive plan to quit smoking. It's important to appreciate that everyone's journey is different, so it's important to find what works best for you in your efforts to quit smoking.'

The article notes that while bananas may aid smoking cessation, no direct scientific evidence links banana consumption directly to smoking cessation. Two studies (Lal et al. 2017 and a study in International Journal of Biology Research) reported that bananas help supply required vitamins and minerals to smokers trying to quit, and that craving for nicotine is reduced by banana consumption. A market survey by Chennakrishnan (2011) suggested bananas may replenish nutrients like vitamins C, A1, B6, B12 and minerals like potassium and magnesium, potentially easing the quitting process. However, these are indirect nutritional benefits, not a direct causal mechanism for smoking cessation.

title: Fact Check: Can eating capsicum treat rough and frizzy hair?
claim_text: If you have rough and frizzy hair, eat capsicum!
quick_take: A social media post tells viewers to eat capsicum for rough hair. It claims that eating capsicum can address the issue of rough and frizzy hair. After fact checking, we termed this claim false.
doctor_explanation: The fact check explains that while capsicum is a nutrient-rich vegetable containing vitamins A and C, which play roles in hair health, there is no scientific evidence that eating capsicum directly reduces hair frizz or smooths rough hair. Capsicum contains vitamin C which is essential for collagen production, helping maintain hair follicle structure. A lack of vitamin C can lead to dry, brittle hair. Vitamin A supports hair growth by promoting cell development in the scalp. Capsicum also contains capsaicin, and a 2007 study found that oral administration of capsaicin (6 mg/day) combined with isoflavone (75 mg/day) increased IGF-I production, promoting hair growth in 64.5% of volunteers with alopecia compared to 11.8% in the placebo group. However, this study focused on hair growth, not hair texture or frizz reduction. Frizz occurs when the hair cuticle lifts, allowing moisture from the air to enter and cause strands to swell, triggered by external factors like humidity, heat styling, or chemical treatments. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, 'Capsicum, or bell pepper, is rich in vitamin C, which helps the body absorb iron and also supports collagen production. Collagen is important for maintaining the strength and structure of hair. Capsicum also contains vitamin A, which supports scalp health by keeping it moisturised and promoting healthy hair follicles. While eating capsicum can contribute to overall hair health as part of a balanced diet, it's not a quick fix for rough or frizzy hair. Good nutrition works best when combined with proper hair care habits.' Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, says, 'Yes, there are definitely better ways to manage rough and frizzy hair. The key is to keep the hair well-moisturised and protect it from damage. Use a gentle, sulphate-free shampoo and follow it up with a good conditioner. Avoid excessive heat styling, and try using leave-in serums or oils that help lock in moisture. Diet matters too—eating a balanced diet with enough protein, iron and healthy fats supports hair health from within. If the frizz is severe or persistent, it's a good idea to see a dermatologist to check for any underlying scalp or hair issues.' The article concludes that while eating capsicum may contribute to overall hair health due to its rich nutrient profile including vitamins A and C, which support collagen production and hair growth, there is no scientific evidence that it specifically treats rough or frizzy hair. Frizz is primarily caused by external factors and is better managed through targeted hair care products and practices.

title: Can eating cardamom cure erectile dysfunction in men?
claim_text: An Instagram post claims that eating two cardamoms before bed eliminates impotence and improves male sexual performance.
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating cardamom can cure erectile dysfunction in men. We fact checked this claim and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific proof that cardamom can cure erectile dysfunction (ED), which is commonly referred to as male impotence. ED is a complex medical condition that can be caused by a range of physical issues, such as diabetes, heart disease, obesity, hypertension or hormone imbalances. It can also result from psychological factors like anxiety, depression, or stress. Cardamom has been linked to sexual wellness in some traditional practices, but that doesn't mean it works as a cure. Modern medicine does not recognise cardamom as an effective treatment for ED. In fact, relying on such claims may delay proper diagnosis and treatment. On the other hand, claims that cardamom harms fertility are false. ED is best managed through lifestyle changes, psychological support, and medical care, depending on its cause. Dr Mohit Sandhu, Ayurveda Consultant from Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh, said: 'In Ayurveda, cardamom is known for its warming and digestive properties. It supports agni, the digestive fire, and can help reduce stress-related imbalances. But we do not consider it a direct cure for erectile dysfunction. ED in Ayurveda is seen as a condition with multiple causes, like physical, emotional, and lifestyle-related. Treatment usually involves a personalised approach with herbs, diet, lifestyle correction, and sometimes therapies like Vajikarana. Cardamom may be part of the diet, but not the sole remedy.' Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician, Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, explained: 'There's no evidence in modern medicine that cardamom can cure erectile dysfunction. ED is usually a result of underlying health issues, like obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, or stress. So, even though cardamom may support general health due to its antioxidants, it doesn't address the root causes of ED. I often tell my patients that depending on spices or herbs or home remedies alone delays proper treatment. If someone is experiencing ED, it's important to speak to a doctor and look at the bigger health picture.' Regarding sexual performance: Some early studies on animals suggest that cardamom may affect sperm count or hormone levels under certain conditions, such as in obese or hypothyroid mice. Other studies indicate that cardamom might have aphrodisiac properties. However, these findings do not mean that cardamom improves sexual performance in healthy human males. Cardamom provides antioxidants and may improve blood circulation, which supports overall health. But eating it alone won't address sexual performance problems or cure ED. Good sexual health depends on overall well-being, such as eating well, staying active, and managing stress, not on using a single spice. Regarding testosterone: Some small animal studies suggest that cardamom might affect testosterone or other hormones under certain conditions. A 2020 study found that cardamom increased testosterone levels in young male mice. But this happened after the mice were given cardamom during early development, not as adults. The study also reported changes that may not be helpful, like reduced movement and social behaviour. So far, no reliable research shows that cardamom boosts testosterone in healthy men. Human bodies are very different from mice, and what works in animals doesn't always work in people. Even if cardamom had a slight effect on hormones, it wouldn't be enough to treat erectile dysfunction (ED), which can have many causes. Hormones are just one part of the picture. To conclude, the claim that eating cardamom can cure erectile dysfunction in men is false. Even though cardamom may offer some general health benefits and has traditional uses, there is no scientific evidence that it treats erectile dysfunction. ED is a medical condition that requires proper diagnosis and management, not home remedies.
