title: Fact check: Can eating specific foods once a week prevent cancer?
claim_text: According to a Facebook post by Nari, including specific foods in our diets—like broccoli, tomatoes, and blueberries—just once a week is sufficient to prevent the development of cancer cells.
quick_take: According to a social media post, eating specific foods such as blueberries, tomatoes, and broccoli once a week can help prevent cancer. After verifying the claim, we determined that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Cancer development, or carcinogenesis, usually originates from a sequence of genetic mutations that interfere with normal cell growth and regulation. These mutations can be passed down through generations or acquired over time, mostly as a result of lifestyle and environmental influences. While cancer prevention is of great significance, it is essential to comprehend that not all malignancies can be entirely avoided due to the complicated multifactorial aetiology of cancer development, which encompasses risk factors that are both modifiable and non-modifiable. A major proportion of malignancies are associated with modifiable risk factors; hence, adopting healthy lifestyle choices may considerably reduce their risk. These practices could include consuming nutraceuticals (cancer-preventive bioactive compounds), staying away from tobacco, limiting alcohol, shielding the skin from the sun, and maintaining a healthy weight. Diet plays a pivotal role in cancer prevention. An unbalanced diet heavy in processed foods, red meat, refined sugars, and saturated fats has a major impact on several malignancies, including breast, prostate, and colon cancers. Doctors usually recommend following a plant-based or Mediterranean diet that is comprised of essential micronutrients, fibre, proteins, and omega-3 fatty acids. Plant-based diets high in antioxidants, fibre, and phytochemicals may aid in lowering inflammation and oxidative stress, two major factors in carcinogenesis. The mindful food consumption should be complemented with consistent dietary patterns, which may have a cumulative impact on overall cancer risk. Dr. Manish Singhal, Oncologist, Apollo Hospital, Delhi, stated in an interview with THIP Media that having processed foods and refined sugars every day while disregarding weight gain is an unhealthy practice. Dr. Singhal stresses the importance of including vital micronutrients and antioxidants in addition to eating the proper amounts of fats, protein, and carbs. He also maintains that one should consume food at appropriate times and that one should not put off eating. Regarding the specific foods: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, a carotenoid that is a potent antioxidant. The ability of lycopene has been extensively studied for reducing the incidence of prostate cancer. However, these benefits are usually associated with frequent and sustained consumption rather than occasional intake. Broccoli is a cruciferous vegetable that has been linked to a lower risk of breast, lung, and colorectal cancers because it contains glucosinolates, which break down into substances like sulforaphane that are biologically active and exhibit cancer-fighting abilities. However, these findings are confined to preclinical research and the advantage results from consistent and sustained dietary inclusion. Blueberries are packed with anthocyanins, flavonoids, and other polyphenols, which have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory characteristics. Due to these properties, blueberries have demonstrated the ability to reduce oxidative stress, inhibit the development of tumours, and even improve the efficiency of radiation therapy. However, for optimal outcomes, they should be frequently included in a balanced diet. Dr Sarthak Moharir, Chief Radiation Oncologist at Apollo Cancer Centre, Bilaspur, advised that cancer is not a single disease. It is a group of over 200 different diseases with different causes and no single food or dietary intervention absolutely guarantees prevention. Daily and sustained intake over years of green vegetables and fruits reduces the risk of certain types of cancer. The benefits of eating foods that reduce oxidative stress or influence inflammatory pathways (that is, fresh fruits and green leafy vegetables) are seen over years and decades of sustained intake. A once-a-week intake of these food items is likely not going to help as much as making it a habit and eating it every day. There are no so-called anti-cancer foods because cancer is an extremely complicated illness, and eating certain types of food may not be sufficient to completely prevent its developmental risk. Therefore, it is necessary to combine a well-nourished diet with other beneficial practices. Most significantly, there is no 100% accurate, quick fix for preventing cancer, and it can affect healthy people who have no recognised risk factors.

title: Fact Check: Can eating sugarcane kill cancer cells?
claim_text: Sugarcane: Sugarcane is a good source of vitamin C and antioxidants that may boost your immunity. Presence flavonoids – help the body stave off cancerous cells, especially prostate and breast cancer. Sugarcane juice work excellent for digestive and liver problems
quick_take: A social media post suggests sugarcane kills cancer cells, implying that consuming it can cure cancer. We fact-checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: The current cancer treatments include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, hormone therapy, stem cell transplants and precision medicine. Treatment choices depend on the type and stage of cancer, tailored to each patient's needs and guided by oncologists. Diet can play a significant role in reducing the risk of certain types of cancer. But cancer is a complex disease which is influenced by various factors, including genetics, environmental exposures, and lifestyle choices. So, adopting a healthy diet can be a proactive step in cancer prevention. But diet alone cannot prevent cancer. Also, a healthy diet improves the outcome of cancer treatment. But it can only aid in cancer prevention and should not be considered a replacement for conventional cancer treatments. Shivashankar T., Chief Clinical Nutritionist and Dietician at Tata Memorial Cancer Hospital, Mumbai confirms the same: 'A healthy diet plays an important role in supporting overall health and well-being during cancer treatment. A diet high in good protein and no simple carbohydrates as well as inflammatory proteins can be beneficial for the cancer patients. However, this diet advice needs to be altered for every patient according to the requirements of their body.' There is no evidence that shows eating sugarcane kills cancer cells. Moreover, no conclusive scientific evidence supports the claim that flavonoids in sugarcane can directly stave off cancerous cells, particularly in the case of prostate and breast cancer. While flavonoids are a group of naturally occurring compounds found in various plants and have been studied for their potential health benefits, their role in cancer prevention is complex and not fully understood. It is important to note that all cells in the body require sugar to survive. Cancer cells do have a higher demand for glucose (sugar) compared to normal cells. They tend to take up more glucose and produce energy through a less efficient process called glycolysis, even in the presence of oxygen (aerobic glycolysis), rather than the more efficient oxidative phosphorylation that occurs in normal cells. Our research also shows that even though cancer cells have an increased need for glucose, they do not necessarily need sugar to survive. No evidence suggests that sugar feeds cancer or that a sugar-free diet lowers cancer risk. Cancer cells are versatile and can adapt their metabolism to use other fuel sources, such as amino acids and fatty acids, in addition to glucose. They do it through a process called metabolic reprogramming. It is a way for cancer cells to change their normal way of getting energy and nutrients, so they can grow and spread more easily. It's like a survival strategy that helps cancer cells become stronger and more dangerous. The reason why cancer cells show a preference for glucose is not entirely clear, but it is believed to provide several advantages for tumor growth and survival. Glucose metabolism can supply intermediates for cell growth and proliferation, and it can also generate antioxidants that help protect cancer cells from oxidative stress. Additionally, high glucose uptake can promote an environment, which can be advantageous for tumor growth. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director, Amrita School of Ayurveda said, 'Cancer is not a single disease and there is no remedy for cancer. Different types of cancer are treated with different procedures of chemotherapy. One drug does not work across all cancers.' Our research further shows that cancer treatment typically involves a multidisciplinary approach, including medical interventions like chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, and targeted therapies. Dr. Sarthak Moharir, Chief Radiation Oncologist Apollo Cancer Centre, Bilaspur further adds, 'Special diet or diet modifications do not cure cancer. Diet is very important for patients undergoing cancer treatment and it is advised they take a balanced meal with all macros and micronutrients as prescribed by their dietary counsellor.' He further states, 'Sugarcane, its derivatives, and any flavonoid are not included in the management algorithm of any cancer. Even if a compound demonstrates anti-cancer activity in a laboratory setting, its effects may vary significantly inside the human body. Sugarcane juice primarily serves as a source of glucose and does not offer any other notable nutritional benefits.' The dangers of trying to cure cancer through diet and not seeking medical advice include: Cancer is a complicated disease that requires more than lotus root for treatment. Relying solely on home remedies and not seeking proper medical treatment can worsen the condition making cancer incurable. Cancer multiplies quickly and spreads throughout the body in a short span. Any delay in the treatment will make the condition difficult to treat.

title: Fact check: Can eating three oranges daily help control unbridled lustful desires that may be difficult to manage through other means and methods?
claim_text: Eating three oranges daily helps control unbridled lustful desires that may be difficult to manage through other means and methods.
verdict_original: The claim is false. Hence, the claim that eating three oranges daily helps control unbridled lustful desires that may be difficult to manage through other means and methods is False.
quick_take: No, eating oranges cannot help control unbridled lustful desires. Oranges on the other hand do have mild aphrodisiac properties. After thorough research it is clear that their consumption to manage libido does not have any scientific evidence.
doctor_explanation: Libido refers to a person's overall sexual desire for sexual activity. It is affected by various biological, physiological and social factors. Biologically, libido is affected by the hormones estrogen, progesterone and testosterone; it is also affected by neurotransmitters dopamine and serotonin, which play a role in a person's mood. Libido is a complex and multifaceted aspect of human sexuality which can greatly vary from person to person. High libido refers to high sexual desire or the emotion and mental energy related to sex. Another term for it is 'sex drive.' A high libido potentially becomes a problem when it results in sexual activity that feels out of control. Dr T. Siddhartha, MBBS, MS, Consultant Urologist and Andrologist, Prashanth Hospital, Kolathur, said: 'Libido can be defined as a drive for sex. It's a very dynamic process that varies from person to person. Multiple factors, such as biological, physiological and social, affect libido. High libido is very hard to define or quantify; it's only easy to assess if it causes problems in day-to-day life.' An orange has over 170 different phytochemicals and more than 60 flavonoids, providing various health benefits. Oranges contain a large number of essential vitamins, minerals and nutrients. They are rich in potassium and contain other minerals like phosphorus, manganese, magnesium, selenium, and copper. Oranges also have choline and anti-oxidants like zeaxanthin and carotenoids. They also contain vitamins like thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, Vitamin B-6, pantothenic acid and folate. There is no such evidence that consuming oranges can control or decrease libido or sexual desires. In fact, oranges do have mild aphrodisiac properties and thus can help in dealing with sexual problems like erectile dysfunction, frigidity and disinterest in sex. Orange peel could be a functional food for erectile dysfunction. It can improve sexual behaviour and also inhibit the activities of enzymes implicated in erectile dysfunction. However, no relevant clinical data has been presented to prove this. Dr. Nishanth Puliyath, Senior Resident, Dept of Urology & Andrology, Calicut Medical College, Kerala, said: 'It's a myth, and people should be aware of such claims. We do not support such claims as no clinical evidence is present to date. My only advice to patients with any such issue is to eat a balanced diet, exercise regularly, and get 8 hours of sleep. We can only embrace a holistic lifestyle.' Dr. Poonam Gulati, Senior Consultant Urology and Renal Transplant at Batra Hospital, said: 'While there are foods with known aphrodisiac quality, foods with natural phytoestrogens are known to decrease libido, oranges are not amongst foods that decrease sexual drive.' Conclusion: eating oranges cannot help control unbridled lustful desires. Oranges actually have mild aphrodisiac properties and their consumption to manage libido does not have any scientific evidence.

title: Fact Check: Can eating three times a day make you sick?
claim_text: An Instagram post suggests a hierarchy of eating frequencies: those who eat once a day are yogis, those who eat twice are bhogos (enjoyers), and those who eat thrice a day are rogi (sick people). The video argues that excessive mealtimes, including frequent snacking, are the primary cause of illness. title: Can chewing tulsi leaves in the morning treat urine problems?

doctor_explanation: The claim that chewing tulsi leaves in the morning can treat urine problems is mostly false. Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum or holy basil) and mint (Mentha species, commonly called pudina) are different plants with distinct properties and uses. Tulsi has applications as a medicinal herb in traditional Indian medicine, while mint is widely used in cooking and for digestive relief. The Instagram post confuses the two by showing a picture of mint leaves while talking about tulsi. Traditional sources claim that tulsi has diuretic properties, meaning it may help the body produce more urine and flush out toxins, which could be beneficial for urinary health. Some sources suggest that consuming tulsi detox water or tulsi leaf juice with honey may help in expelling kidney stones and normalising uric acid levels. However, these claims are largely based on traditional use and not on robust scientific studies. Clinical research on tulsi's effects on urinary problems in humans is very limited and lacks strong evidence. Mint has been used historically for various digestive and some urinary complaints. Some ancient texts mention mint as a mild diuretic and suggest it could help with urinary flow and bladder stones. Modern research shows mint may have antibacterial properties in test-tube studies, but there is no strong clinical evidence supporting its use for urinary tract infections or other urinary problems in humans. A 2009 study tested 17 Indian medicinal plants, including tulsi, against drug-resistant bacteria linked to urinary tract infections (UTIs). Tulsi's ethanol extract showed some antibacterial activity in the lab, particularly against Klebsiella pneumoniae and Enterococcus faecalis. However, these effects were seen only in petri dishes, not in real patients. Dr Almas Fatma, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, said: 'While tulsi is a respected herb in traditional medicine and may have some antibacterial properties in lab settings, eating a few tulsi leaves in the morning is unlikely to treat urinary problems. Urine issues, such as burning, pain, or frequent urination, often point to infections or other underlying conditions that need proper medical attention. It's important not to rely solely on home remedies for UTI. Instead, drink plenty of water and see your doctor if symptoms persist. Early treatment can prevent complications.' Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic in New Delhi, said: 'Mint is a refreshing herb often used in food and drinks, and while it may help with digestion or offer a cooling effect, it does not treat urinary problems. Issues like burning sensation, frequent urination, or pain usually suggest an infection or another medical concern that needs proper diagnosis. Chewing mint leaves alone will not address the root cause. If symptoms last more than a day or two, it's best to see a doctor.' While tulsi may have some traditional uses for urinary health, these are not proven by modern science. Adding tulsi detox water to your routine may offer hydration and traditional wellness support, but it is not a cure.

title: Can eating two bananas a day fuel 90 minutes of exercise?
claim_text: Eating two bananas daily provides enough energy for 90 minutes of exercise and is also considered a fruit that brings happiness.
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating two bananas a day can fuel 90 minutes of exercise and make you happier. We conducted a thorough fact check and found the claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Can two bananas power a 90-minute workout? No, not for most people or types of workouts. Bananas are rich in carbohydrates and natural sugars like glucose, fructose and sucrose. A medium banana has around 100 to 110 calories and about 27 to 29 grams of carbohydrates. Two bananas would give you roughly 200 to 220 calories in total. This may be enough for a short burst of light to moderate activity. But 90 minutes of continuous moderate or intense exercise usually needs much more energy. Depending on the intensity and the individual, it could take 400 to 800 calories or more. That's far more than what two bananas can provide. Athletes and regular gym-goers often need a mix of carbohydrates, proteins and fats before a long workout. Bananas can be a good pre-workout snack because they are easy to digest and contain potassium, which supports muscle function. Still, suggesting they alone can fuel a full 90-minute workout is misleading. Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, says, "Two bananas can give you a good amount of quick energy because they are rich in natural sugars and carbohydrates. They are especially useful before a workout as they help fuel your muscles. However, whether they can power a full 90-minute session depends on the intensity of the exercise and your overall nutrition. For longer or more intense workouts, your body may need more than just bananas, such as a mix of carbs, protein, and fluids to keep going strong." Do bananas make people feel happier? Maybe, but not in the way the post suggests. Bananas contain tryptophan, an amino acid that the body can use to produce serotonin (a brain chemical that helps regulate mood, sleep, and overall wellbeing). However, the tryptophan from bananas must first be absorbed into the bloodstream and then transported to the brain before it can be converted into serotonin. The serotonin naturally found in bananas cannot cross the blood–brain barrier, so eating bananas does not directly raise serotonin levels in the brain or instantly improve mood. Bananas contain vitamin B6, which helps convert tryptophan into serotonin. However, eating one or two bananas won't noticeably improve mood. Any mood effect is mild and depends on many factors like diet and mental health. The idea of bananas as a "happy fruit" comes from their link to serotonin, but there's no strong proof they directly make you happier. A 2020 study found moderate banana eating (1–3 times a week) linked to fewer depression signs in men, but high intake (4+ times a week) linked to more signs in women. The study cannot prove that bananas cause these effects because it only shows a connection, not a cause. Mood is affected by many things, including sleep, exercise, mental health and overall diet. While food plays a role, no single fruit can change how you feel in a big way. Are there any other benefits of eating bananas? Yes, bananas are nutritious when eaten in moderation. They are a good source of potassium, which helps keep blood pressure in check and supports heart health. Bananas also provide fibre for digestion, along with vitamin C and antioxidants. That said, eating too many bananas, especially for people with blood sugar concerns, may not be ideal. Their natural sugar content can lead to spikes in blood glucose levels if not balanced with other foods. So, while bananas are healthy, it is important to eat them as part of a varied and balanced diet rather than relying on them alone. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, "Bananas offer more than just a tasty snack. They provide important nutrients like potassium, which helps keep blood pressure healthy, and vitamin C, which supports the immune system. The fibre in bananas also helps in digestion and keeps you feeling full longer. Plus, their natural sugars give you a quick energy boost, making bananas a smart choice before or after exercise." THIP Media Take: The claim that eating two bananas a day can fuel 90 minutes of exercise and make you happier is mostly false. Bananas are a healthy snack and a good pre-workout option, but claiming that two bananas alone can fuel 90 minutes of exercise is an exaggeration. The idea that they directly make you feel happy is also too simple. They do support overall health and mood, but they are not a quick fix. Balanced meals and a healthy lifestyle are far more important.

The gallbladder holds a digestive fluid called bile between the meals when there is no fat to be digested. However, when we eat food gallbladder contracts to squeeze out the bile through the bile duct into the small intestine. Besides bile, the gallbladder also stores cholesterol and bilirubin (which makes urine yellow and stool brown). Due to some chemical imbalance, these stored compounds in the gallbladder produce stones. Gallstones stuck in the gallbladder can only be treated through surgical procedures including endoscopy, laparoscopy, cholecystectomy or open surgery. But gallstones range from the size of a sand grain to a golf ball. So, small gallstones may leave the gallbladder and pass into the bile duct to reach the small intestine and stool. The available evidence only suggests that eating a healthy diet reduces the risk of developing gallstones. However, we could not find evidence that confirms natural remedies like yoghurt, honey and lemon can cure gallstones completely. Dr Sharad Malhotra, Gastroenterologist, stated: "Gallstones occur because of supersaturation of cholesterol or infection in bile. Since no food elements will change the bile composition, no food can be offered as a cure for gallstones". A 2020 study showed Bifidobacteria and Lactobacilli bacteria catalyse the bile salts to prevent them from forming a stone. Yoghurt being a probiotic drink is full of bacteria, so incorporating yoghurt into the routine diet may prevent the formation of gallstones. Another 2009 study showed vitamin C can reduce the risk of gallstones. As lemons are rich in vitamin C, introducing lemons to a routine diet can be a healthy choice. A 2020 research showed honey can degrade the Salmonella typhi biofilm on the gallbladder to expose the gallbladder for treatment or to be passed through the stool on its own. However, we could not find any evidence of optimum dosage of lemon yoghurt and honey that can prevent the risk of gallbladder. Dr Dakshini also adds: "There is also evidence from prospective cohort studies indicating that the highest level of yogurt consumption compared with the lowest intake category was associated with a reduced risk of hip fracture, however, the quality of evidence is low for this". A (2013) study showed 'Milk and yogurt intakes were associated with hip but not spine BMD, while cream may adversely influence BMD. Thus, not all dairy products are equally beneficial for the skeleton'. This study further recommends 'suggestive fracture results for milk and yogurt intakes need further confirmation'. Harvard University health researchers recommend that women limit their dairy consumption to no more than two servings per day, since the potential risks of dairy, including the tie to ovarian cancer, can outweigh the potential advantages. Galactose, a type of sugar found in yogurt and produced from lactose, also has a potential association with ovarian cancer." title: Fact Check: Can elbow tapping cure heart blockages?
claim_text: A post shared on Instagram claims to cure heart blockages through elbow tapping (Lymphatic tapping or Lymphatic drainage).
quick_take: One particular post on Instagram claims to cure heart blockages through elbow tapping or lymphatic tapping. However, after conducting a fact check, we determined this claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Social media is full of posts offering advice on health conditions, especially those related to the heart. This saturation of information makes individuals vulnerable to trusting any health-related content they find online. What is the lymphatic system? The lymphatic system comprises vessels and organs beneath the skin, and is necessary for maintaining a healthy immune system. It functions similar to a garbage disposal, carrying out waste and bacteria filtration within the body. The lymphatic system includes various components vital for immune function. Bone marrow, found within bones, produces blood cells. The thymus, situated in the chest, facilitates the maturation of immune T cells. Tonsils and adenoids, located in the throat and nasal cavity, capture germs from ingested food and inhaled air. The spleen, positioned beneath the ribs and above the stomach, filters out old or damaged blood cells. Lymph nodes, found in the neck, armpits, and groin, serve to filter viruses and bacteria from lymph fluid as it passes through them. Additionally, mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), lining areas such as the tonsils, airways, small intestine, and appendix, helps in germ detection and elimination. What is lymphatic tapping or lymphatic drainage? Lymphatic tapping, also known as lymphatic drainage, is a gentle massage technique to stimulate the lymphatic system. During lymphatic tapping, a trained therapist applies light pressure and rhythmic movements to specific areas of the body where lymph nodes are located. This encourages the movement of lymph fluid through the lymphatic vessels, helping in the elimination of toxins and waste products. The benefits of lymphatic tapping include reducing swelling, improving circulation, and supporting immune function. It improves the quality of life in people with fibromyalgia. It can also help with conditions such as lymphedema, which involves the buildup of fluid in certain parts of the body. Can elbow tapping really cure heart blockages? No, elbow tapping cannot cure heart blockages. We did reverse image search to identify the person in the video when it was first shared. We found out the person is Chunyi Lin, he shared it on Facebook on June 9, 2019. He has 108,000 followers. The video features heart health techniques titled "How can you enhance your heart's circulation and protect your heart?" However, our Google search did not yield any credible medical reports supporting the effectiveness of these techniques for treating heart problems. Lymphatic tapping, while beneficial for promoting overall health and supporting the lymphatic system, is not a treatment for heart blockages. Heart blockages, caused by a buildup of plaque in the coronary arteries, require specific medical interventions. These approaches improve blood flow to the heart. We found no published research papers supporting the claim of lymphatic tapping being able to cure heart blockages. In fact, during our research we found that people with heart diseases or blood clot disorders should not go for lymphatic drainage. It's important for individuals with heart-related concerns to consult with a cardiologist for appropriate diagnosis and treatment options. What do the experts say? Dr Anusha Dewan, a General Physician at Jeevan Anmol Hospital in New Delhi: "It's important to understand that home remedies should not be seen as replacements for scientifically proven treatments. While some home remedies may offer health benefits, they should not be relied upon solely for addressing conditions like hypertension or arterial blockages. Unlike pharma drugs, home remedies do not undergo the same rigorous testing and regulation. This leads to variations in their effectiveness and safety." Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, a General Physician from Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi: "In addressing the claim that lymphatic drainage can cure heart blockages, it is essential to clarify that this is false. There is no evidence to support the idea that hand or elbow exercises can cure heart blockages. In fact, lymphatic drainage is generally not recommended for individuals suffering from heart disease, kidney disease, or cellulitis. Always seek advice from a medical professional for appropriate diagnosis and treatment." What does heart blockage mean? Heart blockage here refers to blocked arteries (coronary artery disease). Coronary artery blockage happens when the coronary arteries, which carry oxygen-rich blood to the heart muscle, get partially or completely blocked. This blockage occurs due to plaque buildup made of cholesterol, fat, and other substances on the artery walls. As plaque accumulates, it narrows the arteries, restricting blood flow to the heart. Reduced blood flow to the heart can cause symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, fatigue, and in severe cases, heart attack or cardiac arrest. Heart blockage is often linked with coronary artery disease (CAD). CAD develops over time due to various risk factors such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes, obesity, and a sedentary lifestyle. What is the cure for heart blockages? Treatments for heart blockages may include lifestyle changes such as a heart-healthy diet, regular exercise, quitting smoking, maintaining a healthy weight and addressing other risk factors. Some of the other risk factors include family history, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes. Your doctor may also prescribe drugs to manage risk factors like high cholesterol and high blood pressure. In more severe cases, procedures such as angioplasty, stenting, or bypass surgery may be needed to restore proper blood flow to the heart muscle. Early detection and management of heart blockage are essential for reducing the risk of serious heart-related events and improving overall heart health. Who is at risk for heart blockages? Numerous risk factors contribute to heart blockages, or blocked arteries, including high blood pressure and cholesterol levels, smoking, obesity, diabetes, sedentary lifestyle, and consumption of a diet rich in unhealthy fats and processed foods. Other significant factors are advancing age, family history of heart disease, and underlying medical conditions such as kidney disease and autoimmune disorders.

title: Fact Check: Can eliminating inflammation result in fast weight loss?
claim_text: A video on social media featuring actress Vidya Balan claims that reducing inflammation can lead to fast weight loss, presenting it as a shortcut to shedding extra kilos. The video claims that targeting inflammation alone eliminates the need for traditional weight-loss methods like diet and exercise.
quick_take: A social media post claims that eliminating inflammation results in fast weight loss. We conducted a fact check and found that the claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: No, reducing inflammation alone does not directly lead to weight loss. Chronic inflammation can affect hormones like insulin and leptin, which are involved in regulating metabolism and appetite. This disruption can make it harder to lose weight. However, addressing inflammation through diet or stress management can support a healthier weight loss journey when combined with proper nutrition and exercise. Studies support that weight loss itself can help reduce inflammation. A 2018 study found that weight loss through a low-calorie diet or surgery lowered inflammation markers, regardless of diet composition. Another study in 2008 showed that losing at least 10% of body weight reduces harmful inflammation and boosts protective substances. However, maintaining weight loss is essential for lasting health benefits. In 2019, research highlighted that even healthy individuals experience reduced inflammation after weight loss, but these benefits fade with weight regain. Furthermore, a 2020 study demonstrated that an anti-inflammatory diet helped individuals with obesity lose weight, particularly abdominal fat, and lowered inflammation markers like C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), which is linked to heart disease. This evidence shows that a combination of weight loss and diet can play a crucial role in managing inflammation and improving overall health. Deepalakshmi Sriram, Registered Dietitian at The Cleft & Craniofacial Centre and Sree Balaji Medical College & Hospital, Chennai, says, "Reducing inflammation alone won't make you lose weight. Inflammation can mess with hormones that control appetite and metabolism, which might make it harder to shed pounds. But to actually lose weight, you need a combination of a balanced diet, exercise, and a calorie deficit." Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad explains, "Reducing inflammation is like laying a solid foundation for better health. It supports your weight loss efforts but doesn't replace key habits like eating well and staying active. Lowering inflammation helps your body respond better to healthy habits, making it an excellent starting point, but not the ultimate goal." Anti-inflammatory foods like berries, nuts, and fatty fish can improve your health but don't serve as a miracle for quick weight loss. Supplements which claim to fight inflammation often lack strong scientific backing for weight reduction. Studies show that anti-inflammatory diets like the Mediterranean diet can improve heart health and reduce chronic inflammation. However, weight loss from such diets comes from reduced calorie intake and healthier eating habits, not the inflammation reduction itself. Weight loss involves a calorie deficit, where energy expenditure exceeds intake. Reducing inflammation helps improve overall health and may make it easier to stick to a healthy lifestyle. However, it doesn't change the basic science of weight loss. Factors like genetics, activity level, and gut health also play significant roles. A 2016 study highlighted that gut microbiota (microscopic organisms that help digestion), influenced by diet, could impact weight gain and inflammation. However, reducing inflammation without addressing calorie intake or physical activity rarely results in meaningful weight changes. Managing chronic inflammation is important for health but not for quick weight loss. Chronic inflammation is linked to conditions like diabetes, heart disease, and arthritis. Reducing inflammation can improve energy levels and metabolic health, making sustainable weight loss easier over time.

title: Fact Check: Can emotional stress cause cancer in the throat?
claim_text: According to an Instagram video, holding up emotions inside can affect the throat chakra causing throat cancer. The video further says rotating a lapis lazuli crystal can help open the throat chakra.
quick_take: A social media video claims that emotional distress can cause throat cancer. The video suggests stress causes cancer. We did the fact check to term it as Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
The fact check explains that throat cancer refers to cancers that develop in the throat (pharynx), voice box (larynx), or tonsils. It generally originates in the cells lining the throat, with the most common types being squamous cell carcinomas. The throat chakra (Vishuddha) is the fifth chakra in alternative medicine and spirituality, believed to be located at the throat and associated with communication, self-expression, and truth.

There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that emotional distress causes throat cancer or stress causes cancer. Cancer, including throat cancer, primarily results from genetic mutations that lead to uncontrolled cell growth. These mutations can arise due to various factors such as tobacco use, excessive alcohol consumption, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, and exposure to certain chemicals. Emotional distress, while impactful on overall health, does not directly cause the genetic mutations that result in cancer.

Regarding negative emotions causing cancer: chronic emotional distress and negative emotions can weaken the immune system and affect overall well-being, but they do not directly cause cancer. Cancer is fundamentally a disease of cellular mutations and genetic alterations. According to the National Cancer Institute, there exists no direct causal link between negative emotions and cancer. While managing stress and maintaining mental health is important for overall well-being, attributing cancer to negative emotions alone is misleading and lacks scientific basis.

Dr Pooja Khullar, a Radiation Oncologist at Dharamshila Narayana Superspeciality Hospital, New Delhi, shares: "Although stress can impact overall health and weaken the immune system, there is no direct link between stress and cancer. Effective cancer prevention strategies include reducing known risk factors such as smoking, limiting alcohol consumption, getting vaccine shots against HPV, and maintaining a healthy diet and lifestyle."

Dr Rakesh Kumar Sharma, a Medical Oncologist at Max Healthcare, Saket, New Delhi, shares: "Throat cancer is caused by tobacco use in any form, this has been proven by various studies. Emotional distress is a consequence of neuro-psychological disorders. These disorders are due to imbalance of neurotransmitters. If we are holding our thoughts, they are held in our brain not in our throat or thyroid gland. As of today there is no scientific evidence to prove the association of emotional distress and throat or thyroid cancer."

Well-established risk factors for throat cancer include tobacco use (in any form), excessive alcohol consumption, HPV infection, and exposure to certain chemicals. Throat cancer is curable, especially if detected early, with treatment options including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapy.

Regarding lapis lazuli: it is a deep-blue metamorphic rock used as a semi-precious stone. In various alternative medicine practices, it is believed to have healing properties and is associated with the throat chakra. However, these claims are not supported by scientific evidence. The use of crystals like lapis lazuli is based on traditional beliefs and should be seen as a complementary practice rather than a medical treatment.

The conclusion states that the claim that emotional stress causes cancer in the throat is mostly false. Throat cancer is mainly due to genetic mutations influenced by factors such as tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and HPV infection. While managing stress and emotions is important for overall health, there is no scientific evidence that says stress causes cancer. Practices involving lapis lazuli and throat chakra are rooted in alternative medicine and lack empirical support.

title: Fact Check: Can Entod Pharma's PresVu get rid of reading glasses?
claim_text: Entod Pharma's PresVu eye drops can completely get rid of reading glasses and serve as a spectacular, revolutionary breakthrough treatment for presbyopia.
verdict_original: The claim that Presvu can get rid of reading glasses is Misleading. The press release and the various reports are misleading as they seem to overstate the role of Presvu as a breakthrough or a revolutionary drug that can get rid of reading glasses.
quick_take: PresVu eye drops may reduce dependence on reading glasses for certain individuals with presbyopia, but it is unlikely to fully 'get rid of' the need for reading glasses in all cases. Presbyopia is a progressive, age-related condition, and while eye drops may improve near vision temporarily, they are not a cure.
doctor_explanation:
Dr. Ishan Kataria, Ophthalmologist, stated: 'It would be incorrect to classify this drug as a breakthrough treatment for presbyopia. It contains a diluted form of pilocarpine, which provides a temporary 'pinpoint effect' by constricting the pupil and ciliary muscles, similar to looking through a keyhole where light converges to enhance near vision. While this may reduce dependency on reading glasses, it cannot fully eliminate the need for them, as presbyopia is a natural, age-related condition that typically affects those over 40. For individuals above 50, the drops might reduce the need for stronger lenses, e.g.- potentially bringing a prescription of +3.0 down to +1.5, but no further. Although the drops work within 15 minutes, their effect is temporary, and without regular use, the benefits will diminish. Additionally, pilocarpine has a known history of side effects, including headaches and, in rare cases, retinal detachment, particularly when used in higher concentrations for glaucoma. Therefore, it may not be suitable for everyone.'

The article further explains that Presvu is a brand name of pilocarpine hydrochloride ophthalmic solution 1.25%, a cholinergic muscarinic agonist which activates muscarinic receptors at the iris sphincter muscle and ciliary muscle, contracting them to constrict the pupil and improve near and intermediate visual acuity. The drug was first approved in the US in 1974 for glaucoma and ocular hypertension, and was approved under the brand name Vuity by the US FDA in 2021 for presbyopia. A clinical trial by George O. Waring et al. found the onset effect of AGN-190584 (Allergan/AbbVie) formulation of pilocarpine hydrochloride 1.25% was at 15 minutes. The most common adverse reactions (>5%) include headache and conjunctival hyperemia. The drug is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to pilocarpine or excipients.

Drug officials publicly condemned the media coverage, stating the claims made by ENTOD Pharmaceuticals were 'unethical and false presentation of facts' and that an explanation had been sought from the company by the drug regulator.

Lifestyle modifications such as regular exercise, a healthy diet, stress management, and sufficient sleep can contribute to overall sexual health. title: Can everyone gain weight using a single Ayurvedic medication?
claim_text: An Ayurvedic medication called Sanyasi Ayurvedic Sehat Tablet can help everyone gain weight by enhancing nutritional absorption through improved digestive process, contributing to bone health, blood circulation, and overall health status.
quick_take: A social media post asserts that an Ayurvedic medication may help people gain weight. After verifying the claim, we discovered that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Weight is one metric used by doctors to assess optimal wellness. The concept of a healthy weight is subjective, yet it is necessary for optimal physiological functioning, hormone balance, immune response, and illness prevention. Any deviation from the normal range may indicate an underlying medical issue. When an individual weighs lower than expected, they are usually referred to as underweight. Medically, being underweight is defined as having a body mass index below 18.5. Low weight is often a concern for adolescents, senior adults, those who have eating disorders, individuals with chronic illnesses, or people with high metabolic requirements. Many factors contribute to being underweight, including malignancies, hyperthyroidism, and coeliac disease; persistent medical diseases that induce malabsorption or increased metabolic demands; and nutritional inadequacies or insufficient caloric intake. Anxiety and depression are two psychological conditions that can lead to appetite loss. Low weight can also be attributed to eating disorders, particularly bulimia and anorexia nervosa. Senior adults may also lose weight due to changes in taste perception, dental issues, medication, and cognitive impairment. High levels of physical activity and genetic variables may also lead to decreased body weight, making calorie intake insufficient. Addressing the underlying cause of low body weight is essential since successful therapy relies on resolving the fundamental issue, ensuring nutritional rehabilitation, and, if required, implementing medicinal or psychological interventions. While consuming more calories than one utilises for energy is often thought of as the simple solution to weight gain, this is an oversimplification of a complex physiological mechanism. Excessive calorie consumption and effective nutrient absorption are critical for weight gain, but they are only one part of a larger interaction between various elements. These mostly include sleep quality, intestinal microbes, metabolic rate, hormone regulation, inheritance, and psychological health. The hormones such as insulin, leptin, ghrelin, and cortisol have a major impact on energy expenditure, appetite, and fat accumulation. Among these, disruption of leptin signalling may affect satisfaction and lead to overeating even when caloric intake is adequate. Long-term stress, mental health issues, and insufficient sleep can disrupt circadian rhythm and cause hormone imbalances that can result in the accumulation of fat in the abdominal area. Recently, the gut microbiota has been identified as an essential element for the harvesting and preservation of energy. However, certain people may have specific microbial communities that extract more calories from a regular diet, which could lead to weight gain. As a result, managing weight is a complex issue, and focussing solely on a single aspect may have limited or transient results. Ayurveda views weight gain beyond excessive calorie intake. The traditional science considers it as a reflection of internal balance, Agni or digestive fire, optimal metabolism, and well-nourished tissues (dhatuposhan). The holistic nature of the ancient science addresses optimal nutrient absorption by enhancing metabolic rate and intestinal health, and addressing underlying imbalances that may prevent healthy weight gain. Addressing improper digestion or impaired agni is the cornerstone of Ayurvedic weight gain management. The ultimate objective of the therapy is nutritional assimilation, irrespective of the kind of food consumed. Ashwagandha, Shatavari, and Yashtimadhu are often employed to strengthen digestion and promote anabolic processes in the body. Moreover, these herbs promote ojas, which is essential for vitality, immunity, and maintaining a healthy weight. Another important consideration is that Ayurvedic remedies are always customised for each patient. Authentic Ayurvedic care involves a comprehensive evaluation of the individual's constitution, safety considerations, and underlying problem. Most significantly, using online Ayurvedic medications for the management of any medical problem—including weight gain—is not advised. This is due to the fact that these shortcuts could overlook the constitution, safety considerations, or the underlying problem. Without a comprehensive Ayurvedic evaluation, these practices could make a person's condition worse and put them in severe complications. Dr. Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, supports this by stating that 'some people can benefit from Ayurvedic remedies to help with digestion, especially when combined with a healthy diet. Herbs like amla, ashwagandha, and trikatu have long been used to enhance intestinal health and hunger. When combined with a healthy diet, these do help some people feel better. However, it's critical to recognise that not all Ayurvedic treatments are equally effective for everyone, and many of them still lack solid scientific evidence. So, while they might be beneficial when incorporated into a holistic regimen, they shouldn't take the place of personalised medical advice or a well-balanced diet.' Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, also cautions by suggesting that gaining weight too quickly is an unhealthy practice that can put unnecessary pressure on your body. It may seem like a good thing if someone is underweight, but rapid weight gain can lead to fat being stored in unhealthy areas, such as around the liver or abdomen. This raises the risk of poor metabolic health, hypertension, and insulin resistance. The objective should be to increase strength and muscular mass rather than just gaining weight, even if that is your goal. Long-term results are far better with a healthy, progressive approach backed by strength training, a nutritious diet, and adequate sleep. Even though Ayurvedic medicine supports healthy weight gain, a generic remedy might not be the answer for everyone. Hence, consuming such online unsupervised preparations is not recommended. Ayurvedic medicine is usually perceived as natural, holistic, and safer than allopathic options. However, the notion that all Ayurvedic medications are naturally side-effect-free is not entirely accurate. While many ayurvedic remedies are primarily botanical extracts, they can still be associated with adverse consequences, especially when consumed without supervision. Some of the recognised toxic effects are due to contamination, heavy metals, or improper dosing of herbal preparations. The assumption that 'natural equals safe' can be dangerously deceptive. When individuals indulge in self-medicating practices by buying online Ayurvedic medication without a prescription, they are adding an extra layer of risk. The practice may bypass the essential diagnostic steps, leading to misdiagnosis, delaying the treatment required, or may lead to harmful interactions between the herbs and prescribed pharmaceutical medicines. The World Health Organisation acknowledges that while Ayurvedic medicine has a significant role, professional supervision, standardisation, and regulation are necessary for its safe and efficient application.

title: Fact Check: Can exercises correct the gap between the knees?
claim_text: Exercises can correct the gap between the knees. A specific routine involving a towel roll placed between the knees with pressure applied toward the front (10 repetitions, 2 sets, twice daily) and a straight leg stretch with toes pulled toward the body (10 seconds hold, 10 sets per leg) can reduce or eliminate the gap between the knees and relieve associated pain and difficulty walking.
quick_take: While exercise can help alleviate knee pain, it cannot fully correct skeletal misalignment. Knock Knees (genu valgum) is a structural condition that often requires medical intervention such as bracing, physical therapy, or in more severe cases, surgery.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Prasad Dakshinamoorthy, Robotic Arthroplasty and Arthroscopy, Consultant – Orthopaedics, SRM Global Hospitals, Chennai, stated: 'Exercises cannot correct a structural gap between the knees, commonly referred to as bow legs (genu varum) or knock knees (genu valgum), when it is caused by the underlying alignment of the bones. The distance between the knees or the ankles is primarily determined by the shape and alignment of the femur (thigh bone), tibia (shin bone), and the knee joint itself. Because this alignment is related to bone structure, exercise alone cannot change the position or shape of these bones. Many people believe that targeted workouts or stretching routines can bring the knees closer together or eliminate the gap. However, from an orthopedic perspective, exercises mainly help strengthen the surrounding muscles, such as the quadriceps, hamstrings, and hip muscles. While this can improve joint stability, posture, and overall knee function, it does not alter the skeletal alignment responsible for the gap. In children, mild bowing or knock knees may sometimes correct naturally as the bones grow and develop. However, in adolescents and adults, once the bones have matured, the alignment is generally permanent unless treated medically. In cases where the gap is severe and leads to pain, abnormal gait, or joint problems, doctors may consider orthopaedic interventions such as braces in growing children or corrective surgery in adults. It is also important to understand that not every gap between the knees is abnormal. In many individuals, a small degree of variation in leg alignment is completely normal and does not require treatment unless it causes symptoms or functional limitations. Therefore, while regular exercise is beneficial for maintaining muscle strength, mobility, and joint health, it cannot correct or eliminate a structural gap between the knees. Anyone concerned about leg alignment should consult an orthopedic specialist for proper evaluation and guidance rather than relying on exercise-based claims circulating online.' Dr. Prakash Ayyadurai, Consultant, Orthopedics, Arthroscopy & Sports Medicine, Rela Hospital, Chennai, further added: 'Strengthening exercises can help improve muscle strength, balance, joint stability, and overall knee function, which are important for maintaining healthy joints. However, these exercises do not change the shape or alignment of the bones, which primarily determines the gap between the knees. When the gap between the knees is due to the natural alignment of the leg bones, exercises alone are generally not able to correct it. The distance between the knees is largely influenced by the structure and positioning of the femur and tibia, and this underlying alignment cannot be altered through workouts. If the gap between the knees is noticeable, painful, or causes difficulty while walking, it is advisable to seek evaluation from an orthopedic specialist. Depending on the cause and severity, management may involve observation during growth in children, bracing in certain cases, or corrective surgery in adults when medically indicated.' The article further explains that genu valgum (knock knees) refers to abnormal alignment where knees angle inward, creating a space between the ankles when standing with knees together. This deformity typically occurs in childhood, beginning around age 2, and is most prominent between ages 3 to 4. It may occur naturally or due to factors such as genetics, injury, or conditions like rickets or arthritis. According to Vicky Duong et al. (PubMed: 37874571), first-line management for knee pain should focus on conservative approaches including structured exercise, patient education, and self-management strategies. According to Allyn M. Susko et al. (PMC5074793), exercise is an effective intervention for alleviating knee pain but not for correcting skeletal alignment. According to Madhish Patel et al. (NBK559244), treatment for knock knees typically includes observation for mild cases or children under 6 years with a tibiofemoral angle <15 degrees; more severe cases may require guided growth, osteotomies for adults, or medical management for metabolic disorders.

title: Fact Check: Can eye colour be changed through diet? - THIP Media
claim_text: In a Facebook video, the narrator states that eyes can change color if you detox the body from the heavy metals, toxins and diseases, consume a raw fruit diet or fast for a period of time or take specific herbs, such as contribo that detox the body and bring oxygen to your brain.
quick_take: A social media post claims that eye colour of a person can be changed after consuming a raw vegan diet or detox or a herb called contribo. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation:
How is the eye color determined? The color of eyes is determined by the combination of genetic factors inherited from their parents. Eye color is primarily influenced by the amount and distribution of a pigment called melanin in the iris. It is the colored part of the eye. Melanin comes in three forms: eumelanin, pheomelanin, and neuromelanin. The specific genes involved in eye color inheritance are complex and not fully understood. However, it is known that multiple genes play a role in determining eye color. Variations in the OCA2 gene, as well as other genes such as HERC2, can influence the amount and type of melanin in the iris, resulting in different eye colors. The inheritance of eye color follows a complex pattern. It is generally believed that brown eye color is dominant over blue or green eye color. However, the actual inheritance can be more intricate, as other genetic factors and interactions between genes can influence eye color inheritance. It is possible for parents with brown eyes to have a child with blue or green eyes if they carry certain genetic variations that affect eye color. It is important to note that eye color can also be influenced by other factors, such as lighting conditions, the scattering of light in the iris, diseases, medications and trauma.

Can eye color of a person change after consuming a raw vegan diet or detox or a herb called contribo? No. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that eye color can change after consuming a raw vegan diet, detox, or the herb contribo. Eye color is determined by the amount of melanin in the iris, and there is no known way to change the amount of melanin in the iris through diet or supplements. Even no evidence confirms that eyes predict disease. Even if some people claim that their eye color has changed after consuming a raw vegan diet or detox, it is impossible to know whether this is due to the diet or detox. It is possible that the eye color changed naturally over time, or that they suffer from a disease which might have led to the change. Also, while certain factors like lighting conditions or pupil dilation can create the illusion of temporary changes in eye color, these changes are not permanent and do not alter the underlying genetic makeup or pigmentation of the iris.

Can the eye color of a person change? Not exactly. In most cases, the eye color of a person remains stable throughout their lifetime. However, there are a few rare instances where eye color can change or appear to change. Here are some possible reasons for such changes: It is important to note that significant and spontaneous changes in eye color are relatively rare and should be evaluated by an eye care professional to rule out any underlying medical conditions or eye disorders.

title: Fact Check: Can eye exercises improve your vision? - THIP Media
claim_text: Eye exercises can improve vision and reverse the need for spectacles
quick_take: Several media articles and social media post recommends various eye exercises to improve vision. Many of these even claim to reverse the use of spectacles. We fact-checked the validity of such claims and found them to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: No. There is no scientific evidence regarding this. Most medical professionals maintain that eye exercises do not help in improving vision in any way. A detailed study done regarding this matter concludes, "There is no clear scientific evidence published in the mainstream literature supporting the use of eye exercises in the remainder of the areas reviewed, and their use therefore remains controversial." However, eye exercises done properly not harm either. They have their own set of benefits. Eye specialist Dr Pradeep Dahale, MS, DNB says, "Eye exercises can reduce strain on your eyes. They may help prevent certain eye conditions or contribute to your overall well-being. But there is no way eye exercises can improve vision." A small-scale research was done to study 'Effects of yogic eye exercises for myopia among students' done on notes, 48 individuals who performed eye yoga for 4 weeks "showed meagre improvement, but it was not statistically significant." Another study done on Chinese students shows that myopia may progress slowly due to eye exercises but there is no reversal of the eye power. The study notes, "The children with high-quality performance of the exercises had slightly less myopia progression." Dr Dahale explains, "Eyeglasses are given by Ophthalmologists or Optometrists to correct vision. These glasses are given to correct vision problems that occur due to anatomical variations of eyeball dimensions. Exercises, eye drops or diet supplements can't alter eye dimensions like axial length, Corneal Curvature, etc. So it is naive to believe that you will be able to correct your vision naturally and take your glasses off just by exercising."

title: Can eye floaters and cataracts be cured with Castor oil? - THIP
claim_text: They don't want you to know that you can heal your eyes with Castor Oil. All you need is a drop or two in each eye before bed • helps remove floaters • reduces redness/inflammation • clears cataracts. Make sure to buy it cold pressed, hexane free, and in glass
quick_take: A social media post claims that eye floaters and cataracts can be completely cured with Castor oil. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Eye floaters are small, dark shapes that float across your vision, looking like specks, dots, lines, or cobwebs. They are created when tiny clumps form in the clear, jelly-like substance (the vitreous humour) inside the eyeball and are usually harmless. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that castor oil can cure eye floaters. In fact, putting castor oil directly in the eye can cause various problems such as eye irritation, reduced tear quality, blurred vision and allergic reactions. It can also block lubricating glands in the eyelid, resulting in dry eyes. Dr. Aditya Sethi, Cataract, Refractive, Paediatric Ophthalmologist and Strabismus surgeon at Gurgaon states, 'While some anecdotal evidence suggests that people use castor oil to alleviate eye floaters, there is no robust scientific support for its efficacy. Eye floaters are often caused by age-related changes in the vitreous humor. Consultation with an ophthalmologist is crucial for a proper diagnosis and recommended treatments, which may not include castor oil.' For cataracts, castor oil is often promoted in alternative medicine as a potential remedy, but there is no scientific evidence to support that it can cure or reverse cataracts. Cataracts involve the clouding of the eye's natural lens and the primary treatment is surgical removal of the cloudy lens and its replacement with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL). Putting castor oil directly in the eye can be dangerous as it can cause irritation and damage the cornea. Because castor oil is not sterile, using it as eye drops will raise the risk of a dangerous eye infection. Dr. Sethi further states, 'Cataracts are primarily treated through surgical procedures to replace the clouded lens. Castor oil is not recognized as a cure for cataracts within mainstream ophthalmology. Relying on established medical interventions is essential for addressing cataract-related concerns, and seeking professional advice is paramount.' Various other remedies such as herbal drops are believed to cure cataracts, but this is also not possible.

Any single eye drop won't be a cure for all eye diseases. In cases of any permanent damage, it can't be reversed with the use of topical aids. title: Can facial skin be tightened with a hibiscus-based recipe?
claim_text: A hibiscus-based recipe (combination of hibiscus flowers, coconut oil, vitamin E, and aloe vera gel) tightens facial skin in just one week.
quick_take: According to a social media post, a hibiscus-based recipe works well for facial skin tightening. We analysed the assertion and found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Skin tightening is necessary to address laxity and signs of ageing, including wrinkles, fine lines, and sagging. While hibiscus is known as a natural Botox and is rich in antioxidants and might enhance skin elasticity by blocking the activity of the elastase enzyme, coconut oil has substantial anti-inflammatory and moisturising properties, vitamin E is a well-established antioxidant that lowers oxidative stress and neutralises free radicals, and aloe vera gel is a well-recognised ingredient that can help reduce oxidative damage, enhance hydration, and may exhibit collagen-stimulating effects. However, the scientific evidence backing their effectiveness as a skin-tightening intervention remains inconclusive. Dr. Gurman Singh Bhasin, Director & Chief Dermatologist, Skinclarity Clinic, Nagpur, reinforces this by stating that ageing, UV exposure, and lifestyle factors accelerate the breakdown of collagen and elastin, which is the main cause of skin laxity. Even though hibiscus extract has mild antioxidant and phytoestrogen-like properties, aloe vera and coconut oil help calm and hydrate the skin, and none of them have strong clinical evidence to reverse or significantly tighten loose skin. At most, they might enhance surface texture and moisture, which creates a transient plumping effect. True skin tightening necessitates the use of retinoids, peptides, energy-based devices (RF, HIFU, lasers), or procedural therapies that encourage collagen remodelling. Regarding the one-week claim: skin tightening is a progressive biological phenomenon that works by the stimulation of collagen and elastin - the skin's natural structural components. These elements take time to undergo remodelling and regeneration, so skin tightening cannot be achieved in just one week. Dr. Bhasin advises that no natural or topical remedy actually results in noticeable skin tightening in a single week. The biological process of collagen remodelling takes weeks to months. What can happen in a week is a temporary improvement in hydration, a mild reduction in puffiness, or a glow effect, but not actual tightening. Dermatologists treat skin laxity with topical retinoids, peptides, and antioxidants for mild tightening; fractional lasers, radiofrequency, high-intensity focused ultrasound, microneedling and PRP for collagen remodelling; thread lifts and dermal fillers for non-surgical interventions; and surgical face lifts for the most effective and durable procedure.

title: Fact Check: Can fasting cure cancer?
claim_text: A YouTube video has been circulating, claiming that fasting can cure cancer. The video suggests that by depriving the body of food, cancer cells starve and eventually die off, leading to a cure.
quick_take: A video on social media claims that fasting can cure cancer. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim and hence it's False.
doctor_explanation: Autophagy is a vital process where the body basically 'cleans house' by removing damaged cells and making space for new, healthy ones. This process is mainly associated with fasting, as it can be triggered when the body experiences a lack of nutrients. However, it is important to understand that while autophagy supports the body's natural balance, it is not a cure for cancer. Although this process helps maintain cellular health, it does not specifically target or eliminate cancer cells. Therefore, while autophagy offers significant health benefits, it should still not serve as a replacement for cancer treatment approaches. Fasting can provide certain health benefits when done correctly and under proper guidance. Studies suggest that fasting may enhance metabolic health, help in weight management, and reduce inflammation. However, these benefits are primarily for general health improvements and disease prevention, rather than curing serious conditions like cancer. Some social media influencers also promote smoothies and green juices to cure cancer. But cancer does not have a single remedy or cure, it is a complex disease that needs proper medical interventions. Fasting may offer some supportive benefits for cancer patients, but it is not a cure. Early research indicates that fasting might potentially enhance the effectiveness of treatments like chemotherapy by making cancer cells more susceptible. However, these findings are still in the early stages, and more research is needed to fully understand the impact. It is important to emphasise that fasting should never replace conventional cancer treatments. Dr Pooja Khullar, Radiation Oncologist, Dharamshila Narayana Super Specialty Hospital, New Delhi says: 'Fasting is sometimes seen as a potential way to support cancer treatment. But, it's crucial to understand that it is not a cure for cancer. Some studies are investigating whether fasting might make cancer cells more sensitive to treatments like chemotherapy. However, this research is still in its early stages. Cancer is a complex disease, and effective treatment usually requires a combination of proven therapies, including surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. For patients, it's essential to prioritise well-established medical treatments and to consult with their healthcare team before considering fasting or any other alternative approaches. The risks associated with fasting, especially for those undergoing cancer treatment, can include malnutrition and a weakened immune system, both of which could compromise overall health and recovery.' Dr Sarthak Moharir, Chief Radiation Oncologist, Apollo Hospitals, Bilaspur states: 'There is not enough evidence in medical literature to prove that fasting causes the body to eliminate diseased tissues or toxins. The removal of toxins is primarily the function of the kidneys and liver, not fasting or specific diets. Cancer patients, in particular, should avoid fasting, as it can lead to catastrophic consequences. Their bodies are already in a catabolic state, and fasting can result in muscle wasting, malnutrition, and effectively, starvation.' Fasting can have harmful effects, especially for individuals with chronic illnesses like cancer. Even though fasting might pose risks such as dehydration, nutrient deficiencies, and a weakened immune system for the general population, these dangers are even more pronounced for cancer patients. For those undergoing cancer treatment, fasting can lead to severe weight loss, malnutrition, and a reduced ability to handle treatments effectively. These adverse effects can easily outweigh any potential benefits, making fasting a particularly risky practice for cancer patients. The THIP Media Take states: The idea that fasting can cure cancer is not true as per available evidence. Fasting may provide certain health benefits and could potentially complement conventional cancer treatments. But, it is not a cure. Cancer patients should prioritise evidence-based treatments and consult with their healthcare providers before exploring any alternative therapies.

title: Fact Check: Can fasting cure diseases of all kinds?
claim_text: Fasting can cure diseases of all kinds. It is an effective method to enhance immunity, prevent diseases, and act as a universal treatment technique capable of addressing a wide range of health issues from common colds to chronic diseases.
quick_take: An Instagram video claims that fasting can cure diseases of all kinds. It suggests that fasting is a powerful treatment for any illness. We did the fact check and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: The fact check examines multiple aspects of the fasting claim. Regarding Ayurveda, ancient Indian medicine sees fasting as a helpful practice but not a universal remedy. Ayurvedic texts promote fasting to cleanse the body, improve digestion, and balance doshas (Vata, Pitta, Kapha). Fasting should be personalized to individual constitutions and integrated into a holistic health routine, not considered a standalone cure. For disease prevention, there is no scientific evidence that fasting can prevent dengue and malaria, which are caused by viruses and parasites transmitted by mosquitoes. Prevention requires mosquito control, insect repellents, mosquito nets, and eliminating breeding sites. Regarding immunity, intermittent fasting has been studied for potential benefits like reducing inflammation and enhancing autophagy, but there is no conclusive evidence it can cure diseases or provide universal protection. For chronic diseases, research indicates intermittent fasting can improve metabolic health by enhancing insulin sensitivity and helping with weight loss, especially for type 2 diabetes and obesity, but it is not a 'cure' and should be part of a comprehensive treatment plan with medical supervision. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at All India Institute of Ayurveda, explains that Ayurveda has a concept called Langhana which detoxifies the body, but it means keeping the body light by eating only as much as needed, not purely fasting. Langhana is a powerful treatment but does not completely fit the modern definition of fasting. Dr. Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, clarifies that while fasting and fasting-mimicking diets may offer some health benefits, they are not a cure-all for diseases. People should focus on balanced nutrition, regular exercise, and medical guidance. Fasting is not suitable for everyone, especially those with diabetes, eating disorders, or pregnancy, and requires medical advice. Regarding cancer, fasting shows promise in enhancing treatment effectiveness and reducing side effects by potentially weakening cancer cells while protecting normal cells, but these benefits are still being researched and fasting should not be relied upon as the sole treatment. Periodic fasting or fasting-mimicking diets show anticancer effects in mouse models by enhancing treatment effectiveness and triggering anticancer immunity, but as standalone therapies they may have little efficacy against established tumors. The benefits of intermittent fasting include promoting weight loss, reducing insulin resistance, decreasing markers of inflammation, and potentially enhancing brain health through increased BDNF production. However, much research relies on small or short-term animal studies, and more high-quality human studies are needed.

title: Fact Check: Can fasting on water for seven days prevent cancer? - THIP Media
claim_text: Fasting only on water for seven days once a year reduces the risk of cancer by 95%
quick_take: A video on social media shows an influencer claiming seven days of fasting reduces the risk of cancer by 95%. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False. The social media influencer misleadingly referred to a research by Dr Thomas Seyfried, which hypotheses ketogenic diet, a calorie-restricted diet when preceded by three to five days of fasting only on the water, can reduce cancer cell growth.
doctor_explanation: We searched online for Ben Azadi to find that he runs a website named ketokampacademy.com and promotes ketogenic diet and intermittent fasting. Also, he has published many reels on his Instagram account around these topics. However, this time it seems he has misinterpreted the research done by Dr Thomas Seyfried and published a misleading video. Azadi's LinkedIn page shows that he is a functional health practitioner certified by Functional Diagnostic Nutrition (FDN). We could not find any information about course accreditation on the website. In the USA, National Commission for Certifying Agencies (NCCA) accredits programs, including health coach certification. There is no mention of NCCA on the FDN website. Also, anyone can enroll on the self-paced courses offered after paying the fees, which again puts the credibility of certificants in question. It does not seem so. The claim is misleading and does not provide a complete picture of the research by Dr Thomas Seyfried. No evidence confirms fasting only on water for seven days once a year reduces the risk of cancer up to 95%. Even the research by Dr Thomas Seyfried, to whom the claimant referred to in the video, has not confirmed the same. We ran a keyword search and found an article published on The Paleo Diet website that discussed the research by Dr Seyfried. This article shows Dr Seyfried hypotheses ketogenic diet, a calorie-restricted diet when preceded by three to five days of fasting only on the water, can reduce cancer cell growth. The condition is that calories mostly made of fats and proteins should be 30 to 40 per cent of normal intake. We also found that in the article Dr Seyfried promoted such a diet because cancer cells cannot process ketones, but normal cells can process them to generate energy. So, in the presence of ketones and the absence of glucose and glutamine, cancer cells starve, which may shrink the tumour by burning fat instead of carbohydrates. We further researched on this conclusion and found a review published in 2014 that showed ketogenic diet might be a good adjuvant therapy to mitigate the damage to normal cells during radiation therapy and chemotherapy. This diet may also increase the efficiency of treatment with a lesser chance of an adverse event. However, the research on the impact of a ketogenic diet on cancer cells is nascent and not enough to establish any conclusion. Even this review recommends more research in preclinical and clinical settings.
