title: Fact Check: Can fasting prevent rabies after a dog bite?
claim_text: If you get a dog bite, you can avoid rabies infection by fasting for three days and eating only fruits and vegetables. According to this claim, there is no need to take the rabies vaccine, regardless of whether the dog has rabies or not.
quick_take: A social media post claims that fasting can prevent rabies after a dog bite, without a vaccine. We fact checked this and found it to be False.
doctor_explanation:
Rabies is a viral disease that targets the nervous system and can be fatal if not treated promptly. The virus generally transmits through the saliva of an infected animal, most commonly via a bite. There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that dietary changes, such as fasting or altering food intake, can prevent rabies infection following exposure. Given the seriousness of rabies, it is extremely important to address misconceptions about rabies. The only proven method to prevent rabies after potential exposure is to seek immediate medical attention and receive the rabies vaccine as soon as possible. Claims that avoiding food or consuming only fruits and vegetables after a dog bite can prevent rabies are inaccurate as per scientific evidence. Delaying medical treatment in favour of such practices can result in severe and life-threatening consequences.

Dr Anusha Dewan, Practising General Physician and Public Health Professional, Jeevan Anmol Hospital, New Delhi explains: "There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that fasting or consuming fruits and vegetables can prevent rabies. Rabies is a life-threatening disease. And, the only proven way to prevent it after exposure is by getting the rabies vaccine promptly."

Dr Manan Arora, BAMS, Specialised in Chronic Disorders & Mental Wellness, New Delhi states: "Ayurveda does promote the use of natural remedies and a balanced diet for general well-being. But, rabies is a severe viral disease that cannot be managed with dietary changes alone. Immediate medical treatment, including the rabies vaccine, is essential to prevent infection after a dog bite or any other animal's bite."

Dr Yash Choudhary, BAMS, Ayurvedic Consultant & Formulation Expert, New Delhi says: "Ayurveda emphasises the importance of diet and natural remedies for health, but rabies is a serious viral infection that cannot be prevented by fasting or consuming specific foods like fruits and vegetables. In Ayurvedic terms, this harmful entity, requires immediate medical intervention. Post-exposure vaccination is essential to prevent the infection and effectively combat this viral threat."

Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician, Navi Mumbai explains: "The rabies vaccine is essential following a dog bite because rabies is a deadly viral disease. The virus affects the nervous system. Once symptoms appear, it is almost always fatal." She further emphasises: "The rabies vaccine after a dog bite is a lifesaving measure. It is a sure-shot way to stop the virus before it can cause irreversible harm."

Rabies has an incubation period that can vary from days to months, during which the infected animal may not show symptoms. In some cases, a dog can be shedding the virus and still appear normal. If a person who has been exposed to rabies does not receive the vaccine, the virus can spread to the central nervous system. This can eventually lead to the onset of rabies symptoms including fever, headache, muscle weakness, and confusion, which progress to more severe symptoms such as paralysis, coma, and eventually death. title: Fact Check: Can fatty liver and liver fibrosis be cured by tamarind and plum drink? - THIP Media
claim_text: You can cure fatty liver and liver fibrosis by consuming a drink made with tamarind and plum
quick_take: A Facebook post claims that you can cure fatty liver and liver fibrosis by consuming a drink made with tamarind and plum. We fact-checked and found that the claim was False.
doctor_explanation: Fatty liver is a condition in which there is a buildup of fat in the liver. It is of two types, namely, NAFLD (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease) and Alcoholic fatty liver disease. NAFLD is the build-up of extra fat in the liver cell that is not caused by alcohol. Until now, there is no treatment available to cure NAFLD; the only treatment modalities to reverse the fat buildups are diet and lifestyle changes. According to the American Liver Foundation, if more than 5-10% of the liver's weight is fat, it is called fatty liver (steatosis). The more severe form of NAFLD is called Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH). NASH causes the liver to swell and become damaged. Until now, no drugs have been approved specifically to treat NAFLD. When living with NAFLD, lifestyle changes can control or reverse the fat buildup in the liver. A patient with NAFLD should lose weight, lower their cholesterol and triglycerides, control their diabetes, avoid alcohol, etc. Liver fibrosis is the excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins including collagen. It occurs in most types of chronic liver diseases. It causes a buildup of scar tissue in the liver, which causes improper functioning of the liver. There is no standard treatment modality for liver fibrosis. It is usually treated by clearing infections, making lifestyle changes and anti-inflammatory medications. There are multiple benefits of tamarind and plum documented for liver care. However, none of them has proven to cure fatty liver or fibrosis. A 2014 study done by a group of researchers shows that tamarind may have some positive effects on Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD). The study was done on rats. While the study was good to provide insights into the clinical therapeutic potential of tamarind, researchers noted that further studies are required on the same. Similarly, in another research a diet of prunes (plum), dried grapes, carrots, cape gooseberry, pomegranate peel, chicory, sumac, sweet corn, germinated soybeans and vitamins B12, C and D showed to be beneficial for fatty liver. But, once again, it was rat-based study and can hardly be called conclusive evidence in favour of plum alone. Dr. Kashyap Dakshini, General Physician in Mumbai, clarifies: 'Liver fibrosis is scarring of the liver tissue. It may be due to an infection or due to inflammation of the liver, NAFLD or alcoholic liver disease. There are various forms of management, essentially treating the cause. There is no known evidence or study proving the effectiveness of tamarind and plum drink's effectiveness in treating Liver Fibrosis. Also, Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a condition in which excess fat builds up in your liver, which is not caused by heavy alcohol use. The incidence of NAFLD is growing in our country because of a more sedentary lifestyle and food habits. Complications of NAFLD include Cirrhosis of the Liver and Liver Cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and dyslipidemia (abnormality in cholesterol levels). There is no cure for NAFLD; however, lifestyle and dietary changes, exercise, weight loss, and reducing carbohydrate intake help control it. There is no known evidence or study proving the effectiveness of tamarind and plum drink in the treatment of NAFLD.' Clinical Nutritionist Nidhi Sarin further elaborates: 'There is no evidence that plum and tamarind can cure liver fibrosis. But they help detox the liver. However, along with that, one has to live a healthy lifestyle and maintain the right body weight with the right exercise. Also, NAFLD can be cured if patients take the proper guidance from doctors and dieticians for lifestyle changes which include 10 per cent of their body weight, the right diet and exercise. Tamarind and plum are very beneficial for the liver as they flush the toxins. But, consuming only these two can't cure the disease.' Like tamarind and plum, spinach, beans, soy, garlic and even coffee have shown to have beneficial effects on multiple liver conditions. However, multiple experts have confirmed that a single ingredient diet cannot cure any liver disease. A good diet combined with medicines wherever required along with changes in lifestyle (daily exercises to reduce weight, leaving alcohol consumption etc) is the best way to treat liver problems like NAFLD and Fibrosis.

title: Can fatty liver be cured by tamarind and plum drink? - THIP Media

quick_take: A Facebook post claims that a drink made from tamarind and plum can cure fatty liver and liver fibrosis. However, our fact-checking revealed that this claim isfalse.
doctor_explanation:
So far, there are no approved medications specifically for treating non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). If someone has NAFLD but no other underlying health issues, they usually don't need any special medical treatment. Instead, making key lifestyle changes can help manage or even reverse the fat accumulation in the liver. This includes losing weight, reducing cholesterol and triglyceride levels, managing blood sugar if diabetic, and completely avoiding alcohol.

While tamarind and plums are known to offer several benefits for liver health, there's no solid evidence that either can cure fatty liver disease. A 2014 study involving rats suggested that tamarind might have a positive impact on Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD). Although the findings hinted at tamarind's potential in liver therapy, the researchers clearly stated that more research is needed—especially in humans—to confirm these effects. Similarly, another study showed that a diet including prunes (plums), dried grapes, carrots, cape gooseberry, pomegranate peel, chicory, sumac, sweet corn, germinated soybeans, and vitamins B12, C, and D helped improve fatty liver in rats. However, this was also an animal study. So, while the results are interesting, we can't draw firm conclusions about plums alone based on this evidence.

Dr Kashyap Dakshini, a general physician based in Mumbai, explains that non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) occurs when too much fat builds up in the liver. The number of cases is rising in India, largely due to increasingly sedentary lifestyles and poor eating habits. If left unmanaged, NAFLD can lead to serious complications like liver cirrhosis, liver cancer, heart disease, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and abnormal cholesterol levels (dyslipidaemia). While there's currently no cure for NAFLD, it can be managed through lifestyle changes such as regular exercise, weight loss, a healthy diet, and cutting down on carbohydrate intake. Dr Dakshini confirms that there is no scientific proof or reliable study supporting the use of tamarind and plum drinks as a treatment for NAFLD.

Diet plays a significant role in managing and reducing fatty liver. While quick improvements are possible, they depend on individual factors such as weight, metabolism, and overall health. A diet based on whole, unprocessed foods can support weight loss and improve insulin sensitivity, both of which are key to reducing liver fat. For some individuals, a noticeable decrease in liver fat may occur relatively quickly when following a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, lean proteins, and healthy fats. However, long-term commitment to dietary changes and regular physical activity is usually required for sustained improvement.

Dr Sharad Malhotra, Head of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Therapeutic Endoscopy at Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, explained that fatty liver often develops gradually and without early symptoms, but can lead to serious liver damage over time. There is no instant cure or miracle treatment—especially not one that works in just two weeks. The most effective approach involves sustained lifestyle changes, including a balanced diet, reduced intake of sugar and alcohol, regular physical activity, and gradual weight loss. Even losing 5% to 10% of body weight can significantly improve liver function. Dr Malhotra emphasized the importance of regular check-ups, recommending an annual abdominal ultrasound and liver function tests for early detection. In some cases, advanced diagnostics like a Fibroscan or liver biopsy may be necessary. He advised managing blood sugar and cholesterol levels, and warned against using unverified herbal remedies or unnecessary medications.

Clinical Nutritionist Nidhi Sarin clarifies that there is no scientific proof that plum and tamarind can cure fatty liver. She emphasizes the importance of a healthy lifestyle, including maintaining an appropriate body weight through proper diet and exercise. While tamarind and plum offer health benefits, relying solely on them is not effective for treating the condition. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) can be managed successfully with professional guidance from doctors and dietitians, which typically involves losing around 10% of body weight along with adopting the right dietary and exercise habits.

Maintaining a healthy liver requires time, consistency, and informed choices—not quick fixes.

title: Can fennel, carom and cumin tea dissolve kidney stones in 8 days?
claim_text: Kidney stones can be removed in just 8 days using a home remedy of boiling one spoon each of Saunf (fennel), Ajwain (carom seeds), and Jeera (cumin) in a cup of water for 5–10 minutes, straining and taking on an empty stomach every morning, with a 100% guarantee of success.
quick_take: A social media post claims that fennel, carom and cumin tea can dissolve kidney stones in 8 days only. We fact checked this claim and termed it as false.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific proof that this mixture can dissolve kidney stones. Fennel (saunf), carom seeds (ajwain), and cumin (jeera) are often used in home remedies for digestion or bloating. Some also believe they may support urine flow. But no strong medical evidence shows that this mix can break down kidney stones. A 2023 animal study found that fennel seeds and their sprouts helped protect rat kidneys from chemical damage. The sprouted seeds had stronger antioxidant effects and improved kidney function. However, these were high doses tested in rats, not humans, and not directly for kidney stones. Furthermore, a 2024 lab study on cumin showed that its extract may help slow the growth of calcium oxalate crystals (the most common type of kidney stones). It also showed some kidney-protective effects in test tubes. But again, this was not tested in humans or as a stone treatment. Ajwain, though used in traditional medicine, did not show strong results for kidney stone treatment in a 2014 study. This mix may support general health, but there is no medical proof that it can dissolve kidney stones. Similarly, there are other home remedies that make even more exaggerated claims, such as lemon, holy basil, and coconut water curing kidney stones in a day. But this is false. How quickly a kidney stone passes depends on its size and where it is in the urinary tract. Very small stones (less than 5 mm) may pass naturally over days or even weeks. But larger stones often need medical help. There is no evidence that this drink speeds up the process. Expecting it to work in exactly 8 days is not realistic. There is no such thing as a 100% guaranteed cure or treatment for kidney stones, especially not from a home remedy. Every case is different, and even clinically proven medical treatments can't promise exact results. Claiming that this drink works for everyone in just 8 days is not only inaccurate, it's also misleading. 'Home remedies like fennel, carom, and cumin may help improve digestion or urine flow to some extent. But there's no strong evidence that they can treat or dissolve kidney stones. People should avoid using these remedies as a substitute for proper medical care,' he said. He explained that kidney stones are common in tropical countries due to dehydration and said that no home remedy can prevent or cure all cases. 'Reducing risk involves staying well hydrated, limiting salt, maintaining a healthy weight, eating calcium-rich foods, and avoiding high-oxalate foods. For uric acid stones, cutting down on red meat, sugar, refined carbs, alcohol, and smoking may help manage the risk,' he added.

title: Fact Check: Can fennel seeds, rock candy and coriander seeds dissolve kidney stones?
claim_text: An Instagram post by user dryusuf_malik claims that a mixture of 50 grams each of fennel seeds (saunf), rock candy (mishri), and coriander seeds (dhania), ground into powder and taken with a glass of water before bedtime for 10-12 days, can dissolve and help pass kidney stones measuring between 4 to 6 mm.
quick_take: While fennel seeds and coriander seeds have shown some nephroprotective and diuretic effects in animal studies, no scientific evidence or medical consensus supports the claim that these ingredients can effectively dissolve kidney stones in humans. Moreover, rock candy's high sugar content has been associated with an increased risk of kidney stones.
doctor_explanation:
According to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), kidney stones are solid, pebble-like materials that can form in one or both kidneys when high levels of certain minerals are present in urine. Symptoms include sharp pain in the back, side, lower abdomen, groin, or hematuria (blood in urine). Small stones can pass through the urinary tract without symptoms.

Fennel seeds (saunf) have pharmacological effects including anti-allergic, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antibacterial, anti-cancer, anti-stress, and cytotoxicity activity. Coriander seeds (dhaniya) provide protective effects against neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, and metabolic syndrome, with antioxidant, neuroprotective, anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, analgesic, hypoglycemic, hypotensive, antimicrobial, and anti-inflammatory properties. Rock candy (mishri) is a simple carbohydrate consisting mainly of sucrose — it provides quick energy but lacks essential nutrients.

A study by Hassan Barakat et al., published in the Journal Antioxidants, found that fennel seed sprout extracts can potentially restore oxidative stability and improve kidney function, suggesting nephroprotective properties that could help prevent diseases related to oxidative stress. Another article in the Avicenna Journal of Phytomedicine by Sadrefozalayi et al. reported that aqueous fennel seed extract had a beneficial effect on renal function in rats with PCOS.

Coriander has shown diuretic effects in animal studies. A comparative study in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology found that coriander seed extract increased diuresis, excretion of electrolytes (sodium, potassium, and chloride), and glomerular filtration rate in a dose-dependent manner in anesthetized Wistar rats. However, no human evidence supports these diuretic effects.

Conversely, a study by Yin et al. published in Frontiers in Nutrition found a significant association between higher energy intake from added sugars and an increased prevalence of kidney stones. Researchers analyzed data from 28,303 adults (2007–2018, NHANES), finding cross-sectional evidence linking greater added sugar consumption with increased kidney stone risk.

Dr Vivek K Koushik, Consultant Nephrologist, Prashanth Hospitals Kolathur, Chennai, stated: 'While it is difficult to isolate every active compound in a spice/food product, both fennel and coriander appear to act as a diuretic (substance which increases urine output) in animal studies which can reduce stone formation. However, no major randomised trials are available in humans to suggest that they prevent stone formation. Also, evidence suggests that consumption of added sugars like rock candy may increase the likelihood of stone formation in humans.'

Dr Naveen M N, Consultant Urologist and Renal Transplant Surgeon at Gleneagles BGS Hospital, Kengeri, Bengaluru, explained kidney stone management: Medical treatment includes dietary management, disease-specific therapies, and medical expulsion therapy (MET). Increasing urine volume to at least 2 L/day can reduce stone recurrence by 40–50%. Oxalate-rich foods (cucumber, green peppers, beetroot, spinach, soya bean, chocolate, rhubarb, popcorn, sweet potato) should be avoided. Fresh tomato juice has the highest citrate and low oxalate content. Reduction of animal protein intake is suggested for calcium oxalate and uric acid stone formers. Approximately 90% of stones <5 mm and 15% of stones between 5–8 mm pass spontaneously within 4 weeks, while 95% of stones >8 mm require urological intervention.

For surgical management: Simple renal calculi (stone burden <2 cm with normal anatomy) — 80–85% treated successfully with shock wave lithotripsy. Complex renal calculi (>2 cm, staghorn calculi, abnormal anatomy, stones resistant to fragmentation) — percutaneous nephrolithotomy is the treatment of choice. Flexible ureteroscopy is used for proximal ureteral stones. Spontaneous passage of ureteral calculi <5 mm usually occurs within four weeks of symptom onset.

title: Fact Check: Can fenugreek-based oil truly enhance hair growth?
claim_text: According to an Instagram post, fenugreek-based oil is very effective for hair growth. The post with the caption 'करोड़ों लोग आज भी तेल का गलत इस्तेमाल कर रहे हैं' further underlines that the reduced residue of fenugreek seeds, rice, and cloves may not only prevent hair fall but also accelerate hair growth such that one may need a haircut every week.
quick_take: An Instagram post suggests that fenugreek-based oil is a surefire way to strengthen hair. We fact-checked the claim and discovered that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Hair growth is a dynamic biological phenomenon. The process reflects both aesthetic appeal and an underlying health condition. Scalp hair grows in cycles. Healthy hair growth is primarily influenced by a well-nourished diet, stable hormones, and psychological well-being. Any disruption in this cycle might lead to hair thinning or loss. Several variables affect this process. Systemic ones include nutrition, thyroid function, androgen levels, as well as iron and vitamin D status. Environmental stresses, oxidative damage, and specific medications could also interfere with the hair growth cycle.

Herbal formulations have traditionally been used to encourage hair growth. One such combination, prepared with fenugreek seeds, rice, and cloves, has been advocated. Fenugreek seeds have been suggested to help strengthen hair and prevent hair loss. This could be due to their high bioactive profile, good protein content, and elevated concentration of nicotinic acid. Furthermore, their emollient characteristics may promote scalp health. Rice-based preparations are becoming increasingly popular because of their significant levels of amino acids, antioxidants, and minerals. Clove contains eugenol, which possesses antimicrobial effects and can enhance blood circulation to the scalp.

Even while all three ingredients, fenugreek seeds, rice, and cloves, have distinct characteristics that may benefit scalp health, their combined efficiency in promoting hair growth is dubious. Furthermore, the evidence supporting natural formulations for hair growth remains anecdotal.

Dr. Rashi Soni, Dermatologist and Co-Founder of Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, confirms that hair growth is a gradual process. Hair usually grows around half an inch per month. It is absurd to expect a handmade preparation to speed up the process significantly. There is inadequate evidence to back up the dramatic effect of a fenugreek-based recipe. Thus, the assertion is definitely exaggerated.

Employing unregulated home remedies for hair growth can be risky. While anecdotal reports and user testimonials may suggest benefits, they frequently lack scientific validation. Many untrustworthy internet preparations or items might differ dramatically because they may contain hazardous substances or unknown allergens. Most importantly, untested therapies may delay the required evaluation and management of the underlying medical issue causing hair loss. Conditions such as androgenetic alopecia, thyroid-related disorders, and nutritional deficiencies necessitate evidence-based treatment.

Dr Sachin Gupta (MBBS and MD in Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi), who currently works at Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, suggests that hair growth is controlled by a variety of factors, including heredity, hormones, dietary intake, and overall health. Dr. Gupta firmly advises against unverified remedies, emphasising that there is no quick-fix option for accelerating hair growth. He recommends eating nutritiously and proper hair care procedures for optimal hair health, as well as seeking professional guidance for any underlying medical conditions.

Medical experts approach hair growth through a comprehensive, structured framework: Accurate Diagnosis (analysing patient's history, clinical examination, diagnostic procedures such as scalp biopsies or blood work), Therapeutic Interventions (topical minoxidil, oral finasteride, low-level laser therapy, platelet-rich plasma injections, hair transplantation), and Routine Monitoring (follow-up appointments to determine efficacy).

title: Fact Check: Can Fenugreek cure diabetes?
claim_text: Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is an ancient herb widely used in culinary and medicinal practices for 3000 years and is a cure for modern diabetes. The post suggests soaking 1/4 teaspoon of fenugreek seeds and half an inch of Ceylon cinnamon stick in water overnight and drinking the mixture on an empty stomach every morning for three months alongside a balanced, low-GI diet to cure diabetes.
verdict_original: This claim is FALSE. Fenugreek cannot cure diabetes.
quick_take: While fenugreek has been shown to improve glycemic control and lipid profile, contributing to better overall health, no scientific evidence or medical consensus supports the claim that fenugreek can cure diabetes.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Srinath Aswathiah, Consultant Diabetologist & Endocrinologist at Gleneagles BGS Hospital Kengeri, Bengaluru, explained: 'Diabetes is a chronic condition that arises due to issues with insulin production or utilization. The causes differ depending on the type of diabetes. Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disorder where the immune system mistakenly attacks insulin-producing cells in the pancreas, resulting in little or no insulin production. Type 2 diabetes, the more common form, typically occurs due to a combination of genetic predisposition and lifestyle factors such as poor diet, lack of physical activity, and obesity. A key factor in type 2 diabetes is insulin resistance, where the body's cells do not respond effectively to insulin. In addition to these, there are other significant forms of diabetes. MODY (maturity-onset diabetes of the young) is a rare type with a strong genetic component, often running in families. It typically affects lean, young male individuals and responds well to oral medications. LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults), sometimes referred to as Type 1.5 diabetes, shares characteristics of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes but presents differently, requiring its own unique management and treatment approach. Another important form is gestational diabetes, which occurs during pregnancy and usually resolves after childbirth. However, it does increase the risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life. All types of diabetes require careful management to prevent complications and maintain overall health.'

Dr Aswathiah further stated: 'Fenugreek, indeed, has a long history of medicinal use dating back over 3000 years. Historically, it has been utilized in various cultures to manage a range of health issues, including diabetes. Modern research supports its traditional use, showing that fenugreek can positively affect blood glucose levels. Studies indicate that fenugreek seeds can lower fasting blood glucose and HbA1c levels, and improve insulin sensitivity. While it is not a cure for diabetes, fenugreek can be an effective adjunct to conventional treatments, helping manage the condition more effectively. It is essential to use it as part of a comprehensive diabetes management plan, including diet and medication as prescribed by healthcare professionals.'

Ms Karthigaiselvi, Chief Dietitian at Gleneagles BGS Hospital, Kengeri, Bangalore, said: 'There's no cure for diabetes and no way to completely get rid of it. However, diabetes can be reversed in most people. Reversing diabetes means carefully managing blood sugars to a point where medications are no longer necessary, and staying at that manageable point through a healthy routine of diet and exercise. Healthy habits move the slider toward a more manageable state; they cannot switch the diabetes 'off.' Furthermore, the slider can move back toward diabetes if someone fails to maintain healthy habits. Managing diabetes involves stabilizing blood sugar levels through lifestyle modifications and medications. There are also innovative minimally invasive procedures like bariatric surgery can help improve your diabetes management without the need for medication. People with severe obesity have a greater risk than obese people with lower BMIs. Weight around your middle can be a particular problem. Fat can build up around your organs, affecting the function of organs like the liver and pancreas and increasing your risk of developing diabetes. Careful glucose monitoring is a vital part of controlling your diabetes.'

Ms Karthigaiselvi also commented: 'Traditional plant medicines are used throughout the world as alternative therapies to control diabetes. Although numerous herbs are reported to possess some degree of anti-diabetic activity, a significant amount of research, as well as traditional usage suggest that Fenugreek may be among the best in terms of efficacy and safety. Fenugreek seeds (trigonella foenum graecum) are high insoluble fiber which helps lower blood glucose by slowing down digestion and absorption of carbohydrates. It is effective in treating people with diabetes. It can improve most metabolic symptoms associated type 1 and type 2 diabetes by lowering blood glucose levels and improving glucose tolerance. title: Fact Check: Can fenugreek (methi) powder concoction transform skin?
claim_text: Take 2 tbsp of fenugreek powder and add 1 tbsp of curd and mix it well and apply it for 15 minutes and then wash it off. This mask is very helpful in reducing dark spots and blemishes. Use this mask twice a week for skin whitening.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a mixture of fenugreek powder and curd can reduce dark spots and blemishes. Additionally, it claims that using this mask twice a week will tighten the skin. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Dark spots and hyperpigmentation are caused by an overproduction of melanin, the pigment that gives color to our skin, hair, and eyes. Melanin is produced by specialized cells called melanocytes. When these cells become overactive or are stimulated by various factors, they produce more melanin, leading to the appearance of dark spots and patches on the skin. There is no credible scientific evidence to prove that the concoction of fenugreek powder and curd can reduce spots and tighten skin. Fenugreek (methi) and yogurt (curd) are often used in traditional skincare remedies due to their potential benefits for the skin. However, it's important to note that individual responses to such mixtures can vary, and results may not be universal. While these ingredients may offer some benefits, there's limited scientific evidence specifically supporting their ability to reduce spots or tighten the skin. Even though few research papers suggest an anti-aging and anti-collagenase property of fenugreek, skin tightening is a complex process that involves the production of collagen and elastin. It often requires medical or cosmetic procedures, such as laser treatments, radiofrequency therapy, or surgical interventions. Additionally, skin conditions can be influenced by various factors, and what works for one person may not work the same way for another. Dr. Sandeep Arora, MBBS, MD, an experienced dermatologist elaborates on this by stating 'Fenugreek extract has been demonstrated to possess antioxidant, antiradical, anti-inflammatory and collagenase activities in several studies. This collagenase activity is what explains its skin-tightening effects. Unfortunately, the home concentrations of fenugreek may not penetrate across the skin surface to depths where they can cause effective skin tightening in the long term. Curd contains lactic acid which helps lighten the skin. In the long term it may to an extent even out tone, but it cannot eliminate dark spots altogether. The problem with trying too hard with excessive home remedies is the possibility of reactions; in this case, it can then lead to the darkening of the skin.' Remember, home remedies aren't always fruitful in curing all skin problems. One must always consult a dermatologist or skincare professional before trying home remedies, especially if you have specific skin concerns or conditions. They can provide personalized advice based on your skin type and any existing skin issues you may have. Additionally, for issues like skin whitening, it's important to approach it with caution, as promoting natural skin health and radiance is different from attempting to alter one's natural skin tone. Dr Sachin Gupta MBBS, MD (Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi), working with Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, summarizes this and states, 'Natural ingredients are not always synonymous with safety or efficacy in dermatology, and what might seem harmless can actually be risky. Consulting a dermatologist is the safest and most effective approach for anyone experiencing skin issues. Dermatologists offer personalized treatments based on scientific research, clinical expertise, and an understanding of individual skin physiology. This approach ensures that treatments are not only effective but also tailored to your unique skin needs. Remember, your skin's health should always be entrusted to evidence-based medical practices, not kitchen ingredients. What works in the kitchen doesn't always work on your skin.' For preventing hyperpigmentation and dark spots, recommendations include using broad-spectrum sunscreen daily, avoiding prolonged sun exposure, and protecting the skin with appropriate clothing and hats. For existing dark spots, treatments may include topical creams containing ingredients like hydroquinone, retinoids, vitamin C, or alpha hydroxy acids, chemical peels, laser therapies, or microdermabrasion.

title: Fact Check: Can fenugreek seeds accelerate weight loss?
claim_text: An infographic circulating on Pinterest claims that fenugreek seeds offer many benefits including clear skin, better sleep, improved digestion, weight loss, relief from menstrual cramps, treating constipation, and preventing hair fall. The infographic portrays fenugreek as a miracle cure for various health and beauty issues.
quick_take: A social media post claims that fenugreek seeds can accelerate weight loss along with several other benefits. Our fact check says this claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
**Weight Loss Claim:** While fenugreek leaves and seeds may offer some benefits for weight loss, they are not the miracle solution claimed. The high fibre content in fenugreek can help increase feelings of fullness, which may lead to a reduction in calorie consumption. A 2015 study suggested that fenugreek, along with fennel tea, might suppress appetite in overweight women, but the study involved only nine participants—too small to draw reliable conclusions. Additionally, there is no strong evidence that fenugreek causes significant weight loss. Weight loss is a complex process that requires more than adding one food to your diet. A balanced diet, daily exercise, and a healthy lifestyle are essential.

**Expert Quote - Shruti K Bhardwaj (Chief Clinical Nutritionist, Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad):** "Fenugreek seeds are a promising natural ingredient with potential benefits for weight loss. Some studies suggest they may help control appetite and reduce calorie intake. However, we still need more research to confirm this. Remember, a healthy diet, regular exercise, and a balanced lifestyle are essential for sustainable weight loss. Consult a healthcare professional for personalised advice."

**Skin Claim:** Fenugreek seeds contain vitamin C, which is important for skin health. But while vitamin C can help maintain healthy skin, there is no substantial evidence to support the idea that fenugreek can specifically clear up acne or give you glowing skin. Clear skin requires a combination of healthy eating, proper skincare, and good hygiene—not just relying on fenugreek.

**Sleep Claim:** Fenugreek contains compounds like flavonoids and some people use fenugreek water for its potential to ease discomfort from indigestion. This may indirectly improve sleep. However, there are no studies linking fenugreek directly to better sleep. Herbal remedies like chamomile are much more effective for promoting restful sleep.

**Digestion Claim:** Fenugreek is rich in soluble fibre, which can help with digestion and relieve constipation by adding bulk to stools. Some animal studies show that fenugreek may have positive effects on gut health, but it's not a miracle cure for all digestive issues. A varied diet, plenty of water, and exercise are essential for good digestion.

**Menstrual Cramps Claim:** Fenugreek has traditionally been used to relieve menstrual cramps, possibly due to its anti-inflammatory properties. However, there is very limited evidence to prove it works, and its safety isn't well studied. While it might provide some relief, more research is needed to confirm its effectiveness compared to other remedies.

**Constipation Claim:** The high fibre content of fenugreek can help manage constipation by promoting regular bowel movements. However, it's important to drink plenty of water when using fenugreek to avoid bloating or discomfort. Like with any remedy, moderation is key.

**Safety Information:** Fenugreek is safe when used in small amounts, like in cooking. Large amounts can cause nausea, diarrhoea, low blood sugar, and rare liver problems. It is not safe for children or pregnant women and may cause allergies.

**Hair Fall Claim:** Fenugreek seeds contain protein and niacin (vitamin B3), which are beneficial for hair health, but there is no solid scientific evidence to confirm that they can stop hair fall or promote significant hair growth. Some believe that sprouted fenugreek seeds can promote hair regrowth, but this claim also lacks strong scientific backing. While the anti-inflammatory properties of fenugreek might help improve scalp health, tackling hair loss requires a holistic approach, which includes a nutritional diet for hair and proper hair care.

**Expert Quote - Dr Sachin Gupta (Dermatologist, Amrita Hospital, Faridabad):** "While fenugreek is commonly used in traditional hair care routines, its impact on promoting hair growth and strengthening hair is not strongly supported by scientific evidence. It might provide some scalp and hair nourishment, but it's unlikely to deliver significant results on its own. To maintain healthy hair, focusing on overall nutrition, stress management, and choosing the right hair care products is essential."

**THIP Media Take:** Fenugreek seeds are a nutritious food that can offer some health benefits, such as improving digestion and alleviating constipation. However, claims that fenugreek seeds can help in weight loss, offer clear skin, or prevent hair loss are mostly exaggerated and hence we term this as mostly false.

doctor_explanation: Dr. Shireen Furtado (MBBS, MD, FRGUHS), Senior Consultant (Medical & Cosmetic Dermatology) at Aster CMI Hospital, Bangalore, explained that dietary choices can influence skin clarity, though results vary by person. Foods rich in antioxidants like berries and leafy greens help fight inflammation, supporting overall skin health. Omega-3 fatty acids from fish or flaxseed may reduce inflammation-related skin issues, promoting a clearer complexion. Fenugreek contains various nutrients and is used to make skin clean and moisturized, but while it is often included in traditional wellness practices, it is not a proven solution for brightening or clearing skin. Dr. Ruby Sachdev, Consultant Aesthetic Physician, Gleneagles Hospital Bengaluru, stated that fenugreek seeds are known for their beneficial properties and can contribute to a clearer complexion, but should not be considered a miracle solution for skin issues. She recommends fenugreek seeds for their anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, which may help soothe irritated skin and promote a more even skin tone over time. Fenugreek contains compounds like flavonoids, saponins, and alkaloids, which can help reduce skin redness, treat acne, and improve overall skin health. Its ability to balance oil production and its rich content of vitamins and minerals, such as vitamin C, also support healthier skin. Studies have noted that fenugreek seeds possess high nutritious value rich in fibre, phospholipids, glycolipids, oleic acid, linolenic acid, vitamins A, B1, B2, and C, nicotinic acid, and niacin, which are good for health. Studies have mentioned the role of fenugreek seed in combination with other ingredients may show benefits towards retaining skin moisture and making skin smooth, supple, and soft, but there is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that supports the claim that fenugreek seed alone can make skin clear. Waqas et al., a formulation containing fenugreek seed extract and paraffin oil was applied to participants; the findings indicated that this formulation effectively reduced skin melanin content and increased skin moisture levels without causing any irritation, but this study also does not mention that fenugreek seed on its own has any positive impact on the skin. However, the study did not establish any standalone role of fenugreek in achieving clear skin. All these studies have noted the effects of fenugreek seed on skin clarity; however, fenugreek seed alone cannot be considered a proven solution for all skin clarity issues, and there is no medical consensus within the medical community supporting it as a recommended solution for improving skin clarity.

title: Can fermented millet cure liver and kidney problems? - THIP Media
claim_text: Fermented millets – A Rambaad Ilaaj for, Liver & Kidney Health
quick_take: A social media post claims that fermented millet can cure liver or kidney diseases. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Absolutely not. Fermented millet is not a cure for liver or kidney conditions. While it may be a part of a healthy diet, there's no medical evidence to support the idea that it can heal or reverse damage in the liver or kidneys. To be clear, the liver and kidneys are vital organs with complex functions. When they are affected by conditions like hepatitis, fatty liver disease, or chronic kidney disease, treatment requires proper medical care, often involving medications, dietary changes, and sometimes dialysis or surgery. There is no "magic food" that can fix such conditions. Fermented millet, like other fermented foods, may help in digestion and support gut health due to the presence of good bacteria (probiotics). But it's far from curing diseases. Serious health problems need medical attention, not folk remedies without scientific backing. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says "Food can support organ function, but it can't undo disease. It worries me when people believe that just eating something like fermented millet will heal organs. That's not how it works." Fermentation adds nutritional value, not medicinal powers. Fermentation can boost some nutritional aspects of food. For millet, it might reduce anti-nutrients like phytic acid, making minerals such as iron and calcium more absorbable. It can also make the food easier to digest and introduce some beneficial microbes. However, fermentation doesn't turn millet into a miracle cure. It's similar to how fermenting cabbage into sauerkraut doesn't make it a treatment for diabetes or cancer. Nutritional benefits are not the same as therapeutic effects. Saying otherwise spreads false hope and distracts people from proper treatment. Dr Sharad Malhotra, Head of Gastroenterology at Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, says "Fermented millet, rich in antioxidants, fiber, and probiotics, may contribute to general health by reducing inflammation and supporting gut microbiota, which could indirectly benefit liver and kidney function. However, current scientific research does not provide conclusive evidence that fermented millet can directly prevent or treat liver or kidney diseases. Conditions like hepatitis, cirrhosis, or chronic kidney disease require targeted medical interventions, and relying solely on fermented millet is not advisable." It might support general health, but it's not prevention on its own. Eating millet, especially when included in a balanced diet, can be good for your health. It's high in fibre, magnesium, and B vitamins. These nutrients can contribute to better metabolic health, including controlling blood sugar and reducing cholesterol, both important for long-term organ function. But preventing liver or kidney disease takes more than just one food. It's about overall lifestyle, maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding excessive alcohol, managing blood pressure and blood sugar, and staying hydrated. Millet can play a small role in that bigger picture, but it's not a shield against disease. Harita Adhvaryu, Senior Clinical Dietitian at Ezcure Diabetes Care in Ahmedabad, says "I always tell my clients, good health is about the whole plate, not one ingredient. Millet is great, but it's not a substitute for medical treatment or a balanced lifestyle." The claim likely stems from misinformation and cultural myths. Many such claims circulate on social media or through word of mouth, often rooted in traditional beliefs. While traditional diets and ingredients can have value, turning them into unverified cures is risky. People might skip or delay medical care, hoping millet will solve serious health issues. That delay can lead to worsened conditions or even life-threatening situations. Plus, when someone with kidney problems consumes fermented foods without proper dietary guidance, they might actually worsen their condition. For example, some fermented products are high in potassium or sodium, both of which can be harmful for people with kidney disease. If you're dealing with symptoms like fatigue, swelling, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or changes in urination, don't look to millet, fermented or not, for answers. Talk to a doctor. Blood tests and scans can help pinpoint the problem, and timely treatment can make all the difference. It's perfectly fine to enjoy millet as part of your meals. It's nutritious, versatile, and easy to prepare. But remember: food is powerful, just not in the way these viral claims make it out to be. Cure is a big word, and not one to be used lightly. Fermented millet is a healthy food, not a cure. Trust science and medicine when it comes to treating liver and kidney diseases. Healthy eating supports your organs, but it doesn't replace medical care. Always consult a professional before making decisions that affect your health.

Fermented millets are nutritious and may support general health due to their rich fiber, probiotics, and antioxidant content. They can be a part of a kidney-friendly diet in early stages of chronic kidney disease (CKD) if appropriately recommended by a doctor or dietitian. However, relying on them as a sole treatment can delay critical medical care and worsen disease progression. Misleading claims suggesting "miraculous" recovery through food items like fermented millets can fuel dangerous medical misinformation, potentially causing harm to vulnerable patients. Patients with kidney failure should always consult a doctor and follow evidence-based treatment protocols. Incorporating healthy foods must be done under professional guidance, considering potassium, phosphorus, and protein restrictions in CKD diets.'

Dr Aman Rathore, DNB, Critical Care Medicine, Max Super Speciality Hospital, responded: 'Fermented millets are undoubtedly nutrient-rich and may contribute to overall health by supporting gut health and metabolic function. Treatment may involve hospitalization, medications, and in severe cases, a liver transplant. Suggesting that fermented millets can act as a "miracle cure" is not only medically inaccurate but also potentially harmful, particularly if it causes patients to delay or forgo evidence-based care. In advanced liver disease, dietary restrictions are often necessary to manage complications such as ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and disturbances in protein metabolism. Even healthy foods must be consumed cautiously under medical supervision. Management of liver failure should always be guided by a qualified doctor, with individualized treatment plans based on clinical status and liver function tests. title: Can fermented rice give a botox-like tight skin?- THIP Media
claim_text: Applying fermented rice paste on skin makes your skin look tight and lifted.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that applying fermented rice gives a "tightened" look. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Botox works by relaxing specific facial muscles, which softens expression lines. Fermented rice, whether eaten, drunk, or used as "rice water", doesn't switch off muscle movement, so it can't mimic that "frozen-smooth" Botox effect. What fermented rice might do is support the outer layer of your skin (the barrier). Some lab and cosmetic-ingredient research on fermented rice products suggests potential improvements in moisturising factors and barrier-related components, which can make skin look smoother. But that is very different from structurally lifting skin or erasing dynamic wrinkles. Consultant Dermatologist, Dr Sachin Gupta from Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, shares his perspective on the use of unproven natural remedies for wrinkles. He explains that given the limited and inconclusive scientific evidence supporting these approaches, it is wiser to choose treatments that have proven effectiveness and well-established clinical benefits. Although most do-it-yourself skincare remedies are unlikely to cause harm, depending on them excessively is unlikely to result in noticeably firmer or tighter skin. Collagen and elastin are the "scaffolding" that helps skin feel firm. Improving that scaffolding usually takes time, and the strongest evidence-based approaches are things like sun protection and retinoids (topical vitamin A derivatives). Some fermented rice ingredients (like fermented rice bran extracts) have shown collagen-related effects in laboratory or animal settings, which is interesting, but it doesn't automatically translate into a reliable, Botox-level result in real people from eating fermented rice. If you want collagen support from diet, the basics matter more: enough protein overall, and vitamin C (needed for collagen production). Fermented rice may be a healthy food in your routine, but it's not a collagen "shortcut". Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist, Aesthetician and Hair Transplant Surgeon at Rashi Hospital, Mumbai, explains that when it comes to improving skin firmness, doctors prefer treatments supported by strong scientific evidence. She notes that using a good-quality sunscreen every day is one of the most effective ways to prevent further skin damage. Retinoids are also commonly recommended, as they stimulate collagen production and promote healthy cell turnover. She adds that moisturisers containing ceramides or hyaluronic acid help maintain the skin's protective barrier and improve hydration, giving the skin a fuller appearance. Lifestyle habits matter too, avoiding smoking, eating a balanced diet and getting adequate sleep can significantly influence skin health. However, she emphasises that some loss of elasticity with age is completely natural. For more pronounced or deeper wrinkles, in-clinic procedures such as chemical peels or laser treatments may offer better results. It can happen, but it's usually temporary and explainable - there are a few common reasons for temporary tightening effect. Fermented rice may help skin look a bit smoother through hydration and barrier support, but it does not replicate Botox or create a true "tightened" face. If you want the most evidence-backed "firmer skin" strategy, prioritise sun protection, adequate protein and vitamin C, and consider proven topical options like retinoids. Safety note: Cooked rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus. If rice is left at room temperature too long, bacteria can grow and produce toxins that may not be destroyed by reheating. If someone is fermenting rice at home (or storing cooked rice overnight), the safest approach is strict food hygiene: cool quickly, refrigerate promptly, and consume within recommended time limits.

Caesalpinia bonducella is a medicinal plant found throughout India and is widely used in traditional medicine systems like Ayurveda and Siddha. Several studies highlight its strong antioxidant properties due to high levels of phenolics and flavonoids, which help combat free radicals (2011, 2010, 2009). title: Fact Check: Can Fibroids be cured naturally with concoction of lemon juice, baking soda and a clove of garlic?

Dr. Sharmishtha Garg, Associate Consultant, Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, New Delhi, explained: 'Fibroids are common tumours found in females of reproductive age group. The incidence is as high as 20 to 25 percent. Fibroids are estrogen and progesterone-sensitive tumours. The cause of fibroids can be linked to hereditary or genetic causes, as it is quite commonly seen in females from the same family. We talk about the risk factors, including early age of onset of menses, late menopause, obesity, and women suffering from polycystic ovarian syndrome. In some cases, it also presents as infertility or recurrent miscarriages. Sometimes, it presents as abdominal distension. So females harbouring any of these symptoms should consult their connective system on a regular basis, and it is recommended to have regular gynae checker to ensure a healthy body.'

Dr. Smriti Uppal, Consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist, explained: 'Fibroids are benign (non-cancerous) solid tumours of the uterus which are very commonly found in females and may be symptomatic or asymptomatic. The important cause of the development of these is either genetic or hormonal. Genetic—it has been found in studies that a particular gene mutation in the uterine muscles predisposes to fibroid development. Hormonal states of hyperestrogenism cause the development and growth of fibroids.'

Dr. Smriti Uppal further clarified: 'Natural remedies present and talked about are not to cure fibroids but to cope with the symptoms caused by them such as pain and pressure symptoms or heavy menstrual flow. This present claim about treating fibroids completely with this concoction of lemon juice, baking soda and garlic doesn't make any scientific sense. The treatment of fibroids is either medical or surgical. Medical anti-estrogenic medicines suppress the growth of fibroids and bring about a reduction in size.'

Scientific evidence cited: A study by Islam, M. S. (2014) reported that 'Allicin, an organosulfur compound derived from garlic (Allium sativum L.), found that it guards against fibrosis by mitigating reactive oxygen species (ROS)-dependent signalling pathways.' title: Fact Check: Can Fish Prasadam cure respiratory illnesses?
claim_text: Fish Prasadam can cure respiratory illnesses. It claims to treat asthma through the ingestion of a live Murrel fish filled with a secret herbal paste.
quick_take: Fish Prasadam, a traditional remedy from the Bathini Goud family in Hyderabad, India, claims to cure respiratory diseases like asthma. A viral Facebook video suggests Fish Prasadam can cure respiratory illnesses. However, our fact check reveals it is False.
doctor_explanation: Fish Prasadam is a traditional remedy popular in Southern India. The Bathini Goud family in Hyderabad administers this. The treatment involves swallowing a live Murrel fish (Channa striatus), approximately 2-3 inches long, filled with a yellow herbal paste. The practice takes place during the monsoon season and people believe it can cure asthma and other respiratory illnesses. It needs to be taken for 3 consecutive years to be effective. For vegetarians, there is an option of having the herbal paste with jaggery instead of the fish. The Bathini Goud family claims that the fish medicine was received from a Hindu saint in 1845. Since then, they have been administering the treatment annually at the Nampally Exhibition Grounds in Hyderabad. The family insists that the herbal paste's formula is a top secret and that its effectiveness would diminish after commercialisation. NO SCIENTIFIC EVIDENCE EXISTS: Medical professionals and studies have repeatedly indicated that there is no empirical data or clinical trials verifying the claims made by the Bathini Goud family. A systematic review highlighted that while the treatment has cultural significance, it lacks solid scientific validation. Experts have not observed significant improvements in asthma patients who have undergone the treatment. On the other hand, some patients have reported worsened conditions following the remedy. The treatment is often criticised as being unscientific and potentially harmful. Dr Ajit Vigg, Head of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine at Apollo Hospital, Hyderabad, commented: 'There is no evidence that it works. On the contrary, we have seen 10-15% patients whose condition has worsened. In my practice of 20-25 years, I have not seen a single patient whose condition has either improved or who has got completely cured with fish medicine.' Dr Vigg mentioned that they had sent some dozen chronic asthma patients to be treated with fish medicine a few years ago and monitored variables such as their forced vital capacity and forced expiration volume before and after the treatment but found no improvement. There is no cure for asthma as of now. But, there are treatments that can effectively manage the condition and reduce its impact on daily life. These treatments generally include medications like bronchodilators to help open up the airways and reduce inflammation. And, corticosteroids control inflammation in the airways over the long term. Additionally, avoiding triggers that can worsen asthma symptoms, such as allergens or irritants, can also help manage the condition. While Fish Prasadam holds cultural and historical significance, it lacks scientific backing and poses potential risks. Therefore, the claim that Fish Prasadam can cure respiratory illnesses is false. Effective medical treatments and lifestyle adjustments remain the best approaches to managing asthma and other respiratory illnesses.

Often referred to as the 'silent killer,' hypertension is linked to both structural and functional alterations in blood vessels due to its early asymptomatic presentation. Undiagnosed moderately high blood pressure can shorten life expectancy by accelerating vascular damage and compromising organ perfusion. The WHO states that uncontrolled hypertension plays a major role in heart failure, myocardial infarction, stroke, and chronic renal disease, requiring evidence-based medication, lifestyle changes, and early intervention.

Research on flaxseeds shows potential benefits for lowering high blood pressure due to their high levels of dietary fibre, alpha-linolenic acid (ALA), and lignans, which have vascular-protective and anti-inflammatory attributes. Studies show flaxseed consumption may slightly decrease both systolic and diastolic blood pressures in some patients with hypertension by enhancing endothelial function, reducing arterial stiffness, and modifying lipid profiles. However, these effects are not universal and depend on dosage, duration, and individual health status.

CRITICAL: Flax seeds should NOT be considered as a substitute for evidence-based blood pressure medication. Hypertension is a multifaceted illness requiring all-encompassing care. Without medical supervision, relying on unproven home cures like flax seeds can be risky—it may delay timely intervention and contribute to the condition's gradual progression, resulting in serious complications.

Regarding regular consumption: While flax seeds can help enhance lipid profiles, support cardiovascular health, improve glycaemic control, and facilitate digestion, prolonged consumption in excess can cause bloating, diarrhoea, and gastrointestinal distress due to high fibre content. Due to phytoestrogenic qualities, people with hormone-sensitive conditions should use them cautiously. Those using prescribed blood thinners may experience interactions.

Diet cannot replace evidence-based medication. While diet is vital in managing cardiovascular conditions, hypertension requires a multimodal approach combining lifestyle and pharmaceutical therapy. The DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet has demonstrated improvements in lowering blood pressure but is not sufficient for dropping blood pressure to healthy ranges alone. Medical practitioners recommend antihypertensive medications (ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers, thiazide diuretics, and beta-blockers) when lifestyle modifications are insufficient.

Dr. Almas Fatma advises the most effective ways to regulate blood pressure are: consume a nutritious diet, be physically active, limit salt intake, and manage stress. Doctors may also recommend medication in some situations to maintain blood pressure within acceptable limits.

Dr. Ubaid ur Rahman explains that lowering blood pressure takes time and requires both medical assistance and healthy lifestyle choices. Reducing alcohol consumption, quitting smoking, increasing physical activity, and consuming a diet high in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat foods are crucial support strategies. Even if some individuals require medication, lifestyle modifications are always the cornerstone of treatment.

doctor_explanation: Cough (also known as tussis) is a natural reflex of the body to remove irritants such as foreign particles, fluids, mucus, microbes, etc. from the throat and breathing passage through rapid expulsion of air from the lungs. Acute cough is usually self-limiting and rarely needs significant medical intervention, but chronic cough needs medical intervention as it is a crucial symptom of various chronic respiratory diseases. Treatment of cough depends on its cause - if caused by infection, antiviral or antibiotic medication is prescribed. Various cough suppressants or antitussives can aid in relieving symptoms. Hot beverages, honey, fluid consumption, and certain herbs have also been seen to be effective in treating cough. Flu (influenza) is an acute respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses (types A, B, C and D). Flu symptoms include fever, chills, headache, persistent and dry cough, muscle and joint pain, severe malaise, sore throat and runny nose. Treatment of flu depends on severity - patients not in high-risk groups are managed with symptomatic treatment (e.g., antipyretic drugs for fever). In cases of severe or progressive clinical illness, flu antiviral drugs such as neuraminidase inhibitors and corticosteroids are prescribed, along with rest and plenty of fluids. There is no evidence from scientific studies or clinical trials that prove wearing potatoes in socks is effective in curing flu and cough. Potatoes (scientifically called Solanum tuberosum L) indeed have health benefits containing vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and phytochemicals - they benefit the human body as supplementary nutrients and antioxidants, are rich in carbohydrates and are energy-providing food with little fat. Consuming potatoes can help strengthen the immune system and help in dealing with colds and flu. However, there is no proof that the placement of potatoes on feet externally will transfer their benefits to the skin. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) does not list potatoes as a cure for flu or cough among its authorized health claims. Additionally, there are children or patients who can experience potato allergy with symptoms such as red, itchy skin, rhinitis, itchy or stinging eyes, runny or stuffy nose, and sneezing. title: Fact Check: Can fluoride toothpaste lower IQ and damage cells?
claim_text: According to an Instagram post, fluoride in toothpaste is toxic, can lower IQ, and damage cells.
quick_take: A social media post claims that fluoride toothpaste lowers IQ and damages cells. Our fact check says this claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Fluoride in toothpaste does not harm cells when used appropriately. Fluoride is a naturally occurring mineral known for strengthening tooth enamel and preventing cavities. In toothpaste, the fluoride content is strictly regulated and deemed safe for daily use. Research on fluoride-related cellular damage usually involves excessive levels far beyond those found in toothpaste. While prolonged exposure to extremely high doses of fluoride can lead to fluorosis, this condition is rare and typically occurs in regions with excessive natural fluoride in water. For topical use, such as in toothpaste, fluoride exposure to the body is minimal because it is not swallowed. Most of it is rinsed or spat out, limiting systemic absorption. Regulatory bodies like the NHS and the World Health Organization (WHO) confirm that fluoride is safe at recommended levels. Claims that fluoride harms the brain or lowers IQ lack solid evidence. Studies linking high fluoride levels to lower IQ often overlook other factors like arsenic, mercury, or socioeconomic conditions. Fluoride at normal levels, as found in toothpaste and drinking water, does not easily reach the brain and is not harmful. Toxic effects on brain cells occur only at extremely high doses, far beyond typical exposure. Additionally, concerns about aluminium-fluoride compounds suggest that aluminium, not fluoride, may be the primary cause of toxicity. The claim about fluoride lowering IQ comes from limited studies with significant methodological issues. Research linking fluoride to reduced IQ mostly involves high fluoride concentrations in drinking water, not toothpaste. A few studies conducted in regions like China and India with naturally elevated fluoride levels in water have shown potential links to reduced cognitive function. However, these studies often fail to account for other factors such as malnutrition, socioeconomic status, or exposure to environmental toxins like lead, which also affect IQ. When fluoride is used in controlled amounts, as in toothpaste or fluoridated water, there's no credible evidence it impacts intelligence. Dr Sanjeev Bhankhur says, 'The idea that fluoride in toothpaste affects IQ is a misunderstanding of the science. The studies suggesting such links often involve areas with extremely high natural fluoride levels in water, not the controlled doses in toothpaste. Normal fluoride exposure doesn't cross into the brain easily, and there's no evidence it affects cognitive development. It's important to focus on the proven benefits of fluoride for dental health rather than fear unsupported claims.' Fluoride in toothpaste is not toxic when used as intended. 'Toxicity' depends on the dose. Almost anything can be toxic in excess, even water or vitamins. Fluoride in toothpaste is present in small amounts, typically around 1,000–1,500 ppm (parts per million), which is far below harmful levels. Swallowing large quantities of toothpaste could potentially cause stomach discomfort, but this is unlikely unless consumed in excessive amounts. Fluoride toxicity primarily becomes a concern when significantly high doses are ingested, such as industrial exposure or accidents. This is why children's toothpaste has reduced fluoride content and warnings to supervise brushing. Dr Snigdha says, 'Fluoride in toothpaste is not just safe but essential for preventing tooth decay. It works by strengthening tooth enamel and reversing early signs of damage. The fluoride levels in toothpaste are carefully regulated to ensure they're effective and harmless when used as directed. Spitting it out after brushing ensures minimal absorption, making it a safe and vital part of oral hygiene.' The claim that fluoride toothpaste lowers IQ and damages cells is mostly false and lacks strong scientific backing. Fluoride remains an essential tool in dental health, protecting against cavities and strengthening teeth when used at recommended levels.

title: Fact Check: Can food burn more calories than it provides?

doctor_explanation: Negative calorie foods are often claimed to require more energy to digest than they provide, theoretically resulting in a caloric deficit. However, the concept is oversimplified and lacks strong scientific evidence. While some low-calorie foods may contribute to weight loss, the term negative calorie is not widely accepted in the scientific community. The notion of negative-calorie foods, claiming they burn more calories during digestion than they contribute, lacks solid scientific backing. While low-calorie foods play a role in a balanced diet, the idea of negative calories oversimplifies metabolism. There is insufficient evidence to support its validity. Weight management is better approached through a holistic strategy, including a diverse and nutritious diet, regular exercise, and healthy lifestyle habits. While the foods listed in the claimed Instagram video might be nutritious, they do have calories. There is no solid evidence to support the claim that they require more energy to digest than they actually provide. An idea also exists that the energy used while chewing might contribute to the negative-calorie concept. However, research suggests that the extra calories burned during chewing are quite minimal and likely not significant. When it comes to digesting food, our body does use some calories for the process. But the calories burned during digestion are generally less than the calories present in the food. This energy expenditure is a small percentage of the calories eaten, and it varies for carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. Most foods claimed to be negative-calorie are high in water and carbs, with little fat or protein. While it is true they require some energy to digest, it is not likely significantly higher than other carbohydrate-based foods. However, this aspect has not been studied extensively. Both fruits and vegetables contain calories. But it is not that the calories expended in eating, digesting, and processing them exceed the calories they provide. The fiber in some fruits and veggies can make your body work a bit more to digest it. This is because our bodies cannot fully break down fiber. This extra effort the body puts into digesting fiber is like a small workout for the digestive system. However, the extra calories burned are not huge or visible. The main benefit of fiber is keeping the digestion healthy and help people feel full. So, eating fruits and veggies having fiber is good for health. Dr. Swati Dave, a Ph.D. in Food and Nutrition, warns against weight loss misinformation online, likening it to a viral spread of quick fixes and false claims. Deceptive content with unrealistic promises can lead to ineffective or harmful practices, hindering healthy weight loss. Dr. Dave emphasises on the importance of critical evaluation, seeking evidence-based advice, and avoiding misleading trends without scientific support. A food cannot burn more calories than it contains. The calories in food represent the energy it provides when your body digests and processes it. If a food item claims to have negative calories or to burn more calories during digestion than it provides, it is generally a misconception or an exaggeration. While certain foods may require more energy to digest (like those high in fibre), they still contribute calories to your overall energy intake. This means the actual caloric expenditure during digestion is not likely to surpass the caloric content of the food. Weight loss usually occurs when you consume fewer calories than your body uses, creating a calorie deficit.

doctor_explanation: What factors influence the growth of an individual's height? The growth of an individual's height is primarily determined by a combination of genetic, nutritional, and environmental factors. Genetics play a significant role, as a person's potential height is largely inherited from their parents. Proper nutrition, especially during childhood and adolescence, is crucial as a lack of essential nutrients can stunt growth. Hormones, such as growth hormone and thyroid hormones, also play a pivotal role. Additionally, environmental factors like adequate sleep, physical activity, and a healthy living environment can support optimal height development during the growing years. At what age does an individual typically cease growing in height? Individuals typically stop growing in height during their late teens to early twenties, usually around the ages of 18 to 25. This cessation of growth is primarily due to the closure of growth plates in the bones. Can food influence height even after growth has ceased? No, once an individual's growth plates in the bones have closed, typically in late adolescence or early adulthood, further growth in height is not possible, regardless of diet or nutrition. Nutrition primarily supports height growth during the growing years when the body is actively developing. Once growth plates have fused, food and nutrition no longer have the capacity to increase a person's height. Does onion and jaggery increase in height? No, there is no scientific evidence to support the idea that onion and jaggery can increase a person's height. Height is primarily determined by genetics and the closure of growth plates in the bones, which typically occurs in late adolescence. While a balanced diet rich in essential nutrients is essential for overall health, these specific foods, yoga or exercise do not have the ability to alter your genetic predisposition for height or change the growth process once it has stopped. Proper nutrition during childhood and adolescence can help you maximize your height. But once the skeleton has stopped growing, no treatments or nutrition will help you to increase height.

claim_text: Kalonji (nigella sativa) seeds mixed with honey can dissolve gallbladder stones naturally within 30 days
quick_take: A social mediapost suggests that consuming kalonji seeds mixed with honey can dissolve gallstones completely within 30 days, comparing the process to how stones dissolve in water. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: There is no strong clinical evidence (proper human trials with scans before and after) showing that kalonji plus honey dissolves gallbladder stones. What often happens online is 'evidence laundering': a remedy may have general health claims or lab findings, and then it gets promoted as a stone cure, without real proof in patients. You can find research looking at Nigella sativa essential oil and its compounds acting on cholesterol gallstones in vitro (meaning the stone is tested outside the body). In those settings, researchers may see changes in stone surface or partial breakdown. But that's a very controlled environment, nothing like a living gallbladder with bile flow, mucus, inflammation, and stones tucked away in corners. A lab result is a starting point, not a treatment recommendation. Also, gallstones aren't all the same. Some are cholesterol-based, others are pigment stones, and some are mixed or calcified. Even the in-vitro work suggests effects are mainly on cholesterol stones, not pigment stones. So the leap from 'might affect a type of stone in a lab dish' to 'dissolves gallstones in people' is simply too big. From an Ayurvedic viewpoint, Ayurveda does not offer any direct interventional medicine that can reliably dissolve gallstones. Referring to the teachings of Acharya Sushruta, widely regarded as the father of Ayurvedic surgery, gallstones are considered a type of Shalya (foreign body) that develops due to an imbalance of the doshas. According to classical Ayurvedic texts, such Shalyas are meant to be removed from the body through Shalya Karma, or surgical intervention. Only in certain cases based on radiological findings, very small gallstones (typically below 3–4 mm), described as Pitta-Ashmari, may respond to Ayurvedic medicines when prescribed and monitored by a qualified Ayurvedic physician. The only medicine that really dissolves gallbladder stones is ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), a prescription bile acid, used to dissolve small cholesterol gallstones in a working gallbladder. This isn't a folk remedy, it's a medical approach with strict limits. Even when UDCA is appropriate, treatment is typically many months (often quoted around 6–18 months) and works best when stones are small and mostly cholesterol. If stones are large, calcified, pigment-based, or if the gallbladder isn't functioning well, dissolution in 30 days is unlikely. Stones can come back after successful dissolution because the underlying bile chemistry may still favour stone formation. When stones cause repeated pain, inflammation, infection, or block ducts, the standard treatment is usually cholecystectomy (removal of the gallbladder). Gallstones are firm, solid deposits that form inside the gallbladder and cannot be dissolved simply through diet or home remedies. Their presence often indicates that the gallbladder is not working as it should. The biggest risk of relying on home remedies is delay, because gallstones can trigger serious complications that need urgent care. Red flags include severe pain that doesn't settle, fever or chills, yellowing of the skin/eyes (jaundice), or repeated vomiting. These can point to problems like infection/inflammation or a stone blocking a duct, and that can become dangerous. Gallstone pancreatitis, for example, happens when a stone blocks the pancreatic duct area and triggers inflammation; it typically needs hospital care.
