title: Can ginger and lemon juice cure head lice in one wash?
claim_text: According to an Instagram post, you can get rid of head lice in just one use. The video suggests that using a mixture of ginger (adrak) and lemon juice with shampoo is a 100% guaranteed home remedy that can remove all head lice in just one use, leaving the hair as if lice were never present.
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that a homemade remedy of ginger and lemon juice can cure head lice in one wash. Our fact check shows this is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: There is no strong scientific evidence to support the claim. While ginger and lemon juice have some health benefits, their effectiveness against head lice has not been proven in clinical studies. A 2024 lab study tested 6-gingerol (from ginger) and Cymbopogon citratus (lemongrass) on adult head lice. The study found that both compounds killed adult lice by disrupting their enzymes and causing physical damage. However, the study did not examine their effects on lice eggs. Similarly, a 2018 lab study investigated essential oils from white turmeric (Curcuma zedoaria, a member of the ginger family but not ginger itself) and eucalyptus to stop lice eggs from hatching. This study used specific concentrations of oils (10% Curcuma zedoaria and 10% eucalyptus), not random amounts like a few drops of ginger juice. The results showed that this combination of oils prevented the eggs from hatching, but once again, it was tested under controlled lab conditions, not on humans. A 2010 study tested lemon juice (Citrus limon) against head lice in a lab setting. The study found that undiluted lemon juice and half-diluted lemon juice killed 95% and 90% of adult lice, respectively, after three hours. This suggests that lemon juice may have some effect on lice, but further testing on humans is needed to confirm its effectiveness. In contrast, standard medical treatments involve specifically formulated lice-killing medications (pediculicides) and the careful removal of lice eggs (nits), both of which have been proven to be effective in real-world situations. Similarly, claims that a mixture of garlic, lemon juice, and mustard oil can permanently cure lice in just one use also lack scientific backing and are unlikely to provide the desired results. Even clinically proven treatments for head lice often require more than one application, spaced several days apart, to kill both live lice and newly hatched nymphs. Nits are notoriously difficult to remove and often require manual combing with a fine-toothed comb. A single wash with a homemade remedy is unlikely to eradicate all lice and nits effectively. Additionally, re-infestation is possible if proper precautions, like washing bedding and avoiding head-to-head contact with infested individuals, are not followed. The idea that one treatment can make it seem as though lice were 'never there' is therefore misleading. Even though both ginger and lemon have some beneficial properties, their undiluted or improperly used application on the scalp could cause irritation, dryness, or even chemical burns in sensitive individuals. Lemon juice is acidic and can be harsh on the skin, while concentrated ginger extracts can also be irritating. Without proper formulation and testing, the safety of such a homemade remedy is uncertain. Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, explains, 'While ingredients like ginger and lemon juice may show some effects in lab studies, they are not a reliable, one-time solution for head lice. Clinically proven pediculicides remain the most effective and recommended treatment. It's crucial to consult a dermatologist for proper diagnosis and treatment to avoid prolonged infestations and complications.' Dr Rashi Soni, Dermatologist and Co-founder of Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, says, 'The most effective treatments for head lice are scientifically proven pediculicides. These are specially formulated medications to kill lice and sometimes their eggs. These treatments include over-the-counter options like permethrin or pyrethrin, as well as prescription medications such as malathion, spinosad, or ivermectin. It's important to follow the product instructions carefully for the best results. In addition to treatment, thorough nit combing and cleaning bedding and clothing are crucial steps to prevent re-infestation. For a personalised approach, it's always best to consult with a dermatologist or healthcare provider.'

title: Fact Check: Can Ginger Cure Symptoms During Heart Attack?
claim_text: In an Instagram reel, it is claimed that ginger can cure symptoms during a heart attack. The user instructs: 'How to turn your home into an ICU: Step one, if someone has a heart attack or yourself, the step 1 is to change the posture. One heart is your heart and the other heart is calf muscles. Bring these two hearts close together... Sit on the ground with back support. Step two: Take a piece of ginger and put it in the patient's mouth. The ginger will create a reaction, making tears come out of their eyes. Within 15 minutes, the symptoms should start reducing, and in half an hour, symptoms will fade away and they will feel better. Step three: Take a bucket of hot water, around 45 degrees Celsius (geyser water). Make the patient sit on a chair and place their feet in the hot water. Hopefully, this process will help the symptoms go away.'
verdict_original: The claim by the user is FALSE.
quick_take: Ginger is not a cure or treatment for symptoms during a heart attack. It may promote cardiovascular health over time, but during a heart attack, immediate medical attention is critical. The claims that changing posture or soaking feet in hot water can relieve heart attack symptoms are not supported by scientific evidence or medical consensus. Prompt emergency measures remain essential. Call emergency services at the first sign of symptoms.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Prem Aggarwal, MD (Medicine), DNB (Cardiology, Director), Sanjeevan Hospital, Daryaganj, Delhi, said: 'Heart attacks are serious medical emergencies, and the claims about using posture changes, ginger, or hot water to treat them are false and highly misleading. If you or someone around you experiences symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, or discomfort, don't waste time on unproven remedies. Instead, call for emergency medical help immediately. Time is critical during a heart attack, and professional medical care is essential to save lives. Remember, unscientific methods can delay treatment and worsen outcomes. Always prioritize your health and seek expert care without delay.' Dr Manav Aggarwal, MBBS, DM, Interventional Cardiologist, Sanjeevan Hospital, New Delhi, explained: 'The claims about using posture changes, ginger, or hot water to treat a heart attack are false and lack scientific basis. Heart attacks are medical emergencies that require immediate professional intervention. Symptoms like chest pain, breathlessness, or discomfort should prompt calling emergency services. Delays in treatment can be life-threatening. Always prioritize reaching a hospital over unproven remedies.'

Scientific evidence: A heart attack (myocardial infarction) occurs when blood flow to the heart muscle is reduced or blocked, depriving it of oxygen. This typically happens due to atherosclerosis, where coronary arteries narrow from plaque buildup (fat, cholesterol, and other substances). If a plaque ruptures, it can trigger a blood clot that obstructs blood flow. Without timely treatment, the heart muscle begins to die.

While ginger (Zingiber officinale) has well-documented anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties and may support overall cardiovascular health — including potentially lowering cholesterol levels, reducing hypertension, and addressing atherosclerosis (per studies in Nutrition and Current Topics in Functional Food) — ginger cannot dissolve a blood clot or reopen a blocked artery, the primary cause of a heart attack. These preventive benefits apply only when ginger is consumed regularly as part of a balanced diet; they do not constitute a treatment during an active heart attack.

The 'Golden Hour' of a heart attack refers to the critical first hour after onset of symptoms, during which prompt medical intervention (thrombolytic therapy or angioplasty) can significantly improve survival rates. Relying on ginger, posture changes, or hot water immersion during this window can cause life-threatening delays.

The claim that changing posture can cure heart attack symptoms by 'bringing hearts close together' (referring to the chest and calf muscles) and that placing feet in hot water can relieve symptoms are both without scientific backing or medical consensus. All three interventions — postural manipulation, ginger ingestion, and hot water foot soak — lack any evidence as heart attack treatments and are deemed dangerous because they delay proper emergency care.

title: Can ginger decoction help you lose weight in just 15 days?- THIP
claim_text: An Instagram post claims that drinking a ginger decoction prepared with lemon and jaggery every morning can help you lose weight rapidly, sometimes promising visible changes within 10–15 days.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that a herbal drink prepared with ginger, lemon, and jaggery can lead to real and lasting weight loss within just 15 days. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Ginger does not burn stored body fat. Fat loss occurs only when the body consistently uses more energy than it receives from food, a process known as a calorie deficit. Ginger contains bioactive compounds such as gingerols and shogaols, which have been studied for their effect on digestion and metabolism. Some small studies suggest ginger may slightly increase thermogenesis, the process by which the body produces heat, but the increase is minimal. It is not strong enough to cause noticeable fat loss on its own. At best, ginger may help some people feel fuller for longer or experience fewer cravings. This indirect effect can support weight management, but it does not 'melt fat,' detox fat, or target belly fat, claims that have no scientific basis.

Dr P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda, points out that Ayurveda has long recognised obesity as a complex and challenging condition. Classical texts even describe it as 'almost incurable,' captured in the phrase na hi sthulasya bheshajam, which means there is no single medicine that can cure it. He emphasises that there is no quick or magical solution, meaningful improvement comes from managing stress, correcting lifestyle habits, and following an appropriate diet, with medicines serving only a supportive role. Because obesity presents differently in each individual, Ayurveda advocates a personalised, whole-person approach rather than a one-size-fits-all treatment.

Chhavi Kohli, Dietitian and Diabetes Educator at Medanta, stresses the importance of caring for both physical and emotional health by focusing on habits that can be sustained long term. She encourages enjoying favourite foods in moderation, opting for seasonal and minimally processed choices, staying physically active, getting adequate sleep, and maintaining good hydration. She also advises people to be cautious about online health claims and to seek personalised advice from a qualified professional rather than relying on generic tips.

Regarding lemon: Lemon does not speed up fat loss. Lemon juice is often associated with 'detox' claims, but the body does not need external detox drinks. Your liver and kidneys already perform detoxification around the clock. What lemon does provide is vitamin C and flavour. This can encourage people to drink more fluids, which may help reduce unnecessary snacking caused by mild dehydration. However, drinking lemon water does not increase metabolism in any meaningful way and does not cause weight loss on its own. Any short-term change seen after starting lemon water is usually due to improved hydration, not fat loss.

Dr Swati Dave, who holds a PhD in Food and Nutrition, explains that she often reminds clients there is no drink that can instantly burn body fat. While ingredients such as ginger, cinnamon, fenugreek, cumin and ajwain may help digestion and give a small metabolic lift, their effects are too mild to drive significant weight loss on their own. Sustainable fat loss, she notes, comes from maintaining a steady calorie deficit through a balanced diet and regular physical activity.

Regarding jaggery: Jaggery is often perceived as 'healthy' because it is less refined than white sugar, but metabolically, it behaves very similarly. Jaggery is still a concentrated source of carbohydrates and calories. One tablespoon of jaggery adds extra calories to the drink and raises blood sugar levels. From a weight-loss perspective, adding jaggery actually works against fat loss, especially when consumed daily. The small amounts of minerals present in jaggery are nutritionally insignificant and do not enhance metabolism or fat burning.

Sports nutritionist Manasi Bandhu explains that jaggery should not be mistaken for a weight-loss aid. Although it contains small amounts of minerals and antioxidants and may be slightly less refined than white sugar, it is still calorie-dense and has a high glycaemic index. Having jaggery in the morning does not burn fat or speed up weight loss. Effective weight management depends on a broader approach that includes mindful calorie intake, regular physical activity, and healthy lifestyle habits that support energy balance.

Regarding rapid weight loss claims: Safe and sustainable weight loss is gradual. Health experts generally consider 0.5–1 kg per week to be realistic. Rapid weight loss claims often involve dehydration, muscle loss, or extreme calorie restriction, none of which are healthy or long-lasting. No drink can compensate for high-calorie diets, poor sleep, chronic stress, or physical inactivity, all of which strongly influence body weight. So a ginger decoction made with lemon and jaggery cannot help you lose meaningful weight in just 15 days. At best, it may reduce bloating and support digestion. Real fat loss depends on long-term dietary patterns, physical activity, and lifestyle habits, not viral drinks promising quick results.

title: Fact Check: Can ginger, onion, and honey cure piles?
claim_text: Mixing ginger, onion juice, and honey can cure piles.
quick_take: A social media post claims that ginger, onion, and honey cure piles. We fact-checked and found the claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Piles, also known as hemorrhoids, happen when the blood vessels swell around your bottom and rectum. This can lead to pain and discomfort. Some common signs are itching, pain in the bottom, lumps near your back passage, bleeding from your bottom, or even the hemorrhoid coming out. Piles occur when there is too much pressure in the lower part of your rectum. Things like being constipated, lifting heavy things, having chronic diarrhea, or pushing too hard when you go to the bathroom can cause piles. Other factors include being pregnant, getting older, being overweight, and what you eat. To some extent, doctors recommend changing your diet to help with piles. Eating foods with lots of fiber can make your poop soft and easier to pass. Drinking water and other liquids can also help. It is important to talk to your doctor about how much fiber and liquids you should have each day. Dr Sharad Malhotra, Gastroenterologist, Akash Hospital, Delhi, explained: "Eating the right way can't cure piles, but it can make the symptoms better. A good diet should have whole grains, beans, fruits with the skin, and foods with fiber to prevent constipation. Try to stay away from processed foods that have lots of fats and carbs because they slow down your digestion and make constipation worse." Dr. Malhotra also explained that there are treatments for piles including eating more fiber, using things like laxatives or stool softeners, avoiding medications or foods that make constipation worse, taking medicines to reduce pressure in the veins around the anus, and sometimes having medical procedures like injections, banding, or surgery to fix the swollen veins. Regarding the specific claim: There is no evidence about the fact that onion juice and honey can cure piles. The available evidence does show that eating ginger, onion and honey is good for colon health. However, the available evidence does not confirm whether eating these foods cures piles. These foods contain phytochemical, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and antioxidant properties which may soothe the symptoms of piles. However, we found no evidence that confirms ginger, onions, and honey can cure piles. Also, we have no information on the proportion of these ingredients in daily meals to gain health benefits. Dietician Kamna Chauhan says "Diet cannot cure the pile disease but it can reduce the symptoms. Eating food that are high in fiber can make stool softer and easier to pass. This can make piles less painful. Drinking water and other liquids can help the fiber in your diet works better." Dangers of trying to cure piles through home remedies: Trying to treat piles with home remedies without understanding the underlying cause can leave piles untreated. Such a condition can cause anaemia and trap piles in the anal muscles to cause a painful condition called gangrene, which leads to the death of tissues.

However, there is no conclusive evidence to support the teeth whitening benefits of brushing with a homemade paste made of salt, ginger, and lemon in addition to toothpaste.

Lemon juice is a powerful at-home bleaching agent and a rich source of vitamin C. On the other hand, excessive use of lemon juice erodes the tooth enamel which guards against dental disease. It is crucial to stress that your teeth's enamel does not grow back. As a result, regularly applying lemon juice will have a negative impact on its ability to whiten teeth.

Studies have shown that ginger has nutraceutical and medicinal properties. The essential oils of the rhizome are responsible for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties. As a result, the versatile herb helps to maintain oral hygiene and reduce gum disease-related inflammation. However, there isn't much evidence to support the use of ginger juice as a home remedy for teeth whitening.

Salt, or sodium chloride, is a versatile therapeutic agent that is easily used as a toothpaste additive to prevent plaque build-up and maintain oral hygiene, as well as a mouth rinse for mouth ulcers and a pain reliever. However, due to the salt's abrasive nature, its regular application in a homemade paste may be harmful.

Dr. Pooja Bhardwaj (BDS), our dental expert, was asked about the impact of preparation on teeth whitening. She responded that ginger's anti-inflammatory properties help to maintain healthy gums. Additionally, the salt reacts with the citric acid in lemons, which has an acidic pH, to cause the dissociation of the chloride atom and the hydronium ion. This change in reaction causes the pH to become more acidic, which ultimately causes the teeth's enamel to etch. This weakens teeth and makes them more vulnerable to caries.

Please be aware that this homemade paste for teeth whitening that combines toothpaste, ginger, salt, and lemon may actually do more harm than good because there are no established dosages, the ingredients may be abrasive or acidic, and they might ultimately result in tooth sensitivity or enamel damage. In addition, tooth whitening is not guaranteed by this composition.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: Since teeth whitening is a cosmetic procedure, it would be risky to rely on a homemade paste made of ginger, a natural anti-inflammatory, abrasive salt, and acidic lemon juice. This is because they are not well-known teeth whitening products and cannot take the place of teeth whitening done by a professional dentist. Additionally, daily application of these medications may result in tooth sensitivity and enamel erosion in the absence of a dosage that has been proven to have therapeutic efficacy. Therefore, we draw the conclusion that the claim is mostly false.

title: Can ginger, turmeric, and ACV water cure fatty liver in 14 days?
claim_text: A viral Instagram reel suggests that a mix of ginger, turmeric, cinnamon, lemon juice, and apple cider vinegar (ACV) can cure fatty liver in just 14 days. It also links having a "ponch" (belly fat) with guaranteed fatty liver.
quick_take: A social media post claims that ginger, turmeric, and ACV water can cure fatty liver in 14 days. We did the fact check to term this claim as false.

Fatty liver, especially non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), is a condition where fat builds up in the liver. It doesn't have a quick fix.

Ginger and turmeric may help reduce inflammation. Regarding liver health, while studies suggest curcumin, a component of turmeric, may help reduce liver damage and NAFLD severity, larger, longer trials are necessary to confirm its role. Also, the curcumin from turmeric is very hard to absorb in the body due to poor bioavailability. Cinnamon, on the other hand, might help regulate blood sugar. Finally, while apple cider vinegar and lemon juice are often linked with "detox" claims, their actual effect on the liver is minimal and not medically proven to "cure" it.

NAFLD is quietly becoming a major health concern across India, often going unnoticed until it worsens. What works best for managing it is consistent lifestyle change—gradual weight loss, a balanced diet, cutting down on sugar and refined carbs, and staying active. No single drink or herb can replace this.

Despite this, some claims suggest that apple cider vinegar can cure fatty liver from the roots—an idea that is misleading and not backed by strong scientific evidence.

No, belly fat does not mean you definitely have fatty liver. Having a belly (ponch) can be a risk factor for fatty liver, but it's not a diagnosis. Many people with belly fat may have a healthy liver, and some lean people can still have fatty liver. The only way to confirm fatty liver is through proper medical tests, like an ultrasound or a liver function test. Saying there's a 100% guarantee is misleading and medically inaccurate.

Maybe, but with caution—and it won't treat fatty liver. Most of these ingredients are generally safe in small amounts. However, drinking strong ginger-turmeric-cinnamon concoctions regularly might irritate the stomach or interact with medications, especially blood thinners. ACV is acidic and may harm tooth enamel or cause acid reflux if taken undiluted or on an empty stomach daily. Lemon juice and ACV don't "detox" the liver. The liver already has its own natural detox system and doesn't need help from trendy drinks.

No, fatty liver doesn't go away overnight or with a single home remedy. The liver can heal over time, but only with long-term changes. Weight loss of 5–10% over a few months, reducing alcohol intake, following a nutritious diet, avoiding certain foods high in fat and sugar, and engaging in regular physical activity are proven ways to reduce liver fat. In some cases, certain medicines may be prescribed, but no home remedy or drink has been clinically proven to cure fatty liver quickly.

Dr Sharad Malhotra, Head of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Therapeutic Endoscopy at Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, clarified: "Fatty liver usually develops silently and doesn't cause symptoms early on, but it can slowly lead to serious liver damage. There's no quick fix or magic remedy—especially not one that can cure it in just 14 days. The most effective way to manage it is through long-term lifestyle changes like eating a balanced diet, cutting down on sugar and alcohol, staying active, and losing weight gradually. Even a 5% to 10% weight loss can improve liver health."

Dr Malhotra added: "It's important to get a yearly abdominal ultrasound and liver function tests to catch fatty liver early. In some cases, further tests like Fibroscan or a liver biopsy may be needed. Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and avoiding unproven herbal mixtures or unnecessary medications also goes a long way in protecting your liver. A healthy liver takes time and consistency—not shortcuts."

Chhavi Kohli, Chief Diabetes Educator & Certified Clinical Nutritionist at Medanta—The Medicity, Gurgaon, explained: "It's a gradual process that needs consistent lifestyle changes over several months. One of the key things we now understand is the role of the gut-liver axis. She continues: "Including probiotics—like curd, yoghurt, and fermented foods—and prebiotics—like fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and flaxseeds—may help by restoring gut balance. This can reduce inflammation and improve fat metabolism. However, these are not quick-fix solutions or cures. They work best when combined with overall dietary improvements, weight loss, and regular exercise as part of a long-term liver health plan."

A few research done to study the effect of Ginkgo Biloba on glaucoma, has shown that Ginkgo Biloba has the ability to increase blood flow into eyes. However, there is no conclusive evidence on whether increasing blood flow can result into prevention of glaucoma or curing it is not clear. Researchers note, "Conclusive evidence is lacking regarding the effect of Ginkgo Biloba Extracts on clinical outcomes in glaucoma patients such as visual field performance." Similarly, two other small researches done to study the effect of Ginkgo Biloba on age related macular degeneration (AMD). One research was done in France on 20 people and another was done in Germany on 99 people. Both trials reported some positive effects of Ginkgo biloba on vision however their results could not be pooled. A study done on both the research concluded, "The question as to whether people with AMD should take Ginkgo biloba extract to prevent progression of the disease has not been answered by research to date. title: Can giving ginger to a person experiencing a heart attack help?

A heart attack occurs when the flow of blood to part of the heart muscle is obstructed, typically by a blood clot. The interruption in blood flow causes the affected heart tissue to be deprived of oxygen, leading to damage. Once a heart attack is underway, the damage to the heart muscle begins immediately. The most effective way to reduce further damage is through urgent medical intervention. Although ginger contains compounds like gingerols and shogaols, known for their anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, these benefits are preventive and cannot provide immediate help during a heart attack. Ginger may help reduce inflammation and improve circulation over time, potentially lowering the risk of heart disease in the long run, but it is not a solution during a medical emergency. When a heart attack occurs, time is critical. The priority should be to restore blood flow to the heart muscle through medical treatments such as thrombolytic therapy (clot-busting drugs) or surgical procedures like angioplasty or bypass surgery. Ginger does not have the ability to facilitate these processes. Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, notes, "Ginger may help maintain heart health over time, but it is not a quick solution during emergencies. It's best seen as part of a long-term heart-healthy diet." Studies have shown that ginger could play a role in lowering cholesterol levels, improving blood circulation, and even reducing blood pressure—all factors linked to heart disease prevention. A 2022 study suggested that ginger can help reduce oxidative stress, which is an underlying factor in the development of cardiovascular disease. Additionally, research indicates that ginger might assist in lowering levels of bad cholesterol (LDL) and triglycerides, while increasing levels of good cholesterol (HDL). It also might act as a natural anti-inflammatory, which helps prevent the development of conditions like arteriosclerosis. However, these benefits are seen over months or even years of consistent use. Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, says, "When someone is having a heart attack, every second counts. Attempting to use ginger or any unproven remedy in such a critical situation could delay proper treatment, which could have serious consequences. If you suspect that someone is having a heart attack, calling emergency services should be the first and most important action. Heart attacks are life-threatening, and every minute without professional medical care increases the risk of severe heart damage or even death." While ginger is generally safe for consumption, it is not a treatment for heart attack damage. In fact, giving ginger could potentially delay the proper use of more effective treatments like clot-busting medications, blood thinners (such as aspirin), or even emergency surgery. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, shares her perspective saying, "During a heart attack, it's not advisable to eat anything at home. While Ayurveda has various remedies for promoting heart health, emergency situations and critical organ treatment need immediate professional attention. Certain medications also have restrictions. Allopathy is highly effective in emergency care and should be used when required. Once the patient is stable, they can explore alternative medicine for long-term heart health."

title: Fact Check: Can glycerine and cloves tighten skin overnight?

doctor_explanation: Glycerine is a humectant, meaning it draws moisture to the skin, which may temporarily make the skin appear plumper and more hydrated. A 2008 study found that glycerine helps moisturise the skin, improve its elasticity, and support the skin's barrier. However, it does not tighten the skin overnight. However, these benefits took 14 weeks to manifest, not overnight. These results were observed in mice, not humans. Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, says, 'While glycerine helps moisturise and hydrate the skin, it doesn't have the ability to tighten it instantly. Glycerine draws moisture into the skin, which may temporarily make it look plumper and more hydrated, but this effect is superficial and short-lived. Cloves, known for their antioxidant properties, may support skin health when used appropriately, but there's no evidence to suggest they can tighten the skin or provide instant results.' Dr Sachin Gupta, Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, states, 'Glycerine is excellent for keeping the skin hydrated, and cloves offer some antioxidant benefits, but neither can tighten the skin instantly. Professional treatments or long-term skincare routines that support collagen production are necessary for lasting results.' Collagen production is a complex process that cloves and glycerine can't significantly boost. The body makes collagen using nutrients like vitamin C and amino acids. Some skincare treatments, like retinoids or peptides, can help with collagen, but cloves and glycerine don't. The antioxidants in cloves don't absorb well when soaked in glycerine for DIY use. Skincare products need to be properly formulated for these ingredients to work effectively. Skin tightening and anti-ageing require consistent care over time. While some treatments, like hydrating masks or temporary fillers, can provide an immediate but short-lived plumping effect, no remedy can permanently tighten loose skin overnight. Cloves contain eugenol, which can irritate sensitive skin or cause allergic reactions. Applying whole cloves directly to the face, especially for prolonged periods, increases the risk of irritation or burns (like contact urticaria). Glycerine can attract moisture from the air, and in very humid conditions, this can overwhelm the skin's natural barrier, leading to potential irritation.

title: Fact Check: Can GMO food change human DNA? - THIP Media
claim_text: GMO food can change human DNA
quick_take: A social media post claims GMO food can change human DNA. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False. The available research does not confirm GMO food can change human DNA.
doctor_explanation: GMO is an abbreviation for Genetically Modified Organisms. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines GMOs as organisms (plants, animals, or microorganisms) whose DNA has been changed in a way that won't affect the natural process of breeding. The process follows transferring selected genes from one organism to another irrespective of whether they are related. A research paper published in 2017 informs that GMO foods are globally accepted for commercial use because they have perceived benefits to the producer or consumer. They have a lower price and greater health benefits. As per the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) website, GMO foods have various characteristics. The screenshot of some news release along with the caption mentioned in the claimed Instagram post misconstrue people believing GMO food can change human DNA. The caption of the claimed Instagram post links to a Substack article that claims biotech lobbyists admitted in a hearing of a U.S. Missouri House committee that GMO foods can change DNA. From the available log of testimony and documented House Bill HB 1169, it is unclear what that claim is based upon. From the video of the hearing, it is quite evident that GMO has been improperly mixed with the term 'gene editing'. No evidence confirms eating GMO foods can alter human DNA. We could not find any recorded case of human genes being changed by eating GMO foods. We further researched and found that certain organisms can get DNA besides their parents. This practice is called Horizontal Gene Transfer. But it is quite uncommon in GMO foods. The acquisition of genetic material not inherited from a parent, known as horizontal gene transfer, is rare and appears no more likely from GMO food than from non-GMO food. We also found research papers that show plant microRNA is found in animal blood because of horizontal gene transfer. However, we could not find any laboratory experiments that can explain this type of mix. Also, we do not know whether the sample was GMO. Another research paper published in 2022 informs that whatever genetic material enters the body after surviving cooking and digestion is not functional enough to withstand the metabolic barriers of the human body. Besides this, we researched further and found that a few food scientists in 2009 reported food DNA can survive in the gut. This made them think that the new DNA can affect the immune system. However, no evidence confirms that food DNA from the gut or bloodstream can change the DNA. Also, it is essential to understand that there is nothing like a tomato gene or a meat gene. All DNA is made up of bases A, T, U, C, and G.

title: Can Gond Katira help you lose weight in 7 days? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook video claims that consuming only water with two stone-like pieces of Gond Katira resulted in a 15-kilo weight loss in 7 days, flattening a sagging belly.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that consuming just two small rock-sized pieces of Gond Katira with water can aid in weight loss. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
Belief in Gond Katira's weight loss powers often stems from cultural lore and anecdotal buzz. In Ayurvedic practices, it's valued as a cooling agent that swells into a gel when soaked, creating a sense of fullness that might deter overeating. Social media amplifies personal stories, people swear by mixing it into drinks to curb cravings or enhance energy for exercise. Its high soluble fibre appeals too, echoing how fibres like psyllium or oats help manage hunger. Yet, these claims lean heavily on tradition and hype, not rigorous trials. In a world craving quick fixes, its natural, affordable tag makes it enticing, but overlooks that true weight loss demands sustained lifestyle shifts, not isolated remedies.

No, direct scientific evidence linking Gond Katira to significant weight loss is lacking, with studies showing at best indirect benefits from its fibre properties. Derived from Astragalus plants, this gum is primarily soluble fibre, which can absorb water and expand in the gut, potentially slowing digestion and promoting fullness, a mechanism supported by meta-analyses on soluble fibres generally reducing body weight by about 1.25 kg over 12 weeks in overweight adults. However, specific research on tragacanth is sparse. A small human trial with five men consuming 9.9 grams daily for three weeks found no changes in body weight or blood lipids, though it increased faecal output, hinting at mild digestive effects without toxicity. Animal studies offer glimmers: in rats with fatty liver disease, low-molecular-weight oligosaccharides from the gum curbed weight gain compared to controls, lowered blood glucose and insulin, and improved lipid profiles, suggesting metabolic support via better gut health and reduced oxidative stress. Still, these rat findings don't translate directly to humans, and no large-scale randomised trials confirm weight loss from Gond Katira alone. Broader reviews echo this, soluble fibre supplements can trim BMI and fat slightly in obese individuals, but effects are modest and require dietary context, not standalone use. Ultimately, any perks likely stem from fibre's general role in calorie control, not unique magic in this gum.

Sweta Chauhan, MSc in Food and Nutrition working at Kiran Multi-specialist Hospital, Surat, explains, "Many patients are enthusiastic about Gond Katira, citing its Ayurvedic roots and gel-forming properties as a weight loss solution. While its soluble fiber may promote feelings of fullness, this alone doesn't drive significant weight loss. The excitement stems from cultural beliefs and online anecdotes, but without robust clinical evidence, it's unreliable. Sustainable weight loss depends on maintaining a consistent calorie deficit, not a single ingredient."

While generally safe in moderation, pursuing quick weight loss with Gond Katira carries risks, especially from overconsumption or improper use. As a high-fibre substance, it can trigger digestive woes like bloating, gas, diarrhoea, or constipation if introduced suddenly or without ample water, issues noted in reviews where excess fibre ferments in the gut, causing discomfort. Choking hazards arise if not soaked properly, as the dry gum swells rapidly and might block the throat or intestines without fluids. Allergic reactions, though rare, include rashes, itching, or breathing difficulties in sensitive folks. For those with diabetes, it could fluctuate blood sugar, interacting with medications and risking lows or highs. Underweight individuals or those with eating disorders might face malnutrition from suppressed appetite. Short-term studies confirm tolerance at 10 grams daily, but long-term data is thin, urging caution, start low, hydrate well, and consult a doctor to avoid amplifying these side effects in hasty weight loss bids.

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said, "Patients often overlook the risks of natural products like Gond Katira, assuming they're safe because they're plant-based. Overconsuming it can lead to bloating or even dangerous blood sugar swings, especially for diabetics. If you're trying it, start with a small amount, drink plenty of water, and don't expect rapid weight loss. It's a minor player at best sustainable results come from long-term dietary changes and movement, not quick fixes."

Proven paths to sustainable weight loss hinge on balanced, evidence-backed habits like calorie-controlled diets, regular movement, and behavioural tweaks, not single supplements. Aim for a hypocaloric diet, slashing 500-1,000 kcal daily via nutrient-rich foods, think veggies, lean proteins, and whole grains, yielding 5-10% body weight loss in six months when combined with exercise. Meal replacements help maintain this, with trials showing sustained drops in weight and glucose over years. Physical activity is key, burn 1,000-2,000 kcal weekly through brisk walks or strength training to preserve muscle and prevent regain, as per long-term registry data from successful losers averaging 60 minutes daily. Behaviour therapy shines too, self-monitoring food intake curbs calories, while mindful eating combats triggers. Combined approaches outperform solos: diet plus exercise nets 7-8 kg loss over months, with ongoing support like apps or counselling boosting adherence. Fibre-rich diets aid indirectly by enhancing satiety, but pair them with sleep and stress management for lasting results. Forget fads; gradual changes build habits that stick, fostering health beyond the scale.

title: Fact Check: Can Gotu Kola plant cure depression?
claim_text: The Gotu Kola plant cures depression

doctor_explanation: Gotu Kola (Centella asiatica), also known as Mandukaparni, Asiatic Pennywort, or Indian pennywort, is a herbaceous plant native to Asia used in traditional medicine. It has been studied for cognitive enhancement and wound healing, rich in bioactive compounds like triterpenoids. Centella asiatica plant cannot cure depression. However, this plant has shown some promise in potentially helping with symptoms of depression. Therefore, better human trials/research are needed to confirm its effectiveness and understand the mechanisms behind it. Moreover, there can be no substitute for professional treatment. Centella asiatica cannot be a standalone treatment. Herbal medicines can interact with medications and have side effects like stomach upset. So, it is better to consult a healthcare professional before trying any herbal supplement. Dr Rahul Bansal, Consultant psychiatrist in an interview with THIP adds, "Any delay in treatment will worsen the health". Psychiatrist Dr Binda Singh states, "Depression is a disease and needs proper treatment. It can happen due to a variety of reasons, such as situational, trauma, physical health issues, etc. Depression needs intervention, which might include medication, counselling, positive thoughts, communication, etc. Unfortunately, the dietary cure for depression has no scientific evidence". The idea that Centella asiatica alone can cure depression is an oversimplification of a complex condition, and it is essential to approach depression treatment with a comprehensive and individualized approach.

title: Fact Check: Can grape juice cure stomach flu?
claim_text: It's that time of the year… I make my family drink grape juice daily from now until March, Just a few sips each day. It keeps the stomach bug from attaching to your digestive system if you're exposed to the virus
quick_take: A number of social media users claim that grape juice can prevent and cure stomach flu. We fact-checked and found the claim is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Stomach flu is a common term used to refer to a virus born gastrointestinal disease that causes watery diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea or vomiting, and sometimes fever. It is majorly a food or water borne disease. In most common cases, the virus causing stomach flu is Norovirus. However, the disease can also be triggered by bacteria such as E. coli and salmonella. The patient is advised to keep himself rehydrated and rest. The disease can be self-healing with home care, but in extreme cases doctors may administer IV fluid or prescribe antibiotics. Stomach flu caused by Norovirus is not related to the flu, which is caused by influenza virus. Grape Juice has shown to have some antiviral properties in test tube studies, but there are no human trials to provide conclusive evidence. A study done in 1979 showed that grape juice was 'likely to prevent or modify human enterovirus infections.' But this old study could not be replicated in all studies and was not carried forward to test the effectiveness of grape juice on norovirus or other viruses and bacteria causing stomach flu. Some people believe that grape juice can change the pH of the stomach and kill the Norovirus. However, this is also not true. The normal pH of our stomach is a highly acidic. While it is not feasible for a glass of grapes juice to change the stomach pH from acidic to neutral, but even if it happens that may not be a good thing. Research has shown that stomach viruses grow faster in more neutral pH. So, while there are some early promises in test tube research, efficacy of grapes juice to preventing or curing stomach flu is still not yet proven. Another social media post claims that the grapes cure kidney disease and cancer. Grapes contain antioxidants that may prevent kidney disease and cancer.

title: Fact Check: Can graying of hair be reversed with lemon & coconut oil?
claim_text: A Facebook post with the caption, "How to Reverse Gray Hair With Coconut Oil and Lemon Juice" shares a video on how to prepare a mixture of coconut oil and lemon juice which can reverse graying of hair.
quick_take: A social media post claims that the graying of hair be reversed with lemon and coconut oil. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Greying of hair is a natural phenomenon with age. Harvard Health states that the hair follicles produce less color with age, so when hair goes through its natural cycle of dying and being regenerated, it's more likely to grow in the gray beginning after age 35. There is a major role of genetics in this process. Additionally, there are multiple other medical conditions that can contribute to the early onset of greying of hair, popularly known as premature greying. The reasons include vitamin deficiency, thyroid disease, vitiligo, and alopecia. Many people believe even stress contributes to greying of hair. However, there is very little scientific conclusive evidence for the same. Studies even suggest that under stress hair turns grey in mice. But whether the same phenomenon works on the human body is still not yet known. Despite multiple marketing claims by product makers, the greying of hair can never be reversed. Cosmetic coloring aside, once a hair follicle produces hair, the color is set and cannot be changed. The Harvard Blog states that If a single strand of hair starts out brown (or red or black or blond), it is never going to change its color (unless you color your hair). Dr Reena Majithia, Consultant Dermatologist and cosmetologist further confirms, "Hair greying is primarily a result of the natural aging process, and it is influenced by genetic factors. It occurs when the pigment-producing cells in the hair follicles gradually decrease in activity. This reduction in pigment production leads to the appearance of grey or white hair. Lemon and coconut oil may have certain beneficial properties for hair health, such as moisturizing and conditioning, but they cannot alter the underlying causes of greying. Lemon juice is acidic and may help remove excess oil and build-up from the scalp, while coconut oil can provide nourishment to the hair strands. However, neither of these ingredients has the ability to stimulate the production of melanin (the pigment responsible for hair color) or reverse the aging process." Dr. Swati Watwani, Dermatologist and Medical Director, Persianlaly – Skin/Hair/Aesthetics/Ayurveda Clinic says, "Graying of hair starts when you are in your late 40s and early 50s. Premature graying of hair can start as early as in the 20s. So premature hair graying can be slowed down by finding out the cause and treating it accordingly. But it cannot be reversed completely." There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that lemon and coconut oil can reverse the graying of hair. Graying of hair is primarily caused by the reduction of melanin, the pigment responsible for hair color, due to natural aging and genetic factors. While some natural remedies and ingredients might promote hair health, they are unlikely to completely reverse the graying process. Coconut oil remains on the scalp to mask the cuticles and give an oily as well as heavy look to the hair. On the other hand, coconut oil can influence microbes on the scalp and their functions. This means excessive oiling can cause dandruff or produce sebum on the scalp to make hair look flat. In the same manner, if the oil is not properly washed out from the hair, it can cause severe damage to the scalp and strands. Similarly, lemon contains citric acid and antioxidants, which could potentially help with scalp health, but there's no scientific consensus on its ability to restore hair color. Even though lemon is a good source of Vitamin C and is an antioxidant, using lemon directly on the skin is not recommended as it is highly acidic and can change your skin's pH. A component of lemon, limonin could be developed as a useful treatment for hair loss. But, the direct application can lead to skin irritation, dryness, and sun damage, especially if you have sensitive skin. Dr. Sonali Kohli, Consultant Dermatology, Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, comments on why the application of lemon should be avoided by stating, "Lemon is a vibrant source of Vitamin C and has antioxidant and anti-bacterial flavonoid properties which are great for the skin. Lemon juice is highly acidic, and the Vitamin C serums we use are not citric acid but the ascorbic acid version of the lemon juice, which is beneficial for the skin and is stabilized. When a person applies lemon directly, it disturbs the skin's pH and makes it completely acidic. Hence, it must be avoided."

title: Fact Check: Can green juice cure cancer?
claim_text: A YouTube video claims that drinking a green juice containing cucumber, celery, apple, and spinach can cure cancer, lower blood sugar levels, reduce blood pressure, and lower cholesterol.
quick_take: A video claims that a green juice can cure cancer and help with other health conditions too. We did the fact check to term it as Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: No, green juice cannot cure cancer. Green juices made from vegetables and fruits like cucumber, celery, apple, and spinach are rich in vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. But, there is no scientific evidence supporting the claim that they can cure cancer. Cancer is a complex disease that requires treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted therapies. Relying solely on green juice or solutions like fasting to cure cancer could actually delay essential medical interventions and make the prognosis worse. A 2021 study reviewed dietary polyphenols, which are abundant in fruits and vegetables, and their role in cancer prevention. These polyphenols show promise in modulating cancer-related pathways and may work synergistically with conventional therapies. But still, they are not sufficient to treat cancer on their own. The study emphasises their role in supporting overall health but cautions against viewing them as substitutes for standard cancer treatments. Another study from 2018 on apple polyphenols found they could inhibit cell growth and metastasis in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cells in laboratory settings. But, this does not translate into a cure for cancer. Similarly, scientific evidence does not support claims that other natural remedies like alkaline water can cure cancer. These remedies can even be more dangerous if they lead patients to forgo proper medical treatments. Dr Pooja Khullar, a Radiation Oncologist at Dharamshila Narayana Super Speciality Hospital in New Delhi, emphasises the importance of a holistic approach to cancer prevention. She says, "It's essential to understand that no single food or exercise can fully 'fight' cancer. Effective cancer prevention needs a complete approach which includes a balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables, regular physical activity, minimising exposure to carcinogens, avoiding smoking and alcohol, limiting direct sun exposure, and keeping up with regular medical screenings. I recommend focusing on an overall health strategy and seeking expert guidance from medical professionals." Dr P. Rammanohar, Research Director at Amrita School of Ayurveda in Kollam, cautions against depending on a single ingredient or solution to treat cancer. He explains, "Cancer is a complex group of diseases, and there isn't a single cure for it. Different treatment approaches are designed for various types of cancer, and no single drug or remedy is effective for all forms of the disease." Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, Mumbai, says, "Antioxidants play a very important role in protecting our cells from damage due to free radicals. These are the unstable molecules that can lead to oxidative stress and contribute to chronic diseases, including cancer. By neutralising these free radicals, antioxidants help maintain cellular health and support the body's natural defence systems. A diet rich in fruits and vegetables provides a good source of antioxidants. But still, it's important to remember that they work best as part of a balanced diet rather than as a standalone solution." A 2013 study highlighted the anti-cancer potential of cucurbitacins, compounds found in cucumbers. The study shows these compounds could inhibit cancer cell proliferation and induce apoptosis (cell death) in various cancer models. However, while these findings are promising, they do not suggest that consuming cucumbers or green juice can cure cancer. A 2015 study on dietary fibre, abundant in fruits and vegetables, suggested that high fibre intake might reduce the risk of certain cancers, such as colorectal cancer. Another study from 2011 demonstrated the anti-cancer properties of glycoglycerolipids found in spinach, which could inhibit cancer cell growth. A 2012 study showed that dietary spinach could suppress colon carcinogenesis by modulating microRNA profiles and other molecular pathways. This study underscored the potential of spinach in cancer prevention but did not claim it could cure existing cancers. The claim that green juice can cure cancer is mostly false. Although green juices are healthy and packed with essential nutrients and antioxidants, they cannot replace conventional cancer treatments. Cancer is a serious disease that requires professional medical intervention. Incorporating green juices and a healthy diet into your routine can support your overall well-being. However, when it comes to cancer, it's necessary to rely on evidence-based treatments.

No matter how long you've been on BP medicine, 90% of people reportedly stop needing it within 5 to 7 days.
quick_take: Green juice ingredients like mint, coriander, spinach, basil, neem, curry leaves, and amla may support blood pressure management, but there is no scientific evidence that they can cure hypertension or replace antihypertensive medication in 7 days. Stopping prescribed BP medication without medical supervision is dangerous and can increase the risk of stroke, heart attack, or heart failure.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Rajesh Badani, Associate Director, Interventional Cardiologist & Electrophysiologist, Aditya Birla Memorial Hospital told Medical Dialogues: 'Green juices, especially those made from beetroot, spinach, celery, or amla contain natural nitrates, antioxidants, and potassium that may support better blood pressure control. However, to claim they can 'cure' hypertension and replace prescribed medication within 7 days is both unrealistic and dangerous. High blood pressure is a chronic condition influenced by multiple factors: genetics, age, stress, diet, sleep, and physical activity. Discontinuing medication without medical supervision can increase the risk of stroke, heart attack, or heart failure. Green juice can be a valuable dietary addition, but it's not a substitute for evidence-based treatment.' Dr. Annapoorna Kalia, Senior Consultant, Interventional Cardiology at Aditya Birla Memorial Hospital added: 'While certain green juices have shown mild short-term benefits in lowering blood pressure due to their potassium and nitrate content, there is no scientific evidence that they can reverse hypertension or replace antihypertensive drugs in just a week. Blood pressure regulation is a long-term commitment, requiring a holistic approach—medications, diet, exercise, and stress management. Patients should be cautious of viral health claims. Instead of looking for a quick fix, focus on sustainable lifestyle changes under the guidance of your cardiologist. Never stop prescribed medication without a proper medical review.' The article further explains: While some listed ingredients may offer health benefits, there is no clinical proof that any combination of them can replace prescribed antihypertensive medication, especially not within a 7-day period. Relying solely on such juices may put individuals at serious health risk if it leads them to stop taking their medications without a doctor's guidance. The article cites individual studies for each ingredient: neem may exhibit antihypertensive properties via calcium channel inhibition, enhanced eNOS expression, and ERK1/2 signaling pathway activation (Yarmohammadi et al., PubMed); mint may contribute to decreases in systolic/diastolic blood pressure (Nematolahi et al.); curry leaves' high potassium and low sodium content may support BP management (Bioinformation/PMC10640786); tulsi leaf juice showed blood pressure improvement in hypertensive participants (Jamshidi et al., PMC5376420); high-nitrate spinach soup reduced central systolic blood pressure after 7 days (Jovanovski et al., PMC4525132); amla powder supplementation may help lower blood pressure (Attique et al.); coriander demonstrated blood pressure-lowering effects via cholinergic and Ca²⁺ antagonist mechanisms (Journal of Ethnopharmacology). Despite these individual supportive findings, none of these ingredients — individually or combined — have been shown to replace prescription medications or reverse hypertension in 7 days. According to WHO, high blood pressure (140/90 mmHg or higher) can be controlled with lifestyle modifications, diet, and medications but has no cure.

title: Can green leafy vegetable juice cure high blood pressure? - THIP
claim_text: A social media video claims that drinking a juice made from green leafy vegetables like coriander (dhaniya), curry leaves (kadi patta), spinach (palak), fenugreek leaves (methi), and mint (pudina) every morning can completely cure high blood pressure (hypertension), and one can stop taking blood pressure medication after adopting this practice.
quick_take: A social media video claims that drinking a juice made from a combination of green leafy vegetables daily can cure high blood pressure and help you stop taking your medication. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Several research studies have found that consuming green leafy vegetables, especially those rich in nitrates, does not consistently lead to a reduction in high blood pressure. These vegetables are undoubtedly beneficial for heart health, as they are good sources of potassium, magnesium, and dietary nitrates, all of which are associated with blood pressure regulation. However, the evidence on their direct impact on lowering blood pressure is mixed. It's essential to recognise that while green leafy vegetables and their fibre content can support blood pressure management, they don't work like medication. Drinking a few glasses of green juice won't reverse years of unhealthy habits or instantly treat a condition like hypertension. Instead, they should be seen as a valuable part of a heart-healthy diet, not a quick fix or miracle cure. A five-week dietary supplementation with leafy green vegetables or nitrate pills (containing an equal amount of inorganic nitrate) did not lead to a reduction in ambulatory systolic blood pressure in people with elevated blood pressure (2020 Study). In a 2014 study, participants followed either a high-nitrate or low-nitrate diet for seven days. The high-nitrate group increased their nitrate intake by at least 300 mg per day from leafy greens. While this significantly raised nitrate and nitrite levels in both saliva and blood (by at least four times), there was no meaningful difference in ambulatory, home, or clinic blood pressure readings, nor in measures of arterial stiffness. This suggests that a short-term increase in dietary nitrate may not effectively lower blood pressure in people with high-normal readings or at risk of hypertension. Hypertension is a chronic condition. It doesn't simply disappear because you've started drinking a healthy juice every day. The claim that it can be cured with a mix of leafy greens has no credible scientific evidence behind it. While some studies suggest that increasing vegetable and fruits intake can help lower blood pressure over time, there is a big difference between managing a condition and curing it. What's missing from this understanding is that high blood pressure often requires ongoing management through a combination of medication, diet, exercise, stress reduction, and regular monitoring. The danger lies in assuming that your blood pressure is 'fixed' just because your readings improve after making dietary changes. That's often the result of a combination of efforts, not just one juice. Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician shares, 'It might sound appealing that drinking a green smoothie or juice could lower high blood pressure, but the truth isn't that simple. Many people believe a single food or drink can fix their blood pressure, yet there are individuals who struggle to control it even with proper medication. If it were really that easy, we wouldn't see so many people still battling hypertension. That's exactly why modern medicine, or allopathy, exists. Sure, dietary changes can be part of a healthy lifestyle, but if a video tells you to stop your medication and rely only on such remedies, I strongly advise against it.' Never stop or change your blood pressure medication without speaking to your doctor, no matter how promising a home remedy sounds. Dr Almas Fatma, a General Physician from Navi Mumbai with qualifications in MBBS, Family Medicine, and Digital Health explains, 'The most reliable approach to lowering blood pressure involves a mix of healthy lifestyle habits and, when needed, medication. This includes eating a nutritious diet, staying physically active, cutting down on salt, and managing stress. In certain cases, doctors may recommend medication to help maintain healthy blood pressure levels. The goal is to tackle the underlying causes while supporting long-term well-being.' Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic in New Delhi explains, 'Bringing blood pressure down takes time and requires a combination of healthy habits and medical support. I always advise cutting back on alcohol, giving up smoking, and being more physically active. A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and low-fat foods also plays a vital role. While some patients may need medication, lifestyle changes are always the foundation of treatment.' High blood pressure is often called the 'silent killer' because it typically has no symptoms. Yet it can lead to life-threatening complications like stroke, heart attack, and kidney failure if left untreated. Medications prescribed by doctors are carefully chosen and dosed to control the condition and prevent damage to vital organs. Stopping medication because a social media influencer told you to is risky. In fact, many people who suddenly stop taking their medication experience a rebound effect, where their blood pressure shoots up even higher than before. This can result in emergency hospital visits or even fatal outcomes. Not necessarily harmful, but it's not a magical solution either. There's nothing wrong with drinking juice made from fresh greens, as long as it's made hygienically and consumed in moderation. These vegetables offer a wealth of nutrients, including vitamins A, C, and K, fibre, antioxidants, and plant-based compounds that support overall health. But problems arise when people consume it in excess or with unrealistic expectations. For instance, large quantities of methi or curry leaves might not sit well with everyone's digestive system. Some individuals, especially those with kidney disease or on certain medications, need to monitor their intake of potassium and other minerals. Juice should complement your meals, not become the centrepiece of your treatment plan.

title: Can green tea extracts be used to treat acne?
claim_text: A green tea solid cleansing mask contains green tea extract, which has anti-acne potential, effectively cleans skin pores, deeply cleans skin dirt, balances skin water and oil, replenishes skin moisture, and nourishes the skin.
quick_take: A viral Facebook post claims that a green tea face mask can cure acne. We verified the claim. According to our findings, the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
The product shown in the video is not trustworthy. The product is widely available on Amazon and Flipkart, but the names of the green tea extracts implicated have not been disclosed. Furthermore, there is no information about the exact concentrations of the green tea extracts. The product description also lacks the number of times it must be applied, and no precautions or side effects of the products are provided. As a result, the product should not be purchased unless a dermatologist has prescribed the same.

Regarding green tea extracts for acne treatment: Green tea is made from fresh leaves in a way that prevents the polyphenolic components from oxidizing. Catechins are the most common of these components. The main components of green tea beverages are catechins, flavonols, and other flavonoids. Catechins are divided into four types: catechin (C), epicatechin (EC), epicatechin gallate (ECG), epigallocatechin (EGC), and epicatechin-3-gallate (EGCG). The most abundant catechin is EGCG, which has been shown to have skin-health benefits. Acne is caused by excess sebum clogging pores and encouraging bacterial growth. As a result, green tea's EGCG is anti-androgenic and lowers lipid levels. This makes it effective at reducing sebum excretion in the skin. Hence, by reducing sebum production, EGCG can slow or stop the development of acne. Thus, green tea polyphenols could be promising in the treatment of acne vulgaris by reducing sebum production in the skin and acting as anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial agents. Even though studies have shown that green tea-containing topical creams and ointments or supplements may be beneficial, an effective dose is still unknown.

Regarding risks: Relying solely on green tea extracts to treat acne could be risky due to the complex nature of acne. As a result, the majority of treatments are only marginally effective. Traditional acne treatments include topical and systemic therapies, physical modalities, lasers, and photodynamic therapy. Nonetheless, all of these medications predispose people to potentially serious side effects, necessitating the development of more natural therapies with fewer side effects. Much more research is needed to conclusively prove green tea's efficacy as an acne treatment. It is unlikely that using a green tea mask alone will cure acne.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: The product being endorsed cannot be trusted because the names of the green tea extracts and their effective concentration for treating acne are not mentioned. Precautions and side effects are also missing from the product description. Although there is no denying that topical green tea is a safer option, the search yielded a limited number of findings on how green tea may be used in reducing sebum secretion and its role in acne pathology. As a result, more high-quality research studies are needed to determine the effective dosage of topical green tea extracts for the treatment of acne. Therefore, the claim is mostly false.

title: Fact Check: Can greying of hair be reversed with a DIY recipe?
claim_text: A homemade recipe made up of pomegranate peels, amla powder, mustard oil, and kalonji is a natural hair dye. Application of the formulation for 2-3 weeks is capable of turning your hair black for 800 years.
quick_take: A viral Instagram reel claims that a DIY recipe has the potential to permanently reverse greying of hair. We fact-checked the notion and found that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Greying of hair is a natural phenomenon that occurs as hair follicles gradually lose their pigment. Grey hair often appears when the melanocytes, which are the cells that give hair its colour, are less active. These cells eventually lose their effectiveness, which reduces melanin synthesis and causes hair to eventually turn grey. It is important to distinguish between premature and natural greying of the hair. People in their 20s and 30s usually exhibit this early onset of grey or white hair. While the primary cause of both gradual and premature greying of hair is characterised by reduced melanocytes, untimely onset is triggered by genetics, oxidative stress, and unhealthy lifestyle choices. Furthermore, certain systemic illnesses such as autoimmune disorders, vitamin deficits, and cardiovascular issues may also be associated with early greying. Dr. Swati Watwani, consultant dermatologist and medical director of Persianlily Clinic, further elucidates this distinction by stating that premature greying can occur as early as the 20s, while most individuals tend to experience it in their late 40s or early 50s. Determining the underlying cause of early greying—whether it be stress-associated, hormonal, or nutritional—may help delay its onset with appropriate therapy and care.

Regarding the DIY recipe: While natural DIY solutions might be safe, they cannot ensure permanent reversal of the greying. Kalonji, mustard oil, amla powder, and pomegranate peels are often touted as organic alternatives to stop greying, but their effectiveness is questioned. Pomegranate peel is packed with antioxidants and has been extensively studied for its potential to promote hair growth, but there is no credible scientific evidence to suggest it can reverse greying. Mustard oil is a classic hair care solution that promotes hair follicle stimulation and circulation. While it may delay the onset or reduce the appearance of grey hair, it cannot effectively prevent greying of hair. Amla (Indian gooseberry) is high in vitamin C and antioxidants and has demonstrated potential in addressing female androgenic hair loss, promoting the anagen phase, and possibly delaying the onset of greying. Despite these promising benefits, the scientific evidence backing its role in reversing greying remains inconclusive. Kalonji (Black Cumin Seeds) has been linked to several hair health benefits due to the presence of linoleic acid, which supports the functional potential of hair follicles. Additionally, they contain thymoquinone, a potent antioxidant that shields hair and may even promote scalp health. However, these benefits do not extend to reversing greying.

Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda, further supports this by stating that while genetically or age-related greying is irreversible, external factors such as lifestyle choices or environmental stressors may be able to slow it down. In these situations, taking the right actions might help prolong the preservation of hair pigment. While these ingredients may offer hair-related benefits, greying is primarily influenced by genetic factors and the natural ageing process, which cannot be reversed by a natural DIY recipe.

Dermatologists may suggest short-term fixes, including hair dyes and additional cosmetic procedures to cover grey hair. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, a dermatologist, cosmetologist, trichologist, and consultant for aesthetic medicine in Lucknow, explains that the most common alternative is hair dye; depending on your requirements, permanent, semi-permanent, and ammonia-free solutions are available. If you prefer a more natural look, henna can provide a reddish-brown tone; however, it might not completely cover greys. For quick solutions, root touch-up powders and sprays are good for covering greys in between dye sessions. Given that greying is primarily inherited, maintaining good hair can be achieved by consuming a balanced diet that includes adequate amounts of iron, zinc, and vitamin B12. While certain expert treatments, such as microneedling or specific serums, can enhance hair health, they cannot prevent greying. Accepting your grey hair is also a terrific alternative, as many individuals are now celebrating their silver hair with the right care and styling.

Consequently, these triggers induce a persistent inflammatory response, destroying tooth-supporting structures such as the periodontal ligament and alveolar bone. Unlike early gum-related issues that can be conservatively addressed, periodontitis necessitates expert attention. Furthermore, systemic diseases like diabetes, cardiovascular problems, and unfavourable pregnancy outcomes have been correlated with periodontal breakdown. Hence, advanced gum disease or periodontitis is a critical health concern that requires timely diagnosis and comprehensive therapeutic intervention. While guava leaves are one of the popular botanical choices, the scientific evidence backing their use in the management of advanced gum disease is inconclusive. Even while these results are encouraging, they are not sufficient to establish that guava leaves are a validated cure for advanced gum disease. They should therefore be viewed as an addition to established periodontal therapy rather than as a replacement for it. Dr. Ketan Rajput, Periodontist, and Oral Implantologist, Dhule, Maharashtra, adds that while guava leaves have antibacterial, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory properties, they are not an effective way of managing periodontitis. Reliance on such online therapies may conceal the symptoms and result in serious consequences because periodontal disintegration is a progressive condition that requires prompt attention. It is not advisable to rely on uncontrolled social media cures since periodontal disease leads to the deterioration of the tooth-supporting tissues, which may have both oral and systemic implications. Even though some natural remedies, including aloe vera gel, pomegranate, and green tea, have demonstrated better results as adjuncts to professional treatment, they shouldn't be used in place of them. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, an Ayurvedic expert and MD scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, advises that while historical Ayurvedic writings go into great depth about dental care, the assertions made in widely shared social media posts are primarily misleading. Should someone assert that the medication can be found in Ayurvedic texts, they must provide the specific source. This allows skilled Ayurvedic practitioners to properly examine it and direct treatment according to the requirements of each patient. The periodontal management approach involves: Extensive Diagnostic Stage (in-depth assessment including periodontal probing and radiographic evaluation), The non-surgical approach (root planning and scaling to remove supra- and sub-gingival plaque and calculus), Surgical periodontal intervention (pocket reduction and regenerative surgeries for persistent or severe issues), Post-operative phase (stringent maintenance schedule with reinforcement of oral hygiene practices and periodontal examinations). The treatment is not complete without blood sugar control, smoking cessation, and general health maintenance.

title: Fact Check: Can Guava leaves cure tumour?

doctor_explanation: Tumor is an abnormal growth of cells in the body. When cells in your body get damaged due to various factors, they die, forming new cells and replacing those dead cells. Sometimes, this ongoing cycle breaks down, resulting in the growth of abnormal or damaged cells that multiply when they shouldn't. It is a misconception that all tumors are cancerous in nature, some can be non-cancerous too. The cancerous ones widely spread to other parts of the body, increasing the risk of serious health issues. Usually, tumours are categorized into two types: malignant tumours, which are cancerous and benign tumours, which are non-cancerous. Tumours can appear anywhere in the body, including bones, skin, tissues, thigh or shoulder. Early detection of tumours can help save lives and prevent further complications. One could face symptoms such as fatigue, excessive sweat, especially at night, loss of appetite, bloating, sudden weight gain or weight loss, difficulty breathing, sore throat or ulcers lasting more than 3 weeks. It is important to consult experts or doctors to seek medical guidance to combat tumour to minimize further complications. The leaves of the guava plant (P. guajava) have been studied for their health benefits, which are attributed to their plethora of phytochemicals, such as quercetin, avicularin, apigenin, guaijaverin, kaempferol, hyperin, myricetin, gallic acid, catechin, epicatechin, chlorogenic acid, epigallocatechin gallate, and caffeic acid. Some research shows that guava does have some anticancer properties, but no definitive scientific evidence claims that drinking guava leaf juice can cure tumours or melt lumps. A study by Biswas et al. mentioned that 'phytochemicals or bioactive compounds, mainly polyphenols and flavonoids as well as essential oils of guava (P. guajava) fruits and leaves, are suitable for antioxidative, antiproliferative, antitumorigenic, and anticarcinogenic potential.' Another study by Lok et al. reported, 'The various parts of the guava plant have been shown to exhibit medicinal properties, such as antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antidiabetic activities. Recent studies have shown that the bioactive phytochemicals of several parts of the guava plant (P. guajava) exhibit anticancer activity.' Despite studies showing that guava may have some anticancer properties, no scientific evidence or consensus in the medical fraternity supports the claim that it can cure tumours. Dr Tirathram Kaushik stated, 'Various parts of fruits or plants, including leaves, are used for medicinal purposes and curing various health-related issues. Although guava leaf extract is believed to have anti-cancer properties, it might help tackle tumours. Guava leaf juice can help with health-related problems like stomach pain, reduce acne, improve digestion, and heal serious wounds. Overconsumption causes nausea, stomach pain and skin irritation. Moreover, there isn't any scientific research to support or justify this claim. So, there is no knowledge about how it works for the patients. Individuals are advised to seek medical attention for treating serious conditions like tumors instead of fully depending on such hacks. Don't fall prey to anyone, such as trends or forward messages on social media. It is better to discuss with your doctor before following any such quick fixes, as they can do more harm than good. Be alert and stick to the advice given by the expert.' Dr. Philip George Kuttikat added, 'Green leaves may contain antioxidants, which can be present in various types of leaves, not limited to guava leaves. However, to claim that they can resolve tumours is unscientific. Such assertions could mislead patients with tumours, potentially causing delays in receiving proper cancer treatment.'
