title: Fact Check: Can Melasma be treated using apple cider vinegar or lemon? - THIP Media
claim_text: Melasma can be treated at home by applying different home remedies, such as apple cider vinegar or lemon. The YouTube video shows that melasma can be treated by applying lemon or a mixture of apple cider vinegar with water in equal amounts.
quick_take: A social media post claims that Melasma can be treated at home by applying different home remedies, such as apple cider vinegar or lemon. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Melasma is a skin condition that causes patches and spots, usually on the face, which is darker than your natural skin tone. It is characterized by gray-brown patches of skin discoloration on areas of the face exposed to the sun. It is an entirely harmless condition; however, it can make some people feel self-conscious and impact the quality of life. Its cause is not yet completely understood, but there are some known triggering factors such as sun exposure, pregnancy, sexual hormones, inflammatory processes of the skin, and the use of cosmetics, steroids, and photosensitizing drugs. Treatment of melasma, such as creams, cannot make melasma disappear; however, it can help fade the discoloration. The most effective treatment is a sun protective agent and medications applied to the skin. Various treatment options are available to reduce discoloration; however, research states that the most effective and well-studied treatment options are Hydroquinone monotherapy and triple combination cream. Also, there is a high risk of adverse effects with chemical peels and laser- and light-based therapies, even though these treatment modalities are equal to or inferior to topical treatment options. Dr. Swati Watwani, Medical Director, Co-Founder & Chief Consultant, Persianlily – Skin/Hair/Aesthetics/Ayurveda Clinic, says, 'Melasma, Photomelanosis & post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation can be reduced with topical creams such as hydroquinone, tretinoin, topical steroids, alpha hydroxy acid creams, azelaic acid, arbutin, liquorice, kojic acid. If the condition doesn't improve with these medicines then other modalities should be used.' There is no scientific evidence that proves that melasma can be treated at home using ingredients such as lemon or apple cider vinegar. These ingredients are highly acidic in nature and can irritate your skin. The skin irritation can worsen the melasma, eventually leading to the darkening of the spots which you were trying to lighten. Additionally, even though lemon is a good source of Vitamin C and is an antioxidant, using lemon directly on the skin is not recommended as the application of lemon can make the skin more susceptible to sun damage as citrus lemon is a photosensitizer. Dr. Watwani further elaborates by stating, 'Nowadays Internet has no shortage of skin hacks and DIY remedies. While some help to certain extent, others can be harmful as these are anecdotal claims and have not been supported by scientific review. Additionally, things like lemon juice and apple cider vinegar may make melasma worse.' She further elaborates and says, 'The number of patients that visit dermatologists with pigmentary disorders is significant. Patients are often overwhelmed with numerous over-the-counter skin-lightening agents, many without clinical evidence of efficacy. Botanical and natural ingredients have become popular as depigmenting products. However, evidence-based studies on many of these agents are still lacking.'

title: Fact Check: Can men get pregnant?
claim_text: A man has given birth to three children - titled '"Nothing is impossible": The World's First Male Pregnancy and the Birth of His Three Children'
quick_take: An article published on a media website claims that a man has given birth to three children. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: The headline of the article does not give the correct picture of what the article speaks about. Sensationalized headlines or unverified information can cause confusion about sensitive medical procedures among the public. While medical science has made significant strides in assisted reproduction, such as surrogacy and in vitro fertilization, male pregnancy is not a medically recognized phenomenon. While medical science has advanced significantly in the areas of fertility treatments and transgender medicine, male pregnancy is not yet possible.

title: Fact Check: Can menstrual irregularities be managed at home?
claim_text: An Instagram post claims that a homemade concoction of ginger, fennel seeds, and cinnamon combined with honey might help with irregular periods. In addition to helping with menstrual disturbances, consuming it daily may help reduce hormonal imbalances and ease period-related pain or discomfort.
quick_take: According to a well-known Instagram reel, an at-home preparation could manage menstrual irregularities. We analysed the claim and found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: The term 'menstrual irregularities' refers to a wider range of aberrant menstrual cycle patterns. The following factors typically cause irregular menstrual periods in terms of duration, flow, or their absence. Medical examination is vital for the accurate identification and clinical management of menstrual irregularities. A herbal remedy that combines fennel seeds, ginger, cinnamon, and honey is often advertised on social media as a natural remedy for irregular menstruation. Despite having a high bioactive profile, these ingredients' efficacy cannot be relied on for addressing irregular menses. This is supported by Dr. Padmavathi Kapila, Chief Consultant Obstetrician & Gynaecologist, Renova Hospitals, Langar House, Hyderabad, who states that irregular periods include cycles that are shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days, bleeding during the interval, exceptionally painful periods, heavy and prolonged bleeding for more than a week, and fertility issues. Dr. Kapila cautions that while fennel seeds, cinnamon, ginger, and honey have been used as traditional remedies for irregular menstruation, this is not an evidence-based approach. Honey may be a calming carrier for herbs and may help with energy levels if irregular menstruation is linked to overall weakness or nutritional problems. Additionally, there is limited evidence that fennel seeds and ginger can aid with menstrual cramps and that cinnamon can help with irregularities connected to PCOS. Furthermore, endometriosis, PCOS, thyroid issues, and uterine fibroids are among the underlying conditions associated with irregular periods that require medical attention. For any irregularities related to your period, consult a gynaecologist. Herbal infusions and dietary practices, though considered traditional therapies with marginal positive outcomes, exhibit limited clinical evidence to support their use in addressing complex or long-term illnesses. Among the conditions that call for precise diagnosis and targeted treatment approaches are irregular menstrual cycles, diabetes, and hypertension. It is not encouraged to replace established therapies with unverified at-home remedies because relying on them might delay medical assessment, permitting silent progression, leading to irreversible consequences. Self-medication without expert supervision may conceal symptoms, resulting in an incorrect diagnosis. Therefore, under a doctor's strict supervision, it is advised to incorporate safe supportive measures in addition to appropriate treatment. The practice not only facilitates timely intervention but may also prevent worsening of the condition. Changing to a healthier lifestyle is essential to managing menstrual irregularities holistically. Weight regulation is the cornerstone: Regular exercise and a healthy diet may improve cycle regulation and ovulation. Diets high in micronutrients, fibre, legumes, and healthy fats are usually recommended, as is a decrease in processed foods and added sugar. A weekly minimum of 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise has been associated with the regulation of the menstrual cycle. Soumam Dutta, PhD Scholar in Nutrition at the Department of Endocrinology, ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, asserts that the menstrual cycle is a complicated hormonal process that involves several hormones, such as progesterone, oestrogen, FSH, and LH, and cannot be controlled by a single factor like diet. However, maintaining overall menstrual health necessitates consuming a healthy, proportionate diet. Healthy practices of yoga, mindfulness, or meditation exhibit a positive correlation with the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, which ultimately supports cycle regularity. A regular sleep schedule, abstinence from alcohol and caffeine, and additional factors may also have an impact on hormonal stability. These lifestyle interventions complement the medical guidance, thereby offering a safe and sustainable approach to improving menstrual health. If the menstrual cycle is absent for more than three months, the cycles are shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days, or there is major bleeding, excruciating pain, or discharge, medical intervention is necessary. The management process usually begins with a thorough medical history, physical examination, and relevant diagnostic procedures. Among the laboratory tests are diagnostic imaging, hormonal profile, and occasional endometrial examination. Following confirmation of the diagnosis, Gynaecologist Dr. Anita Gupta, Associate Director at Fortis La Femme, New Delhi, advises that the first line of therapy should be pharmaceutical intervention of the underlying cause. Hormone-based medications are usually recommended for the effective regulation of the menstrual cycle. Please be advised that irregular menstruation is a complicated, multifaceted health issue that entails timely, personalised medical therapy. Such an individualised, evidence-based approach ensures effective menstrual cycle regulation while fostering long-term reproductive and overall wellness.

title: Can Methi, Clove, Kalonji and Onion Cure Dandruff for 100 Years?
claim_text: Spraying a mixture of methi, clove, kalonji, and onion on the scalp will not only cure dandruff for 100 years but also promote such rapid hair growth that it will need to be burned off.
quick_take: A social media post claims that spraying a mixture of methi, clove, kalonji, and onion on the scalp will cure dandruff for 100 years. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: The claim that a natural mixture can permanently cure dandruff for 100 years is false. Dandruff is caused by a variety of factors such as scalp dryness, fungal infections (like Malassezia), seborrheic dermatitis, and even certain lifestyle habits. While ingredients like methi, clove, kalonji, and onion may offer temporary relief by soothing the scalp or addressing some causes of dandruff, they cannot offer a one-time cure lasting for 100 years. Scientific evidence has shown that dandruff treatments, including natural remedies, can be effective in managing symptoms in the short term. However, dandruff often requires ongoing care because its underlying causes, such as scalp inflammation or fungal overgrowth, can persist. Thus, promising a cure that lasts for a century is simply not feasible. In a 2014 study, researchers used methi paste and it showed positive results on dandruff. Methi (fenugreek) has antifungal properties, which could help with dandruff caused by fungal infections. It also contains lecithin, which nourishes the scalp and may reduce dryness. Clove has antiseptic and antimicrobial properties that can help maintain a clean scalp, preventing the growth of dandruff-causing fungi. Kalonji, or black seed, is believed to have anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects, which could soothe the scalp and reduce dandruff symptoms. Onion, rich in sulphur, is often used in traditional medicine to combat scalp infections, though its impact on dandruff is still under investigation. While these ingredients can provide temporary relief and soothe an irritated scalp, they won't eliminate dandruff forever. Even if they offer short-term improvements, they cannot prevent the condition from returning. Dr. Sachin Gupta, Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, explained that dandruff is a chronic condition, meaning it can be managed with the right care and treatment but often returns. Medicated shampoos containing active ingredients like zinc pyrithione, selenium sulphide, or ketoconazole are commonly used to treat dandruff. These ingredients address the root causes, such as the overgrowth of the Malassezia fungus or excess oil production on the scalp, but they must be used regularly to maintain their effectiveness. He further added, 'Even prescription treatments or medicated shampoos cannot guarantee a 100-year cure. If not properly managed, dandruff may resurface, especially during times of stress, environmental changes, or hormonal shifts.' Dr. Mohit Sandhu, BAMS, CAD, CAC, and PGDAKS, Founder of the Association for Ayurvedic Palpative Pain Medicine, Gurgaon, said 'Ayurveda highlights that external remedies alone cannot provide a permanent cure for dandruff unless underlying factors like poor diet, stress, or hormonal imbalances are addressed. While the mentioned mixture may offer temporary relief, it is not a 100-year cure. Ayurveda advocates for a holistic approach that combines diet, lifestyle changes, and herbal remedies for long-term, sustainable results.' While the combination of methi, clove, kalonji, and onion may provide relief from dandruff symptoms in the short term, it cannot offer a permanent, lifetime solution. Dandruff is a recurring condition that requires ongoing care and proper treatment.

title: Fact Check: Can methi daana, kalonji, apple cider vinegar, honey, and olive oil water dissolve gallbladder stones naturally in 15 days?
claim_text: Methi daana, kalonji, apple cider vinegar, honey, and olive oil water dissolve gallbladder stones naturally in 15 days, eliminating the need for gallbladder removal surgery.
verdict_original: The claim by the user is FALSE
quick_take: An Instagram post falsely claims that a mixture of methi daana, kalonji, apple cider vinegar, honey, and olive oil can dissolve gallbladder stones naturally in 15 days. There is no scientific evidence supporting this claim. Gallstones typically require medical treatment, including medication or surgery.
doctor_explanation:
Dr K Hemanth Kumar, Consultant - Surgical Gastroenterology, GI Oncology & HPB, Robotic Surgery, Manipal Hospital Old Airport Road, explained: 'The gallbladder is a small organ that stores bile produced by the liver. Gallstones (medically termed cholelithiasis) are hardened deposits that form in the gallbladder. When the bile in the gallbladder becomes concentrated and the substances within it, like cholesterol, bilirubin, and calcium, exceed their solubility limits, they become crystallized and form gallstones. This formation process is categorized into 3 sections: Super Saturation, Crystal Formation, and Crystal Aggregation. There are various factors involved in gallstone formation. High cholesterol levels in bile, incomplete gallbladder emptying, hormonal factors, and certain medications are a few common contributing factors.
Although belief persists, there is no scientific evidence to support that a mixture of fenugreek seeds, black seeds, apple cider vinegar, honey, and olive oil can dissolve gallbladder stones. While some studies indicate that fenugreek may help reduce cholesterol levels and prevent gallstone formation in animals, there is no conclusive evidence that it can dissolve existing gallstones in humans. Some traditional remedies also mention black seeds for gallstones, but there is no scientific evidence for this either. While honey and olive oil may offer some general health benefits, no conclusive report can support their claim to dissolve gallstones. Gallstones typically require medical treatment, which may include medication or surgery, depending on the severity and size of the stones.
Gallstones, when kept in a petri dish and poured with apple cider vinegar, would easily dissolve. This is because vinegar is an acetic acid. However, it's not really possible until you remove gallstones surgically to expose them to acetic acid. Now, you may think you can drink the apple cider vinegar. But the cider goes through the digestive process, breaks down into various chemical components, enters the bloodstream, and by the time it reaches the gallbladder, it's no longer acidic. Therefore, it won't be effective on any stones residing in your gallbladder.'
Dr Kiran B, Consultant - Gastroenterologist, Manipal Hospital, Varthur Road, broke down the individual scientific evidence of the ingredients as follows:
1. Apple Cider Vinegar (ACV): Claim that ACV can dissolve gallstones is Not proven — no scientific proof exists; anecdotal reports may help with pain but do not dissolve stones.
2. Black Seeds (Nigella sativa): Some animal studies show hepatoprotective and anti-inflammatory properties, but no direct evidence of gallstone dissolution in humans. Verdict: Promising for liver health, but not proven for gallstones.
3. Fenugreek Seeds: A few animal studies show fenugreek may reduce cholesterol in bile, which could potentially help prevent gallstone formation, not dissolve existing ones. Verdict: May help in prevention, not treatment.
4. Honey: No evidence that honey has any effect on gallstones beyond general health benefits. Verdict: No proven role in dissolving stones.
5. Olive Oil: The idea of a 'gallbladder flush' using olive oil is not supported by science. What people often pass during a flush are soap-like substances, not actual gallstones. Verdict: Myth; olive oil doesn't dissolve stones.
Dr Kiran B further added: 'While lifestyle changes such as a healthy diet and regular exercise can help prevent gallstones, there is no scientific evidence supporting the use of natural remedies like the combination mentioned above to dissolve existing gallstones. If you suspect you have gallstones or are experiencing symptoms, it's crucial to consult a healthcare professional for appropriate diagnosis and treatment. Relying on unproven natural remedies can delay necessary medical intervention and may lead to complications.'
A study by Agostino Di Ciaula et al. highlights the significant role of diet in the formation of cholesterol gallstones, emphasizing that modifiable environmental factors such as dietary intake affect cholesterol synthesis in the liver, bile composition, and gallbladder motility. The study links obesity, insulin resistance, and poor dietary habits to increased risk, while a diet high in fiber, specific macronutrients, and vitamin C may provide protective effects. quick_take: A social media post claims that methi, kalonji, and kala chana can control diabetes in a month. We fact checked this claim, and found that this is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: No, this mixture cannot cure or control diabetes in a month. Diabetes is a chronic condition that requires long-term management. According to the National Institutes of Health, "There is not enough high-quality evidence to determine whether fenugreek is useful for diabetes." In an earlier conversation with THIP Media, Dr V Mohan discussed diabetes remission and cure. He explained that while the terms "diabetes reversal" and "diabetes cure" have become popular, they are not new ideas. The correct term is "diabetes remission," which means the condition improves temporarily but can return. Currently, there is no permanent cure for diabetes. Dr P Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita School of Ayurveda, explained that Ayurveda categorises diabetes into different stages based on its progression. In the early stage, called Kapha Prameha, lifestyle changes and supportive therapies may help in management and even reversal. As it advances to Pitta Prameha, lifelong medication becomes necessary rather than a cure. In the most severe stage, Vata Prameha, managing diabetes becomes much more challenging. While research continues to explore potential treatments, no single herb or remedy has been scientifically proven to cure diabetes completely. Dr Muskan Thakur, BAMS, Ayurveda Consultant from Indore, explains that Ayurveda classifies diabetes as Prameha, a condition with 20 types, each linked to imbalanced doshas (biological energies), mainly Kapha. Among these, 10 are Kapha-dominant and considered Sadhya (curable), 6 are Pitta-dominant and classified as Yapya (difficult to cure), while 4 are Vata-dominant and regarded as Ashadhya (incurable). Ayurvedic treatments, including herbs like Haridra, Giloy, Fenugreek, Shilajit, Gudmar, and Vijaysar, may help regulate blood sugar, but a complete cure is not always possible—especially in Type 1 diabetes. In Type 2 diabetes, lifestyle changes such as a balanced diet, regular exercise, and stress management may actually help in blood sugar control. However, people should approach exaggerated claims with caution. Dr Thakur further notes that in the early stages of diabetes, Ayurvedic treatment may assist in managing the condition before turning to oral hypoglycaemic agents (OHAs) or insulin. For genetically inherited diabetes, Ayurveda may provide supportive care, but it does not guarantee a permanent cure for all. Do these ingredients have any benefits for diabetes management? Maybe, but only as part of a balanced diet. However, consuming these ingredients alone without addressing other lifestyle factors will not effectively control diabetes. Diabetes management involves a combination of diet, exercise, and medical supervision. There is no shortcut or single ingredient that can replace these essential steps.

title: Can milk cream and lemon mix really erase acne marks?
claim_text: A YouTube video asserts that mixing two teaspoons of milk cream with a few drops of lemon juice can remove acne marks with regular use. It suggests rubbing this mix on the face at night and washing it off with warm water in the morning.
quick_take: A social media post claims that milk cream and lemon mix can really erase acne marks. We fact checked this claim and termed it as false.
doctor_explanation:
Milk cream, particularly dairy-based cream, contains fats and oils that are generally not recommended for acne-prone skin. Moisturisers can help overall skin health, but applying heavy creams can potentially clog pores, known as being comedogenic. Clogged pores can lead to new acne breakouts, which would only add to the problem of acne marks rather than solving it. Effective treatment for acne marks ideally involves ingredients that promote skin cell turnover or reduce pigmentation, neither of which is a primary function of simple dairy cream.

Lemon juice contains citric acid, a type of alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA), and Vitamin C. AHAs help remove dead skin cells, and Vitamin C is an antioxidant that may reduce dark spots and brighten the skin over time. However, the form of Vitamin C in lemon juice doesn't absorb well into the skin because it's water-soluble, so any benefit is quite limited. The bigger concern is its high acidity. Lemon juice has a pH between 2 and 3, which can disturb the skin's natural barrier. This can cause irritation, dryness, redness, or even a burning sensation, especially on sensitive or acne-prone skin. Although lemon juice might give mild exfoliation in theory, lemon juice is too harsh and unsafe for regular use on the face.

It is not safe to leave lemon juice mixture on your face overnight. Lemon juice is highly acidic and can damage the skin's natural barrier when left on for long periods, especially overnight. This can cause severe irritation, chemical burns, and a painful condition called phytophotodermatitis — triggered when the skin is exposed to sunlight after contact with certain plant compounds like lemon. Although milk cream may seem to soften the mixture, it doesn't cancel out the risks and could even clog pores.

Dr Sonali Kohli, Consultant Dermatologist at Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, warns that lemon juice can disturb the skin's natural pH and trigger irritation, especially when exposed to sunlight. This can lead to a condition called phytophotodermatitis. She recommends avoiding direct use of lemon on the face and instead using Vitamin C serums that are formulated to be safe and gentle on the skin.

Dr Rashi Soni, Dermatologist and Co-founder of Rashi Hospital in Mumbai explains: 'Yes, there are much safer and more effective ways to treat acne scars than using harsh home remedies like lemon juice. We usually recommend treatments such as retinoids, chemical peels, microneedling or laser therapy, depending on the type and depth of the scars. Even using a good Vitamin C serum, approved by dermatologists, can help brighten the skin and reduce uneven tone over time. The key is to treat the skin gently and be consistent. Harsh ingredients can often make things worse, especially if the skin is already sensitive or healing. It's always best to speak to a dermatologist before trying anything new on your face.'

Medically approved treatments are far more effective and safer. Dermatologists recommend treatments like retinoids, chemical peels, microneedling or laser therapy. For natural options, ingredients like aloe vera or licorice extract have mild brightening effects and are safer.

title: Fact Check: Can milk, ghee, and mishri cure all weaknesses?
claim_text: An Instagram post suggests that consuming a glass of milk with a teaspoon of cow's ghee and mishri can cure physical, mental, and brain-related weaknesses, according to Ayurvedic principles.
quick_take: A social media post claims that milk, ghee, and mishri can cure all weaknesses related to physical, mental, and brain health. We performed a fact check and determined this claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
## Does milk provide nutritional benefits?
Yes, it does. Milk is a good source of calcium, protein, and essential vitamins and minerals. These nutrients support bone health, muscle function, and overall well-being. Milk contributes to a balanced diet and helps maintain physical health. Despite this, some social media posts misleadingly claim that animal milk weakens bones. However, it does not cure physical, mental, or brain-related weaknesses.

## Does ghee have any health benefits?
Well, yes. Ghee contains fat-soluble vitamins and butyric acid, which may have anti-inflammatory properties. It is known for helping in digestion and providing quick energy. However, ghee is also high in saturated fat, which can negatively impact cardiovascular health if consumed excessively. Moderation is essential. Some studies suggest potential benefits, but we need more research to confirm these claims.

## Does mishri offer any unique health advantages?
Not really. Mishri is a less refined form of sugar. While it is considered more natural than table sugar, it is still primarily composed of sucrose. Mishri provides quick energy but does not offer any unique health benefits. Excessive consumption can lead to weight gain, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular issues. There is no scientific evidence suggesting it is healthier than other types of sugar.

## Can a mixture of milk, ghee, and mishri cure physical weakness?
Maybe. The combination of milk, ghee, and mishri provides calories and some nutrients, which can temporarily boost energy levels and help with certain types of physical weakness related to nutritional deficiencies. However, it is not the ultimate cure for all types of physical weakness. Some conditions, like chronic fatigue, anaemia, or muscle weakness, require specific medical treatments. Therefore, this mixture should not be considered a solution for all physical health issues.

## Can a mixture of milk, ghee, and mishri cure mental weakness?
No, it cannot. Mental weakness can involve stress, anxiety, depression, or cognitive decline. While good nutrition supports overall mental well-being, this mixture is not a proven remedy for mental health issues. Conditions like anxiety or depression require a combination of medical treatment, therapy, and lifestyle changes. Drinking milk with ghee and mishri may provide temporary comfort but is not a substitute for professional care.

## Can a mixture of milk, ghee, and mishri cure brain-related weaknesses?
No, there is no evidence. Brain-related weaknesses can result from neurological disorders, nutritional deficiencies, or age-related cognitive decline. Although milk and ghee contain nutrients that support brain health, such as vitamins B12 and D, there is no evidence to suggest this mixture can cure these conditions. Proper diagnosis and specialised medical care are required for brain-related health issues.

Expert Opinion from Dr Muskan Thakur, BAMS, Ayurveda Consultant from Indore: "While Ayurveda recognises the nourishing qualities of milk and ghee, and their potential to support overall well-being, it's crucial to understand that no single mixture can universally 'cure' all weaknesses. True Ayurvedic practice is about restoring balance in an individual, considering their unique constitution (Prakriti) and imbalances (Vikriti). To claim this specific combination is a 'miracle cure' oversimplifies the complexity of health. Such remedies can be supportive, but should always be used in conjunction with a holistic approach and never as a replacement for necessary medical interventions."

Expert Opinion from Dr Mohit Sandhu, BAMS, Ayurveda Consultant and Kshar Sutra expert from Hamirpur, Himachal Pradesh: "According to Ayurveda, the combination of milk, ghee, and mishri is considered balya (strength-giving) and can nourish the body and mind. It supports ojas (vital energy) and can improve vitality when used appropriately. However, claiming it as a cure for all physical, mental, and brain-related weaknesses is misleading. Ayurveda emphasises balance and individualised treatment, so this mixture may not be suitable for everyone. It's always best to consult a qualified practitioner for specific health concerns."

THIP Media take: The claim that milk, ghee, and mishri can cure all weaknesses is mostly false. While milk, ghee, and mishri provide some nutritional benefits and energy, the claim that this mixture cures all forms of physical, mental, and brain-related weaknesses is misleading. There is no scientific evidence to support such broad health claims. Ayurvedic practices are valuable for overall well-being but should be used alongside conventional medical care, not as a replacement. The Instagram post exaggerates the health benefits, creating false expectations about this traditional mixture.

The US CDC defines brain health as "an ability to perform all the mental processes of cognition, including the ability to learn and judge, use language, and remember." The brain has three primary functions: interpreting sensory information and controlling movement, supporting cognitive processes and mental/emotional well-being, and regulating behaviour and facilitating social interactions. The three main parts of the brain are the cerebrum (responsible for motor/sensory information, emotions, intelligence, memory, and complex thinking), cerebellum (controls smooth/accurate movements, thinking, focusing, language, and emotions), and brainstem (controls breathing, heart rate, body temperature, sleep cycles, digestion, and reflexes). It is incorrect to say the brain functions at 100%. The brain has over 120 billion neurons responsible for transmitting information, and while not all regions are active at the same time, all areas of the brain are active to some degree over the course of the day. Resting-state fMRI studies show the brain continuously communicates between different regions through interconnected networks (e.g., default-mode network), even when not performing specific tasks. While coffee (C. arabica) contains bioactive compounds such as chlorogenic acid, polyphenols, caffeine, and minerals like potassium and magnesium, with some studies suggesting benefits for type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's disease, liver disease, and cardiovascular disease — and lemon (Citrus limon L.) offers vitamin C, antioxidants, heart health benefits, and kidney stone prevention — and cinnamon is known for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, antimicrobial, and heart-protective effects with potential benefits for Parkinson's and Alzheimer's diseases — a systematic review published in Nutritional Neuroscience concluded that cinnamon and its bioactive compounds may positively influence brain function particularly in areas related to memory and learning, but does not mention 100% improvement. A review in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health highlighted that low to moderate coffee consumption may support improvements in cognitive function and mental well-being, but does not suggest 100% increase. A study in Antioxidants on lemon's role in brain function found Lemon IntegroPectin (derived from organic lemon waste) shows potential to protect brain cells and mitochondria from oxidative stress linked to diseases like Alzheimer's, but does not mention lemon juice or any 100% brain function claim. Dr Vikram Sharma, Clinical Director & Senior Consultant Neurologist at CARE Hospitals, Banjara Hills, Hyderabad, told Medical Dialogues: "While a cup of coffee or a squeeze of lemon may energize in their own right, together with cinnamon they form no magic elixir. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that consuming them together on an empty stomach can increase brain function by 100%. Though caffeine can stir alertness and focus in the short term, such household items hold no secret to doubling brain function overnight. Cinnamon may support neural processes through time, and vitamin C aids overall wellness, but their mixture creates no overnight intellectual transformation. It's important to rely on balanced nutrition, regular exercise, and proper sleep for optimal brain health. Always approach such claims critically and consult healthcare professionals for personalized advice." Dr Avinash Kulkarni, DM (Neurology), MRCP SCE (Neurology), Fellowship in Neuroimmunology, added: "Drinking a mixture of coffee, lemon juice, and cinnamon powder on an empty stomach is unlikely to increase brain function by 100%. While each ingredient has individual health benefits — caffeine in coffee can boost alertness, lemon juice is rich in antioxidants, and cinnamon may support blood sugar regulation — there is no scientific evidence to support this specific combination dramatically enhancing brain function. Improving brain health requires a holistic approach, including a balanced diet, regular exercise, proper sleep, and mental stimulation."

title: Fact Check: Can mixture of roasted black sesame seeds, poppy seeds, and jaggery reverse arthritis?
claim_text: A mixture of roasted black sesame seeds, poppy seeds, and jaggery can reverse arthritis. The Instagram post states: "When the greasing (lubrication) finishes, a gap forms between the knees, and when you go to the doctor, they will directly tell you to replace the knees, that surgery is needed. For those whose knee fluid (also called grease) has diminished, or if you feel that there is a sound coming from your knees, this will help. Even for children — if their parents are suffering and they fear that they might develop it later — they should start eating it too. Eat it three to four times a week or even just for 10 days in a month. Along with this, start eating a little bit of pure mineral-rich jaggery. You will notice that knees that were making cracking, stiffening sounds will start feeling relaxed."
verdict_original: The claim is False. Hence, the claim by the user is FALSE.
quick_take: The claim that a mixture of roasted black sesame seeds, poppy seeds, and jaggery can reverse arthritis is false. While black sesame seeds and poppy seeds have anti-inflammatory benefits which may help in the management and treatment of arthritis, there is no clinical evidence to support the idea that this or any food mixture can cure or reverse arthritis.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Srikanth Madikaattu, Consultant - Orthopaedic Surgeon And Joint Replacement Surgeon, Manipal Hospital, Baner, Pune, in a conversation with The Medical Dialogues Fact Check Team said: "Arthritis is a condition commonly seen in older adults, where the cartilage in the joints becomes thin and starts to wear away, a process we refer to as cartilage loss. On an X-ray, this typically appears as a reduction in the joint space. It often occurs due to lack of exercise, reduced strength in the knee, or weakening of the surrounding muscles. These factors increase the chances of cartilage deterioration and the development of arthritis. Arthritis is usually graded as mild, moderate, or severe. In mild to moderate cases, pain can often be managed through physical therapy, exercises, or injections such as viscosupplementation, which help reduce pain. Medications like paracetamol may also help when combined with regular exercise. In severe cases, when pain persists despite medications and therapy, we begin to consider surgical options. Many patients believe that arthritis is a reversible condition that can be cured with medication. However, with age, cartilage naturally wears down. Once damaged, cartilage cannot regenerate. What we can do is slow down its degeneration and manage the symptoms. Strengthening the muscles around the knee, maintaining bone density, and leading a healthy lifestyle are essential for preserving knee function and reducing stress on the cartilage. Patients often ask whether arthritis can be cured with medications. While medicines can help manage pain, they cannot regenerate cartilage. Relying solely on medication may eventually lead to worsening joint deformities, making surgical treatment more complex and less effective. It's important to educate patients that knee arthritis is a progressive condition. To prevent its progression, consistent physical strengthening and proper weight management are crucial. Sometimes, medications are needed to maintain bone health. Patients often express a desire to avoid surgery. To do so, they must maintain a healthy lifestyle and manage their weight. Nowadays, there are also claims in the market about regenerating cartilage and meniscus, but these methods are not proven. We've seen many patients who undergo such treatments and return years later with no relief — by then, the deformity has worsened, making surgery riskier and less effective. Therefore, patients should understand that knee arthritis is a slowly progressive disease. Initial treatment can include paracetamol, viscosupplement injections, and physical therapy. In some cases, offloading braces can help reduce pressure on the joint. However, if the pain continues to worsen and is not relieved by medical or physical therapy, surgery remains a reliable and effective option to restore quality of life."

Dt Priyanka Bandal, Senior dietician, Manipal Hospital, Baner, Pune, further said: "Kale til that is black sesame, white sesame, white til and khaskhas that is poppy seeds as supportive foods in the dietary management of rheumatoid arthritis. These seeds are rich in omega-6 fatty acids, calcium, magnesium and antioxidants which may help reduce inflammation, support joint health and oxidative stress. So, their nutrient density makes them valuable in addressing bone, demineralization, and fatigue. If these are commonly seen in the patients and they should be used in a control portion due to their calorie density and always under supervised dietary planning, especially uh those who are diabetic uh or any metabolic concern."

While ingredients like black sesame seeds and poppy seeds possess anti-inflammatory and nutritional properties that may support the management of arthritis, they are not a cure or a method for reversing the disease. There is no scientific or clinical evidence to validate the claim that consuming a mixture of roasted black sesame seeds, poppy seeds, and jaggery can reverse arthritis. A study published in Molecules found that black sesame seeds are rich in lignans namely sesamin, sesamol, sesaminol, and sesamolin which possess notable antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects — these properties might help in reducing inflammation, a key symptom of arthritis. In a study, Riya Singh et al. found that poppy seeds possess promising health-promoting properties including anti-inflammatory effects. There are no scientific studies supporting the use of jaggery for arthritis.

title: Fact Check: Can mobile phones cause brain cancer?
claim_text: Mobile phone use can lead to brain cancer due to 5G radiation. Additionally, any phone with a SAR value higher than 1.6 W/kg poses a significant health risk.
quick_take: A social media post claims that mobile phones cause brain cancer due to 5G radiation. We fact checked the claim and found it to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Does mobile phone usage cause brain cancer? Not really, the evidence is not strong and still inconclusive. As of now, all the major health organisations do not support the claim that mobile phones can cause cancer or specifically brain cancer. The claim that mobile phones cause brain cancer has been a long-debated topic, but current scientific evidence does not support a direct link between mobile phone use and brain cancer. In 2011, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), part of the World Health Organisation, designated radiofrequency (RF) waves emitted by mobile phones as "possibly carcinogenic" and classified them as Group 2B. This classification was based on limited evidence suggesting a potential connection between long-term mobile phone use (e.g., 30 minutes per day for 10 years) and glioma, a type of brain cancer. However, this does not mean mobile phones definitely cause cancer. It simply indicates that some evidence exists, but it's not enough to confirm a strong, direct link. Dr Akanksha Chhabra, Medical Oncologist, Max Healthcare, New Delhi, states, "While concerns about mobile phone usage remain, it's essential to consider the current evidence. The studies show inconsistent results regarding a direct link between mobile phones and cancer. Ongoing research is critical to understanding any long-term effects. Until then, maintaining a balanced perspective is vital." Dr Pooja Khullar, Radiation Oncologist, Dharamshila Narayana Super Speciality Hospital, New Delhi, says, "Cell phones emit radiation in the radiofrequency region of the electromagnetic spectrum. Second-, third-, and fourth-generation cell phones (2G, 3G, 4G) emit radiofrequency in the range of 0.7–2.7 GHz, while fifth-generation (5G) phones are anticipated to use frequencies up to 80 GHz. Cell phones emit radiation in the form of radiofrequency radiation (RFR or radio waves), and their use is widespread. These frequencies fall in the non-ionising range of the spectrum, which is low frequency and low energy. This energy is too low to damage DNA." Dr Khullar adds, "In contrast, ionising radiation, such as x-rays, radon, and cosmic rays, is high frequency and high energy. Ionising radiation can damage DNA, and DNA damage can cause gene changes that may increase cancer risk. However, current evidence suggests that cell phone use does not cause brain or other types of cancer in humans." Regarding SAR values: The post also mentions the SAR value exceeding 1.6 W/kg as dangerous. SAR measures the rate at which the body absorbs RF energy. Regulatory bodies such as the Ministry of Communications (GoI) have set SAR limits to ensure safety. While it's true that phones must adhere to SAR limits (below 1.6 W/kg in India), a phone with a slightly higher SAR value does not necessarily pose a cancer risk. SAR values keep RF exposure within safe limits, but no study conclusively shows that higher SAR values lead to cancer. THIP Media Take: There is no strong evidence that mobile phones cause brain cancer. Some studies suggest a possible risk for heavy users, but most recent research does not confirm a clear link. Health organisations like the WHO classify mobile phone radiation as "possibly carcinogenic," but this is based on limited evidence. Claims about 5G radiation causing brain cancer or that SAR values above 1.6 W/kg are inherently dangerous are not accurate.

title: Fact Check: Can morning saliva cure acne?
claim_text: Applying morning saliva to your face can cure acne and give you spotless skin
quick_take: An Instagram video claims that morning saliva can cure acne and offer spotless skin. We did a fact check to term it as Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
## What does morning saliva contain?
Morning saliva is a mix of water, enzymes, bacteria, and other substances that contribute to digestion and oral health. Enzymes like amylase and lipase help break down carbohydrates and fats, while antibacterial components such as lysozyme, lactoferrin, and immunoglobulins help control bacterial growth in the mouth. However, after a night of reduced saliva production, the concentration of bacteria in the mouth increases. As a result, morning saliva contains more bacteria, which can be harmful if applied to the skin, especially on open pimples or sensitive areas.

## Why does acne occur?
Acne occurs when several factors work together, primarily involving the production of skin oil, or sebum. When the sebaceous glands produce excess oil, it can combine with dead skin cells, leading to clogged pores. This creates an ideal environment for bacteria, particularly Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes), to grow. The presence of these bacteria triggers an inflammatory response, resulting in the red, swollen pimples commonly associated with acne. Additionally, hormonal changes, stress, certain medications, and diet can exacerbate these factors, making the development of acne more likely.

## Can morning saliva really cure acne and offer spotless skin?
Not really. This claim is based on misconceptions rather than scientific evidence. Saliva does contain antimicrobial enzymes like lysozyme. But, these are not proven to be effective against acne when applied topically. Additionally, the bacteria present in morning saliva could potentially worsen acne rather than help it.

A review of the scientific evidence highlights the potential therapeutic properties of saliva and related treatments, but with clear limitations. A 2017 study found that lysozyme-shelled microbubbles combined with ultrasound significantly inhibited Propionibacterium acnes (P. acnes) growth, suggesting promise for acne treatment, though these results were obtained in controlled laboratory settings. A 2008 study identified histatins in saliva that promote wound healing in vitro, particularly in the oral cavity, but it did not focus on acne treatment.

Similarly, a 2019 study demonstrated that saliva contains peptides like histatins, which help in wound healing by promoting skin cell migration and proliferation, yet it did not directly address acne. Finally, a 2021 study found elevated levels of inflammatory markers in the saliva of acne patients, supporting saliva's potential as a diagnostic tool rather than a treatment. Collectively, these studies suggest potential benefits in specific contexts but do not support the use of saliva as an effective topical treatment for acne.

Dr Rashi Soni, a Dermatologist from Rashi Hospital, Hingoli, Maharashtra, says, "Saliva does have enzymes with antimicrobial properties, but there's no scientific proof that it can treat acne. In fact, putting morning saliva on your face, especially if you have acne-prone skin, might actually introduce more bacteria and make things worse. It's important to stick with proven acne treatments and consult a dermatologist to create a skincare routine that's safe and effective."

Therefore, instead of relying on morning saliva or certain herbs for treating acne, it is essential to consult a dermatologist for proper care. To add, there are claims that eating raw green chillies can clear blemishes and brightens the skin, which is not true.

## Why do people believe in such remedies despite the lack of conclusive evidence?
Many people are drawn to home remedies and myths because they've been passed down through generations or are endorsed by celebrities and influencers. Misinformation spreads really fast on social media, because they promise quick results. Social media's influence, combined with the appeal of quick and easy solutions, often leads people to try unreliable methods in the hope of seeing miraculous results.

It's important to remember that what works for one person may not work for another, and some remedies can even cause harm. Never trust anyone who is not qualified to offer health advice. Consulting a dermatologist or healthcare professional before trying new treatments is really important. Making informed decisions is key to maintaining healthy skin and overall well-being.

## THIP Media Take
The claim that morning saliva can cure acne and offer spotless skin is largely false due to inconclusive scientific evidence. Scientific research has explored the therapeutic properties of saliva, such as its role in wound healing and inflammation monitoring. However, there is no evidence to support its effectiveness in treating acne through casual topical application. Skincare should rely on reliable methods and professional advice, not on misleading and potentially harmful remedies.

title: Can mouth ulcers be treated with apple cider vinegar?
claim_text: A YouTube video titled "Five Effective Home Remedies for Mouth Ulcers" suggests that rinsing your mouth with diluted apple cider vinegar could be a successful method of treating mouth ulcers.
quick_take: According to a YouTube video, mouth ulcers can be treated at home with an ingredient like apple cider vinegar. We confirmed the assertion, and the findings of our research indicate that it is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
Mouth ulcers, also known as canker sores, are oral lesions that cause harm to the mouth's inner lining. They typically form in the soft tissue lining of lips, tongue, inner cheeks, gums, or roof of the mouth. While usually uncomfortable and may make it difficult to eat, drink, or speak, their precise developmental cause is unknown, though hereditary inheritance has been identified as a main etiological factor. Additional catalysts for their development include citrus fruits and foods high in acidity or spices, dental braces, uncomfortable dentures, unfinished dental fillings, stress, anxiety, hormonal changes, specific allergens, insufficient sleep, and particular medications.

Regarding apple cider vinegar (ACV), while it has been hailed as a supplement helping with blood pressure reduction, elevated lipid and cholesterol levels, nutritional support, and antioxidant defense, and its organic acids have been used as dietary supplements safe for eradicating harmful intestinal bacteria, it is NOT strong enough to effectively treat mouth ulcers. Although ACV has antimicrobial characteristics that could eliminate bacteria causing ulcers (particularly Streptococcus or Actinomyces), it is a controversial treatment because it may sting the ulcer when applied and would not be effective for all kinds of mouth ulcers.

Dr. Pooja Bhardwaj, a dental expert (BDS), cautioned that while apple cider vinegar has antimicrobial properties that reduce bacterial activity, it should be avoided for treating mouth ulcers. This could be due to the acidic pH of vinegar, which might irritate oral ulcers. Therefore, rather than relying on these archaic home remedies, one should seek professional help because the etiology may differ in each individual and, if untreated, can be a sign of other serious complications.

Most mouth ulcers, such as non-contagious canker sores, heal on their own in 1–2 weeks and don't usually require medical attention. By consuming plenty of water, using warm saline rinses, and avoiding spicy and hot foods, pain could be lessened and healing could move more quickly. It is never a good idea to ignore unusually large, uncomfortable mouth sores, especially if they persist for more than two weeks. Besides that, it is not advisable to rely on long-lasting mouth sores, particularly those associated with high fever or diarrhea that cannot be treated at home and necessitates medical attention. Furthermore, mouth ulcers could be a sign of a number of different conditions, including HIV/AIDS, Behcet's disease, celiac disease, immune disorders, inflammatory bowel diseases, diabetes, and immune disorders.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: Typically, mouth ulcers are a non-contagious group of lesions. However, if painful or large lesions last longer than two weeks, they may be signs of a more serious condition that needs to be treated right away. Since it could be dangerous to rely solely on natural remedies like apple cider vinegar, we draw the conclusion that this claim is mostly false.

title: Fact Check: Can Mulethi (licorice) and Honey Remove Skin Pigmentation?
claim_text: Applying the mixture of mulethi (licorice) powder and honey removes skin pigmentation. Start your day with mulethi powder, take a small amount of honey, add mulethi powder to it, mix it with your hands, and apply it to your face. Then massage your face for 3 to 4 minutes every day. Honey and mulethi will remove pigmentation, uneven skin tone, and tanning, clean your pores, and your skin will start to glow.
quick_take: While licorice and honey support skin health, their mix is not a proven cure for pigmentation. For lasting results, it's best to consult a dermatologist rather than rely on home remedies.
doctor_explanation: Skin pigmentation differs significantly among individuals, influenced by factors such as genetic makeup, exposure to sunlight, and certain medications. Disorders that affect skin pigmentation can alter a person's physical appearance and may also impact their emotional health and social interactions. Pigmentation issues generally fall into two categories: hyperpigmentation, where an overproduction of pigment leads to darkened areas, and hypopigmentation, where a lack of pigment results in lighter patches. Some commonly seen pigmentation conditions include albinism, melasma, vitiligo, Addison's disease, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, which may arise from conditions like acne, eczema, or reactions to specific drugs. While licorice (mulethi) has been found to help reduce inflammation, fight infections, lower the risk of heart disease and diabetes, ease muscle spasms, and support lung health, and honey is known for its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties with supportive benefits for the respiratory, digestive, cardiovascular, and nervous systems, no scientific evidence or medical consensus supports the claim that a mixture of licorice powder and honey can remove skin pigmentation. A study published in Current Issues in Molecular Biology found that heat-treated Wongam extract (WH-130), a new type of licorice, may help reduce skin pigmentation and could be useful in treating different skin conditions that cause dark spots — but the study only shows a reduction in pigmentation, not a complete or permanent removal. Another study published in the Iranian Journal of Dermatology found that a skin-lightening serum with licorice extract can help brighten the skin by blocking the production of melanin — the pigment that gives skin its color — however, the study does not mention that licorice extract can remove skin pigmentation completely. A third study published in the Research Journal of Pharmacy and Technology used a serum containing licorice root extract as a whitening agent and found that licorice root ethanol extract can be formulated as facial lightening serum preparations; again, this study does not confirm that licorice can permanently remove skin pigmentation. There is no scientific evidence supporting the use of honey for removing skin pigmentation. A study published in the Journal of Microbiology, Immunology and Infection noted that honey has antimicrobial activity, which can help in managing various skin disorders. Another study published in the Central Asian Journal of Global Health reported that honey is effective in promoting the healing of partial-thickness burns. Several studies have highlighted the role of licorice in reducing skin pigmentation, but there is no scientific evidence to support any effect of honey in reducing pigmentation. No research supports the idea that licorice and honey — either alone or combined — can completely remove skin pigmentation, and there is no consensus among medical professionals backing this claim. Dr Shareefa Chause, Dermatologist, Dr Shareefa Skin care clinic, Mumbai, told Medical Dialogues: 'Licorice does have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties; glabridin (flavonoid) found in licorice extract inhibits tyrosinase (enzyme responsible for melanin production). Licorice extract is also used in cosmeceuticals to reduce pigmentation. Honey is also an antioxidant and natural humectant, keeping skin hydrated; it also has antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties, reducing skin irritation and preventing breakouts. So yes, licorice and honey mask can be helpful to reduce pigmentation but not complete removal of pigmentation, as such a process will need more than just licorice and honey mask — like sunscreen, lifestyle modification, diet (antioxidant-rich), exercise, etc. And lastly, it is always advised to check for skin allergy; before applying anything on face, do a patch test on skin behind the ear.' Dr Parul Khot, MBBS, DNB, DVD, Consultant Dermatologist at Holy Family Hospital, Mumbai, added: 'As dermatologists, we emphasize the importance of understanding the cause and depth of pigmentation before choosing a treatment. While a DIY mixture of mulethi (licorice) powder and honey can offer mild skin-brightening benefits, its effectiveness varies. Mulethi inhibits melanin production, and honey provides hydration, making it a gentle option for mild pigmentation. However, for deeper or persistent pigmentation, consulting a dermatologist for treatments is advisable to ensure safe and effective results.' The Medical Dialogues Final Take states: 'Licorice and honey offer several health and skin benefits, but the claim that their mixture can completely remove skin pigmentation is unfounded. There is no proven or medically accepted basis for using this combination as a pigmentation treatment. Relying on such remedies may delay proper care for underlying skin conditions.'

For instance, lentinan from shiitake mushrooms and PSK (polysaccharide-K) from turkey tail mushrooms have demonstrated the potential to increase chemotherapy efficacy and increase cancer patients' chances of survival. Dr. Jyoti Mehta, Radiation and Clinical Oncologist, TGH Onco-Life Cancer Centre, Talegaon, added: 'Mushrooms or medicinal mushrooms are believed to cure cancer as they contain certain anti-cancer components. Agaricus blazei, a type of mushroom, is known to decrease the growth of cancer cells and boost the immune system. Other species of mushrooms, like reishi and maitake, have also shown potential in curing cancer. These mushrooms may carry natural components that might help prevent cancer cells from growing further, but going on hearsay is not a good idea. Don't eat mushrooms just because others are doing so or they have been promoted on social media. Mushrooms can also help strengthen the body's defense mechanism against cancer by improving the immune system and are safe to eat, they will not help you to manage cancer. One will need to undergo combination treatment, including surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, or immunotherapy to battle cancer. You will be shocked to know that wild mushrooms are poisonous and create havoc on your health. Even those suffering from any type of food allergy should avoid mushroom intake. Furthermore, eating mushrooms mindlessly can cause liver or kidney toxicity and give a tough time to an individual. It is better to consult an expert if you are adding mushrooms to your daily diet and be assured about the quantity. Anything consumed in excess can do more harm than good. Cancer patients should strictly follow the treatment plan devised by the doctor only. title: Fact Check: Can muskmelon peel water with sugar remove stones from body in 30 minutes?
claim_text: Boil watermelon peel in water, strain it, and mix in a spoonful of sugar. Drink it, and you won't believe it—within half an hour, the stone may dissolve and pass out.
verdict_original: The user's claim is FALSE. The claim by the user is FALSE.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Arun P, Associate Consultant, Gastroenterology, KIMSHEALTH explained: "Muskmelon contains dietary fiber, carbohydrates, minerals, and electrolytes. However, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that muskmelon peeling water with sugar can remove gallbladder stones from the body. The only definitive treatment for symptomatic gallbladder stones is cholecystectomy, which is the surgical removal of the gallbladder."

Dr Vinayak M, Consultant Department of Nephrology, KIMSHEALTH stated: "Fruits, in general, are rich in citrate and potassium, two substances considered to inhibit renal stone formation. Muskmelon, in particular, is high in both of these, as well as water, and has a low glycemic index, meaning it does not cause a rapid rise in blood sugar levels. Muskmelon peel water, on the other hand, may lack these beneficial ingredients, and the added sugar could worsen the chances of new stone formation. Therefore, muskmelon may be a better choice than the peel water. However, it is important to note that excess sugar consumption is also linked with increased risk of kidney stones. Most importantly, while these factors may help prevent new stone formation, they may not have much effect on already existing renal stones."

Dr Sachin Choudhary, MBBS, MS (General Surgery), FMAS,FIGS, Assistant Professor (General Surgery), Army College of Medical Sciences added: "There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that muskmelon peel water with sugar can remove kidney stones. Kidney stones form due to mineral deposits, and their treatment depends on size and composition. While staying hydrated is essential for kidney health, specific dietary changes and medical interventions—such as increased citrate intake or prescribed medications—are more effective. Large stones may require lithotripsy or surgical removal. Relying on unverified remedies can delay proper treatment and worsen the condition. Always consult a doctor for appropriate management."

Medical Dialogues Final Take: There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that muskmelon peel water with sugar can dissolve or remove kidney or gallbladder stones. While muskmelon is hydrating and contains beneficial nutrients, it does not have proven medicinal properties for stone dissolution. Further, excess sugar and sugary drink consumption is linked with increased risks of kidney stone formation. Moreover, gallstones can be removed only with surgical intervention. There are various types of stones found in the body (gallstones and kidney stones), but the post does not specify them. Gallstones can only be removed through surgical procedures, and kidney stones cannot be eliminated within 30 minutes. The article further explains that gallstones (cholelithiasis) are solid deposits that form within the gallbladder or biliary tract due to an imbalance in bile components, categorized as cholesterol gallstones (from excess cholesterol) and pigment gallstones (from elevated bilirubin, seen in liver conditions or blood disorders). Kidney stones (renal calculi/nephrolithiasis/urolithiasis) are solid pebble-like masses formed from calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, cystine, struvite, magnesium ammonium phosphate, and uric acid, and are linked to higher risk of chronic kidney disease, end-stage renal failure, cardiovascular conditions, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Treatment options include Shock Wave Lithotripsy, Cystoscopy and Ureteroscopy, Percutaneous Nephrolithotomy, laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy, and ERCP. Evidence also shows that excessive sugar consumption may increase the risk of kidney stones: a study in Frontiers in Nutrition found that a greater percentage of energy derived from added sugars is significantly associated with a higher prevalence of kidney stones, and a study by Pietro Manuel Ferraro et al. concluded that consuming sugar-sweetened soda and punch is associated with a higher likelihood of stone formation.

title: Fact Check: Can mustard oil and herbs remove varicose veins?
claim_text: A homemade oil made by heating mustard oil, bay leaves, rosemary leaves, cinnamon sticks, and castor oil can remove varicose veins. The post also claims that running or gymming contributes to varicose veins.
quick_take: A social media post claims that mustard oil and herbs can remove varicose veins. We fact checked this claim and termed it as mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Aseem Sharma, Director and Chief Dermatologist, Skin Saga Centre for Dermatology, Mumbai, explains: 'Oil massage may provide short-term relief from discomfort like heaviness or itching, but it does nothing to treat the actual cause of varicose veins. These veins usually form due to weakened valves and damaged blood vessels. Effective treatment often involves medical options like sclerotherapy (injecting a sealing agent), laser therapy, or minor surgery. It's best to consult a vascular specialist for proper diagnosis and care.'

Topical oils may soothe the skin or provide a mild sense of relief due to massage or warmth, but they cannot fix damaged veins. Varicose veins are a structural issue involving weakened valves inside blood vessels. Rubbing oil on the skin can't reverse these changes. At best, some ingredients like mustard oil and rosemary might offer minor anti-inflammatory effects, but there's no evidence that they can reduce or cure varicose veins.

Some of these ingredients have been studied for their general properties. For example, mustard oil is often used in traditional remedies for its warming and circulation-boosting effects. Rosemary leaves have antioxidant effects, cinnamon may improve circulation, and castor oil is known for its skin-soothing nature. But these effects are mild, and not targeted enough to influence deep vein health or cure vein disorders. None of these herbs or oils is known to strengthen vein valves, reduce vein diameter, or treat vein disease.

Regarding exercise: No, exercise does not cause varicose veins. In fact, regular movement, including running, walking, and gym workouts, improves blood circulation. These activities help reduce the risk of varicose veins by strengthening leg muscles, which push blood back to the heart. Varicose veins occur when the valves inside veins weaken or get damaged, causing blood to pool. Risk factors include genetics, obesity, prolonged standing, pregnancy, and age; not regular workouts. Staying inactive or sitting for long hours poses a greater risk of developing varicose veins than exercising.

Dr Almas Fatma, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, explains: 'Varicose veins may look like a skin issue on the surface, but they're actually a sign of deeper vein trouble. Thankfully, treatment has come a long way. Early on, we usually advise lifestyle changes, things like regular walking, leg elevation, and compression stockings to support blood flow. But if the veins are large, painful, or causing skin changes, we refer patients for specialised treatments. These can include laser procedures, injections that close off faulty veins, or even minor surgeries. All of these are done with minimal downtime. It's not a one-size-fits-all approach, so seeing a doctor helps determine what's right for each person.'

Effective treatments include compression stockings, lifestyle changes (like regular movement), and medical procedures such as laser therapy or vein stripping. Self-care helps in early stages, but advanced varicose veins need professional care. Homemade oils do not replace evidence-based treatment.

Sometimes, doctors can also recommend phototherapy (light therapy) for large areas of skin. Dr Ekansh Shekhar says, 'Psoriasis is a long-term skin condition where skin cells grow too quickly, causing red, scaly patches and inflammation. It happens because the immune system mistakenly attacks healthy skin cells. While mustard oil and neem powder have some properties that may help with skin health, like anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial effects, there's no strong evidence that they can cure psoriasis.' title: Can mustard oil, salt, and turmeric prevent all dental diseases?

Mustard oil, often used in traditional practices, also has some antimicrobial properties. Salt can act as a mild abrasive to scrub away surface debris. However, cleaning teeth with your finger lacks the mechanical action of a toothbrush, which is crucial for removing plaque—a sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth. Toothpastes also contain fluoride, which strengthens enamel and prevents cavities, something this mixture cannot do. Relying solely on this method could leave plaque behind, increasing the risk of dental issues over time. Dr Sanjeev Kumar, BDS, MPH, Senior Consultant (Medical), NPCCHH (MoHFW), Centre for Community Medicine, AIIMS, New Delhi, clarifies: 'Proper oral hygiene requires brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste, flossing daily to clean between teeth, and using a toothbrush to effectively remove plaque. The claim that 'no dental disease will exist' is an overstatement. Dental diseases, such as cavities, gum disease, and tooth decay, are caused by multiple factors, including poor oral hygiene, high sugar intake, and lack of fluoride. While turmeric and mustard oil have antibacterial properties that might reduce some harmful bacteria in the mouth, they cannot address all causes of dental diseases. For example, cavities form when bacteria produce acids that erode enamel, a process that requires fluoride to counteract—something this mixture lacks. The National Health Service emphasizes that preventing dental diseases involves brushing twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, flossing, and regular dental check-ups. A 2024 study highlights that fluoride is key to reducing cavity risk, a benefit this remedy does not provide. title: Can natural home remedies reverse premature greying of hair?
claim_text: A widely shared Facebook reel asserts a natural way to reverse or prevent premature greying of hair. Furthermore, the claim implies that kalonji seeds, mustard oil, bhringraj, and mehndi powder combined in an iron wok (kadhai) are not only useful for premature greying, but that the natural preparation may enhance hair health and reduce hair fall.
quick_take: According to a social media post, an alternative remedy can effectively reverse premature greying of hair. We fact-checked the notion and found that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
The onset of grey or white hair strands before the age of 20 or 30 years is known as premature greying. In medical terms, greying of hair is brought on by a gradual decline in melanocyte activity within hair follicles. This reduces melanin, the pigment responsible for hair colour. The chief contributors to premature greying are: stress-related, hormonal, or nutritional factors. Premature greying is not a medical condition; yet, its occurrence has a considerable impact on self-esteem and, in some situations, may even be an indication of underlying systemic challenges. Addressing premature greying involves both cosmetic and pharmacological approaches. Natural hair care remedies are strongly established in traditional medicine. One such herbal combination of kalonji, bhringraj, mehndi, and mustard oil prepared in an iron kadhai has been suggested for reversing premature greying.

Analysis of each ingredient:

**Black cumin seeds (Kalonji/Nigella sativa):** Strong in thymoquinone, has potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and may protect hair follicle melanocytes from oxidative damage. These findings, while promising, require large-scale clinical trials.

**Bhringraj (Eclipta Alba):** Known as 'keshraj' in Ayurveda, the chemical is known for its potential to promote hair pigmentation and prevent hair follicle ageing. However, these results are limited to exploratory or experimental studies.

**Mehndi (henna/Lawsonia inermis):** A popular natural dye that deposits a reddish-brown pigment on the hair shaft. Nevertheless, while the component gives the impression of darker hair, it does not stimulate melanin production.

**Mustard oil:** Contributes to hair vitality by promoting scalp health and enhancing hair strength because it includes both needed fatty acids and antioxidants. However, no credible studies support its role in reversing premature greying.

**Iron wok (kadhai):** The usage of an iron vessel may result in trace levels of iron, a mineral associated with hair health; however, these effects are theoretical.

While these ingredients exhibit individual benefits, there is limited clinical evidence from randomised trials to support their efficacy in reversing or preventing premature greying of hair.

Dr. Swati Watwani, consultant dermatologist and medical director of Persianlily Clinic, adds that premature greying may begin as early as the 20s and cannot be treated with random therapies. Although premature greying cannot be completely reversed, recognising the underlying cause—whether stress-related, hormonal, or nutritional—can contribute to delaying its progression with appropriate therapy and care.

Hair loss is primarily caused by dietary inadequacies, hormonal imbalances, or scalp conditions, whereas premature greying is brought on by oxidative stress and a hereditary predisposition that lowers melanocyte activity. Empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of a single therapy for both hair loss and premature greying remains inadequate. While certain botanical extracts may possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects that may enhance scalp health, these benefits are confined to preliminary research. These unverified cures may be ineffective in addressing underlying illnesses that require therapeutic intervention. Organic remedies can be used in conjunction with the evidence-based therapeutic approach, but they are not a cure-all for the two hair-related concerns.

**Medical management of premature greying:** Begins with identifying the underlying cause through exhaustive medical history and clinical examination. Diagnostic evaluations may help identify reversible contributors. Once correctable causes are identified, skin professionals may propose supplements or treatment for the underlying medical condition. Furthermore, food rich in antioxidants or oral supplements may be prescribed to reduce oxidative stress. Topical therapies, confined to cosmetic concealment, may temporarily restore lost pigmentation. Certain experimental techniques, such as melanin-stimulating agents and photobiomodulation (PBM), are being studied but lack definitive evidence.

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar recommends practical alternatives for grey or white strands: hair dye (permanent, semi-permanent, and ammonia-free options); henna for a more natural appearance producing reddish-brown tone but may not completely conceal grey hair; root touch-up powders and sprays for covering greys in between dye sessions. Given that greying is mostly inherited, maintaining healthy hair requires a well-balanced diet rich in iron, zinc, and vitamin B12. Medical experts may recommend specific procedures such as microneedling or specialised serums, which may enhance hair health but cannot prevent premature greying. Dr. Shekhar suggests that adopting your grey hair is a good alternative, as many individuals appreciate their silver hair with proper management and care.

However, there is insufficient empirical evidence to support the role of navel therapy for enhancing eyesight. Furthermore, eye development and visual pathways are predominantly controlled by the retina, optic nerve, and visual cortex, none of which have a direct physical or physiological association with the umbilical cord.

Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at Amrita School of Ayurveda, confirms that "applying oils to the navel for curing diseases is not supported by traditional Ayurvedic texts and has no scientific validity." Herbal medications containing highly alkaline or acidic ingredients, on the other hand, may alter the natural pH of the eye, causing severe dryness or damage. Furthermore, replacing proven vision-corrective procedures with unregulated ones can result in infections if contaminated practices persist.

Dr. Bhanu Prakash M, Senior Consultant Cataract, Cornea and Refractive Surgery at Yashoda Hospitals in Hyderabad, suggests treating children with myopia with prescription Myatro 0.01% eye drops. Excessive neem intake can have detrimental consequences and should not be regarded as a stand-alone diabetic therapy alternative. Diabetes mellitus is a chronic disease that, while it can be controlled, cannot be completely cured by a single herbal remedy like neem. Consuming neem leaves uncontrolled on a daily basis may do more harm than good - it may result in hormonal imbalances, gastrointestinal distress, hepatic damage, or even miscarriage. A chronic metabolic illness such as diabetes cannot be cured; however, it may occasionally enter a state of remission.
