title: Can turmeric kill cancerous cells?
claim_text: Turmeric can eliminate/kill cancer cells (from the YouTube video "Cancer dies when you eat these three foods?")
quick_take: A well-liked YouTube video claims that turmeric can eliminate cancer cells. We checked the assertion. Our analysis shows that the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
Cancer is a condition wherein a few of the body's cells grow out of control and spread to other body regions. This is primarily a genetic disease, meaning that it is brought on by changes to the genes that regulate how our cells function, particularly how they grow and divide. Proto-oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and DNA repair genes are the three main gene classes that cause cancerous changes. These are referred to as cancer's 'drivers.'

Turmeric has a long history in traditional Asian medicine because it contains curcumin. Clinical trials are currently being conducted on curcumin due to its anti-inflammatory properties. These trials suggest that the properties of curcumin might counteract the inflammatory response, which is a significant characteristic of cancer. Although the findings are promising, there isn't any definite evidence that turmeric or curcumin can cure or prevent cancer in humans.

Moreover, there are some restrictions on the use of curcumin. These include the right dosage, absorption, and medication safety of turmeric. Due to all of these drawbacks, it appears that more clinical trials are needed before turmeric can be used to treat cancer. Furthermore, oncologists believe that although turmeric appears promising, there is still much work to be done before it can be considered an effective cure for cancer.

Diet and body weight are two important modifiable risk factors in cancer prevention. According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), a healthy diet is one that is rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, low in red and processed meats, refined grains, sugar, and alcohol. Cruciferous foods like broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, collard greens, and Brussels sprouts have been linked to a lower risk of colorectal, gastric, and lung cancers in women.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: It makes sense that someone would want to try alternative medicine to combat or treat cancer. Please be aware that while turmeric is typically well tolerated, it is not yet recognized as a treatment for cancer. Additionally, more research must be done with a larger sample size. Thus, we draw the conclusion that the assertion is mostly false.

title: Fact Check: Can Turmeric lemonade treat depression better than Prozac?
claim_text: An Instagram post claims that Turmeric lemonade may treat depression better than Prozac. The post claims that consuming a mixture of four cups of distilled or filtered water, two tablespoons of turmeric (grated or powdered), juice from one and a half lemons, juice from one blood orange, and Stevia extract may treat depression.
quick_take: In the field of medical research there has been no head-on comparison between turmeric lemonade and Prozac. Turmeric lemonade is not proven to treat depression better than Prozac or any other clinically approved antidepressant medication like fluoxetine. Most studies on curcumin's effects on depression involve high doses of concentrated curcumin extracts, not turmeric in its natural form, and certainly not in lemonade, which would contain far lower levels of curcumin.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Meenakshi Jain, Assistant Professor, Psychiatry, Amrita Hospital Faridabad, explained that depressive disorders include a range of illnesses like premenstrual dysphoric disorder, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, major depressive disorder, etc. These are characterized by symptoms like severe recurrent temper outbursts, verbal rage, irritability, anger, low mood, limited or diminished interest in activities, weight loss, disturbed sleep, tiredness, reduced attention and concentration, feelings of worthlessness, and in severe cases suicidal thoughts. She noted that research has not concluded a single definite cause for depression — multiple risk factors are involved: traumatic childhood experiences, stressful life events, genetic factors, negative affective temperament, hormonal changes (menstrual cycle, menopause, altered testosterone), illnesses like hypothyroidism, Parkinson's disease, cancer, insomnia, and substances such as alcohol, cannabis, and opioids.

Regarding turmeric, Dr Krithishree S S, Consultant Psychiatrist KMC Hospital, stated that curcumin, the active compound in turmeric, only makes up about 0.3% to 8.6% of turmeric's composition and has low bioavailability when ingested. Its absorption in the intestines is poor, it has a rapid metabolism and short half-life, and it is lipophilic, meaning it does not easily stay in body fluids. Due to its low molecular weight, curcumin struggles to cross the blood-brain barrier effectively. Consequently, conventional doses of curcumin might not provide the necessary levels in the brain to have a significant neuromodulation effect. She emphasized that curcumin is still a long way from becoming an approved antidepressant treatment due to these challenges. Despite its potential as a nootropic (may enhance mental alertness and energy levels), it is not suitable as a primary treatment for major depressive disorders. Recent advances in pharmacology have led to the development of newer antidepressants that are more effective, faster-acting, better tolerated, and have fewer side effects, making them preferable over curcumin for treating depression.

Key scientific evidence cited: A study by Lopresti et al. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25046624/) reported that while greater antidepressant effects of curcumin compared to placebo were observed from weeks 4 to 8, when evaluating the whole treatment period (baseline to week 8), curcumin was not found to be significantly more effective than placebo in reducing depressive and anxiety symptoms. The study's findings are limited by a small sample size of only about 50 participants, affecting reliability and statistical power. A study by Sanmukhani J et al. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23832433/) tracked 60 adults diagnosed with MDD who scored above 7 on the HAMD-17 scale, assigned to three groups: 1000 mg curcumin, 20 mg fluoxetine, and combined treatment. After eight weeks, the combined group showed 77.8% improvement, while fluoxetine-only was 64.7% and curcumin-only was 62.5% — not statistically significant. Goel et al. noted that regular turmeric powder contains only 2-5% curcumin and may not be potent enough for medicinal purposes; concentrated curcumin extract (BCM-95) is needed to achieve therapeutic benefits. The article also references Fluoxetine (Prozac) as an FDA-approved SSRI with demonstrated efficacy across major depressive disorder, OCD, panic disorder, bulimia, binge eating disorder, premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and bipolar depression (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459223/).

title: Fact Check: Can turmeric, methi, and black pepper restart stopped periods in one day?
claim_text: Drink turmeric, methi, and black pepper and your periods, stopped for a year, will restart within a day.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that a mix of turmeric, fenugreek (methi), and black pepper can switch a year-absent period back on in 24 hours. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Menstruation happens when the uterine lining (endometrium) builds up under oestrogen and progesterone, then sheds if pregnancy doesn't occur. That build-up takes weeks of hormonal cycling from the brain–ovary axis (hypothalamus, pituitary, ovaries). If you haven't bled for a year, either you've reached menopause (12 months without a period is the usual clinical marker), or there's another cause such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), thyroid issues, high prolactin, low body weight, intense exercise, stress-related hypothalamic amenorrhoea, uterine scarring, or certain medicines. None of those conditions can be reversed in 24 hours by a spice drink. Biology needs time and the right signals. Turmeric's active component, curcumin, is known for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects; it doesn't deliver clinically proven, cycle-restoring hormone changes. Fenugreek seeds contain saponins and phyto-compounds sometimes called phytoestrogens, but their oestrogen-like activity is weak and inconsistent in humans. Black pepper mainly offers piperine, which helps the body absorb certain nutrients and drugs; it is not a hormone. Even when studied for menstrual discomfort or general wellness, these spices haven't shown reliable, medically significant effects on ovulation or the endometrium that would restart a long-absent period alone within a day. A period is not a switch board. To bleed, the endometrium must first thicken over the follicular phase (roughly two weeks), then progesterone must rise after ovulation, and finally drop to trigger shedding. If you haven't cycled for a year, your lining likely hasn't been building. You can't shed what isn't there. Medical treatments that bring on a withdrawal bleed (for example, a short course of progesterone) still take several days and are guided by a clinician after ruling out pregnancy and other causes. A 24-hour turnaround contradicts how the reproductive system works. For PCOS, the cornerstone is lifestyle change (weight management if needed, regular movement, sleep) plus targeted medical options like metformin or hormonal therapy, depending on goals. For stress-related or weight-related amenorrhoea, restoring energy balance, addressing stress, and gradually normalising exercise patterns are key. Spices can be part of a healthy diet, but they don't replace the hormonal and metabolic shifts required to resume ovulation. Dietician Nidhi Sarin explained: "What you eat can significantly impact your wellbeing during periods. Certain foods may support hormone activity, helping regulate cycles and ease menstrual discomfort. However, it's important to remember that these so-called superfoods only act as supportive aids to lessen the intensity of symptoms. They cannot be considered a cure or treatment for irregular periods." Turmeric at high doses can upset the stomach and may interact with blood thinners and some gallbladder conditions. Fenugreek can lower blood sugar (a concern if you're on diabetes medicines), cause digestive discomfort, and may trigger allergies in those sensitive to legumes/peanuts. Black pepper (piperine) can alter how the body handles several medicines by affecting liver enzymes, potentially changing drug levels (think some blood thinners, seizure medicines, antidepressants). Large, concentrated shots increase these risks without proven benefit. Dr Anita Gupta, Gynaecologist and Associate Director at Fortis La Femme, New Delhi, emphasises that the key to managing irregular periods is first to identify and treat any underlying medical or gynaecological issues. In several cases, gynaecologists may prescribe hormone-based medicines, which can be effective in bringing the menstrual cycle back to balance.

title: Fact Check: Can Turmeric Milk Purify Blood?
claim_text: Turmeric milk purifies blood
verdict_original: The claim by Pinterest User is FALSE.
quick_take: Curcumin, the active compound in turmeric, is known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties and may help reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease and diabetes. However, there is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to support the claim that turmeric milk can purify blood. Hence, the claim is FALSE.
doctor_explanation:
Dr. Jeny Elizabeth George, Associate Consultant, Transfusion Medicine, Apollo Adlux Hospital Ernakulam, said: "The scientific evidence in modern medicine for using turmeric milk to purify blood is very limited. Scientifically, it is not proven. In traditional medicine, many findings claim it helps, but in modern medicine, there is no hematological evidence supporting the use of turmeric milk for purifying blood or increasing the number of blood cells. That's why we wouldn't recommend it without sufficient scientific studies. However, it is considered to be an antioxidant and is supposed to have anti-inflammatory effects, but these claims are more related to naturopathy or Ayurveda. Modern science does not endorse them."

Dr. Govind Eriat, Consultant- Hematology & BMT Medicine, Gleneagles BGS Hospital Kengeri Bengaluru, further explained: "Purification of blood and regeneration of your blood pool every day involves trafficking billions of senescent cells to be reclaimed by the reticuloendothelial system and producing new cells in the bone marrow. This complex affair may be aided by affecting the cellular milieu, with micro and macronutrients, and exercise. Curcumin has been known to ancient medicine cultures in healing, with special reference to topical and systemic use as antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, anticancer, hepatoprotective, and cardioprotective effects. In the last decades, modern science is researching these claims for scientific validation with mammalian tissue in genetic laboratories. Some clear cellular expression profiles have been shown to regulate the genes implicated in tumor cell proliferation, metastasis, chemotherapy resistance, and angiogenesis. New targetable biological therapy is being considered due to the pharmacokinetics of curcumin and it's low bioavailability. A recent paper ScienceDirect 2023 on Curcuma longa's effects Endothelial progenitor cells (EPCs) have been recently described in the peripheral blood as cells contributing to both physiological and pathological angiogenesis. Recent data shows curcumin as a systematic agent can heal these endothelial cells by decreasing oxidative stress, inflammation, abnormal Nitric oxide bioavailability, and cell adhesion. Better angiogenesis would decrease end-organ damage in diseases ranging from diabetes, hypertension, atherosclerosis, dementia and vasculitis to cardiometabolic multimorbidity. It is important to note that turmeric milk alone cannot purify the blood."

The article further explains: Turmeric's active compound, curcumin, has been studied for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, which may contribute to general detoxification but there is no scientific evidence to support the benefits of milk in blood purification. The kidneys play a key role in purifying blood within the body — healthy kidneys filter about half a cup of blood each minute, eliminating waste and excess water. Blood purification therapy (dialysis, filtration, adsorption) is a clinical procedure used in emergency care (plasmapheresis), life support (hemodialysis for kidney failure), and treatment of metabolic or immune disorders. While a paper in Pharmacological Research suggests curcumin may help manage cardiovascular-metabolic multimorbidity by improving endothelial function, reducing inflammation, and enhancing blood circulation, more research is needed. A study led by Javad Sharifi-Rad et al. found curcumin offers antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, neuroprotective, liver-protective, and heart-protective benefits. A study by Debjit Bhowmik et al. noted traditional use of turmeric for blood purification and skin conditions but emphasized anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. A review in the Nutrition Journal found turmeric and curcumin may help protect individuals at risk of cardiovascular disease by improving serum lipid levels. A review in the Journal of Functional Foods found curcumin can lower the risk of cardiovascular diseases and diabetes. While turmeric may promote general well-being, there is no evidence to support the claim that turmeric milk purifies the blood.

title: Fact Check: Can turmeric prevent atherosclerosis? - THIP Media
claim_text: Turmeric prevents atherosclerosis (some posts claim it can cure atherosclerosis)
quick_take: A number of social media posts claim that turmeric prevents atherosclerosis. We fact-checked and found that the claim is half true. Most of the posts miss a very important context.
doctor_explanation: Atherosclerosis is a disease in which plaque builds up inside our arteries. Plaque is made up of fat, cholesterol, calcium, and other substances found in the blood. It hardens and narrows the arteries and limits the flow of oxygen-rich blood to our organs. This can lead to serious health problems, and sometimes even death. Yes, a number of research has shown that curcumin is effective for decreasing the aortic atherosclerotic lesion area as well as for lowering lipid profiles. Curcumin is a polyphenolic compound derived from the dietary spice turmeric. However, the quality of such researches have been questioned by many other researchers. Many of these researches are done on mice. The researchers noted, "curcumin can improve the permeability of atherosclerotic coronary artery to inhibit lipid deposition and inflammatory cell infiltration, and delay and stabilize atheromatous plaque formation." But, the mouse model of atherosclerosis was still different from atherosclerosis in human beings in some aspects. For instance, the atherosclerotic plaque of humans tended to occur in the coronary artery while it would gather in the aortic root in mice. Also, the dosage of curcumin required to prevent or cure atherosclerosis has not been established. While researchers observed that the optimal dosage of curcumin is around 207 mg/kg body weight per day, they noted, "it needs further optimal dose-setting study to confirm the result." No, it is not advisable to depend on turmeric to prevent or cure atherosclerosis. It is important to note that systematic studies to understand the molecular basis of disease preventing or therapeutic properties of curcumin began to appear in the scientific literature only during the last 40 years. Therefore, more scientific evidences are required to support the claim.

title: Fact check: Can turmeric promote a longer lifespan? - THIP Media
claim_text: Turmeric promotes a longer lifespan by reducing inflammation, preventing chronic diseases, and enhancing overall health
quick_take: An image on Pinterest claims that turmeric can promote a longer lifespan. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: There is no conclusive evidence that turmeric directly increases lifespan. Turmeric contains curcumin, a bioactive compound celebrated for its health-promoting properties. Curcumin's ability to combat inflammation and oxidative stress has positioned turmeric as a possible help in managing chronic diseases. However, when it comes to extending lifespan directly, the evidence falls short. Most studies linking curcumin to longevity have been conducted on animals or in laboratory conditions. For instance, research involving worms and mice suggests curcumin may activate genes associated with longevity and reduce markers of cellular damage. However, humans are far more complex, and these findings cannot be easily extrapolated to our species. Moreover, the doses of curcumin used in such studies are significantly higher than what can be achieved through typical dietary turmeric consumption. To date, long-term human studies directly linking turmeric to extended lifespan are lacking. According to Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, 'a teaspoon daily of turmeric with water or with milk will provide some sort of potential benefits, BUT ADD YEARS TO YOUR LIFE- NOT POSSIBLE.' Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, 'Yes, turmeric may help reduce inflammation, but it's not a magic bullet.' She further explains that chronic inflammation plays a pivotal role in the ageing process and the development of age-related conditions such as arthritis, heart disease, and diabetes. Curcumin has been shown to inhibit inflammatory pathways in the body, suppressing molecules like cytokines and enzymes responsible for inflammation. A 2017 review highlighted curcumin's potential to manage inflammation-related conditions, particularly when consumed in higher doses or as supplements. However, curcumin is not unique in its anti-inflammatory properties. A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and omega-3 fatty acids can also significantly reduce inflammation. Additionally, turmeric's impact on inflammation is limited by its poor bioavailability—how well it is absorbed and utilised by the body. Combining turmeric with black pepper, which contains piperine, can boost curcumin absorption by up to 2000%, but even then, its effects are not transformative enough to single-handedly combat the complexities of ageing. Regarding chronic diseases: curcumin may support cardiovascular health by improving endothelial function (the lining of blood vessels), which plays a critical role in regulating blood pressure and blood flow. A 2024 study found that curcumin supplementation improved vascular function in postmenopausal women, offering benefits comparable to moderate exercise. However, these findings do not establish curcumin as a substitute for proven heart-health practices such as exercise, a balanced diet, and avoiding smoking. For cancer prevention, turmeric has been investigated for its potential to prevent or slow the progression of cancer. Curcumin may inhibit tumour growth and promote the death of cancerous cells. Research has shown encouraging results, particularly in laboratory and animal studies, for cancers such as colorectal and breast cancer. However, these findings are largely based on curcumin concentrations far higher than what can be consumed through diet. For neurodegenerative conditions, turmeric's ability to cross the blood-brain barrier has made it a candidate for research into Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases. Curcumin may reduce the buildup of amyloid plaques in the brain, a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. Yet, human trials remain limited and have yet to confirm turmeric's role in significantly altering the course of these conditions. Conclusion: Yes, turmeric can be a valuable addition to a healthy diet, but it's not a miracle ingredient. Turmeric is a versatile spice with proven health benefits, particularly for reducing inflammation and supporting digestion. Some lab and animal studies have explored whether baking soda for cancer can influence tumour growth. In very specific conditions, sodium bicarbonate has been shown to affect the pH around tumours in mice. Moreover, a small study in 2018 tested a new method to treat liver cancer. Doctors added baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) directly into the tumour during a common treatment called TACE. This mix worked much better than TACE alone, because it helped shrink tumours in all patients in the study. The idea is that baking soda reduces acidity inside tumours, making it harder for cancer cells to survive. But this has not translated to safe or effective treatment in humans through large clinical trials. Experts, including those from the Cancer Research UK, do not recommend baking soda as a treatment for cancer. No approved cancer therapy includes drinking baking soda or combining it with lemon juice. The claim that this drink lowers the glycaemic index (GI) of the body is flawed. GI refers to how fast a particular food raises blood sugar. It is not a property of the body itself, and drinking lemon juice with baking soda will not change how other foods are processed. Misleadingly, some people claim that baking soda can cure diabetes in just three days. Moreover, the suggestion that diarrhoea is part of a "healing crisis" is also incorrect. Diarrhoea is a sign of irritation in the gut or an unwanted reaction, not a sign of cleansing or detox. The body already has organs like the liver and kidneys to remove toxins naturally. It's not something that applies to the body itself, and drinking lemon and baking soda won't change how your body processes other foods. It's always better to focus on eating whole grains, fruits, vegetables, and getting regular exercise, rather than relying on quick fixes or internet trends." Drinking large amounts of baking soda and lemon for cancer or other purposes can lead to side effects such as: For people on medications or with high blood pressure or kidney problems, the high sodium content of baking soda can be dangerous. title: Fact Check: Can using Coconut Oil Reverse Tooth Cavity?

quick_take: Coconut oil can promote better oral hygiene but cannot reverse cavities or heal decomposed teeth. Preventing tooth decay requires consistent oral care and professional dental treatment for existing issues.
doctor_explanation: Tooth cavity or decomposed tooth in medical terms is known as Dental Caries. Shafers in 1993 defined dental caries as an irreversible microbial disease of the calcified tissues of the teeth, characterized by demineralization of the inorganic portion and destruction of the organic substance of the tooth, which often leads to cavitation. This common chronic condition is mainly caused by cariogenic bacteria like Streptococcus mutans, which adhere to the teeth. These bacteria convert sugars into acid, leading to the gradual erosion and weakening of tooth structure. The development of dental caries relies on four essential factors: bacterial biofilm (plaque), fermentable carbohydrates, dental hard tissues, and an adequate amount of time. There is no cure for tooth cavities — once they have taken place, they cannot be reverted back. Coconut oil offers various health benefits like antimicrobial, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, and it is easily digestible oil; however, there is no scientific evidence or medical consensus from within the dental community that supports the claim that coconut oil can be used to reverse cavities. Studies have shown that oil pulling may have antibacterial activity against Candida albicans and Streptococcus mutans using coconut oil, where S. mutans is one of the essential factors for the development of dental caries. However, these studies do not talk about the reversal of dental caries once formed. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of the International Oral Health highlighted coconut oil's effectiveness as an antimicrobial agent in reducing bacterial colonization and significantly improving oral hygiene through oil pulling, but the study does not support the claim that coconut oil can reverse dental caries. Another study published in the Journal of Global Oral Health concluded that oil pulling with coconut oil is effective in reducing plaque and gingivitis, describing coconut oil as a safe, affordable, and effective option with minimal side effects. However, no studies have indicated that coconut oil has the ability to reverse cavities or heal decayed teeth. Dr. Prinita Tirkey, MDS Periodontist, Rajmata Smt. Devendra Kumari Singh Deo Govt Medical College and Hospital Ambikapur, Surguja, Chhattisgarh, told Medical Dialogues: "Claiming that coconut oil can reverse cavities is an overstatement. Once dental caries begin, they cannot be reversed, as there is no cure or ingredient, including coconut oil, capable of repairing cavities. Maintaining proper oral hygiene through regular brushing, flossing, and professional dental care is the best way to prevent cavities and protect your teeth." Dr. Deepika Jain, Orthodontist, Samda Superspeciality Hospital, Rajnandgaon, C.G, added: "Cavities occur when tooth decay damages the structure of the tooth, and this damage is irreversible and can only be restored with dental treatment. While coconut oil may support oral hygiene by reducing bacteria, it cannot repair cavities. For optimal dental health, focus on consistent brushing, flossing, and regular dental check-ups to prevent tooth decay in the first place."

title: Can using elephant yam for weight loss be more effective than green tea?
claim_text: Jimikand or suran or elephant yam (elephant foot yam) "burns fat more effectively than green tea" and also improves digestion, metabolism and hormonal balance.
quick_take: A social media post claims that suran or elephant yam for weight loss is more effective than green tea. We fact checked this claim and found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
How does Jimikand support fat loss? Jimikand or elephant yam doesn't directly burn fat. It's a starchy, fibre-rich vegetable, so it can help you feel full and potentially support weight control by reducing hunger. Foods high in fibre are often linked to better weight management because they make you less likely to overeat. However, there is no evidence that eating Jimikand makes your body burn extra calories or fat. In short, it may help with satiety (just like any filling food), but it isn't a metabolic "fat-melter". Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says: "Jimikand, or elephant foot yam, doesn't actually burn fat, but it can support weight management in a more natural and sustainable way. It's rich in fibre, which helps you feel full for longer and reduces the urge to snack unnecessarily. It's also low in calories for the volume it provides, so it fills up your plate without adding too many calories. When combined with an overall balanced diet, this can help you control your appetite and manage your weight better. But no food, including Jimikand, can melt fat on its own." 

Can elephant yam for weight loss be more effective than green tea? No. There's no research showing Suran or Jimikand outperforms green tea. In fact, green tea has been tested in multiple studies and does have a mild fat-burning effect (from its caffeine and catechins). Green tea catechins can slightly increase calorie burn, although the effect is small. Jimikand, by comparison, does not contain such compounds (it has virtually no caffeine and epigallocatechin gallato or EGCG). Its benefit comes from fibre and nutrients, not from boosting metabolism. In one sense, eating Jimikand instead of a high-calorie snack might help reduce calories (due to its fullness effect), but it's not actively burning fat. Malvika Fulwani, Founder and Chief Dietitian at Healthitude, explains: "Green tea has been studied quite a bit for its mild fat-burning effect, mostly because of compounds like caffeine and catechins that may slightly increase metabolism. Jimikand, on the other hand, doesn't have these active compounds. It's more of a filling, fibrous vegetable that supports digestion and helps with satiety. So, while both can play a role in a healthy diet, it's not accurate to say Jimikand burns more fat than green tea. They work very differently."

Can Jimikand help digestion and reduce bloating? Yes, to an extent. Jimikand is rich in dietary fibre, which does support digestion. Fibre adds bulk to stools and helps food move smoothly through the gut. In traditional medicine, Elephant yam is used to ease digestive issues. Lab studies in animals back this up: an extract of Jimikand increased bowel movements and gut motility in rats, effectively relieving constipation. By easing constipation and regulating stools, it can indirectly reduce bloating and gas in people prone to those issues. However, bear in mind the evidence is mostly anecdotal or from small studies. Saying it cures digestive problems or bloating in everyone is an overstatement. But as a high-fibre food, Jimikand or suran can be part of a diet that improves digestion and reduces mild bloating.

Does elephant yam improve metabolism and hormone balance? Maybe, but evidence is weak. There's no proof that Jimikand speeds up your metabolism. It contains no caffeine or stimulants known to raise metabolic rate. It is nutritious (carbs, fibre, vitamins), but simply eating it won't make your body burn calories faster. On hormones, Jimikand does contain plant steroids like diosgenin, which is sometimes described as a phytoestrogen. Some sources say this could help relieve menopause symptoms by mildly mimicking oestrogen. In fact, another study notes that diosgenin in Elephant yam "mimics oestrogen" and might ease hot flashes or mood swings. However, people must exercise caution because these same compounds could disrupt hormone balance if consumed in excess. In short, while Jimikand has bioactive steroids, there's no confirmatory clinical evidence that eating it will balance hormones in men or women. The hormone claims are based on the presence of these compounds, not on solid human studies.

Why must Jimikand be boiled before eating? Yes. Elephant yam must be cooked thoroughly before eating. That's because its raw flesh contains calcium oxalate crystals and irritants that cause itching and burning in the mouth or throat. If you chew it raw, you might feel intense itch or irritation on your tongue and lips. For this reason, traditional recipes always boil or soak Jimikand (often in vinegar or tamarind water) right after peeling. The cooking process and acidic soak neutralise the oxalates and allergens. In practice, you should always boil Jimikand (sometimes with a bit of lemon or vinegar) to make it safe and non-irritating before using it in curries or salads.

In summary, the claim that using suran or elephant yam for weight loss is more effective than green tea is misleading.

title: Fact Check: Can using fluoride toothpaste lower IQ ?
claim_text: Fluoride toothpaste is recommended but; fluoride is toxic, it can lower your IQ and damage cells.
quick_take: While excessive fluoride can be toxic, the levels used in toothpaste and fluoridated water are considered safe and effective for preventing tooth decay by reputable organizations like the WHO and ADA. This post mixes valid concerns about excessive fluoride exposure with exaggerated and unsupported assertions about commonly used fluoride levels, creating a false and misleading narrative.
doctor_explanation: Fluoride has been widely used to prevent tooth decay through various methods such as toothpaste, water, milk, mouth rinses, tooth gels, and varnishes. Regular toothbrushing is advised to maintain oral health and prevent decay, with a general recommendation to brush for 2 minutes twice daily using fluoride toothpaste. The fluoride concentration in standard or family toothpaste typically ranges from 1000 to 1500 parts per million (ppm). The American Dental Association (ADA) recommends that caregivers brush children's teeth with water and consult a dentist or physician before introducing fluoride toothpaste for children under 2 years old. For children aged 2 to 6 years, a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste is advised. Prolonged consumption of excessive fluoride during infancy and childhood, a critical period when teeth are developing, can result in dental fluorosis — presenting with white streaks or spots to prominent white or brown discolourations on the teeth. Most toothpaste contains fluoride, typically sodium fluoride or monofluorophosphate, at levels of 1,000 to 1,100 mg/L (approximately 1.3 mg per typical brushing amount). Daily fluoride intake from toothpaste is estimated at 0.1–0.25 mg for children under 5 years, 0.2–0.3 mg for children aged 6–12 years, and 0.1 mg for adults — levels well below the daily adequate intake of fluoride. Excessive fluoride exposure, often from rare incidents such as overly fluoridated water, accidental ingestion of fluoride products meant for topical dental use, or improper administration of fluoride supplements to children, can lead to symptoms like nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, periostitis, and, in very rare cases, death. An acute dose of 5 mg/kg (e.g., 375 mg for a 75 kg individual) could cause serious systemic toxicity. Studies examining chronic fluoride exposure include: A study in Molecular Biology Reports shows that high and chronic exposure to fluoride causes cellular apoptosis (cell damage). A study in Archives of Toxicology mentions that extended exposure to elevated fluoride levels causes extensive damage to cellular organelles (the cell surface, mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, and nucleus), influenced by duration and concentration of exposure. However, these studies focus on excessive fluoride exposure and do not address fluoride exposure from toothpaste. A study published in the Journal of Neurosciences in Rural Practice concludes that children in endemic areas of fluorosis are at risk for impaired development of intelligence — related to endemic/high environmental fluoride, not toothpaste. Intelligence refers to the capacity to think logically, learn efficiently, comprehend complex concepts, and adapt to one's surroundings. IQ measures an individual's intelligence in comparison to peers of the same age. IQ is highly heritable and is a reliable predictor of life outcomes. Cellular damage refers to harm caused to cells due to external influences or internal malfunctions, arising from environmental, chemical, and biophysical stimuli. Cells adapt to injuries through four main types of responses: ischaemic/lack of oxygen response, oxidative stress response, heat shock response, and acute phase response. All these studies highlight the effects of excessive or chronic fluoride exposure on IQ and cellular damage. However, no studies have been found indicating that fluoride toothpaste causes cellular damage or lowers IQ. Fluoride levels in toothpaste are insufficient to cause excessive fluoride ingestion. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus to support claims that fluoride toothpaste, which contains standardly safe amounts of fluoride, can lead to lower IQ or cellular damage. Fluoride in toothpaste has scientifically documented benefits including inhibition and reversal of the initiation and progression of dental caries (tooth decay) and stimulates new bone formation. Dr Meenakshi Sahu, Senior Associate Dentist, Vyas Dental Inn, Raipur (C.G): 'Fluoride toothpaste is a trusted and safe way to strengthen teeth and prevent cavities. Its fluoride levels are carefully controlled, making it safe for daily use without causing harm. When used correctly—such as a pea-sized amount for children and proper brushing—it supports healthy teeth without risks. Fluoride toothpaste remains a key part of maintaining good oral hygiene.' Dr Ritu Thawait, Dental Surgeon, Medical Officer, CHC, Risali, Durg, C.G: 'Using fluoride toothpaste is recommended as it helps protect teeth from cavities. However, it should be used cautiously in small children less than 2 years and as directed by your dentist. When used appropriately, fluoride toothpaste prevents excessive fluoride exposure and poses no harm when following the recommended dosage.'

title: Fact Check: Can using ghee and bronze to release toxins work?
claim_text: An Instagram video suggests that dipping a bronze bowl in ghee and massaging the feet can release toxins, reduce acidity, and heat from the body, improve sleep, and nourish nerve endings, as part of a practice called Padabhyanga. The black residue on the skin is evidence of toxins being pulled out.
quick_take: A social media post claims that massaging your feet with ghee using a bronze bowl to release toxins works wonders for your health. It reduces acidity and cools the body. We conducted a thorough fact check and found the claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Padabhyanga is a real Ayurvedic practice, but its benefits are limited. It is an Ayurvedic foot massage technique that uses oils, often ghee, to relax the body. Studies suggest it can reduce stress, improve sleep, and promote relaxation by stimulating pressure points in the feet. However, there is no scientific evidence that massaging with warm ghee and using bronze to release toxins, acidity, or heat from the body is effective. The calming benefits of bronze plate massage come from the massage itself, not from detox processes. Dr Muskan Thakur, Ayurvedic Consultant from Indore says, 'Padabhyanga is much more than a relaxing ritual. When done regularly, especially before bedtime, it helps calm the nervous system, improve blood circulation, and support better sleep. In Ayurveda, we believe the feet connect to important energy channels in the body. By gently massaging them with warm herbal oils, we stimulate these pathways, balance the doshas, and nourish the skin and nerves. It can also help relieve fatigue, reduce stress, ease leg stiffness, and even soothe eye strain. Padabhyanga is a simple yet powerful way to restore balance and promote overall well-being.' Regarding metals like bronze, Dr Almas Fatma, General Physician from Navi Mumbai explains, 'There's no scientific evidence that metals like bronze or silver can pull toxins out of the body through the skin. The idea may sound appealing, but it doesn't match how the human body actually works. Our main organs for detox are the liver, kidneys, and gut. The skin acts as a protective barrier, not a detox tool. Rubbing metal on the skin or using it during massage might feel soothing, but it won't draw out toxins or acidity. These claims are misleading and should be viewed with caution.' Scientific research shows that detoxification happens primarily through the liver and kidneys, not the skin. Bronze, an alloy of copper and tin, has no proven ability to extract toxins. Regarding the black residue seen after massaging with a bronze bowl, this is likely a mix of ghee, dead skin cells, dirt, or oxidation from the bronze itself. Bronze can react with oils or sweat, creating a dark film, but this is not a sign of toxins being removed. The body does not release toxicity through the skin in this way, and no studies support the idea that such residue indicates detoxification. In summary, while Padabhyanga may promote relaxation and improve sleep, there is no scientific evidence that it can release toxicity, acidity, or heat from the body. Ghee may moisturise the skin, but its role in nourishing nerve endings is unproven. Detoxification happens through the liver and kidneys, not through foot massages with bronze bowls. For relaxation, a simple foot massage with any safe oil can be just as effective without the misleading claims.

title: Fact Check: Can using ginger regrow your hair in 21 days? - THIP Media
claim_text: Ginger extract can make thin hair look fuller and thicker in 21 days and can cure bald spots and alopecia
quick_take: A video on social media claims ginger extract can make thin hair look fuller and thicker in 21 days. We fact-checked and found the claim is misleading, hence Mostly False. No scientific evidence confirms ginger extract can prevent hair loss and reduce bald spots to make hair look fuller and thicker.
doctor_explanation: Not exactly. We could not find credible scientific evidence that can confirm ginger extract has a curative effect against bald spots, and regular use for 21 days can make hair look fuller. During our fact check, we found that the video is promoting a website named HairyFormula.com that claims ginger can regrow hair. The website is promoting a hair spray GingerGRO HairReborn Oil which claims to have components that can cure alopecia. The website has not listed the product ingredients and has only mentioned safflower, black sesame and ginger extract as the main ingredients. We ran a Google reverse image search on the images of people shown as testimonials on the website. We found that most of the images used in the ad are taken from different sources. This raises an authenticity about the product and the video promoting it. We could not find any scientific evidence that confirms ginger extract triggers hair follicles to promote hair growth. The video claims that as the product touches the inner part of the scalp, it triggers cells which are responsible for hair regrowth and prevents the recurrence of alopecia in future. We asked Dr Jyothy Kannangath, Dermatologist, how deep topical products can go when applied onto the scalp. To this, she said 'The follicular penetration is a complex process, whose effectiveness and efficiency strongly depends on a diversity of different factors including follicular density and size, activity status of hair follicles and physicochemical properties of the topically applied substances.' This means applying ginger will not give similar results on every scalp. A study published in 2013 measured 6-Gingerol, the main active component in ginger, on hair growth in mice to find that this chemical component is a potential hair growth suppressive drug which can be used to remove hair. There is no research online that has studied the impact of this component on human beings. Another study published in 2014 has shown that ginger has anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities that may improve the scalp environment to support healthy hair growth. Dr Kanangath says 'No scientific evidence proves ginger helps treat baldness. Most of the evidence seems anecdotal.' Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disorder that causes patchy hair loss. People with the condition often grow back hair on their own with steroids, vasodilators, an anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive drug, photodynamic therapy and managing stress. Some advanced and severe forms of alopecia include Alopecia totalis, Alopecia universalis and Ophiasis alopecia. None of these variants of alopecia can be treated using only ginger extract. Alopecia alters the anagen phase of the hair cycle, declines hair diameter and increases the waiting period between hair fall and onset of regrowth. The stages of hair growth begin with the anagen phase. It is the longest phase which grows the hair out from follicles. In the next stage catagen, hair follicles shrink, and the hair growth slows. This stage is followed by the telogen phase in which new hairs form in the follicles but haven't fallen out from the head. Lastly, the shedding of hair is marked by the exogen stage where it is common for a person to lose 50 to 100 strands per day. No evidence shows how ginger extract impacts these cycles to make the hair grow and look fuller as well as thicker. What can be the dangers of trying to cure hair fall through home remedies and not seek medical advice? Using home remedies to treat hair fall don't necessarily cause problems for most people. Commonly used home remedies like oils, henna, onion juice or aloe vera are not harmful to the scalp or hair. But some people can be allergic to raw ingredients. Allergic reactions often go on their own. However, it is better to consult a doctor if the symptoms last longer than expected. Dr Kanangath adds to this by saying 'People with allergies may develop red rash, hives or welts, itchiness, inflammation or swelling in the affected area. Also, self treatments can be dangerous as they may lead to infections if not applied properly. Prolonged application may lead to folliculitis which causes small boils on the scalp.'

title: Can using triphala powder for eye wash detox and soothe eyes?
claim_text: An Instagram video promotes Triphala eyewashes using eye cups, claiming that this practice gives "rest, relaxation, clarity, clean and calm" to the eyes. The caption further describes Triphala as a natural remedy that detoxes, soothes, and strengthens tired eyes.
quick_take: An Instagram video claims that using triphala powder for eye wash can provide rest, relaxation, clarity, and a clean, calm feeling. After fact checking, we found that the claim is only half true.
doctor_explanation:
The claim comes from Nupur Pittie, who runs ChakraSutra and promotes herself as a lifestyle and wellness mentor. Her professional profile shows that she has a background in commerce and has completed short-term certifications such as Laughter Therapy and basic NLP. She also refers to herself as a Guinness World Record holder, though the nature of the record isn't specified. Notably, she does not hold any recognised qualification in medicine, be it modern, Ayurvedic, or homoeopathic. Without a clinical or scientific background, she is not qualified to offer advice on health-related matters, especially those involving sensitive areas like the eyes.

Triphala is a blend of three fruits, namely, Amla, Haritaki, and Bibhitaki, used in Ayurveda, a traditional Indian healing system. It's commonly taken as a powder or tablet to support digestion, liver health, and overall wellness. Traditionally, Triphala is not widely documented for eye treatments in Ayurvedic texts, though some sources mention its use for eye health. Its primary focus is internal health, not external applications like eye rinsing with triphala powder for eye wash.

Yes, there is some scientific evidence suggesting triphala for eyes may be beneficial. A 2010 study tested Triphala on rats to see if it could prevent cataracts caused by a chemical. The researchers gave Triphala internally, not as an eye wash. The study found some protective effects on the eye lens, likely due to Triphala's antioxidant properties. However, this research does not support using Triphala water directly in human eyes, and there is no evidence it can clean or soothe tired eyes when used as an eyewash.

A 2019 study on 80 people with screen-related eye strain found that using Triphala eyewash with eye exercises gave about 55% relief. It worked better than using plain water, but the study does not confirm if it's fully safe or suitable for everyone. Also, these studies don't isolate the effect of triphala water for eyes alone, and direct evidence for eye washing remains limited.

Dr Muskan Thakur, Ayurveda Consultant from Indore, says, "Yes, Triphala powder is traditionally used in Ayurveda as an eye wash to detoxify, soothe, and rejuvenate the eyes. It is considered Chakshushya (beneficial for eye health) and may help reduce dryness, redness, and eye strain, especially from screen exposure or fatigue. To use safely, a decoction is prepared by boiling Triphala in water, cooling it, and filtering it multiple times to ensure it is completely sterile and particle-free before use. However, it should be avoided in cases of active eye infections or recent eye surgery, and it's best used under the guidance of an Ayurvedic practitioner."

Dr Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, explains, "Triphala is a powerful herbal blend in Ayurveda, known for balancing all three doshas and supporting many body systems, including the eyes. Traditionally, it is used in various forms, including decoctions for internal use. Some people use Triphala water as an eyewash, believing it helps soothe the eyes. While this may provide temporary comfort, the concept of detoxing the eyes is not clearly defined in Ayurveda. We must also be cautious, as applying anything directly to the eyes needs sterile conditions. Without proper preparation, such practices may do more harm than good. Always consult a trained practitioner before trying such remedies."

Maybe, but people should exercise caution. While Triphala is generally safe when taken orally, using triphala powder for eye wash carries risks. Homemade solutions may not be sterile, potentially introducing bacteria or fungi, which can cause infections like conjunctivitis or keratitis, a serious condition that may harm vision. Experts emphasise using clean, filtered water and straining the solution thoroughly to remove particles. A 2013 study reported no adverse reactions during a trial of Triphala Kwath for allergic conjunctivitis, but it stressed proper preparation. Consulting an eye care professional or Ayurvedic practitioner is essential, especially for those with existing eye conditions or injuries.

Yes, there is evidence that triphala powder for eye wash can help reduce screen-related eye strain. The abovementioned 2019 study found that Triphala Kwath eyewash, combined with eye exercises, provided significant relief from CVS symptoms, including eye strain, in 40 participants over 42 days. The group using Triphala saw a 55% improvement in symptoms, while the distilled water group saw only 13%. However, the study included eye exercises, so the exact role of Triphala alone is unclear. Still, this suggests triphala for eyes may help soothe tired eyes from screen use.

No, the concept of "detoxing" the eyes lacks scientific support. The eyes have natural mechanisms, like tears and blinking, to remove dust and debris. While Triphala's antioxidant properties may support overall eye health by reducing oxidative stress, as shown in the cataract study on rats from 2010, there's no evidence that triphala water for eyes removes toxins or improves clarity through "detoxing." Claims of "detoxing" are often vague and not backed by science, especially for external eye applications.

title: Can Vaidban Kala Gond kit really relieve joint pain without surgery?
claim_text: A social media post claims that a kit containing 5 ayurvedic medicines (Vaidban Kala Gond Kit) can effectively ease joint pain and eliminate the need for surgery within two weeks, without side effects.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a kit that contains 5 ayurvedic medicines, can effectively ease joint pain and eliminate the need for surgery. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Smit Dave, Orthopaedic Surgeon at Sterling and Orthocure Hospitals in Ahmedabad, emphasises that total knee replacement remains the only reliable treatment for advanced knee arthritis. He notes that oils, gels, creams, or home remedies may offer temporary comfort but cannot cure the condition. Dr Dave warns people not to fall for unverified claims on social media that promote such products as substitutes for surgery in repairing knee damage.

Regarding gond (edible gum): No, edible gum does not have strong evidence for treating arthritis or chronic joint pain. Kala gond or edible gum is derived from tree resins such as Acacia species. Traditionally in Ayurveda, it is used as a strengthening agent, often given to women post-pregnancy for recovery or consumed in sweets during winters for warmth and energy. Some laboratory studies on gum arabic and tragacanth have shown antioxidant or anti-inflammatory properties in test tubes. However, these effects are very limited and have not been proven in large, human clinical trials for arthritis. Unlike NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) or disease-modifying drugs prescribed by doctors, gond has no proven ability to reduce swelling, repair cartilage, or halt joint degeneration. At best, it may provide general nourishment, but it cannot be relied upon as a treatment for arthritis.

Regarding arthritis reversibility: Arthritis damage cannot be reversed so quickly. Arthritis, whether osteoarthritis (wear-and-tear of joints) or rheumatoid arthritis (autoimmune inflammation), is a chronic, long-term condition. Once the cartilage (the cushion between bones) is worn down, it cannot regrow naturally. Modern medicine itself has no permanent cure; instead, treatments aim to manage pain, improve mobility, and slow progression. Even effective interventions like physiotherapy or weight loss take weeks to months, not just 14 days, to show visible results. The claim of "pain-free movement in 2 weeks" oversimplifies a complex medical condition and risks misleading people into unrealistic expectations.

Regarding side effects: Natural does not always mean side effect free. The kit is advertised as having "no steroids, no side effects." While it may not contain steroids, herbal and Ayurvedic products can still cause problems, especially if used without proper regulation. Concerns include adulteration, inherent constituents like alkaloids that may cause adverse events. While mild users may tolerate it, claiming that it is universally "safe for all" is scientifically inaccurate.

Dr. Sushant Srivastava, Orthopaedic Surgeon at Mata Gujri Memorial Medical College and Lions Seva Kendra Hospital, Kishanganj, Bihar, explains that successful treatment of joint pain depends on correctly identifying its root cause. Whether the pain arises from osteoarthritis, injury, inflammation, or infection, treatment cannot be effective without this understanding. Joint pain is not limited to the knees, back, or waist; it can affect multiple joints in the body. Without thorough medical evaluation, it is misleading to claim that any kit can completely cure joint pain.

Regarding customer testimonials: The brand highlights "6 lakh+ satisfied customers", but popularity is not evidence of medical benefit. Many products, from herbal oils to magnetic bracelets, are sold widely, yet scientific reviews often show little to no therapeutic effect. Testimonials are subjective, influenced by placebo effects (feeling better because you expect to), temporary relief, or unrelated lifestyle changes. The gold standard for testing any health product is randomised controlled trials (RCTs) published in peer-reviewed journals. At present, there are no clinical trials available for Vaidban Kala Gond Kit. Without this level of evidence, its claims remain anecdotal and marketing-driven.

The claim that Vaidban Kala Gond Kit can relieve joint pain naturally within two weeks, without side effects or surgery, is not supported by credible scientific evidence. While edible gums may have mild antioxidant or soothing properties, they cannot reverse arthritis or restore damaged joints.

title: Fact Check: Can varicose veins be treated using an oil? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook post promotes a Korean varicose veins essential oil for slim legs without edema, claiming it is made from natural ingredients and can reduce symptoms, relieve pain, support blood circulation, and improve muscle and nerve function.
quick_take: A social media post claims that varicose veins can be treated by applying a Korean varicose vein essential oil. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Varicose veins are enlarged, swollen, and twisted veins that commonly occur in the legs. They develop when the valves within the veins become weakened or damaged, causing blood to pool and the veins to enlarge. Varicose veins are often blue or purple in colour and may be visible through the skin. They can cause symptoms such as pain, aching, heaviness, itching, and swelling in the affected area. Risk factors include a family history of varicose veins, pregnancy, obesity, standing or sitting for long periods, and aging. Varicose veins is a medical condition caused by underlying issues with the veins' valves and blood flow, and they typically require appropriate medical treatment for resolution. External application of oil alone is unlikely to eliminate varicose veins. While certain oils may provide temporary relief for symptoms like discomfort or dry skin associated with varicose veins, they do not address the underlying causes or structural issues of the veins themselves. Essential oils, such as cypress, horse chestnut, or witch hazel, are occasionally mentioned as potential natural remedies for varicose veins, but their efficacy in treating or eliminating varicose veins is not well-established through scientific research. The oil consists of three ingredients namely papaya, glycerol and garden balsam stem. We could not find any scientific research related to these ingredients that can support the claim. However, limited research is available for Glycerol which was used in conjunction with other ingredients for treating varicose veins. We need more research to establish the sole use of glycerol. Dr. Aseem Sharma, DNB (Dermatology), MBA & FMUHS (Trichology & Hair Disorders) informs: 'Massaging with oil may temporarily alleviate discomfort associated with varicose veins. However, it does not do ANYTHING to the underlying condition. Typically weak vein valves and broken blood vessels causes varicose veins. Their treatment typically involves medical interventions such as injection of hardening agents, laser therapy or surgical procedures. Consulting a vascular specialist is better for appropriate evaluation and treatment.' Treatment options for varicose veins may include lifestyle changes (such as exercise and weight management). In many cases, medical interventions such as sclerotherapy, laser therapy, ligation and stripping or surgical procedures may be necessary to effectively treat varicose veins and alleviate symptoms. These approaches directly target the underlying issues and can be more effective in treating varicose veins compared to topical applications of oils. Oils may offer temporary relief or contribute to overall skin health. However, it is essential to consult with a healthcare professional for a proper diagnosis and guidance on appropriate treatment options for varicose veins.

title: Can Vaseline and lemon juice reduce pigmentation in a week?
claim_text: A popular Instagram post suggests that Vaseline is a multifunctional ingredient that may address a range of skin-related issues. One of these is a combination of Vaseline and lemon juice that can effectively reduce dark spots in just one week, along with enhancing facial glow.
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, applying Vaseline and lemon juice could reduce pigmentation in just one week. We verified the claim and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Pigmented skin typically originates from either uneven stimulation or hyperactivation of melanin, resulting in spots, blotches, and extensive facial discolouration. Possible primary triggers include excessive sun exposure, hormonal swings, acne-related inflammation, trauma, and certain medications. The primary culprit of these is UV exposure, which accelerates the formation of melanin and intensifies pre-existing pigmentation. Moreover, disorders like melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation might be major contributors. Because pigmentation can be recurring and persistent, a timely and accurate evaluation is crucial. Evidence-based therapeutic approaches are often suggested for their management. Thus, effective and long-term skin preservation still hinges on early management and rigorous sun protection.

Do Vaseline and lemon juice work well for pigmentation? No, not exactly. Despite the combination of Vaseline and lemon juice being touted as an effective fix for facial pigmentation, its applicability is confined to social media. Since the two ingredients are being considered for facial application, they should be carefully analysed.

We begin with Vaseline. Petroleum jelly is often portrayed as a therapeutic agent that can lock in moisture and supposedly enhance skin repair. Even though it is an occlusive moisturiser that aids in lowering transepidermal water loss, it has no depigmenting impact; it neither prevents the development of melanin nor speeds up pigment clearance.

The lemon juice comes next. This ingredient is packed with citric acid and vitamin C content, which may exhibit mild exfoliating and antioxidant effects. Direct application, however, can be extremely acidic and may even damage the skin's protective layer, which may trigger irritation and possibly aggravate post-inflammatory-induced pigmentation, especially on sun exposure.

While Vaseline may help moisturise skin and lemon juice may be erroneously assumed to lighten skin, neither of these constituents can effectively or safely address pigmentation.

Can skin pigmentation be reduced in a week? No, it is not attainable to drastically reduce hyperpigmented spots in a single week. Intense skincare regimens may cause fading, although noticeable results may take weeks or months to manifest. This may be explained by the fact that melanin disruption and skin cell turnover are both gradual processes that call for consistent exfoliation, sun protection, and prescription pigment inhibitors. Therefore, it is essential to seek medical attention for the issue as soon as possible.

Is it advisable to employ unregulated online pigmentation remedies? No, absolutely not. Even though social media platforms and beauty blogs often promote unregulated quick fixes as easily accessible, affordable, natural, and risk-free alternatives for conventional skin care products, relying on them is unscientific and impractical. Furthermore, such unregulated web-based remedies lack standardisation in terms of composition, dosage, efficacy, and safety. Above all, excessive or incorrect application can exacerbate pigmentation via photosensitivity or discomfort.

This is further supported by Lucknow-based Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, who explains that prolonged facial pigmentation might be attributed to hormonal fluctuations, consistent sun exposure, or skin inflammation associated with acne. Dark spots or patches may also appear as a result of the skin releasing more melanin in reaction to an injury or irritation. Melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are two prominent manifestations. It's also critical to know that inadequate sun protection may make pigmentation worse. Understanding why it occurs enables medical experts to take the appropriate action to prevent it from recurring. Hence, while unregulated online options may appear convenient, relying on them without medical supervision can delay appropriate intervention and compromise skin care.

What is the dermatological approach to skin pigmentation? When addressing hyperpigmentation, clinicians usually employ a meticulous approach. The condition is handled at both the cellular and surface levels, contingent upon skin type, sensitivity, and the severity of pigmentation. Comprehensive photoprotection is typically the first step in the management process. Using broad-spectrum sunscreen is typically part of the required daily routine to prevent excessive UV exposure – the primary cause of facial pigmentation. Melanin suppression and skin regeneration may benefit from prescription topical therapies such as hydroquinone, retinoids, azelaic acid, kojic acid, and niacinamide. Intense pulsed light (IPL), therapeutic lasers, and chemical peels are further methods for addressing pigmented lesions. Ferulic acid, vitamin C, or antioxidant-rich formulations might enhance the therapeutic outcome by alleviating oxidative stress.

Dr. Rashi Soni, a Consultant Dermatologist and co-founder of Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, affirms that doctors frequently employ a progressive approach when correcting severe pigmentation. "Given that UV rays aggravate pigmentation, the first and most crucial step is to protect oneself from the sun every day. It is then advised to use active ingredients that gradually lighten dark spots, like vitamin C, retinoids, or niacinamide. For deeper pigmentation, doctors may suggest laser therapies or chemical peels. Thus, with persistence and a tailored strategy, an observable and long-lasting impact can be achieved. By improving general skin texture and decreasing noticeable pigmentation, the holistic, tried-and-true regimen may help prevent skin photoageing."

title: Can Vicks with turmeric and coconut oil cure piles in 7 days?
claim_text: Applying a mixture of Vicks, turmeric, and coconut oil directly on piles can shrink them within 7 days.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that applying a Vicks mixture can cure piles in just 7 days. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Piles are swollen blood vessels in and around the back passage. When people say 'cure', they often mean the itching, swelling, or burning has settled, and yes, mild hemorrhoid symptoms can calm down in a few days when the main trigger (usually constipation and straining) is fixed. But that's not the same as reversing the underlying tendency for those veins to swell again. Guidelines and reputable patient information consistently point to conservative care first: soften stools, reduce straining, and avoid long toilet sitting. Fibre and fluids reduce bleeding and irritation in early disease, but they don't promise permanent removal of piles in a week. Piles are not one single thing. A small internal pile that flares after constipation behaves very differently from a painful external clot or a prolapsing pile that sticks out. Those don't follow a neat '7-day' script.

Vicks VapoRub is designed for external skin use for cough/cold symptom relief. It commonly contains ingredients such as menthol and camphor, which can cause a strong cooling/burning sensation and skin irritation. On thin, sensitive, or inflamed skin (which is exactly what you have during a pile flare), that irritation risk goes up. If there are tiny cracks or broken skin, it can sting badly and worsen inflammation.

Dr Almas Fatma, General Physician, Navi Mumbai, highlighted that 'Vicks VapoRub is not formulated for use on sensitive anal tissue. It contains menthol, camphor, and eucalyptus oil—ingredients that can cause significant burning, irritation, and inflammation, especially on already swollen or fissured hemorrhoids. Hemorrhoids involve inflamed and fragile blood vessels. While strong counter-irritants may create a temporary cooling sensation, they do not treat the underlying condition and can actually worsen pain, swelling, or skin damage. There is no scientific evidence supporting Vicks as a treatment for piles.'

The anal area is a 'high-friction, high-moisture' zone. Products that are fine on the chest can behave very differently there. Even if someone feels temporary numbness or cooling, that doesn't mean healing is happening, it may just be sensory distraction. In the worst case, irritation leads to more swelling, more scratching, and a longer flare.

Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, said, 'A cooling or numbing sensation does not equal healing. In haemorrhoids, the goal is to reduce inflammation and protect the tissue. Applying strong, non-prescribed balms to the anal area may increase burning, swelling, and prolong the flare-up. It's always safer to use treatments specifically designed for haemorrhoids.'

Dr. V.P Singh, Director & HOD – General, Laser and Laparoscopic Surgery, Dharamshila Narayana Superspeciality Hospital, Delhi: 'Products like Vicks VapoRub are not formulated for use on sensitive anal tissue. Ingredients such as menthol and camphor may cause significant irritation, especially when the skin is already inflamed or compromised, as in piles. Using inappropriate topical agents can worsen symptoms rather than relieve them.'

Turmeric (curcumin) has anti-inflammatory properties in lab studies, and it's often used traditionally on skin. But 'popular' isn't the same as 'proven for piles.' There isn't strong clinical evidence showing that a turmeric paste can treat haemorrhoids effectively, let alone cure them in a week. Importantly, turmeric can also be a skin allergen. Medical literature documents allergic contact dermatitis and irritation from turmeric/curcumin in topical use. In a sore, already-inflamed anal area, an irritant or allergy reaction can feel like the piles are 'getting worse,' when the real issue is dermatitis on top of piles.

Coconut oil can work as an emollient, basically a moisturiser that reduces friction and may soothe dryness. There is some limited research suggesting symptom improvement with coconut oil ointment in specific groups (for example, a trial in pregnant women with grade 1–2 haemorrhoids reported improvement in symptoms). But that is not the same as 'cure', and it doesn't justify a 7-day guarantee for the general population. If coconut oil helps, it's likely by making wiping less painful and reducing irritation, useful, but not a treatment that shrinks the swollen vein in a predictable, permanent way.

The fastest safe wins are boring, but they work. Most pile flares improve when you reduce pressure in the area and make stools easy to pass. If pain is severe, bleeding is heavy, or symptoms don't improve, that's when assessment matters, because sometimes you need medical treatments beyond home care.

Consequently, the natural colour of your urine can cause the vinegar to change colour, which has nothing to do with hCG levels (commonly called the pregnancy hormone) and isn't indicative of pregnancy. Lack of scientific evidence leads to the conclusion that vinegar does not react with hCG specifically to help detect pregnancy. The article notes that other DIY/homemade techniques using sugar, baking soda, shampoo, and garlic have also been debunked. Doctors check for beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) levels in urine or blood, conduct ultrasound scans to visualise the foetus, perform physical examinations, gather medical history, and conduct lab tests. Dr Shiba Mittal states: 'The most reliable method for confirming pregnancy in women is to test for beta-hCG levels in both urine and blood. Pregnancy kits, whether used at home or in a medical setting, detect HCG in urine. The accuracy of home tests depends on the precision of the testing process. Blood tests are particularly useful for detecting pregnancy in its early stages.' Dr Saumya explains: 'Unfortunately, homemade pregnancy tests/methods are widely prevalent among both rural and urban populations due to the stigma associated with unwanted pregnancy or the lack of autonomy for women. However, these DIY methods lack any scientific basis and should not be relied upon for confirming pregnancy, given the significance of the matter. Pregnancy testing kits (hCG tests) readily available at local pharmacies are generally reliable and accurate. Nevertheless, following an hCG test, it is advisable to undergo a confirmatory test—beta hCG test using a blood sample—at a healthcare facility under the supervision of a qualified doctor. Additionally, an ultrasound of the lower abdomen can be useful in confirming pregnancy, determining foetal age, identifying any abnormalities, and detecting the presence of multiple pregnancies.' Dr Pooja Luthra emphasizes: 'Utilising vinegar to detect pregnancy at home is not a reliable approach. Despite numerous old wives' tales circulating, they lack scientific validation. For dependable results, I recommend utilising commercially available pregnancy test kits, which detect the presence of the hormone hCG in urine. These tests have undergone extensive testing and have been demonstrated to be highly accurate when utilised correctly. It is advisable to seek medical attention promptly following hCG testing to proceed with appropriate professional care.' Early detection is important for initiating prenatal care, monitoring maternal and foetal health, nutritional guidance, emotional support, and in cases of unwanted pregnancy, considering options like medical abortion which can only be initiated in early stages.
