title: Do ginger & clove benefit skin, digestion, & testosterone in men?
claim_text: Ginger and clove can act as a potent internal cleanser, purifying the body while supporting skin health, helps in digestion, and serving as effective natural testosterone enhancers
quick_take: A social media post suggests that consuming ginger and clove provides powerful benefits, acting like a dynamic duo to improve digestion, enhance skin health, and boost testosterone levels. We fact checked and found the claim to be Half True.
doctor_explanation: The claim that ginger and clove can 'clean your body like fire' from the inside out is not supported by scientific evidence. The phrase suggests a dramatic detoxification process, but their benefits stem from antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties which support overall health without directly 'cleansing' toxins. Ginger (Zingiber officinale) contains bioactive compounds like gingerol and shogaol. A 2024 review highlights ginger's antioxidants (e.g., vitamin C, quercetin) that reduce oxidative stress by neutralizing free radicals, which may protect cells from damage. Ginger also enhances gastric motility and reduces nausea, as shown in a 2025 Clinical Nutrition Open Science. These effects may be mistaken for detoxification, but no studies confirm ginger enhances liver or kidney detox pathways. Cloves (Syzygium aromaticum) are rich in eugenol, which has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. A 2018 study in Nigerian Journal of Physiological Sciences showed cloves reduced oxidative damage in diabetic rats, supporting organ health. However, no peer-reviewed research supports cloves as a broad detoxifier. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said "Ginger and clove are incredibly valuable in everyday cooking, thanks to their antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. However, it's important to understand that these spices don't function like medicine when taken casually. The idea that ginger and clove can 'clean the body like fire' is not backed by any credible clinical evidence. While they support, they do not detoxify the liver or flush out toxins in the way many viral claims suggest. The liver and kidneys do that job naturally, and no single food or spice can replace those organs' functions." Dr Divya Chauhan, Senior Ayurveda Researcher (R & D Team), DesiLLM Private Limited said "In Ayurveda, each person's unique 'prakriti' means ginger and clove affect everyone differently, not as a universal detox. They boost 'Agni,' the digestive fire, enhancing metabolism and digestion to help the body eliminate toxins naturally. However, too much can disrupt balance, especially Pitta dosha, causing issues like skin irritation or overheating. Overusing these spices as supplements, not food, may also lead to stomach issues like grahani or IBS-like symptoms. Moderation is key, and don't fall for exaggerated claims." Dr Thulasi K, BAMS, MD (Ayurveda) said "It depends upon the state of digestive tract or koshta. If you are a person with difficulty in digesting heavy meals it would benefit. But if you are a person with acidity and heart burn – it can backfire. So every home remedy or medicine is subjective." Regarding testosterone: Ginger shows potential as a testosterone booster, but evidence is limited to animal studies and small human trials. A 2018 review in Biomolecules analyzed in vivo studies, primarily on diabetic rats, and found ginger increased serum testosterone by enhancing luteinizing hormone (LH) production, increasing testicular cholesterol (a testosterone precursor), reducing oxidative stress, and improving testicular blood flow. A study reported a 17.7% testosterone increase in infertile men taking ginger, but the study's small sample size and lack of detailed methodology limit its reliability. No robust human clinical trials confirm ginger's effects in healthy men. Cloves have even less evidence. A 2004 study in BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine found that a 50% ethanolic clove extract increased sexual behavior in male rats, suggesting a possible testosterone boost. Manasi Banduni, Senior Nutritionist at Clinic Living Plus, Bangalore said "I often see people turning to ginger and clove benefits with the hope that these will boost testosterone or detox the body overnight. But that's an oversimplification of how nutrition works. Ginger does have some emerging evidence. But the human data is still early and limited. Similarly, cloves are high in antioxidants and useful in managing oxidative stress, which could theoretically benefit hormonal balance but we can't label them as natural testosterone boosters based on a few small-scale studies." Regarding skin health: Ginger contains bioactive compounds like gingerol and shogaol, which help combat oxidative stress that can prevent premature aging, wrinkles, and UV-induced skin damage, as demonstrated in a 2022 study. Its anti-inflammatory effects may reduce inflammation associated with acne, psoriasis, or dermatitis. Additionally, a study showed ginger's ability to enhance wound healing by promoting collagen synthesis. Clove, rich in eugenol, boasts one of the highest antioxidant capacities among spices, protecting skin from free radical damage, as per a 2021 study. It also provides mild anesthetic effects, reducing itchiness. While generally safe in moderation, ginger may interact with blood thinners and undiluted clove oil can cause burns. Dr Almas Fatma, General Physician from Navi Mumbai said "As a physician, I encourage my patients to enjoy spices like ginger and clove as part of a healthy diet, but I caution them against exaggerated claims seen online. Detoxing, for example, is a natural process handled efficiently by the liver and kidneys. No herb or spice 'burns out' toxins from the body like fire. When it comes to testosterone or hormone-related claims, most of the studies cited are conducted on animals, and very few are reliable human trials. People must understand the difference between food-based support for overall health and clinical treatment. These spices support wellness but are not substitutes for medical therapies."

title: Do green leafy vegetables melt bones and cause memory loss?
claim_text: A video shared by the account haryanalive_official features a man wearing a saffron cloth claiming that consuming green leafy vegetables like sarso (mustard greens), methi (fenugreek), and palak (spinach) can be harmful to health. He suggests that these vegetables may lead to melting of bone, memory loss, and skin issues.
quick_take: A social media post claims that consuming green leafy vegetables, such as sarso (mustard greens), methi (fenugreek), and palak (spinach), can be harmful to your health. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Green leafy vegetables do not harm bones or cause memory loss. In fact, they are a powerhouse of nutrients that support bone health. These vegetables are packed with vitamins and minerals like vitamin K, calcium, magnesium, and folate, all of which are essential for maintaining strong and healthy bones. Vitamin K plays a crucial role in calcium absorption and bone mineralisation, helping prevent fractures. Calcium is also found in significant amounts in these vegetables. The idea that these greens 'melt' bones stems from a misunderstanding of oxalates, naturally occurring compounds found in foods like spinach and methi. Oxalates can bind with calcium and reduce its absorption in the body. However, this effect is very minimal unless consumed in extremely large amounts over long periods of time, which is highly unlikely for the average person. Regarding memory loss, green leafy vegetables may actually help improve brain function. They are loaded with antioxidants, vitamins (especially folate and vitamin K), and minerals that support brain health. Folate is essential for proper brain function and has been shown to improve cognitive performance. Vitamin K has also been linked to better memory and cognitive function. Several studies suggest that a diet rich in these nutrients can help protect against cognitive decline and age-related memory loss. Antioxidants in these vegetables help fight oxidative stress, which is known to damage brain cells and contribute to conditions like dementia. Manasi Banduni, Senior nutritionist, Clinic Living Plus, Bangalore said: 'Green leafy vegetables do not harm your bones. In fact, they are beneficial for bone health, as they are rich in calcium, vitamin K, and other essential nutrients. While some greens like spinach contain oxalates, which can bind to calcium and slightly reduce its absorption, this effect is minimal and unlikely to cause harm, particularly if you maintain a balanced diet with other calcium-rich foods. The claim that bones can 'melt' as suggested in the video is a significant exaggeration.' Dr. Mohit Sandhu, BAMS, CAD, CAC, and PGDAKS, Founder of the Association for Ayurvedic Palpative Pain Medicine, Gurgaon said: 'According to Ayurveda, eating sarson (mustard greens), methi (fenugreek leaves), and palak (spinach) does not 'melt bones.' These leafy greens are nutritious when consumed in moderation. While palak contains oxalates that may reduce calcium absorption if overconsumed, all three greens support digestion and metabolism. Moderation and proper cooking methods (like with ghee and spices) enhance their benefits. Overconsumption can create Ama (toxins), indirectly affecting bone health.' Dietician Kamana Chauhan said: 'It's well known that vegetables are beneficial for overall health. Research shows that foods high in vitamin K, such as spinach, kale, methi, sarso, asparagus, and Brussels sprouts, can help slow cognitive decline with age. What's good for the heart is also good for the brain. A nutrient-rich diet, along with regular exercise and avoiding smoking, can lower the risk of dementia.' Dr. Sharad Malhotra, Senior Gastroenterologist at Akash Healthcare explained: 'Spinach, methi and sarson are a great source of iron and vitamins. However, it's important to consume all foods in moderation as part of a balanced diet. If there are any specific health concerns, then spinach may need to be avoided.' The concern with these vegetables often comes from their high oxalate content, which can potentially contribute to kidney stones in susceptible individuals. However, this risk is typically only a concern for people who are prone to forming kidney stones, and it can be managed by balancing oxalate-rich foods with other foods and staying well-hydrated. The benefits of consuming these vegetables far outweigh the minimal risks for most people.

title: Do honey and lemon juice work well for skin pigmentation?
claim_text: Honey and lemon juice can effectively handle skin pigmentation
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, honey and lemon juice can effectively handle skin pigmentation. We fact-checked the claim and found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Skin pigmentation is usually induced by the hyperactivation or uneven stimulation of the melanin, resulting in spots, blotches, and extensive facial discolouration. Primary contributors include ultraviolet (UV) light, which worsens pre-existing pigmentation and speeds up melanin production, as well as disorders such as melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Honey and lemon juice are being circulated as natural therapies for skin pigmentation; their relevance is confined to social media. Even if the combination has been recommended for topical skin application, a thorough analysis of its components is essential.

Starting with lemon juice - it includes citric acid, a naturally occurring moderate exfoliator that may aid in the removal of superficial dead skin cells and might have a skin-brightening impact. However, lemon juice's citric acid is excessively acidic to be applied directly to the skin, as it can cause irritation and burns and even exacerbate post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Regarding honey - it has been extensively researched for dermatological usage because it contains a variety of phytochemicals, including flavonoids, dicarboxylic acids, coumarins, and phenolic acids. Thus, honey exhibits antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, antiaging, antioxidant, anticancer, depigmenting, photoprotective, wound-healing, and skin barrier-enhancing properties. Despite being valued for its moisturising and anti-inflammatory qualities, honey lacks the melanin-inhibiting qualities required to target deeper pigment pathways.

Even though the lemon-honey combination may brighten skin temporarily, it is not clinically verified to be effective in addressing existing pigmentation disorders, such as melasma or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Dermatologist-guided skincare remains the most reliable and secure approach.

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, a Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine consultant in Lucknow, explains that frequent sun exposure, hormonal changes, or skin inflammation linked to acne are major causes for prolonged facial pigmentation. Dark spots or patches can also arise from the skin releasing more melanin in reaction to an injury or irritation. Melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation are two frequent manifestations. Furthermore, inadequate sun protection can aggravate pigmentation. These online options usually overlook oxidative stress and photoaging, which are the primary causes of pigmentation.

Dr. Rashi Soni, Consultant Dermatologist and co-founder of Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, explains that when correcting severe pigmentation, they frequently employ a graded approach. The first and most important step is to shield yourself from the sun every day because UV rays exacerbate pigmentation. After that, it is recommended to utilise active components such as vitamin C, retinoids, or niacinamide that progressively lighten dark spots. Doctors may recommend chemical peels or laser therapies to alleviate deeper discolouration.

The most reliable treatment approaches include: comprehensive photoprotection using broad-spectrum sunscreens; prescription topical medications like hydroquinone, retinoids, azelaic acid, kojic acid, and niacinamide for melanin suppression and skin regeneration; chemical peels, therapeutic lasers, and intense pulsed light (IPL); and antioxidant-rich formulations like ferulic acid or vitamin C to reduce oxidative stress.

title: Do jaggery and lukewarm water work well for kidney stones?
claim_text: Consuming jaggery with lukewarm water can successfully dissolve renal stones. The post suggests taking the combination before bedtime could help with joint discomfort and heartburn.
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, combining jaggery with lukewarm water can help dissolve kidney stones. After verifying the claim, it was found to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Renal stones, or calculi, are hard, pebble-like aggregates that develop in the renal calyces and pelvis. They usually develop from the crystallisation of salts and minerals such as calcium, oxalate, and uric acid in extremely concentrated urine. The most frequent causes include familial inheritance, dehydration, certain medical illnesses, and high-protein dietary choices. Male patients between the ages of 30 and 50 tend to be at higher risk.

Jaggery, frequently referred to as 'gur' or 'guda', is consumed as a nutritious ingredient because it is packed with minerals such as iron, potassium, magnesium, and calcium. Traditional sweetener is considered beneficial for digestion, cleansing, and overall metabolism. Due to the detox-related benefits of the combination, it is believed that it may help flush out stones; however, there are no credible scientific studies to support the notion that jaggery, either by itself or with lukewarm water, can dissolve or break up renal stones. Additionally, the temperature of the water may not have a very significant impact on kidney stone dissolution.

On the other hand, consuming a lot of carbohydrates and added sugars may raise the risk of developing renal calculi. Fructose and additional sugars enhance urinary excretion of calcium and oxalate, key stone-forming components. Research found those who consumed more than 25% of their energy from added sugars were 88% more likely to develop renal stones than people who consumed less than 5%. Elevated blood sugar levels may also promote lower urinary pH levels.

Dr. Bhanu Mishra, Consultant Nephrologist at Delhi's BLK Max Hospital, states that the aforementioned combination is ineffective at dissolving stones. While drinking adequate water and calcium can help prevent kidney stones from forming, it is not a valid idea that a drink will dissolve and flush kidney stones effectively. Patients should get medical help right away if they suspect kidney stones or if they are exhibiting symptoms like fever with chills, burning sensation in the urine, nausea or vomiting, or back pain.

Dr. Archana Daftardar, consultant nephrologist and physician specialising in hypertension and transplants at Renova Hospitals in Kompally, Hyderabad, suggests that there are numerous misconceptions regarding kidney stone management and prevention. However, untested natural substitutes could worsen the condition rather than improve it. Such unsubstantiated alternative therapies could give a false sense of assurance or even interfere with prescribed medications. This can exacerbate the condition or delay required medical care.

Treatment options: For stones 5-10 mm, alpha-blocker-based medical expulsive therapy is used. For larger stones associated with infection, hydronephrosis, or persistent discomfort: percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy (ESWL), and ureteroscopy are employed.

title: Fact Check: Do magnets at the corner of your eyes really calm anger?
claim_text: A Facebook post claims that sticking a small magnet or even a dried pea on the outer corners of the eyes or eyebrows helps 'channel out' anger or bring emotional balance.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that placing a magnet or a pea near the corners of your eyes or eyebrows can calm anger. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Magnet therapy has been around for centuries, often promoted for pain, stress, and circulation. However, when it comes to emotions such as anger or anxiety, there's no credible research showing magnets can influence brain function. The magnetic fields produced by small household magnets are extremely weak - they simply cannot penetrate deep enough to affect the brain or its emotional centres such as the amygdala, which is responsible for processing fear, stress, and anger. Clinical treatments like Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) do use magnetic fields to influence brain activity, but they require large, medically approved devices that deliver precise electromagnetic pulses under expert supervision. A tiny magnet stuck to the skin, especially near the eye, does not have any comparable effect. In short, the magnets you find at home or in bracelets are thousands of times weaker than what is needed to affect mood or emotions. Dr Varun Jaitpal, MBBS, MD, DNB(Psychiatry), explained that one of the biggest challenges society faces today is the widespread lack of awareness and misinformation about mental health. He noted that harmful beliefs like seeing mental illness as a weakness often stop people from seeking help. Another common myth, he added, is that depression can be beaten through willpower alone, without professional guidance. Many also fear that psychiatric medications cause dependency or severe side effects, while some expect therapy to work instantly. Such misconceptions, Dr. Jaitpal warned, can prevent people from accessing proper care and may worsen their mental health struggles. Regarding pressing the corners of the eyes - applying gentle pressure near the eyes or brows may create a sense of calm simply because of the relaxation response. When you press or massage the skin, it activates touch receptors that signal the brain to relax muscles and slow the heartbeat. This has nothing to do with magnets or peas - it's just the body's natural reaction to soothing touch. Some alternative medicine traditions, like magnetic acupressure, describe points near the temples and eyebrows as calming spots. Modern science suggests that any benefit likely comes from increased awareness of breathing, temporary distraction from stress, and sensory comfort, not energy flow or magnetic influence. As physiotherapist Prachi Bharwani explains, 'Pressing or massaging around the eyes can feel relaxing because it shifts your focus away from emotional tension. It helps you pause, breathe, and physically unwind. But there's no evidence that a magnet or a pea does anything special.' Her words highlight what most professionals agree on: relaxation comes from your body's response to touch and mindfulness, not from the object used. The placebo effect is when you experience real improvements simply because you believe a treatment will work. If you expect calmness from a magnet or pea, your brain releases chemicals like endorphins and reduces stress hormones such as cortisol. This doesn't mean the object has magical powers - rather, your belief triggers a chain of mental and physical reactions that mimic true relaxation. Evidence-backed, practical strategies work far better than untested tricks. These methods are backed by consistent evidence and can be practiced anywhere without risk.

quick_take: An article published by NewsPunch titled "Official Study Concludes That Masks Caused More COVID" was published on May 11, 2022. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Research states that "A primary route of transmission of COVID-19 is via respiratory particles. Reducing disease spread requires two things: limiting contacts of infected individuals via physical distancing and other measures and reducing the transmission probability per contact. Current evidence indicates that mask wearing reduces transmissibility per contact by reducing transmission of infected respiratory particles." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also recommends the use of mask by stating, "Wear a Mask to Protect Yourself and Others." According to the WHO, "Masks should be used as part of a comprehensive strategy of measures to suppress transmission and save lives; the use of a mask alone is not sufficient to provide an adequate level of protection against COVID-19." There is no substantial scientific evidence that proves that masks can cause COVID. We did not find any official study by a government or medical organization. Even in context with this story, the study is written by an individual. The conclusions section of his reports says, "no cause-effect conclusions could be inferred from this observational analysis." Also, a report by the Office of National Statistics in the United Kingdom published on September 2021 report shows that people who never wore masks or felt they weren't needed in enclosed spaces were more than 1.5 times more likely to test positive for COVID. title: Fact Check: Do mobile phones send electric waves through the body when used while on charging? - THIP Media
claim_text: It is unsafe to use a mobile phone while it is charging because it allows electric waves to pass through the body
quick_take: A social media video claims that it's unsafe to use the phone while it's charging because it allows electric waves to pass through the body. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Not exactly. No scientific evidence confirms that mobile phones are unsafe because they send electric waves through the body. A voltage stick tells whether there is live voltage within the device. So, any cable plugged into the wall will show the same result. The phone charger has a rectifier which converts dangerous mains voltage into harmless low DC voltage. A (2021) research has shown that a current of 1 milliampere is enough to feel an electric shock. The smartphone batteries have around 4 volts of voltage. One milliampere is 1/1000th of one ampere. So, 0.001 milliampere is just too low to cause any effect on the human body. It means the tiny amount of live voltage picked by the voltage stick is not enough to cause any damage to the human body. However, this may not be the case with cheap chargers. In cheap chargers, the output voltage is not consistent and fluctuates to have a high-frequency leakage. This leakage can make the cheap charger catch fire while plugged into the wall. A (2009) study states that 'the body has resistance to current flow. More than 99% of the body's resistance to electric current flow is at the skin'. It means only in rarest of cases the fully failed cheap charger can electrocute people. Yes. Electrical injuries are common and can occur as a result of lightning, low-voltage, or high-voltage injury to cause high morbidity and mortality. A research states, 'There are four main types of electrical injuries: flash, flame, lightning, and true. Flash injuries, caused by an arc flash, are typically associated with superficial burns, as no electrical current travels past the skin. Flame injuries occur when an arc flash ignites an individual's clothing, and electrical current may or may not pass the skin in these cases. Lightning injuries, involving extremely short but very high voltage electrical energy, are associated with an electrical current flowing through the individual's entire body. True electrical injuries involve an individual becoming part of an electrical circuit'. The available published studies recommend people to not use cheap and damaged electrical devices or leave them unattended while plugged into the wall. THIP MEDIA TAKE: Mobile phones do send the electric current. However, the tiny amount is not enough to cause damage to the human body. Hence, the claim is Mostly False until proven otherwise.

title: Fact Check: Do mouth ulcers have an instant Ayurvedic remedy?
claim_text: Heat brought on by liver-related abnormalities is the root cause of mouth ulcers, which can be instantly resolved by an Ayurvedic formulation. A combination of black peppercorns, long pepper, and dry ginger powder can provide instant relief from mouth ulcers.
quick_take: A trending Facebook post claims that an Ayurvedic remedy can effectively address mouth ulcers. We fact-checked and found that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Mouth ulcers, also referred to as aphthous ulcerative lesions, are erosions or ruptures in the mucosal lining of the oral cavity. These are frequently spherical or oval ulcers with a yellowish or whitish base and an elevated red border. The most frequent causes include unintentional biting, sharp teeth, abrasive foods, bacterial or viral infections, immune-mediated reactions, nutritional deficiencies, systemic illnesses, and drug-related reactions. Contrary to common perception, liver imbalance is not necessarily the cause of mouth ulcers. While some oral symptoms, such as xerostomia and mucosal ulcerations, are associated with a chronic liver condition, these associations are secondary. Therefore, oral ulcers are usually systemic or local in origin; however, they are not necessarily associated with gastrointestinal conditions. The phrase 'Ayurvedic therapy' is widely used on a number of social media platforms and conveys a misleading impression that the suggested treatment is universally applicable, safe, and efficient. However, the highly specialised practice of Ayurveda, the traditional science, promotes a customised approach based on each individual's specific tridosha imbalance. Classical Ayurvedic texts call mouth ulcers 'Mukhapaka'. The choice of therapeutic intervention depends upon the type of ulcer—Pitta-type ulcers are frequently inflamed and burning, whereas Vata-type ulcers might be dry and cracked—as well as the patient's constitution and severity. Dr. Thulasi K, who is currently associated with Kottakkal Arya Vaidyasala and Punarjani, states that as per Ayurveda, Pitta dushti or Kapha pitta dushti causes Asya paka, or mouth ulcers. She underlines that traditional medicine encompasses both local and systemic care because the primary contributors include poor eating habits, an irregular waking cycle, and lifestyle decisions that impede digestion. Rinsing with buttermilk or triphala kashayam is a frequently employed method to achieve localised control. For systemic rectification, Ayurvedic practitioners use pitta/kapha pitta samana medications, such as patoladi kashayam or guluchyadi kashayam, to correct digestion, based on the status of the gut for the person. Both the local and systemic management approaches are supported with individual or specific dietary changes. People frequently turn to organic options because mouth ulcers can be extremely painful and even persistent. One such online remedy that has been suggested is a combination of black peppercorns, long pepper, and dry ginger powder. The three ingredients are being considered because of their mild anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, or antibacterial qualities. Among these, dried ginger has been most extensively explored for oral conditions. Ginger extract may help people with recurrent aphthous stomatitis with their discomfort; however, it may not have an impact on ulcer healing time or shrinkage. Despite these benefits, there is a lack of solid clinical evidence to support the use of black peppercorns, long pepper, or dry ginger powder to heal mouth ulcers. Dr. Gagandeep Singh Sodhi, a dentist in Delhi, supports this further, suggesting that adopting questionable home remedies for mouth ulcers before seeing a doctor could delay necessary care, worsen symptoms, and result in unanticipated complications. Therefore, for timely and comprehensive intervention, one should consult with a qualified dental specialist. Please note that not all online suggestions may always be safe, and reliance on them may pose risks. Furthermore, delaying evidence-based treatment can exacerbate pre-existing conditions and possibly result in infections. Therefore, the use of such spice-based therapies for mouth ulcers should be limited to their application as an adjuvant rather than as their primary treatment. A systematic, scientifically validated approach to mouth ulcer prevention places a strong emphasis on limiting contributing factors, promoting oral cleanliness, and addressing the underlying medical conditions. Self-care measures primarily include meticulous oral hygiene practices, which is the cornerstone of the prevention protocol. This entails using medicated toothpaste that is devoid of sodium lauryl sulphate twice a day, rinsing your mouth with mouthwashes that don't include alcohol, managing stress, and getting sufficient nutrition. Dr. Surya Kiran Mudigonda, Consultant Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeon at Renova Hospitals in Hyderabad, points out that applying ice, butter, or ghee to mouth ulcers usually reduces discomfort while preserving moisture for wound healing. However, these are not the approved options for managing mouth ulcers. Do not apply any irritants, such as clove oil or turmeric powder, to mouth ulcers. They might worsen the discomfort and irritation. Professional intervention begins with topical corticosteroids. Severe cases can be managed with systemic medication. For certain patients with both vaginal and oral lesions, immunosuppressants may be recommended. It is essential to acknowledge that mouth ulcers are unpleasant oral lesions that need personalised treatment. Because of their complexity, ulcerative lesions may not be fully addressed by a single Ayurvedic treatment. Therefore, one should seek medical guidance before incorporating any dubious online advice into an ongoing treatment regimen.

title: Fact Check: Can dried coconut cure mouth ulcers?
claim_text: According to a style_tuber Instagram post, eating dry coconut is effective for mouth ulcers. The post titled "सबको पता होना चाहिए शेयर जरूर करें" suggests that consuming dried coconut could immediately heal existing mouth ulcers.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that consuming dried coconut can help cure mouth ulcers. After analysing the assertion, we discovered that it isfalse.
doctor_explanation: Mouth ulcers are uncomfortable lesions that appear in the oral cavity. They usually originate in the soft tissues that line the tongue, buccal mucosa, gingiva, lips, and roof of the mouth. Canker sores usually constitute the most prevalent kind of mouth ulcer. Usually unpleasant, these lesions can make it challenging to consume food, drink, or even converse. While the exact developmental source is unknown, their primary etiological factor has been determined to be genetic inheritance. Furthermore, a few factors could serve as accelerators for their development. These include orthodontic braces, irritating dentures, incomplete dental fillings, chronic stress, anxiety, hormonal fluctuations, certain allergens, lack of sleep, excessive consumption of citrus fruits or spices, and specific medications. These prevalent oral lesions fall into one of the following categories: Can the consumption of dried coconut help get rid of mouth ulcers? No, not at all. Despite being regarded as a safe choice, there is conflicting scientific evidence regarding its potential use for healing mouth ulcers. Coconut oil contains medium-chain fatty acids (MCFAs), especially lauric acid, which are usually regarded as beneficial. Monolaurin, a derivative of lauric acid, possesses antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and wound-healing qualities. Lauric acid has also demonstrated strong bactericidal effectiveness against a range of oral infections, including Streptococcus mutans, Staphylococcus aureus, Lactobacillus species, and even Candida. Most significantly, using virgin coconut oil along with 5% amlexanox reduced the ulcer size significantly by the fifth day. However, these coconut-related benefits are only relevant to preliminary studies. Dr. Pooja Siwach, Oral and Maxillofacial pathologist, advises that mouth ulcers, though small, can cause significant discomfort. Gentle remedies—saltwater rinses cleanse, honey soothes, aloe vera heals, and ice might ease the pain. Avoiding irritants and maintaining oral hygiene can prevent recurrence. These simple, natural treatments often work wonders, supporting the body's healing process. However, persistent or severe sores may signal deeper health issues and deserve professional attention. Dr. Surya Kiran Mudigonda, Consultant Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeon, Renora Hospitals, Hyderabad, adds credence to this by highlighting that application of ice, butter, or ghee over the mouth ulcers usually provides symptomatic relief to relieve discomfort and preserve moisture for the wound healing. Nonetheless, they are not the definitive treatment methods for mouth ulcers. Never apply turmeric powder, clove oil, or any such irritants to mouth ulcers. They will worsen the condition. It is crucial to clarify that there is no clinical data available that establishes dried coconut as an effective remedy for mouth ulcers. While most of the mouth ulcers may heal on their own, conventional topical agents are usually recommended for symptomatic relief. Hence, it is simply a folkloric remedy rather than an evidence-based intervention. Should one depend on unverified home remedies for mouth ulcers? No, not really. While minor aphthous ulcers often heal spontaneously in a week or two, persistent and larger lesions necessitate established therapeutic intervention. Certain natural remedies, including aloe vera, honey, and salt-water rinses, are frequently utilised. This may be explained by their soothing, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory characteristics. Among these, aloe vera in particular has demonstrated potential for both decreasing ulcer size and alleviating discomfort while maintaining a low risk of adverse consequences. Furthermore, a number of additional natural extracts show a beneficial correlation with notable decreases in exudate, erythema, ulcer size, and pain intensity. These outcomes, however, are frequently associated with specific standardised herbal formulations rather than random or unregulated online home remedies, which may do more harm than benefit. Variations in potency, preparation method, and dosage further raise concerns with regard to the safety and reliability of unverified herbal remedies. Dr. Gagandeep Singh Sodhi, a Delhi-based dentist, supports it further by stating that adopting untested home remedies for mouth ulcers before seeking medical consultation can delay necessary care, worsen symptoms, and present unanticipated health risks. Even though certain natural therapies may have minor benefits when carefully evaluated, it is not recommended to rely primarily on them without professional supervision. These home remedies should only be used in conjunction with established treatments, especially when the mouth ulcers are severe, persistent, or recurrent. When should someone with mouth ulcers seek medical intervention? As was previously stated, most oral ulcers are small, non-contagious canker sores that usually heal on their own without requiring specific medical attention. Some at-home practices that may help reduce oral discomfort and possibly enhance the healing process involve employing warm saline rinses, avoiding hot, spicy, and acidic meals, and drinking enough water to keep the mouth moist. Additionally, salt can establish an alkaline oral environment that hinders the survival of dental microorganisms. title: Fact Check: Do mRNA Covid vaccines impair long-term immunity? - THIP Media
claim_text: Unvaccinated people are much more likely to develop broad antibody immunity after Covid infections than people who have received mRNA shots, a new study shows. mRNA vaccines impair long-term immunity after Covid infection. COVID boosters are destroying the immune system.
quick_take: A preprint server medRxiv published a preprint article that analysed the level of antibody named anti-nucleocapsid antibody (anti-N Ab) post-infection in people vaccinated with the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine (mRNA-1273 vaccine) and compared the result with those who received a placebo. Referring to this article, several social media posts claimed mRNA vaccines impair long-term immunity after Covid infection. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: It does not seem so. No evidence confirms that mRNA Covid vaccines impair long-term immunity. The preprint article referred to by social media users nowhere confirms that the mRNA vaccines impair long-term immunity after Covid infection. The preprint article was conducted before the occurrence of Delta and Omicron variants. This article analysed the level of antibody named anti-nucleocapsid antibody (anti-N Ab) post-infection in people vaccinated with the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine (mRNA-1273 vaccine) and compared the result with those who received a placebo. How are people diagnosed with Covid infection? The available antibody tests for Covid assess proteins formed in response to either Spike protein or Nucleocapsid protein. The mRNA covid vaccines recognize the formed proteins on the spike proteins to show a positive test for Covid infection in the cases with prior infection and/or vaccination. However, the formed proteins can also recognize nucleocapsids. So, tests are available that can recognize these proteins on nucleocapsid to show a positive result for cases with prior Covid infection having a history of Covid vaccination. Anti-N antibodies are produced when a person gets infected with Covid infection. Anti-N antibodies only recognize Nucleocapsid – a molecule present inside the Covid virus. Whereas, Anti-S antibodies recognize spike protein present on the surface of the Covid virus. Anti-S antibodies can be present within the body after a Covid infection and a vaccine. This is because mRNA from vaccines enters 'the muscle cells and instructs the cells' machinery to produce a harmless piece' of the spike protein. The mRNA Covid vaccines do not promote the production of anti-N antibodies but recognize anti-S antibodies. The preprint article has shown that 40% of vaccinated people formed anti-N antibodies at a median of 53 days after the diagnosis which was 93% in the placebo group. It seems, because the unvaccinated people had more anti-N antibodies after the Covid infection than vaccinated people, the preprint article claimed Covid-19 vaccines impair long-term immunity. However, the article does not confirm if more anti-N antibodies provide strong immunity or if these antibodies confirm vaccines are effective against Covid infection. Also, the article did not confirm if Covid vaccines have any role in developing fewer anti-N antibodies after the Covid infection to impair long-term immunity. Does the human body rely only on immunity from vaccines? No. The human body experiences innate and adaptive immunity against viruses such as Covid. Innate immunity is the defence system people are born with. It is the early response against the virus, which is then followed by adaptive immunity. Adaptive immunity is the process through which the body develops a stronger immune response against viruses using B and T cells. The B cells produce anti-S and anti-N antibodies. The mRNA Covid vaccines target spike protein because it is where the virus attaches to the healthy cell and multiplies. So, the best thing is to inhibit the virus from attaching itself to the healthy cell, which mRNA vaccines do. Besides spike protein, nucleocapsid also gets affected by the virus. However, from the perspective of mRNA Covid vaccine, spike protein is more important as it is the first point of contact with the virus. From the conclusion of the preprint article, it is clear that more research is needed on anti-N immune responses along with vaccines to produce immunity against Covid infection. Besides this, more evidence is needed to confirm if combined immunity of anti-S and anti-N antibodies is better against Covid infection. A study has shown that vaccination against Covid infection and reinfection can reduce the number of anti-N antibodies. But this should not have any impact on the overall immunity. THIP MEDIA TAKE: The available evidence does not suggest mRNA Covid vaccines impair long-term immunity after Covid infection. We need more studies to understand better the mechanism of mRNA Covid vaccines and the combined effect of all types of immunity against Covid infection.

title: Fact Check: Do mRNA vaccines cause large blood clots?
claim_text: A post on X by Richard Hirschman shows a picture of a 19-inch long clot removed from an artery, implying such clots are a new phenomenon directly linked to mRNA vaccines (such as those used to prevent COVID-19). The post suggests these clots did not occur before 2021 and that the vaccine is the most likely cause.
quick_take: A post on X claims that mRNA vaccines cause large blood clots. We did a thorough fact check to term this claim as False.
doctor_explanation: mRNA vaccines are not causing large blood clots. The claim that mRNA vaccines cause large blood clots lacks scientific evidence. Blood clotting is a complex physiological process that can happen due to various factors. And, none of these risk factors or verified data are linking mRNA vaccines to the formation of such large clots. There were concerns about a rare clotting condition, VITT (vaccine-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenia), linked to adenoviral vector vaccines. However, mRNA vaccines such as Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna have not been associated with this issue. By January 2022, over ten billion COVID-19 vaccine doses had been administered globally. Data from millions of mRNA vaccine recipients show no significant connection to large clots. VTE (venous thromboembolism) is a common condition, affecting 1 to 2 in 1000 people annually. So, some cases will occur by chance after vaccination. However, detailed studies have not shown a direct link between mRNA vaccines and these clots, making such claims more about misinterpretation than science. The development of blood clots has been a recognised but rare side effect associated with certain vaccines. This specifically applies to the AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson COVID-19 vaccines, which are not mRNA vaccines. This condition, known as VITT, is different from the general blood clotting process and involves a combination of blood clots and low platelet counts. However, these cases are exceptionally rare. In recent studies, VITT has been found to occur at a rate of roughly 1 case per 100,000 vaccinations. Still, the risk of dying from COVID-19 without vaccination is much higher than the rare chance of clots from the Johnson & Johnson or AstraZeneca vaccines. There is no significant or conclusive evidence that mRNA vaccines, such as those produced by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, cause unusual or large blood clots. The mRNA vaccines work by instructing cells to produce a protein that triggers an immune response, and they have no association with the mechanisms that cause blood clot formation. Large blood clots are not a new phenomenon and can occur under various medical conditions including deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, and arterial thrombosis. These clots have been documented well before the COVID-19 pandemic and the introduction of vaccines. The blood clot could likely have been formed during the embalming process. During embalming, blood is often removed from the body and replaced with preservative fluids. This process can sometimes cause clots to form or be more noticeable. Moreover, clots can become more prominent or exaggerated post-mortem due to the lack of circulation and the natural settling of blood in the body. Such clots are not indicative of vaccine side effects and have been observed in the embalming process long before COVID-19 vaccines were developed. The risk of blood clotting is significantly greater after contracting COVID-19 than after vaccination.

title: Do natural remedies help a child grow taller in only a month?
claim_text: A home cure consisting of sesame seeds, fennel seeds, almonds, and fox nuts (makhanas) can help a child grow taller in just one month.
quick_take: A popular Instagram post claims that a child can grow taller in just a month by consuming an all-natural preparation. After verifying the claim, we discovered that it is completelyfalse.
doctor_explanation: The combination of sesame seeds, fox nuts, fennel seeds, and almonds is a nutrient-dense preparation, but their direct impact on height growth is limited. Dr. Unmesh Upadhyay, President of the Paediatric Association of Ahmedabad (2023–24) and Founder and Senior Consultant Paediatrician, Vismay Childcare Hospital, Ahmedabad, Gujarat, asserts that almonds, sesame seeds, fennel seeds, and fox nuts (makhana) may provide essential nutrients like zinc, calcium, protein, and healthy fats that may help a child by promoting strong bones and adequate hormonal function. However, they won't alter a child’s genetically set height. Dr. Unmesh Upadhyay further explains that height is a progressive phenomenon that happens over time, with spurts between childhood and adolescence. Consequently, it is unrealistic to anticipate that certain dietary choices will result in appreciable height gains in a few weeks. Manasi Banduni, Senior Nutritionist at Clinic Living Plus in Bangalore, emphasises that although there is a common desire to grow taller, one must realise that height is mostly determined by genetics and early nutrition. The growth phase might also have an impact on mental health. Even while certain home remedies might provide healthy nutrition, it is not advised to employ them because they lack scientific validation. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, discusses the Ayurvedic perspective on height growth by emphasising that it mostly depends on genetics and the environment throughout the natural growth phase, which concludes when the growth plates close. Even while certain herbs are well recognised for their health benefits, Ayurveda and modern science do not support that they have the potential to increase height once this stage is over. Despite their ability to boost general health and vitality, such herbs cannot alter a person’s genetic makeup or encourage bone growth. Sesame seeds are high in calcium, magnesium, and zinc which could aid in bone development, but many children have sesame allergies, and consuming them despite an allergy could delay the child’s development. Fox nuts are nutritious and high in fibre and protein, but there is limited concrete evidence that they directly affect a child’s height. Fennel seeds provide essential elements like fibre, calcium, iron, and magnesium that may help with digestion and systemic wellness and exhibit antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, but there is no clinical evidence to support that fennel seeds influence height growth in children. Almonds include vitamin E, protein, and healthy fats which may be beneficial for undernourished preschoolers, but they have no direct effect on height development. Parents' reliance on untested home remedies is primarily due to cultural beliefs, anecdotal success tales, and the accessibility of natural therapies. These untested solutions are being advertised on social media platforms as traditional boosters. However, there is no scientific evidence to support the notion that such therapies may enhance a child’s height beyond their genetic potential. The term 'Ayurveda' is frequently employed to promote such untested cures, remedies, or formulations. However, traditional science stresses a holistic approach and does not support specific herbal remedies for height gain.

title: Do nutrient deficiencies cause food cravings? - THIP Media
claim_text: In a social media video, a dietician Mehaar Bakshhi explains how various nutrient deficiencies lead to food cravings. For example, many teenagers and school-aged children may consume chalk or mud, indicating iron and zinc deficiencies.
quick_take: A social media video talks about how different nutrient deficiencies cause food cravings. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
The fact-check article examines multiple specific claims about nutrient deficiencies causing food cravings:

**Chocolate and Magnesium Deficiency:** A 1991 study notes that while there are some correlations between chocolate cravings and preferences for other sweet or sensory foods, these do not strongly support the idea that cravings are due to a lack of certain nutrients like magnesium or theobromine. Craving chocolate doesn't necessarily mean you are magnesium deficient. Instead, the desire for chocolate seems more linked to its sensory qualities and possibly hormonal factors, rather than a nutritional deficiency. Dr Mohit Sandhu, B.A.M.S., C.A.D., C.A.C., PGDAKS from Shri Shubhda Ayurveda Wellness Clinic, Gurgaon explains: "In Ayurveda, cravings, including those for chocolate, are generally not interpreted in terms of specific nutrient deficiencies like magnesium, as is done in modern nutrition. Instead, Ayurveda views cravings as signals of imbalance in the doshas, particularly related to emotional and mental states."

**French Fries and Sodium Deficiency:** A 2015 research explains how a lack of sodium (salt) can significantly impact psychology and behaviour. When animals (including humans) don't get enough sodium, they start to crave salty foods and find salt more rewarding. This craving is connected to specific areas in the brain that help detect sodium levels and trigger the desire for salty substances. The study mentions that sodium deficiency can lead to trouble concentrating, fatigue, and even feelings similar to depression. However, sodium deficiencies are quite uncommon - consuming too much sodium is more typical, particularly in developed regions. Therefore, just because you crave salty foods doesn't automatically indicate that you're sodium deficient.

**Sugar and Chromium Deficiency:** Craving sugar does not necessarily mean you are chromium deficient. While chromium plays a role in insulin function and may influence sugar metabolism, cravings can arise from various factors such as emotional triggers, dietary habits, or imbalances in blood sugar levels. Some studies suggest chromium supplementation might help reduce sugar cravings, but evidence is mixed because a 2017 meta-analysis revealed that chromium supplementation had no significant effect on fasting glucose levels in both diabetic and non-diabetic groups, suggesting it offers little benefit in populations where chromium deficiency is unlikely. Dr Krutika Ingle, Consultant Diabetologist and Physician, Sugar.fit, Saifee Healthcare, Mumbai explains: "High sugar cravings frequently arise from emotional factors and eating habits. Tackling these cravings demands an approach that encourages balanced nutrition allowing us to better understand the body's signals." Dr. Shalin Nagori, MBBS, MD from Halol, Gujarat mentions he is familiar with Pica but has not encountered cases of sugar cravings linked to chromium deficiency.

**Chalk or Mud Cravings (Pica) and Iron/Zinc Deficiency:** Craving non-food items like chalk or mud can indicate a condition called Pica, often associated with nutritional deficiencies. Specifically, craving chalk may suggest a deficiency in iron or zinc, as these minerals play vital roles in the body's functioning. Similarly, cravings for mud are commonly linked to iron deficiency. While these cravings can be a sign of underlying health issues, they can also stem from psychological factors. If you experience such cravings, it is important to consult a healthcare professional for proper testing and guidance.

title: Do onion and beetroot cure piles in just 7 days? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook post claims that onion and beetroot can cure piles in 7 days, even in people who have had the condition for many years.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that consuming onion and beetroot can cure piles of any stage. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Do onion and beetroot actually cure piles within a week? No. Piles are swollen and inflamed blood vessels in or around the anus. They develop due to pressure most commonly from chronic constipation, straining during bowel movements, pregnancy, obesity, or sitting on the toilet for long periods. Because piles are a structural problem involving veins, they do not simply disappear because of one or two foods. In mild cases, symptoms like itching, discomfort, or slight bleeding may reduce within a few days if straining stops and stools become softer. However, this improvement is often mistaken for a "cure." Medically speaking, symptom relief is not the same as healing the underlying swollen veins. A guaranteed seven-day cure, especially from kitchen ingredients alone, is unrealistic.

Can onion and beetroot reduce piles by improving digestion? Partially, yes, but indirectly. Onion and beetroot contain dietary fibre, which helps add bulk to stools and supports smoother bowel movements. Softer stools mean less straining, and less straining reduces irritation of haemorrhoids. However, the fibre content of these vegetables alone is not high enough to treat constipation if the rest of the diet is poor. A single beetroot or a small serving of onion cannot compensate for an overall low-fibre diet, inadequate water intake, or poor toilet habits. Their benefit comes only when they are part of a broader pattern of eating fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and pulses regularly. So while onion and beetroot may support bowel health, they do not directly treat piles.

Do onion or beetroot have properties that shrink haemorrhoids? No. You may hear claims that onion is "anti-inflammatory" or beetroot "improves blood flow," and while these ideas come from nutrition research, they are often taken out of context. Onions contain plant compounds such as quercetin, and beetroot contains betalains and nitrates. These compounds have been studied for general anti-inflammatory or cardiovascular effects, not for curing haemorrhoids. There are no clinical trials showing that eating onion or beetroot reduces the size of piles, stops bleeding, or repairs damaged rectal veins. In medicine, when natural substances help haemorrhoids, they are usually studied in specific doses and forms (for example, certain flavonoid supplements), not as everyday vegetables promoted as miracle cures.

Why does the "7-day cure" idea sound believable to many people? Because symptoms can fluctuate. Piles often behave unpredictably. A painful flare-up may calm down within days if constipation eases or if irritation reduces. When this happens after someone starts a home remedy, the improvement is wrongly credited to that remedy. This creates a powerful illusion: "I ate onion and beetroot and felt better in a week." In reality, the improvement likely came from reduced straining, better hydration, or simply the natural settling of inflammation, not from the foods themselves. Social media and home-remedy posts often rely on personal stories rather than medical evidence, making the claim sound convincing but unreliable.

Dr Almas Fatma, a General Physician based in Navi Mumbai with in Family Medicine, and a PG degree in Digital Health, shares her expert perspective on this claim. She explains that natural approaches such as dietary modifications may help ease symptoms in mild cases of piles, but they are not sufficient for treating severe conditions like grade 4 piles, which are often painful and debilitating. She notes that while natural remedies can help soothe inflammation and support bowel regularity, grade 4 piles involve prolapsed haemorrhoids that cannot be pushed back manually, making medical or surgical intervention necessary. In such cases, treatments like rubber band ligation, sclerotherapy, or haemorrhoidectomy are far more effective, as they address the underlying cause and reduce the risk of complications. Dr Fatma further emphasises that although natural remedies may provide temporary symptom relief, they cannot replace proven medical treatments. In summary, she highlights that natural remedies can play a supportive role alongside medical care, but they should not be relied upon as a standalone solution, particularly in advanced cases such as grade 4 piles.

What actually helps piles improve within days to weeks? Evidence-based self-care does. Most mild to moderate piles improve when pressure on the veins is reduced and the area is allowed to heal.

Can diet alone permanently cure piles? No. Diet is important, but it is only one part of management. Even people who eat well can develop piles if they strain, lift heavy weights incorrectly, sit for long hours, or have repeated bouts of constipation or diarrhoea. Long-term control depends on consistent habits, regular bowel movements, balanced meals, physical activity, and proper toilet posture. In some cases, medical procedures are needed when piles do not respond to lifestyle changes.

Can home remedies replace medical treatment? Home remedies may help relieve mild discomfort, but they cannot cure piles or replace proper medical care. Beetroot and onion may offer temporary digestive relief, but they do not treat the underlying problem. In mild cases, piles may improve with dietary changes, increased fibre intake, and healthier toilet habits. However, if symptoms are persistent, painful, or worsening, relying only on home remedies can delay treatment and make the condition more serious.

Dr Ubaid ur Rahman, General Physician at Holy Mission Clinic, New Delhi, explains that while home remedies may provide short-term comfort, they are not a substitute for medical treatment. He stresses that piles which bleed, cause pain, or keep recurring need proper evaluation and diagnosis. Depending solely on herbal drinks or kitchen spices may allow the condition to progress. Doctors encourage healthy lifestyle practices, but also emphasise recognising when professional medical help is necessary.

title: Fact Check: Do Onion, Black Tea, Curry Leaves, and Rice really help regrow hair?
claim_text: Applying mixtures made from onion, black tea, curry leaves, and rice to the scalp can stimulate hair follicles and promote hair regrowth.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that applying onion, black tea, curry leaves, and rice water can promote hair growth. However, our fact-check found that this claim is false.
doctor_explanation:
ONION JUICE: A small study from 2002 reported that individuals who applied onion juice twice a day for two months experienced better hair regrowth compared to those who used plain water. However, this effect was mainly observed in people with Alopecia Areata, a genetic condition that causes patchy hair loss. Onions contain sulphur compounds, which are sometimes believed to improve blood circulation to the scalp and support keratin production, a protein that forms hair strands. More importantly, there is no convincing evidence that onion juice helps regrow hair in common types of hair loss such as pattern baldness, stress-related shedding, or age-related thinning. These conditions are driven by hormonal changes, genetics, or follicle damage, which topical onion juice cannot reverse. At best, onion juice may act as a mild scalp cleanser or provide some antioxidants. At worst, it can irritate the scalp, especially in people with sensitive skin. Dr Sachin Gupta explains that there is very limited strong scientific evidence showing that onion can significantly speed up hair growth. While such ingredients may offer some supportive benefits, they should not be considered primary treatments for hair regrowth. He emphasises that focusing on overall health, proper nutrition, and clinically proven treatments is far more important for achieving meaningful results.

BLACK TEA: Black tea does not stimulate new hair growth. Black tea is often recommended as a hair rinse because it contains caffeine and antioxidants. Some online claims suggest that caffeine can block the hormone responsible for hair thinning. However, most research on caffeine and hair follicles has been conducted in laboratory settings using isolated hair cells. Applying brewed black tea to the scalp is unlikely to deliver enough caffeine to affect hair follicle activity in a meaningful way. What black tea may actually do is temporarily improve the appearance of hair. Its tannins can slightly darken hair strands and make them look shinier. This cosmetic effect can create the illusion of thicker hair, but it does not trigger new hair growth or repair damaged follicles.

CURRY LEAVES: Curry leaves cannot regrow hair when applied externally. Curry leaves are rich in antioxidants, iron, and certain vitamins, which is why they are sometimes associated with hair health in traditional practices. However, nutrients such as iron, vitamins, and proteins primarily benefit hair when they are consumed as part of a balanced diet. Hair follicles receive nourishment through the bloodstream, not through topical plant pastes applied to the scalp. Applying curry leaf paste or oil may help condition the scalp or hair strands, similar to many herbal oils. But there is no medical evidence showing that curry leaves can reactivate dormant hair follicles or reverse thinning hair. Dr Rashi Soni explains that natural ingredients such as curry leaves have traditionally been used to support hair health, but there is limited scientific evidence proving that they can significantly boost hair growth or stop hair loss. According to her, these remedies may offer minor benefits, such as improving hair texture or reducing mild hair shedding. However, for noticeable hair loss or persistent problems, it is better to consult a specialist and consider evidence-based medical treatments.

RICE WATER: Rice water does not trigger hair regrowth. Rice water has gained popularity due to historical references to its use in traditional hair care practices. It contains starch, amino acids, and a compound called inositol, which may help smooth and strengthen hair strands. When used as a rinse, rice water can make hair feel softer and may reduce breakage by coating the hair shaft. This can improve hair appearance and manageability. However, strengthening existing hair is not the same as stimulating new hair growth. Hair regrowth requires activation of hair follicles within the scalp. There is currently no scientific evidence showing that rice water can influence follicle activity or restart hair growth cycles. Dr Ekansh Shekhar explains, "Rice water may help nourish the hair and improve its appearance, but it does not work the same way for everyone. Unfortunately, it cannot regenerate hair or stimulate new growth in people who are experiencing medical hair loss conditions. It is important to be realistic about what such home remedies can and cannot do."

EVIDENCE-BASED APPROACHES: Evidence-based approaches focus on addressing the root cause of hair loss. Hair thinning can occur due to genetics, hormonal changes, nutritional deficiencies, stress, thyroid disorders, or certain medical conditions. Supporting hair health usually involves maintaining a balanced diet rich in protein, iron, zinc, and essential vitamins, along with proper scalp care. In some cases, medical treatments such as clinically approved topical solutions or medications may be recommended by doctors. While natural ingredients like onion, tea, curry leaves, or rice water may improve hair texture or scalp comfort, they should not be viewed as reliable treatments for hair regrowth.

title: Fact Check: Do onions have the potential to unclog arteries?
claim_text: Consuming raw onions may have potential health benefits, such as opening blocked arteries and regulating blood pressure, which can contribute to maintaining good heart health.
quick_take: Social media has been the source of claims suggesting eating raw onions will clear clogged arteries. Our fact-checking revealed that the assertion is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Arteries play a crucial role in circulating oxygen-rich blood throughout the body. However, clogged arteries can occur due to the accumulation of plaque, which can obstruct blood flow and increase the likelihood of heart attack and stroke. Arterial plaque is composed of calcium, fat, cholesterol, cellular waste, and fibrin, which lead to heart conditions such as atherosclerosis, a process that causes arteries to narrow and harden. Atherosclerosis is mainly caused by high levels of 'bad' cholesterol (LDL) and high blood pressure, while smoking, diabetes, high blood sugar levels, family history, stress, a sedentary lifestyle, and obesity are additional risk factors. Plaque development can start as early as childhood or adolescence and become more prominent in middle age or later. Dr. Amit Bhushan Sharma, Associate Director and Unit Head of Cardiology at Paras Hospitals, Gurugram, suggests that a heart attack or stroke may occur when a piece of plaque breaks off and lodges in the bloodstream, reducing blood flow. He further advises that blockages in arteries can also result in brain strokes, angina, and peripheral artery disease. Are onions capable of opening clogged arteries? No, not really. Onions offer potential benefits for heart health and artery function due to their high antioxidant content, particularly quercetin. While they cannot directly unclog arteries, the anti-inflammatory properties of onions can help reduce oxidative stress and contribute to overall heart health. Additionally, onions may help regulate blood pressure, which is an important factor in maintaining a healthy heart. It is important to keep in mind that using onions alone as a solution to unclog arteries is not strongly supported by scientific evidence. Atherosclerosis, a condition that involves the buildup of plaque in the arteries, is a multifaceted issue that can be influenced by various factors such as diet, genetics, and lifestyle. Therefore, while adding heart-healthy foods like onions to your diet can be beneficial, it should be done in conjunction with a comprehensive approach that includes exercise, quitting smoking, and prescribed medical interventions. Dr. Mohit Bhagwati, MBBS, DNB (General Medicine), and DNB (Cardiology), advises that onions may have compounds that could indirectly contribute to cardiovascular health. Onions contain quercetin, a potent antioxidant that may help reduce the oxidation of low-density lipoproteins (LDL) and inflammation. These are key factors in the development of atherosclerosis, which can lead to blocked arteries. Additionally, onions contain allicin, which is responsible for their pungent aroma. Allicin exhibits antiplatelet and blood-thinning properties, potentially preventing blood clots. Onions also contain sulphur compounds that may aid in lowering blood pressure. However, it is important to note that while these individual components show promise in epidemiological studies, there is currently no solid scientific data to fully support these claims. Therefore, it is crucial to include onions as part of a well-rounded diet and lifestyle that also includes other heart-healthy practices, such as regular exercise, to effectively support cardiovascular well-being. When asked about the role of diet in managing clogged arteries, Dr. Sharma explained that when plaques build up inside a person's arteries, they can become clogged, leading to restricted blood flow. While individual foods cannot remove plaque from the arteries, a healthy diet can help manage and prevent heart disease. It is worth noting that statins have a pleotropic effect, which means they can prevent strokes in both the brain and heart by regressing plaque and transforming it from a thin to a thick cap, thus reducing the risk of plaque rupture. A comprehensive approach is necessary for managing clogged arteries, which may involve various tests such as angiography and CT scans. These tests help to accurately determine the level of blockage. To maintain healthy arteries in the long term, it is essential to adopt a heart-healthy lifestyle, including a balanced diet, regular physical activity, and quitting smoking. Prescribed medications may be necessary to lower cholesterol levels and prevent blood clots. In severe cases, procedures such as angioplasty or surgery may be required.

title: Fact Check: Do onions under your feet really helps?
claim_text: A Instagram post claims that sleeping with raw onions under your feet improves blood flow, detoxifies the body, reduces inflammation, fights bacteria, and boosts the immune system.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that wrapping onion slices under your feet boost circulation and detox your body. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Can onions absorb toxins through the soles of your feet? No, onions do not pull toxins from your body through your feet. The idea that onions can extract toxins from the body through the skin, especially from the soles of your feet, is not supported by science. Human skin acts as a barrier, not a filter. Toxins cannot be 'sucked out' simply by placing food on the surface of the skin. While onions do contain compounds like sulphur and antioxidants, these benefits are only active when eaten, not when applied externally. This myth likely stems from the way onions change colour or smell after being left out in the open. Some believe that they help cure cold and flu toxins from their surroundings, but this is more a case of oxidation and bacterial growth than detoxification. No scientific evidence shows that placing onions under your feet removes any harmful substances from the body. Do onions improve blood circulation when placed on the feet? No, they do not affect circulation through skin contact. Blood circulation is influenced by heart health, physical activity, diet, and conditions like diabetes or high blood pressure. There's no evidence that applying onions externally improves blood flow. While onions contain quercetin, a compound linked to better blood vessel function, this effect occurs when onions are consumed, not when placed on the body. To truly support circulation, you're better off walking, stretching, eating heart-healthy foods, and managing stress. Simply putting onions in your socks overnight will not change your circulation in any meaningful way. Can raw onions fight infections through foot contact? No, onions cannot fight bacteria or viruses through your feet. Onions do have antibacterial properties when eaten raw or cooked, thanks to their natural sulphur compounds. Some studies have shown they can inhibit certain bacteria in lab conditions. However, this applies only when the onion is ingested or directly applied in a controlled medical context, not when placed under your feet. Your feet don't have a direct pathway to your internal immune system in the way these claims suggest. Sleeping with onions in your socks will not prevent colds, flu, or infections. Good hygiene, handwashing, vaccination, and a healthy diet are proven ways to support your immune health. Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician shares, "The idea that placing onions on your feet can draw out toxins or cure illnesses is simply not grounded in science. Our bodies already have efficient systems—like the liver and kidneys—to detoxify naturally. No food, applied externally, can replace that." Does this remedy reduce inflammation in the body? No, onions on the feet do not lower inflammation. Onions contain antioxidants that may reduce inflammation, when eaten as part of a healthy diet. There is absolutely no evidence that resting onions on the skin, especially the feet, has any systemic anti-inflammatory effect. Inflammation is an internal process, and topical onion contact doesn't influence it. If you're dealing with inflammation-related issues, it's better to consume anti-inflammatory foods (like leafy greens, berries, olive oil), reduce stress, and stay physically active. Onion slices on the soles of your feet are unlikely to make a difference. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, added, "There's no biological mechanism by which an onion under your foot can impact your immune system or circulation. It's an old folk remedy that may give people comfort, but it's not doing what they think it is." Manasi Banduni, Senior Nutritionist at Clinic Living Plus, Bangalore, shares, "Onions have antibacterial properties when eaten, not when used topically. The skin is a protective barrier, not a sponge for detox. Believing otherwise can delay people from seeking real treatment when they need it." Is there any real benefit to placing onions under your feet? No proven medical benefit exists, only a temporary placebo or cooling effect. The only thing you might feel from placing onions under your feet is a cooling or tingling sensation. This can create a short-lived feeling of relief or relaxation, possibly due to the moisture or strong aroma of the onion. Some people find comfort in rituals, and the placebo effect is powerful, but it doesn't equal real, measurable health improvement.
