title: Fact check: Can we diagnose ourselves without a medical degree? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook video claims that understanding your health isn't as complicated as it seems and that day-to-day health can be managed with a simple checklist: a strong sense of hunger, clear skin, uninterrupted sleep, high energy, and natural bowel movements — implying you can self-diagnose health problems without a medical degree or professional medical help.
quick_take: A social media caption claims that just by ticking the checklist one can self diagnose the problem one is going through without any medical help. We fact checked it and found this claim Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Self-diagnosing is when an individual tries to identify the cause of their own medical condition or health issue without consulting a qualified healthcare professional. This often involves using online resources, books, or personal knowledge to match symptoms to potential medical conditions. However, self-diagnosis can be unreliable and risky as it lacks the expertise and precision of a trained medical professional, potentially leading to incorrect assessments or delayed proper treatment. Self-diagnosis is generally not considered safe for several reasons: Inaccuracy - Without proper medical training and expertise, individuals may misinterpret symptoms, leading to incorrect self-diagnosis. This can result in unnecessary worry, anxiety, and potentially harmful actions or treatments. Delayed treatment - Relying on self-diagnosis may cause delays in seeking professional medical help, especially for serious or underlying health conditions. Early detection and treatment are crucial for better health outcomes. Lack of proper examination - Self-diagnosis lacks the physical examination and diagnostic tests that healthcare professionals can perform, which may lead to missed or overlooked factors affecting the condition. Complex conditions - Many health conditions have similar symptoms, making it challenging for non-experts to distinguish between them accurately. We need to go to medical professionals for diagnosis because they have the necessary training, experience, and medical knowledge to properly evaluate our symptoms and medical history. They can conduct appropriate tests and examinations, leading to accurate diagnoses of underlying health conditions. Self-diagnosis or seeking advice from unqualified sources can lead to misinterpretation of symptoms and delay in receiving appropriate care, potentially worsening our health outcomes. Understanding one's own health can be a complex and multifaceted process. Numerous factors come into play, ranging from individual genetics and lifestyle choices to environmental influences and access to healthcare. The human body is a highly intricate system, and health issues often involve a combination of interconnected factors. Identifying the root causes of symptoms or conditions can be perplexing, requiring medical expertise and comprehensive diagnostic methods. Genetics and family history can play a significant role in determining a person's predisposition to certain health conditions. Understanding and interpreting this information can be overwhelming and might necessitate professional guidance. Lifestyle choices, including diet, exercise, sleep, and stress management, have a profound impact on overall health. Social determinants of health, such as socioeconomic status, access to healthcare, and support systems, can greatly influence one's well-being. While having a strong sense of hunger, clear skin, uninterrupted deep sleep, high energy, and natural bowel movements can indicate good health, they may not be sufficient to provide a comprehensive assessment of your overall health. While these signs can reflect positive aspects of your lifestyle, there are many other health factors that may not be evident from these observations alone. Blood tests and other medical assessments play a crucial role in detecting health conditions, monitoring specific health markers, and providing a more in-depth understanding of health. These tests can reveal important information about your blood sugar levels, cholesterol levels, organ function, nutrient levels, and much more. Regular medical check-ups and blood tests are essential for early detection, even if you currently feel healthy. Dr Atul Vashishtha says, 'Consulting a medical professional for health diagnosis is a safer practice than self diagnosing because they have the expertise to check symptoms accurately.' Dr Vashishtha emphasizes that, 'A strong appetite is influenced not only by stomach stretching but also by blood glucose levels. Diabetics may experience hunger despite eating due to irregularities in basal insulin levels. Skin conditions can result from metabolic changes but should be treated externally with antimicrobials and steroids for optimal results. Addressing interrupted sleep is crucial for overall health and involves factors like stress, sunlight exposure, diet, and metabolic disorders. High energy levels vary among individuals, and adequate rest is essential for maximum productivity. Bowel habits can be affected by digestive issues, disease, or constipation, requiring proper medical assessment and guidance. Therefore, it is essential to seek professional help for personalised care and solutions. Their guidance ensures a proper understanding of the issues and helps preserve overall health and well-being.'

title: Fact Check: Do women bear 57 del (unit) pain at the time of delivery? - THIP Media
claim_text: A human body can bear only up to 45 del (unit) of pain. Yet at time of giving birth, a mother feels up to 57 del (unit) of pain. This is similar to 20 bones getting fractured at a time
quick_take: Multiple social media posts suggest a human body can only bear up to 45 del (unit) of pain where women bear up to 57 del at the time of delivery. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: No evidence suggests women bear 57 del (unit) pain at the time of delivery. While researching the topic, we found no unit with the name 'del' to measure pain. A research paper showed the unit of measuring pain is 'dol' which is measured using a dolorimeter. This research paper has shown that the maximum dols women can experience during pregnancy is 10.5 which is way too less than the numbers mentioned in the Instagram post. The Harvard Medical School has developed a 10-point pain scale to analyse the severity of pain. 0 means no pain whereas 10 means extreme pain. This scale is often used by doctors and other healthcare professionals to document and monitor the extent of pain and prescribe treatment accordingly. However, even this method does not seem efficient enough because the extent of pain can be at different rates on the same value. Pain during delivery is highly subjective as every birth experience is different. Pain is often inconsistent during the labour process because of breaks between contractions or while pushing. Pain seems to increase after water breaks or during labour. This increase in the intensity of pain occurs when the duration of break shortens with time. However, this intensity of pain experienced by each woman is different. We have now evidence that shows pain is not only an isolated physical sensation, rather, it is affected by fear, mood, memories, personality and other factors like the duration and overall experience of delivery. Dr. Anita Gupta further adds, 'This pain feeling can be reduced by epidural analgesia but intensity of labour pain cannot be reduced to enable a smooth labour and delivery. Also, if childbirth is done at home and there is no equipment to measure the baby's heart beat then at times the baby may be delivered in a not too good condition.' Dr. Gupta's quote has also highlighted the fact that women do not always undergo normal delivery. Women with c-section do not experience the same extent of pain like those with normal delivery. THIP MEDIA TAKE: No evidence suggests women bear 57 del (unit) pain at the time of delivery. The unit of measuring pain is 'dol' not 'del' and labour pain is measured using cardiotocograph in millimetres of mercury in Indian settings.

title: Do women store the DNA of every man they have sex with? THIP
claim_text: Women Store DNA From Every Man They've Ever Made Love With, Study Finds - women retain and store, for life, the DNA of every man they've ever had sexual intercourse with through male microchimerism
quick_take: A social media post claims that scientists have discovered that women retain and store, for life, the DNA of every man they've ever had sexual intercourse with. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: When we checked about the claim with Dr Ekta Singh, a specialist in Obstetrics and Gynaecology currently working at Cloudnine Hospital, Noida, she explained, 'There is a lack of authentic scientific evidence which proves that a woman stores the DNA of every man she had a sexual relationship with. The scant evidence which indicates any such association lacks credible scientific backup. However, when a pregnancy occurs, the DNA of the foetus circulates in the body of the mother which can be confirmed with non invasive prenatal testing. However, microchimerism is not a result of sexual activity or intercourse with different partners. It has not been proven that it is a mechanism for storing the DNA of every sexual partner a woman may have. Each pregnancy carries the potential for microchimerism, but it doesn't accumulate with every sexual partner. The presence of male microchimerism is primarily linked to a woman's history of pregnancies, not her history of sexual partners. The link is currently only speculative. There is no evidence that this potential DNA transfer could apply to every sexual act between a man and a woman.' Gynaecologist Dr. Puja Sharma, MBBS, MD, FMAS, and FICOG, serving as the director of Daksh Clinic in Hauz Khas, Delhi, says, 'There are no concrete literature supporting this. Microchimerism is exchange of cells between two different individuals and is observed physiologically during pregnancy, miscarriage, blood transfusion and organ transplant. Small number of transferred cells may remain in mother's body even decades after childbirth. However, fetal microchimerism is mostly protective for mother, it may have certain negative effects in cases of recurrent pregnancy loss.' Dr. Garima Gupta, MBBS, MD (Obstetrics & Gynaecology) states, 'Microchimerism refers to the presence of a small number of cells that originate from another individual and are found in a person's body. This phenomenon can occur during pregnancy when fetal cells pass into the mother's bloodstream and vice versa. While microchimerism is a well-documented occurrence between a mother and her child, the idea that women store the DNA of every man they have sex with is not accurate. The notion that women retain the DNA of every sexual partner likely stems from a misunderstanding or misinterpretation of scientific concepts. It is crucial to distinguish between microchimerism associated with pregnancy and the idea that every sexual encounter leads to the permanent storage of an individual's DNA in a woman's body. In summary, microchimerism occurs between a mother and her biological child during pregnancy, but it does not involve the storage of the DNA of every sexual partner a woman may have.' Microchimerism is the presence of cells from one individual to another genetically distinct individual. Male microchimerism refers to the presence of a small number of male cells (typically carrying a Y chromosome) in the body of a female. This phenomenon occurs when male cells, often from a male fetus during pregnancy, enter the bloodstream of the mother and become integrated into her tissues. These male cells can persist in the female's body for many years, and they are referred to as 'microchimeric' because they exist in relatively small quantities compared to the female's own cells. The most common source of male microchimerism is the transfer of fetal cells (stem cells) from a male fetus to the mother during pregnancy. These cells can then migrate to various tissues and organs in the mother's body. While the exact reasons for this phenomenon are not fully understood, a few causes could be unrecognized spontaneous abortion, a vanished male twin, and an older brother transferred by maternal circulation. There is not enough scientific evidence to prove that women store the DNA of every man they have sex with through microchimerism. Microchimerism typically occurs as a result of pregnancy when a woman carries a male fetus. Data suggests that male microchimerism in young girls may originate from an older brother either fully born or from a discontinued pregnancy or from transfusion during pregnancy. The study mentioned found male DNA in 63 percent of the female subjects' autopsied brain tissue specimens. But, the researchers did not suggest that the origin of this male DNA found in female brain tissue was 'harvested' or 'stored' from every past lover. Some studies have suggested that sexual intercourse may be a possible cause of male microchimerism. However, there is no scientific evidence to prove that this DNA comes from having sex.

title: Fact Check: Do worm secretions cause halitosis, headache and pimples?
claim_text: An Instagram post shares a video in which the claimant states that the causative agent of various conditions, such as headaches, bad breath or halitosis and pimples is the presence of ammonia, which is released from worms as urine.
quick_take: A social media post claims that worm urine raises ammonia levels in the body which causes bad breath, headaches and pimples. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: The claim that worm secretions cause halitosis, headaches, and pimples is false. Ammonia is a naturally occurring compound in the human body and is a waste product of various metabolic processes, particularly the breakdown of proteins. Elevated levels of ammonia in the blood can be a sign of health issues, such as liver or kidney problems, where the body is unable to properly metabolize and eliminate ammonia. Worms, such as intestinal parasites, can potentially infest the human body, but their presence and activities are typically associated with specific symptoms and health issues related to the parasitic or helminth infection. While some parasitic worms may release waste products, including ammonia-like compounds, into the host's body, the detection of ammonia in the blood alone is not a reliable indicator of a worm infestation. There is no scientific evidence to suggest that worm secretions and urine can cause halitosis (bad breath), headaches, and pimples. Dr. Ketan Rajput, BDS, MDS (Periodontology and Implantology) states: "Halitosis or bad breath is an unpleasant, persistent foul odour in the exhaled breath or in the oral cavity. Halitosis is a wide terminology and can have many systemic and local factors contributing to it. Persistent hyperacidity or gastric secretions do result in halitosis due to the gases expelled. Treating the main cause i.e., hyper-acidity accompanied by professional teeth cleaning can help reduce/ eliminate halitosis/ foul odour. This fact has been proved by many international and national publications. In a medically compromised condition where the patient is bedridden and not maintaining regular oral hygiene and also has some kind of infection is likely to get halitosis due to the fact that he/she is not maintaining regular oral hygiene. Hence to my knowledge and experience, I would like to quote that halitosis is a vague term and can be linked directly or indirectly to some or the other medical condition the patient is suffering from. Maintaining good oral hygiene and also having a healthy lifestyle surely helps reduce/ eliminate bad breath." Regarding pimples, Dr. Soumya Sachdeva, Consultant Dermatologist comments: "There is a mite called Demodex, which can infest and start living in the hair follicles of your skin as an ectoparasite and have a role in worsening acne. Similar papules, pustules and nodules, as seen in acne vulgaris, can be seen with Demodex mite infestation. Other than that, of course, not keeping your face clean and being exposed to worms, mites, and insects, will of course lead to the worsening of acne. However, there is no specific evidence of any particular worm secretion/ urine causing pimples." The narrator in the video mentions pimples on the arms, which can even be due to a condition called keratosis pilaris, a harmless condition that can occur when hair follicles become blocked with a build-up of keratin. Parasitic infections can cause a variety of symptoms, depending on the type of worm involved and the location of the infection. Common symptoms of parasitic infections can include abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss, fatigue, and sometimes skin rashes or itching. However, the presence of halitosis, headache and pimples do not typically characterize the presence of worms in the body.

title: Fact Check: Do yoni pearls cleanse the vagina? - THIP Media
claim_text: yoni pearls are herbal tampons that clean the vagina of yeast, bacteria, and other issues in the womb
quick_take: A video on social media claims yoni pearls cleanse vagina. These pearls are herbal tampons that clean the vagina of yeast, bacteria, and other issues in the womb. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False. A woman's body does not need yoni pearls and has its system of cleansing the vagina.
doctor_explanation: Yoni pearls are a bunch of herbs wrapped in cloth meant for cleaning vaginas. These are called vaginal pearls, herbal tampons, and vaginal detox pearls. It seems the claimed video on Facebook selling these yoni pearls. The claimant named Shayla's solutions has attached the website link from where people can place an order. We could not find credible evidence that enlists these herbs. So, we referred to a blog that informs yoni pearls contain osthol, rhizoma, borneol, rhubarb, safflower, motherwort, peach, kernel, and angelica root. This blog further highlights that some brands claim to be organic but contain toxic chemicals. No scientific evidence proves yoni pearls cleanse vagina. A few research papers have shown that the vagina is a self-cleaning organ. These studies also warned against inserting external products to get a sense of 'feeling clean'. A simple search about yoni pearls on PubMed showed zero results on yoni pearls. We searched about yoni pearls on Google Scholar and found a case study published in 2022. This case study shows a 41-year-old hospitalized after inserting a yoni pearl for 36 hours. Yoni pearls increase the risk of sepsis and toxic shock syndrome. Regular use of these pearls can reduce blood flow to kill tissues, create holes in body organs and abnormally connect body parts. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) website does not recommend using yoni pearls. FDA has banned a brand selling yoni pearls and has warned against using such a product regularly. We often find inconsistent social media posts that claim to improve vaginal health using quick home remedies. Similar to this story, we also debunked that groundnut water tightens the vagina.

title: Fact Check: Does a chemical make stale vegetables look fresh?
claim_text: Chlorpyrifos and cypermethrin are the chemicals used to revive wilted rocket leaves when soaked in them. These vegetables are sold fresh in markets. No matter how much we wash this chemical, when it is absorbed by the vegetables and when we cook and eat it, how much harm will it cause to our bodies? Chemical name 'Chlorpyrifos, Cypermethrin' is very dangerous for liver and kidney functions.
quick_take: A video shared on Facebook alleges that soaking rocket leaves in a certain chemical solution can rejuvenate withered herbs. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: The claim incorrectly identified chlorpyrifos and cypermethrin as chemicals used to revive wilted herbs. However, these are both chemical pesticides whose primary purpose is to control pests and insects that may damage plants, including herbs. They are not intended for use as a means to 'revive' herbs or any other plants. Using these chemicals on herbs or any other vegetation that is not affected by pests can be harmful and counterproductive. Regarding chlorpyrifos toxicity: Yes, chlorpyrifos can be toxic to humans and has the potential to be lethal, especially when ingested in large amounts or in cases of severe exposure. It is an organophosphate insecticide that affects the nervous system. Acute poisoning with chlorpyrifos can lead to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, muscle tremors, difficulty breathing, and, in extreme cases, seizures, paralysis, and death. Regarding cypermethrin toxicity: Yes, cypermethrin is a synthetic pyrethroid insecticide commonly used in agriculture and household pest control. While it is generally considered less toxic to humans than some other pesticides, it can still be harmful if not used properly. In humans, exposure to cypermethrin can lead to a range of symptoms, including skin and eye irritation, headache, dizziness, nausea, and in some cases, more severe symptoms such as respiratory distress and neurological effects like muscle twitching or seizures. In extremely rare cases of very high exposure, cypermethrin can be fatal. The effectiveness of reducing pesticide residues relies on factors such as the washing methods employed, the chemical structure of the pesticide, and additional preparatory steps taken.

title: Fact Check: Does a cold-water bath improve blood circulation and reduce muscle soreness? - THIP Media
claim_text: The moment cold water hits your body, your blood is forced to circulate a lot faster in an effort to maintain its temperature. Thus they improve blood circulation and reduce muscle soreness
quick_take: A social media post suggests a cold-water bath improves blood circulation and reduces muscle soreness. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly True.
doctor_explanation: It seems so. The available scientific evidence shows cold water immersions can improve blood circulation and reduce muscle soreness. Because cold water has a higher temperature than the body, the circulatory system works harder to maintain the body's core temperature. Dr Kashyap Dakshini, General Physician, says "Cold water bath stimulates blood circulation, however it also induces changes in the body such as increase in heart rate, blood pressure, metabolism, and reduction in blood flow to the brain (as the blood flow is diverted to the skin & muscles). While a cold water bath may help improve the look of the skin, making it look clearer, one must be careful and avoid very cold water, especially amongst those who may have or are unaware of their heart condition, diabetes, high blood pressure, etc. Cold water may reduce muscle soreness by constricting the blood vessels, which may give some relief to the swelling and soreness in the muscles after a workout, however this may be restricted to only easing post-workout aches, as the cold temperature numbs the nerve stimulus. If one has to push through pain during exercise, one might be ignoring an underlying injury. However, cold water / ice packs do help in pain relief and reduce the swelling." Cold water on the body constricts the blood vessels to decrease the blood flow to the skin and minimize the heat loss from the warm blood. This condition is called vasoconstriction that narrows the inside of blood vessels to increase the pressure of the blood. The increased pressure improves the overall blood circulation. Evidence also suggests that cold water immersion replenishes oxygen in the tissues to cure muscle soreness. While searching for any potential disadvantages of cold water immersion, we found research papers that claim cold-water immersion can reduce blood flow to the brain. Another research paper claimed cold water baths can be harmful to people with heart conditions. A website has also highlighted that frequent cold baths may also induce cold urticaria – a condition in which skin becomes red, welts and itches due to exposure to cold temperatures. THIP MEDIA TAKE: A cold-water bath can improve blood circulation and reduce muscle soreness. However, the cold water on the body can generate unknown allergic reactions or harm the organs of the body.

title: Does a combination of hypoglycemic herbs help reverse diabetes?
claim_text: A herbal drink can reverse and help manage diabetes
quick_take: A video on social media claims that a herbal drink can help reverse and manage diabetes. Though diabetes cannot be reversed, management can be done with proper diet and lifestyle. We fact checked and found the claim to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Hypoglycemic herbs are plants used to help lower blood sugar levels. These herbs can support the management of diabetes or prediabetes by improving insulin sensitivity, mimicking insulin effects, or regulating glucose metabolism. Examples include fenugreek, bitter melon, vijaysar, gurmar, cinnamon and many more.

Diabetes can sometimes be put into remission, but it's not fully reversible. While Type 1 diabetes and Type 2 diabetes cannot be completely reversed naturally, some people with Type 2 diabetes may achieve remission through major lifestyle changes and medical treatments. Remission means that diabetes symptoms improve and blood sugar levels normalise without medication, but symptoms can return if an unhealthy lifestyle is resumed.

Dr V Mohan stated in an interview with THIP Media: While the term "Diabetes Reversal" has gained popularity, it is not a new concept. He emphasized that the more accurate term is "Remission of Diabetes," as remission suggests that the disease or disorder is temporarily under control but may resurface at any time.

Dr Aashirwad Pawar, diabetologist at Sai Aashirwad Hospital in Mumbai, explained: "It's crucial to distinguish between remission and reversal. Remission means that your diabetes symptoms have improved and your blood sugar levels are normal without medication, thanks to lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, and weight loss. However, this does not equate to a cure; the condition can return if these changes aren't sustained."

The ingredients mentioned in the claim—Karela (bitter melon), Vijaysar (Indian kino tree bark), Gurmar (Gymnema sylvestre), Jamun beej (Indian blackberry seeds), Methi dana (fenugreek seeds), Kutki (Picrorhiza kurroa), and Bel patra (bael leaf)—are often touted in traditional medicine for their potential benefits in managing diabetes. However, these herbs cannot reverse diabetes.

Dr. Swati Dave, Ph.D. in Nutrition and Dietetics, noted that the herbs mentioned are hypoglycemic, meaning they help lower blood sugar levels. However, this doesn't mean one should abandon other treatments in favor of these herbs. While she might recommend these herbs to her patients, she emphasizes that they should continue their medication, maintain a healthy diet, and exercise. Dr. Dave stresses the importance of comprehensive diabetes management and warns against falling for reversal diabetes scams.

While these ingredients might contribute to better blood sugar management when used as part of a balanced diet, they should not be seen as a replacement for conventional diabetes treatments. Diabetes management typically requires a combination of lifestyle changes, such as diet and exercise, and, if prescribed, medication.

Similarly, claims that Ayurveda can always cure diabetes are not true. While Ayurveda can support the management of diabetes, it cannot cure the condition.

title: Does a DIY baby oil blend help remove wrinkles from face? - THIP
claim_text: An Instagram post claims that a homemade botox mixture containing baby oil, clove, lemon, turmeric, raw honey, green tea, rose water, aloe vera gel, and vitamin E capsules can erase wrinkles.
quick_take: A social media post claims that mixing baby oil with clove, lemon, turmeric, and other ingredients and applying just four drops daily can erase wrinkles. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Wrinkles cannot be permanently removed by any topical home remedy because they are caused by deep structural changes in the skin. As we age, the skin gradually loses collagen and elastin, proteins that provide firmness, strength, and elasticity. At the same time, repeated facial movements, long-term sun exposure, pollution, and reduced cell renewal cause the skin to thin and fold more easily. These processes occur in the deeper layers of the skin, far beyond the reach of DIY mixtures. When this blend appears to 'work', it is usually because oils and humectants temporarily swell the outer skin layer with moisture, visually softening fine lines. This is a cosmetic illusion, not biological repair, and the effect disappears once the product is washed off. Dr Sachin Gupta, Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital in Faridabad, highlights the risks of using unverified natural remedies for wrinkles. He notes that due to the limited and inconclusive evidence supporting these treatments, it is far safer and more effective to rely on options that have proven clinical benefits and documented effectiveness. Clove does not tighten skin or stimulate collagen, and there is no scientific evidence supporting its use as an anti-ageing facial ingredient. Clove contains eugenol, a powerful chemical compound known for its antimicrobial and numbing properties. While eugenol may cause a warming or tingling sensation on the skin, this is not a sign of tightening or rejuvenation. It is a sign of irritation. Dermatological research recognises eugenol as a common cause of contact dermatitis, particularly on sensitive areas like the face. Repeated irritation damages the skin barrier, increases water loss, and triggers inflammation, processes that actually accelerate wrinkle formation rather than prevent it. Lemon and turmeric are neither safe nor effective wrinkle treatments when applied directly to facial skin. Lemon juice is highly acidic and disrupts the skin's natural pH balance, stripping away protective oils and weakening the barrier that keeps moisture in and irritants out. This makes the skin more vulnerable to sun damage, pigmentation, and fine lines. Turmeric, although beneficial when consumed in food, contains compounds that can irritate the skin when used topically in raw or concentrated form. It may cause redness, itching, staining, or allergic reactions. Dr Sonali Kohli, Consultant Dermatologist at Sir HN Reliance Foundation Hospital, explains that while lemon is naturally rich in vitamin C and contains antioxidant and antibacterial flavonoids that sound beneficial for the skin, it is not suitable to be applied directly to the face. She points out that professionally formulated vitamin C serums are carefully designed with stabilised ingredients and added components that maintain the skin's normal pH. These serums use ascorbic acid, a controlled and skin-safe form of vitamin C, rather than raw citric acid found in lemon juice. Applying lemon juice directly makes the skin overly acidic, disrupts its protective barrier, and increases sensitivity. In such a state, even mild sun exposure can trigger phytophotodermatitis, a painful skin reaction. Honey, aloe vera, and rose water support skin comfort but do not reverse ageing or remove wrinkles. Raw honey acts as a humectant, drawing moisture to the skin's surface. Aloe vera soothes dryness and mild irritation, while rose water provides a cooling and refreshing sensation. These effects can temporarily improve how the skin feels and looks, especially if it is dry. However, hydration does not equal repair. These ingredients do not influence collagen production, elastin regeneration, or cellular ageing. Green tea does not significantly reduce wrinkles when used in DIY topical mixtures. While green tea contains antioxidants that help protect cells from damage, these compounds are highly unstable. They break down quickly when exposed to air, light, and heat. In professionally formulated skincare products, antioxidants are stabilised and delivered at effective concentrations. A homemade green tea solution applied to the face may feel soothing, but it does not penetrate deeply enough or remain active long enough to affect wrinkle formation or skin firmness. Vitamin E oil does not repair wrinkles and is often misunderstood as an anti-ageing solution. While vitamin E plays a role in skin health when consumed as part of a balanced diet, topical vitamin E from capsules is heavy, occlusive, and poorly absorbed. It does not stimulate collagen or reverse ageing. In some people, especially those with sensitive or acne-prone skin, it can clog pores and cause irritation. Dr Ekansh Shekhar, a Dermatologist, Cosmetician, Trichologist, and Consultant in Aesthetic Medicine in Lucknow, explains that vitamin E can offer certain benefits for the skin, such as protecting against dryness and early signs of ageing. He notes that it helps maintain skin hydration, which can improve overall skin texture, although it is not a definitive solution for removing wrinkles. Regular use of this blend can harm the skin barrier and accelerate visible ageing. Ingredients like clove, lemon, and turmeric can cause chronic low-grade inflammation when applied repeatedly. Persistent inflammation disrupts the skin's ability to retain moisture, repair itself, and protect against environmental damage. Over time, this leads to dryness, uneven tone, increased sensitivity, and more noticeable wrinkles, exactly the opposite of what the blend claims to achieve.

title: Does a fenugreek-based recipe help with irregular menstruation?
claim_text: the early morning consumption of fenugreek seed-soaked water is a highly effective remedy for menstrual irregularities
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, fenugreek-soaked seed water helps address menstrual irregularities. We fact-checked the claim and discovered that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: While fenugreek-soaked-seed water preparation continues to rise in popularity as an intervention for menstrual or period-related issues, scientific evidence supporting its efficacy remains equivocal. Fenugreek seeds, scientifically known as Trigonella foenum-graecum, are exceptionally high in phytoestrogens and saponins. This high bioactive profile is responsible for the oestrogen-like activity, which may aid in hormonal balance. Given that fenugreek seeds have anti-inflammatory and analgesic characteristics, clinical research suggests their role in reducing premenstrual symptoms and relieving period pain. Furthermore, there is evidence of marginal benefits in PCOS-related menstrual issues. Despite these advantages, most studies evaluate fenugreek as a standardised extract rather than as a simple soaked-water preparation. This could be attributed to the inconsistent, lower, or uncertain efficacy of fenugreek-based DIY remedies. Soumam Dutta, PhD Scholar in Nutrition at the Department of Endocrinology, ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, asserts that while eating a healthy, proportionate diet can enhance overall menstrual health, it cannot substitute for recognised treatments for menstrual irregularity. This is because the menstrual cycle is a complex hormonal phenomenon involving numerous hormones, including progesterone, oestrogen, FSH, and LH, which cannot be influenced by a single factor, such as nutrition. Considering such options may delay the essential procedure. While fenugreek seeds may be useful, in the absence of large-scale randomised clinical trials, their role is confined to being a supportive measure. The aforementioned preparation should not be regarded as the definitive treatment for irregular menstruation. Women who experience recurrent period-related abnormalities should see a gynaecologist for an accurate diagnosis and timely therapy. Dr. Saumya, Consultant Gynaecologist, ESIC Medical College and Hospital, Patna, adds, 'While home remedies can provide some nutritional benefits and help with hydration, it's important to remember that they are not a magic cure for menstrual issues.' Period-related issues might be caused by underlying concerns such as hormone imbalances or additional medical disorders, which should be evaluated by a medical professional. Dr. Saumya continues, 'If you solely depend on natural remedies, you may delay receiving the proper treatment you require, which could lead to subsequent greater issues.' Patients with irregular or heavy periods should always consult their medical professional. Timely intervention may aid in developing a multimodal plan that includes well-nourished meals and an active lifestyle. Fear of medication-related side effects and resorting to unverified cures might mask major health issues, resulting in their silent progression. As a result, the procedure may not only exacerbate the medical condition but also jeopardise fertility. Certain natural remedies may play a complementary role; therefore, they should be used in conjunction with evidence-based therapies under medical supervision. Gynaecologist Dr. Anita Gupta, Associate Director at Fortis La Femme in New Delhi, recommends pharmaceutical intervention to address the root cause. Hormone-based therapies are usually prescribed to effectively regulate the menstrual cycle.

title: Does a herbal recipe work well for skin ageing pigmentation?
claim_text: A homemade recipe made with papaya leaves, besan, honey, and lemon juice can effectively manage skin ageing pigmentation and make a 50-year-old look 25.
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, a herbal recipe can effectively manage skin ageing pigmentation. After fact-checking the claim, we found that it is completely false.
doctor_explanation: Skin ageing pigmentation is the term used to describe the uneven darkening of skin brought on by ageing, which usually shows up on the hands, face, and neck. The most common signs of pigmentation include uneven skin tone, lentigines, and age spots. The condition usually stems from a complicated interaction between prolonged UV exposure, which accelerates melanogenesis by enhancing melanocyte activity, damaging DNA, and contributing to localised melanin accumulation, and age-related collagen and elastin deterioration which further modifies the structure of the skin, increasing the visibility of pigmentation. Age-related pigmentation affects the skin at the cellular level and goes beyond appearance and self-esteem. Therefore, it is crucial to address the issue of skin ageing pigmentation with clinically proven depigmenting therapies to restore skin health by preventing premature ageing. While the combination of papaya leaves, besan, honey, and lemon juice is touted as a highly effective natural remedy for skin ageing pigmentation, it lacks scientific validation. Papaya leaves contain antioxidants and enzymes like papain that may help exfoliate dead skin cells and reduce oxidative stress. Besan (gram flour) is frequently used in face packs because of its cleansing and mildly exfoliating effects. Honey is a naturally occurring humectant that is widely used for its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Lemon juice is packed with vitamin C and has been reported to exhibit a skin-lightening impact. However, there is no clinical evidence to support the herbal recipe's effect on skin ageing pigmentation. Furthermore, because lemon juice is acidic, applying it directly to the skin, particularly on the face, may aggravate or even exacerbate the condition. These herbal remedies should only be taken as a supplement or to slightly improve the texture of the skin; they should not be used instead of dermatologist-approved therapies for pigmentation. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, explains that recurrent sun exposure, hormonal fluctuations, or skin inflammation associated with acne are common causes of persistent facial pigmentation. Dark spots or patches may result from the skin producing more melanin in response to injury or irritation. Common examples include post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation and melasma. Inadequate sun protection may worsen pigmentation. Dermatologists typically address the condition on both superficial and cellular levels, beginning with stringent photoprotection using broad-spectrum sunscreens. The prescribed topical agents, such as hydroquinone, retinoids, azelaic acid, kojic acid, and niacinamide may help with the inhibition of melanin synthesis and may even encourage skin renewal. Pigmented lesions may be dealt with chemical peels and procedures like laser therapy or intense pulsed light (IPL). Antioxidant-rich formulations packed with Vitamin C or ferulic acid may also be utilised to reduce oxidative stress and enhance treatment outcomes. Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital, Mumbai, says, 'When it comes to stubborn pigmentation, we usually take a layered approach. The first and most important step is daily sun protection, because UV rays make pigmentation worse. Then we use creams that contain active ingredients like vitamin C, retinoids or niacinamide, which help lighten dark spots over time. In some cases, we recommend chemical peels or laser treatments to target deeper pigmentation. It's not a one-size-fits-all process, and it does take patience, but with the right plan, we can achieve noticeable and lasting results.'

title: Fact Check: Does a home remedy work well for vision correction?
claim_text: Vision correction can be achieved using a homemade treatment composed of fennel seeds, almonds, rock sugar, and white pepper. The formulation is equally beneficial for other vision-related problems such as eye-related redness, blurriness, and discharges.
quick_take: A social media post is promoting a natural remedy for vision correction. After fact-checking the claim, we determined that it is false.
doctor_explanation:

title: Fact Check: Does a homemade formula work well for hair fall?
claim_text: According to an Instagram reel, a homemade shampoo-based formulation could potentially reduce hair fall and premature greying of hair. The post with the caption: बस शैंपू में ये चीज़ें मिला लो और बाल झड़ना, टूटना, और रुका हुआ बढ़ना सब कुछ होगा खत्म! asserts that fenugreek seeds, curry leaves, rice, black tea, and shampoo boiled in water may assist with hair loss as well as hair regrowth in just three to four weeks.
quick_take: A well-circulated Instagram post is promoting a homemade hair fall formula. We analysed the claim and discovered that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: The term 'hair fall' implies pathological hair loss. The condition, which shows up as bald patches, thinning, and a notable decrease in hair density, is brought on by disruption of the natural cycle of hair growth. The most prevalent triggers include specific medications, metabolic stress, and hormonal shifts. Since the disorder is associated with hair loss, it should not be confused with normal hair shedding, which is a vital component of the hair's natural cycle of growth. The two can be differentiated based on their extent and pattern. Normal shedding is usually persistent, undetectable, and uniformly distributed, as opposed to pathological hair fall, which is excessive, may be caused by specific circumstances, and shows up as noticeable thinning or shedding beyond the average daily range. A homemade concoction combining black tea, curry leaves, fenugreek seeds, and rice with shampoo is being promoted for hair benefits; however, the formulation cannot be effective for hair fall because: Black tea contains caffeine and antioxidants that may stimulate hair growth and enhance hair health. Components of black tea, such as EGCG, may also reduce oxidative stress and inhibit the hormone activity that leads to hair loss. While black tea is being considered for enhancing scalp health, these findings are limited to preliminary studies. Next are fenugreek seeds, which when applied topically, are quite beneficial for those who have mild to moderate hair loss. This may be due to the proteins, flavonoids, and saponins. They may also support scalp wellness due to their anti-inflammatory, anti-androgenic, and vasodilatory characteristics. Even with the positive correlation, further study is required to completely comprehend these results. Curry leaves are a great source of antioxidants, vitamins (including Vit C and B), and minerals (such as calcium and iron) that may help fortify hair follicles and prevent premature greying of the hair. In a similar vein, rice water may strengthen hair and reduce thinning by nourishing the hair and scalp. Both of these, however, might be helpful for normal hair shedding, not pathological hair fall. Dr. Gurman Singh Bhasin, Director & Chief Dermatologist, Skinclarity Clinic, Nagpur, advises that while these ingredients, like fenugreek and curry leaves, are rich in nutrients that can condition the scalp and improve hair texture, there's no credible scientific evidence that they can stop hair fall on their own. Hair fall is often caused by underlying factors like genetics, hormonal imbalance, or nutritional deficiencies, and tackling it usually requires a focused, medically directed strategy. These home remedies may complement care, but they are not a cure in and of themselves. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, a dermatologist, cosmetologist, trichologist, and aesthetic medicine consultant from Lucknow, states that combining a boiling tea leaf and fenugreek seed solution with shampoo won't boost hair growth. This approach lacks a scientific foundation and is unlikely to produce any significant results beyond a basic cleansing. No shampoo formulation can counteract the fact that hair growth is influenced by a number of factors, including hormones, nutrition, genetics, and overall wellness. While the combination may sound promising, its role in the prevention of hair fall lacks robust human clinical trials. Dr. Gurman Singh Bhasin acknowledges that regeneration and prevention are two very distinct goals. Prevention of hair loss can be occasionally achieved by avoiding damage and improving scalp health, but in cases like androgenetic alopecia, regrowth requires clinically validated treatments such as PRP or minoxidil. While it is unlikely that a single home cure will be able to effectively address both, it may assist in maintaining overall hair quality when combined with the right medical care. Dr. Rashi Soni, co-founder and consultant dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, further clarifies that a healthy diet packed with proteins, vitamins, and minerals is crucial for reducing hair fall and enhancing hair strength. Additionally, she suggests moderate hair care practices, including avoiding harsh chemicals and very hot styling. Selecting gentle shampoos and conditioners that are appropriate for your hair type is equally crucial. If hormone imbalances or genetic factors are the cause of thinning hair, treatments such as minoxidil or other prescription medications may be necessary. The aforementioned combination may complement, but not replace, the evidence-based hair fall therapy. Some of the ingredients are beneficial at preliminary levels, but after bypassing professional medical intervention, they may be risky. Considering the complexity of hair loss, a homemade recipe might not be the best option for everyone who experiences it. Always seek medical advice if one loses more than the standard amount of hair daily.

title: Fact Check: Does a laxative contain ethylene glycol?
claim_text: A laxative called MiraLAX contains PEG3350 which is ethylene glycol (antifreeze), and ethylene glycol is poisonous for humans when ingested.
quick_take: A video on social media shows a laxative claiming it has ethylene glycol, which is poisonous when ingested. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Laxatives are drugs or medicines that stimulate bowel movement. They are prescribed to treat constipation when lifestyle changes do not work. MiraLAX contains PEG3350, which is an abbreviation for polyethylene glycol 3350. As per the National Library of Medicine, PEG3350 is an osmotic laxative and is used to treat occasional constipation. This compound is safe for human consumption and helps soften the stool by retaining the water to increase the number of bowel movements. However, we researched further and found that MiraLax contains antifreeze ingredients which is a highly controversial topic. There is no mention of antifreeze in the laxative on the MiraLAX website. However, a website has shown that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) tested eight batches of MiraLAX and found ethylene glycol (EG) and diethylene glycol (DEG) in them. These antifreeze were impurities added during the manufacturing process. The claim is mostly false because while PEG3350 is NOT ethylene glycol (they are different chemical compounds), there were some impurity concerns found in FDA testing. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website informs that ethylene glycol is present in antifreeze which keeps a car safe from overheating or freezing in the winter. Ethylene glycol can be poisonous for humans if ingested.

title: Does a magical herbal mouthwash work well for mouth ulcers?
claim_text: A viral Instagram post claims that using warm water with turmeric, honey, lemon juice, and rock salt can naturally heal all types of mouth ulcers and prevent their recurrence. The Hindi caption translates to: 'Mouth ulcers will no longer be the enemy of your smile! This small desi remedy will do wonders — both pain and burning will disappear.'
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, a magical herbal mouthwash can naturally heal all types of mouth ulcers. We fact-checked and found that it is completely false.
doctor_explanation:
Mouth ulcers, also referred to as canker sores or aphthous ulcers, are small, painful lesions with white or yellowish cores and a red, inflammatory border. These lesions usually develop in the mucosal lining of the mouth, including the tongue, lips, and inner cheeks. While mouth ulcers are often small and resolve in one to two weeks, they can cause significant discomfort that can make it challenging to consume food, speak, and maintain satisfactory dental hygiene. While their precise cause is still unknown, factors such as autoimmune conditions, stress, nutritional deficiencies, infections, and trauma may contribute to their development. Occasional ulcers aren't a serious concern; however, persistent or unusually large or major lesions warrant medical evaluation and management.

The claim that warm water with turmeric, honey, lemon juice, and rock salt can cure mouth ulcers is completely false. The popularity of such remedies is confined to social media and is not supported by scientific research. Each ingredient was analyzed:

1. TURMERIC: Despite its well-known anti-inflammatory, healing, and antioxidant properties due to its active component curcumin, there is insufficient clinical evidence to support its direct use in healing oral ulcers.

2. HONEY: Although honey can provide antimicrobial protection and aid in tissue healing, and its administration can reduce pain and duration of mouth ulcers, it does not correlate with the resolution of mouth ulcers.

3. LEMON JUICE: Although this vitamin C-rich component might help with oral hygiene, it might not have an impact on healing. Additionally, because lemon juice has an acidic nature, administering it excessively or incorrectly can irritate the ulcerated mucosa and perhaps delay the healing process.

4. WARM SALINE RINSES (with rock salt): This is most commonly prescribed by experts. The practice may help keep the mouth clean, reduce swelling and may even prevent infection, but excessive use of rock salt may induce discomfort.

Despite several anecdotal reports stating that the aforementioned ingredients may help provide short-term symptomatic relief, they cannot replace targeted therapy for mouth ulcers. Moreover, mouth ulcers are multifactorial in origin; a single home remedy cannot address the entire causative spectrum. Ulcers that are persistent, recurrent, or extremely painful may be a sign of an underlying problem that requires proper therapy.

Regarding prevention of recurrence: Recurrent mouth ulcers are an ongoing inflammatory condition of the oral mucosa that continues to come back even after therapy. Even if their precise cause is unknown, those linked to autoimmune diseases, stress, and malnutrition necessitate extra caution. Although clinically validated medical intervention may reduce the severity and frequency of ulcers, it cannot guarantee complete prevention of recurrence.

Why high-risk patients should refrain from unverified home remedies: Mouth ulcers tend to be more common in people with diabetes, infections, or autoimmune disorders. Using unreliable web-based remedies for oral lesions may not only delay required treatment but may also worsen the existing condition. Direct application of several home-based recipes, including salt, turmeric, or acidic fruits, can cause secondary infections, disrupt mucosal healing, or conceal underlying systemic diseases, leading to their silent progression. Furthermore, vulnerable individuals with minor mucosal breaches can serve as entry points for pathogens, increasing the risk of severe infections or sepsis.

Dr. Gagandeep Singh Sodhi, a dental expert from Delhi, advises that using unsubstantiated home cures for mouth ulcers before consulting an expert may delay critical treatment, exacerbate symptoms, and lead to unanticipated complications. Therefore, a trained dental professional should be consulted for timely and effective therapy.

How clinicians handle mouth ulcers: The therapeutic regimen begins with a thorough medical history and oral examination to rule out underlying causes (systemic diseases, infections, oral injuries, or medications). Based on the exact cause, clinical experts may prescribe topical corticosteroids, antiseptic or anesthetic mouthwashes, and protective topical applicants to reduce inflammation, pain, and bacterial colonization. Supplements including iron, vitamin B12, or folate may be suggested for ulcers caused by dietary deficiencies. Immunomodulatory medicines or laser therapy may be administered for recurrent aphthous stomatitis to promote healing and reduce recurrence.

Dr. Surya Kiran Mudigonda, Consultant Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeon at Renova Hospitals in Hyderabad, explains: 'Applying ice, butter, or ghee to mouth ulcers usually reduces discomfort while maintaining moisture for wound healing.' However, these are not the recommended approaches to addressing mouth ulcers. When handling oral ulcers, avoid using any irritants such as turmeric powder or clove oil as they might intensify discomfort and inflammation. Topical corticosteroids constitute the first line of professional intervention; severe cases can be managed via systemic medication. For certain patients with both oral and vaginal lesions, immunosuppressants may be recommended.

title: Fact Check: Does a microwave destroy every food value in the food and make it toxic? - THIP Media
claim_text: The microwave is basically destroying every food value that's in the food and turning it into a toxin. So, everything out of the microwave is highly toxic and the food value is completely zero. Another user claimed: 'I haven't used a microwave in years ~ They destroy the nutritional value of food along with taste.'
quick_take: A social media post claims that a microwave is toxic and it destroys every food value in the food. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: According to the FDA, 'Microwaves are produced inside the oven by an electron tube called a magnetron. The microwaves are reflected within the metal interior of the oven where they are absorbed by food. Microwaves cause water molecules in food to vibrate, producing heat that cooks the food. That's why foods that are high in water content, like fresh vegetables, can be cooked more quickly than other foods. The microwave energy is changed to heat as it is absorbed by food, and does not make food 'radioactive' or 'contaminated'. No. There is no evidence that they destroy every food value in the food and make it toxic. Generally, any form of cooking damages the chemical structure of the nutrient, to some degree. Since microwave ovens often use less heat than conventional methods and involve shorter cooking times, they generally have the least destructive effects. Microwaves are even better than other cooking methods at preserving nutrients and preventing the formation of harmful compounds. A study highlighted that 'Pressure-cooking showed a more pronounced effect on the reduction of the dietary fibre components than ordinary and microwave cooking.' Another research that studied the effect of microwaves on nutrient value of food states that, 'No significant nutritional differences exist between foods prepared by conventional and microwave methods. Any differences reported in the literature are minimal.' On studying the influence of cooking methods on antioxidant activity of vegetables, it was noted that microwaving and baking preserved antioxidants the best, while pressure cooking and boiling did the worst. A false social media posts also shared that consuming food cooked in a microwave causes colon cancer. Further proving this claim to be false, the FDA states, 'Foods cooked in a microwave oven may keep more of their vitamins and minerals, because microwave ovens can cook more quickly and without adding water.' In conclusion, microwaves are a safe, effective, and highly convenient cooking method which do not turn your food toxic.

title: Does a mixture of honey and baking soda make skin radiant?
claim_text: A YouTube video claims that combining honey and baking soda can make the skin noticeably fairer and remove blemishes.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that applying a mixture of honey and baking soda can whiten the skin and remove blemishes. Our fact check found this claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: A paste made from honey and baking soda cannot whiten the skin, nor can it significantly lighten the skin at all. Each ingredient is commonly found in households, but none has properties that can alter melanin, the pigment that controls skin tone. Honey, although known for its moisturising and soothing effects, does not contain compounds capable of bleaching or lightening the skin. It may help calm irritation or support healing, but it has no impact on melanin production. Baking soda, or sodium bicarbonate, is another risky ingredient. Because of its alkaline nature, it disrupts the skin's natural acidic pH balance. This barrier imbalance may lead to dryness, sensitivity, irritation, and even micro-damage. None of these effects contribute to skin lightening. There is also no scientific research that supports the idea that combining these ingredients can have any bleaching effect. Skin colour is largely determined by genetics and melanin pathways, which cannot be changed with home remedies or daily pantry items. No home remedy or cosmetic product, natural or chemical, can permanently change skin tone. Skin colour is regulated by melanin, genetics, and environmental factors like sun exposure. Even if a product temporarily reduces pigmentation, it cannot permanently stop melanin production. The skin constantly renews itself. In younger adults, this cycle takes about 28–30 days, while in older adults, it may take 45–50 days. Any temporary brightening fades as new cells form. Skin darkening happens primarily due to UV exposure. When the skin senses sunlight, it increases melanin production as a form of protection. This mixture contains no SPF, which means it offers no defence against UV rays. Without sunscreen or physical protection, the skin will naturally tan or darken when exposed to the sun, no matter what DIY remedy is used. Using this mixture on the skin is not recommended and may do more harm than good. Dermatologists strongly caution against applying toothpaste, baking soda, shampoo, or lemon juice on the skin due to their harsh, irritating nature. Dr Swati Watwani, Medical Director at Persianlily Clinic, explains that baking soda is overly alkaline and disrupts the skin's natural acidity. This can lead to rashes, dryness, and increased sensitivity. Its rough texture can also over-exfoliate and cause micro-tears. Dr Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital, Mumbai, states that shampoo is formulated for the scalp and hair. Many shampoos contain surfactants and fragrances that strip the skin of moisture and damage the protective barrier. Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, warns that lemon is highly acidic and can cause severe irritation. When exposed to sunlight, lemon can trigger phytophotodermatitis, a painful condition that leads to burning and dark patches. When combined, these harsh ingredients greatly increase the risk of irritation, redness, allergic reactions, and long-term skin damage. Some natural remedies, such as mulethi (liquorice) with honey, may help to mildly brighten the skin over time. However, their effects are limited, vary with skin type, and require consistent, careful use. For genuine skin brightening or pigmentation concerns, consult a dermatologist. Scientifically backed ingredients such as vitamin C, niacinamide, AHAs, and daily sun protection are far safer and more effective than social media myths.

title: Does a papaya seed-based recipe dissolve kidney stones?
claim_text: A trending Instagram reel with the caption "पथरी गलाने वाला जबरदस्त नुस्खा" suggests that a homemade recipe prepared by grinding raw papaya seeds, papaya peels, black peppercorns, and kalonji seeds makes a definitive solution for all forms of kidney stones.
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that a papaya-seed-based recipe is a potent solution for kidney stones. We fact-checked the assertion and found it to be false.
doctor_explanation: Kidney stones (renal calculi) are mineral-based formations in the renal calyces and pelvis that arise when organic and crystalline components like calcium, oxalate, or uric acid become supersaturated in urine. Calcium oxalate stones are most common and develop due to inadequate water intake, high protein or sodium consumption, weight issues, and specific metabolic and familial illnesses. Raw papaya seeds and peels may demonstrate nephroprotective and antioxidant properties because they are packed with glucosinolates and benzyl isothiocyanate. However, these benefits are confined to animal studies. Additionally, uncontrolled use of papaya-seed extracts may be dangerous because they can be cytotoxic and physiologically active at large concentrations in experimental settings. Black peppercorns (Piper nigrum) contain piperine, known for anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects. While the polyphenolic extract may demonstrate antioxidant potential against sodium oxalate-induced imbalance in rat kidneys, additional comprehensive studies are required. More significantly, black peppercorns are a high-oxalate dietary option that may need to be restricted for those prone to calcium oxalate kidney stones. Kalonji (Nigella sativa) contains thymoquinone and could potentially have anti-urolithic properties, but these outcomes are confined to preclinical examinations and small clinical trials. Dr. Bhanu Mishra, consultant nephrologist at Delhi's BLK Max Hospital, confirms that the combination is not effective at dissolving stones. Even when consuming calcium and drinking sufficient water may help prevent kidney stones from developing, the concept that an at-home formulation would successfully dissolve and eliminate kidney stones is inaccurate. Combining ingredients does not always improve safety or effectiveness - no robust clinical data suggests that such home preparations dissolve existing renal calculi or match clinically validated conventional therapy. Dr. Sharad Malhotra, HOD Gastroenterology, Hepatology & Therapeutic Endoscopy at Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, recommends against employing home remedies as a long-term kidney stone cure, warning that these unregulated cures shouldn't be considered a substitute for standard medical therapies because they lack substantial scientific evidence. People at high risk often turn to unregulated home remedies due to pain, inconvenience, financial constraints, and side effects of standard prescription medications. Phytotherapeutics for renal stone evacuation are limited to complementing rather than replacing conventional therapeutic modalities. Several herbal remedies lack standardization in dosage, formulation, duration of use, and safety. Kidney stone removal is determined by three factors: anatomical position, chemical formulation, and calculus measurement. For small confirmed cases, specialists may recommend medication, hydration therapy, and dietary changes. Medical or surgical procedures may be necessary for larger and obstructive calculi. Medical expulsive therapy employing alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin can be beneficial for stone transit. Tailored dietary modifications, increased fluid intake, and alkaline citrate supplements continue to be more successful in reducing recurrence.

title: Fact Check: Does a Paste of Pepper, Cloves, and Mustard Oil Relieve Toothache Faster Than a Painkiller?
claim_text: A thick paste of crushed pepper, cloves, and mustard oil relieves toothache faster than a painkiller.
doctor_explanation: Clove, black pepper, and mustard oil may offer mild relief and antibacterial effects, but there is no scientific proof they relieve toothache faster than painkillers. Toothache (odontogenic pain) refers to pain originating from the teeth or surrounding structures, most commonly caused by inflammation of the dental pulp due to dental caries. Other causes include tooth sensitivity, abscesses, bruxism, or pain following dental procedures. Management focuses on relieving pain using over-the-counter NSAIDs as first-line treatment per guidelines developed in collaboration with the American Dental Association; antibiotics are given when infection is spreading; and root canal treatment or extraction is recommended for root canal system infections. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and ketorolac typically begin pain relief within 30 to 60 minutes orally. Black pepper (Piper nigrum) contains piperine, which has demonstrated antimicrobial, antioxidant, antidiabetic, and cholesterol-lowering effects. Clove is rich in phenolic compounds like eugenol, eugenol acetate, and gallic acid, possessing stronger antioxidant and antimicrobial properties than many fruits, vegetables, and spices. Mustard oil exhibits antibacterial, antifungal, and antiallergic properties. The study by Sweta V R et al. demonstrated that clove and black pepper have very good antibacterial activity against S. mutans (the bacteria responsible for dental caries), but does not suggest they relieve toothache faster than a painkiller. A review article in the Indian Journal of Research in Pharmacy and Biotechnology discusses clove's role in managing toothache but provides no evidence for faster relief than painkillers. A review article in Evidence-based Complementary and Alternative Medicine suggests inflamed gums may be managed with turmeric, salt, and mustard oil paste but does not support the idea that mustard oil relieves toothache faster than a painkiller. Dr. Prakhar Pragya, MDS (Orthodontics and Dentofacial Orthopaedics), Consultant Orthodontist, South Delhi Region, said: 'Toothache caused by conditions like pulpitis or a dental abscess is usually severe and cannot be treated effectively with home remedies applied on the surface. Clove oil may have a mild numbing effect, but it can't reach the deeper tissues where the infection is. Painkillers are important for relief, but proper treatment often requires procedures like a root canal.' Dr. Ritika, MDS (OMFS), Senior Lecturer, ITS Dental College, Muradnagar, added: 'Clove and other natural ingredients have been used in traditional remedies for years, and they may offer some short-term relief. But there's no scientific proof that they work faster or better than proper pain medications. In fact, relying only on home remedies for a toothache can delay real treatment and allow the condition to get worse. Tooth pain is often a sign of something deeper, like infection or nerve damage, which needs professional care.' There is no scientific evidence that paste made of pepper, clove, and mustard oil works faster or better than standard painkiller medications. While clove contains eugenol, which may offer temporary relief from mild toothache, it must be present in pharmacologically active concentrations to have a meaningful effect, and there is no scientific data supporting the claim that clove alone can completely relieve toothache, especially not faster than a painkiller. There is no consensus within the dental community supporting the idea that applying these ingredients can relieve a toothache more quickly than a painkiller.

title: Does a patent show that 5G cell towers are brainwashing people?
claim_text: In a Facebook video, a woman claims that 5G towers are used for brainwashing people. She says these towers are all over the place and they can actually make you feel the emotions they want you to feel.
quick_take: In a social media video, a woman claims that 5G cell towers brainwash people. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: The claim that a patent shows 5G cell towers are used for brainwashing is false. The patent in question, U.S. patent No. 5356368A, is unrelated to 5G technology or cell phone towers. It is a system and method for influencing brain waves. This patent was filed in 1991 and expired in 2011, predating the launch of 5G networks. It is worth noting that the patent pertains to audio technology used in meditation, not telecommunications or 5G technology. The patent does not specifically mention 5G, nor does it describe a way to use 5G to brainwash people. In fact, there is no scientific evidence to support the claim that 5G can be used to brainwash people. 5G is a type of cellular network that uses radio waves to transmit data. Radio waves are non-ionizing radiation, which means they do not have enough energy to damage DNA. Non-ionizing radiation is generally considered to be safe for humans, even at high levels of exposure. The idea that 5G can be used to brainwash people seems like a conspiracy theory and there is no evidence to support it.

title: Fact Check: Does a recent social media video shows LGBT Parade in Spain?

The post questioned whether pedophilia was publicly accepted in the LGBT community, citing the video as evidence. title: Does a single Ayurvedic formula address all dental pains?
claim_text: An Ayurvedic tooth powder can be used to address external tooth stains, dental pains, gum bleeding, and tooth decay.
quick_take: According to a social media post, an Ayurvedic powder is an all-in-one solution for all dental pains. After verifying the claim, we discovered that it is mostly false.
doctor_explanation: The Ayurvedic powder being promoted claims to address both gingival (gum) discomfort and tooth-related pains. However, the efficacy of a specific product across a range of dental conditions raises questions about its blanket claims. This is because while the aforementioned pains may affect the oral cavity but are distinctive in terms of their development and treatment interventions. A toothache is a symptom rather than a disease in and of itself. It is frequently associated with carious lesions, pulpitis, or tooth sensitivity and entails completely distinct approaches to endodontic or restorative procedures. Conversely, gum-related discomfort is brought on by inflammation due to poor oral hygiene, leading to gingival bleeding and advanced gum conditions. The management of gingival issues often requires plaque control, prescribed antimicrobial therapy, or even surgical intervention. In the absence of proper intervention, the condition may exacerbate, leading to tooth loss and may even contribute to systemic conditions such as cardiovascular disease. Given these differences, it can be highly deceptive to think that a single Ayurvedic formulation can effectively resolve both of these distinctive dental problems. Another essential consideration is the lack of information on the formulation's composition, dosage, and application technique. During the internet search, the herbal constituents identified were Nimbapatra, Amlaki, and Haritaki. Of these, Haritaki has been specifically highlighted for its ability to resolve all dental problems. Dr. Muskan Thakur, an Indore-based Ayurvedic consultant, explained that in Ayurveda, Haritaki is a Rasayana, a herb that promotes lifespan and overall wellness and exhibits therapeutic, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial characteristics. Owing to these qualities, it has long been used to enhance gum health, lower plaque, and relieve ailments including mouth ulcers and foul breath. Dr. Thakur further adds that its application in dantya roga (dental diseases) is mentioned in classical writings such as the Charaka Samhita. Even while Ayurvedic medicine widely acknowledges these advantages, not everyone will experience them in the same way. For comprehensive dental care, it is always recommended to seek professional counsel. Dr. Ketan Rajput, Periodontist and Oral Implantologist, Advanced Dental Clinic and Implant Centre, Dhule, Maharashtra, suggests that an Ayurvedic tooth powder might be an effective organic solution to improve oral health by lowering gum inflammation, irritation, and oral malodour in otherwise healthy individuals. However, a single remedy with specific ingredients may not be sufficient to address all oral health issues. Hence, if you're experiencing a severe toothache or extensive gum discomfort, it's essential to visit a dentist to identify the underlying cause. These Ayurvedic remedies can therefore be used as supplements because using a single formulation to address all forms of oral issues may have adverse consequences. Regarding scientific evidence, no peer-reviewed publications were found for Aditya herbal tooth powder on PubMed. Additionally, the herbal combination has not been approved by the Indian Dental Association (IDA). The product is also not listed in the Ministry of AYUSH's searchable portal for authorised medicines. Self-medication can be highly risky because unverified online products frequently mask symptoms while the underlying condition worsens. Unsupervised oral health practices may raise the risk of complications including tooth loss and systemic infections by delaying prompt clinical intervention.
