title: Fact Check: Does a smoothie diet help in weight loss?
claim_text: A Facebook video by the account sizzums closet shows avocado, banana, cucumber, and carrot blended as a smoothie for weight loss. The video claims this smoothie combination helps in weight loss.
quick_take: A social media post showcases a recipe of avocado, banana, carrot, cucumber smoothie as a part of a weight loss smoothie. Upon fact-checking, it has been determined that the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
A smoothie diet revolves around the consumption of blended mixtures of fruits and vegetables. These smoothies are created by combining whole fruits and vegetables, ensuring that their nutritional value remains intact. Since fruits and vegetables are rich in essential nutrients crucial for a healthy diet, incorporating them into one's daily meals is important. Unfortunately, many individuals do not consume an adequate amount of these food groups. To address this gap and promote higher fruit and vegetable intake, beverages like smoothies have gained popularity.

When it comes to losing weight, many folks turn to smoothies, hoping for a quick fix. But the truth is, there's no clear-cut answer. In 2022, Tufts University Health and Nutrition warned that those juice cleanses you see advertised as a way to detox and shed pounds might not be as effective as they claim. In fact, there's not a lot of solid scientific evidence to back them up. What's worse, juice cleanses can leave you feeling tired, lacking essential nutrients, and loaded with sugar, which can actually make you gain weight and lead to other health problems.

Similarly, a review from 2014 found that just adding more fruits and veggies, often done through smoothies and juices, doesn't have a big impact on weight loss. It suggested that if you want to lose weight for good, you need to make a combination of changes in your diet and get more active. So, before you jump into a juice cleanse or smoothie diet, it's a good idea to think it through carefully. There's no magic trick for losing weight without some effort.

The combination of avocado, cucumber, banana, and carrot can be a healthy addition to your diet, but it won't guarantee weight loss on its own. While these ingredients are nutritious and low in calories, weight loss depends on various factors such as your overall diet, calorie intake, physical activity, and metabolism. Avocado is a good source of healthy fats and fibre, which can help you feel full and satisfied. Cucumber and carrot are low-calorie vegetables that provide essential nutrients and fibre. Bananas add natural sweetness and additional nutrients. But the video didn't provide specific guidance on portion sizes, meal timing, or whether this smoothie should be consumed alongside other meals or as a meal replacement. It's important to clarify these aspects to use this smoothie effectively as a part of your diet.

Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA), emphasises that, "According to Ayurvedic principles, addressing obesity is a complex challenge, and there are no quick-fix solutions. Ayurveda views obesity as a condition that is difficult to completely cure, highlighting the significance of stress management, lifestyle adjustments, and dietary changes as the primary approaches to managing it. Medications, whether taken internally or applied externally, play a supportive role, with the key emphasis placed on adhering to a comprehensive treatment plan for better outcomes. Managing obesity effectively in Ayurveda necessitates a personalized and tailored treatment strategy."

Dt. Priyanka recommends that achieving successful weight loss requires a holistic strategy. This approach involves identifying the fundamental reasons for weight gain, which can encompass factors like inflammation, leaky gut, hormonal imbalances, toxin exposure, slow metabolism, or the use of specific medications. Once the underlying cause is pinpointed, suitable adjustments in diet and lifestyle can be implemented to facilitate effective weight loss.

Pariksha Rao, a nutritionist, emphasizes that achieving lasting and healthy weight loss necessitates a multifaceted approach. This approach includes a reduced-calorie diet, consistent physical activity, and the adoption of a disciplined lifestyle and behavioral changes. Rao also acknowledges the potential benefits of additional weight loss aids like pharmacotherapy and bariatric surgery. Notably, Rao underscores that any weight loss plan, when complemented with regular physical activity, plays a crucial role in preventing weight regain.

title: Fact Check: Does a sticker on fruit mean it has pesticides?
claim_text: A sticker on fruits with a four-digit number where the first digit is three or four means the fruit has been sprayed with pesticides.
quick_take: A social media post claims fruit stickers with a four-digit mean the fruit has been sprayed with pesticides. We fact-checked and found the claim has a missing context, hence Half True. A four-digit sticker on fruits means they are grown conventionally and may or may not have pesticides.
doctor_explanation: As per the IFPS website, a four-digit code on stickers shows that the fruit is grown conventionally. However, conventional farming means the seeds have been genetically altered using traditional breeding methods and are not certified as 'organic'. It means the seeds may not always contain pesticides. Stickers on fruits are a common practice worldwide that provides information about traceability, grade and prices. The International Federation for Produce Standards (IFPS) website shows that the number depicts Price Look Up (PLU) codes. According to the IFPS website, PLU codes have been in use since 1990 by supermarkets to improve the check-out and inventory control process. The website also shows that the PLU coding system is voluntary and has not been made mandatory by any governing body worldwide. In India, fruits and vegetables with stickers are often considered premium quality. However, it is not the case. The stickers used by traders in India often do not contain any information except 'Brand name of Traders' or 'Tested Ok' or 'Best Quality' or 'Name of the Product'. As per the Food Safety and Standards Act (2006), no business provider can store and distribute food whose quality can harm human health. No evidence confirms whether Food Safety and Standards Regulations have set specific requirements for packaging fruits with reference to the adhesive on stickers.

title: Fact Check: Does a tumor collect all the poison from your body and save your life? - THIP Media
claim_text: People need to understand that a tumour is there to save your life. When your body is full with poison, toxaemic and acidosis and you are basically going to die of that poison — your body builds a bag and collects all the poison from your body into this bag, which they call a tumour. And now they come and they say 'We need to do a needle biopsy and pinch into this highly toxic tumour' which of course now explodes and pours all the poison into the body.
quick_take: A social media post claims that when your body is full with poison, toxaemic, and acidosis, your body builds a bag and collects all the poison from your body into this bag, which they call a tumour. It further claims that needle biopsy explodes and pours all the poison into the body. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: A tumour is an abnormal growth of cells that forms a solid mass of tissue. Tumors can affect bones, skin, tissue, organs, and glands. Tumours grow and behave differently, depending on whether they are cancerous (malignant), non-cancerous (benign), or precancerous. Even if they are benign, they still may need treatment. When a tumour is malignant or cancerous, it can be life-threatening and requires cancer treatment. According to Cancer Research UK, Cancer cells stay inside the tissue from which they have developed. They grow and divide, creating more cells that form a tumour. Sometimes, as many as a million cancer cells can form a tumour. There is a basement membrane that keeps all the cells of the body tissue inside it. Unfortunately, the cancer cells have the power to break this membrane. Thus, this would be called invasive cancer. As the size of the tumour increases, its center moves away from the blood vessels it is growing, depriving it of oxygen and nutrients. In such cases, the cancer cells can't live without them and they send signals called angiogenic factors which encourage new blood vessels to grow in the tumour. This process is called angiogenesis. With the increasing size, they cover more and more areas in the body, thereby, suppressing the surrounding organs and hampering their function. There is absolutely no scientific evidence that supports this claim. Rather, a tumor, whether benign or malignant, needs emergency treatment. They destroy the normal cells around it and damage the body's healthy tissues, making a person sick. Therefore, the claim is false. Dr. Manish Singhal, Senior Oncologist, Apollo Hospital, says, 'There is absolutely no truth in the claim that a tumour collects all the poison from your body and saves your life. However, a tumour can push itself or grow into nearby blood vessels, nerves, and organs and affect the body's normal functioning. Therefore, it is necessary to consult a doctor, irrespective of the tumour being benign or malignant.' Regarding biopsy spreading cancer: Very rarely. The American Society of Clinical Oncology says a biopsy is often the best way to definitively say whether a person has cancer. Some researchers say 'Tumor seeding or needle seeding refers to rare occurrences when the needle inserted into a tumor during a biopsy dislodges and spreads cancer cells. It is sometimes called needle track or tract seeding because the cancer cells grow along the needle's track.' Several studies and reports of individual cases confirm that tumor seeding is a rare event and that the benefits of biopsies far outweigh the risks. According to the National Cancer Institute, 'The chance that surgery will cause cancer to spread to other parts of the body is extremely low. Following standard procedures, surgeons use special methods and take many steps to prevent cancer cells from spreading during biopsies or surgery to remove tumors.'

title: Does a two-week course of ash gourd juice detoxify the body?
claim_text: Drinking ash gourd juice daily for 14 days removes harmful toxins from the body
quick_take: A social media post claims that ash gourd juice detoxifies the body in two weeks. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: No, there is no scientific evidence that ash gourd juice removes toxins from the body. The word toxin itself is used very loosely online. Most posts don't explain what toxins these juices are supposed to remove, how much toxin exists or how a vegetable juice can suddenly pull them out. In medicine, toxins are very specific chemicals, and removing them usually requires the liver, kidneys or advanced medical treatment, not a fruit or vegetable juice. Ash gourd juice is largely water, along with a small amount of vitamins, antioxidants and mild cooling properties. While these can make you feel refreshed, they do not target harmful substances inside the body. Your internal detox system is already working 24/7. Drinking ash gourd for two weeks does not 'speed up' that built-in system or give it extra power. People may feel lighter or cleaner, but this is usually because they are drinking more fluid and eating lighter meals, not because toxins are being flushed out. It is a perception, not a physiological detox. Dr Durga Priyadarshini R, PhD (Nutrition) said, 'People often believe that a juice cleanse will pull toxins out of the body, but that isn't how human physiology works. Your liver, kidneys and gut are constantly detoxifying on their own. Ash gourd juice is hydrating, but it cannot cleanse the body in the medical sense.' Dr Thulasi K, BAMS, MD (Ayurveda) said 'Ash gourd is known for its cooling properties, but Ayurveda does not consider any single ingredient to be a complete solution for the accumulation of toxins (ama) in the body. Treatment first focuses on identifying and avoiding the root cause—whether related to ahara (diet) or vihara (lifestyle habits). This is followed by restoring balance to the aggravated doshas through shodhana (cleansing therapies) or shamana (pacifying measures). Consuming ash gourd juice alone cannot address these aspects, and therefore, the claim does not hold true from an Ayurvedic standpoint.' Dr Divya Chauhan, Senior Ayurveda Researcher (R&D Team), DesiLLM Private Limited added 'Ash gourd juice is often promoted for detox and weight loss because its properties support gentle cleansing, though Ayurveda does not endorse a fixed two-week detox, as each body has different needs. An important consideration is that ash gourd's effects vary with its stage of maturity and the part used. Immature fruit helps pacify Pitta; Half-ripened fruit may aggravate Kapha; Fully mature fruit (Kushmanda) is widely used in cooking and medicine and is considered pathya ahara (wholesome food). For cleansing purposes, the mature fruit is preferred. However, the form of consumption—juice, pulp, or seed oil—and the duration of use differ based on an individual's prakriti, body condition, and daily routine (dinacharya), including lifestyle and work patterns.' The liver and kidneys are incredibly efficient organs. The liver breaks down medicines, alcohol, chemicals and metabolic waste. The kidneys filter blood and remove excess water and salts through urine. These processes are automatic and don't need external cleansing unless someone has a diagnosed medical condition. Some laboratory studies show that ash gourd contains antioxidants like vitamin C, flavonoids and phenolic compounds. These compounds may help reduce oxidative stress inside lab settings. But that doesn't translate into your liver functioning better simply because you drank the juice. Human clinical studies proving that ash gourd juice improves detoxification, lowers toxin levels or repairs liver cells are absent. So, the idea that two weeks of juice can 'reset' the liver or kidneys is a social media myth, not a medically supported fact. While ash gourd juice can be safe in moderation, it is not an evidence-based detox method. It is low-calorie and hydrating, but using it as a replacement for meals or depending on it as a detox method may cause problems. Juice-only routines can reduce your intake of protein, healthy fats, fibre and essential nutrients. For people with diabetes, ash gourd juice may unexpectedly lower blood sugar and cause dizziness or weakness. For individuals prone to digestive issues, drinking it on an empty stomach may trigger discomfort. Most importantly, a detox-like juice routine creates the illusion that the body needs external help to stay clean, which is not true. Unless someone has a medical disorder affecting the liver or kidneys, the body handles waste products perfectly well on its own. No vegetable juice can outperform your natural detox organs. Ash gourd juice is healthy, refreshing and nutritious, but it is not a detox agent. It cannot clean the body, remove toxins, boost liver function or reset your system in just two weeks. The safest and most effective way to support the body's natural detox processes is through everyday habits: eating fresh foods, staying hydrated, avoiding excess alcohol, sleeping well and exercising regularly.

title: Fact Check: Does adding some ingredients to black coffee offer any real health benefits? - THIP Media
claim_text: Drinking black coffee with shilajit, cinnamon and dates will control hunger, boost metabolism and help you lose 10 kgs
quick_take: A social media post suggests that drinking black coffee with shilajit, cinnamon and dates will control hunger. Boost metabolism and help you lose 10 kgs. We fact checked and found the claim to beFalse.
doctor_explanation: The fact check examines several claims about black coffee with added ingredients: 1) Black coffee significantly boosts metabolism and burns fat: No. Caffeine in black coffee gives your metabolism a gentle nudge. A 2019 study in The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition found caffeine can increase energy expenditure by 5-10% for a few hours, burning roughly 10-20 extra calories daily for the average person. A 2023 study found that caffeine was combined with ephedrine (200 mg caffeine/20 mg ephedrine). The impact of caffeine alone, as typically consumed through common sources like coffee or tea, is likely to be less significant for weight loss. A 2020 Nutrients review adds that regular coffee drinkers develop tolerance, further dimming the metabolic spark. For real fat loss, you need a calorie deficit through diet and exercise. 2) Adding dates to coffee prevents energy crashes and provides stamina: Somewhat. Dates are a natural source of sugars (glucose and fructose) and fibre, which slow digestion and help avoid blood sugar rollercoasters. Four dates (about 30g) add 80-100 calories, offering a quick boost. Tossing them into hot coffee might make a sticky mess without unique benefits. 3) Shilajit with honey in coffee boosts testosterone and workout performance: Not really. A 2016 Andrologia study with 38 men showed 250mg daily raised testosterone in those with low levels, but the evidence is shaky for healthy folks, and no studies test it in coffee. Honey adds carbs (17g per tablespoon), which might fuel a workout but doesn't boost testosterone. 4) Cinnamon in coffee suppresses appetite and controls sugar cravings: To an extent. Cinnamon's compounds, like cinnamaldehyde, may improve insulin sensitivity, potentially easing sugar cravings by stabilising blood sugar. But studies use 1-6g daily, way more than a pinch in your brew. A 2023 review found inconsistent results on cinnamon's effect on appetite hormones. 5) Coconut oil or ghee in coffee provides clean energy for fasting: Not exactly. Coconut oil (12g saturated fat per tablespoon) and ghee (8g per tablespoon) are calorie-dense, packing 120-130 calories. A 2021 Nutrition Reviews study found no fat-loss edge over a standard low-carb diet. The 'clean energy' label is misleading. 6) Combining these ingredients helps lose 10 kg faster: No. There's no evidence that combining coffee with dates, shilajit, honey, cinnamon, coconut oil, or ghee accelerates weight loss, let alone by 10 kg. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, 'The trend of turning coffee into a so-called superdrink by adding ingredients like cinnamon, shilajit, ghee, and more is driven more by hype than solid science. People often assume that mixing several powerful ingredients makes the drink more effective, but that's a misconception. Black coffee on its own may slightly boost focus and metabolism, but it's no substitute for a healthy, balanced diet. Cinnamon might help with blood sugar control, but only at studied doses usually in supplement form, not just a sprinkle in your mug. Ghee and coconut oil can help with fullness in some low-carb diets, but they're calorie-dense and may slow weight loss if overused. And natural sweeteners like dates or honey can still cause energy crashes unless paired with protein or fibre. Coffee can be part of a healthy lifestyle, but it won't fix metabolism, hormones, or body weight on its own. True results come from steady habits, not shortcut drinks.' Dietitian Kamana Chauhanshares, 'I often see people treating their morning coffee like a supplement cocktail, adding honey for stamina, dates for energy, cinnamon for cravings, and even shilajit for testosterone. Unfortunately, most of these claims are exaggerated. For instance, dates and honey do offer natural sugars and some fibre or antioxidants, but they still contribute to your calorie count. Shilajit does show some testosterone benefits in specific, small studies, but that doesn't mean tossing it into coffee will do anything for a healthy adult. And coconut oil or ghee, though popular in keto diets, are dense in calories and don't provide cleaner energy than any other fat source. If weight loss is your goal, I recommend sticking to black coffee and focusing on meals that nourish your body without excess hype.'

title: Does HIV medication weaken the immune system? - THIP Media
claim_text: A video on Instagram by yada_awakening claims that AIDS/HIV medications weaken the immune system. The claim states: 'AIDS/HIV is a virus of a weak immune system, right? That means we need to make our immune system strong. But what happens if you take these drugs? They weaken your immune system. quick_take: A video on social media claims that AIDS/HIV medications weaken the immune system. We fact checked this claim and found it to be False.
doctor_explanation: AIDS (Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome) is a severe condition caused by HIV (human immunodeficiency virus). HIV harms the body's immune system by targeting CD4 cells, which are vital in battling infections. As HIV remains untreated, it weakens these defences, leading to more complications. If HIV is not treated, it can advance to AIDS, at which point the defences are badly damaged. Although there is no cure for HIV/AIDS, a treatment called antiretroviral therapy (ART) can control the virus, allowing people with HIV to live a healthy, full life. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, AIDS/HIV medication (ART) works by stopping the HIV virus from proliferating in the body. These medications target different stages of the HIV life cycle, which helps to keep the virus under control. By doing this, ART slows down the progression of HIV, protects the immune system, and prevents serious health problems related to AIDS. Effective ART can also reduce the amount of HIV in the blood to very low levels (undetectable), making it less likely to transmit the virus to others. No, AIDS/HIV medication (ART) does not hurt the immune system. In fact, ART is specifically designed to help strengthen the immune system by suppressing the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and preventing it from damaging immune cells. By controlling viral replication, ART helps to slow down the progression of HIV infection and preserve immune function. Effective ART can also reduce the level of HIV in the blood to undetectable levels, which not only improves the health and quality of life of people living with HIV but also significantly reduces the risk of transmitting the virus to others. Overall, ART plays a crucial role in supporting and maintaining a healthy immune system in individuals living with HIV. Dr. Sarthak Moharir, Radiation Oncologist at Apollo Cancer Centre in Bilaspur, states: 'AIDS is a serious health problem caused by HIV. But don't worry, modern science has made HIV treatable. Medicine, if taken correctly, allows people with HIV to live long without progressing to AIDS. There are set rules that doctors follow to keep their patients healthy. The way modern medicine works is simple. It uses clear and undeniable proof to decide on treatments.'

title: Fact Check: Does alcohol have any health benefits?
claim_text: According to an article published on a website, there are health benefits of alcohol consumption.
quick_take: An article on social media claims that alcohol consumption offers multiple positive effects for health. We did the fact check and found out it is half true.
doctor_explanation: The debate over the health benefits of alcohol consumption has persisted for years. There are conflicting studies and widespread myths about alcohol, which often clouds public perception. Are there any health benefits of alcohol consumption? Yes, but the potential health benefits of alcohol are very limited and often outweighed by the risks. Some studies suggest that moderate alcohol consumption might help raise good cholesterol (HDL) and lower the risk of heart disease. However, these benefits are modest and can be achieved through other means like diet and exercise. Moderate drinking may also lower the risk of type 2 diabetes by improving insulin sensitivity, but this effect is small and varies by individual. Some research even indicates that moderate drinkers might live longer than non-drinkers, likely due to other healthy lifestyle factors they engage in. Research also indicates that alcohol consumption decreases the risk of dementia. However, the risks associated with alcohol consumption are significant. Heavy drinking can lead to liver diseases like cirrhosis and liver cancer. Alcohol increases the risk of various cancers, including mouth, throat, liver, and breast cancer. While a small amount might benefit the heart, too much alcohol increases the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease. Long-term alcohol use can also lead to mental health issues such as depression, anxiety, and addiction. Chronic drinking can cause problems with memory and thinking clearly, and alcohol can irritate the stomach, leading to inflammation and other digestive issues. Excessive drinking is also associated with increased risk of obesity. Additionally, excessive drinking can weaken the immune system, making it harder for your body to fight off infections. Alcohol consumption is also associated with higher incidences of accidents, injuries and violence. Dr Amit Harshana says, "As a doctor, I often get questions about the health benefits of alcohol consumption. While some studies suggest that moderate alcohol intake, particularly red wine, might offer certain heart benefits, these findings are often exaggerated and must be carefully weighed against the significant risks of alcohol use. The proposed benefits, like increased good cholesterol (HDL) and antioxidants such as resveratrol, are minimal compared to the well-known harmful effects, including liver disease, various cancers, mental health disorders, and addiction. It's important to know that any potential benefits from moderate drinking can be easily obtained through safer choices like a balanced diet and regular exercise." Dr Harshana warns people regarding the adverse effects of alcohol: "I strongly advise my patients not to start drinking alcohol for supposed health benefits. The myths about alcohol's positive effects are often blown out of proportion and not substantial enough to justify drinking, especially considering the risk of abuse and addiction. The harms of alcohol far outweigh the modest benefits suggested by some studies. For those who already drink, I recommend reducing intake to minimise health risks. Keeping a healthy lifestyle through proper nutrition, physical activity, and social connections is a much safer and more effective way to achieve long-term health and well-being." Regarding safe consumption levels, Dr Harshana states, "As per the latest WHO report, it clearly states that no level of alcohol consumption is safe for our health. Alcohol is a toxic, psychoactive, and dependence-producing substance and has been classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer decades ago – this is the highest risk group, which also includes asbestos, radiation, and tobacco." Dr Amit Harshana concludes with, "We cannot talk about a so-called safe level of alcohol use. It doesn't matter how much you drink – the risk to the drinker's health starts from the first drop of any alcoholic beverage. The only thing that we can say for sure is that the more you drink, the more harmful it is – or, in other words, the less you drink, the safer it is." The article also addresses other myths like wrapping alcohol soaked cloth around the neck to cure coughs, which is medically incorrect.

doctor_explanation: High alkaline foods are foods with a pH level above 7, which is considered alkaline or basic. These foods include fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, and certain grains. They help balance the body's pH levels and promote health by reducing acidity in the body as per people claiming. Examples of high alkaline foods include leafy greens, cucumbers, broccoli, almonds, and tofu. However, scientific evidence supporting the health benefits of consuming high alkaline foods is limited, and their impact on overall health remains a subject of debate among researchers and health professionals. COVID-19 isn't 'immune' to organisms with higher pH. A 1991 study clarifies that the study focused on a different coronavirus known as mouse hepatitis virus type 4 (MHV4), not the coronavirus responsible for COVID-19. A 2021 study says maintaining a balanced pH might offer health benefits, but it's not a guaranteed defence against COVID-19. Vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and following public health guidelines remain the most effective ways to reduce transmission. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, emerged in December 2019, leading to a global pandemic with millions infected and thousands of deaths. Alkaline foods, such as lemons, may leave an alkaline residue after digestion, supporting the immune system. While no specific food or supplement can prevent COVID-19, a nutrient-rich diet can aid immune health. Vitamin D supplements and foods high in vitamin D may also support the immune system during quarantine. Consuming alkaline foods or water may temporarily influence the pH of urine, but they typically do not have a significant or lasting effect on the overall pH balance. The body tightly regulates its pH levels to maintain optimal function, and any changes caused by diet are usually short-lived and balanced by the body's buffering systems. Therefore, while consuming alkaline foods or water may affect certain bodily fluids' pH levels, they generally do not alter the blood or body's overall pH. According to Oncologist Dr. Manish Singhal, even a slight change in the pH of our blood can lead to a person being admitted to the ICU. The topic of alkaline food and alkaline water has been extensively discussed, often with claims suggesting that alkaline pH can cure cancer. However, upon fact-checking, it's evident that these claims lack solid scientific research backing. title: Does alkaline water really support detoxification?
claim_text: A social media post named Vijaymangam uploaded a carousel claiming that alkaline water supports detoxification and enhances energy levels by removing toxins more effectively, thereby improving overall health.
quick_take: A social media post claims that there are various benefits of alkaline water. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly false.
doctor_explanation: No, alkaline water does not detoxify the body in the way people often claim. The idea that alkaline water support detoxification helps the body get rid of toxins is a popular one, but it doesn't have scientific backing. The body is naturally equipped to detoxify itself through the liver, kidneys, and digestive system. These organs work tirelessly to filter out toxins without the need for any special drink or supplement. Alkaline water, which typically has a higher pH level than regular water, is often marketed as having various health benefits, including detoxification. However, the body maintains a tightly controlled pH balance in the blood, and drinking alkaline water doesn't really change this. In fact, the stomach itself is highly acidic to break down food, so any effect from alkaline water is unlikely to make a significant difference in overall detoxification. While alkaline water is often discussed for its detoxification benefits, other traditional practices, like drinking ghee water, are also gaining attention for their potential health benefits, including weight management. Regarding pH balance: No, it doesn't have a major effect on your body's pH balance. While alkaline water is more basic (higher pH) than regular tap water, the human body's pH levels are well-regulated and don't change dramatically based on what you consume. Your blood pH, for example, is tightly controlled by your lungs and kidneys, and it's generally maintained at around 7.4, which is slightly alkaline. Drinking alkaline water won't influence this balance in any meaningful way. The body works hard to keep your pH stable, and drinking water with a different pH level won't override this system. Any slight change in pH from alkaline water is usually neutralised by stomach acid before it even has a chance to affect your system. Therefore, the idea that alkaline water can balance the body's pH is more of a marketing myth than a proven fact. Regarding health benefits: Not significantly—any benefits are likely to be overstated. The health benefits associated with drinking alkaline water are mostly anecdotal and not supported by strong scientific evidence. Some small studies suggest that alkaline water may improve hydration or reduce acid reflux symptoms. However, these studies are limited in scope and don't provide enough evidence to make broad claims about the water's detoxifying properties. Regarding diabetes: Some studies have suggested that alkaline ionized water (AIW) could have positive effects on blood glucose levels in animal models of diabetes. However, these findings are not conclusive, and more robust clinical research on humans is necessary to determine whether AIW is effective or safe for managing diabetes. Dr. Ayush Chandra, a Diabetologist and founder of Nivaran Health in Delhi NCR, explains, "Managing diabetes requires the right medications or insulin therapy under professional guidance. A balanced diet rich in essential nutrients, regular exercise, adequate water intake, mental well-being, and consistent blood sugar monitoring are all important factors." Regarding high blood pressure: The relationship between alkaline water and blood pressure is similarly unclear. Although some people believe that the alkalinity of the water could help help reduce blood pressure, there is limited scientific evidence to support this claim. Dr. Shalin Nagori, a Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, adds, "The impact of alkaline water on blood pressure remains unclear, and scientific evidence is limited. Blood pressure management involves many factors, and it's best to consult a healthcare professional for personalised advice." Regarding cancer: Cancer is a complex disease influenced by genetic factors, lifestyle, and environmental exposures. The idea that altering the body's pH with alkaline water affects cancer cells is not backed by credible research. Cancer cells can thrive in both acidic and alkaline environments, and the body regulates its pH through the kidneys, lungs, and buffer systems, making it impossible to significantly change blood pH with diet or water consumption. While the alkaline diet promotes healthy eating, such as consuming more fruits and vegetables, it's an exaggeration to claim it can prevent cancer. Dr. Pooja Khullar, a Radiation Oncologist at Dharamshila Narayana Superspecialty Hospital, New Delhi, explains, "There's no solid science to back up the idea of alkaline water preventing cancer. Cancer is complex, and drinking water with a different pH won't stop its development. A balanced diet and healthy lifestyle are the best ways to reduce cancer risk." Regarding harm: Generally, no, but excessive consumption could lead to issues. For most people, drinking alkaline water in moderation isn't harmful. However, if you consume large amounts regularly, it could potentially interfere with your stomach's natural acidity, possibly leading to digestive issues like bloating or discomfort. title: Does an aloe vera-based composition ensure long hair?
claim_text: An Instagram post with the caption दुनिया के 70 करोड़ लोग आज मूर्ख बन रहे हैं लेकिन आप मत बनो! suggests that combining rice, curry leaves, and aloe vera gel with shampoo can be a very successful way to stimulate hair growth.
quick_take: A trending Instagram reel claims that an aloe vera-based composition ensures long hair. After fact-checking the claim, we found it to be false.
doctor_explanation: The term 'hair growth' refers to a coordinated mechanism that is controlled by hormones that stimulate hair follicles to develop new hair. During the three stages of the cyclical process of hair growth—growth (anagen), regression (catagen), and rest (telogen)—hair follicles grow and shed hair strands. The anagen phase, which is much longer than the preceding stages, is when adult hair follicles are primarily found. Hair length is determined by the duration of the anagen, or growth phase; longer anagen periods allow hair to grow to a suitable length before moving on to the next stages of hair growth. The homemade formulation composed of aloe vera, rice water, and curry leaves has been promoted as a natural enhancer of hair length and strength. Aloe vera gel comprises proteolytic enzymes that may help break down dead skin cells on the scalp, clearing clogged follicles and promoting optimal hair growth. It might also provide vital micronutrients that nourish hair follicles, such as minerals and vitamins A, C, and E. Furthermore, its anti-fungal and anti-inflammatory qualities could enhance scalp health and potentially alleviate dryness. Rice water is widely utilised as it is rich in minerals, inositol, and amino acids. Amino acids help strengthen and repair the hair shaft, while vitamins B and E and minerals like magnesium stimulate hair follicles and promote a healthier scalp environment. Inositol can stimulate the scalp to reduce friction-induced breakage and penetrate the hair to repair damage. Curry leaves are utilised extensively due to their potent nutritional profile. Their nutritional and antioxidant concentration may promote general scalp health. Although this combination may help nourish hair, minimise damage, and perhaps establish an environment that is conducive to hair growth, there is insufficient reliable, substantial clinical research to support the claims that it significantly accelerates hair growth. Dr. Sachin Gupta (MBBS and MD in Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi) of Amrita Hospital in Faridabad explains that there is no instant approach to promoting hair growth. He firmly advises against the use of untested therapies. Dr. Gupta emphasises that while hair development is regulated by a range of factors, including hormonal levels, nutrition, genetics, and general well-being, depending only on unregulated formulations may not be beneficial. Healthy hair development can be promoted by a well-balanced diet, appropriate hair care practices, and expert advice for any existing medical issues. Dr. Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consultant Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Hingoli, Maharashtra, adds that 'natural ingredients have been used for generations to promote healthy hair, but their role in achieving significant hair growth or preventing hair loss is still questionable.' These remedies may be useful for minor hair loss and texture issues, but it's preferable to see an expert and look into the evidence-based medical interventions. Unregulated web-based solutions lack scientific validation, and there are concerns over their safety due to the risk that they contain irritants, contaminated substances, or uneven concentrations. Furthermore, some dubious online resources may exacerbate scalp inflammation, trigger allergic reactions, or even impair the skin barrier. Most significantly, depending too much on ineffective remedies can interfere with ongoing medications and delay timely medical evaluation of conditions that call for specific medical attention, such as iron deficiency, thyroid dysfunction, or telogen effluvium. Even though the aforementioned formulation, prepared with rice, curry leaves, and aloe vera, may enhance the health of the scalp, there is no empirical evidence that it guarantees long hair. Further research is required to verify its efficacy. Long hair ultimately depends on genetics, hormonal balance, nutritional status, and underlying medical status. Hence, this combination may help maintain healthier-looking hair, but it cannot override biological growth cycles. For long and strong hair in the true sense, evidence-based care with balanced nutrition and proper medical management remains the cornerstone.

The visible changes from these remedies might be due to hydration, temporary plumping, or sheer coincidence, not long-term change. This can delay people from getting real treatment for skin concerns like acne scars, sun damage, or melasma.

title: Does applying beetroot juice remove dark spots and pigmentation?
claim_text: Beetroot + coffee works as a scrub and removes dark spots quickly, and Beetroot + atta + besan can "clear pigmentation" in just one use.

doctor_explanation: Beetroot juice cannot erase dark spots or pigmentation instantly. And that's because pigmentation isn't something sitting on the skin like dirt that can be wiped away with one wash. Dark spots, whether from acne, tanning, or melasma, form when the skin produces extra melanin, the pigment that gives skin its colour. This pigment is made deeper within the skin and slowly moves upward as the skin renews itself. That renewal cycle takes weeks, sometimes months, not a few minutes after applying a DIY mask. Beetroot does contain antioxidants (like betalains) and small amounts of vitamin C, both of which are generally good for skin health. In properly formulated skincare products, vitamin C can support gradual brightening. But rubbing raw beetroot juice directly on the face is very different from using a stable, skin-tested product. Raw beetroot juice: That "instant glow" people notice is usually just temporary hydration plus surface staining, not real pigment reduction. Once the colour fades or the skin settles, the dark spots are still there. According to Dr Ekansh Shekhar, a dermatologist, cosmetologist, trichologist, and aesthetic medicine consultant based in Lucknow, facial pigmentation often lingers because of repeated sun exposure, hormonal fluctuations, or ongoing skin inflammation especially after acne. In many cases, dark spots develop when the skin produces excess melanin as a protective response to irritation or injury. Two of the most common forms seen in clinical practice are melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. What's often overlooked is the role of poor or inconsistent sun protection, which can continuously trigger and worsen pigmentation, even when treatments are being used. Understanding why pigmentation develops is essential—only then can steps be taken to prevent it from coming back. Many online remedies and viral skincare hacks fail to address deeper contributors such as oxidative stress and photoaging, which play a significant role in pigment formation. This is why dermatologist-guided treatments are far more effective and safer in the long run. When it comes to skincare, it's wise to be cautious of internet trends and prioritise medical advice over quick-fix fads. Coffee scrubs do not fade pigmentation quickly, and they can actually make it worse. Coffee grounds work as a physical scrub. They remove dead surface cells, which can make skin feel smooth and look slightly brighter for a short time. But most pigmentation sits below the surface, especially marks left after acne, waxing burns, friction, or rashes. While caffeine can temporarily reduce puffiness, that's not the same as treating pigmentation. A coffee scrub mainly works by friction, not by correcting pigment biology. If exfoliation is needed, gentle chemical exfoliants (used correctly and infrequently) are usually far safer than rough kitchen scrubs. Dr Rashi Soni, consulting dermatologist at Rashi Hospital, explains that beetroot does contain certain skin-supportive nutrients, including vitamin C, which is known to play a role in regulating melanin production. However, she points out that the vitamin C content in beetroot juice is quite small when compared to the concentrations used in scientifically proven skincare formulations. Applying beetroot juice or using face packs made with wheat flour and besan may feel soothing or refreshing, but these methods are unlikely to reduce dark spots in a meaningful or lasting way. For people struggling with pigmentation, she advises choosing ingredients such as niacinamide or retinoids, which have stronger clinical evidence behind them. While natural remedies can complement skincare, Dr Soni emphasises that they are most effective when used alongside well-researched treatments and a consistent, protective skincare routine rather than as standalone solutions. The "worked" feeling comes because clean, oil-free skin always looks brighter. Reduced shine can make dark spots appear lighter. And beetroot's tint can visually blur uneven tone for a short while. True pigment reduction requires: This DIY mix doesn't reliably do any of that. And if it's rubbed in like a scrub or used too often, it can irritate the skin and worsen pigmentation over time. Because pigmentation fades through slow biological processes, not instant fixes. Think of pigmentation like ink that has soaked into layers of paper, it can't be scrubbed away in one go. Even surface-level pigment needs time for the skin to shed old cells and replace them with new ones. For most people, visible improvement takes 4–12 weeks, depending on: Sunlight and heat are major triggers. That's why someone may see a temporary glow after a mask, step outside without sunscreen, and feel like "nothing works." Prevention is just as important as treatment. Dr Sachin Gupta, MBBS, MD (Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi), currently working at Amrita Hospital, points out that natural ingredients should not automatically be assumed to be safe or effective. In some cases, substances that seem harmless can actually irritate the skin or cause harm. This is why he emphasises that consulting a dermatologist remains the safest and most effective way to manage skin-related concerns. He also explains that a healthier-looking glow often seen with improved hydration or skin care should not be confused with a reduction in one's natural skin pigmentation. While certain natural ingredients may support overall skin health, there is currently no scientific evidence to show that they can safely or effectively whiten the skin. Real results come from consistency, not instant fixes, and sunscreen is non-negotiable.

title: Fact Check: Does applying beetroot juice on the face help reduce wrinkles?
claim_text: Applying beetroot juice ice cube on the face helps reduce wrinkles.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that applying beetroot juice to your face reduces wrinkles in a meaningful way. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Wrinkles can be influenced by genetics or develop gradually with age. They usually appear as fine lines or deeper folds on areas such as the face, neck, and hands. Both ageing and environmental factors play a major role in their development. As we grow older, the skin slowly loses collagen, elastin, and moisture. This makes it less firm, less stretchy, and more likely to crease. The outer layer of the skin also becomes thinner, weakening the support structure underneath. At the same time, increased oxidative stress and slower skin cell renewal further reduce the skin's ability to repair itself. Together, these changes cause the skin to sag, become more fragile, and form permanent lines and wrinkles over time. External factors can speed up this process. Habits and exposures such as smoking, air pollution, prolonged sun exposure, dehydration, and repeated facial expressions all contribute to earlier and more noticeable skin ageing.

No. There's no solid clinical evidence in humans showing that rubbing beetroot juice on the face reduces wrinkles. Wrinkles form mainly because of collagen breakdown, loss of elasticity, and long-term sun exposure. To prove an ingredient reduces wrinkles, we'd need well-designed human studies (with before–after measurements, control groups, and enough participants). That kind of evidence doesn't exist for plain beetroot juice.

Some lab and animal research suggests beetroot compounds could influence skin ageing pathways (like oxidative stress). For example, a rat study using a beetroot extract cream reported changes linked to collagen breakdown after UVB exposure, but animal studies don't reliably translate to real-life facial wrinkles in people.

Dr Rashi Soni, Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital, notes that beetroot does contain some nutrients that support skin health, including vitamin C, which is involved in melanin regulation. However, she explains that the amount of vitamin C present in beetroot juice is very low compared with the concentrations used in skincare products that have been scientifically proven to work. As a result, applying beetroot juice directly to the skin is unlikely to have any real effect on wrinkles. She also emphasises that it is always important to consult a dermatologist before trying untested or home-based skincare methods for wrinkle prevention or treatment.

Unlikely. Beetroot contains pigments called betalains, which have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in research settings. In theory, antioxidants can support skin by reducing damage from "oxidative stress" (one contributor to visible ageing). But here's the catch: antioxidants only help wrinkles if they're stable, absorbed into the skin, and present at an effective dose, and beetroot juice isn't designed for any of that. It oxidises easily, and isn't formulated to penetrate the skin barrier well. So while beetroot is interesting on paper, rubbing a beetroot juice ice cube on your face is a big leap.

Dr Sachin Gupta, Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, said, "Natural" doesn't automatically mean "skin-safe". Beetroot can trigger allergy in some people (rare, but reported), and anything acidic or plant-based can cause stinging, redness, or a rash, especially on sensitive skin or around the eyes. Also, homemade mixes come with hygiene issues (bacteria contamination), which can worsen breakouts or irritation.

Since wrinkles develop due to collagen breakdown, loss of elastin, long-term sun exposure, oxidative stress, and natural ageing that affects the deeper layers of the skin, relying on rubbing an ice cube on the face is unlikely to be effective. The cold may temporarily numb the skin or make it appear slightly tighter, but this effect is short-lived and does not address the underlying causes of wrinkles. Therefore, wrinkle care should be based on treatments that are clinically proven, rather than following viral or social media skincare trends.

title: Fact Check: Does AstraZeneca vaccine use aborted fetus?
claim_text: Through a Facebook video, a person claims that the AstraZeneca vaccine, known as the Vaxzevria contains Human Embryo Kidney cells (HEK-293 cells) from an aborted fetus.
quick_take: A social media video claims that AstraZeneca vaccine use aborted fetus cells. We fact-checked and based on available evidence found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Not exactly. The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine named Vaxzevria does not contain aborted fetus cells. The vaccine uses a viral vector, which is a virus from the adenovirus family that carries the genetic material for the spike protein of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The vaccine does not list Human Embryo Kidney cells (HEK-293 cells) as active or inactive ingredients. On the contrary, the HEK-293 cell line is an important part of the manufacturing process, as written in a public information document of this vaccine. Our research shows that the AstraZeneca vaccine was made using a cell line called HEK-293 from fetal kidney cells in 1973. Over time, these cells have been significantly altered and made immortal. These modified cells are used to speed up vaccine production. The HEK-293 cell line is a widely used tool in scientific research and is used in the production of many other vaccines and medications besides the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Similar cell lines have been used in making vaccines for diseases like rabies, hepatitis A, chickenpox, and shingles. HEK-293 cell line does not contain any fetal tissue or DNA. Therefore, the AstraZeneca vaccine itself does not contain any aborted fetal cells. The distant origin of the HEK-293 cell line in aborted fetal tissue remains a concern for some people. Ultimately, the decision of whether or not to get the AstraZeneca vaccine is a personal one.

Founder of Chetanya Ayurveda in Varanasi, Dr. Pallav Prajapati, BAMS, further explains this by advising that Ayurveda is a very specific therapeutic approach that classifies patients according to life stages such as old age, childhood, youth, pregnancy, and a delicate constitution known as Sukumar. Dr. Prajapati explains that the same medical illness is treated differently in Ayurveda depending on an individual's age, body constitution (determined by their doshas), medical history, and the severity of their condition. This thorough assessment usually helps in determining the type of formulation, appropriate dosage, the dietary regimen, and necessary lifestyle modifications. Ayurvedic remedies are not universally safe across all age groups, necessitating age-specific preparations. Moreover, the medicine system employs a holistic approach that involves specific herbal formulations, altered dietary regimens, and modified therapeutic procedures. The fundamental objective is to address the underlying cause by re-establishing equilibrium among the three doshas. Ayurvedic principles align with modern pharmacogenomics in tailoring therapies by age, body constitution and the severity of the medical illness. Regarding paediatrics, Ayurveda mentions Kaumarbhritya. The Kashyapa Samhita, the canonical text on Ayurvedic paediatrics, gives the subject of Ayurveda a lot of attention, with paediatric medication dosages being carefully assessed based on the child's age. Ayurvedic physicians consider various factors when determining the appropriate dosage for children. Adult formulations are strong and complex, while those given to children are milder because their immune and digestive systems are usually still developing. Ghee-based preparations, syrups, or decoctions with honey are usually given to children for better absorption and compliance. Regarding single preparations for all health issues, Ayurveda has always stressed a personalised approach, crafted to an individual's prakriti (body constitution), vikiriti (body-related imbalances), and specific health conditions that need attention. There is no single preparation that can effectively cure digestive diseases, cardiac issues, or haemoglobin insufficiency in all individuals. Every medical ailment has a unique pathophysiology that calls for specific herbs and dosages. Certain Ayurvedic medications are classified as Rasayana Therapy, which aims to revitalise and rejuvenate the body. These preparations are believed to improve longevity, enhance intelligence and memory, support healthy digestion, bring the body back into equilibrium, improve complexion, clarify the voice, and even sharpen the senses. While Rasayana therapy helps maintain balance among the three doshas and may prevent the recurrence of illnesses, it is not designed to treat any specific diseases. Regarding labeling, Regulation 161 of the 1945 Drugs and Cosmetics Rules specifies how Ayurvedic, Siddha, and Unani (ASU) medications must be labelled. The rule mandates that Ayurvedic products bear labels that include the manufacturer's data, manufacturing license number, batch number, manufacturing and expiration dates, and contents list. While it isn't often stated clearly as a distinct age usage instruction, the requirements do need that the target customer group be specified. Ayurvedic medications, however, are not always branded with age-appropriate directions. In a prior interview with THIP Media, Dr Thulasi K, currently associated with Kottakkal Arya Vaidyasala and Punarjani, further supports the importance of health literacy by stating that while the internet can be a helpful resource for basic awareness, it frequently leads to inaccurate information, unnecessary anxiety, or erroneous self-diagnosis. The finest advice based on an accurate assessment can only be given by a professional healthcare provider because every person's health status is unique. Relying on online resources rather than medical experts can delay treatment and do more damage than good.

title: Fact Check: Does Ayurveda suggest drinking water only while sitting down? - THIP Media
claim_text: As per Ayurveda, you should not drink water while standing; you should always sit down while drinking water. Some versions claim water enters esophagus and stomach with high pressure when drinking while standing, others claim the force of water hits the knees and causes arthritis.
quick_take: A lot of people claim that as per Ayurveda you should not drink water while standing, rather you should always sit down while drinking water. We fact-check and found that the claim is false.
doctor_explanation: No. There is no scientific evidence that a particular posture is suggested while drinking water. No such recommendation is also given in Ayurveda. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director, Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA) says, "Ayurveda suggests that food should be consumed while sitting down to avoid choking. There is no recommendation on how to drink water. But it's common sense that you should not consume water in a hurry, or drink too much water too fast, or drink while in a wrong position. Those things can cause choking." No. There is no scientific evidence that suggests that drinking water while standing up can cause any health problems. The claims about water entering the stomach at a high force damaging the walls of the intestine are unscientific too. Whenever we swallow food or water, it enters our digestive system through the esophagus. The large, hollow organs of the GI tract contain a layer of muscle that enables their walls to move. The movement of organ walls—called peristalsis—propels food and liquid through the GI tract and mixes the contents within each organ. Peristalsis looks like an ocean wave traveling through the muscle as it contracts and relaxes. Hence, the water doesn't directly 'fall' into the stomach. General Physician Dr. S Krishna Prasanthi, MBBS, MD (PGIMER) explains, "The peristaltic movement is an involuntary mechanism in the body that happens as soon as the food (either liquid or solid) is swallowed. Contrary to the popular claim that the liquid is moved directly under the effect of gravity, it is this peristalsis that propels the distal movement of food. So, there is no scientific validation behind not drinking water while standing. There is no risk of damage done to the digestive tract, and also risks lungs and heart functions if we drink water while standing."

title: Does Ayurvedic medicine help in breast enlargement?- THIP Media
claim_text: A social media reel claims that the herbal product 'Grow Cup' contains a special formula supposedly used by actresses to make their breasts fuller and achieve a perfectly rounded shape. The promoter in the video further states that the 'Grow Cup' is made from rare ingredients that can permanently increase breast size.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that Ayurvedic medicines by the name Grow Cup can permanently increase breast size. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation:
Can shatavari, methi, gambhari, and ashwagandha really help in breast enlargement? No, shatavari, methi (fenugreek), gambhari, and ashwagandha do not have proven effects on breast enlargement. Some of these herbs, like fenugreek and shatavari, contain phytoestrogens plant compounds that weakly mimic the female hormone oestrogen but their action is too mild to stimulate breast tissue growth. Ashwagandha is better known for stress relief and overall vitality, while gambhari is used in Ayurveda for general wellness, not cosmetic changes. Scientific studies on these herbs focus mostly on fertility, lactation, or hormonal balance, not breast size. Breast development depends on genetics, hormones, and body fat, not on herbal supplements. So while these herbs may support health in other ways, they cannot increase breast size in a safe or permanent manner.

Dr Mohit Sandhu, BAMS, CAD, CAC, and PGDAKS, Founder of the Association for Ayurvedic Palpative Pain Medicine, explains that Stanya-vardhak dravyas (galactagogues) such as Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) and Methi (Trigonella foenum-graecum) have traditionally been used in Ayurveda to support breast milk production and strengthen the female reproductive system. Gambhari (Gmelina arborea), a herb from the Dashmool group, is known for its nourishing (brimhana) properties, which may aid in tissue development. Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is considered both balya (strengthening) and rasayana (rejuvenating), helping improve overall vitality, hormonal balance, and tissue nourishment. In Ayurvedic terms, these herbs are believed to nourish the rasa and meda dhatu (body tissues), which can indirectly influence the size, shape, and firmness of the breasts. They are not specifically labelled as "breast enlargement" herbs, but rather as stanya-poshak (milk-nourishing) and dhatu-vardhak (tissue-supporting).

Why has this belief become so popular? The popularity of this belief stems from cultural expectations and persuasive marketing rather than solid science. For centuries, fuller breasts have been tied to ideals of beauty and femininity. This has created demand for natural, "side-effect free" solutions. Social media and online advertisements amplify the idea that simple herbal remedies can achieve what surgery does, without risk or cost. In reality, many women may experience temporary fullness due to hormonal fluctuations, weight gain, or pregnancy, and wrongly credit an Ayurvedic product they were using at the time. This coincidence fuels the myth further.

Dr Kashyap Dakshini, a General Physician from Mumbai, shares that for many years, products like devices, special diets, smoothies, creams, and lotions have been advertised as ways to enhance breast size. But scientific studies confirm that none of these methods, nor exercises or quick fixes, can truly increase breast size. While certain exercises may tone and strengthen the chest muscles beneath the breasts, they do not lead to any noticeable enlargement.

Are herbal breast enlargement products safe to use? Not necessarily, many of these products can be unsafe. Some "Ayurvedic" pills, powders, or oils marketed for breast enlargement are unregulated and may even contain hidden synthetic hormones. These can cause serious side effects, from menstrual irregularities to risks for hormone-sensitive conditions. Even when they are truly herbal, safety is not guaranteed. Fenugreek may interact with medicines for diabetes or blood clotting. Shatavari and fennel can affect hormone balance, which could be risky for women with conditions like breast cancer. Using such products without proper medical guidance is not recommended.

What are the proven options for breast enlargement? The only medically proven methods to increase breast size are surgical procedures such as implants or fat transfer. Non-surgical alternatives like padded bras, special clothing, or posture exercises can enhance appearance but do not change size. For women who struggle with confidence, counselling or guidance from a healthcare professional may help more than turning to unproven herbal products.

title: Fact check: Does applying banana peel on face cure skin abnormalities? - THIP Media
claim_text: massaging the white part of a banana peel with four drops of rose water for two minutes every day can aid in treating acne, combat aging, heal scars, and enhance the skin's radiance
quick_take: A social media post claims that massaging white part of banana peel with rose water can cure acne, fight ageing, cure scars and makes skin glowing. We fact checked and found the claim to be Half True.
doctor_explanation:
Banana peel is a rich source of bioactive compounds including phenolic and non-phenolic antioxidants like ascorbic acid, carotene, and cyanidin. These antioxidants are crucial in preventing inflammation by inhibiting reactive oxygen species, protecting protease inhibitors from oxidative damage, and preventing fibroblasts degradation. Banana peel also contains anti-inflammatory agents like trigonelline, isovanillic acid, and ferulic acid. Trigonelline can inhibit bacterial enzymes and nucleic acid synthesis. While isovanillic acid suppresses TNF-α production induced by LPS. Ferulic acid suppresses proinflammatory signalling and cytokine production.

Regarding acne: No evidence shows that rubbing banana peel removes acne. But it can help prevent acne proliferation. A research paper published in 2022 shows that banana peel has potential anti-inflammatory properties, but more research is needed to confirm banana peel can cure acne. A 2018 study investigated banana peel effectiveness for treating acne vulgaris. Before application, 62.2% (28) subjects had mild acne, 33.3% (15) had moderate, and 4.4% (2) had severe. After rubbing ripe banana peel on acne daily for seven days (30 minutes to an hour), the prevalence remained the same BUT 57.9% of subjects who previously had moderate acne vulgaris had their acne recede to mild. The Wilcoxon signed rank test showed significant difference in efficacy.

Regarding skin glowing: Banana peels contain Lutein and zeaxanthin, powerful antioxidants. A study on 60 healthy women given 10mg lutein and 2mg zeaxanthin isomers daily for 12 weeks showed significant improvement in overall skin tone and lightening compared to placebo, with increase in skin yellowness and decrease in skin redness.

Regarding ageing: Banana peel contains phenolics and alkaloids that fight against acne-causing bacteria (Staphylococcus epidermidis) and has antioxidant properties that can help prevent premature skin ageing.

Regarding scars: Banana peel contains antioxidants like vitamin C and lutein with skin-healing properties. The peel's enzymes and minerals may help reduce inflammation and promote collagen production. However, effectiveness is not scientifically proven - more research is needed.

Dr. Jyothy Kannangath (Consultant Dermatologist) states: 'Fruit peels hold some of the vital health-benefiting constituents such as dietary fibre and phytonutrients like carotenoids, flavonoids, vitamins, potassium, minerals, etc. They have several health benefits if taken along with the fruit pulp. Some of the fruit peels like orange, apple, papaya, banana, kiwi and pomegranate may brighten or lighten the complexion temporarily. Even though some fruit peels have a collagen stimulating effect, I don't think they can effectively reverse or delay the ageing process. Likewise, with a simple fruit peel we can't treat acne scars. Scar tissue requires advanced treatments like lasers or radio frequency to make it better.'

title: Fact Check: Does Banana Peel Tea Detox the Liver?
claim_text: Mixing banana peel with cloves, bay leaves, and cinnamon offers several health benefits, including cleansing and detoxing the liver.
quick_take: A social media post suggest that banana peel tea combined with other herbs can detox and cleanse the liver. Our fact check found this claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: The liver is already the body's primary detox organ, working continuously without any outside help. Every minute, it filters blood, breaks down alcohol and medicines, converts harmful substances into safer forms, and removes waste through bile, urine, and stool. If the liver truly needed a tea or drink to cleanse itself, humans would not survive beyond infancy. Medical science does not recognise any process where toxins quietly build up in a healthy liver and can then be flushed out with a beverage. When the liver is damaged, the solution is medical care and long-term lifestyle changes, not detox teas. Dr. Sharad Malhotra, Senior Consultant and Head of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Therapeutic Endoscopy at Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, stated: 'no homemade drink can magically detox the liver. This vital organ already works continuously, filtering toxins on its own without any need for special juices, teas, or concoctions. While ingredients such as pudina may add flavour and some nutritional value to meals, they should not be mistaken for miracle remedies.' Dr. Malhotra also stressed that genuine liver health is built through everyday habits: eating a balanced diet, staying well hydrated, limiting alcohol and ultra-processed foods, managing stress, and staying physically active. There are no shortcuts or quick fixes. While banana peels do contain antioxidants such as polyphenols and flavonoids, and these compounds help protect plant cells from damage and may help reduce oxidative stress in the body, antioxidants in food do not automatically translate into liver detoxification. Most research on banana peel antioxidants comes from laboratory or animal studies using concentrated extracts, not from people drinking peel tea. How much of these compounds actually enter the water during boiling is unclear and likely minimal. There are no good-quality human studies showing that banana peel tea lowers liver enzymes, reverses fatty liver, or repairs liver damage. Claims promising visible improvement 'within days' are especially misleading. When liver markers do improve, it is usually due to changes such as reduced alcohol intake, better overall diet quality, gradual weight loss, improved blood sugar control, or stopping harmful medications, not because of a detox drink. The fact check also found no evidence to support claims that banana peel tea can treat insomnia or other chronic health conditions. The belief that it offers these benefits stems from a misunderstanding of how detoxification actually works and an exaggerated interpretation of the role antioxidants play in the body. While you may enjoy banana peel tea as a warm, comforting drink if you like the taste, it should not be viewed as a liver cleanse or a therapeutic remedy.

title: Fact Check: Does bee sting cure HIV?
claim_text: Bee sting can kill HIV virus/ cure HIV patient. A Bee Sting, Possible Cure for HIV. Researchers say the hidden cure to the HIV virus that causes AIDS may be in the sting of a bumble bee.
quick_take: Various social media posts claim that bee venom contains toxins that can destroy HIV, and its sting can cure HIV. We fact-checked and found this claim to beMostlyFalse.
doctor_explanation: Not exactly. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that bee stings or any other natural remedy can cure HIV. As of now, there is no cure for HIV. However, Antiretroviral treatment (ART) can control the infection. Thus, the virus multiplication in the body is limited, which can lead to long and healthy lives. The treatment lowers the viral load (concentration of the virus in the blood). Successful viral suppression restores the immune system, halts the onset and progression of the disease, and reduces the chances of getting opportunistic infections. Researchers have found that bee venom's principal toxin is melittin, a small protein. They have found that the nanoparticles carrying a toxin found in bee venom can destroy human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) while leaving surrounding cells unharmed. Another research also states that honey bee venom may be safe and therapeutic in a specified dose. It also states that the uptake of melittin by HIV-infected cells can possibly cause a decrease in HIV gene expression and replication. However, much more research will be required before these results can be put to use in people. Also, the research is based only on a single component, melittin. However, the bee venom contains various other components such as peptides like apamin, mast cell degranulating (MCD) peptide, and adolapin, enzymes such as phospholipase A2 (PLA2) and hyaluronidase, and amino acids and volatile compounds. One cannot be dependent on bee stings as not only it can have adverse effects, the possibility of any therapeutic effect is currently dependent on a component that is derived from the venom and not the entire venom. Dr. K. S. Satish, Senior Chest Specialist and HIV Physician at Fortis Cunningham Road and Manipal Hospital, Millers Road, Bangalore, clarifies this by stating, While a person living with HIV can suppress the virus with antiretrovirals, there is no cure for HIV till date. A cure for HIV would refer to the total eradication of the virus from the body, which is still under research. Why relying on bee stings to cure HIV can be dangerous: Relying on bee stings or any other unproven remedy to cure HIV can be dangerous and it is not recommended as it may delay or even prevent individuals from seeking and receiving the proper medical care they need. This can result in the progression of the virus, increasing the risk of complications and even death. Additionally, depending on bee stings as a cure for HIV can increase the risk of adverse reactions and complications. Bee stings can cause allergic reactions, ranging from mild to severe, in some people. In rare cases, bee stings can cause a life-threatening condition called anaphylactic shock. Any unproven remedies can give false hope to individuals and lead to disappointment, frustration, and despair when they do not see any improvement in their condition.

title: Fact Check: Does beer help in reducing the risk of bone fractures?
claim_text: Beer helps reduce the risk of fracture.
verdict_original: The claim is Misleading. The claim without specifying the quantity of consumption, proclaims that consumption of beer can be helpful in reducing risk of fracture, whereas in reality, high amounts of beer consumption can be detrimental to bone health.
doctor_explanation:
Fractures are usually caused by trauma ranging from a trivial fall at home to accidents. Undisplaced fractures may be treated with immobilisation in a plaster cast, whereas displaced fractures may necessitate surgical fixation by plating or nailing. Stress fractures result from repetitive strain on a bone, commonly seen in the foot. Rest, activity modification, and braces or crutches are needed to offload the affected area. Fragility fractures, such as osteoporotic bones or pathologic fractures, such as tumours, are seen in weakened bones even without trauma or fall. In such fractures, the underlying disease causing bone weakness must be treated along with the fracture. — Dr. Anup Khatri, Senior Consultant-Orthopedics, Gleneagles Hospital, Parel, Mumbai.

Multiple studies demonstrated that alcohol consumption in the form of beer of 0 to 22 g/d was linked to a slight decrease in the risk of osteoporotic fractures and hip fractures, whereas beer consumption of >49 g/d and >40 g/d was correlated with a significantly elevated risk of osteoporotic and hip fractures, respectively. But because of other harmful effects of beer, such as affecting nutritional status and the intake of micronutrients, leading to malnutrition and deficiencies in calcium and vitamin D, beer consumption can be considered counterproductive in fracture healing. — Dr. Daivik T Shetty, Orthopaedic Surgeon, KMC Hospital, Mangalore.

The scientific community does not strongly agree that beer consumption directly reduces fracture risk. At the same time, there is some evidence suggesting potential benefits associated with beer's silicon content. However, these advantages only apply to moderate beer drinking and are not strong enough to support the active recommendation of beer as a fracture prevention strategy. Although some evidence supports the positive effects of some ingredients in beer, such as silicon, on bone density, the benefits are not clear-cut. The potential risks of higher consumption and the associated negative health impacts, such as loss of bone mass and other health issues, heavily rely on moderation. Hence, the claim 'beer consumption can reduce the risk of fractures' without any explanation on the quantity and emphasis on moderation is best assessed as 'misleading' based on the available evidence.

title: Fact Check: Does Ben Carson have a cure for dementia? - THIP
claim_text: Dr. Ben Carson has a cure for dementia and his innovative treatment can restore memory to the level it was at age 21 within seven days.
quick_take: A social media post is a testimonial claiming that Dr Ben Carson has a cure for dementia. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Our research shows that Dr. Ben Carson is a retired pediatric neurosurgeon. His expertise lies in brain surgery, not in dementia research or treatment. There is no evidence to support claims of a cure for dementia discovered by Dr. Carson. Our research only shows a podcast in which Carson addressed the ongoing development of new drugs for Alzheimer's. He expressed optimism about their potential, stating that they show promise by purportedly targeting the root cause of the disease rather than just alleviating symptoms. Notably, he did not mention anything that the new drugs have the ability to reverse dementia within a week. Additionally, we found different versions of the claimed Facebook post where Ben Carson was seen with Bruce Willis and Dolly Parton. Similar to the claimed Facebook post, these posts also serve as a testimonial expressing gratitude towards Dr. Ben Carson for his successful treatment of dementia. The post further claims that Dr. Ben Carson's innovative approach to treating dementia/Alzheimer's disease, without dependence on pharmaceuticals, has garnered widespread attention. In the end, the post discusses a promising development, suggesting that within seven days, one's memory could potentially be restored to the level it was at the age of 21. Regarding dementia itself: Dementia is a broad term that does not refer to a specific disease but encompasses a range of conditions characterized by difficulties in remembering, thinking, or making decisions, ultimately hindering the ability to carry out daily activities. Among the various types of dementia, Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent. While dementia predominantly impacts older adults, it is important to note that it is not an inherent aspect of normal aging. Also, the available evidence only indicates that dementia cannot be cured but can only be treated.
