title: Does benign prostatic hyperplasia respond to a bee venom inhaler?
claim_text: Using a bee venom based inhaler just once a day will help reduce symptoms of benign prostate hyperplasia (BPH), prostatitis, and support prostate function and reduce inflammation.
quick_take: According to one Facebook post, using a bee venom based inhaler just once a day will help reduce symptoms of benign prostate hyperplasia, or BPH. We verified the claim and found that it is false.
doctor_explanation: While the potential application of a bee venom inhaler to manage benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a developing field of research, it is not yet a commonly accepted or clinically established treatment for the condition. Bee venom therapy is being considered due to bioactive components that have been studied for their potential to manage a range of inflammatory and immunological conditions due to their anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and immune-modulating characteristics, there is limited scientific evidence supporting the use of bee venom as a therapy for managing BPH symptoms. Another crucial consideration is the mode of administration. Although bee venom has been investigated for inflammatory disorders in topical and injectable forms, inhaled bee venom therapy for BPH has not yet been demonstrated. Therefore, before it can be regarded as a feasible therapy option, additional clinical trials are required to determine its safety, dose, and long-term effects for the management of BPH symptoms. It is usually advised to see a physician before using any such alternative therapeutic modalities. BPH management depends upon the severity of symptoms, prostate size, patient preference, and adverse effects. Initial medical therapy for symptomatic BPH may include α-blockers, which relax the muscles in the bladder neck and prostate to improve urine flow. For men with noticeably enlarged prostates, 5α-reductase inhibitors reduce prostate size by preventing hormonal changes. It has been shown that combination therapy with both α-blockers and 5α-reductase inhibitors is more successful in symptom alleviation and halting the progression of the disease. Additionally, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, such as tadalafil, can be utilised to improve both sexual and urinary function, especially in males with erectile dysfunction. Surgical intervention should be considered for patients who do not respond to or tolerate medicinal therapy.

title: Does Bhringraj work well for premature greying of hair?
claim_text: A trending Facebook post by India's Gardening promotes Bhringraj (भृंगराज) for hair health, claiming the well-known herb strengthens hair, encourages hair growth, decreases hair loss, helps make hair lustrous and black, and regular use can help with premature greying.
quick_take: According to a well-shared Facebook post, Bhringraj has the potential to prevent premature greying of hair. After fact-checking, we found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation: Premature greying, also known as premature canities, is the early fading of natural hair colour associated with noticeable grey or white strands before the ages of 20 to 30. The condition is usually brought on by: Genetic factors (main cause - associated with IRF4 gene and family history); Biological parameters (elevated reactive oxygen species (ROS) concentration associated with melanocyte depletion in hair follicles); External contributors (sedentary lifestyles, inadequate dietary intake, cigarette smoking, deficits in calcium, ferritin, folic acid, B12, and biotin). Bhringraj, also known as Eclipta alba or Eclipta prostrata, is a long-used Ayurvedic herbal element that is often praised for pigment-supporting qualities and hair development; however, it does not directly restore colour in human follicles. It is widely utilised because it is rich in phytochemicals, including flavonoids and coumestans, which may help strengthen hair follicles, nourish the scalp, and even delay hair greying. Scientific evidence confirming Eclipta alba extracts' capacity to promote hair growth suggests that they may indirectly promote melanocyte function and delay premature greying. However, these findings are confined to animal research; rigorous human clinical trials would be required to establish that Bhringraj alone may reliably prevent or reverse premature greying—melanin repigmentation. Dr. Swati Watwani, consultant dermatologist & medical director of Persianlily Clinic, explains that premature greying may begin as early as the 20s and cannot be cured with random remedies. While it is impossible to completely prevent premature greying, identifying the underlying cause—whether it be hormonal, nutritional, or stress-related—can help delay its progression with appropriate intervention. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda, maintains that while age-related or hereditary greying is inevitable, addressing lifestyle choices or environmental stressors may be able to delay the progression. Relying on unsubstantiated alternatives can result in misguided optimism and a failure to identify underlying conditions, including autoimmune diseases or thyroid abnormalities. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Consultant in Aesthetic Medicine from Lucknow, recommends hair dye (permanent, semi-permanent, ammonia-free), henna for natural look, root touch-up powders and sprays, and maintaining a diet rich in iron, zinc, and B12. He notes that microneedling or carefully prepared serums can enhance hair health but cannot prevent greying.

title: Fact Check: Does black salt and lemon for gas really work?
claim_text: An Instagram video claims that heating a lemon on a flame, squeezing out its juice, and mixing it with black salt creates a black salt and lemon for gas remedy that can cure gas, heartburn, and bloating from the root when taken every morning on an empty stomach.
quick_take: An Instagram video promotes a home remedy for gas problem by claiming that heating a lemon, squeezing its juice, and mixing it with black salt can permanently cure gas. Our fact check reveals this claim is false.
doctor_explanation: Is there scientific evidence for black salt and lemon for gas? No. Reputable health sources, such as Johns Hopkins Medicine, do not list this specific combination—black salt and lemon for gas—as a treatment for gas, heartburn, or bloating. While lemon juice and black salt are used in traditional practices like Ayurveda, no rigorous scientific studies confirm their effectiveness for permanently curing these conditions. Most evidence is anecdotal or based on traditional use, not clinical research. For those hoping for relief, this lack of evidence suggests caution. Can warm lemon juice help with bloating or heartburn? Maybe. Some sources suggest that a small amount of lemon juice mixed with warm water and honey may have an alkalising effect, potentially neutralising stomach acid and easing heartburn for some. However, lemon juice is acidic and can worsen heartburn in others, especially those with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). A 2022 study found that lemon juice increased stomach contents by 1.5 times, which could aggravate acid reflux symptoms. Regarding warm lemon juice for bloating, there is no specific evidence that it directly reduces bloating, though some people might find it soothing. The effect varies, so it's not a reliable solution for everyone. What are the black salt benefits for digestion? Black salt, or kala namak, is used in Ayurvedic medicine to help digestion. It's said to balance stomach acid and reduce bloating due to its mineral content, like sodium chloride and sulphate. These are the black salt benefits for digestion often cited in traditional practices. However, scientific evidence supporting these claims is scarce. While it may offer temporary relief for some, it's not proven to cure digestive issues permanently. Is permanent relief possible with this remedy? Unlikely. Gas, heartburn, and bloating are often chronic or triggered by diet, lifestyle, or underlying conditions like GERD. The idea of a "permanent cure" from a single remedy like black salt and lemon for gas is not supported by medical science. Leading healthcare organisations emphasise ongoing management through diet and lifestyle changes, not one-time fixes. Claims of permanent relief oversimplify complex digestive issues, which can be frustrating for those seeking lasting solutions. Are there risks involved with this remedy? Possibly. Lemon juice's acidity could irritate the stomach or esophagus, particularly in people with acid reflux or sensitive digestive systems. Black salt contains sodium, which might be a concern for those with high blood pressure or kidney issues. Overuse or improper preparation could lead to discomfort, delayed treatment or other health concerns, especially without medical guidance. Therefore, it is important to approach such remedies with care. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, says, "Lemon and black salt may offer short-term relief in some cases of gas or bloating, but using them daily, especially as a permanent cure, can be harmful. Drinking lemon juice every morning on an empty stomach may irritate the stomach lining, especially in people who have acidity, ulcers, or a sensitive gut. It can actually make heartburn worse for some. Also, regular use of black salt increases sodium intake, which isn't safe for everyone. It's important to understand that such home remedies are not a cure. For lasting relief, a balanced diet and medical advice are much more reliable."

title: Does blue light from electronic devices increase risk of blindness?

doctor_explanation: White light is composed of seven different wavelenghts. (VIBGYOR = Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red). The colour blue in this composition has shorter wavelengths and higher energy than other colors. It is mixed in potentially all forms of lights including natural sunlight. We are exposed to blue light majorly from sun rays. Other than that, household items like fluorescent lights, CFL (compact fluorescent light) bulbs, LED lights, Flat-screen LED televisions, computer monitors, smartphones, and tablet screens, etc. also contribute to the amount of blue light our eyes are exposed to. According to research, the blue light exposure to eyes from household items is much lesser compared to blue light exposure from the sun. Yet, due to the proximity of the blue light from household items (computers and mobile screen included), they remain to be a matter of concern. Yes. If exposed to a certain wavelength (emission peak below 450 nm) of blue light for a longer duration, blue light may affect eyes. Many researches have shown that 'blue light can also produce different degree of damage to corneal, crystal lens and retina.' However, there are few missing context in the generalised statement – 'Blue light hurts eyes.' For starters, researchers say that for short time exposure to digital displays 'It is unscientific to equate all blue light as directly causing eye injury and unilaterally.' Not all blue lights will hurt eyes. Only, at a certain wavelength (emission peak below 450 nm) it may hurt eyes. As per an extensive study done on this matter, researchers conclude, 'Although we are convinced that exposure to blue light from LEDs in the range 470–480 nm for a short to medium period (days to a few weeks) should not significantly increase the risk of development of ocular pathologies, this conclusion cannot be generalized to a long-term exposure (months to years).' Also, most studies do not take into account the modern day innovation in lighting or gadgets technology. In Harvard Health Blog, Dr. David Ramsey writes, 'consumer electronics are not harmful to the retina because of the amount of light emitted. For example, recent iPhones have a maximum brightness of around 625 candelas per square meter (cd/m2)…many retail stores have an ambient illumination twice as great.' Most experts believe, it is infrequent blinking while staring at screens that causes the eye strain and not the blue light from the device. On a related note, there are claims like blue light can harm the skin. But, this lacks scientific backing. Yes. Blue light has a few advantages too. Researches have shown that blue light boosts alertness, elevates mood and regulates the circadian rhythm (the body's natural wake and sleep cycle). Further still, Early studies show a deficiency in blue light exposure could contribute to the recent increase in myopia/nearsightedness. Though some researchers suggest, 'it is necessary to take appropriate protective measures when using blue light-related products, especially at night,' most experts are not convinced about the effectiveness of blue light blocking lenses or blue cut lenses. Research also supports Dr. Aftab's advice. A research done on 13 teenagers, show that people who have excess exposure to blue light at night may benefit from blue cut lenses to help their sleeping. But the experts at American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) advices caution, 'taking preventive measures against blue light even though there is no evidence of damage could be more harmful than the blue light itself,' notes the AAO website.

title: Fact Check: Does Bovaer harm health and the environment?

doctor_explanation: Cows produce methane because of the way they digest food. They have a special stomach called the rumen, where tiny microbes break down the grass and other plants they eat. During this process, methane gas is made, which the cows release into the air mostly by burping. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. It traps heat in the atmosphere much more than carbon dioxide, making it a big cause of climate change. Since cows are a major source of methane, reducing the amount they release can help slow down global warming and protect our planet. Regarding health risks: No, current evidence does not support this claim. Bovaer is primarily used to reduce methane emissions in cattle by inhibiting an enzyme in their digestive systems. Its active ingredient, 3-NOP (3-nitrooxypropanol), has undergone rigorous safety assessments by regulatory agencies, including the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). Studies show that Bovaer does not accumulate in milk or meat, ensuring its safety for human consumption. Side effects, such as skin irritation or breathing difficulties, are occupational hazards during manufacturing or handling concentrated forms of the additive. Proper safety protocols, including personal protective equipment (PPE), address these concerns. For consumers, these risks are irrelevant as the additive does not persist in animal products. Despite the lack of evidence, false claims continue to circulate, suggesting that Bovaer harms both cows and humans, often in an attempt to promote fake meat. Regarding male infertility or DNA damage: No, this claim is misleading. There is no evidence linking Bovaer to male infertility or DNA damage. The references cited in the post do not directly associate 3-NOP with genotoxicity, infertility, or birth defects in humans. Instead, these stem from speculative concerns rather than validated scientific research. Regulatory reviews consistently conclude that Bovaer is safe for use within prescribed limits, with no adverse effects on animal health, human consumers, or the environment. Regarding manure from treated cattle: No, manure from cattle fed Bovaer is not harmful to crops. Studies evaluating the environmental impact of Bovaer have found that its active ingredient breaks down quickly and does not persist in the environment. Its degradation products do not affect soil health, plant growth, or groundwater. Manure continues to serve as an effective natural fertiliser, maintaining agricultural sustainability. Regarding insufficient testing: No, this claim is inaccurate. Bovaer has undergone extensive testing in multiple countries, and reputable authorities, including EFSA and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), have reviewed it. Research spanning over a decade confirms its efficacy in reducing enteric methane emissions without compromising food safety. The trial involving 30 UK farmers is part of ongoing efforts to validate its benefits under real-world conditions. Such trials are a standard process in adopting new agricultural technologies and do not imply uncertainty about the additive's safety. The recent claims are incorrect—dsm-firmenich owns Bovaer and has no connection to Bill Gates or external investors. Some suggest that the video of Bill Gates was erased from the internet, but this isn't true—it is still accessible. Another popular claim suggests that Bill Gates invented a wireless birth control chip, which is also false.

title: Fact Check: Does Budwig diet help in cancer treatment? - THIP
claim_text: The Budwig diet (combination of cottage cheese and flaxseed oil) is beneficial for cancer treatment
quick_take: A video on social media discusses the Budwig diet, claiming that its beneficial for cancer treatment. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: The Budwig diet is a nutritional approach developed by German biochemist Dr. Johanna Budwig in the 1950s. It is made by the combination of cottage cheese (or quark) and flaxseed oil as its central component. The diet suggests consuming this mixture daily, often accompanied by fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. Advocates claim it can improve overall health and help in managing certain diseases. Though scientific evidence supporting these claims is limited. The Budwig diet operates on the principle that combining cottage cheese with flaxseed oil provides essential nutrients like omega-3 fatty acids and sulfur-rich proteins. Dr. Johanna Budwig, the diet's founder, believed this mixture could enhance cellular health, improve oxygenation, and aid detoxification. However, scientific evidence supporting these claims is limited. Budwig assumed that cancer patients needed highly unsaturated fatty acids, particularly linoleic acid and linolenic acid, to support cell membrane formation and cellular respiration. Inadequate intake of these fatty acids led to an oxygen-deficient environment, hindering cellular metabolism. Flaxseed oil, containing significant amounts of LA and LNA, was a cornerstone of Budwig's diet. She believed that when these fatty acids interacted with sulfhydryl groups from cottage cheese, they released stored energy. While Budwig's theories were based on older understandings of carcinogenesis, recent research highlights the role of oxygen free radicals in cancer development. The only major problem with the Budwig Diet is that there haven't been any clinical trials to test. The evidence we have mainly comes from people's personal stories, not from scientific studies. So, it's hard to say for sure if this diet can actually help treat cancer. While some parts of the diet might be good for your health and could lower your chances of getting cancer, you should never rely on it or any other diet as your only treatment for cancer. It's important to talk to your doctor and follow their advice for the best treatment options. Voomika Mukherjee, a Health and Nutrition Life Coach, highlights, 'While certain foods or food groups cannot guarantee cancer prevention, avoiding specific items may not necessarily lower the risk. For cancer treatment, maintaining a healthy body weight, reducing visceral fat, and increasing muscle strength are vital alongside a balanced diet.' She advises a well-rounded diet and limiting sugar, caffeine, salt, and alcohol intake. She stresses that consuming nutritious meals in adequate amounts can help reduce the risk of cancer and other chronic diseases. However, it's important to understand that no single food can cure cancer. Shivashankar T., Chief Clinical Nutritionist and Dietician at Tata Memorial Cancer Hospital, Mumbai, explains that maintaining a balanced diet is essential for achieving a healthy weight and supplying the body with essential nutrients to bolster the immune system. He recommends the Mediterranean diet as the optimal 'anti-cancer diet', which encourages reduced consumption of red meat and increased intake of white meat.

While bulletproof coffee may provide a feeling of fullness, it is not a balanced meal replacement. For weight loss, a healthy, balanced diet is crucial, and bulletproof coffee falls short in providing essential nutrients. Caffeine is known to temporarily boost metabolism by increasing energy expenditure, but this effect is limited. title: Does cancer stem from damaged mitochondria, not genes?
claim_text: Cancer happens due to damaged mitochondria, not bad genes or bad luck, citing biologist Thomas Seyfried
quick_take: A social media post claims that cancer stems from damaged mitochondria, not genes. We did the research and termed this claim as mostly false.

The prevailing scientific view attributes cancer to a complex interplay of genetic mutations, environmental factors, and lifestyle choices. Genes that control cell growth, division, and death are crucial in cancer development. When these genes mutate, they can lead to uncontrolled cell proliferation, the hallmark of cancer. Dr Pooja Khullar, Radiation Oncologist at Dharamshila Narayana Super Speciality Hospital, New Delhi explains: "The Mitochondrial Metabolic Theory by Dr Thomas Seyfried suggests that cancer starts from problems in how cells make energy, especially due to damaged mitochondria, rather than just from genetic mutations. This theory has gained attention and encourages exploring low-carb or ketogenic diets as supportive options. However, it's not widely accepted as the main explanation for cancer. Most scientists see cancer as a complex disease involving both genetic changes and metabolic disruptions, and standard treatments like surgery, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy remain essential." Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition states: "We do know that many cancer cells rely heavily on glucose to grow and survive, which is why low-carb or ketogenic diets are being researched as supportive strategies. These diets may help slow tumour growth in some cases, but they are not a cure. They should never replace medical treatment and must always be followed under professional supervision, especially during cancer therapy." While mitochondrial dysfunction can contribute to cancer development, it is not the sole cause. Mitochondria damage often occurs as a consequence of genetic mutations, not as the initial cause. Thomas Seyfried's Mitochondrial Metabolic Theory is a minority view and does not reflect mainstream scientific understanding.

title: Does Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) tolerance calm anxiety? - THIP Media
claim_text: Training oneself to tolerate higher levels of CO₂, through breath-holding, CO₂ exposure, or special 'CO₂ tolerance' exercises, will reduce anxiety for most people.
quick_take: A social media post claims that by increasing CO₂ tolerance, a person can stay relaxed and feel more positive. It also suggests that this effect may support people with depression by lifting their mood. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Scientific studies consistently show that inhaling air enriched with CO₂ can actually trigger anxiety and panic, rather than calm it. Researchers use CO₂ inhalation as a controlled method to induce panic-like symptoms in laboratory settings. When CO₂ levels rise in the bloodstream, specialized brain receptors detect the change and send signals to the body's alarm system. This leads to rapid breathing, heart palpitations, dizziness, and a sense of breathlessness, all sensations that are commonly associated with panic. In people with panic disorder or high anxiety sensitivity, even modest increase in CO₂ can provoke strong anxiety reactions. This effect has been repeatedly documented in clinical research and forms the basis of the CO₂ 'challenge test', a tool used to study panic mechanisms. In other words, CO₂ acts as a natural panic trigger for many, rather than a calming agent. Suggesting that inhaling more CO₂ will soothe anxiety ignores this well-established physiological response. Dr Satya Ranjan Sahu, Senior Consultant–Pulmonology at Narayana Superspeciality Hospital, Gurugram, explains, 'Carbon dioxide is a natural part of the air we exhale and helps regulate how fast and deeply we breathe. But this does not mean that inhaling concentrated CO₂ offers any healing benefits. In reality, higher CO₂ levels can upset the body's oxygen balance and quickly cause headaches, dizziness, rapid breathing, confusion, and shortness of breath. In severe situations, it may lead to fainting or even become life-threatening by displacing oxygen.' He adds that in certain scientific studies, researchers use very small and carefully monitored amounts of CO₂ to understand how the body responds to stress or anxiety. These are controlled research techniques, not home remedies, and require strict supervision because even slight variations in CO₂ levels can pose health risks. Regarding panic or hyperventilation: Some individuals with panic disorder breathe too quickly or deeply on a chronic basis, a pattern known as hyperventilation. It reduces the concentration of CO₂ in the blood (hypocapnia), which can intensify physical symptoms such as tingling in the fingers, light-headedness, and shortness of breath. Capnometry-assisted breathing therapies have been developed to address this problem. These therapies use real-time monitoring of CO₂ levels to help patients learn to slow their breathing, thereby raising their CO₂ back to normal levels (eucapnia). Clinical trials have shown that this approach can reduce panic symptoms, improve breathing stability, and give patients a sense of control over their bodily sensations. The crucial point is that these interventions do not aim to raise CO₂ beyond normal physiological levels. Rather, they correct an imbalance caused by over-breathing. Promoting CO₂ tolerance exercises or breath-holding routines as a universal anxiety cure is unsafe and scientifically unsupported. People vary greatly in their sensitivity to CO₂. Exposing someone to elevated CO₂ without supervision can trigger acute panic, dizziness, fainting, or even more serious cardiorespiratory stress. The safest and most effective way to address breathing-related anxiety is through supervised respiratory training that monitors CO₂ levels.

title: Fact Check: Does castor oil cure vaginal itching?
claim_text: Apply castor oil around the vaginal opening to cure vaginal itching. The person in the video claims it can heal wounds, itching, and infections.
quick_take: A social media post suggests castor oil for vaginal itching. It claims that castor oil can cure vaginal itching at home. After fact checking, we found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Vaginal itching is a common issue that can arise from multiple causes. Infections, such as yeast infections (caused by the fungus Candida albicans), bacterial vaginosis, or sexually transmitted infections (STIs), are frequent culprits. Other causes include allergic reactions to products like soaps, detergents, or feminine hygiene sprays, as well as skin conditions such as eczema or psoriasis. Hormonal changes, particularly during menopause or breastfeeding, can lead to vaginal dryness, which may also cause itching. Friction from tight clothing or irritation from scented hygiene or menstrual products can further contribute to discomfort. Dr Charmi Shah, MS OBGYN & Laparoscopic Surgeon, Valsad, Gujarat says: 'Clean the genital area every day with mild, unscented soap and water. Avoid using harsh soaps, scented pads, tampons, or feminine sprays, as these can irritate the area and disturb the natural pH balance. Stick to cotton underwear and avoid tight-fitting clothes that trap heat and moisture, as this creates a perfect environment for yeast to grow. Always use condoms properly to reduce the risk of infections, and only take antibiotics when prescribed, since they can upset the body's natural balance and increase the chances of a yeast infection.' There is no evidence for using castor oil for vaginal itching. It is not a recommended treatment for vaginal itching by medical professionals. Some studies suggest that castor oil, particularly its component undecylenic acid, has antifungal properties that can reduce Candida albicans growth in laboratory settings or specific contexts, such as denture cleaning or root canal treatments. A 2013 study found that castor oil reduced Candida in root canals after 21 days. However, these studies do not apply directly to vaginal use, as the vaginal environment is highly sensitive and requires targeted treatments. Medical guidelines, such as those from the NHS, recommend antifungal medications for yeast infections, antibiotics for bacterial infections, or other specific therapies based on the diagnosed cause. There is no clinical evidence supporting castor oil as an effective or safe treatment for vaginal itching, and relying on it may delay proper medical care. Dr Sachin Gupta, Senior Consultant Dermatologist at Amrita Hospital, Faridabad said: 'Clean the outer vaginal area once a day using plain water or a mild, unscented soap. Avoid scrubbing, and stay away from harsh soaps, wipes, or scented products, as they can disturb the natural pH and cause irritation. Vaginal washes or douches are not necessary for daily use and may do more harm than good.' He added: 'Wear cotton underwear and avoid tight clothes that trap heat and moisture. After sweating or working out, change into dry clothes quickly. Drink enough water to support healthy skin. title: Fact Check: Does chanting Vitthal mantra prevent heart attacks?
claim_text: chanting the Vitthal mantra can prevent heart attacks and cure heart problems
quick_take: A social media post claims that chanting the Vitthal mantra can prevent heart attacks. We did the fact check to term it as False.
doctor_explanation: In an era where health misinformation can spread rapidly through social media, it's extremely important to scrutinise claims that lack scientific backing. The term 'Vitthal' refers to a Hindu deity who is a form of Lord Vishnu, particularly worshipped in Maharashtra, India. Vitthal, also known as Vithoba or Panduranga, is the central figure of devotion in the Bhakti movement. Devotees often engage in practices such as chanting his name, singing devotional songs, and participating in pilgrimages to his temples. No, chanting the Vitthal mantra cannot prevent heart attacks. No scientific studies or clinical trials support the notion that chanting the name Vitthal can prevent heart attacks or prevent heart diseases. Heart disease comprises a range of conditions, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, arrhythmias, and heart failure. All of these require medical diagnosis and treatment. Even though chanting and meditation can contribute to overall mental well-being, there is no conclusive evidence, yet, to suggest they can directly cure physical conditions such as heart disease. The placebo effect, which can occur when patients believe in the efficacy of a treatment, might offer some subjective improvements. But it still cannot replace standard medical interventions. The study titled 'Effect of chanting Vitthal on Heart: A Clinical Study,' published in 2014, investigated the effects of chanting 'Vitthal' on heart parameters and Heart Chakra energy. Conducted with only 30 healthy volunteers, the study assessed changes before and after chanting 'Vitthal' for 9 minutes. The study shows statistically significant improvements in heart rate, blood pressure, pulse rate, and ejection fraction, suggesting enhanced heart function. Additionally, there was an increase in the energy associated with the Heart Chakra. This study does not say that chanting the Vitthal mantra can prevent heart attacks anywhere. After analysing carefully, we found out the study has several limitations. Dr Ashok Kumar Boss, Cardiologist at HDNA Aarogyam Hospital, Patna, shares his expertise, 'As of now, no authentic study supports this. Drawing conclusions from a one-year study on only 30 subjects in such a chronic disease is insufficient.' People should not believe these claims. Mantra chanting and meditation can be beneficial for mental health and stress reduction, which can support overall well-being. But still, they cannot prevent heart attacks or cure heart disease. Dr Shailesh Singh, an Interventional Cardiologist, at Fortis Escorts Heart Institute, New Delhi advises, 'Heart disease can only be prevented by a good lifestyle and exercise. People should consider the following to stay away from heart diseases: Stop smoking, manage their diabetes and cholesterol levels better, regularly monitor the blood pressure, and exercise regularly.' Mantra chanting has gained recognition for its potential health benefits, particularly in relation to mental and cardiovascular well-being. Rigorous scientific research is still ongoing, but available data suggest several benefits of mantra chanting. Scientifically, meditation and mantra chanting show potential to influence cardiovascular health positively. But methodological issues in past research make larger, randomised trials necessary with longer follow-up periods to validate these effects. In clinical practice, these practices can complement conventional treatments for cardiovascular risk due to their non-invasive and cost-effective nature. Addressing psychosocial factors like stress, depression, and anxiety through meditation and Ayurvedic massages may enhance overall quality of life. Current evidence supports the potential benefits of incorporating mantra chanting into daily routines for improved mental and physical health. Still, we must reiterate that you should not rely solely on chanting mantras to cure health problems. The claim that chanting Vitthal mantra can prevent heart attacks and cure heart problems is not true. It is not backed by scientific evidence and is thus false. Spiritual practices such as chanting or meditation can enhance mental well-being and reduce stress. But, they are not substitutes for medical treatments and interventions. You can maintain your heart health through a combination of a balanced diet, regular exercise, avoiding smoking, managing stress, and adhering to medical advice. For anyone with heart-related concerns, consulting a healthcare professional is essential.

title: Does chlorophyll water neutralise odour and help clear skin? - THIP
claim_text: Drinking chlorophyll water for just seven days improves digestion, clears up the skin, and neutralises body odour, leaving you fresher, healthier, and basically glowing from within.
quick_take: A social media post claims that drinking chlorophyll water helps eliminate body odour, clears up the skin, and improves digestion. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
## Does chlorophyll water actually remove or neutralise body odour? No, there's no strong scientific proof that chlorophyll water neutralises body odour from within. This popular idea likely stems from studies done in the 1940s and 1950s where Sodium copper chlorophyllin (a semi-synthetic mixture of water-soluble sodium copper salts derived from chlorophyll) was used to reduce odours in hospital patients with colostomies and other medical conditions. However, those were specific cases involving concentrated doses, not a few drops of chlorophyll in water. Today, there's no robust evidence showing that drinking chlorophyll water can significantly change how your body smells. Body odour is largely caused by bacteria breaking down sweat, especially in areas like armpits, not by what you drink. Sure, hydration helps reduce strong-smelling urine or bad breath in some cases, but that's not unique to chlorophyll. At best, chlorophyll water might make your breath feel fresher if it helps with hydration or masks minor smells. But don't expect it to replace your deodorant. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition says, "There's very little scientific backing for the idea that chlorophyll water can reduce body odour. While it may have some mild deodorising properties in certain medical conditions, it's not a reliable fix. Good hygiene and a balanced diet are far more important."

## Can chlorophyll water really improve digestion in a week? No, chlorophyll water does not directly improve digestion in any medically proven way. Digestion is a complex process involving enzymes, gut bacteria, bile, and more. While chlorophyll is sometimes marketed as a "gut healer," there's very little solid research to back this up. One small study found that chlorophyllin might reduce constipation and gas in people taking it alongside a high-protein diet, but again, this involved a specific form, not the drops found in wellness waters. If people feel better after drinking chlorophyll water, it's often because they're drinking more fluids or eating cleaner at the same time. That's the effect of lifestyle change, not chlorophyll itself. Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, General Physician from Navi Mumbai, said, "There's no magic in chlorophyll water. While chlorophyll itself has some antioxidant properties, drinking it won't drastically change your digestion overnight or even in a week. A balanced diet with enough fibre and hydration is far more effective."

## Does chlorophyll water clear the skin? No, there is no clinical proof that drinking chlorophyll clears acne or improves skin clarity. Some social media influencers swear their skin glowed after a week of chlorophyll water, but glowing skin isn't proof. Most of these stories are anecdotal. There are some studies showing that applying topical chlorophyllin might help reduce acne and inflammation, but that's on the skin, not inside your body. Your skin's health depends on hormones, genetics, skincare habits, and diet. Drinking chlorophyll water won't cancel out a lack of sleep, excess sugar, or not washing your face properly. Staying hydrated, eating balanced meals, and avoiding harsh skin products will do far more good for your skin than chlorophyll drops. Dermatologist Dr Jyothy Kannangath pointed out that while chlorophyll water has gained popularity, largely thanks to social media influencers, there's little solid scientific evidence to support its effectiveness. Although chlorophyll does have antioxidant properties, its ability to protect the skin from oxidative damage caused by harmful carcinogens hasn't been conclusively proven. Dr Kannangath cautions against using liquid chlorophyll as a remedy for acne, noting that excessive intake could potentially have harmful effects. However, she did mention that chlorophyll might play a role in professional skin treatments like photodynamic therapy, but such methods should be carried out under medical supervision, not as DIY solutions.

## Will your body "thank you" after 7 days of drinking chlorophyll water? No, your body likely won't notice much difference, because chlorophyll water isn't a miracle cure. This line is often used in marketing to promise vague wellness benefits. But unless you're deficient in something or severely dehydrated, adding chlorophyll water for a week probably won't make any meaningful changes. The human body is already excellent at detoxifying through the liver, kidneys, and digestive system; it doesn't need chlorophyll's help to do what it's designed to do. If you feel better after a week, it might be the placebo effect, or simply because you're drinking more water and paying attention to your habits.

## So, is there any benefit to drinking chlorophyll water at all? Yes, but only as part of a healthy lifestyle, and mostly from increased hydration. Chlorophyll itself contains antioxidants and may have anti-inflammatory properties. But these benefits are mostly studied in isolated lab settings or through topical use. If you enjoy the taste or it reminds you to drink more water, that's great. But don't rely on it to detox your organs or clear your pores. Also, be cautious, some chlorophyll supplements can cause stomach cramps, green stool, or make you more sensitive to sunlight.

## Final Verdict Chlorophyll water is more hype than health hero. It won't magically clean you out or make you odour-free in a week. While it's not dangerous in moderation, don't be swayed by bold claims without solid proof. Save your money, or spend it on leafy greens, which are far better sources of chlorophyll anyway.

title: Does consuming artificial sweetener make you slim? - THIP Media
claim_text: Artificial sweetener doesn't cause obesity and will keep you slim. Consuming water and drinking soda with artificial sweeteners are nearly equivalent.
quick_take: A social media post says that artificial sweeteners help in weight loss and maintaining a slim figure. We fact checked and found the claim to be Mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
According to his website Ekansh Taneja was previously overweight and has since lost weight. We have checked his website, yet could not find any certification that shows a formal training in medicine. His assertion that artificial sugars will help in slimming down and won't lead to weight gain should be approached with caution, as it comes from a non-professional individual. For accurate advice on the consumption of artificial sweeteners, it's advisable to consult a doctor or a registered dietitian.

NOT REALLY - ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS AND OBESITY: Artificial sweeteners were originally developed to replace sugar and help with insulin resistance and obesity. In 2017 a research indicated that it may actually contribute to metabolic syndrome and the obesity problem. Studies in both animals and humans suggest that artificial sweeteners can alter the microbiome, reduce feelings of fullness after eating, and disrupt how our bodies manage sugar levels. Surprisingly, they might even lead to consuming more calories and gaining weight.

In 2010 large-scale studies showed a positive correlation between artificial sweetener consumption and weight gain. The San Antonio Heart Study observed that adults who consumed artificially sweetened beverages had higher BMIs over a seven to eight-year period linked to greater weight gain. Similarly, studies by the American Cancer Society and Nurses' Health Study reported associations between artificial sweetener use, particularly saccharin, and weight gain in women over several years. Children's studies also support these findings. High consumption of diet sodas among children was linked to higher BMI scores over time in various longitudinal studies, such as the Growing Up Today Study and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Growth and Health Study.

Experimental studies shed light on potential mechanisms. Preload experiments indicate that sweet tastes, whether from sugar or artificial sweeteners, can stimulate appetite and increase subsequent food intake. A 2020 review explores how artificial sweeteners affect body weight and glucose regulation differently than sugars due to their unique metabolic pathways, impacting gut microbiota, insulin response, and other physiological processes. While some studies suggest neutral or beneficial effects on weight and glucose control in humans, evidence is limited by short study durations and varying metabolic responses among different sweeteners.

CANCER LINK: According to the National Cancer Institute, (2023) individuals who consumed higher quantities of artificial sweeteners showed a slightly elevated risk of obesity-related cancers compared to those who did not use artificial sweeteners. The debate over artificial sweeteners and cancer risk arose after a study showed elevated rates of bladder cancer in mice given very high doses of saccharin and cyclamate. As a result, cyclamate was banned in the U.S. However, subsequent research indicated that cyclamate does not actually pose a cancer risk.

CARDIOVASCULAR SIDE EFFECTS: In 2023 a research paper listed a number of harms artificial sweeteners can cause to our heart. Artificial sweeteners could potentially harm cardiovascular health by disrupting the balance of gut bacteria, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and immune function. This imbalance has been linked to diseases like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease (CVD). By altering gene expression involved in carbohydrate metabolism, artificial sweeteners may affect how gut bacteria grow and function, leading to metabolic and inflammatory changes that contribute to vascular dysfunction and cardiovascular problems. Moreover, artificial sweeteners might impair the function of certain proteins like ApoA-I, a key component of HDL (good cholesterol), which is crucial for preventing atherosclerosis (hardening of arteries). Changes in ApoA-I caused by artificial sweeteners could reduce its ability to act as an antioxidant and transport lipids effectively, promoting oxidative stress and accelerating the development of atherosclerosis. Some artificial sweeteners, like aspartame, have been associated with oxidative stress in heart tissues and adverse effects on cardiac function. This includes decreased heart rate variability and a loss of protective nervous system functions, potentially increasing susceptibility to cardiovascular diseases. Long-term consumption of artificial sweeteners has also been linked to structural changes in the heart and complications like impaired relaxation of the heart's chambers (left ventricular end-diastolic pressure elevation). Additionally, certain artificial sweeteners aspartame, can act as excitotoxins in cardiac tissue, potentially leading to arrhythmias like atrial fibrillation. These substances can overstimulate glutamate receptors in the heart, disrupting normal electrical activity and increasing the risk of abnormal heart rhythms, especially in individuals without other heart conditions like high blood pressure or coronary artery disease.

Dr. Neha Singh, BHMS, MAPC, Bhavil Homoeopathic Clinic New Delhi said, "Artificial sweeteners are promoted as a healthier option to sugar. However, clinical data indicates that their anticipated benefits often do not align with real-world outcomes. Although artificial sweeteners are generally safe, that does not imply one should keep on drinking diet sodas or juices loaded with artificial sweeteners without any limit. Surprisingly, human data on the effects of artificial sweeteners on the human body are low and need further scientific research. Consumption in moderation is the key, and individuals should consult healthcare providers to understand personal health implications."

Dr. Ashirwad Pawar, MBBS, Diabetologist, Sai Aashirwad Hospital, Mumbai said, "Artificial sweeteners such as Aspartame, Sucralose, Saccharin, Acesulfame Potassium, and Stevia offer several potential benefits. However, it's important to note the potential drawbacks. Studies suggest that artificial sweeteners may affect metabolism and gut microbiota. There is also evidence linking them to glucose intolerance in some individuals and an increase in appetite or cravings for sweet foods. My recommendation is to use these artificial sweeteners in moderation. Consider gradually reducing their intake until no sweeteners are added at all. Focus on a balanced diet rich in whole foods to promote overall health and well-being."

Mumbai-based diabetologist Dr. Almas Fatma advises against unlimited consumption of diet sodas, citing concerns over artificial sweeteners like aspartame, sucralose, and saccharin. She says, "Despite their lower calorie content compared to regular sodas, excessive intake of these sweeteners may pose health risks, including potential metabolic issues such as insulin resistance, as suggested by some studies."

Dr. Kunal Gupta, MD (Physician) and Emergency Physician at Accord Superspeciality Hospital, Faridabad, also warns against excessive consumption of diet coke, citing research linking it to potential weight gain. He recommends limiting intake to one or two cans per day, suggesting that regular soda may be a preferable option over diet coke.

title: Fact Check: Does consuming salt relieve anxiety? - THIP Media
claim_text: Putting salt on the tongue can help distract from anxiety and ground one by engaging their senses.
quick_take: According to an Instagram post, salt consumption reduces anxiety. We checked the claim. According to our findings, the claim is False.
doctor_explanation:
Anxiety is a person's overall reaction to a threat or danger. Each anxiety experience includes a perception of danger, thoughts about harm, and a physiological alarm and activation process. The most common of these disorders are panic disorders, phobias, generalized anxiety disorders, and OCDS. These conditions typically affect one's mood, thought process, behaviour, and physiological activities. The main symptoms include restlessness, feeling tense, easily fatigued, difficulty concentrating or going blank, muscle tension, and irritability.

No. There is no substantial evidence that it is possible to get rid of anxiety disorders by taking common salt. It should be noted that cardiovascular disease is closely linked to a variety of neuropsychiatric disorders. These conditions include PTSD, depression, and anxiety disorders. It should also be noted that excessive salt consumption is widely recognized as a dietary risk factor for cardiovascular disease. This is because salt has been linked to a notable increase in anxiety. Therefore, these anxiety-salt interactions are thought to play a role in the close relationship between neuropsychiatric diseases and cardiovascular disease.

Anxiety disorders and depression, on the other hand, are associated with electrolyte inadequacies. Furthermore, some foods are thought to play an important role in anxiety reduction. Thus, we discovered in our analysis that dietary magnesium intake is slightly negatively correlated with anxiety. Clinical evidence suggests that magnesium supplementation may have a relaxing effect. This is because magnesium inhibits NMDA receptors. As a result, this blockage may help reduce nervous stimulation. However, this correlation requires more evidence. Furthermore, salt contains a lot of sodium, which is necessary for fluid balance, nerve health, nutrient absorption, and muscle function, but too much salt consumption may not reduce anxiety.

We asked Psychologist Dr Manisha Gaur if salt consumption could help relieve anxiety. She cautioned that "Anxiety disorders could cause people to overindulge in salty, fatty foods." She explained that this could be more detrimental than beneficial because the recurrent pattern of overeating could lead to obesity, hypertension, diabetes, and even cardiac ailments. Thus, in order to manage anxiety, one should seek psychiatric advice.

The two primary treatments for anxiety disorders are psychotherapy and medication. A combination of the two may be most effective for anxiety relief. Please keep in mind that management varies from person to person. Psychotherapy, also known as psychological counselling, implies working with a therapist to reduce its symptoms. It has the potential to be an effective treatment for anxiety. The most beneficial type of psychotherapy is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT). Additionally, depending on the type of anxiety disorder, the psychiatrist may prescribe various medications to relieve symptoms.

THIP MEDIA TAKE: Salt is high in sodium. Sodium is an essential nutrient that the body requires for a variety of vital functions. However, most health organizations recommend that healthy adults limit their intake of sodium. Furthermore, sodium may trigger anxiety rather than alleviate it. Further, it can cause hypertension. As a result, we conclude that salt consumption does not reduce anxiety. Hence, the assertion is false.

While cucumbers are a healthy food choice, low in calories and high in water, they lack magical properties that directly trigger fat loss. The foundation of weight loss is a calorie deficit: burning more calories than you consume. Regularly including cucumbers can aid in controlling calorie intake by promoting fullness, but they won't independently drive pounds off the scale. Cucumbers fit well into a healthy diet, but consuming them 1-2 times daily won't deliver results without an overall balanced eating plan and physical activity. Sustainable weight loss demands a holistic strategy.

Does eating cucumbers help curb hunger? Yes, cucumbers can temporarily reduce hunger. Their fiber and high water content expand in the stomach, fostering a sense of fullness that may curb appetite briefly and encourage lower daily calorie consumption, indirectly aiding weight management. That said, this satiety is short-lived. Cucumbers make a solid low-calorie snack, but for sustained hunger control, pair them with balanced meals featuring protein, healthy fats, and complex carbs. Relying solely on cucumbers won't suffice for ongoing appetite management.

Are cucumbers low in calories? Absolutely, cucumbers are exceptionally low in calories, ideal for weight loss or calorie reduction. Swapping them for high-calorie options like chips, chocolate, or sodas can slash your total intake, supporting better weight control. However, they shouldn't dominate your diet. A varied plan with proteins, fibers, vitamins, and minerals, beyond what cucumbers offer, is crucial. Eating them 1-2 times a day may trim calories, but it won't dissolve fat on its own.

Do cucumbers help you stay hydrated? Yes, cucumbers excel at hydration, boasting about 96% water content to keep you refreshed. Proper hydration benefits overall health and can stop overeating, as thirst is sometimes mistaken for hunger, curbing unnecessary snacks. Incorporating cucumbers boosts fluid intake, which may indirectly help weight loss by easing hunger pangs. Yet, hydration isn't a standalone fat-burner, combine it with balanced nutrition and exercise.

Can eating cucumbers 1-2 times a day help you lose weight in the long run? Only within a balanced, calorie-controlled diet. Snacking on cucumbers 1-2 times daily can contribute to long-term weight loss by bulking up meals or replacing calorie-dense foods, fostering a deficit without excess energy. But solo reliance yields minimal, unsustainable results.

title: Fact Check: Does consuming female animal meat increase estrogen in males? - THIP Media
claim_text: A Facebook reel claims that we only get female animals to eat, which means that we are taking estrogen. Males should consume testosterone and not this, and consuming female animal meat will change their hormones.
quick_take: A social media post claims that we only get female animals to eat, and this means that we are taking estrogen, and males should consume testosterone and not this. We fact-checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
The fact-check addresses three key questions:

1. Are male bodies only composed of testosterone hormones? Not exactly. While testosterone is the primary male sex hormone, it is not the only hormone in the male body. There are many other hormones in the male body that play essential roles in various physiological processes. In addition to testosterone, males also produce other androgens, such as dihydrotestosterone (DHT) and androstenedione. Males also contain estrogen, although in much lower amounts than females. Estrogen is typically thought of as a female hormone, but it is actually present in both males and females. In males, estrogen is produced primarily by the testes and adrenal glands.

2. Do we consume meat made up of only female animals? No, we do not consume meat made up of only female animals. Both male and female animals are used for meat production. In many cases, male animals are raised specifically for meat production, such as beef cattle and pigs. In other cases, both male and female animals are raised for meat production, such as chickens and turkeys. Males intended for meat are routinely castrated. Some cultures even favour the meat of male sheep and goats.

3. Does eating female animal meat increase estrogen in males? Not exactly. There is a lack of credible scientific evidence to prove that consuming meat will lead to an increased estrogen level in males. Firstly, as stated above, we consume meat irrespective of the gender of the cattle. Secondly, the estrogen consumed through meat is negligible. The amount of estrogen in the animals that we eat is not sufficient enough to elevate the female hormones. Our bodies produce much more levels of estrogen than we could ever consume in meat. Another research concluded that compared to a commonly prescribed hormone replacement therapy for women after hysterectomy or menopause, the estrogenic activity in a tofu burger was three times higher. On the other hand, a quarter-pound ground beef burger with approximately the same calorie count, a serving of milk, or rice, all had at least 750-fold less estrogenic activity. Therefore, further research is needed to prove this claim, and until there is definitive evidence to prove this, the claim stands mostly false.

title: Does consuming ghee water help reduce belly fat? - THIP Media
claim_text: Drinking ghee water with lemon juice on an empty stomach may help reduce belly fat by enhancing metabolism, improving digestion, detoxifying the body, curbing appetite, and promoting fat breakdown. It also aids in hormone regulation and supports skin health.

doctor_explanation:
Ghee does not directly help in burning belly fat. Ghee, a type of clarified butter, has been used in traditional Indian cooking and medicine for centuries. It's often praised for its high concentration of healthy fats and believed to have anti-inflammatory properties. However, when it comes to losing belly fat specifically, ghee alone doesn't play a significant role. Many say the Conjugated Linoleic Acid found in ghee can help people lose weight, while studies have not found any significant effect. A review of 18 high-quality studies found that people who took 3.2 grams CLA lost an average of 0.05 kg per week more than those who took a placebo. However, this is a small amount of weight loss. Several studies have investigated the impact of Conjugated Linoleic Acid (CLA) on weight loss in humans. One review of these studies assessed the long-term effects of CLA supplementation on fat loss in overweight and obese individuals. It found that taking 2.4–6 grams per day for 6–12 months led to a reduction of about 1.33 kg of body fat compared to a placebo. This reduction, while statistically significant, is relatively small when compared to the placebo group. Other studies have also shown mixed results, with CLA offering little to no real-world benefits for fat loss and there were no changes in the waist circumference, even when combined with exercise. Overall, current research suggests that CLA has minimal effects on weight loss, both in the short and long term. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said, 'Fat loss doesn't occur just by adding a specific food or drink to your diet. It's a complex process that requires an overall reduction in calorie intake, regular physical activity, and a consistent approach to healthy eating. Simply drinking ghee water won't magically target fat in your belly area.' So, ghee in moderation may be a healthy addition to your diet, but it won't cause belly fat to vanish.

Regarding lemon juice: No, lemon juice by itself does not melt belly fat. Lemon juice is often touted for its supposed detoxifying properties and its role in boosting metabolism. While lemons are high in vitamin C, the idea that lemon juice can target belly fat is misleading. Lemon juice has been linked to a variety of health benefits. However, there's no solid scientific evidence showing that it directly contributes to fat loss, especially in the belly area. Nutritionist Dr. Umesh Wadhavani emphasizes that overall health is influenced by a range of factors, not just individual foods. Aspects such as daily habits, work-related stress, personal relationships, sleep quality, and physical activity all play a significant role. To manage belly fat, it's important to take a holistic approach that addresses multiple areas of a healthy lifestyle.

Regarding combining ghee and lemon juice: Harita Adhvaryu, a senior dietician from Ahmedabad said, 'No, combining ghee and lemon juice will not lead to belly fat loss. There is no evidence that combining these two ingredients will result in a fat-burning miracle.' The idea behind this combination is that the acidity of lemon might help the body absorb the fat from ghee more efficiently, or that the lemon could 'cut' the richness of ghee, making it easier to digest. However, the truth is that consuming fat with lemon juice will not dramatically change how the body processes fat or lead to fat burning. The body breaks down and processes fats in a specific way, and it requires a balanced approach to diet and exercise to lose weight. In fact, drinking ghee water with lemon juice may actually increase your total calorie intake, making it harder to maintain a calorie deficit, which is the most effective way to lose belly fat.

Regarding detoxification: No, there is no scientific evidence that ghee water with lemon juice detoxifies the body. The concept of 'detoxification' is widely discussed in wellness circles, but the body already has a built-in detox system – your liver, kidneys, and digestive system work tirelessly to filter and remove toxins from your body. There's no need to rely on special drinks or diets to detoxify. Ghee and lemon juice don't provide any additional detox benefits. While lemon juice may support liver function with its vitamin C content, there's no evidence that combining it with ghee helps to detoxify the body. Dr. Sharad Malhotra, Senior Consultant and Head of Gastroenterology, Hepatology, and Therapeutic Endoscopy at Aakash Healthcare, New Delhi, shares his expertise on homemade drinks for body detox and digestive issues. He explains, 'No single drink can detoxify the body. Our body is an incredibly efficient organ that naturally detoxifies itself, without the need for special drinks to assist in this process.'

title: Does consuming ginger thrice in a week remove fat from liver?

However, these effects are indirect and not powerful enough to eliminate fat deposits in the liver. Managing these underlying conditions requires a comprehensive approach involving a well-balanced diet, increased physical activity, and in some cases, medical interventions. While ginger can complement these efforts, it is not a cure-all method for reducing liver fat." Scientific research highlights ginger's potential to benefit the liver in several ways: its antioxidant properties help reduce oxidative stress—a condition that contributes to liver damage in conditions like NAFLD; ginger's anti-inflammatory effects may help combat chronic low-grade inflammation, which is often associated with liver fat accumulation. Studies also suggest that ginger may help in regulating lipid metabolism. By lowering triglyceride and cholesterol levels, ginger could indirectly reduce the factors that lead to fatty deposits in the liver. However, these findings indicate supportive benefits rather than a direct fat-removal effect. The best way to maintain liver health is through a combination of dietary adjustments, regular exercise, and when necessary, medical care. title: Fact Check: Does consuming milk reduce calcium in bones?
claim_text: People who drink more milk have the least amount of calcium left in their bones. Humans are deficient in the enzyme lactase, which breaks down lactose in milk, just as our bodies are deficient in the enzymes needed to break down glass or metal. When milk is consumed, it becomes acidic in the stomach, causing lactic acid to be produced. As the spread of this lactic acid might cause sudden death, the release of calcium from the bones neutralises the acidity of the stomach, leaving the bones demineralized or calcium-depleted.
quick_take: A well-circulated Instagram post asserts that consuming milk reduces calcium in the bones, demineralizing them. We verified the facts and discovered that the claim is False.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Gulhima Arora, renowned Dermatologist, cautions against medical misinformation. She insists that you should always trust a qualified professional with your health concerns. Avoid following trends and fads. Since every patient has a unique genetic makeup and set of triggers for their particular illness, following your doctor's recommendations ensures that you receive the right medical therapy and avoid medical misconceptions.

Lactase is an enzyme that is usually present in the brush border of the human small intestine. Its primary function is to break down the lactose sugar found in milk into glucose and galactose, two easier-to-digest carbohydrates. Infants acquire significant amounts of lactase to help with the digestion of breast milk; however, adult lactase levels may decrease with age. Additionally, a drop in lactase enzyme levels leads to the onset of lactose intolerance, a common condition that manifests as symptoms like bloating, diarrhoea, and gas after consuming dairy products. Other enzymes, besides lactase, are also involved in milk digestion. Even though lactase is essential for the breakdown of lactose, the main sugar in milk, other enzymes aid in the digestion of milk. Among these are the digestive enzymes responsible for milk's fat and protein content. The digestion of milk proteins like casein and whey is aided by proteases, which are enzymes that break down proteins into amino acids. Lipases facilitate the breakdown of triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol, aiding in the digestion of milk fats.

Regarding lactic acid: Lactose is broken down by the enzyme lactase into glucose and galactose; however, lactose travels through the colon undigested when lactase activity is low. In this scenario, gut bacteria called lactic acid bacteria (LAB) digest lactose and make lactic acid as a byproduct. Fermentation breaks down the components of milk even further, facilitating digestion and absorption. Lactic acidosis is caused by an excessive buildup of lactic acid. Elevated amounts of lactic acid are not directly induced by milk digestion but can be a result of faulty lactose fermentation in people with severe lactose intolerance or malabsorption problems.

On bones being deprived of calcium: There is no substantial evidence suggesting that consuming milk reduces calcium in bones. Milk is traditionally promoted for its calcium content, which is essential for bone health. Calcium fortifies bones and helps in the prevention of diseases like osteoporosis. Therefore, consuming milk and other dairy products has been associated with higher bone mineral density. Research indicates that fermented dairy products, regardless of their calcium level, have a favourable impact on bone health.

There might be detrimental effects of milk on bone health. A 2014 study uses self-reported data, which increases the risk of recall bias and inaccurate measurements of milk intake, which cannot be applied to other populations other than Swedish people. Most importantly, the results could also have been influenced by uncontrolled food and lifestyle factors that affect fracture risks and death rates. According to another study, milk contains D-galactose, which may be harmful to bones. These studies highlight the question of whether consuming an excessive amount of milk over time may eventually cause bone deterioration. Furthermore, the substantial impact of genes, dietary and lifestyle factors on bone health provides a conflicting perspective regarding the necessity of milk drinking for strong bones.

Therefore, the evidence predominantly supports milk's positive role in maintaining bone health when consumed in moderation, making milk and dairy products an integral part of a balanced diet.

Milk has rightly earned the title of "complete food" for the human body due to the multitude of health advantages its life-giving nectar offers. Milk is the easiest, most affordable, and most accessible primary source of calcium. Calcium, the body's primary structural element, is essential for the production of bone tissue, a major factor in the measurement of bone mineral density. In addition to increasing bone density, calcium has been demonstrated to reduce the incidence of stroke and cardiovascular disease. Milk and dairy products are strong sources of compounds with antioxidant properties. Since milk fermentation results in the production of antioxidant peptides, dairy products have a higher potential for antioxidants. Children who don't get enough cow's milk are more likely to break their bones when they get hurt, and they will take longer to recover if they don't get enough calcium to help rebuild their bone mass.

Limitations: Milk might not be beneficial to everyone, particularly for people who have lactose intolerance, a condition brought on by a lack of the enzyme lactase. Allergies to milk are another reason to stay away from it. As opposed to lactose intolerance, which is characterised by trouble digesting milk sugar, a milk allergy is an immunological reaction to casein or whey proteins found in milk. Other than these conditions, the fat content of milk and other substances has the potential to aggravate certain digestive conditions, such as irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

title: Does consuming milk with fish or salt cause white patches on skin-
claim_text: Consuming combinations like milk with salt and milk with fish causes leucoderma (white skin patches)
quick_take: A social media post claimed that certain food combinations, such as milk with fish or salt causes white patches on skin, leucoderma. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Leucoderma, also known as vitiligo, is a skin condition characterised by the loss of pigmentation. This results in white patches appearing on various parts of the body. The condition occurs when melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing melanin (the pigment that gives skin its colour), stop functioning. Leucoderma is caused by the loss of melanocytes, the cells that produce melanin, the pigment responsible for skin colour. The exact cause of this loss is not entirely understood, but several factors are believed to contribute: 1) Autoimmune Response: The most common theory is that leucoderma is an autoimmune disorder. The immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys melanocytes. 2) Genetic Factors: There is a hereditary component, as vitiligo often runs in families. Certain genes may increase the susceptibility to the condition. 3) Neurogenic Factors: Nerve endings may release substances that are toxic to melanocytes. 4) Oxidative Stress: An imbalance between free radicals and antioxidants in the body may damage melanocytes. 5) Environmental Triggers: Exposure to certain chemicals or significant sunburn can trigger the onset in susceptible individuals. 6) Stress: Emotional or physical stress may precipitate or exacerbate the condition. Consuming milk and salt together does not cause leucoderma. No scientific evidence supports the claim that dietary combinations, such as milk and salt, trigger leucoderma. This misconception likely arises from traditional beliefs or anecdotal reports, not from validated medical research. Factors contributing to leucoderma include genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, stress, and possibly certain autoimmune or endocrine conditions. Dr Sachin Gupta, Dermatologist, Amrita Hospital, Faridabad, said, "There is no scientific evidence that eating milk and salt causes leucoderma. It is an autoimmune condition where the body's white blood cells destroy the cells (melanocytes) that produce skin colour. No foods or diet cause leucoderma, so no dietary restrictions is in need. There are many treatments available, like creams, oral medicines, phototherapy, and even surgery. Visit a dermatologist to get proper treatment based on the stage of leucoderma." Consuming milk and fish together does not cause leucoderma. This is a myth with no scientific evidence. Leucoderma is an autoimmune condition influenced by genetic, environmental, and immunological factors, not by diet. You can safely consume milk and fish together without fear of developing leucoderma.

title: Does consuming Okra help with vaginal dryness? - THIP Media
claim_text: A social media post suggests that if a doctor tells you that you have vaginal dryness, you should start eating bhindi (lady fingers).
quick_take: A dietitian's social media post suggested that lady fingers can help relieve vaginal dryness. However, upon fact checking the statement we found that the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: No, there is no scientific mechanism or evidence to support that. The main reason okra feels "slimy" is because of mucilage, a type of soluble fibre composed of complex plant carbohydrates (polysaccharides) and glycoproteins. This mucilage gives okra its characteristic texture when you cut or cook it, and has been studied mainly for its food and functional properties, such as its ability to thicken soups, hold water, and behave in the digestive tract. However, digestion breaks down food into its basic chemical components, and those molecules are absorbed into the bloodstream. There is no biological pathway by which the mucilage or "slipperiness" of okra is transported to the vagina or acts as a vaginal lubricant. Vaginal lubrication is controlled by local tissue health, blood flow, nervous-system responses during arousal, and hormone effects on the vaginal lining, particularly oestrogen. Mucilage from okra does not influence those processes, and no clinical trial has measured its effect on vaginal dryness. Although okra is nutritious and can benefit general health, its nutrients do not act like a pharmaceutical or topical agent within the vaginal environment. Therefore, the claim that okra improves vaginal lubrication is not supported by physiology or research. Dr Sunita Sharma, Senior Consultant Obstetrician & Gynaecologist and Infertility Specialist at Fortis Nagarbhavi, Bangalore, explains that the leading cause of vaginal dryness is low oestrogen levels. Oestrogen plays a key role in keeping the vaginal lining thick, well-lubricated, and flexible. When levels drop, the tissues can become thinner and less elastic. This can result in discomfort during sexual activity, which may gradually reduce interest in intimacy. Dryness can also make physical activities such as sports or other high-impact movements uncomfortable. Additionally, reduced natural lubrication may increase susceptibility to vaginal infections, as the protective balance of the vaginal environment can be affected. No, there are no clinical trials or research studies demonstrating this. Scientific research on okra has focused on a range of topics, such as its nutritional content, effects on blood sugar levels, antioxidant properties, or applications in food and pharmaceuticals, but none of this literature shows that okra improves vaginal dryness. For example, studies on okra mucilage examine its role in antidiabetic effects or its potential as a pharmaceutical excipient, not its ability to affect vaginal tissues. By contrast, when researchers study treatments for vaginal dryness, they measure real outcomes like symptom severity, vaginal pH, tissue thickness, or patient-reported improvements in comfort. So far, no study has positioned okra as a treatment in this context. Dr Tanuj Lawania, MBBS, DNB (OBGYN), Centre Head at Indira IVF, Saket Nagar, Kanpur said "As a gynaecologist, I've seen the recent claims about okra (bhindi) helping with vaginal dryness. While okra feels slippery because of its natural fibre, there is no scientific proof that eating it or using it locally can treat vaginal dryness. Natural remedies can sound harmless, but when it comes to intimate health, it's always better to rely on evidence-based care instead of social media trends." Not in a way that targets vaginal dryness specifically. Okra is a nutritious vegetable rich in fiber, vitamins (like C, A and K), minerals, and antioxidants that benefit general health. Eating a balanced diet and staying hydrated can improve overall wellbeing, but those general benefits do not specifically translate into increased vaginal lubrication. General hydration or good nutrition helps the body overall, but it does not directly restore moisture to the vaginal lining if dryness is caused by tissue changes or lowered oestrogen. Vaginal dryness often arises from conditions like menopause, postpartum hormonal shifts, breastfeeding, certain medications, irritation from products, or autoimmune issues. These causes affect the vaginal mucosa's structure and secretory function, changes that simple dietary fibre or plant compounds don't directly reverse. Several options have clear research backing: lubricants, moisturisers, hyaluronic acid, or clinician-supervised hormonal treatments are far more likely to work than dietary hacks.
