title: Does eating 100 grams of Lychee help burn belly fat? - THIP Media
claim_text: eating 100 grams of lychee daily helps in burning belly fat effectively
quick_take: A social media post suggests that eating 100 grams of lychee daily can help burn belly fat. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: The straightforward answer is no. Lychee, like most fruits, contains vitamins, minerals, fibre, and antioxidants that contribute to good health, but it does not contain any special ingredients that 'burn' fat directly. The idea of 'fat-burning foods' is popular in diet culture, but it is largely a myth. Fat loss occurs when your body uses stored fat as energy because it's in a calorie deficit, meaning you consume fewer calories than you burn. This process cannot be triggered or targeted by any specific food, including lychee. You cannot selectively lose fat from your belly by eating any one fruit. Scientific research confirms that fat loss happens systemically, not spot-reduced in a particular area. Lychee provides nutrition and energy, but it does not contain compounds that target fat cells or increase the rate of fat breakdown in the belly region. For metabolism: The short answer is no significant metabolic boost comes from lychee consumption. Metabolism refers to the chemical processes in your body that convert food into energy. Some foods like green tea or chili peppers have mild metabolism-boosting effects due to their caffeine or capsaicin content, but lychee lacks these components. Lychee is mostly water, carbohydrates (mainly natural sugars like fructose), and small amounts of fibre. While sugars in lychee give quick energy, they do not increase your metabolic rate enough to cause fat loss. The body's metabolic rate depends on many factors like muscle mass, age, genetics, and physical activity levels; no fruit alone will speed it up dramatically. Regarding the 100 gram amount: Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said, 'The quantity of lychee you eat doesn't play a meaningful role in fat loss. One hundred grams of fresh lychee typically provides about 60 to 70 calories and around 15 grams of natural sugar. This makes it a healthy and low-calorie snack option compared to processed sweets. But eating 100 grams of lychee every day won't lead to fat loss by itself.' Hakim Bharmal, a Master Trainer and Contest Prep Coach from Maharashtra, said 'Weight loss depends on your total calorie intake versus your total calorie expenditure throughout the day. Simply adding lychee without reducing calories elsewhere or increasing activity could even add unwanted calories. So, it's not about the amount of lychee, but your overall calorie balance and diet quality that matter.' Regarding indirect weight management: Yes, eating only lychees and nothing else might result in weight loss, but that's simply due to extreme restriction of overall food intake. Such weight loss would occur through starvation, not in a healthy or sustainable way. This is definitely not a method we recommend or support. Fruits like lychee and chikoo are seasonal delicacies and should be enjoyed in moderation for their flavour not pursued for specific health benefits. However, lychee's fibre content is moderate compared to other fruits like apples, pears, or berries, so its impact on fullness and weight management will be modest. Including lychee as part of a balanced diet rich in fibre, vegetables, lean proteins, and whole grains can contribute to healthier eating habits, but it's not a silver bullet for belly fat loss. Scientific evidence: Most scientific studies on lychee focus on its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and nutritional benefits rather than direct fat-burning effects. For instance, a study published in the Brazilian Archives of Biology and Technology investigated the effects of lychee flour supplementation in rats fed a high-calorie diet. The study observed a reduction in visceral fat and certain metabolic improvements in the rats given lychee flour. This suggests lychee's bioactive compounds might support metabolic health and fat metabolism in animal models. However, it's crucial to understand that this research used lychee flour (a processed form of lychee) and involved rats, not humans eating fresh lychee fruit. Animal studies don't always translate directly to humans because of physiological differences. Plus, consuming lychee flour is very different from eating fresh lychee fruit, especially in terms of quantity and concentration of bioactive compounds. Currently, there is no robust clinical evidence in humans proving that eating fresh lychee, whether 100 grams or more, results in fat loss or specifically targets belly fat.

title: Fact Check: Does eating 2 slices of onions a day treat depression? - THIP Media
claim_text: Eating 2 onions daily helps increase immunity, treat depression, fight the common cold and flu being a potent natural antibiotic, and it helps you sleep better!
quick_take: A social media post claims that along with various benefits of daily consumption of onions, it can also be used to treat depression. We fact-checked and found that the claim lacks credible scientific evidence and, thus, is Mostly False until proven otherwise.
doctor_explanation: Depression (major depressive disorder) is a common and serious medical illness that negatively affects how you feel, the way you think and how you act. It can lead to a variety of physical and emotional problems by causing a persistent feeling of sadness and loss of interest in everything. According to WHO, Depression affects about an estimated 3.8% of the population, including 5.0% among adults and 5.7% among adults older than 60 years. Depression, even if diagnosed at a later stage, can be treated. The treatment modalities of depression include medications (antidepressants), psychotherapy (such as one-to-one counselling) and cognitive behavioural therapy, or a combination of these two. If in case, the symptoms do not reduce with these options, Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT) and other brain stimulation therapies are explored. No compelling research can give scientific proof of onions working as a treatment for depression. Onions are definitely good for health as they are proven to have anti-inflammatory properties and antioxidant properties due to the presence of Vitamin E. Furthermore, onions can also help reduce atherosclerosis and cardiovascular disease, eye diseases and the risk of thrombosis, but their benefit in treating depression is not yet proven. Although research done on rats suggest that onion exerted antidepressant-like activity when administered daily in rats, neither such study was done on humans, nor did the study claim that similar effects will definitely be seen in humans. People who suffer from depression must seek out evidence-based interventions as a treatment modality. Psychiatrist Dr. Binda Singh states: 'No. Depression is a disease and needs proper treatment. It can happen due to a variety of reasons, such as situational, trauma, physical health issues, etc. Normally eating onions and other fruits and vegetables help in getting rid of inflammation. They are good antioxidants hence help in keeping your body and brain healthy, and do reduce stress but eating these things cannot cure acute depression or anxiety. No scientific studies prove that consuming two slices of onion a day will cure depression. It needs intervention, which might include medication, counselling, positive thoughts, communication, etc. Unfortunately, the dietary cure for depression has no scientific evidence. In conclusion, the consumption of onion may be beneficial for health, but it can't be used as a therapeutic measure to treat depression.'

title: Does eating almonds reverse the greying of hair - THIP Media
claim_text: Consuming almonds has the natural ability to transform grey hair into black
quick_take: A social media post suggests that consuming almonds can naturally reverse the greying of hair to black. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that eating almonds can reverse greying of hair. Greying of hair is primarily attributed to natural ageing and genetic factors that lead to a reduction in melanin production. Melanin is the pigment responsible for hair colour. According to Dr. Swati Watwani, a Dermatologist and Medical Director at Persianlily Clinic, "Grey hair typically begins in the late 40s to early 50s, while premature greying can start in one's 20s. Slowing down premature greying involves identifying its cause and providing appropriate treatment. However, complete reversal of grey hair is not possible." According to Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA), "Greying of hair is a natural part of aging influenced by genetics and environmental factors. Age-related or genetically determined greying cannot be reversed. However, greying caused by environmental and lifestyle factors can be slowed down with appropriate measures." Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition said, "Consuming foods rich in protein, folic acid, iron, Vitamin D, Vitamin B12, Vitamin E, Copper, and Selenium is crucial for maintaining healthy hair and skin, including a healthy scalp. Almonds are particularly beneficial and should be included in your daily diet. However, these dietary changes are most effective when adopted consistently over a long period. If started after hair greying has already occurred, they may not reverse the hair to its original colour of black." While almonds are nutritious and contain beneficial nutrients such as vitamin E, biotin, and essential fatty acids which are important for overall hair health, these nutrients may support hair strength, shine, and growth, but they do not specifically target melanin production or reverse greying. Factors contributing to grey hair include genetics, ageing, stress and oxidative stress, nutritional deficiencies (particularly B vitamins like B12 and folate), and medical conditions such as autoimmune diseases and thyroid disorders.

title: Fact Check: Does eating apples fight asthma?
claim_text: Apple 'Help fight asthma' (as claimed in a Twitter post listing benefits of apples)
quick_take: A social media post claims eating apples helps fight asthma. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Half True.
doctor_explanation: Asthma is a disease of the respiratory tract that narrows and swells the airway with extra mucus. Such a condition makes breathing difficult supported by a wheezing sound when people air out. Besides this, people with the condition also suffer from excessive coughing and shortness of breath. We asked Pulmonologist Dr Muhammed Anas, NMC HealthCare, if asthma can be cured completely. To this, he said "It is highly unlikely that asthma can be cured completely. It is a lifelong disease which can only be controlled with medicines and a healthy lifestyle. Once fully controlled, people can stop medicines and continue to control asthma with lifestyle changes. But anytime in life if people get exposed to their triggers again, asthma can come back for which medicines will be required again. Triggering factors can be allergens like climate change or pollution and others". It does not seem so. The scant evidence only suggests eating apples fight asthma but does not confirm the same. While some papers suggested apple juice is better for asthma, others rejected this claim. We further researched the chemical composition of apples that might make them a favourable dietary option against asthma. As a result, we found a study that shows apples have phytochemicals like flavonoids and antioxidants that may reduce the symptoms of asthma. We researched more to find a paper that shows flavonoids have anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-allergic and immune-modulating effects. Another paper showed antioxidants can affect the development of asthma and impairment of pulmonary function. Both the studies seem to suggest that eating apples may reduce the severity of symptoms to make it easy for people to deal with asthma. However, these studies do not provide confirmatory outcomes. Also, we do not know how many apples we need to eat to meet the exact dosage of phytochemicals and antioxidants required to fight against asthma. Dt. Kamna Tank says "Fruits and vegetables can be helpful against asthma because the ingredients have nutrients, antioxidant, anti-allergic and anti-inflammatory properties. Adding fruits and vegetables to your diet can reduce inflammation and 'Free Radicals' that stop cell damage. However, eating apples or any kind of fruit cannot cure asthma completely but may reduce the risk". We further asked Dr Anas to explain if diet can cure asthma. To this, he said "It is unlikely that diet can cure asthma. As people can be allergic to certain food items, it is better to know your food triggers and avoid them completely. It is crucial to not believe that diet can cure asthma as it can delay the required line of treatment. In India, asthma is treated as per the global GINA guidelines."

title: Does eating as much watermelon as you can help with fat loss?
claim_text: Eating as much watermelon as you can helps in fat loss
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating as much watermelon helps in fat loss. We fact checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Watermelon is a hydrating fruit with a low calorie content. It is rich in vitamins A and C, as well as antioxidants like lycopene, which may help protect against certain diseases. However, watermelon has a high glycemic index (GI), meaning it can cause a rapid increase in blood sugar levels. Despite this, its glycemic load (GL), which takes into account both the quantity and quality of carbohydrates in a serving of food, is relatively low due to its high water and fibre content. This means that while watermelon may cause a spike in blood sugar, its overall impact on blood sugar levels is moderate. Consuming too much watermelon can potentially lead to adverse effects due to its high water content and natural sugars. Over consumption may cause digestive discomfort such as bloating, gas, and diarrhoea, especially in individuals with sensitive stomachs or those prone to gastrointestinal issues. Additionally, excessive intake of watermelon can contribute to an imbalance in electrolytes, particularly if consumed in large quantities without adequate hydration from other sources. Therefore, moderation is key when incorporating watermelon into your diet. Furthermore, while watermelon is low in calories and can be part of a healthy diet, consuming it in excess without considering overall calorie intake and physical activity levels may contribute to weight gain. Despite its high water content, watermelon still contains natural sugars, which can add up in calories if consumed excessively. As with any food, portion control and moderation are important factors to consider for weight management. Dr. Swati Dave (Ph.D. in Food and Nutrition) said: "Watermelon is a thirst-quenching fruit with few macronutrients, including protein and fat. Also, it contains nutrients such as lycopene, citrulline, and vitamins A, C. Extreme, restricted diets and cleanses are not advisable during the summer heat. It's not healthy to eat as much watermelon as you can without limits. Large amounts of watermelon might cause diarrhea in many cases. It is a high-GI fruit and is not recommended for diabetics." Dr. Dave further warns about the dangers of weight loss misinformation. She likens it to a virus spreading rapidly on the internet, with captivating captions promising quick fixes and false claims. Deceptive information sets unrealistic expectations, leading people to adopt ineffective or harmful practices that hinder sustainable and healthy weight loss. Dr. Dave emphasises the importance of critically evaluating online content, seeking evidence-based advice, and avoiding misleading trends lacking scientific support. Dietician Harita highlights that there's no one-size-fits-all approach to weight loss and points out common weight loss misconceptions.

Each vegetable/fruit contains a unique combination of vitamins, minerals, and phytonutrients essential for overall health. Consuming a variety ensures a broader spectrum of nutrients, supporting various bodily functions and promoting optimal health. Additionally, repetitive consumption might lead to flavour fatigue, reducing overall enjoyment of meals. Rotation of vegetables/fruits helps maintain interest, ensures adequate nutrient intake, and supports a balanced diet. title: Does eating bananas improve mood swings? - THIP Media
claim_text: Bananas improve mood swings because they increase serotonin and instantly lift your mood.
quick_take: A social media post created confusion by displaying an image of a banana while the caption discussed cucumber in the photo and claimed they help with mood swings. After reviewing the available scientific evidence, we found that the claim was misleading and false.
doctor_explanation:
Dr Pubali Chaudhuri, MBBS, MD (Psychiatry), Consultant Neuro-Psychiatrist based in Kolkata, West Bengal, explains that serotonin and melatonin are naturally produced brain chemicals derived from the amino acid tryptophan. Melatonin plays a key role in regulating healthy, restorative sleep, particularly improving sleep quality and depth. Serotonin, often referred to as the happiness hormone, contributes to sleep by promoting a sense of calm and emotional stability. Its role becomes especially significant in conditions such as anxiety disorders and depression, where lower serotonin levels are commonly linked to disturbed or poor-quality sleep.

Bananas contain small amounts of tryptophan, an amino acid used to make serotonin, often called the feel-good chemical. This has led to the assumption that eating bananas raises serotonin levels in the brain. However, the body does not work in such a simple way. Serotonin in the brain is produced through a tightly regulated process. Tryptophan from food must first compete with other amino acids to cross into the brain. The amount found in a single banana is relatively modest. Eating one does not create a dramatic or immediate rise in brain serotonin. Moreover, most serotonin in the body is actually produced in the gut, where it regulates digestion rather than mood. So while bananas contain nutrients involved in serotonin production, they do not act like a natural antidepressant or instant mood stabiliser.

Can bananas reduce irritability caused by blood sugar dips? In certain situations, bananas may help, but not in the way many people assume. Mood swings are sometimes linked to changes in blood glucose levels. When someone skips meals or eats foods high in sugar but low in fibre or protein, blood sugar can spike quickly and then crash. That sudden drop may leave a person feeling tired, shaky, or unusually irritable. Bananas provide natural carbohydrates along with fibre, which helps slow digestion slightly. When eaten as a snack, especially when combined with protein or healthy fats such as yoghurt or a small handful of nuts, they can support steadier energy release. More stable energy can mean fewer mood dips caused by sudden sugar crashes. However, this benefit relates to energy regulation rather than direct changes in brain chemistry. If mood swings stem from hormonal fluctuations, ongoing stress, poor sleep, or underlying mental health conditions, eating a banana will not address the underlying cause. Research also notes that serotonin found in bananas cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. This means it cannot directly enter the brain to elevate mood. So while bananas contain nutrients linked to neurotransmitter production, they do not function as instant mood enhancers.

Vitamin B6 in bananas: Unlikely on its own. Bananas are a source of vitamin B6, a nutrient involved in the production of neurotransmitters such as serotonin and dopamine. Vitamin B6 deficiency can contribute to low mood, but true deficiency is uncommon in people who eat a varied diet. A medium banana provides roughly 20-25% of the daily recommended intake of vitamin B6. While that contributes to overall nutritional adequacy, there is no strong evidence that adding one banana per day significantly reduces mood swings in individuals who are not deficient.

Is there scientific evidence that bananas improve mood swings? The evidence is limited and not conclusive. Some observational studies suggest that higher fruit consumption is associated with better mental wellbeing. However, such studies cannot prove that bananas themselves improve mood. People who eat more fruit often have healthier overall lifestyles, including better sleep, more physical activity, and lower intake of ultra-processed foods. There are small studies exploring fruit intake and depressive symptoms, but these are not robust enough to confirm that bananas specifically reduce mood swings. At present, the research does not support a clear cause-and-effect relationship.

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, Mumbai, explains that although banana tea is often believed to help with mood swings, there is limited scientific evidence to strongly support this claim. Instead, she advises choosing whole bananas. Whole bananas provide potassium, magnesium, and tryptophan nutrients that may support relaxation to some extent and contribute to overall nutritional balance, rather than acting as a direct or powerful mood remedy.

So bananas do not directly cure or prevent mood swings. They do not dramatically increase serotonin in the brain, nor do they function as a natural mood stabiliser. However, they can help maintain steady energy levels and contribute useful nutrients as part of a balanced diet. If mood swings are frequent, severe, or disruptive, they should not be self-treated with dietary fixes alone. A healthcare professional can help explore potential causes and provide appropriate support.

title: Fact Check: Does eating breakfast after 9 am pose the risk of diabetes?
claim_text: According to a study mentioned in a blog on Mail Online, the assertion is that having breakfast after 9 am and consuming meals later in the day may have the potential to raise the likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes.
quick_take: According to a blog, a recent study indicated that having breakfast after 9 am might elevate the risk of diabetes. Our fact-checking process revealed that this claim is partially accurate, earning a rating of Half true.
doctor_explanation: The claim is partially accurate. While there is some evidence linking breakfast timing to diabetes risk, the relationship is nuanced and not absolute. What is the the circadian clock? The body's biological clock, also known as the circadian clock, is an internal timekeeping system that regulates various daily activities, including sleep and eating. These internal clocks are sensitive to external signals like light and food. When our circadian clocks are out of sync with our surroundings, it can have negative effects on our health. For instance, eating when our body expects us to sleep can disrupt our metabolism. However, maintaining a consistent schedule for eating and fasting can help maintain the health of our biological clocks and improve our metabolism. This scientific understanding is providing us with new insights into the optimal times for meals to promote our overall health. Does the circadian clock impact blood sugar levels? Yes, in 2021 a study was conducted where they kept healthy volunteers awake when they'd normally be asleep. At the same time, they gave them a steady supply of sugar. This helped them separate the body's internal clock from the usual ups and downs of blood sugar. Findings showed that the internal body clock has a big role in how blood sugar behaves. In the constant sugar infusion method, people had high blood sugar and insulin levels when they'd normally be sleeping. This suggests that the body clock affects how blood sugar works. Is it true that breakfast after 9 am increases the diabetes risk? The answer is uncertain, because there are many mixed studies. A 2022 study said people who had breakfast after 9 AM had a lower risk of diabetes compared to those who ate between 7-9 AM. However, this association was more significant for individuals with high blood sugar levels at the beginning of the study and not as clear for those with normal blood sugar levels. Breakfast habits alone may not determine diabetes risk, as other factors also play a role. In a 2023 study it was written that individuals who had their breakfast between 8 AM and 9 AM demonstrated the best diabetes control, with 28.5% classified as having normal control and a significant 54.8% showing good control. In contrast, those who delayed breakfast until between 9 AM and 10 AM exhibited poorer diabetes control, with only 3.4% categorised as having normal control and nearly half, at 49.7%, falling into the poor control category. The most concerning trend emerged when breakfast was postponed until between 10 AM and 11 AM, as none had normal diabetes control, and a staggering 92.7% had poor control of diabetes. Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, City Pathology Laboratory, Panchmahal, Gujarat, said: "The timing of your breakfast, such as eating it after 9 am, doesn't inherently cause a rise in blood sugar levels. Instead, it's primarily influenced by the composition of your breakfast, portion size, and individual metabolic factors. Foods with a high glycemic index, like sugary cereals or pastries, can lead to rapid blood sugar spikes regardless of the time you consume them. To manage blood sugar levels, it's advisable to opt for lower GI foods, control portion sizes, and consider your overall diet. Keep in mind that individuals vary in their response to meals and meal timing due to factors like genetics and insulin sensitivity. Engaging in physical activity after breakfast can also help regulate blood sugar levels, and consistency in meal timing is beneficial for overall stability."

title: Fact Check: Does eating bugs cause cancer or lung disease?
claim_text: A video on Facebook claims that eating bugs causes cancer or lung disease, based on research papers about parasites in edible insects and chitin. The video also claimed that 'the powerful 0.1% want us lower castes to eat bugs, while they save the best for themselves' because 'they want us all to get sick and die'.
quick_take: A video on social media claims that eating bugs cause cancer or lung disease. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: The research paper referred to in the video itself does not confirm the claim. From the methodology section of the research paper, researchers took samples of insects from 300 farms and found disease-causing parasites in 91 farms. However, it is not clear enough whether eating insects from these farms will cause disease in humans. Also, it is not clear whether any clinical testing has been done to identify the number of parasites that can cause disease in humans. This research paper also talks about unhygienic practices including feeding insects moldy food and feces within these farms. It is not clear from these research papers whether such practices are followed within the sample farms or other farms as well. Also, we do not know whether parasites are present within the animal feed. Besides this, we also researched and found the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website which informs that meat may contain disease-causing parasites. However, a document also informs that the number of parasites in meat can be reduced with preventative farming practices. In context with chitin, the claim is partially incorrect. The claimed video informs that 'we cannot digest it (chitin), and it is known to cause several health issues with humans who consume it, including respiratory issues and the accelerated growth of cancer cells.' Chitin is a fibrous material present in the exoskeleton of arthropods and the cell walls of fungi. Evidence suggests that humans cannot digest chitin, however, it is not an issue. The undigested food passes through the intestine and excretes from the stool. On the contrary, a research paper informs that increasing fiber consumption is considered good for health. We also went through the research paper referred to in the claimed video and found that it is an exploratory study that analyzed the role of chitinase, an enzyme that breaks down chitin, in generating a series of harmful and disease-causing responses within the body. This research paper nowhere associates the consumption of chitin with inflammation or cancer and lung disease. Besides this, we researched and found no evidence that has discussed the health impacts of chitin in humans. In context with the claim about the powerful 0.1% wanting lower castes to get sick and die, it is not clear to whom the statement is referred. Many international organizations have put their stance forward on this topic. From this evidence, it is clear that the possibility of parasites causing illness among humans cannot be negated completely. Hence, we need more studies to hold the claim true.

title: Fact Check: Does eating Chicken help you beat Corona?
claim_text: Eat Chicken, Beat Corona
quick_take: A lot of Facebook posts have put up different Ad creatives that read, "Eat Chicken, Beat Corona". We have done a Fact Check of the same and found that the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: While Chicken meat has important nutrients, they cannot be building our immunity alone. Medical websites have listed chicken(and poultry) as immunity-boosting foods. United States health department website NIH lists poultry products as a primary source of Vitamin B6. Kajal Gupta, Dietitian and Nutritionist, says, "Chickens are lean meat i.e. high source of protein, low in fat. This makes them a good nutrient to be added to the diet as proteins are building blocks to our immunity." The health website of Harvard mentions the following about Chicken, "A warm bowl of chicken soup is a popular go-to when we're feeling under the weather. Is there scientific evidence that it aids in healing? The short answer is no; there aren't any clinical trials that show that chicken soup speeds healing any more than other foods. But when breaking down its ingredients, it does appear a worthwhile remedy to try." No. Immunity is a sum total of multiple functions in our body. As per the website of CDC, "Immunity to a disease is achieved through the presence of antibodies to that disease in a person's system." While protein in Chicken can surely help in building immunity powers, it cannot singularly prevent a infectious disease like COVID-19. Kajal Gupta, Dietitian and Nutritionist say, "There is no alternative to eating healthy. That is an important step towards building a healthy body. But, a single substance diet alone cannot build immunity against COVID-19. It's necessary to take all the recommended precautions along with eating a variety of fruits, vegetables, and proteins." We could track the source of the slogan "Eat Chicken, Beat Corona" to an advertisement by the Karnataka Poultry Farmers and Breeders Association and Vencobb — part of All India Poultry Development and Services Private Limited. The advertisement apparently seemed like a response to rumor that "eating chicken and eggs during the pandemic is not safe". However, the slogan initially chosen to educate the audience, went wrong when it was used out of context by many other companies. The original advertisement was also condemned by the Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) and the advertisement was asked to be taken down. This reportedly happened after PETA India lodged a complaint against the Advertisement.

title: Fact Check: Does eating dates enhance memory?
claim_text: Dates can enhance memory
quick_take: A social media post talks about benefits of eating claiming that dates can enhance memory. We fact checked and found this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
The claim that dates can enhance memory has some basis in scientific evidence but remains limited. Dates are rich in various nutrients, including carbohydrates (mainly sugars like glucose and fructose), fibre, vitamins (such as vitamin B6 and vitamin K), and minerals (such as potassium, magnesium, copper, and manganese). They also contain small amounts of protein and fat and are a good source of antioxidants, including flavonoids, carotenoids, and phenolic acid.

While diet can impact memory - with a well-balanced diet full of antioxidants, omega-3 fatty acids, vitamins B6, B12, and folate promoting brain health and cognitive performance - the direct evidence linking dates to memory enhancement remains limited. 

In 2018, research suggested that dates, containing simple sugars like glucose and fructose, might temporarily boost short-term memory by providing readily available energy to the brain. Studies on mice fed date diets showed improved memory and learning abilities. Experiments on elementary school students consuming dates indicated significant post-test score differences compared to control groups. Studies in 2015 found that long-term consumption of date fruits improved memory, learning, and motor coordination in mice with Alzheimer's disease, with antioxidants like ferulic acid potentially responsible for these benefits.

Preliminary research in 2014 on date extracts suggested potential memory improvement in rats. Dates reduced scopolamine-induced amnesia and increased learning and memory performance, possibly due to antioxidant properties. Additionally, dates decreased acetylcholine esterase activity, improving cognitive function.

A 2015 study investigated the impact of long-term dietary supplementation with date fruit on spatial memory, learning ability, and anxiety in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Results showed significant improvements in learning and memory deficits, motor coordination, and reduced anxiety levels in mice receiving date fruit supplementation.

Expert Opinion from Chaitali Bharatiya, M.Sc. Specialized Dietetics in Diabetes and Cardiac Nutrition: 'The claim that dates can boost memory function has some basis in scientific evidence, primarily due to their nutrient content. Dates are rich in antioxidants, vitamins, and minerals that support brain health and cognitive function. title: Fact Check: Does eating egg whites increase the risk of biotin deficiency?
claim_text: It has been observed that eating egg whites may increase the risk of biotin deficiency. Avidin, a protein present in egg whites rubs off biotin from the body, increasing the risk of biotin deficiency, thereby increasing the risk of possible side effects.
quick_take: A few social media posts and a few health articles on different media platforms suggest that it is harmful to eat eggs daily. They claim eggs whites increase the risk of biotin deficiency in the body. We fact-checked and found that the claim is half true. Such posts miss an important context while quoting the research related to this fact.
doctor_explanation: Biotin, also called vitamin B7 or vitamin H, is a water-soluble vitamin that belongs to the B vitamin family. Biotin (Vitamin B7) plays an important role in food metabolism and keeping our endocrine system healthy. A single, large egg contains between 13 and 25 micrograms of biotin. Other dietary sources of biotin (Vitamin B7) include fish, meat, milk, fruits like bananas, and vegetables like sweet potato, cauliflower, broccoli, etc. Avidin is a particular protein that is present in birds, reptiles, and amphibians and is passed on their eggs. The exact role of Avidin is still not known, however, in the human body it is considered to be an antinutrient (a substance that prevents absorption of nutrients). Avidin binds the biotin (Vitamin B7) present in the egg closely and prevents its absorption in the human body. Theoretically, Yes. Avidin binds to biotin and stops its absorption in the body. Worst still, Avidin does not only bind to the biotin in the egg, it also binds biotin from other food sources and prevents them from getting absorbed in our body, thereby creating a risk of biotin deficiency in the body. However, there is a very important context that needs to be mentioned here. Avidin binds biotin in Egg majorly in its raw form. Hence, the risk of biotin deficiency, if any from Avidin, is only to someone who consumes raw eggs (or egg whites). Research has shown that Avidin is denatured and its biotin-binding capabilities are drastically reduced over 75 to 80 degrees centigrade. Another research shows that a complete deactivation of Avidin's biotin-binding ability happens when boiled for over 4 minutes. Also, even though raw egg whites contain Avidin, it is unlikely to cause any major effect like Vitamin deficiency unless a lot of raw eggs are consumed daily for many days. Researchers note, 'Nutritional biotin deficiency is rare' but at the same time warns that 'consumption of raw eggs on a regular basis may cause biotin deficiency.' So, to be at risk of biotin deficiency from eating eggs, you will have to be eating raw eggs daily for a prolonged period of time.

The breast tissue was oestrogen receptor-positive, prompting a discussion about the potential impact of phytoestrogens. Flaxseeds are primarily valued for their high fibre, omega-3 fatty acids, and antioxidant content. Additionally, the size of breasts depends on genetics, body weight, hormonal levels, and life stages, not the consumption of a particular food. title: Does eating one elaichi before sunset really boost hair growth?
claim_text: Having one cardamom (elaichi) with warm water before sunset may provide certain benefits, such as supporting faster hair growth, helping to reduce hair fall, refreshing breath, and possibly strengthening immunity against colds and flu.

doctor_explanation:
CAN ELAICHI ACTUALLY PROMOTE FASTER HAIR GROWTH?
No, not directly. Cardamom (Elaichi) contains nutrients like antioxidants, zinc, and magnesium, which are good for overall health. These elements can support a healthy scalp if included in a balanced diet over time. However, there is no scientific evidence that eating one cardamom pod with hot water will directly speed up hair growth. Hair growth depends on many factors, such as genetics, hormones, diet, and scalp condition. A single cardamom pod does not provide enough nutrients to make a noticeable difference. For example, it has very small amounts of zinc—far less than what your body needs daily for hair health. While cardamom may improve digestion and blood flow, which could help nutrient absorption, it cannot single-handedly lead to faster hair growth. For better results, a diet rich in proteins, vitamins, and minerals is more effective than relying on one spice.

DOES IT REALLY REDUCE HAIR FALL?
No, cardamom on its own is not proven to prevent hair loss. Although cardamom is rich in antioxidants that support overall health, there is currently no solid scientific evidence directly linking its consumption to reduced hair fall. That said, a 2022 study found that Alpinetin (AP), a compound present in cardamom, may promote hair growth by prolonging the active phase of hair follicles and stimulating certain stem cells through Wnt signalling—a process that encourages cell growth and development. In experiments on mice, AP performed better than standard treatments and appeared safe for both human and mouse skin cells. However, these findings still need to be confirmed through human studies.

We spoke to Dr Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic Medicine Consultant in Lucknow, to get his expert take on using cardamom for hair fall. He explains, "Although cardamom does offer certain health benefits thanks to its antioxidant content, there is no scientific proof that it can reduce hair loss. When it comes to maintaining healthy hair, the key lies in following a balanced diet, maintaining proper hair hygiene, and opting for medically proven treatments."

CAN IT HELP GET RID OF BAD BREATH?
Yes, but only for a short time. Cardamom has natural oils, such as cineole, that can kill some bacteria in the mouth. This is why chewing it can make your breath feel fresh temporarily. Studies have shown that these oils have antibacterial effects, which support its use as a quick breath freshener in many cultures. However, this effect does not last long, usually less than an hour. If bad breath continues, it may be due to some foods, dental problems, poor oral hygiene, or stomach issues. Cardamom can mask the odor briefly, but it does not fix the root cause. For lasting relief, proper dental care and a visit to the dentist are necessary.

DOES IT PREVENT COLD AND FLU?
No, it does not. Colds and flu are caused by viruses. Cardamom has antioxidants and slight immune-boosting properties that might help your body in small ways. It can also soothe a sore throat or ease congestion when added to warm drinks. However, no scientific studies prove that eating one cardamom pod with hot water prevents these illnesses. Building strong immunity requires a healthy diet, good sleep, and habits like handwashing or getting vaccinated. Cardamom may support general health as part of a balanced diet, but it is not a substitute for proven methods to avoid colds and flu.

IS TIMING 'BEFORE SUNSET' IMPORTANT?
No, it is not. The idea of eating cardamom before sunset likely comes from traditional beliefs rather than science. Your body processes nutrients the same way at any time of day. There is no evidence that eating cardamom before sunset works better than doing it at another time. What matters is including healthy foods in your diet regularly, not the specific timing of one spice.

THE BOTTOM LINE: Cardamom is a flavorful spice with some health benefits. It contains nutrients that may support digestion, freshen breath for a short time, and contribute to overall wellness when part of a good diet. However, the claim that eating one elaichi with hot water before sunset can boost hair growth, stop hair fall, cure bad breath, and prevent colds and flu is not supported by science.

title: Does eating peacock feathers help conceive a baby? - THIP Media

doctor_explanation: Does eating peacock feathers improve fertility in men or women? No. There is no evidence that eating peacock feathers improves fertility in either men or women. Human fertility is governed by a complex interaction between hormones, reproductive organs, genetics, and overall health. In women, factors such as ovulation, egg quality, uterine health, and hormonal balance play key roles. In men, sperm count, sperm quality, and hormone levels matter most. Peacock feathers do not influence any of these processes. Medical research into fertility consistently focuses on well-studied areas such as nutritional deficiencies, endocrine disorders, age-related changes, stress, body weight, and lifestyle habits. Peacock feathers are not mentioned in any scientific literature related to reproductive health. Dr Thulasi K, BAMS, MD (Ayurveda), Kottakkal Arya Vaidyasala and Punarjani TreatmentCentre says, "The post is just another myth regarding reproductive health. Neither Ayurveda nor any medical science would approve of such myths. Ayurveda views reproduction as a process that involves preparing mind and body of parents for the process through lifestyle modification and treatments that clear the root cause of infertility if any. Even for healthy couple, preconception care helps in improving the general health of parents, quality of sperm and ovum and thus the quality of offspring. Thus such claims are rootless and just try to make use of emotional vulnerability of couple." Is there any scientific or biological basis for this belief? No. There is no scientific or biological mechanism that explains how peacock feathers could enhance fertility. The belief appears to be symbolic rather than biological. In many cultures, peacocks are associated with beauty, abundance, or divine energy, which may lead people to link them emotionally with creation or childbirth. However, symbolism and tradition do not create physiological effects in the human body. Biology relies on measurable chemical reactions, nutrients, hormones, and cellular processes. Peacock feathers do not contain substances that can trigger or support these mechanisms. Can the body digest peacock feathers or absorb anything useful from them? No. Peacock feathers are made primarily of keratin, a tough, fibrous protein that the human digestive system cannot break down effectively. Unlike dietary proteins found in lentils, milk, eggs, or fish, keratin does not provide usable amino acids. This means the body cannot absorb nutrients from feathers or convert them into anything that supports fertility. In simple terms, eating feathers offers no nutritional benefit. They pass through the digestive system without contributing vitamins, minerals, or energy. Are there health risks linked to eating peacock feathers? Yes. Eating peacock feathers can be unsafe. Feathers may carry bacteria, parasites, fungi, or chemical residues from the environment. Grinding feathers into powder does not remove these risks. There is also the possibility of choking, gut irritation, or intestinal blockage, especially if consumed repeatedly. Ingesting non-food items can irritate the digestive tract and may interfere with nutrient absorption, which can negatively affect overall health including reproductive health. Fertility is best supported by balanced nutrition, adequate calorie intake, and key nutrients such as folate, iron, iodine, zinc, selenium, and omega-3 fats. Maintaining a healthy body weight, managing stress, getting enough sleep, and avoiding smoking and excessive alcohol also play important roles. Medical evaluation can identify treatable issues such as thyroid imbalance, PCOS, low sperm count, or vitamin deficiencies. Addressing these factors has real, measurable benefits, unlike unproven remedies. So Eating peacock feathers does not help you conceive a baby. The claim has no scientific foundation, no nutritional value, and carries potential health risks. Fertility is influenced by complex biological processes, not symbolic substances or rituals. When it comes to conception, evidence-based nutrition, lifestyle changes, and appropriate medical guidance remain the safest and most effective path forward.

title: Fact Check: Does eating raw radish improve vision? - THIP Media

doctor_explanation: Can radishes improve vision because of their vitamin content? No, radishes cannot significantly improve eyesight through their vitamin content alone. Radishes are rich in vitamin C, potassium, folate, and small amounts of B vitamins. Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant, which helps protect cells from damage caused by free radicals, including cells in the eyes. However, the vitamins critical for vision are vitamin A and carotenoids like lutein and zeaxanthin. Vitamin A is essential for forming rhodopsin, a pigment in the retina that allows us to see in dim light. Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from harmful blue light and oxidative stress. Radishes contain almost no vitamin A or carotenoids, which means their contribution to directly improving vision is minimal. Eating radishes can support overall health and immunity, but their effect on eyesight is indirect at best and cannot correct refractive errors such as nearsightedness, farsightedness, or astigmatism. Could regular radish consumption enhance night vision or clarity? No, there is no scientific basis for radishes improving night vision or visual clarity. Night vision relies primarily on retinal function and adequate vitamin A intake, which supports rhodopsin production in the eyes. Consuming radishes does not increase rhodopsin levels because they lack vitamin A. Visual clarity also depends on the health of the cornea, lens, retina, and the nervous system, none of which are directly improved by eating radishes. While radishes are hydrating, low in calories, and contain nutrients that support general health, they do not enhance visual acuity or sensitivity to light. Clinical studies and nutrition research consistently recommend foods high in vitamin A, lutein, and zeaxanthin for supporting night vision and eye function, with radishes offering no significant contribution. Dr Naveen Gupta, DNB in Ophthalmology from Delhi, explains, "There's a difference between being 'good for eye health' and 'improving vision.' Many people mix up these two concepts. However, it's incorrect to assume that improving eyesight means reducing the need for glasses. Maintaining eye health involves eating a nutritious diet and leading a healthy lifestyle." Why is it risky to rely on unverified home remedies, and how does critical thinking help in making informed choices? Relying on unverified home remedies for vision issues can be dangerous due to several factors. These remedies may be ineffective, inappropriate, or even harmful. Relying on such treatments might cause individuals to delay proper medical intervention, allowing the underlying condition to worsen unnoticed. Many natural remedies haven't been scientifically tested, making it difficult to assess their safety and effectiveness. The risks associated with unapproved remedies are often subtle or delayed, depending on factors like dosage, age, genetic traits, co-existing health conditions, and concurrent medications. For this reason, it is unwise to use local herbs or unproven treatments for eye-related problems. Dr Aftab Alam, an eye surgeon from Bareilly, points out that while plant-based diets may be beneficial for overall eye health, they don't necessarily improve eyesight. He emphasizes that there's no scientific evidence supporting the idea that untested home remedies can enhance vision. Critical thinking plays a crucial role in helping individuals evaluate health claims. It enables people to assess the quality of the evidence, identify the difference between anecdotal accounts and scientifically controlled studies, and make informed decisions based on facts rather than misconceptions. While home remedies might seem harmless, they lack the rigorous testing needed to ensure their safety and efficacy. Critical thinking allows people to make decisions grounded in evidence, helping them avoid potential health risks. Dr Isha Agarwalla, an ophthalmologist at Drishti Netralaya in Dibrugarh, Assam, clarifies that the treatment for eye health issues depends on the root cause. Vision problems can often be corrected with glasses, contact lenses, or LASIK surgery. However, if cataracts are the cause, surgery is typically needed to restore vision. The key to finding the most effective solution is a proper diagnosis from an eye care specialist, who can guide you to the best treatment for your specific condition. Eating raw radish is healthy, supports overall nutrition, and may provide minor antioxidant benefits, but it does not improve eyesight directly. Claims that radishes can strengthen the eyes, enhance night vision, or prevent vision problems are myths, rooted in folk traditions rather than scientific evidence. Eye health depends on nutrients like vitamin A, lutein, zeaxanthin, and omega-3 fatty acids, which are found in carrots, leafy greens, eggs, and fatty fish. Including radishes in a balanced diet can support your overall health, but relying on them alone for better vision is misleading. For optimal eye health, focus on a varied diet, protect your eyes from UV light, reduce prolonged screen exposure, and schedule regular eye examinations.

title: Fact Check: Does eating rice at night lead to weight gain?
claim_text: Eat less rice at night because it causes weight gain.
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating rice at night can cause weight gain. After fact checking, we found this to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
No, eating rice at night does not directly cause weight gain. Scientific studies show that weight gain is mainly about your total calorie intake versus how much you burn, not the specific time you eat rice. Your body continues to use energy even while you sleep, so calories from rice are not automatically stored as fat just because it's eaten at night. The idea that rice alone causes weight gain is part of the larger rice and weight gain myth. The real issue is eating more calories than your body needs, regardless of the time.

Yes, portion size is the real culprit. Rice is a source of carbohydrates and provides energy. An ideal serving of cooked rice contains about 200 calories. If you eat large portions, especially with high-fat or oily side dishes, your calorie intake can easily exceed what your body needs, leading to weight gain over time. This is why portion control with rice is far more important than the time of day you eat it. Eating moderate portions and balancing rice with protein (like dal, fish, or paneer) and vegetables helps keep your meal healthy and filling.

Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, explains, "Meal timing does play a role in weight management, but portion size has a bigger impact. Eating large amounts of rice, especially with heavy sides, can lead to weight gain, no matter when you eat. Keeping portions moderate and meals balanced is the key."

Rice can influence digestion and sleep, but the effects aren't always negative. Some people may experience bloating or discomfort if they eat large amounts of rice late at night, as digestion slows down in the evening. However, research shows that eating carbs before bedtime, like rice, can improve sleep quality by boosting serotonin (a hormone that helps you relax). Good sleep can even help with weight management the next day by reducing cravings.

Yes, brown or whole grain rice is a better choice for weight management. Brown rice contains more fibre and nutrients than white rice, which helps you feel full for longer and supports healthy digestion. Fibre-rich foods are linked to better weight control. If you prefer white rice, try to keep portions small and pair it with plenty of vegetables and lean protein.

Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition says, "Rice often gets a bad name, but it really depends on how and what you eat with it. Brown rice offers more fibre and nutrients, but the key is balance. Think of your plate as a whole, include colourful vegetables, protein like lentils, paneer or chicken, and keep the rice to a reasonable portion. Even white rice can be part of a healthy diet if the rest of the meal is well-planned. It's not about one ingredient, but the overall pattern of eating."

In summary, the claim that eating rice at night causes weight gain is mostly false. Scientific evidence shows that weight gain depends on overall calorie intake, not the timing of your meals. So, giving up rice may not lead to weight loss if other factors, like portion size and food choices, are not addressed. Eating rice at night won't lead to weight gain unless you consistently consume more calories than your body needs. Focus on portion control, balanced meals, and healthy habits instead of cutting out rice.

title: Does eating rock salt lowers blood pressure? - THIP Media
claim_text: Eating rock salt/kala namak lowers blood pressure
quick_take: A social media post claims that eating rock salt/kala namak lower blood pressure. After fact-checking, it has been determined that this claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: The claim that rock salt lowers blood pressure lacks sufficient scientific evidence. Uncontrolled blood pressure (hypertension) is defined as diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg and/or systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg, and is a major risk factor for heart attack, heart failure, stroke, and other complications. Eating too much salt can make blood pressure go up because salt makes the body hold onto more water, increasing blood volume and messing up the sodium-potassium balance. The recommended daily salt intake is less than 5 grams (2 grams sodium), and processed foods should be avoided. Rock salt (Himalayan salt/halite) from the Khewra Salt Mine in Pakistan is similar to table salt, composed mainly of sodium chloride (95-98% NaCl), with 2-4% polyhalite containing potassium, calcium, magnesium, sulphur, oxygen, and hydrogen, plus trace amounts of fluoride, iodine, and other minerals. Table salt contains 99% NaCl while Himalayan salt contains about 98% NaCl. The answer is uncertain - there is not enough scientific evidence to confirm that eating rock salt or kala namak lowers blood pressure. The primary component of both rock salt and common table salt is sodium chloride, and excessive sodium intake can cause hypertension in some individuals by increasing blood volume and putting strain on the cardiovascular system. A 2022 study showed no significant differences in blood pressure and urinary sodium concentration between Himalayan salt and table salt, though more research is needed. However, another study with 600 participants using Himalayan salt showed significant reductions in blood pressure (systolic decreased by 6-8 mmHg, diastolic by 3-5 mmHg) compared to table salt group (570 participants), with improved cardiac function and heart rate variability. Still, more research including randomized controlled trials is needed to confirm these findings. According to Dietician Kamana Chauhan: 'Rock salt is a known cooling spice in Ayurveda that has digestive and healing properties. A diet high in sodium can cause high blood pressure. Excess sodium can increase water retention in the body. This leads to a higher blood volume and puts more strain on the heart, resulting in elevated blood pressure. The recommended daily sodium intake is 6g. But for individuals with high blood pressure, it is around 3.75g. Rock salt has fewer additives compared to common table salt, as it undergoes minimal processing. This makes rock salt a healthier option, as it does not contain additives like Aluminium silicate, potassium iodate, or caking agents. However, people should still consume it in moderation for optimal health benefits.'

title: Does eating soya bean strengthen the liver? THIP Media

There is no specific time of day that is inherently better for consuming soy to strengthen the liver. Instead, focus on incorporating soy into a balanced and varied diet consistently. Spread soy-based foods throughout the day to ensure a steady intake of its beneficial nutrients. title: Fact Check: Does eating spicy food increase your lifespan?

Another study from the US also found that eating hot red chilli peppers was linked to a 12% lower risk of dying over 19 years. This effect was most noticeable for overall mortality, but not for deaths from heart disease or blood vessel problems. However, more research is needed to confirm these findings. Both the Chinese and US studies suggest that eating spicy foods, like chilli peppers, might lower the risk of death. But the effect is small, and these studies only show a connection, not cause-and-effect. More research is needed to confirm these findings. Spicy food may offer some health benefits, but it's not a standalone solution for longer lifespan. Capsaicin, the active compound in green chillies, has been studied for its potential health benefits including antioxidant properties, anti-inflammatory effects, metabolism boost, and pain relief. However, there have been claims suggesting that green chillies can cure heart attacks and reduce the risk of lung cancer. However, these benefits are not proven. Overconsumption of spicy foods can cause issues for some people. While moderate consumption can be part of a healthy diet, excessive intake may lead to stomach irritation, acid reflux, or digestive issues. Shruti K Bhardwaj, Chief Clinical Nutritionist at Zydus Hospital, Ahmedabad, says, "Yes, eating too much spicy food can be harmful for some people. Longevity is influenced by many factors, including genetics, physical activity, mental health, and a balanced diet. While incorporating spicy foods into your meals can offer some health benefits, they are just one piece of the puzzle. Other dietary habits, such as consuming fresh fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and lean proteins, are just as—if not more—important for overall health and longevity. title: Does eating tamarind candy lower your blood sugar? - THIP Media
claim_text: An Instagram video features a thumbnail showing karela marked with a cross and tamarind marked with a tick. In the video, the speaker claims that eating sour-sweet tamarind candy helped lower her blood sugar so dramatically that her reading dropped to 36 mg/dL.
quick_take: A social media post suggests that tamarind candy lowers blood sugar level. We fact checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: Dr Krutika Ingle, Consultant Diabetologist and Physician, Sugar.fit, Saifee Healthcare, Mumbai said, 'Tamarind candy cannot reduce blood sugar because it contains significant amounts of added sugar, which directly increases glucose levels in the blood.' When you eat tamarind candy, the body does not see 'tamarind' first, it sees carbohydrates. Most tamarind candies are made using tamarind pulp mixed with jaggery, sugar, glucose syrup, or date paste. These ingredients are rapidly digested into glucose, which enters the bloodstream and raises blood sugar levels within minutes. There is no biological pathway through which tamarind candy can actively bring glucose down. Blood sugar reduction requires insulin action, improved insulin sensitivity, delayed carbohydrate absorption, or reduced glucose production by the liver. Tamarind candy does none of these. Dr Rahul Desai, Consultant Diabetologist answered, 'Lowering blood sugar requires physiological mechanisms like insulin response or reduced glucose absorption. Sugar-based candies, regardless of flavour, work in the opposite direction.' Dr Shalin Nagori, Consultant Pathologist and Industrial Physician, said, 'Any food made with added sugar will raise blood glucose. The body responds to the total carbohydrate load, not to traditional beliefs attached to an ingredient.' Dr Durga Priyadarshini, PhD, Nutrition Researcher & Founder, Nutrition Research Hub, Chennai, says, 'People often confuse a natural ingredient with a healthy product. Tamarind candy is still a concentrated sugar source, and its glycaemic impact matters far more than the presence of tamarind.' Regarding karela vs tamarind: Karela has been widely studied for its anti-diabetic properties and contains active compounds such as charantin, vicine, and polypeptide-p, which have insulin-like effects and help improve glucose uptake by cells. Regular consumption of karela, especially as a vegetable or juice, has been shown to help reduce fasting and post-meal blood sugar levels in some people with diabetes. Tamarind, on the other hand, contains fibre and polyphenols that may slightly slow carbohydrate digestion and improve insulin sensitivity. However, it is also naturally high in carbohydrates and sugars, which can raise blood glucose if consumed in large amounts or in processed forms like candies or sweetened drinks. While small quantities of tamarind can be included in a balanced diabetic diet for flavour, it should not be relied on for blood sugar control. Overall, karela remains the more effective and safer choice. The claim mixes tradition with half-truths. Tamarind has a long history in traditional diets, and traditional use is often mistaken for medical proof. Sugar behaves like sugar in the body, regardless of cultural context. Sour does not mean sugar-free, and candy, no matter the ingredient, is still candy. Real blood sugar management comes from balanced meals, medical guidance, and evidence-based nutrition, not viral ticks and crosses.

title: Does eating turmeric, onion, and banana cure arthritis in 3 days?
claim_text: A Pinterest account uploaded a video demonstrating a recipe that involves blending turmeric, banana, and onion into a drink, falsely claiming that it can cure joint pain and arthritis in 3 days.
quick_take: A social media post claims that consuming banana, onion and turmeric can cure arthritis in 3 days. We did the fact check to term this claim as false.
doctor_explanation: Arthritis cannot be cured in three days. Arthritis is a chronic condition that affects the joints, often causing pain, stiffness, and inflammation. There are over 100 types of arthritis, with osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis being the most common. Currently, no cure exists for arthritis. Treatments aim to manage symptoms, slow progression, and improve quality of life. Even potent medical interventions take weeks or months to show significant improvements. The idea that three common foods can completely cure arthritis in just three days contradicts everything known about joint diseases and their treatment. Turmeric contains curcumin, a compound with anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. Some studies suggest that curcumin can help reduce inflammation in arthritis patients, but these effects are neither immediate nor curative. Moreover, curcumin has poor bioavailability, meaning the body struggles to absorb it unless consumed with black pepper or a fat source like oil or ghee. Even with optimal absorption, curcumin must be consumed consistently over weeks or months before any noticeable improvement occurs. While turmeric may be a helpful dietary addition for arthritis patients, it is not a substitute for proven medical treatments. Onions contain quercetin, a flavonoid with anti-inflammatory properties. Some studies suggest quercetin may help reduce inflammation, but this does not equate to joint repair or arthritis cure. Arthritis-related joint damage, particularly in osteoarthritis, involves cartilage breakdown, a process that cannot be reversed simply by eating onions. Joint repair requires medical interventions such as physical therapy, weight management, and in severe cases, joint replacement surgery. Bananas are rich in potassium, vitamin B6, and fibre, all of which support general health. Some evidence suggests that potassium plays a role in reducing inflammation, but this effect is mild compared to pharmaceutical anti-inflammatory treatments. While a diet rich in fruits and vegetables can help manage inflammation over time, no single food—including bananas—can eliminate arthritis-related inflammation in a matter of days. Additionally, some arthritis patients with conditions like gout must monitor their banana intake due to its fructose content, which can contribute to uric acid buildup. Dr Almas Fatma, MBBS, Diploma in Family Medicine, PG in Digital Health, and a General Physician from Navi Mumbai, shared her insights on this claim. She clarifies, "Arthritis has no definitive cure. It is a condition characterised by joint inflammation and damage, which cannot be reversed. While turmeric, onion, and banana each have some anti-inflammatory properties, they do not have the ability to repair joint tissues or halt the progression of arthritis. Proper management requires a combination of medical treatments, physiotherapy, and lifestyle changes. Relying solely on this unusual combination could significantly delay appropriate medical care." Diet alone cannot cure arthritis, but it can help manage symptoms. A balanced diet plays an essential role in arthritis management. Anti-inflammatory foods such as fatty fish, nuts, seeds, leafy greens, and berries can help reduce inflammation, while processed foods and excessive sugar may worsen symptoms. However, diet alone cannot cure arthritis. Effective arthritis management typically includes a combination of medication, physical activity, weight control, and sometimes surgical interventions. Misleading claims that diet alone can cure arthritis may prevent individuals from seeking proper medical care, worsening their condition over time.

title: Fact Check: Does eating vitamin D protect you from Covid infection?
claim_text: A YouTube video claims that vitamin D supplements can reduce the risk of admission to intensive care during the coronavirus pandemic.
verdict_original: Mostly False (as shown in the rating image: mostly-false.png)
quick_take: A video on social media claims eating vitamin D can reduce the risk of Covid infection. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: There is currently limited evidence to suggest that vitamin D supplementation may help protect against severe outcomes of COVID-19. Vitamin D is essential for overall health, and a deficiency can lead to the risk of several health problems, including Covid infection. However, it is not a cure for COVID-19 and should not be relied on as a sole means of protection against the virus. It is important to note that while some studies have shown an association between low vitamin D levels and an increased risk of severe COVID-19, more research is needed to determine a cause-and-effect relationship. Even the research paper titled 'Protective Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on COVID-19-Related Intensive Care Hospitalization and Mortality: Definitive Evidence from Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis' as talked about in the YouTube video only speculates about the protective role of vitamin D against Covid infection. Nutritionist Kamna Chauhan adds, "Eating vitamin D will not completely protect you from covid infection but it may reduce the complication and prevent death in those who are infected. Vitamin D is a fat soluble vitamin which is produced by exposure to sunlight. Ultraviolet B rays in sun activate protein in skin called 7-dehydrocholesterol which then metabolize to active form of vitamin D. Vitamin plays an important role in promoting immune response. It has both anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory properties. Besides this, it is also known to enhance function of immune cells, including T-cells and macrophages." Dr Kashyap Dakshini, General Physician practicing in Mumbai, confirms, "There have been conclusive reports of various meta-analyses and trial sequential analysis proving that bolus supplementation of Vitamin D can reduce the severity of COVID-19 infection. Its consumption can reduce ICU stay and mortality in elderly patients." Even if vitamin D might have a curative effect against COVID infection, more research on optimal dose acceptable for human consumption is needed.

title: Fact check: Does erythrosine cause cancer?
claim_text: Watermelon injected with artificial colour and chemicals causes cancer
quick_take: Several social media posts claim that watermelons sold nowadays are injected with artificial colors and chemicals, suggesting that these dye erythrosine cause cancer. We fact checked and found the claim to behalf true.
doctor_explanation: Erythrosine, also known as Red No. 3, is a synthetic red dye commonly used in various food, pharmaceuticals, and cosmetics. Chemically, it belongs to the xanthene class of dyes. Its approval is based on its perceived safety for human consumption in regulated amounts. However, concerns have been raised about its potential adverse effects, which may affect physiological processes such as those related to the pituitary gland and spermatogenesis. While erythrosine's genotoxic and mutagenic properties remain inconclusive, further research is warranted. The link between erythrosine and cancer is still a topic of debate and ongoing research. Some studies have suggested association between erythrosine and cancer development, while others have not found conclusive evidence. In 2015 a study looked at how erythrosine in tablets and food, affects liver health (liver cancer in rats). They found that erythrosine cause cancer and also affected various markers of liver health. It also altered the levels of antioxidant enzymes in the liver. Regarding human consumption, a daily intake of 0.1 mg per kilogram of body weight is safe, but its use has been linked with allergic reactions. Some in vitro studies suggest genotoxicity, in vivo studies show contradictory results. In a 1990 study, rats fed a diet containing 4% erythrosine for 30 months showed more growths in their thyroid glands. Eating erythrosine led to higher levels of thyroid hormones T4 and T3 in their blood, along with an increased response of the pituitary gland to TRH, a hormone that stimulates TSH production. This effect was attributed to reduced levels of the enzyme 5'-deiodinase in the liver, which converts T4 to T3. In a 2011 study, experts found that Erythrosine can cause thyroid tumours in rats, but it's because of how it affects the thyroid, not because it directly damages genes. They think these effects might not be very relevant to humans. Even at high consumption levels, people are still below the safe limit. Botanist Nidhi Singh supports the point by saying, "While not all watermelons have erythrosine dye, it's crucial to continue enjoying them during the season. Remember, this dye is also observed in many other foods we eat. Even if some fruits and veggies have pesticides, the health benefits outweigh the risks. To avoid chemical-treated fruits, watch for signs like powdery residue, overly bright red insides, and any holes or cracks." Red watermelons are safe to eat and are a nutritious and refreshing fruit that provides hydration, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. The red color of watermelon flesh comes from the presence of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant known for its potential health benefits, including supporting heart health and protecting against certain types of cancer.

title: Does eucalyptus oil work as a cure for hallucinations and autism?
claim_text: Inhaling concentrated eucalyptus oil can reduce visual hallucinations and reverse autism symptoms, allowing autistic children to understand emotions better and communicate.
quick_take: In a Facebook post, it was suggested that eucalyptus oil could be used to treat visual hallucinations and autism. We verified the claim's accuracy, and our analysis revealed that the claim is Mostly False.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Abhishek Juneja, Neurologist, was consulted regarding the use of essential oil therapy for autism and hallucinations. He advised against using essential oils, despite the fact that some of them have a calming and anxiety-relieving effect. He said, "They are being evaluated as an additive therapy for the treatment of behavioral and psychological symptoms in dementia patients. There is, however, still no conclusive evidence to support their efficacy in treating neuro-developmental or degenerative disorders." The fact-check also examined whether Dr. Mark Huber (who appears in the video) actually exists - a reverse image search failed to turn up any such neurologist, and no hospital employing a neurologist with that name could be found. The article explains that hallucinations are defined as "the intimate belief of actually perceiving a sensation for which there is no existing object" - one of the main symptoms of schizophrenia. Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by difficulties with social interaction, limited interests, and repetitive behaviors. While people with ASD may experience auditory hallucinations, there is no evidence eucalyptus oil can treat these conditions. Regarding eucalyptus oil composition: flavonoids, alkaloids, tannins, and prostanoids appear to be present in significant quantities, and 1,8-cineole has demonstrated efficacy in treating inflammatory airway diseases like asthma and COPD. However, no significant evidence supports its use in treating autism or psychosis. The article emphasizes that autism is primarily brought on before and may even occur during childbirth - pregnant women must avoid lead, tin, thallium-contaminated food, thalidomide, alcohol, tobacco, anticonvulsants, and polluted air. Antipsychotics work best for hallucinations associated with functional or organic psychosis, and hallucinations in schizophrenia have been suggested to be treated with repetitive TMS (rTMS), along with coping mechanisms, psychoeducation, and cognitive behavior therapy. While essential oils have varying levels of antimicrobial activity, antiviral, nematicidal, antifungal, insecticidal, and antioxidant properties, there is no evidence that aromatherapy is an effective cure for any psychotic or neurodevelopmental illness - it has only been mentioned as a possible therapeutic support strategy. The claim that autism can be reversed is not true - as of now, there isn't a cure for autism.

title: Fact Check: Does every 1 in 500 children who received Pfizer vaccine are hospitalized? - THIP Media
claim_text: One in Every 500 Small Children Who Receive the Pfizer Vaccine are Hospitalised By It
quick_take: A social media post shares a screenshot of an article published on a media website that claims every 1 in 500 children who received the Pfizer vaccine are hospitalized by it. We fact-checked and found the claim to be Half True.
doctor_explanation: The claim made by the article published on a media website named The Daily Sceptic is based on recent research published in 2022. This research was published in the journal named JAMA Network and compared the safety of the Pfizer covid vaccine with other approved vaccines in children younger than five years. The research concluded that only ten out of 7,800 children who participated in the study were hospitalized due to severe symptoms. These children received three micrograms dose of the Pfizer vaccine. It seems the result of this research is concerning for a small number of children because kids under the age of five who are not the participants of the study were not given the dosage that resulted in hospitalization. A press release uploaded on the Pfizer website confirms that 3 micrograms dose of the vaccine was carefully selected after studying safety, tolerability, and immunogenicity in children under five years of age.

One must consult a healthcare professional who can evaluate the nutritional status, consider any underlying conditions, and guide people on appropriate supplementation or dietary adjustments for optimal mental health.
