title: Fact Check: Is the Tetanus vaccine used just to sterilize people? - THIP Media
claim_text: An Instagram post shares a video in which a woman says, "I've never heard of anyone dying [of tetanus] that way. So, come to find out, that is a lie. No one has died that way. Nobody in the entire world, in history, modern history, right? So, why are they giving it [the tetanus vaccine] out if that's a lie, right?…" She further states, "But I saw there is a huge difference in fertility, huge, in people who didn't get it was extremely fertile. The people who did have a lot of problems. I Googled it then and sure enough, you can still find this if you Google it that the World Health Organization and NIH have since 1972 been developing the tetanus vaccine as an abortion or sterilization vaccine."
quick_take: A social media post claims that tetanus vaccines are used as a measure to sterilize people and no one has ever died of Tetanus. We fact-checked and found this claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: Tetanus, also known as lockjaw, is a serious bacterial infection caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani. The bacterium produces a toxin called tetanospasmin, which affects the nervous system and leads to muscle stiffness and spasms. Tetanus bacteria are commonly found in soil, dust, and manure. Tetanus can enter the body through open wounds, such as cuts, burns, or puncture wounds, especially when they are contaminated with soil or other materials containing the bacteria. Once inside the body, the bacteria release the toxin (tetanospasmin), which travels through the bloodstream and affects the nerves that control muscle movement. The muscle contractions can be so severe that they can lead to lockjaw, difficulty breathing, seizures, and even death. Tetanus vaccination is necessary because immunity can wane over time, so routine booster doses are necessary to maintain protection. No, tetanus vaccination does not cause sterilization. There is no scientific evidence to support the claim that tetanus vaccination can lead to infertility or affect reproductive health in any way even though there have been various speculations around this in the past. Tetanus vaccines are designed to stimulate the immune system to produce protective antibodies against the tetanus toxin. They contain inactivated or attenuated forms of the bacterium Clostridium tetani or specific components of the bacterium that are responsible for producing the toxin. This claim has been debunked by UNICEF which states that these vaccines do not contain any substances or ingredients that can interfere with fertility or reproductive function. Dr Kashyap Dakshini, General physician practicing in Mumbai explains, "Tetanus vaccines are generally safe and do not have any serious side effects. Most side effects like pain, heaviness of the shoulder/arm are not serious. Serious side effects (which are rare) include allergic reaction to tetanus toxoid, dizziness, muscle weakness, pain and fever. He further informs, "If an individual is not immunised with tetanus vaccine (also known as tetanus toxoid) then there is a risk of a rare but fatal bacterial infection called tetanus (lockjaw) which may lead to difficulty to swallow, breathe and speak, fever, muscle spasms, paralysis, and seizures. A tetanus shot comprises of inactivated bacteria which provide immunity against tetanus." The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) states that tetanus causes an estimated 213,000 to 293,000 deaths worldwide every year. It also states that it is responsible for 5 to 7% of all neonatal deaths and 5% of maternal deaths globally. The Vaccine Knowledge Project at Oxford University mentions that tetanus is always serious and often fatal. Therefore, the claim that no one has died from tetanus is absolutely false. Additionally, vaccines, including the tetanus vaccine, undergo rigorous testing and are approved by regulatory authorities before they are made available to the public. They are considered safe and effective in preventing tetanus and its complications. It must be noted that the above clip originated from a longer podcast interview with Carrie Madej, who has been previously associated to be a COVID-19 misinformation spreader as can be seen on Google Fact Check Explorer.
doctor_name: Dr Kashyap Dakshini
doctor_specialization: General Physician

title: Fact Check: Is the U.S. Measles outbreak disease X? - THIP Media
claim_text: An Instagram video claims that measles is the new pandemic. The video displays on-screen text featuring the phrase Election 2024 along with a red arrow pointing to the words Disease X.
quick_take: Recent reports have shown that passengers in Virginia, USA have highly contagious measles. After this, a social media video subsequently claims that the current U.S. measles outbreak is the mysterious disease X. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious viral infection caused by the measles virus (MeV). People with measles often suffer from fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a distinctive red rash. Measles spreads through respiratory droplets and is preventable through vaccination. We also found that there have been concerns about measles outbreaks due to vaccine hesitancy. Vaccines are often wrongly associated with causing diseases instead of curing them. In a story, we debunked that mass vaccinations caused the Spanish flu pandemic. In another instance, we refuted the claim that COVID-19 vaccines cause cancer. However, in most of the cases, the risks of vaccines outweigh the benefits. Is the U.S. measles outbreak disease X? No. Measles is not disease X. There is no proof that measles exposure has anything to do with Disease X. Disease X is just a term for a made-up infectious agent. This word is used by the World Health Organization (WHO) for potential diseases that could cause a big epidemic. There is no evidence that this made-up disease is responsible for measles cases at the airports, despite what an Instagram post says. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) website informs that the measles vaccine has reduced the cases of measles in the U.S. However, people can bring it in from other places, for example when they travel. In 2023, there were 56 reported cases of measles in the U.S. Lately, there has been a rise in measles cases in the USA, with reported instances at two airports within the country. The health departments in D.C. and Virginia have issued warnings urging people to be cautious and vigilant about measles. Another post claims that measles virus does not exist, and there is no scientific study that can prove the existence of the virus.

title: Fact Check: Is the viral lobotomy poster from the 20th century?
claim_text: A social media post displays a widely circulated graphic claimed to be a genuine 20th-century advertisement depicting an anatomical head with an icepick-like instrument being inserted into the brain through the eye socket. The poster reads: 'Feeling depressed? Dealing with anxiety and migraines? You might require a lobotomy.' It advocates for lobotomy as a solution for difficult family members and mentions Walter Freeman, an American physician who introduced this procedure to the United States in 1936 and conducted over 3,500 lobotomies.
quick_take: A social media post claims that the viral lobotomy poster is from the 20th century. We fact-checked and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: A lobotomy is a surgery that doctors use to cut or damage parts of the brain to try and help people with severe mental problems. They believed it could make them feel better by changing their feelings or behavior. This surgery became popular during the 1940s and 1950s. Doctors thought that by disturbing certain parts of the brain, they could ease symptoms of mental illnesses like depression or schizophrenia. Usually, they would reach the brain by making holes in the skull or by putting a sharp tool, like an icepick, through the eye socket to damage some brain nerves. But this surgery caused big problems. People often change in ways that cannot be fixed, like losing their emotions and thinking abilities, or even dying. As better medicines and treatments came along, lobotomy stopped being used because it was risky and had bad effects on people. The viral lobotomy poster is not from the 20th century. Someone made a funny advertisement for lobotomy. It is a treatment for mental illness that is not used anymore and was popular in the past. We ran a quick Google reverse image search and found that the post was made by a social media user named Demonic Pinfestation. The user also operates a website https://demonicpinfestation.bigcartel.com/ selling lifestyle product pins. It seems the claimed social media post was made to create a backstory to sell one of their pins. Same has been confirmed by Demonic Pinfestation spokesperson to USA Today. But now, this advertisement is being shared online as if it is a real old flyer promoting the treatment. This is making people doubt science. We even found that this brand has made such advertisements for its other products in the past.

title: Fact Check: Is the viral monkeypox photo really from Singapore?
claim_text: A viral photo circulating on Facebook claims to show the first case of Monkeypox in Singapore in 2024. The post implies that the outbreak is severe, urging people to take precautions such as wearing masks and avoiding crowds, as the disease is highly contagious.
quick_take: A social media post featuring a viral photo claims to show the first case of Monkeypox in Singapore in 2024. However, our fact check finds this claim to be Mostly False.
doctor_explanation:
The viral image circulating on social media is not from Singapore in 2024. After a reverse Google image search we got to know this is an image from Mexico. The image in the Facebook post is originally from October 2022 in Mexico. Then, Mexican infectious disease specialist José Hiram Hernández Jerónimo shared this post. The patient shown in the photo had a severe case of Mpox, with over 250 sores and a compromised immune system. This image has no connection to Singapore's current situation. The viral post has used an old image out of context, causing unnecessary fear by falsely linking it to a new outbreak in Singapore. Similarly, there was another Facebook post that falsely alleged Trump is advising against lockdowns during the 2024 Mpox outbreak. Therefore, it is extremely important to cross-check every claim you see on social media, as taking things out of context is a very common practice.

Is Mpox spreading in Singapore in 2024? Yes, Mpox cases have been reported in Singapore in 2024. As of 22 August 2024, Singapore's Ministry of Health confirmed 13 cases of Mpox. All these cases are of the less severe Clade II type. No cases of the more dangerous Clade I strain have emerged in Singapore. However, the viral image going around doesn't actually reflect the current Mpox situation in Singapore. The severe case shown in the photo has nothing to do with what's happening there in 2024.

What is the Mpox situation in India in 2024? The World Health Organisation (WHO) declared Mpox a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) on 14th August 2024 due to the emergence of a new strain, Clade Ib. This strain has spread rapidly, and India has reported 30 cases so far, with one death occurring in Kerala in March 2024. India's health authorities, including the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), have designated 35 laboratories across the country for testing Mpox, which includes AIIMS, Nagpur. AIIMS, Nagpur has been equipped with kits and reagents for Mpox testing and will continue to monitor cases in Vidarbha and nearby regions.

Dr Meinkaa Aakash, Senior Manager, Office of Public Health & Research, Max Healthcare, New Delhi, provided insights: "India is taking important steps to protect its people from Mpox and is preparing for any potential outbreaks. After the World Health Organization (WHO) raised concerns globally, the Indian government quickly ramped up their efforts. They've boosted their surveillance and monitoring systems, especially at airports and other points of entry. This means travellers from countries with known cases are being screened early, which helps catch and isolate any suspected cases, reducing the chance of the virus spreading." She further explained that awareness campaigns are helping people recognize symptoms and understand transmission. Hospitals are equipped with diagnostic tools and healthcare workers have received training. India is working with WHO on vaccine recommendations and setting up isolation wards. She advised not to panic, noting that programs like the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) allow for quick detection of outbreaks.

How does Mpox spread, and should you be worried? Mpox mainly spreads through direct contact with the rash, sores, or bodily fluids of an infected person. It can also spread through contact with contaminated items like bedding or clothing (fomite borne). Importantly, Mpox is not airborne, so it does not spread through the air like COVID-19 or the flu. The symptoms of Mpox include fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, and a rash that begins in the mouth and spreads to other parts of the body. Lymph node swelling is also common.

Should masks be worn to prevent Mpox? Wearing masks may help reduce the spread of some viruses, but since Mpox is not airborne, masks are not the primary preventive measure. People with Mpox should wear a well-fitting medical mask if they can't avoid close contact, like when getting medical care. Others in the household should wear a respirator or a mask when within 6 feet of the infected person for longer periods. The best way to prevent Mpox is by avoiding direct contact with infected individuals and maintaining proper hygiene.

doctor_specialization: Senior Manager, Office of Public Health & Research, Max Healthcare, New Delhi

title: Fact Check: Is the viral video of a devil baby from Rajasthan real?
claim_text: A baby born in Rajasthan was labelled a 'devil,' and the mother approached the court seeking permission to kill the child.
quick_take: A social media post claims that a devil baby was born in Rajasthan and that the mother asked the court for permission to kill it. However, our fact check shows this claim is false.
doctor_explanation: The claim is false. The baby shown in the viral video is not a 'devil,' but may be suffering from a rare genetic condition known as Harlequin Ichthyosis, which severely affects the skin. The baby's unusual appearance—often misunderstood—can be explained medically, not supernaturally. We performed a reverse image search but could not find any credible news source confirming the claims made in the viral post. While the video appears to be linked to a recent case from Rajasthan, there is no official record or trustworthy report stating that a mother approached the court seeking permission to end her baby's life. The caption circulating with the video is sensationalised and unsupported by evidence. It misrepresents a serious medical condition and contributes to harmful misinformation. The baby's appearance—white, tight skin, large eyes, and an unusual facial structure—is consistent with Harlequin Ichthyosis, a rare and severe genetic disorder that affects the skin. Babies born with this condition often have cracked, thickened skin that can resemble a hardened shell. It can distort facial features and make movements difficult. This condition has nothing to do with superstition or being a 'devil.' India’s Constitution strongly protects the right to life of every citizen, including newborns. There is no law that allows a court to approve the killing of a child because of how they look or due to any disability. Such a request would be illegal and could lead to serious punishment under the Indian Penal Code. Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, making it clear that all lives are protected equally under the law. Harlequin Ichthyosis is caused by a mutation in the ABCA12 gene, which affects how skin develops. It has nothing to do with supernatural forces, demons, or any cultural belief. Spreading such myths adds stigma and fear, making life harder for families already struggling with a difficult diagnosis. It also distracts from the real issue—such babies need immediate medical care, not superstition or social rejection.

title: Is the viral video of Mukesh Ambani talking about a diabetes cure real?
claim_text: A Facebook video circulating on social media shows Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani endorsing a miracle cure for diabetes. In the clip, Ambani appears to say that eating a single fruit every day can "reset the pancreas", restore metabolism, and bring blood sugar back to 90 by next Monday, thus eliminating the need for Metformin, finger pricks, or dietary control. He also claims to have assembled a scientific team led by "India's top endocrinologist Dr Devi Shetty" to develop this method.
quick_take: A social media post claims that the viral video of Mukesh Ambani talking about a diabetes cure is real. After thorough investigation, we found that this claim is false.
doctor_explanation: The viral clip uses footage from a 2020 virtual discussion between Mukesh Ambani and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg. This video was published on Reliance Industries' official YouTube channel. At around the 4-minute mark — the same segment reused in the viral Facebook video — Ambani talks about digital transformation in India during the pandemic. He does not mention diabetes, a fruit remedy, or any medical advice. The viral version uses AI-generated audio to falsely make it seem like Ambani is endorsing a cure. Dr Devi Shetty is a respected cardiac surgeon and not an endocrinologist, which is the medical specialty that deals with diabetes. There are no credible reports, research publications, or official statements linking him to any team developing a diabetes remedy using fruit or a simple fridge ingredient. The video misrepresents his credentials and falsely associates him with the claim. Diabetes—especially Type 2—is a long-term condition involving insulin resistance and complex metabolic processes. While lifestyle changes, weight management, and dietary modifications can help control or even reverse Type 2 diabetes in some individuals, there is no fruit or food that can "reset the pancreas" or cure the condition within days. Type 1 diabetes, on the other hand, is not reversible. Any claim of an instant or one-step cure is medically baseless. Dr Swati Dave, PhD in Food and Nutrition, explains, "There is no fruit that can reset the pancreas or cure diabetes in just a few days. Diabetes, particularly Type 2, is a chronic condition which involves insulin resistance and other metabolic issues. So, while some fruits are rich in fibre and antioxidants and can support blood sugar control when eaten in moderation, no single fruit has the power to reverse or cure the condition. To manage diabetes one needs to have a balanced diet, regular physical activity, weight control, and at times, medication under expert supervision. Claims that one food can replace all of that are not only unscientific but also risky." Managing diabetes usually requires a combination of medication, balanced diet, physical activity, and regular blood sugar monitoring. Completely abandoning medication or dietary precautions based on unverified remedies can lead to dangerous complications such as nerve damage, kidney issues, or even diabetic coma. No legitimate doctor would advise skipping medicines based on an internet video. Dr Surajeet Kumar Patra, Director & Consultant Diabetologist, Dr Surajeet Patra's Diabetes Clinic, Bhubaneswar, says, "There is no home remedy that can cure diabetes. Some natural foods like bitter gourd may help in managing blood sugar, but they should never be seen as a replacement for medicines. What many people refer to as 'reversing diabetes' is actually called diabetes remission. This means maintaining healthy sugar levels without medicines for a few months, but it's not possible for everyone. Only a diabetologist can decide if someone is a suitable candidate for remission, based on their overall health and history. Self-treatment or relying only on home remedies can be harmful and people should always avoid those." The original video has no such content. The clip used in the viral claim is taken from a publicly available conversation on the Reliance Updates YouTube channel dated 15 December 2020. The visuals are real, but the audio has been replaced to promote false health information. This is a clear case of digital manipulation, not a hidden or suppressed broadcast. The video does not name any real ingredient. Despite making bold claims, it never reveals what the so-called "fridge ingredient" is. Instead, it urges viewers to click on an unrelated link, which leads to a generic article about diabetes with no mention of quick remedies. Such tactics are a common practice in scams to lure users into increasing page views, buying fake products, or revealing personal information. The video offers no scientific or medical explanation.

doctor_specialization: PhD in Food and Nutrition; Director & Consultant Diabetologist

doctor_explanation: After a thorough research about the latest news on the official WHO website and other reliable sources, we found no such information. While the WHO is the leading global agency looking after the health of all people around the globe, it does not plan on taking over the sovereignty of its member nations. The WHO formulates guidelines for disease control and prevention, health education and awareness, healthcare equity and promotes well-being. During our research we found the original video which is the source of the above-mentioned misinformation. After carefully watching both the videos, we can conclude that the claim video is false and manipulated. Whatever is being said in the claim video goes absolutely against the core values of WHO. Regarding the pandemic agreement, some people have spread false information about it, like saying it would threaten countries' sovereignty or that the WHO would send troops to enforce it. But those claims are not true. The agreement is actually designed to countries' rights and sovereignty, following the rules of international law. It's up to each nation whether they want to agree to it or not, and the WHO can't force anyone to do anything. The WHO's role is to offer advice and guidance on health matters, not to make laws or enforce them. They have never pushed for vaccine mandates, and their power is limited to international health issues, not national ones.

title: Fact Check: Is there a blue banana that tastes like vanilla ice cream? - THIP Media
claim_text: This is Blue Java Banana and it tastes like Vanilla Ice Cream
quick_take: A number of social media users are sharing a photo of a blue variety of bananas. The claim associated with it is that the seedless variety of bananas tastes like Vanilla Ice Cream. We fact-check the claim and find it to be True.
doctor_explanation: Yes, they are. Blue bananas, popularly known as Blue Java Bananas, are hybrid of two different species of bananas – Musa balbisiana and Musa acuminata. They are majorly grown in South East Asia. NOTE: Only the skin colour of the banana is blue. The flesh is always white. The unusual blue colour of the peel is due to the natural wax coating on the fruit. The blue colour tends to fade out as the banana ripens. (In some photos on Facebook, the banana looks dark blue and the flesh also seems to have a bluish tinge. title: Fact Check: Is there a good time to drink water? - THIP Media
claim_text: Various Facebook and Pinterest posts claim there are specific optimal times to drink water: after waking up, before and after meals, after workout, before a bath, before sleep, and while standing. These posts suggest drinking water at these specific times provides specific health benefits.
quick_take: A number of Facebook posts suggest various timings on when one should drink water. We fact-checked and found the suggestions to be False. There are no scientifically proven benefits of drinking water at any specific time. Neither modern medicine, nor Ayurvedic medicinal practice has any specific instructions about drinking water at any specific time of the day.
doctor_explanation: NO. There is no 'right time' for drinking water. In a 2019 study on water consumption researchers mention, "The timing of beverage consumption in the course of the day may have additional implications for adequate hydration. There is emerging mythology about the correct time to drink water in the course of the day. However, evidence in support of those strategies is limited." Since such claims are often wrongly credited to Ayurveda, we consulted Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director, Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda (ĀCĀRA). Dr. Rammanohar says, "Thirst is a vega or natural reflex according to Ayurveda. The rule is that one must drink whenever one is thirsty. Thirst should not be ignored. Having said that, Ayurveda does not recommend drinking water in large quantities at a time, except in summer and autumn when there is more heat and sweating. In these seasons, one should replenish one's body with enough water as it is lost by sweating. In other seasons, one must drink water when thirsty and in small quantities throughout the day. There is no special recommended time for drinking water in Ayurveda." 1. After waking up: A number of articles that suggest drinking water as soon as you wake up suggest the need for hydration. However, the benefits of drinking water are universal and there is no scientific evidence that suggests our body needs extra hydration after waking up. Dr. Rammanohar says, "Ayurveda suggests sipping hot water in the morning but it is for bowel movements." General Physician Dr. S Krishna Prasanthi, MBBS, MD (PGIMER) agrees, "Human body has a homeostasis mechanism to maintain the hydration levels in the body. The liver and kidney work efficiently throughout day and night to remove toxins. However, if a person has difficulty in passing stools, consuming warm water increases bowel movements and relieves constipation to a certain extent, provided the consumed food has adequate fibre." 2. Before and After Meal: Once again, there is no particular research that suggests any direct benefit of having water before and after meals. Many people believe drinking water before and after meals helps in digestion, while many others believe drinking water close to mealtimes or during meals will disturb digestion. There is no scientific evidence to support either of the claims. However, there is a small study that found that drinking water before a meal helped men and women eat less and feel just as satisfied as a group who didn't drink water before. Dr. Rammanohar says, "there is no question of not drinking water. Rather Ayurveda suggests drinking water in small sips along with meals. Large quantities of water should be avoided." 3. After Workout: There are some benefits of drinking water after a workout. However, evidence suggests that there are benefits of drinking water before a workout and during a workout too. While research has shown that, "Prevention of dehydration after exercise by oral water intake, or oral water intake per se has a role in maintaining post-exercise mean arterial blood pressure." However, similar research has proved that drinking water before and during workouts also has benefits. 4. Before a bath: Many people who suggested this believes that drinking water before a bath will help reduce blood pressure. A Washington University article debunks this as a Myth. The article suggests, "Your blood pressure will not be affected because it is under the tight control of various hormones. If you are severely dehydrated and your blood pressure drops below the normal level, that system of hormones will cause you to feel thirsty. In the case of dehydration, drinking water will actually help increase blood pressure to a normal level." Dr. Prasanthi says, "This claim too doesn't have any scientific validity. Blood pressure in the body is maintained by a complex mechanism of Renin-Angiotension-Aldosterone mechanism. While extreme dehydration due to vomitings, diarrhea might result in lowering of blood pressure, there is no specific benefit for drinking water before bath." 5. Before Sleep: There is little evidence to suggest any specific benefits of drinking water at bedtime. Rather drinking more water before bedtime can result in Nocturia. Nocturia is the increased need to urinate at night. Repeatedly getting up can reduce both the duration and quality of sleep which in turn can lead to risks of stroke and heart attack. There are multiple debates on 'how much' water should an adult consume daily and suggestions from the public health experts have also changed from time to time. As per an article on Nature, "The amount of fluid needed varies between people and according to age, time of year, climatic conditions, diet and levels of physical activity, so it is difficult to set DRVs (dietary reference values)" One research has shown that "The recommended total daily fluid intake of 3,000 ml for men and of 2,200 ml for women is more than adequate." The same research also mentions, "Higher fluid intake does not have any convincing health benefits, except perhaps in preventing (recurrent) kidney stones." No. There is no scientific evidence that a particular posture is suggested while drinking water. No such recommendation is also given in Ayurveda. Dr. Rammanohar says, "Ayurveda suggests that food should be consumed while sitting down to avoid choking. There is no recommendation on how to drink water. But it's common sense that you should not consume water in a hurry, or drink too much water too fast, or drink while in a wrong position. Those things can cause choking." Dr. Prasanthi says, "People who make this claim believes drinking water while standing hampers the absorption of nutrients from the digestive tract, and also risks lungs and heart functions. There is a involuntary mechanism in the body called peristaltic movement that begins at the oesophagus, as soon as the food (either liquid or solid) is swallowed. Contrary to the popular claim that the liquid is moved directly under the effect of gravity, it is this peristalsis that propels the distal movement of food. So, there is no scientific validation behind not drinking water while standing. However, one must avoid consuming liquids while lying in bed as it may result in aspiration (liquid food entering respiratory tract and lungs) that may result in infections."

title: Fact Check: Is there a herbal medicine that can cure HIV and herpes?
claim_text: A post on Threads promotes a permanent treatment for infectious viral conditions such as HIV and herpes. The post further states that the product made of pure and natural roots can cure any type of sickness, virus, or infection.
quick_take: According to a post on the thread, there is a permanent herbal remedy for HIV and herpes. We fact-checked the assertion and found that the claim is completely false.
doctor_explanation:
The fact-check examines multiple aspects of the claim. First, regarding the claimant's credibility: The medications are marketed under "Doctor IZoya," who claims to treat both STDs and non-STDs. However, none of these pages indicate any professional experience in allopathic medicine. The account holder holds certification as a traditional practitioner, not a licensed medical doctor. Ms. Malvika Phulwani, Clinical Dietician and diabetes educator, advises patients to check the credentials of people offering health information online and stresses the validity of information shared by licensed health educators, doctors, nurses, and other qualified healthcare professionals.

Second, regarding the herbal product's reliability: Upon using Google's translation tool on one of the viral photos, the Nigerian product lacked certain specifications. Since the drug cover did not make it obvious whether NAFDAC (Nigeria's food and drug regulatory body) had evaluated the product, we checked Nigeria's Registered Drug Product Database on the NAFDAC's official site but were unable to discover the product there. There are no essential details on the medication cover, including adverse effects, contraindications, and quantities and purposes of the ingredients. The product makes no mention of any accreditations that attest to the efficacy and safety of medications, such as ISO 15378 Certification or WHO Certification.

Third, regarding supporting research: Each medication provided to treat a particular condition needs to go through a rigorous testing and monitoring process. Clinical trials ensure manufacturers adhere to rigorous research protocols, uphold ethical standards, safeguard patient safety, and create reliable data for evidence-based treatment. When searching for research pertaining to the recommended product on the NAFDAC website, no results were found.

Regarding self-medication: Self-medication is the practice of using medication to treat illnesses or symptoms identified without visiting a physician. Risks include drug resistance, probable delays in obtaining adequate medical therapy (which can be fatal), and ineffectiveness for treating HIV and herpes, which can aggravate or worsen the illness.

Dr. Kashyap Dakshini, General Physician, when asked if patients with herpes or HIV might self-medicate, sternly advised against it, citing the high contagiousness of these viral conditions and the need for an immediate diagnosis and treatment plan that can only be created by a medical professional. Dr. Dakshini explains: "To ensure proper symptomatic treatment, only clinicians should prescribe and monitor the antiviral medications for the treatment of herpes and antiretroviral therapy. Self-medication without medical supervision can result in inadequate treatment and adverse outcomes."

Regarding herbal medicine efficacy: Herbal medications lack substantial scientific evidence. They might provide symptomatic relief but may not be able to completely eliminate infectious conditions. Their purpose should be confined to as an adjuvant.

HIV cannot be cured despite significant advances in medical science. AIDS-causing HIV, also known as the human immunodeficiency virus, persists in the body even after treatment because the virus incorporates itself into the host's DNA. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) successfully inhibits HIV replication, allowing those who are afflicted to live reasonably healthy lives. It does not, nevertheless, eliminate the viral infection.

The herpes simplex virus, which causes genital and oral infections, is difficult to completely eradicate from the body. Herpes symptoms are managed using antiviral medications such as Acyclovir and Famciclovir that are prescribed. While the prescribed medication may reduce the occurrence of HSV symptoms and might reduce the spread, it cannot completely clear the virus from the system. The persistence of HSV symptoms can be a high-risk factor for the development of HIV infection.

Dr. Dakshini adds that although there is research demonstrating the antiviral properties of some herbal remedies, they are not fully effective in treating these infections. He underlines that although these herbs are a safer and natural symptomatic relief, they cannot take the place of the prescribed conventional antiviral drugs. Therefore, it is recommended that patients consult their respective physicians to receive the proper diagnosis and treatment.

title: Is there a magical recipe that can remove dark circles overnight?
claim_text: A Facebook post titled "Get Rid Of Dark Circles Under Eye In One Night" proposes using coffee, aloe vera gel, vitamin E capsules, and coconut oil to get rid of dark circles.
quick_take: A well-liked Facebook post promotes a magical recipe that can remove dark circles overnight. We analysed the claim and found that it is false.
doctor_explanation:
Dark shadows beneath the eyes are called dark circles, or periorbital hyperpigmentation. Individuals of all ages are affected by this prevalent cosmetic challenge. Based on their appearance, they fall into the following categories: The scientific literature states that ageing, genetic susceptibility, thinning of the periorbital skin, hyperpigmentation, poor blood circulation, and unhealthy lifestyle choices are the main causes of dark circles. Prolonged screen time, the habit of eye rubbing, and certain allergies can be significant contributors. Even while dark circles don't cause any symptoms, their obvious effects on appearance and their correlation with fatigue, stress, or medical issues make them worrisome. Considering the periorbital region is aesthetically significant, even minor discolourations are obvious and have an impact on confidence and self-esteem; therefore, they should be efficiently addressed.

Do vitamin E capsules, coffee, aloe vera gel, and coconut oil work well for dark circles? No, not exactly. While the ingredients, such as coffee, aloe vera gel, vitamin E capsules, and coconut oil, are often touted as natural remedies for dark circles, their popularity is confined to social media platforms only. Given that the ingredients are being considered for the delicate periorbital area, an extensive evaluation is essential. We begin with coffee, which is the most prevalent household option for dark circles. It exhibits vasoconstrictive effects due to the presence of antioxidants and caffeine, which may provide temporary relief from puffiness and even aid with the appearance of tired eyes. Furthermore, using caffeine-based formulations topically can improve skin tone and reduce periorbital oedema. Next is the aloe vera gel, which is utilized because it contains aloesin, which may reduce pigmentation by influencing the production of melanin. Aloe vera gel is well-known for its calming and moisturising properties. This is followed by vitamin E capsules. This antioxidant-rich component may shield against oxidative stress and aid in skin restoration. Finally, we discuss coconut oil. This usually provides emollient and anti-inflammatory benefits that can enhance skin texture and hydration. Despite the aforementioned ingredients exhibiting modest benefits, there is a dearth of substantial scientific evidence supporting their direct role in the elimination of dark circles. Another crucial consideration is that under-eye pigmentation develops due to multiple causes. Therefore, a single topical remedy cannot address the entire spectrum. Furthermore, in sensitive people, misuse or incorrect application of thick or greasy formulations may exacerbate puffiness or clog pores. While these ingredients may provide symptomatic relief, they should not replace evidence-based dermatological care.

Can a magical recipe help get rid of dark circles overnight? No, absolutely not. Such unrealistic expectations are the most concerning aspect of the claim. Consequently, it should be made clear that there isn't a magical formula for removing dark circles rapidly. This may be explained by their multifactorial origin, which cannot be readily reversible. Moreover, the under-eye area is among the thinnest in the body, making it more susceptible to injury and hyperpigmentation when exposed to harsh or unverified remedies. While certain supervised at-home measures can provide temporary improvement by reducing swelling or enhancing circulation, they cannot address persistent dark circles. Contrarily, extensive or severe hyperpigmentation necessitates targeted interventions like topical retinoids, vitamin C, hyaluronic acid, chemical peels, or laser therapy. Considering that one night of adequate rest and proper eye care can be a revitalising experience, complete eradication of dark circles is a progressive phenomenon that requires time, consistent medical monitoring, and adherence to dermatologist-recommended regimens. Therefore, it is advised to stay away from such impractical online solutions.

Why do high-risk people employ untested remedies for dark circles? Is relying on them recommended? Unreliable home cures for dark circles are usually employed by those who are struggling with persistent stress, sleep deprivation, hormonal fluctuations, or specific health issues. This is further encouraged when social media claims promote such remedies as quick, inexpensive, natural, and chemical-free botanical extracts. However, it is crucial to clarify that social media trends that equate 'natural' with 'safe' are based on anecdotal reports and not concrete scientific evidence. Moreover, a single remedy may not address all contributors.

Dr. Iftekhar Khan, MD (Dermatology), Assistant Professor at SMS Medical College in Jaipur, provides support by stating that, contrary to popular belief, home remedies are not the best approach for addressing under-eye discolouration. Considering the skin beneath the eyes is much thinner and more delicate, using unsupervised therapies could exacerbate the condition. Effective under-eye therapy requires a comprehensive evaluation of the issue and diligent effort.

Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, Dermatologist, Cosmetician, Trichologist, and Consultant for Aesthetic Medicine in Lucknow clarifies that not all herbal therapies are always beneficial for the skin. Many organic components, including lemon juice or turmeric, may bring about burns, irritation, or even allergic responses when applied directly. Lab-based products undergo extensive testing to ensure their safe and effective operation. For instance, the strong acidity of lemon juice may damage the skin's barrier, while glycolic acid in skincare products softly exfoliates skin. Therefore, despite their apparent attraction, natural cosmetics aren't always the best or safest option for your complexion. Dermatologists advise against such methods since they can postpone appropriate assessment and treatment. To ensure safe and successful dark circle intervention, one must speak with a qualified clinician.

In what ways do dermatologists handle dark circles? Medical professionals correct dark circles with a thoughtful, all-encompassing approach. The therapeutic regimen is usually based on the underlying cause. Pigmented dark circles frequently respond to evidence-based topical medications such as hydroquinone, azelaic acid, kojic acid, or retinoids, which help reduce melanin formation and improve skin tone. Vascular under-eye pigmentation can be handled by topical vitamin K or caffeine formulations – these may enhance circulation and strengthen capillaries. Persistent discolouration could benefit from intense pulsed light (IPL), laser therapy, and chemical peels using lactic or glycolic acid. Hyaluronic acid fillers can be used to address structural hyperpigmentations developed from collagen or fat loss. The procedure might minimise shadowing and restore the volume. Supervised stress management, getting enough sleep, protecting oneself from the sun, staying well hydrated, and preventing photoaging can all help these therapeutic techniques. Please be advised that treatment outcomes are always gradual, even with evidence-based interventions. While dark circles usually are not harmful, they are an indicator of lifestyle choices, underlying health conditions, and the body's general state of rest and rejuvenation. Web-based therapies are not advised for sensitive periorbital skin due to their dubious safety and effectiveness.

doctor_explanation: Oral malodour, often known as halitosis in dentistry, is a foul, unpleasant stench emanating from the mouth. While it is prevalent to wake up with unpleasant breath, this condition, sometimes referred to as physiological halitosis, is considered to be transient. However, the persistent bad breath that results from the production of proteins and amino acids by oral anaerobic bacteria necessitates professional intervention. The anaerobic microbial activity usually induces volatile sulphur compounds, or VSCs, along with volatile components, including amines and diamines, responsible for bad breath. Key contributors include poor dental care, tongue coatings, advanced gum condition, particularly aggressive gingival condition, along with additional issues such as systemic illnesses, infections, certain medications, dry mouth, or xerostomia. While natural ingredients such as salt, lemon juice, and cloves are commonly promoted as quick fixes for unpleasant odours, they cannot be utilised as permanent solutions. Lemon juice's high acidity may stimulate salivation, which could offer short-term relief. However, its long-term use is not recommended primarily due to the risk of enamel erosion and questionable efficacy. Dental professionals frequently recommend salt water rinses to lower the oral bacteria load, yet this approach is not a definitive solution for halitosis. It is vital to emphasise that halitosis is associated with underlying causes. If the relevant contributors aren't identified and timely addressed, the issue won't be resolved. Professional intervention, along with consistent self-care practices, may help in the significant reduction of oral malodour levels. At-home options such as clove, fennel, cardamom, or herbal teas are traditionally used to mask bad breath. However, halitosis may also be an indicator of a metabolic illness like diabetes or periodontitis. Dependence on such unsubstantiated alternative therapies might delay necessary examination and therapy. This delay may ultimately lead to silent progression of the underlying cause, perhaps making the condition worse. Furthermore, prolonged consumption of certain ingredients may cause mucosal irritation and disrupt the oral microbiome. Dr. Pooja Sharma, BDS, MDS, of NIMS University in Jaipur, states that home remedies can occasionally cause more harm than good—not because the ingredients are unsafe, but rather because they can create the false impression that medical attention isn't required. Dental conditions such as cavities and gum infections don't go away on their own; they need to be accurately identified and managed. It is always better to visit a dentist right away rather than waiting for the issue to deteriorate. Dr. Ketan Rajput, Periodontist, and Oral Implantologist, Dhule, Maharashtra, supports this by stating that bad breath, or halitosis, is an unpleasant, persistent, foul odour that can be brought on by several local and systemic factors. In light of this, Dr. Rajput recommends both treating the underlying reason and seeking professional therapeutic intervention. While home remedies could be somewhat helpful, relying solely on them is not clinically or scientifically valid. A comprehensive strategy including professional dental evaluation, self-care practices, and therapeutic intervention is required for the management of oral malodour.

title: Is there a permanent natural remedy for premature greying of hair?

doctor_explanation: The fact check explains why premature greying occurs and why the claimed remedy cannot work. Premature greying (premature canities) is the early loss of natural hair colour, with white or grey hair strands usually apparent before the age of 20 to 30. The condition is influenced by: 1) Familial inheritance - This is the principal contributor. Specific genetic variations of the IRF4 gene have been associated with hair colour and greying. A positive family history is a significant predictor. 2) Environmental triggers - Cigarette smoking, insufficient dietary intake, and a sedentary lifestyle are associated with early grey or white hair strands. B12, biotin, folic acid, calcium, and ferritin deficiencies are contributing factors. 3) Biological considerations - The accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) might result in premature greying. Reduced oxidative stress causes melanocyte depletion in hair follicles, which results in early greying. Regarding the herbal recipe claim: While a formula composed of roasted onion peel powder, aloe vera gel, and coconut oil is frequently promoted as a natural solution for reversing premature greying, it cannot be regarded as an efficient remedy. Each ingredient offers individual benefits, but there is no specific scientific proof to support the claim that the combination may permanently reverse premature greying. Given that this condition is essentially inherited, a natural dye may temporarily conceal appearances, but it cannot replace clinically proven therapy. Regarding home management: It is not recommended to address premature greying at home. While various home cures may provide short-term cosmetic benefits, they do not address the root causes of early greying. Unverified web-based cures such as herbal oils, onion juice, or amla are commonly used to manage premature greying. While they could enhance scalp health and hair texture, they cannot address the reduction in melanocytes. Adherence to at-home measures may aid in the maintenance of professional intervention from a medical health expert, but they cannot replace it. A dermatologist examines the potential underlying reasons, such as vitamin deficiencies or hormonal abnormalities. Dr. P. Rammanohar, Research Director at the Amrita Centre for Advanced Research in Ayurveda, states that while genetic or age-related greying is unavoidable, external influences such as lifestyle choices or environmental stressors may be able to slow down the progression. The right approach requires a multimodal approach combining prescription medications, lifestyle adjustments, and nutritional support. Dermatologists typically prescribe medications based on the underlying cause, such as thyroid dysfunction or autoimmune illnesses like vitiligo. The therapeutic regimen includes the use of topical medications or supplements. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, a Dermatologist, Cosmetologist, Trichologist, and Aesthetic medicine consultant in Lucknow, explains that the most prevalent option is hair dye; depending on requirements, permanent, semi-permanent, and ammonia-free options are available. If preferring a more natural appearance, henna can produce a reddish-brown tone but may not completely conceal grey hair. Root touch-up powders and sprays are effective for covering greys between successive dye sessions. Given that greying is mostly inherited, maintaining healthy hair requires a nutritious diet rich in iron, zinc, and vitamin B12. Certain specialist therapies such as microneedling or customised serums may enhance hair health but cannot prevent greying. Embracing grey hair is also a good decision.

Dr. Thakur adds, 'Ayurvedic treatment can help manage diabetes in its early stages before using insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents (OHAs).' While Ayurveda may provide supportive treatment for genetically inherited diabetes, it does not provide a lasting cure for all patients. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, clarifies: 'Ayurveda takes a holistic approach to diabetes, focusing on digestion, metabolism, and overall well-being. Herbs such as neem, turmeric, and triphala may help improve insulin sensitivity, but managing diabetes effectively requires consistency in diet, physical activity, and mental well-being. While Ayurvedic treatments may significantly improve the condition for certain individuals with type 2 diabetes in its early stages, this does not imply that there is a universal remedy. Integrating Ayurvedic knowledge with contemporary medical advice is crucial instead of depending just on one approach.' Hyperglycemia (diabetes) is a chronic metabolic disease that no medical system is capable of curing. Instead, lifestyle changes, prescribed medications, and herbal remedies as an adjuvant can help regulate the illness. Several plants such as Allium sativum (garlic), Gymnema sylvestre, Murraya koenigii (curry leaf), Allium cepa (onion), Withania somnifera (ashwagandha), Ferula foetida, Neem, and turmeric are noteworthy for their antidiabetic characteristics. The bioactive substances in these plants including coumarins, phenolics, flavonoids, and terpenoids have demonstrated encouraging results in lowering blood glucose levels. While herbal medicines have the potential to lower blood sugar levels, particularly in cases of type 2 or insulin-dependent diabetes, their effectiveness is limited, making them a useful supplement. Moreover, there may be substantial variations in dosage, interactions with other drugs, and individual responses. Relying on botanical interventions without clinical supervision can be risky; herbal ingredients should be used as complementary measures and not as a substitute for established medical treatment. In India, no medical system is permitted to make claims about curing diabetes in advertisements or product marketing due to the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act of 1954. Furthermore, diabetes is listed in Schedule J of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, as one of the conditions that no pharmaceutical or drug may claim to cure unless specifically authorised by regulatory bodies such as the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO). Relying on unapproved home cures or diabetes advice from social media can postpone necessary medical intervention, increasing the risk of severe complications, delayed wound healing, and even irreversible organ damage. Treatments lacking clinical validation may not only be of poor quality, but may also cause harmful drug interactions and be inefficient at controlling blood sugar levels. Unreliable herbal formulations might include unidentified pharmacologically active ingredients, including steroids or even allopathic medications, in unsafe dosages that could have adverse health consequences. Discontinuing prescribed medications for unproven remedies might result in unregulated blood sugar levels, particularly for those receiving insulin therapy for type 1. A well-crafted long-term management plan is essential for effective control of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. In people with T1D, the pancreas either produces too little or no insulin, requiring lifelong insulin therapy. Type 2 diabetes requires medication in addition to tailored food planning, consistent physical activity, weight management, and continual surveillance.

title: Fact Check: Is there an effective herbal remedy for vitiligo patches?
claim_text: A Facebook post suggests a herbal remedy for vitiligo patches composed of three ingredients: blue henon bamboo powder, coconut oil, and tea tree oil. The viral post with the description 'How to cure Vitiligo at Home with Natural Remedies' suggests that applying the formulation on a daily basis for 6 months can completely remove the depigmented patches.
quick_take: A highly circulated Facebook post suggests a herbal remedy for vitiligo patches. We analysed the claim and found that it is completely false.
doctor_explanation: Vitiligo is an autoimmune dermatological illness characterised by depigmented or hypopigmented skin lesions. The disorder is characterised by an unintentional harm to the melanin-synthesising cells that contribute to the pigmentation of the skin, hair, and eyes. The consequent milky white skin lesions may differ in their dimensions and location. Even while the illness provides little risk to life or bodily harm, its visibility has a significant psychological impact. Vitiligo's specific aetiology is uncertain. Nonetheless, the dermatological illness is frequently associated with both hereditary and environmental variables, which can influence its onset and severity. Given its visible nature, vitiligo requires immediate medical attention as well as continuing psychological support to effectively handle its impact on the lives of persons coping with the skin condition. The herbal formulation combining bamboo powder, coconut oil, and tea tree oil cannot replace scientifically validated therapy for the repigmentation of the vitiligo lesions. Bamboo powder is touted as a mild exfoliator and a good source of silica. Coconut oil has moisturising effects and works as a carrier. Tea tree oil has both antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory benefits in specific dermatological conditions. Despite these positive effects, vitiligo patients must prioritise their safety. Physical exfoliation with unproven products might irritate their skin and result in the development of new vitiligo patches at the trauma sites. In addition, tea tree oil is a known contact sensitiser that can cause allergic or irritating dermatitis. As a result, continued use of such unsupervised home remedies could aggravate depigmentation or delay the required corrective measures. Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition with a complicated, unknown aetiology. The challenging interplay of various causative aspects makes it difficult to pinpoint the specific cause of its emergence. The fact that vitiligo is usually associated with other autoimmune disorders suggests a systemic immune dysregulation that specifically targets pigment cells. Melanocyte-related oxidative damage can enhance sensitivity, and external stressors such as emotional stress or sunburn may worsen hypopigmentation. Another significant impediment to management is the condition's unpredictable progression. Because these lesions might advance quickly or remain stable for years, intervention may not always be effective. Hence, contemporary procedures are not always effective and frequently result in transient or short-term repigmentation. Above all, melanocyte regeneration is limited in vitiligo-affected areas due to a paucity of healthy stem cells in depigmented skin. To achieve a complete and long-term recovery, therapies must address the underlying autoimmune damage and gradually restore melanocytes. In a previous interview with THIP Media, Dr. Swati Watwani, an aesthetic dermatologist and cosmetologist who is the chief consultant and medical director of Persian Lily in Maharashtra, reinforces this by stating that vitiligo cannot be completely cured due to its genetic basis. Despite the remarkable outcomes of the most recent medical procedures and advanced prescription medications, the hypopigmented lesions or patches may resurface again. Dr. Ekansh Shekhar, a dermatologist, cosmetician, trichologist, and aesthetic medicine consultant from Lucknow, further supports this by asserting that there is currently no permanent solution for vitiligo. Conventional therapy can help regulate the condition, restore some skin pigmentation, and keep it from spreading while also providing relief and enhancing attractiveness. As a result, it is critical to work closely with a dermatologist to determine the appropriate therapy for your specific requirements. Dermatologists' approach to autoimmune disease focuses on preventing progression and restoring pigmentation. First-line therapies include prescribed topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors. Nonetheless, phototherapeutic intervention, particularly narrowband UVB, remains essential. Excimer laser therapy can be utilised for managing resistant or widespread cases, providing tailored solutions. Systemic immunomodulators can be used to address rapidly spreading depigmented patches. Surgical procedures, such as melanocyte or skin grafting, are frequently employed for managing stable or localised lesions. In addition to medical therapeutic measures, doctors prioritise counselling and psychological support to build an all-encompassing and patient-centred approach to vitiligo management. Dr. Rashi Soni, Co-founder and Consulting Dermatologist at Rashi Hospital in Mumbai, provided her expert opinion on vitiligo therapy options. She explains, 'Vitiligo is frequently addressed with a combination of medicines aimed at restoring skin colour or preventing the illness from spreading.' This may involve topical therapies such as corticosteroids, light therapy, and, in certain cases, surgical intervention. The objective of therapy is to manage the issue and enhance the skin's appearance, but keep in mind that treatment outcomes are very individualistic. Always contact a dermatologist to determine the best therapy for your unique condition. Health literacy is essential in the treatment of vitiligo. The appropriate knowledge has a direct impact on the patient's awareness of the disease, adherence to prescribed medical care, and ability to prevent harmful practices. Patients with higher health literacy are more likely to seek dermatological care on time and even adhere to their recommended therapies. Furthermore, well-informed patients tend to have realistic expectations regarding the therapeutic outcomes. Contrarily, limited knowledge often leads to delayed care, reliance on unproven remedies, and self-medication. Self-medication is strongly discouraged in vitiligo management. Medication-related factors such as discontinuation, overconsumption, and reliance on unproven home remedies might worsen the disease. Dermatologists highlight the importance of evidence-based therapies that are tailored to the severity and stability of the illness.

title: Fact Check: Is there an effective quick home remedy for cancer?
claim_text: A mixture of carrot, onion, garlic, and lime juice is an effective remedy for cancer that can cure cancers in stages one through three.
quick_take: A social media video claims that there is an effective quick home remedy for cancer. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: A mixture of carrot, onion, garlic, and lime juice is not an effective remedy for cancer. The assertion made by the claimant regarding 'one treatment for different cancers' lacks credibility due to its absence of scientific backing. In the video, the claimant appears to advocate the belief that consuming natural ingredients serves as an effective remedy for various cancers. However, upon further investigation, we were unable to find any information about the speaker besides the fact that he identifies himself as Dr. Roots. Consequently, we lack clarity on whether the claimant possesses a valid medical license. He discusses an effective remedy claiming to be capable of curing cancers in stages one through three. The remedy consisted of vague instructions, including enough carrots, enough onions, and enough garlic. There are no specific measurements provided in the video. The instruction is to mix the pounded vegetables with freshly extracted lime juice in a bottle and consume it as a shot twice daily until improvement is observed. Notably, the video lacked any evidence supporting the claim that this mixture has curative properties. Dr. Sarthak Moharir, Chief Radiation Oncologist Apollo Cancer Centre, Bilaspur further adds, "Special diet or diet modifications do not cure cancer. Diet is very important for patients undergoing cancer treatment and it is advised they take a balanced meal with all macros and micronutrients as prescribed by their dietary counsellor." Furthermore, the American Society of Cancer website informs that cancer treatment depends on several factors such as cancer type, stage, available treatment options, and other important variables. This comprehensive perspective sheds light on the complexity of the situation and the fact that a mere quick home remedy cannot cure cancer. Cancer patients need tailored treatment approaches depending on their health condition. It is important to emphasize that there is no singular technique effective for treating all forms of cancer. Carrots, onions, garlic, and lime juice cannot effectively treat cancers. These foods contain various vitamins, minerals, and compounds that may have some cancer-fighting properties, such as beta-carotene in carrots, flavonoids in onions, and allicin in garlic, which have been studied for their potential to combat cancer cells and reduce the risk of certain cancers. Lime juice, rich in vitamin C, also contains antioxidants that may contribute to overall health and potentially aid in preventing cell damage caused by free radicals. However, there is no conclusive scientific evidence to support the claim that consuming them alone can effectively treat cancers. These available research papers only speculates carrot, onion, garlic, and lime juice have anti-cancer properties. None of these papers confirms that eating them will treat cancer. Evidence only shows that a healthy diet rich in fruits and vegetables, including carrots, onions, garlic, and citrus fruits like lime, can be beneficial for overall health. Their chemical composition may reduce the risk of certain cancers. However, it is important to note that these foods should not be considered as standalone treatments for cancer. Cancer is a complex disease, and its treatment usually requires a multifaceted approach involving various medical interventions, such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapies, among others. Voomika Mukherjee, our Health & Nutrition Life coach, explains, "No food or food group can prevent cancer and that avoiding certain foods will not reduce your risk. Maintaining body weight, particularly visceral fat, and muscle strength, in addition to a balanced diet, is critical while treating cancer. The best way is to eat a well-balanced diet rich in lean proteins, fruits and vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy. Reduce your intake of sugar, caffeine, salt, and alcohol." She emphasized that eating meals of adequate quality and quantity can help you lower your risk of cancer and other chronic diseases. However, no food can cure cancer. Shivashankar T., Chief Clinical Nutritionist and Dietician at Tata Memorial Cancer Hospital, Mumbai confirms the same. He informs that a good diet is important in cancer treatment. He further explains that "A healthy diet plays an important role in supporting overall health and well-being during cancer treatment. A diet high in good protein and no simple carbohydrates as well as inflammatory proteins can be beneficial for the cancer patients. However, this diet advice needs to be altered for every patient according to the requirements of their body." Attempting to cure cancer exclusively through dietary changes without seeking medical advice can pose significant dangers. Cancer is a complex illness that demands more than reliance on dietary elements for effective treatment. Depending solely on home remedies and neglecting professional medical guidance might exacerbate the condition, rendering cancer harder to treat or potentially incurable. Cancer cells proliferate rapidly, swiftly spreading throughout the body. Any delay in seeking proper medical treatment can escalate the severity of the condition, making it more challenging to manage and treat effectively.

title: Fact Check: Is there an instant herbal skin whitening formulation?
claim_text: A trending Instagram reel with the caption 'गर्मी में भी ग्लोइंग स्किन चाहिए?' claims that a combination of roasted turmeric, coffee, honey, curd, and lemon juice is an excellent way to whiten skin instantly.
quick_take: An Instagram post claims that a herbal formulation may whiten skin instantly. We analysed the assertion and found that it is completely false.
doctor_explanation: Skin colour refers to the perceived shade or tone of the skin, depending on the form and concentration of melanin. Skin pigmentation varies widely and is influenced by melanocytes, carotene, oxygenated haemoglobin, and local blood circulation. Melanin comes in two varieties: Pheomelanin (contributes to yellow to crimson) and Eumelanin (induces brown to black). Skin pigmentation is influenced by approximately 150 genes, including MC1R, SLC24A5, and TYR. External triggers like UV rays have the greatest influence on modifying skin tone. Although 'tan removal' and 'skin whitening' are often used synonymously, they are fundamentally different processes. De-tanning aims to eliminate transient darkening from sun exposure, while skin lightening aims to permanently reduce melanin synthesis. Regarding the specific ingredients: Turmeric has potent anti-inflammatory and antioxidant qualities due to curcumin, but no substantial effect on melanin development. Coffee may improve circulation and exfoliation due to polyphenols, giving transient sheen but not permanent whitening. Curd provides lactic acid for mild exfoliation enhancing texture but not pigmentation. Lemon juice may exhibit modest depigmenting potential but direct application may irritate or damage the skin barrier. Honey has humectant and antibacterial effects for moisturization and healing but does not lighten skin tone. Dr Sachin Gupta, MBBS, MD (Dermatology and Venereology from AIIMS Delhi), of Amrita Hospital, emphasizes that 'natural ingredients are not always synonymous with safety or efficacy, and what might seem harmless can actually be risky'. Dr. Annusuiya Gohil, MD Scholar at the All India Institute of Ayurveda, maintains that heredity and environmental factors are the main causes of skin pigmentation. While there are several approaches to make the skin more radiant, skin pigmentation cannot be altered; it can only be improved. The natural skin pigmentation lost over time due to ageing, exposure to harsh environments, food, and medication can be restored, but skin colour cannot be transformed by topical therapies. Many online instant herbal remedies contain mercury compounds, steroids, or hydroquinone which can cause skin thinning, sensitivity, pigmentation return, and systemic toxicity.

Cumin seeds are known for their rich antioxidant content, which can help combat oxidative stress in the body. Some studies suggest that cumin may enhance fat loss by increasing metabolic rate and promoting fat oxidation. Additionally, cumin is known to improve digestion and gut health, which are crucial for effective weight management. Coriander seeds possess diuretic properties, which can help reduce water retention and bloating. Moreover, coriander can regulate blood sugar levels, potentially reducing cravings for unhealthy snacks and helping in appetite control. Maintaining stable blood sugar is key for effective weight loss, as it helps manage hunger levels. Fennel seeds are traditionally believed to relieve digestive issues, such as gas and bloating. But a 2017 study indicated that women in the fennel group experienced a slight increase in bodyweight and fat distribution. Is it possible to easily burn belly fat by drinking a specific decoction? No, relying on a drink alone to burn belly fat is not effective. While beverages like green tea, lemon water, or apple cider vinegar might slightly boost metabolism, they are not miracle solutions. Losing belly fat requires a combination of a healthy diet, regular exercise, and lifestyle changes. While drinks can help support these efforts, they cannot replace a balanced approach. Dr. Jyothy Kannangath, Dermatologist emphasises that there are no quick fixes for reducing belly fat. The most effective options are lifestyle changes, liposuction, or cryolipolysis. Does the claimed 5000 years old formula have any scientific backup? No. Dr Mohit Sandhu, B.A.M.S.|C.A.D.|C.A.C.|PGDAKS|, Gurgaon, said, 'In Ayurveda, ancient texts outline various remedies and practices aimed at promoting overall health and addressing excess fat, specifically meda dhatu imbalance. While there isn't a specific 5,000-year-old recipe for belly fat reduction, several traditional approaches can support overall weight management and digestion like triphala, guggul and many pungent spices (trikatu). Ayurveda also encourages people to drink ginger tea, fenugreek seed and aloe vera juice. These Ayurvedic methods, alongside a healthy lifestyle, can help gradually reduce belly fat by reducing overall fat and promote overall balance.' Are there any side effects of drinking this 5000 years old formula? There is no fatal risk of drinking this so-called 5000 years old formula. But one should be very cautious. Individuals can drink this as a complimentary remedy and expecting that it will help you lose belly fat is a misinformation. There are many drinks available on social media that claim drinking a decoction of spice and herbs can help reduce belly fat. One should know that spot reduction is not possible just by drinking the claim or any decoction. A proper exercise regime focusing on core muscle and a proper diet is important. When selective evidence is presented, such as showcasing only one side of the story it creates an unrealistic expectation that everyone will achieve similar results. This often leads people to overlook the potential risks and side effects associated with certain diets or supplements, which can harm their health. Moreover, failing to consider individual variances—like differences in metabolism, genetics, and lifestyle—means that many may adopt approaches that are not suited to their unique circumstances, resulting in frustration or even adverse effects. Additionally, a focus on short-term successes can mislead individuals into neglecting the importance of sustainability, leading them to pursue quick fixes rather than adopting healthier, long-term habits. Overall, the lack of information can foster confusion, disappointment, and a cycle of ineffective belly fat reduction attempts.

title: Fact Check: Is there COVID-19 in the U.S. water supply?
claim_text: There is a much stronger strain of COVID-19 in the U.S. water supply, and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has released this information.

doctor_explanation: No. There is no evidence supporting that COVID-19 is present in the U.S. water supply. Although the claimant in a full video referenced CDC data to suggest COVID-19 detection in wastewater, the CDC has not confirmed it. Moreover, we realized that the claimant is interchangeably using water supply and wastewater. However, it is important to understand that both have different meanings. The water supply is typically known as drinking or tap water whereas wastewater is called sewage. The claimant, Steve Ram, is a real estate investor, YouTuber, and entrepreneur. He regularly shares information in the form of breaking news on his Instagram profile, but he does not provide any links to the references he uses for making the videos. Our research shows that traces of viral RNA (genetic material) from SARS-CoV-2 can be detected in water. However, the likelihood of finding this RNA decreases in the case of drinking water due to multiple processes it undergoes, making it suitable for consumption. This suggests that the viral RNA might have entered the water via sewage or from infected individuals. Nevertheless, detecting RNA fragments does not necessarily indicate the presence of infectious virus particles. RNA can degrade rapidly and does not assure that the virus remains viable. The CDC has established the National Wastewater Surveillance System (NWSS) to track the SARS-CoV-2 virus in U.S. wastewater. On a separate note, our previous fact-checks also clarified that introducing the vaccine into the water supply is not feasible. We debunked a claim suggesting that the World Economic Forum (WEF) has planned to add vaccines to the water supply. Additionally, we also refuted that New Zealand put COVID-19 vaccines in the water supply. In a post tap water is testing positive of COVID when tested with rapid test strips. title: Fact Check: Is too much carbon on the Earth not harmful?
claim_text: A speaker in a social media video claims that too much carbon is not harmful. He claims that increasing levels of carbon is not an actual problem because all life forms on Earth is carbon-based. He expresses his dedication to increasing his carbon footprint and states 'While the world faces numerous challenges, carbon is certainly not one of them.'
quick_take: The speaker in a social media video claims that too much carbon is not harmful. He claims that increasing levels of carbon is not an actual problem because all life forms on Earth is carbon-based. We fact-checked and found the claim to be False.
doctor_explanation: No, too much carbon on Earth is indeed harmful. Carbon is an essential element and plays a crucial role in various natural processes. But excessive carbon in certain forms, particularly carbon dioxide (CO2), can have detrimental effects on the environment and human health. The increase in carbon dioxide levels in the Earth's atmosphere, primarily due to human activities such as burning fossil fuels and deforestation, is a significant contributor to climate change. Carbon is a fundamental building block of life. But it doesn't mean that Earth can absorb unlimited amounts of it without consequences. Excessive carbon dioxide in the environment can disrupt the natural carbon cycle, which involves the movement of carbon in and out of Earth's reservoirs through processes like photosynthesis, burning fossil fuels, and respiration. The burning of energy stored in Earth's reserves at an accelerated rate throws off the planet's natural cycles. While the world will eventually adjust to this shift, it carries severe consequences for life as we know it. The consequences of climate change include more frequent and severe extreme weather events like hurricanes, droughts, heat waves, and floods. It can also cause disruptions to ecosystems, loss of biodiversity, rising sea levels, ocean acidification, and changes in agricultural patterns. These impacts pose risks to human societies, economies, and overall planetary stability. Furthermore, excessive carbon emissions can contribute to air pollution, leading to adverse effects on human health. High levels of carbon monoxide (CO) and other pollutants can cause respiratory problems, cardiovascular issues, and other respiratory diseases. We also found evidence that shows carbon dioxide acts as a greenhouse gas, influencing climate patterns. Excess CO2 acts as a greenhouse gas, trapping heat in the atmosphere and leading to a rise in global temperatures. This phenomenon is known as the greenhouse effect. The increasing frequency of record-breaking heat events worldwide in recent years demonstrates this impact. Evidence shows that heat events affect various organisms, including humans. Additionally, the rising levels of CO2 dissolving in oceans and other bodies of water lead to changes in pH, negatively affecting certain marine organisms, particularly invertebrates. Climate change, largely driven by carbon dioxide emissions, has already resulted in illness and death due to extreme weather events, disruptions in food systems, and the spread of diseases and mental health issues, as reported by the World Health Organization. Reducing carbon footprint is generally considered crucial for mitigating climate change and its impacts. Therefore, humans should try to decrease their carbon footprint to help address this global challenge. Carbon footprint refers to the total greenhouse gas emissions, including carbon dioxide (CO2) and other greenhouse gases, generated by human activities such as transportation, energy production, industrial processes, and deforestation. By reducing their carbon footprint, individuals and communities can contribute to reducing the concentration of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, which is essential for reducing the effects of climate change.
