The post doesn't mention the type of mask (N95, Surgical, HomeMade etc.). We evaluated the claim from multiple perspective and found it to be Mostly True. NOTE: Some fact checking platforms (India Today;Snopes) have rated this claim as 'Mostly False' with the caveat that people should wear right fitted, surgical or cloth made masks. We believe, the issue needs a deeper look keeping in mind your age, medical condition and type of mask you are using (especially in India where home-made masks are popular)
doctor_explanation: Hypoxia is a condition in which there is an absence of enough oxygen in the body or a region of the body at the tissue level. There is a split verdict on this. But most of the experts THIP talked to says it's possible. Various researches at various points of time have revealed that prolonged usage of masks can reduce intake of oxygen. An old research published in ResearchGate.com — a survey among healthcare workers for whom wearing N95 face masks was mandatory during the 2003 severe acute respiratory distress syndrome epidemic — found that over 37% of surveyed candidates complained of headaches. Commenting on a story in Scroll.in in 2017, Dr D Saha, scientist and additional director at the Central Pollution Control Board, said, '(Masks) can lead to oxygen shortage, suffocation, respiration trouble, and heart attacks.' In a recent news published on the Stanford website, John Xu, a research scientist at Stanford, created 'a new type of protective face mask that extracts and concentrates oxygen from the air to avoid the considerable side effects of oxygen deficiency while preventing the spread of the virus.' Explaining the need for the new invention, Xu explained, 'N95 masks are estimated to reduce oxygen intake by anywhere from 5 to 20 percent. That's significant, even for a healthy person. It can cause dizziness and light headedness. If you wear a mask long enough, it can damage the lungs. For a patient in respiratory distress, it can even be life threatening.' Dr Sanjeev Bagai, chairman of Nephron Clinic (per India Today's fact-check), mentions masks will not cause suffocation if they are '… of appropriate size and shape. It should not be so tight on your face that it makes you feel uncomfortable.' Snopes' fact-check emphasizes the right material, with the caveat that 'people wearing cloth or surgical masks are in little to no danger of breathing in unhealthy amounts of carbon dioxide.' The WHO guidelines state, 'The prolonged use of medical masks can be uncomfortable. However, it does not lead to CO2 intoxication nor oxygen deficiency. While wearing a medical mask, make sure it fits properly and that it is tight enough to allow you to breathe normally. Do not re-use a disposable mask and always change it as soon as it gets damp.' It needs to be noted the WHO guideline mentions medical/surgical masks and talks about proper fitting. The Vanguard article and Facebook posts do not talk about mask type, material, or size — the advisory was against wearing masks in general for prolonged periods. Dr. Sai Praveen Haranath, Intensivist and Pulmonologist, Apollo Hospitals, Hyderabad says, 'Depending on the correct fit and the type of mask there will be resistance to air movement. If in an isolated area with low risk of exposure or risk of exposing others to infection can remove the mask. Masks can lead to difficulty in breathing and sometimes can affect the exchange of gases causing a rise in carbon dioxide and a drop in oxygen level. Using the correct mask based on the exposure risk will be the right choice.' Dr. Smarajit Maiti, Consultant Paediatrician and Neonatologist, Bhagirathi Neotia Woman and Child Care Centre, Kolkata, says, 'Hypoxia due to masks is not an uncommon thing. It is always recommended to use a mask which is well fitted and is provided with a respiratory valve.' According to Henry Ford Hospital guidance, 'Do not use paper or plastic bags, scouring pads or sponges as masks. These things won't give you the protection you need, and in the case of plastic bags, they could lead to suffocation and death.' Dr. Sanjeev Jain, Consultant – Pulmonologist, Fortis Hospital, Delhi, says, 'Persons with pre-existing respiratory problems should also wear the mask same way. However, since prolonged wearing of mask has a chance to cause hypoxia, intermittent fresh air should be taken as advised. Any mask that a person wears should be used as a barrier and not as a sealant. It should allow intermittent passage of fresh air. Only in areas where there are high chances of getting a possible infection, it is advisable to wear a more sealing mask. If possible mask should be removed intermittently and fresh air should be inhaled.' Dr. Smarajit Maiti (Paediatrician) adds, 'Masks without respiratory valve is not advisable for children. If an adult can fall prey to Hypoxia due to mask, a child can too. It is necessary to ensure you are buying a mask with well ventilation facility for your child. As for babies, masks are not a feasible option. It can lead to dangerous situation like suffocation if goes unnoticed. Rather, hygiene and proper protection of the care givers, maintenance of cough protocol and off course awareness may be helpful.' Dr. Joyeeta Chowdhury, MD, Assistant Professor, Dermatology, NRS Medical College and Hospital adds, 'It is natural to feel suffocated after 10-15 mins of wearing a mask, afterall not all of us are wearing scientifically designed well ventilated masks. You need to readjust the mask at that time or breathe in fresh air. But the most critical thing to remember is to clean or sanitize your hands while touching the mask. Also, while adjusting don't flip the outside surface inwards. Sometimes colour from dyed masks may cause irritant contact dermatitis or even contact urticaria. But this remains to be established as we have only heard of a couple of isolated cases like these so far.' Expert Advisories: Dr. Jain says, 'Masks are required only when you are in a crowded place.' WHO guidelines read: 'If you are healthy, you only need to wear a mask if you are taking care of a person with COVID-19. Wear a mask if you are coughing or sneezing. Masks are effective only when used in combination with frequent hand-cleaning with alcohol-based hand rub or soap and water.' Dr. Smarajit Maiti (Paediatrician) says, 'Schools are high risk zones. You cannot expect a child to always maintain social distancing properly. Ideally, a child should enter the school wearing a mask and not take it off before they come back home. In between, they should not take the mask off with unclean hands or touch the insides of the mask. However, it's a bit difficult to ensure all the rules are followed when you are dealing with children. So, ensure you provide them a mask with a respiratory valve. This will lessen the chance of suffocation or hypoxia.' Dr. Sanjeev Jain (Pulmonologist) says, 'It needs to be emphasized that the new Coronavirus is not an air-borne pathogen. Apart from surface touch, it only transmits through close physical or breathing contact. So, a mask is only required in crowded areas. There is no reason to wear a mask while driving a car.' Dr. Joyeeta Chowdhury (Dermatologist) says, 'Masks are now being sold in footpaths. These are majorly cloth masks and they need to be cleaned and sterilized properly before use. There should not be issues with skin if you maintain a proper hygiene of your mask. If you are using surgical masks, learn to discard them properly by cutting them in between so that they are not picked up and recycled.' Dr. Rachna Khanna Singh, Director, The Mind and Wellness Studio says, 'Initially there can be a sense of confinement but that should go away as we condition our mind and start accepting this as a new normal. Children should be taught this as a habit as common as wearing clothes. Even if someone feels a bit restricted due to wearing mask, it should not be as severe as feeling suffocated. Gradually this feeling of restriction should go away as you get used to wearing a mask.'

title: The message about 'Coronavirus does not settle in the air' is not from UNICEF - THIP Media
claim_text: The virus does not settle in the air but is grounded, so it is not transmitted by air.
quick_take: An image has been put up on Facebook by a page posing as a circular from UNICEF. The message claims that Coronavirus does not settle in the air and is not transmitted by air. We investigated and found that the message is not from UNICEF. Though it is true that Coronavirus is not an airborne virus but the virus can stay suspended in the air for some time. We mark this as Half True.
doctor_explanation: Dr. Prafful Bharadwaj, Health Officer at UNICEF, has talked to Vishvas News clarifying that UNICEF has not issued any such guidelines or advisory. WHO does not categorize the novel Coronavirus as an airborne virus. On its website WHO mentions, "Current evidence suggests that COVID-19 spreads between people through direct, indirect (through contaminated objects or surfaces), or close contact with infected people via mouth and nose secretions. These include saliva, respiratory secretions, or secretion droplets. These are released from the mouth or nose when an infected person coughs, sneezes speaks, or sings, for example. People who are in close contact (within 1 meter) with an infected person can catch COVID-19 when those infectious droplets get into their mouth, nose, or eyes." WHO also advises people to maintain a distance of 1 meter. This means that, even though the virus is not categorized as 'airborne', it can stay suspended in the air for some time after coming out of an infected person (e.g. through sneeze) before it falls on the ground. So, Coronavirus is not an airborne virus technically but can still stay suspended in air for a shorter length. Hence, precautions like masks and social distancing are not to be taken lightly.

title: The post about Coronavirus transmitted through fruits and vegetables 'may be' fake; but you still need to be careful
claim_text: URGENT MESSAGE….From trusted source in Hong Kong medical lab today: "In our laboratory, we found trace amount of the virus on the skin of fruits and vegetables after 12 hours of being touched by another customer who was infected. We recommend our staff to avoid salads. Do not eat the fruits within 48 hours of purchase, or pour some boiling water over the fruit before cutting. Berries, apples, cucumbers and tomatoes are the worst because some people eat the skin. This explains why the virus is spreading faster in the west than Asia. Most Asians do not eat salad and very few people eat the skin of any fruit. We have to assume anything that comes from outside our home within 48 hours is infected. Shoes, clothes, our hair, all food." Hope that helps, pls take extreme care. Kind Regards.
quick_take: A viral post has been doing rounds on about coronavirus getting transmitted through fruits and vegetables. Fact checkers at Vishvas news and AFP have already written it off as misleading and fake respectively. We investigate and find out that though the particular post can be fake but there is still merits in the message. We label it as half true.
doctor_explanation: All the posts mentioned that the findings were from 'In our Laboratory'. But, like most viral fake posts, none of the messages mentioned the name of any specific laboratory or elaborated further on the source of the claim. The message has all the signatures of a viral fake. Hong Kong's Centre for Food and Safety has put out a Facebook post against the message stating, 'no evidence has shown people can be infected with the 2019 coronavirus disease from food'. Major food safety authorities say that so far there is 'No evidence' about the Novel coronavirus spreading through food. The CDC says, 'there is no evidence to support transmission of COVID-19 associated with food'. The US Food and Drug Administration says, 'there is no evidence of food or food packaging being associated with transmission of COVID-19'. Fact checking platforms like Vishvas News and AP have written off the credibility of the viral message and called it fake solely based on these facts. While we agree with the origin of the message being fake and that the claimant doesn't look credible either, we look at the content on its standalone merit. All communication put out by authorities in recent days are based on lack of evidence or any knowledge about whether the virus can spread through food. This is where a more detailed investigation is needed. We need to remember that this is a situation we know very little about. The researchers are still trying to understand all the nuances of the virus and the pandemic it has caused. Can fruits and vegetables get infected from coronavirus? Unlikely, since the novel coronavirus is a virus that attacks the respiratory tract of humans. But, can coronavirus stay on the skin of a fruit especially after it is being previously touched by an infected person? The honest answer is, we do not know clearly. There are multiple studies happening currently across the world on the ability of the new coronavirus to survive on various surfaces. One such study originally published in the preprint database medRxiv on March 11, and then the revised version published on March 17 in The New England Journal of Medicine, claims that the virus can remain viable in the air for up to 3 hours, on copper for up to 4 hours, on cardboard up to 24 hours and on plastic and stainless steel up to 72 hours. Another study published in February in The Journal of Hospital Infection analyzed several dozen previously published papers on human coronaviruses (other than the new coronavirus) to get a better idea of how long they can survive outside of the body. They concluded that if this new coronavirus resembles other human coronaviruses, such as its 'cousins' that cause SARS and MERS, it can stay on surfaces — such as metal, glass or plastic — for as long as nine days. Somehow, these studies have not talked about fruits and vegetables as a surface. The WHO site on its page about Covid19 states, 'It is not certain how long the virus that causes COVID-19 survives on surfaces, but it seems to behave like other coronaviruses.' The same WHO site hosts a review report on Surface decontamination of fruits and vegetables prepared by Larry R. Beuchat. The report lists Coronavirus as Pathogens of Most Concern in decontamination of fruits and vegetables. The report on its page 13 states, 'Studies have shown that viruses may persist for weeks or even months on vegetable crops… rotavirus, astrovirus, enteroviruses, parvoviruses and coronaviruses have been reported to be transmitted by foods on occasion.' NOTE: This report is old and does not talk about Novel Coronavirus that causes Covid19. We are saying, ignore the viral Facebook message. It may be false. But, be careful while you buy fruits and vegetables.

title: This mobile game is a good exercise but not a valid COVID-19 test - THIP Media
claim_text: A small mobile game (a breathing exercise where a cursor moves on a square and you breathe in or breathe out as instructed) is a valid self COVID-19 test — if you can hold your breath for a certain time, it means you do not have COVID-19.
quick_take: A small mobile game is being forwarded on WhatsApp. The game which is a breathing exercise is being claimed as a self COVID test. We consulted doctors and found the claim to be false.
doctor_explanation: This game is based on two flawed assumptions: (1) that managing to hold your breath for a certain time means you are free from COVID-19, and (2) that all COVID-19 patients will have breathing difficulties — which is not true. Holding your breath does not mean you are COVID safe; it only means you have decent control on your lungs and breathing. The only valid test for COVID-19 is a proper blood test. As per Sanjeev Jain, Consultant – Pulmonologist, Fortis Hospital, Delhi, 'We are seeing only a handful patients who actually complain of breathing problems. It is lesser than half of the COVID patients we treat.' Even as per WHO guidelines (as on August 2, 2020), 'Being able to hold your breath for 10 seconds or more without coughing or feeling discomfort DOES NOT mean you are free from COVID-19.' The game itself is not harmful for common people — it is a controlled breathing exercise. However, it will not prevent you from COVID-19 and cannot be used as a diagnostic tool. As per various research, breathing exercises can help reduce stress. As per the British Lung Foundation, deep breathing can help clear mucus from the lungs after pneumonia, allowing more air to circulate. NOTE: These are general recommendations for any breathing exercise and not specifically for this game. Pregnant women, children, or individuals with pre-existing conditions like hypertension, asthma, or high blood pressure should not try such random exercises without consulting a doctor.

title: Tweet claims diabetes cured in 2 days: Is it possible? - THIP Media
claim_text: Diabetes can be cured in 2 days at Naiminath Homoeopathic Hospital, Agra, India
quick_take: A tweet claiming that diabetes can be reversed in 2 days by using homoeopathy medicine has been trending. We verified the claim and found it to be mostly false.
doctor_explanation:
Our investigation confirmed that Naiminath Homoeopathic Hospital exists in Agra and holds NABH accreditation as 'India's first NABH accredited Homoeopathic Hospital' (verified via the NABH website list of accredited AYUSH hospitals). Dr. Pradeep Kumar Gupta is listed on the hospital's website as Principal Professor and Head of Department for the PG Department of Materia Medica.

When contacted, a hospital representative (speaking anonymously) confirmed that a patient did experience a reversal of diabetes in 2 days after following specific diet and lifestyle changes prescribed by the hospital. The representative stated: 'The case mentioned in the tweet is about that particular person. His diabetes was completely cured in 2 days. This doesn't mean it will apply to all the diabetes patients. There was a certain diet and lifestyle which we made him follow. It wasn't momentary. He is completely cured of diabetes now. If he follows the same diet and lifestyle, it will never come back.'

Dr. Sushil Bahl (DHMS, DI.Hom), a homoeopath with over 40 years of experience, says: 'It is impossible to reverse diabetes in 2 days, no matter whatever medicine or dietary restrictions you put the patient in.'

Kajal Gupta, Dietician and Nutritionist on THIP Medical Review Team, says: 'Diabetes occurs due to permanent damage of pancreatic cells or it becomes sensitive to insulin, so it can't be cured completely but can be managed through proper medication, diet and lifestyle changes.'

Multiple credible homeopathy sources were consulted. The National Health Portal of India describes homeopathy's constitutional remedy approach ('individualisation' based on Similia principle) as akin to personalised medicine, but makes no claim of cure in 2 days. The British Homoeopathic Organisation states: 'Homoeopathic treatment can help improve the general health of a person with diabetes... If a person with diabetes is in good health, his or her insulin requirements will be steady and the blood glucose well controlled.' The Dr Prasanta Banerji Homoeopathic Research Foundation in Kolkata (SIRO-accredited by DSIR) describes using remedies such as Helonias 200, Iodum 200, and Syzygium Jambolanum θ (Mother Tincture) in diabetes treatment, and notes patients already on insulin should continue replacement therapy while starting homeopathic medicines, tapering off conventional therapy over months — again, no 2-day cure claim.

The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) raised concerns on August 20, 2019 that the tweet 'appears to be in violation of #DMR regulations as well in violation of the advisory by Central Council of Indian Medicine #CCIM.' Under the Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954, no product or treatment can claim to cure diabetes.

THIP Media Take: The hospital and the claimant are authentic, and multiple credible sources support controlling diabetes through lifestyle changes, diet, and homeopathic medicines. However, the claim that 'diabetes is cured in 2 days' cannot be corroborated and appears to be misleading. Even the claimant hospital confirms this is a single case and not applicable to all patients. Social media is full of miraculous cures for diabetes such as massaging and acupressure for diabetes or that diabetes can be reversed through diet and exercise — these claims remain misleading and should not serve as primary treatment approach.

title: Updated Fact Check: Can Dettol kill COVID-19 causing Coronavirus?
claim_text: Dettol can kill Coronavirus (COVID-19 causing virus)
verdict_original: True (verified via company confirmation and peer-reviewed evidence — surface disinfectant use only)
quick_take: Several Facebook posts and WhatsApp messages claimed at the start of the pandemic that Dettol can kill Coronavirus. THIP Media and most Fact Checking platforms had flagged off the claim on the basis of non-availability of evidence. However, in recent testing Dettol has been proved to be effective against novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV), the virus causing COVID-19.
doctor_explanation: Yes. Dettol is effective against Novel Coronavirus that is causing COVID-19. This has been confirmed by Reckitt Benckiser (RB), the manufacturer of Dettol, in an official tweet dated June 8, 2020. Following extensive 3rd party laboratory testing, specific Dettol family of products demonstrated effectiveness (>99.9% inactivation) against 2019 Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19), SARS-CoV-2 when used in accordance with directions for use. The American Journal of Infection Control (2020) has confirmed that various components in Dettol and Lysol are effective against the Coronavirus causing COVID-19. RB stated: 'We are pleased to be the first to have recognition from a scientific journal, @AJICJournal, confirming that several of the active ingredients in the Dettol & Lysol family of brands are effective at inactivating #COVID19 virus.' IMPORTANT SAFETY WARNING: The use of Dettol to kill Coronavirus is strictly as a surface disinfectant. Drinking Dettol to kill Coronavirus inside your body is a dangerous thought. Drinking Dettol can be seriously harmful to health. The COVID-19 pandemic situation is a fast evolving situation. Researchers are constantly working to find new ways to tackle the virus. Most Fact Check stories regarding 'Dettol can kill Coronavirus' were fact checked in early 2020 when the pandemic had just set in and Dettol had not been tested against the latest virus. The article notes that THIP Media had earlier fact-checked this topic (published earlier) when no evidence was available, and this story is an update to that earlier fact check reflecting new evidence.

title: Using UV rays to kill Coronavirus: Can sunlight be effective?
claim_text: Live in under the sun…. cause UV ray can kill CORONA Virus … take care everybody…. we will be better soon i believe that… pray more / eat well / sleep well and stay at home.
quick_take: A social media post claims that UV rays can kill Coronavirus. We investigated the claim and found it to be Half True.
doctor_explanation: As per the National Academy of Sciences, 'UV light has been shown to destroy other Coronaviruses, so it will probably work on the novel Coronavirus'. UV-C can destroy the genetic material of a Virus or Bacteria and is therefore used to disinfect public places. Government agencies in most countries are experimenting with the same methodology in case of novel Coronavirus. Based on the facts known so far, sunlight cannot kill Coronavirus directly. UV rays coming from the sun are 3 types – Type A (known as UV-A), Type B (known as UV-B) and Type C (known as UV-C). Out of these, UV-C has the strongest radiation and can easily kill all virus and bacteria by altering their RNA and DNA. But only UV-A and UV-B reaches the earth's surface and UV-C does not reach the earth's surface. UV-C gets trapped by the Ozone layer of the earth. This is fortunate because UV-C, had it reached earth, would have caused severe skin burn and cancer in humans too. In fact UV-A and UV-B which reach the earth is also often associated with premature aging, skin burns and skin cancer in humans after prolonged exposure. UV-A and UV-B are known to kill bacteria and pathogens. UV-A and UV-B also make some viruses like the Influenza viruses less effective. But at the same time, sunlight (UV-A and UV-B) has been ineffective against some viruses like the SARS virus (which is also a type of Coronavirus) after 15 minutes of exposure. What is used as UV lamps and used as disinfectants of surfaces and public amenities are man-made UV rays in the same frequency as UV-C. While it can be a good disinfectant, it can be potentially very dangerous to humans. Scientists believe the man-made UV-C lights can also kill the Novel Coronavirus since they seem to have worked against similar viruses in the past. IMPORTANT NOTE: All the above facts about UV rays effective (or ineffective) on viruses is only when the virus is outside the body and is exposed to the sunlight. Once the virus enters the body, no amount of sunlight or UV light can kill it. WHO has given strict guidelines against using UV lamps to sanitize hands. The UV lamps can have major negative effects on human cells and cause more damage than good. The WHO website says, 'Ultra-violet (UV) lamps should not be used to disinfect hands or other areas of your skin. UV radiation can cause skin irritation and damage your eyes.' Sunlight can be a great source of Vitamin D provided you expose a larger part of skin to sun rays every day for a limited period of time. Dr. Manish Singhal, Senior Oncologist, was consulted on this topic and confirmed that while moderate sunlight exposure is beneficial for Vitamin D, excessive UV exposure carries significant skin cancer risks and cannot treat or kill the Coronavirus once it has entered the body.

title: Fact Check: Video Claim that Lying in a Cowshed Cures Cancer and Rubbing a Cow's Back Reduces Need for BP Medication is False
claim_text: Rubbing a cow's back can reduce high blood pressure medication dosage from 20 mg to 10 mg within 10 days, and lying down where a cow sits and cleaning the cowshed area can cure cancer.
verdict_original: completely false. The claim is FALSE.
quick_take: The claims that rubbing a cow's back can reduce high blood pressure medication and that lying in a cow's resting spot can cure cancer are completely false. No scientific evidence or medical consensus supports these assertions. High blood pressure medications should only be adjusted under a doctor's guidance, and cancer can only reach remission through appropriate medical treatment.
doctor_explanation:
Dr. Prem Aggarwal MBBS, MD (Medicine), DNB Cardiology, Director, Sanjeevan Hospital, Daryaganj, Delhi said: 'Rubbing a cow's back cannot reduce the dosage of high blood pressure from 20 mg to 10 mg; this claim is not just false and frankly, quite absurd. Hypertension is a serious medical condition that requires proper medical management. It involves lifestyle changes, regular monitoring, and prescribed medications to control blood pressure levels. Ignoring medical advice and resorting to unproven remedies can lead to serious health risks, including heart attack and stroke. Promoting such baseless claims can be harmful and should not be supported. Always seek evidence-based treatment and consult your doctor for proper medical guidance.'

Prof. Dr. Somashekhar S P, Lead Consultant - Surgical & Gynaecological Oncology & Robotic Surgeon, Aster CMI Hospital, Bangalore said: 'This statement, however, has no basis in scientific fact and has been widely condemned by medical professionals. Cancer is a complex disease that arises from the uncontrolled growth of abnormal cells, and its treatment requires a combination of well-established medical therapies, such as surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation. There is no scientific evidence to support the idea that cleaning a cowshed or spending time in such an environment could cure cancer. In fact, such baseless claims can put patients at risk by encouraging them to forgo proven treatments in favor of unfounded, potentially harmful alternatives. Suggesting that something as unrelated as cleaning a cowshed could cure cancer is not just misleading—it's dangerous. The problem is that such claims concern a broader challenge involving the spread of health misinformation, particularly in rural communities where quality healthcare and trustworthy information can be scarce. The minister's suggestion also highlights the growing trend of politicians and public figures offering unverified health advice, often under the guise of traditional wisdom. While traditional practices can offer cultural value and sometimes even complementary health benefits, they should never be presented as substitutes for scientifically validated medical treatments, especially when it comes to diseases as serious as cancer. The consequences of such remarks are potentially far-reaching. Patients who believe in these myths might delay or even abandon life-saving treatments, choosing instead to rely on practices that are at best ineffective and at worst harmful. Public figures must exercise responsibility when discussing health issues, particularly when the well-being of vulnerable individuals is at stake.'

The article further states: High blood pressure (hypertension) according to WHO is when blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg or higher. It can be controlled with lifestyle modifications, diet, and medications, but there is no cure. The American Heart Association notes: 'While there is no cure for high blood pressure, it is important for patients to take steps that matter, such as making effective lifestyle changes and taking BP-lowering medications as prescribed by their physicians.' Regarding cancer, WHO defines it as a large group of diseases where abnormal cells grow uncontrollably and can metastasize. Cancer is the second leading cause of death globally, accounting for an estimated 9.6 million deaths (1 in 6 deaths) in 2018. The American Cancer Society states: 'Whether a person's cancer can be cured depends on the type and stage of the cancer, the type of treatment they can get, and other factors. Some cancers are more likely to be cured than others. But each cancer needs to be treated differently. There isn't one cure for cancer.' Cancer treatment encompasses chemotherapy, hormone therapy, hyperthermia, immunotherapy, photodynamic therapy, radiation therapy, stem cell transplants, surgery, and targeted therapy — all evidence-based medical approaches. There is no scientific evidence or medical consensus that rubbing a cow's back reduces high blood pressure medication or that lying in a cow's resting spot cures cancer.

title: Was Pfizer CEO arrested and charged with fraud? - THIP Media
claim_text: CEO of Pfizer Albert Bourla was arrested at his home in Scarsdale, New York, by the FBI and charged with multiple counts of fraud for 'his role in deceiving customers' about the COVID-19 vaccine's effectiveness.
quick_take: A news article and corresponding Facebook posts claim that the CEO of Pfizer was arrested on November first week by the FBI for 'his role in deceiving customers' about the COVID-19 vaccine's effectiveness. We fact checked and found that the claim is False.
doctor_explanation: The claim that Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla was arrested by the FBI is false. An event of such scale would trigger massive media coverage worldwide. There were no news reports anywhere about the arrest of Pfizer's CEO. Multiple news websites have published confirmed reports quoting company sources that Pfizer's CEO Dr Albert Bourla was not arrested by the FBI. Bourla also appeared on various television channels including CNBC, CNN, and Bloomberg giving interviews on 5th and 6th of November when the article about his arrest was published. He has also been active on his social media handles. The article source appears to be the website Conservative Beaver, which published the false claim titled 'CEO of Pfizer arrested, charged with fraud – media blackout as #PfizerGate trends.' Related claims mentioned include: Pfizer paid the highest fine ever by a healthcare company for wrongful marketing; revenue from blood clot treatments; and false narratives suggesting WHO is offering jobs for personal information. The article notes that scrutiny surrounding Pfizer's financial practices raises questions about revenue from blood clot treatments and the overall transparency of the company's leadership amid ongoing investigations.
